title: Part 8: Lineage and Practical Migration Notes
text:
Conceptual Lineage
regularizeNd is inspired by earlier regularized surface fitting tools in the MATLAB ecosystem. Two tools are particularly relevant as a conceptual starting point:

gridfit (John D’Errico) (D’Errico 2016) — a 2-D input surface fitting tool using a similar regularization philosophy. gridfit introduced many users to the idea of balancing data fidelity against smoothness on a grid.
RegularizeData3D (Jamal 2014) — extended the concept to cubic interpolation. Made the smoothness parameter reusable across problems by scaling the regularization relative to the fidelity term.

regularizeNd generalizes the approach to an arbitrary number of input dimensions, fixed some all zero rows in gridfit and RegularizeData3D,exposes the underlying matrices for constrained problems, and provides multiple solver options including iterative solvers for large systems.
The Math for Mere Mortals articles on regularizing 2D and 3D data (Math for Mere Mortals, 2013) are a separate educational lineage. They explain the method through worked examples and spreadsheets. They are not the source of gridfit, RegularizeData3D, or regularizeNd. The maintained local versions are the foundation pages: 2D data, spreadsheet solve, and 3D data.
Important framing: regularizeNd is inspired by this prior work and shares the regularization concept, but it is an independent implementation.

title: Part 8: Lineage and Practical Migration Notes
text:
Migrating from gridfit

Conceptual mapping







gridfit concept
regularizeNd equivalent




gx, gy (grid vectors)
xGrid = {gx, gy}


'smoothness' property (default 1), scalar, vector
smoothness positional arg (similar role, different scaling/defaults), scalar, vector


g = gridfit(x,y,z,gx,gy,s)
g = regularizeNd([x,y], z, {gx,gy}, s)


'interp' property ('triangle', 'bilinear', 'nearest')
5th positional arg ( 'nearest', 'linear', 'cubic'). 'bilinear' = 'linear'


'regularizer' property ('gradient', 'diffusion'/'laplacian', 'springs')
regularizeNd’s regularization is fixed to the gradient regularizer because the others don’t work well.


Output is in meshgrid format
Output is in ndgrid format — transpose before plotting with surf





Minimal gridfit → regularizeNd rewrite
% --- gridfit (old) ---
% g = gridfit(x, y, z, gx, gy, smoothness);
% surf(gx, gy, g)      % gridfit output is meshgrid-formatted

% --- regularizeNd (new) ---
g = regularizeNd([x,y], z, {gx, gy}, smoothness);
surf(gx, gy, g')       % note the transpose: regularizeNd output is ndgrid-formatted
The transpose g' is the most common source of confusion. regularizeNd stores the output in ndgrid format (g(i,j) indexes gx(i), gy(j)), while MATLAB’s surf expects meshgrid format (g(j,i)).


Topographic data demo rewrite
Below is the first section of demo_from_gridfit.m rewritten in clean regularizeNd style. The original used bluff_data.mat (Two ravines on a hillside, scanned from a topographic map of upstate New York).

clc; clear; close all;
load bluff_data
x = bluff_data(:,1);
y = bluff_data(:,2);
z = bluff_data(:,3);

gx = 0:4:264;
gy = 0:4:400;
smoothness = 1e-5;

g = regularizeNd([x,y], z, {gx, gy}, smoothness);

figure
colormap(hot(256))
surf(gx, gy, g')        % transpose for surf
camlight right; lighting phong; shading interp
line(x, y, z, 'Marker', '.', 'MarkerSize', 4, 'LineStyle', 'none')
title('Topographic surface — regularizeNd rewrite of gridfit demo')
xlabel('x'); ylabel('y'); zlabel('z')

Unrecognized function or variable 'regularizeNd'.

title: Part 8: Lineage and Practical Migration Notes
Part 8: Lineage and Practical Migration Notes
text:
What regularizeNd Does Not Do
To be precise about scope:

It does not guarantee interpolation through every data point — it is a weighted least-squares fit. Use smoothness → 0 if you want near-interpolation behavior (at the cost of the smoother no longer regularizing effectively).
It does not enforce physical constraints automatically. Use regularizeNdMatrices + lsqlin or lsqConstrainedAlternative for that (see Part 6).
It does not currently support unstructured output grids. The output is always on a rectilinear ndgrid.

title: Part 8: Lineage and Practical Migration Notes
section: Quick Reference: Common Output Format Confusion
text:
Quick Reference: Common Output Format Confusion
regularizeNd outputs in ndgrid format. Most MATLAB visualization functions expect meshgrid format. The relationship is:
% regularizeNd output: zGrid(i,j) ↔ xGrid{1}(i), xGrid{2}(j)
% surf/mesh/contourf expect: Z(j,i) for plotting against x, y vectors

surf(xGrid{1}, xGrid{2}, zGrid')   % 2-D case: transpose zGrid
For 3-D and higher, use permute or griddedInterpolant to handle the indexing convention explicitly.

You have applied the transpose g' where needed for surf / mesh visualization.
You have verified that the migration produces the same surface shape at the same smoothness.
You have read the framing note: regularizeNd is inspired by prior work, not a derived copy.

title: Part 6: Constraints and Mappings
text:
Practical Goal

Apply monotonic and bounded-output constraints to regularized lookup tables.
Understand matrix-form constrained solving with regularizeNd building blocks.
Use input-variable mappings to improve fit behavior on uneven domains.

title: Part 6: Constraints and Mappings
text:
Example Anchor
Primary script: regularizeNd/Examples/a06_constraint_and_mapping_example.m
Download the example data file a06_constraints_and_mapping.mat to run this script.

title: Part 6: Constraints and Mappings
text:
Why Constraints Matter
The unconstrained solver minimizes a weighted sum of fidelity and smoothness and is completely agnostic about the shape of the resulting lookup table. Two common engineering requirements break that assumption:

Monotonicity — the output should be non-decreasing along a given dimension (think efficiency maps, calibration curves, throttle response).
Bounded output — the table values must stay above (or below) a physical limit.

Both are linear inequality constraints of the form \(A \mathbf{y}_\text{grid} \leq \mathbf{b}\).

title: Part 6: Constraints and Mappings
text:
The Matrix Formulation
regularizeNd solves a least-squares problem inside, but you can access the individual matrices with regularizeNdMatrices:
[Afidelity, Lreg] = regularizeNdMatrices(x, xGrid, smoothness, interpMethod)
Afidelity maps grid values to predicted outputs at each data point. Lreg is a cell array of second-derivative penalty matrices, one per dimension. Stack them and you have the full system:
\[
\min_{\mathbf{y}_\text{grid}} \frac{1}{2} \left\| C \mathbf{y}_\text{grid} - \mathbf{d} \right\|_2^2
\quad \text{subject to} \quad A \mathbf{y}_\text{grid} \leq \mathbf{b}
\]
where
\[
C = \begin{bmatrix} A_\text{fidelity} \\ L_\text{reg} \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{d} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{y}_\text{data} \\ \mathbf{0} \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Two solvers can handle this system:








Solver
Requires
Notes




lsqConstrainedAlternative
base MATLAB
Bundled with regularizeNd; convergence less robust


lsqlin
Optimization Toolbox
More robust; supports equality constraints

title: Part 6: Constraints and Mappings
text:
Monotonic Constraint
monotonicConstraint builds the \(A\), \(\mathbf{b}\) pair for a monotonically-increasing constraint across a chosen dimension:
[Amonotonic, bMonotonic] = monotonicConstraint(xGrid)            % dimension 1 (default)
[Amonotonic, bMonotonic] = monotonicConstraint(xGrid, dim)       % specific dimension
[Amonotonic, bMonotonic] = monotonicConstraint(xGrid, dim, dxMin) % enforce minimum step
For a monotonically decreasing constraint negate the matrix: use (-Amonotonic, bMonotonic).

Have you verified the difference vector diff(yGrid) is everywhere ≥ 0?
If the raw data has a steep section, have you tried a log-axis or a piecewise mapping?

title: Part 4: Boundary Behavior and Convex Hull
text:
Practical Goal

Understand why convex-hull geometry can break scattered interpolation.
Compare boundary behavior between scatteredInterpolant and regularizeNd.
Build intuition for why regularization stabilizes sparse edge regions.

title: Part 4: Boundary Behavior and Convex Hull
text:
Example Anchor
Primary script: regularizeNd/Examples/a04_example_scattered_data_near_convex_hull.m

title: Part 4: Boundary Behavior and Convex Hull
text:
Conceptual Model
scatteredInterpolant depends on Delaunay triangles and can become unstable when triangles near the convex hull are long and sliver-like. regularizeNd instead solves a global least-squares system with a smoothness penalty, so sparsely supported regions are governed by nearby trend continuation rather than local triangulation artifacts.

title: Part 4: Boundary Behavior and Convex Hull
section: The Dataset: A Deliberately Pathological Point Cloud
text:
The Dataset: A Deliberately Pathological Point Cloud
The example data is a synthetic 2-D point cloud shaped like a lens:

Two arcs (upper and lower) tracing portions of a unit circle.
A thin horizontal bar connecting them through the middle.

This geometry is designed so that the Delaunay triangulation used internally by scatteredInterpolant produces extremely sliver-like triangles in the nearly-empty corners of the convex hull. The true underlying surface is the paraboloid \(z = x^2 + y^2\).

clc; clear; close all;


% --- build the lens-shaped point cloud ---
t  = 0.4*pi : 0.02 : 0.6*pi;
x1 = cos(t)';    y1 = sin(t)' - 1.02;   % bottom arc
x2 = x1;         y2 = -y1;              % top arc (mirror)
x3 = linspace(-0.3, 0.3, 16)';  y3 = zeros(16,1);  % horizontal bar

x = [x1; x2; x3];
y = [y1; y2; y3];
z = x.^2 + y.^2;   % true paraboloid

k = convhull(x, y);

figure('Color', 'w', 'Position', [100, 100, 760, 520])
scatter(x, y, 54, z, 'filled', ...
   'MarkerEdgeColor', [0.15, 0.15, 0.15], 'LineWidth', 0.3, 'MarkerFaceAlpha', 0.95)
hold on
plot(x(k), y(k), '-', 'Color', [0.10, 0.10, 0.10], 'LineWidth', 1.8)
colormap(turbo)
cb = colorbar;
cb.Label.String = 'z = x^2 + y^2';
xlabel('x'); ylabel('y')
title('Point cloud with convex hull')
set(gca, 'FontSize', 11, 'LineWidth', 0.8)
grid on; box on
axis equal tight
xlim([-0.35, 0.35]); ylim([-0.12, 0.12])








Notice that the convex hull covers a much larger area than the data itself. The four corner regions are almost entirely unsupported.

title: Part 4: Boundary Behavior and Convex Hull
section: Why scatteredInterpolant Fails Near This Hull
text:
Why scatteredInterpolant Fails Near This Hull
scatteredInterpolant builds a Delaunay triangulation of the input points and then interpolates within each triangle. In the corner regions the triangles are sliver-shaped — connecting points that are far apart and nearly collinear. Interpolation inside a sliver triangle amplifies numerical error, leading to wildly wrong surface values near the hull boundary.

title: Part 4: Boundary Behavior and Convex Hull
text:
regularizeNd Does Not Fail Here
regularizeNd is not an interpolant. It solves a weighted least-squares problem:
\[
\min_{\mathbf{y}_\text{grid}} \left\| A_\text{fidelity}\,\mathbf{y}_\text{grid} - \mathbf{z}_\text{data} \right\|^2
+ \lambda^2 \left\| L\,\mathbf{y}_\text{grid} \right\|^2
\]
Where:

\(\mathbf{y}_\text{grid}\) is the unknown vector of grid values to solve for.
\(A_\text{fidelity}\) maps grid values to the sample locations (data-fit operator).
\(\mathbf{z}_\text{data}\) is the vector of measured data values at the sample points.
\(L\) is the regularization operator (for example, finite-difference derivatives on the grid).
\(\lambda\) is the smoothness weight that balances data fit and regularization.

Where data is sparse the regularization term takes over and enforces a smooth continuation of whatever trend exists nearby. It does not need a well-shaped triangulation.

title: Part 4: Boundary Behavior and Convex Hull
Part 4: Boundary Behavior and Convex Hull
Part 4: Boundary Behavior and Convex Hull
text:
Key Takeaways









scatteredInterpolant
regularizeNd




Uses triangulation
Yes
No


Requires well-sampled hull interior
Yes
No


Behavior near sparse hull boundary
Can spike/degrade
Smooth regularized continuation


Is it an interpolant?
Yes — passes through every point
No — weighted least-squares fit


Control over boundary behavior
None
Via smoothness parameter

title: Part 4: Boundary Behavior and Convex Hull
section: What Controls Edge Behavior in regularizeNd
text:
What Controls Edge Behavior in regularizeNd

Smoothness magnitude — the dominant control. Away from the the data, the solution is essentially a smooth continuation of nearby trends.
Derivative order — second-order regularization enforces near-linear continuation; a first-order variant would enforce near-constant continuation.
Grid extent relative to data coverage — keeping the grid tightly bounded by the data limits how far the model is asked to extrapolate.
Anisotropic smoothness — per-dimension smoothness values (as used above: [0.001, 0.005]) let you tune propagation differently along each axis.

title: Part 4: Boundary Behavior and Convex Hull
text:
Boundary Tuning Protocol

Fix interpolation mode ('linear' is the recommended baseline).
Start with equal per-dimension smoothness and compare with the true or reference surface.
If boundary behavior is implausible, increase smoothness in the offending dimension.
Re-check interior residuals after any smoothness increase — over-smoothing will degrade the interior fit.

title: Part 4: Boundary Behavior and Convex Hull
text:
Checklist Before Part 5

You have plotted the data geometry and identified the convex hull.
You have compared your method against a known reference surface where one exists.
You have inspected the boundary and corner regions explicitly, not just the dense interior.
You have selected a smoothness value that gives plausible behavior across the full grid domain.

Practical Goal

title: Part 2: 1D Smoothing and Parameter Tuning
text:
Why 1D First
In higher dimensions, you may not immediately distinguish noise tracking from true structure. In 1D, the failure modes are visually obvious, so you can establish parameter discipline before moving to 2D and nD cases.

title: Part 2: 1D Smoothing and Parameter Tuning
Part 2: 1D Smoothing and Parameter Tuning
Part 2: 1D Smoothing and Parameter Tuning
text:
Interpretation Rules

If curve oscillations appear between sparse data points, smoothness is likely too low.
If the curve misses clear trend changes, smoothness is likely too high.
If coarse and fine grids tell opposite stories, treat that as a warning and retune.

title: Part 2: 1D Smoothing and Parameter Tuning
text:
Repeatable Tuning Workflow

Start at 1e-2 or 5e-3.
Move by factors of 10 only.
Lock a candidate value where trend fidelity and smoothness are both acceptable.
Validate with at least one alternate grid density.

title: Part 2: 1D Smoothing and Parameter Tuning
text:
Common Mistakes

Changing smoothness, interpolation, and solver all at once.
Using linear-scale sweeps such as 0.001, 0.002, 0.003 before understanding order-of-magnitude behavior. Use linear scaling after you have a good candidate value to fine-tune around.
Ignoring conditioning warnings at tiny smoothness values.

title: Tri-Diagonal Matrices
text:
Background
In many applications — particularly in cubic spline construction, finite-difference boundary value problems, and parabolic PDE solvers — the coefficient matrix has a special banded structure. A sparse matrix contains a large majority of zero entries. Exploiting that structure leads to algorithms that are far more efficient in both time and storage than general Gaussian elimination. The most common case is the tridiagonal matrix.






NoteDefinition — Tridiagonal Matrix



An \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\) is called a tridiagonal matrix if \(a_{ij} = 0\) whenever \(|i-j| > 1\). A tridiagonal matrix has the form
\[
A =
\begin{pmatrix}
a_{1,1} & a_{1,2} & 0       & 0       & \cdots & 0       \\
a_{2,1} & a_{2,2} & a_{2,3} & 0       & \cdots & 0       \\
0       & a_{3,2} & a_{3,3} & a_{3,4} & \cdots & 0       \\
\vdots  &         & \ddots  & \ddots  & \ddots & \vdots  \\
0       & \cdots  & 0       & 0       & a_{n,n-1} & a_{n,n}
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{1}
\]

title: Tri-Diagonal Matrices
text:
Compact Vector Notation
A full \(n\times n\) storage for a tridiagonal matrix wastes \(n^2 - 3n + 2\) zeros. Instead, it is more efficient to store only the three diagonals as vectors:








Symbol
Length
Meaning




\(d_k\)
\(n\)
Main diagonal: \(d_k = a_{k,k}\)


\(a_k\)
\(n-1\)
Sub-diagonal: \(a_k = a_{k+1,k}\) (element below \(d_k\))


\(c_k\)
\(n-1\)
Super-diagonal: \(c_k = a_{k,k+1}\) (element to the right of \(d_k\), directly above \(d_{k+1}\))



With this single-subscript notation the matrix becomes
\[
A =
\begin{pmatrix}
d_1 & c_1 & 0   & 0   & \cdots & 0 \\
a_1 & d_2 & c_2 & 0   & \cdots & 0 \\
0   & a_2 & d_3 & c_3 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots &   & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & \cdots & 0 & a_{n-2} & d_{n-1} & c_{n-1} \\
0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & a_{n-1} & d_n
\end{pmatrix}
\tag{2}
\]
and the system \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) expands to
\[
\begin{aligned}
d_1 x_1 + c_1 x_2 &= b_1, \\
a_{k-1} x_{k-1} + d_k x_k + c_k x_{k+1} &= b_k, \quad k = 2,\ldots,n-1,\\
a_{n-1} x_{n-1} + d_n x_n &= b_n.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
\]






WarningStorage savings



An \(n\times n\) tridiagonal system requires storing only \(3n - 2\) numbers instead of \(n^2\). For \(n = 31\) (the system of Example 2 below) this is \(91\) versus \(961\) — a reduction to about \(9.5\%\) of the naive storage. For \(n = 1000\) (common in finite-difference PDE work) the savings reach \(99.7\%\).

title: Tri-Diagonal Matrices
text:
Uniqueness Theorem






TipTheorem — Tridiagonal Unique Solution



Suppose the tridiagonal system \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) has \(a_k \ne 0\) and \(c_k \ne 0\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, n-1\), and that
\[
|d_1| > |c_1|,
\qquad
|d_k| \ge |a_{k-1}| + |c_k|, \quad k = 2, \ldots, n-1,
\qquad
|d_n| > |a_{n-1}|.
\]
Then there exists a unique solution. (The condition is diagonal dominance, strict in the first and last rows.) If the inequality is strict in every row, the hypothesis that the \(a_k\) and \(c_k\) are nonzero can be dropped.

title: Tri-Diagonal Matrices
text:
Thomas Algorithm
The Thomas algorithm (also called the tridiagonal matrix algorithm, TDMA) applies LU factorization specialized to the tridiagonal structure. It proceeds in two passes.
Forward sweep — eliminate the sub-diagonal.
For \(k = 2, 3, \ldots, n\), compute the multiplier
\[
w_k = \frac{a_{k-1}}{d_{k-1}}
\tag{4}
\]
and update
\[
d_k \;\leftarrow\; d_k - w_k\, c_{k-1},
\qquad
b_k \;\leftarrow\; b_k - w_k\, b_{k-1}.
\tag{5}
\]
Back substitution — solve the resulting upper-bidiagonal system.
\[
x_n = \frac{b_n}{d_n},
\qquad
x_k = \frac{b_k - c_k\, x_{k+1}}{d_k},
\quad k = n-1,\, n-2,\, \ldots,\, 1.
\tag{6}
\]
The algorithm requires only \(O(n)\) operations (versus \(O(n^3)\) for general Gaussian elimination) and needs no pivoting when the hypotheses of the theorem above hold: every modified diagonal entry \(d_k\) is then nonzero.

title: Tri-Diagonal Matrices
text:
Example 1 — Symmetric 4×4 Tridiagonal System
Solve the tridiagonal system \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) where
\[
A =
\begin{pmatrix}
2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & 2
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf{b} =
\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The diagonal vectors are \(\mathbf{d} = (2,2,2,2)\), \(\mathbf{a} = \mathbf{c} = (1,1,1)\), and \(\mathbf{b} = (1,0,0,1)\).

Forward Sweep
Step \(k=2\): \[
w_2 = \frac{a_1}{d_1} = \frac{1}{2},
\quad
d_2 \leftarrow 2 - \tfrac{1}{2}(1) = \tfrac{3}{2},
\quad
b_2 \leftarrow 0 - \tfrac{1}{2}(1) = -\tfrac{1}{2}.
\]
Step \(k=3\): \[
w_3 = \frac{a_2}{d_2} = \frac{1}{3/2} = \frac{2}{3},
\quad
d_3 \leftarrow 2 - \tfrac{2}{3}(1) = \tfrac{4}{3},
\quad
b_3 \leftarrow 0 - \tfrac{2}{3}\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\right) = \tfrac{1}{3}.
\]
Step \(k=4\): \[
w_4 = \frac{a_3}{d_3} = \frac{1}{4/3} = \frac{3}{4},
\quad
d_4 \leftarrow 2 - \tfrac{3}{4}(1) = \tfrac{5}{4},
\quad
b_4 \leftarrow 1 - \tfrac{3}{4}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{3}\right) = \tfrac{3}{4}.
\]
After the sweep the system reduces to the upper-bidiagonal form with modified diagonals \(\mathbf{d}' = (2,\,\tfrac{3}{2},\,\tfrac{4}{3},\,\tfrac{5}{4})\) and right-hand sides \(\mathbf{b}' = (1,\,-\tfrac{1}{2},\,\tfrac{1}{3},\,\tfrac{3}{4})\).


Back Substitution
\[
x_4 = \frac{b_4'}{d_4'} = \frac{3/4}{5/4} = \frac{3}{5}.
\]
\[
x_3 = \frac{b_3' - c_3\,x_4}{d_3'} = \frac{\tfrac{1}{3} - 1\cdot\tfrac{3}{5}}{\tfrac{4}{3}}
     = \frac{-\tfrac{4}{15}}{\tfrac{4}{3}} = -\frac{1}{5}.
\]
\[
x_2 = \frac{b_2' - c_2\,x_3}{d_2'} = \frac{-\tfrac{1}{2} - 1\cdot(-\tfrac{1}{5})}{\tfrac{3}{2}}
     = \frac{-\tfrac{3}{10}}{\tfrac{3}{2}} = -\frac{1}{5}.
\]
\[
x_1 = \frac{b_1' - c_1\,x_2}{d_1'} = \frac{1 - 1\cdot(-\tfrac{1}{5})}{2}
     = \frac{\tfrac{6}{5}}{2} = \frac{3}{5}.
\]
The solution is
\[
\mathbf{x} = \left(\tfrac{3}{5},\,-\tfrac{1}{5},\,-\tfrac{1}{5},\,\tfrac{3}{5}\right).
\]

title: Tri-Diagonal Matrices
text:
Applications
Tridiagonal systems arise naturally in:

Cubic splines — the continuity conditions for the second derivatives produce a tridiagonal system for the spline coefficients.
Finite-difference BVPs — discretizing \(u'' = f\) on a uniform grid yields a tridiagonal system of dimension equal to the number of interior grid points.
Parabolic PDEs — the Crank–Nicolson scheme for the heat equation generates a tridiagonal system at every time step.

In each of these contexts the dimension \(n\) can be very large (hundreds to thousands), making the \(O(n)\) Thomas algorithm essential.

This shows that the Taylor polynomial is the limiting position of the Newton interpolating parabola.

title: Simpson’s 3/8 Rule for Numerical Integration
text:
Description
Simpson’s 3/8 rule approximates a definite integral \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) from values of \(f\) at equally spaced points. It splits \([a,b]\) into \(n\) subintervals of width \(h=(b-a)/n\), with nodes \(x_i=a+ih\) for \(i=0,1,\dots,n\), and on each block of three subintervals \([x_{3k-3},x_{3k}]\) it replaces \(f\) by the cubic through the four nodes. Adding the areas under the cubics gives the composite rule \[
S^{3/8}_n = \frac{3h}{8}\sum_{k=1}^{n/3}\left[f(x_{3k-3})+3f(x_{3k-2})+3f(x_{3k-1})+f(x_{3k})\right],
\] or, collecting the weights, \[
S^{3/8}_n = \frac{3h}{8}\left[f(x_0)+f(x_n)+3\sum_{0<i<n,\ i\not\equiv 0\,(\mathrm{mod}\,3)} f(x_i)+2\sum_{0<i<n,\ i\equiv 0\,(\mathrm{mod}\,3)} f(x_i)\right].
\]
Each cubic spans three subintervals, so \(n\) must be a multiple of 3. The sums converge to the integral for any continuous \(f\), but the error formula below needs \(f\) to be four times continuously differentiable on \([a,b]\), \(f\in C^4[a,b]\).
Like Simpson’s rule, the 3/8 rule is exact for every cubic. The general result, as Mathews states it: if \(f\in C^4[a,b]\), there is a \(c\) with \(a<c<b\) such that \[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx - S^{3/8}_n = -\frac{(b-a)\,f^{(4)}(c)}{80}\,h^4 .
\] The error is therefore \(O(h^4)\), and halving \(h\) typically divides it by about 16. The order is the same as Simpson’s rule, but the constant \(1/80\) is \(9/4\) times Simpson’s \(1/180\), so for smooth \(f\) at the same \(h\) the 3/8 rule’s error is typically about 2.25 times larger. The animation on this page does not show the \(h^4\) rate, because its integrand is not in \(C^4[0,2]\).
Case 1 shows what happens when that hypothesis fails. Its integrand \(f(x)=e^{-x}\sin(8x^{2/3})+1\) has \(f'\) unbounded at \(x=0\), and the error shrinks only like \(h^{5/3}\): in the table below, halving \(h\) divides it by 4.32, then 3.40, then 3.22, approaching \(2^{5/3}\approx 3.17\), not 16. The coarse frames also show the cost of wide panels: at \(n=6\) the first cubic, on \([0,1]\), never rises above 1.37 while \(f\) peaks at about 1.92 near \(x=0.080\), and the error grows from \(-0.132\) at \(n=3\) to \(-0.226\).

Simpson’s 3/8 rule is the degree-3 member of the Newton-Cotes family, between Simpson’s Rule and Boole’s Rule, and the two Simpson rules combine: when \(n\ge 5\) is odd, one 3/8 block plus Simpson’s rule on the remaining even number of subintervals covers \([a,b]\).

The error grows from 4 to 7 sample points, then shrinks at every later frame; the last frame (121 sample points) gives 2.01581, about 0.00047 low. The \(x^{2/3}\) term makes \(f'\) unbounded at \(x=0\) (\(f'(x)\approx \tfrac{16}{3}x^{-1/3}\) near \(0\)), so the textbook error order, which assumes smooth \(f\), does not hold for this integrand. The measured error shrinks like \(O(h^{5/3})\) rather than \(O(h^4)\): halving \(h\) divides it by about 3.22 (from 60 to 120 subintervals), tending to \(2^{5/3}\approx 3.17\), instead of 16.

title: Secant Method
text:
Animations
Each animation below shows the secant diagram for the Secant Method. At each step, a secant line is drawn through the two most recent iterates \((p_{n-1}, f(p_{n-1}))\) and \((p_n, f(p_n))\); its x-intercept becomes \(p_{n+1}\). Unlike Newton’s method, no derivative is required — the slope is approximated from two function evaluations. The method can converge quickly, converge slowly near repeated roots, oscillate while converging, or diverge entirely depending on the function and starting points.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Fast Convergence, \(f(x) = 3e^x - 4\cos(x)\), \(p_0 = 1.0\), \(p_1 = 0.9\)
Behavior: The secant method converges quickly to the root near \(x \approx 0.2549\). Both starting points are on the same side of the root and the function is well-behaved. The first secant step lands at \(p_2 \approx 0.456\), still 0.20 from the root; after that the error falls rapidly (0.066 at \(p_3\), 0.0089 at \(p_4\), \(4.4 \times 10^{-4}\) at \(p_5\), \(3.1 \times 10^{-6}\) at \(p_6\)), consistent with the secant method’s order \(\approx 1.618\) at this simple root.
Julia source



Secant method animation for f(x)=3eˣ−4cos(x): secant line drawn through two iterates, x-intercept converges rapidly to the root near x=0.2549




Case 2 — Slow Convergence (Double Root), \(f(x) = 1 - 10x + 25x^2\), \(p_0 = 1.0\), \(p_1 = 0.9\)
Behavior: The function \((1-5x)^2\) has a double root at \(x = 0.2\) where \(f'(0.2) = 0\). The secant method converges, but only linearly: here \(f(x) = 25(x-0.2)^2\), and the ratio of successive errors settles at \((\sqrt{5}-1)/2 \approx 0.618\), so each step removes only about 38% of the remaining error and the iterates creep toward the root over many iterations.
Julia source



Secant method animation for f(x)=(1-5x)²: iterates slowly approach the double root at x=0.2, demonstrating linear convergence behavior




Case 3 — Convergence with Oscillation, \(f(x) = \arctan(x)\), \(p_0 = 1.35\), \(p_1 = 1.30\)
Behavior: The secant method converges to the root at \(x = 0\), but the iterates oscillate — jumping to the opposite side of the root each step before settling. The relatively flat slope of \(\arctan\) near the starting points causes the secant line to overshoot to negative \(x\) on the first step. The animation ends at \(p_8\), which double precision returns as exactly 0: at \(p_6 \approx -6.9 \times 10^{-12}\) and \(p_7 \approx 4.8 \times 10^{-25}\) the computed \(\arctan(x)\) equals \(x\), so the secant through them passes through the origin. In exact arithmetic \(p_8 \approx -7.6 \times 10^{-48}\).
Julia source



Secant method animation for f(x)=arctan(x) with p0=1.35, p1=1.30: iterates oscillate across x=0 with decreasing amplitude before converging




Case 4 — Convergence (Oscillating Path to Distant Root), \(f(x) = x^3 - x + 3\), \(p_0 = 2.0\), \(p_1 = 1.0\)
Behavior: The cubic \(x^3 - x + 3\) has a real root near \(x \approx -1.672\). Starting from positive values far from the root, the secant iterates wander — including a large positive excursion — before eventually converging. This case illustrates that convergence can occur even when the path is non-monotone and the starting points are far from the root.
Julia source



Secant method animation for f(x)=x³−x+3: iterates wander through positive and negative values before converging to the root near x=-1.672




Case 5 — NON Convergence (Diverging to Infinity), \(f(x) = x e^{-x}\), \(p_0 = 1.5\), \(p_1 = 2.0\)
Behavior: Although \(f(x) = x e^{-x}\) has a root at \(x = 0\), the secant method diverges with these starting points. The function decreases toward zero for large \(x\), so the secant line through points on the decaying tail has a shallow negative slope whose x-intercept falls to the right — each step pushes the estimate further from the root. The divergence is slow: after the first jump to \(p_2 \approx 4.11\), each step moves right by less than 1 (the step tends to \(\ln 2 \approx 0.693\)). The animation stops at \(p_{10} \approx 10.57\), the first iterate past the right edge of the window; \(p_{16} \approx 15.11\).

title: Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg Method
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg Method
text:
Description
The Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg method (RKF45) is an adaptive-step one-step solver for the initial value problem \(y' = f(t, y)\), \(y(t_0) = y_0\). At each step it computes embedded 4th- and 5th-order approximations from the same stage evaluations, estimates the local error from their difference, and adjusts the step size to meet a tolerance. From the current point \((t_j, y_j)\) and a trial step \(h\), the six stages are
\[
\begin{aligned}
k_1 &= h\,f(t_j,\ y_j),\\
k_2 &= h\,f\!\left(t_j + \tfrac{1}{4}h,\ y_j + \tfrac{1}{4}k_1\right),\\
k_3 &= h\,f\!\left(t_j + \tfrac{3}{8}h,\ y_j + \tfrac{3}{32}k_1 + \tfrac{9}{32}k_2\right),\\
k_4 &= h\,f\!\left(t_j + \tfrac{12}{13}h,\ y_j + \tfrac{1932}{2197}k_1 - \tfrac{7200}{2197}k_2 + \tfrac{7296}{2197}k_3\right),\\
k_5 &= h\,f\!\left(t_j + h,\ y_j + \tfrac{439}{216}k_1 - 8k_2 + \tfrac{3680}{513}k_3 - \tfrac{845}{4104}k_4\right),\\
k_6 &= h\,f\!\left(t_j + \tfrac{1}{2}h,\ y_j - \tfrac{8}{27}k_1 + 2k_2 - \tfrac{3544}{2565}k_3 + \tfrac{1859}{4104}k_4 - \tfrac{11}{40}k_5\right),
\end{aligned}
\]
and the 4th- and 5th-order updates are
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_4 &= y_j + \tfrac{25}{216}k_1 + \tfrac{1408}{2565}k_3 + \tfrac{2197}{4104}k_4 - \tfrac{1}{5}k_5,\\
y_5 &= y_j + \tfrac{16}{135}k_1 + \tfrac{6656}{12825}k_3 + \tfrac{28561}{56430}k_4 - \tfrac{9}{50}k_5 + \tfrac{2}{55}k_6.
\end{aligned}
\]
The difference \(|y_5 - y_4|\) estimates the local error of \(y_4\). It shrinks like \(h^5\), so \(|y_5 - y_4|/h\) is an error per unit step that shrinks like \(h^4\). A step is accepted when \(|y_5 - y_4|/h \le \varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the requested tolerance; RKF45 then carries \(y_{j+1} = y_4\) forward, and the variant RKF54 carries \(y_5\). Accepted or not, the next step size is
\[
h_{new} = s\,h, \qquad s = 0.84\left(\frac{\varepsilon h}{|y_5 - y_4|}\right)^{1/4},
\]
clamped to at most \(h_{max}=0.25\) (and at least \(h_{min}=10^{-6}\), which neither case reaches), and a rejected step is retried from the same point. The factor \(0.84\) rounds Mathews’ \(2^{-1/4}\); if \(|y_5 - y_4|\) scaled exactly like \(h^5\), the new step would bring \(|y_5 - y_4|/h\) to about \(\varepsilon/2\).
The method needs \(f\) continuous and Lipschitz in \(y\) near the solution, so that the solution is unique, and \(f\) smooth enough for the orders below. In Case 2, \(f = 1 - t\sqrt[3]{y}\) is not differentiable at \(y = 0\), but the solution stays above \(y(5) \approx 0.00812\).
In general, if \(f\) has continuous partial derivatives through order 5 near the solution (which makes \(y \in C^6\)), the 4th- and 5th-order formulas have local errors \(O(h^5)\) and \(O(h^6)\), so for small \(h\), \(y_5 - y_4\) is dominated by the error of \(y_4\); with fixed steps the global errors are \(O(h^4)\) and \(O(h^5)\). On Case 1’s problem, halving one step at \(t = 0\) from \(0.025\) to \(0.0125\) divides \(|y_5 - y_4|\) by \(30.7\) and the errors of \(y_4\) and \(y_5\) by \(27.9\) and \(65.6\), near \(2^5 = 32\) and \(2^6 = 64\). The animations show the step-size controller, not these rates.
The tolerance bounds local, not global, error. In Case 1 the accepted \(|y_5 - y_4|\) sum to \(5.6\times10^{-7}\), yet RKF45 ends \(4.5\times10^{-3}\) from \(y(1.1) = 139.88\): near the pole of \(\tan(t + \arctan 0.5)\) at \(t \approx 1.1071\), errors grow up to \(1.6\times10^{4}\)-fold by \(t = 1.1\), but the individually grown estimates give only \(2.2\times10^{-3}\). The estimate needs small \(h\): the step \(h = 0.136\) from \(t = 0.1\) underestimates its error 10.5-fold, causing nearly half the final error (\(h = 0.25\) from \(t = 0\): 34-fold, Animations introduction).
The Euler, Heun, Taylor Series, Runge-Kutta, Adams-Bashforth-Moulton and Milne-Simpson pages solve Case 2’s problem with fixed steps, and Adaptive Simpson’s Rule uses the same compare-two-estimates idea for integrals.

title: Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg Method
text:
Animations
The first animation below reconstructs the legacy Example 1 setup from the Mathews module: \(y' = 1 + y^2\), \(y(0)=0.5\), on \([0,1.1]\). The dashed black curve is the exact solution \(y(t)=\tan\!\left(t + \arctan(0.5)\right)\). The step controller is not the module’s: its RKF45 and RKF54 subroutines accept a step when \(|y_5 - y_4| < \varepsilon\) or \(h < 2h_{min}\), start from \(h=0.25\) (here \(0.1\)) and have a minimum step size \(h_{min}=0.001\). At the same \(\varepsilon=10^{-6}\) they take 120 points; the step reaches \(h_{min}\) at \(t \approx 1.055\), and the last 8 of the 119 steps, from \(t \approx 1.092\) on, are accepted only by the \(h < 2h_{min}\) condition. They end with errors of \(7.0\times10^{-2}\) (RKF45) and \(6.5\times10^{-2}\) (RKF54) at \(t=1.1\), against \(4.5\times10^{-3}\) and \(3.2\times10^{-3}\) here (Case 1). Most of that difference is the first step of \(0.25\): its error estimate, \(1.7\times10^{-7}\), passes either acceptance test, but its true error is \(5.6\)–\(5.7\times10^{-6}\), which this problem magnifies about \(1.1\times10^{4}\) times by \(t=1.1\); started from \(h=0.25\), the controller used here ends with errors of \(6.6\times10^{-2}\) and \(6.3\times10^{-2}\).
Because the recovered archive did not include legacy RKF animated GIF portals for this topic, the first animation is reconstructed from the worked-example equations and plot behavior in the module links/images. The module’s Examples 6–8, which solve a second problem, the Riccati equation \(y' = t^2 + y^2\), with the module’s RKF45 and RKF54 subroutines (Example 6), compare those results with its closed-form Bessel-function solution (Example 7) and derive that solution with Mathematica’s DSolve (Example 8), are not animated here.
The second animation uses the same IVP shown on the Euler’s Method page (in both its forward Euler and modified Euler cases) and on the Runge-Kutta, Taylor Series and Adams-Bashforth-Moulton pages: \(y' = 1 - t\sqrt[3]{y}\), \(y(0)=1\), on \([0,5]\), with a dashed high-accuracy reference trajectory from fixed-step RK4 at \(h=10^{-4}\). This IVP is not one of the module’s examples; it is used here so that this page can be compared with those pages.

Case 1 - Adaptive RKF45 vs RKF54, \(y' = 1 + y^2\), \(y(0)=0.5\), \(t \in [0,1.1]\)
Behavior: Both adaptive traces follow the exact solution to within a relative error of \(3.3\times10^{-5}\) all the way to \(y(1.1)=139.88\), just short of the pole of \(\tan\) at \(t=1.1071\); the logarithmic \(y\)-axis keeps the whole run in view. The step shrinks from \(0.136\) near \(t=0.1\) to \(5\times10^{-5}\) near \(t=1.1\), so 187 of the 259 computed points lie in \(t \ge 1.05\) and the marker slows as it nears the pole (each frame adds up to four accepted steps). RKF45 and RKF54 share the error estimate and the step rule, so their steps agree to within \(0.05\%\) and the curves coincide (blue over magenta). They differ only in whether \(y_4\) or \(y_5\) is carried forward, and RKF54 ends closer to the exact value: errors \(3.2\times10^{-3}\) against \(4.5\times10^{-3}\) at \(t=1.1\).

Adaptive RKF45 and RKF54 trajectories versus exact solution for y’ = 1 + y^2, y(0)=0.5 on [0,1.1], with y on a logarithmic axis




Case 2 - Adaptive RKF45 vs RKF54, \(y' = 1 - t\sqrt[3]{y}\), \(y(0)=1\), \(t \in [0,5]\)
Behavior: RKF45 and RKF54 match the dashed reference to within \(7\times10^{-7}\) at every accepted point. The controller takes the maximum step \(h=0.25\) over the hump (\(0.1 \le t \le 1.35\)) and keeps \(h\) between \(0.189\) and \(0.25\) until \(t \approx 2.4\), past the steepest point (\(y'=-0.930\) at \(t=2.19\)). It then cuts the step as the solution bends into its flat tail: below \(0.04\) from \(t=3\) on, and the smallest step it chooses is \(0.027\), near \(t=3.27\). The corners visible on the hump are the straight segments drawn between accepted points \(0.25\) apart (up to \(0.0091\) below the curve, near \(t=0.48\)), not integration error. These steps are set by the tolerance, not by stability: \(\partial f/\partial y=-t/(3y^{2/3})\) reaches \(-41.3\) at \(t=5\), so for fixed steps longer than about \(h=0.0732\), \(h\,|\partial f/\partial y|\) would exceed the 4th-order RKF update’s stability limit \(3.02\) before \(t=5\), while every accepted step here keeps \(h\,|\partial f/\partial y|\) below \(1.3\).

text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Romberg Integration
text:
Description
Romberg integration approximates \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) by building a lower triangular table from composite trapezoidal sums and taking a diagonal entry as the answer. Row \(k\) starts with the trapezoidal sum \(T_{2^{k-1}}\) on \(2^{k-1}\) subintervals of width \(h=(b-a)/2^{k-1}\), which uses \(m=2^{k-1}+1\) sample points. Halving \(h\) keeps every old sample, so a new row costs only the new midpoints. Richardson extrapolation then fills in the rest of the row: \[
R_{k,1}=T_{2^{k-1}},
\] \[
R_{k,j}=R_{k,j-1}+\frac{R_{k,j-1}-R_{k-1,j-1}}{4^{j-1}-1}, \qquad j=2,\dots,k.
\] As Mathews runs it, the table grows one row at a time until two successive diagonal entries agree, \(|R_{k,k}-R_{k-1,k-1}|<\text{tol}\), and \(R_{k,k}\) is the estimate.
The weights rest on a general result about the trapezoidal rule. For smooth \(f\) (\(f\in C^{2j}[a,b]\) for column \(j\)), the trapezoidal error expands in even powers of \(h\), \(T_n-I=c_1h^2+c_2h^4+\cdots\); each extrapolation removes the leading term, so column \(j\) has error \(O(h^{2j})\), and halving \(h\) divides it by about \(4^j\). The second column is Simpson’s rule and the third is Boole’s rule, each on \(2^{k-1}\) subintervals. This builds a triangular table whose diagonal entries converge quickly for smooth integrands, often outperforming raw trapezoidal refinement for the same function evaluations.
The animation on this page shows what happens when the smoothness hypothesis fails. In Case 1, \(f(x)=1+e^{-x}\sin(8x^{2/3})\) has \(f'\) unbounded at \(x=0\), the error no longer expands in even powers of \(h\), and the extrapolation weights cancel the wrong terms. From 64 to 128 subintervals, halving \(h\) divides the error of every column by 3.16 to 3.20, close to \(2^{5/3}\approx 3.17\), so \(R_{8,8}\) is only about 4.4 times closer to \(I\) than \(R_{8,1}\). On the coarse rows extrapolation even hurts: at \(m=3\) and \(m=5\) the diagonal error is larger than the trapezoidal error. The cure is to remove the singularity first. After the substitution \(x=t^3\), the integrand \(3t^2\left(1+e^{-t^3}\sin 8t^2\right)\) on \([0,\sqrt[3]{2}]\) is smooth, and the same 129 sample points give an \(R_{8,8}\) within \(4\times10^{-10}\) of \(I\).
Romberg integration is Richardson Extrapolation applied to the Trapezoidal Rule; Gauss-Legendre Quadrature and Adaptive Simpson’s Rule are the alternatives on this site that place or refine nodes instead.

title: Romberg Integration
text:
Animations
Each animation below shows the Romberg refinement process for \(f(x)=1+e^{-x}\sin(8x^{2/3})\) on \([0,2]\). The graph and table are updated together as the trapezoidal mesh is globally refined with sample counts \(m=2,3,5,9,17,33,65,129\).
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Romberg Table Construction, \(f(x)=1+e^{-x}\sin(8x^{2/3})\), \([0,2]\)
Behavior: After an opening frame that shows \(f\) alone with an empty table, each frame adds one Romberg row from a denser trapezoidal partition and then applies Richardson extrapolation across the row. The diagonal entry \(R_{k,k}\) is the table’s estimate at each stage; it is the most accurate entry in its row from \(m=9\) on, but at \(m=3\) and \(m=5\) it is the least accurate. Its error is not monotone: \(|R_{k,k}-I|\) is \(1.6\times10^{-3}\) at \(m=2\), then \(0.47\), \(0.46\), \(0.046\), \(8.1\times10^{-3}\), \(2.8\times10^{-3}\), \(8.7\times10^{-4}\), \(2.7\times10^{-4}\); the one-panel value at \(m=2\), \(f(0)+f(2)=2.017925\), is close only by coincidence. The \(x^{2/3}\) term makes \(f'\) unbounded at \(x=0\) (\(f'(x)\approx \tfrac{16}{3}x^{-1/3}\) near \(0\)), so the textbook error order, which assumes smooth \(f\), does not hold for this integrand. The measured error of every column, the diagonal included, shrinks like \(O(h^{5/3})\) rather than \(O(h^{2j})\): halving \(h\) divides the diagonal error by about 3.18 (from 64 to 128 subintervals), tending to \(2^{5/3}\approx 3.17\), so extrapolation lowers the error only by a constant factor (about 4.4 against the trapezoid column at 129 sample points). The last frame’s \(R_{8,8}=2.016007\) is still \(2.7\times10^{-4}\) below \(I\approx 2.016280\).

title: Richardson Extrapolation
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Richardson Extrapolation
text:
Description
Richardson extrapolation improves an approximation that depends on a step size \(h\) by combining its values at two step sizes so that the leading term of its error cancels. Mathews applies it to numerical differentiation, where it turns the three-point central difference for \(f'(x)\) into a five-point formula; this page animates that step for \(f(x)=e^{-x}\sin(x)\) over \([0,\pi]\).
The three-point central difference is
\[
D_3(x,h)=\frac{f(x+h)-f(x-h)}{2h}.
\]
For smooth \(f\), Taylor expansion gives \(D_3(x,h)=f'(x)+\tfrac{f'''(x)}{6}h^2+\tfrac{f^{(5)}(x)}{120}h^4+\cdots\), with only even powers of \(h\). Halving \(h\) divides the \(h^2\) term by 4, so the combination
\[
D_5(x,h)=\frac{4D_3(x,h/2)-D_3(x,h)}{3}=\frac{f(x-h)-8f(x-h/2)+8f(x+h/2)-f(x+h)}{6h}
\]
removes it. This is Mathews’ five-point central difference with spacing \(h/2\). In general, if \(A(h)=A+c\,h^p+O(h^q)\) with \(q>p\), then \(\bigl(2^pA(h/2)-A(h)\bigr)/(2^p-1)=A+O(h^q)\).
The method assumes that the exponent \(p\) of the leading error term is known and that this term dominates, which needs \(f\) smooth enough. As a general result, if \(f\in C^3[x-h,x+h]\) then \(f'(x)-D_3(x,h)=-\tfrac{f'''(c)}{6}h^2\), and if \(f\in C^5[x-h,x+h]\) then
\[
f'(x)-D_5(x,h)=\frac{f^{(5)}(c)}{480}\,h^4
\]
for some \(c\) in that interval, which is Mathews’ five-point remainder \(\tfrac{f^{(5)}(c)}{30}k^4\) with \(k=h/2\). So halving \(h\) divides the error of \(D_3\) by about 4 and that of \(D_5\) by about 16. In Case 1, going from \(h=0.02\) to \(h=0.01\) takes the maximum error over \([0,\pi]\) from \(1.33\times10^{-4}\) to \(3.33\times10^{-5}\) for \(D_3\) and from \(1.33\times10^{-9}\) to \(8.33\times10^{-11}\) for \(D_5\). In Case 2, at \(x=1\), the log-log slopes between successive step sizes are 2.000 to 2.007 for \(D_3\) and 3.905 to 4.005 for \(D_5\), from \(h=0.5\) down to \(h=0.006\).
Rounding error eventually wins. Both formulas subtract nearly equal values of \(f\) and divide by \(h\), so rounding errors grow as \(h\) shrinks while the truncation error of \(D_5\) falls like \(h^4\). The last two points of Case 2 leave the \(h^4\) line: at \(h=0.0015\) the computed error of \(D_5\) is \(1.29\times10^{-14}\), about 2.8 times the truncation error \(4.67\times10^{-15}\) found in 50-digit arithmetic. Wrong weights also mislead: a one-sided difference \(A(h)=\bigl(f(x+h)-f(x)\bigr)/h\) has an error starting with an \(h\) term, so the weights 4 and \(-1\) leave an \(O(h)\) error, and the right combination is \(2A(h/2)-A(h)\).
The difference formulas themselves are on Numerical Differentiation and Derive Numerical Differentiation Formulae, the \(O(h^p)\) notation is on Big “O” Truncation Error, Romberg Integration applies the same step repeatedly to the trapezoidal rule, and Aitken’s Method accelerates a sequence without a step size.

title: Richardson Extrapolation
text:
Animations
Each animation below compares the base central difference with Richardson extrapolation for the legacy test function and interval. Case 2 plots the error of the estimate in the legacy module’s Example 8: \(D_5(x,h)\) is that example’s five-point formula for \(f'\) with spacing \(h/2\), evaluated here over a different list of step sizes. Examples 9–10, which use five-point central-difference formulas to approximate the second and third derivatives at the same point, are not animated here, and neither are the pictures that Examples 8–10 draw: the five stencil points with a line, parabola or cubic through the centre point. Nor are the module’s truncation-error-bound examples: Examples 1, 3, 4 and 5 estimate \(M_5=\max|f^{(5)}|\) on \([0,\pi]\) from a graph of \(f^{(5)}\), check the resulting five-point error bound against the actual error, show the bound’s \(O(h^4)\) scaling, and compare it with the three-point bound; Case 1 annotates the actual maximum errors instead. Example 7, the module’s worked extrapolation, combines \(D_3(1,0.02)\) and \(D_3(1,0.01)\) into the five-point value at spacing \(0.01\), which is \(D_5(1,0.02)\); its error is the \(h=0.02\) point of Case 2 and is not shown separately, and Example 2(b)’s plot of the five-point formula at spacing \(0.01\) over \([0,\pi]\) is the \(h=0.02\) frame of Case 1. Example 2(a)’s table at \(x=0,1,2,3\) and Example 6’s proof that the five-point formula at spacing \(h\) equals \(\frac{4D_3(x,h)-D_3(x,2h)}{3}\) are not animated either.

title: Richardson Extrapolation
text:
Derivation Notes
If \(D_3(x,h)=f'(x)+C_2 h^2 + C_4 h^4 + \cdots\), then
\[
\frac{4D_3(x,h/2)-D_3(x,h)}{3}
= f'(x) + O(h^4),
\]
because the \(C_2 h^2\) contribution cancels exactly.

title: Numerical Differentiation
text:
Description
Numerical differentiation replaces analytic derivatives with finite-difference quotients built from nearby function values. In the Mathews examples for this module, the test function is \(f(x)=e^{-x}\sin(x)\) on \([0,\pi]\) with representative steps \(h=0.1,0.01,0.001\). Each formula below differentiates, at \(x\), the polynomial that interpolates \(f\) at the equally spaced points it uses.
The three-point central approximation for the first derivative is
\[
f'(x) \approx D_3(x,h) = \frac{f(x+h)-f(x-h)}{2h},
\]
with truncation error \(O(h^2)\) when \(f\) is sufficiently smooth. When \(f\) is known on only one side of \(x\), as at the end of a table, the forward (\(+\)) and backward (\(-\)) formulas use \(x\) and points on that side; the subscript counts the points:
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_2^{+}(x,h) &= \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}, &
D_3^{+}(x,h) &= \frac{-3f(x)+4f(x+h)-f(x+2h)}{2h}, \\
D_2^{-}(x,h) &= \frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}{h}, &
D_3^{-}(x,h) &= \frac{3f(x)-4f(x-h)+f(x-2h)}{2h}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The three-point central formula for the second derivative is
\[
f''(x) \approx D_3^{(2)}(x,h) = \frac{f(x+h)-2f(x)+f(x-h)}{h^2}.
\]
In general, if the derivative of \(f\) in an error term (\(f''\), \(f'''\) or \(f^{(4)}\)) is continuous on the interval spanned by the points used, each equation below holds for some \(c\) in that interval:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x) &= D_2^{\pm}(x,h) \mp \tfrac{h}{2}\,f''(c), &
f'(x) &= D_3^{\pm}(x,h) + \tfrac{h^2}{3}\,f'''(c), \\
f'(x) &= D_3(x,h) - \tfrac{h^2}{6}\,f'''(c), &
f''(x) &= D_3^{(2)}(x,h) - \tfrac{h^2}{12}\,f^{(4)}(c).
\end{aligned}
\]
So the two-point formulas are \(O(h)\) (Cases 3 and 5) and the three-point formulas are \(O(h^2)\) (Cases 4 and 6), and the central constant \(\tfrac16\) is half the one-sided \(\tfrac13\). Case 1 and Case 2 show \(D_3\) approaching \(f'\) as \(h\) falls to \(0.001\). The table follows \(x = 1\) down to \(h = 10^{-8}\); its entries are the errors \(f'(1) - D\) for each first-derivative formula \(D\), and \(f''(1) - D_3^{(2)}\), in double precision:

Each tenfold cut in \(h\) divides the \(O(h)\) error by about \(10\) and the \(O(h^2)\) errors by about \(100\), until roundoff takes over. Down to \(h = 10^{-4}\), the backward formulas’ errors are within about \(20\%\) of these, and that of \(D_2^-\) has the opposite sign.
As \(h\) decreases, truncation error improves, but eventually roundoff and cancellation can limit accuracy. For small \(h\), \(f(x \pm h)\) and \(f(x)\) share leading digits that cancel in the difference, and the rounding error of each value, of order \(\varepsilon\,|f(x)|\) with \(\varepsilon \approx 2.2 \times 10^{-16}\), is divided by \(h\), or by \(h^2\) in \(D_3^{(2)}\). At \(x = 1\), among powers of ten, \(D_2^+\) is most accurate at \(h = 10^{-8}\), \(D_3\) at \(h = 10^{-5}\) (error of order \(10^{-11}\)), and \(D_3^{(2)}\) at \(h = 10^{-4}\); at \(h = 10^{-8}\) the error of \(D_3^{(2)}\) is \(40\%\) of \(|f''(1)|\). Errors in measured data are magnified in the same way.
Derive Numerical Differentiation Formulae derives central formulas from Taylor expansions, Richardson Extrapolation combines \(D_3(x,h)\) and \(D_3(x,h/2)\) into an \(O(h^4)\) estimate, Big “O” Truncation Error explains the order notation, and the Finite Difference Method for ODE’s applies central differences to boundary value problems.

Animations
Each animation below shows finite-difference derivative behavior for \(f(x)=e^{-x}\sin(x)\) on legacy interval settings from the source module.
Case 1 extends Example 2(c) of Mathews’ module, the plot of \(D_3(x,h)\) against \(f'(x)\) on \([0,\pi]\), from the single step \(h=0.01\) to a sequence of steps, and Case 2 follows Examples 11 and 14, the central difference at \(x_0=1\). Cases 3–6 rebuild Mathews’ animations for Examples 9, 12, 10 and 13, the forward differences \(D_2^+\) and \(D_3^+\) and the backward differences \(D_2^-\) and \(D_3^-\) at \(x_0=1\), with his steps \(h\) and his window \(0 \le x \le 2.1\); the true tangent, also drawn in Case 2, is added to his picture, and every value of \(f'(1)\) his frames print is reproduced to his six decimals. His last frame prints \(h=0.001\) to three decimals, but in the \(O(h)\) animations its printed value is that of \(h=0.0005\), which ends all four cases here. The module’s other examples are not animated here: in Project I, the graph of \(f'''\) used to bound the error (Example 1), the tables of approximations (Examples 2(a) and 2(b)), the plot of the absolute error against the error bound (Example 3) and the study of how the bound shrinks with \(h\) (Example 4); and the formulas for the second derivative (Project II, Examples 5–8, and Examples 15–17).

Behavior: The numerical derivative curve approaches \(f'(x)\) as \(h\) shrinks, consistent with second-order truncation error for the central stencil.

Case 2 - secant to tangent at \(x_0=1\), \(h \to 0\)

As in Example 14, each frame also draws the parabola through the three stencil points and the line through \((x_0,f(x_0))\) with the secant slope; that slope is the parabola’s derivative at \(x_0\), so the line touches the parabola there and runs parallel to the chord.

title: Numerical Differentiation
text:
Derivation Notes
For smooth \(f\), Taylor expansions about \(x\) give
\[
f(x\pm h) = f(x) \pm h f'(x) + \frac{h^2}{2}f''(x) \pm \frac{h^3}{6}f^{(3)}(\xi_\pm),
\]
which leads to the central three-point first-derivative rule with error proportional to \(h^2\).

title: Newton-Raphson Method
text:
Animations
Each animation below shows the tangent-line diagram for the Newton-Raphson method. At each iterate \(x_n\), a tangent line to \(f(x)\) is drawn; its x-intercept gives \(x_{n+1} = x_n - \tfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\). The sequence of tangent lines shows whether the iterates converge to a root, fall into a cycle, or diverge.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Quadratic convergence, \(f(x) = 3e^x - 4\cos(x)\), \(x_0 = 1.0\)
Behavior: The function has a single positive root, \(x^* \approx 0.2549\) (it also has infinitely many negative roots, outside the plotted window). Starting at \(x_0 = 1.0\) to the right of the root, where \(f > 0\) and \(f'' > 0\), each tangent line lands between the root and the previous iterate, so the iterates decrease monotonically to \(x^*\) (1, 0.4798, 0.2857, 0.2556, 0.254850, …); the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step — the quadratic convergence typical of Newton-Raphson near a simple root.
Julia source



Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=3eˣ−4cos(x): rapid, monotone convergence from x₀=1.0 down to the root at x≈0.2549




Case 2 — Linear convergence (double root), \(f(x) = (1-5x)^2\), \(x_0 = 1.0\)
Behavior: A double root at \(x^* = 0.2\). Because \(f'(x^*) = 0\), the standard convergence proof breaks down and Newton-Raphson degrades to linear convergence — each step roughly halves the error rather than squaring it.
Julia source



Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=(1−5x)²: slow linear convergence to the double root at x=0.2




Case 3 — Convergence with oscillation, \(f(x) = \arctan(x)\), \(x_0 = 1.35\)
Behavior: The only root is \(x^* = 0\). For \(f(x) = \arctan(x)\), Newton-Raphson converges only when \(|x_0| < x_c \approx 1.3917\). Starting at \(x_0 = 1.35\) (just inside the convergence radius), the method converges but requires several oscillating steps before settling in.
Julia source



Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=arctan(x): convergent case starting just inside the critical radius at x₀=1.35




Case 4 — Cycling (non-convergence), \(f(x) = x^3 - x + 3\), \(x_0 = 0.0\)
Behavior: \(f\) has one real root, \(x^* \approx -1.6717\), where the curve crosses the axis at the left of the window. Starting at \(x_0 = 0\), the iterates are drawn into an attracting 4-cycle ≈ 0.0074 → 3.0005 → 1.9619 → 1.1475 → … and never approach the root — Newton-Raphson can fail even when a root exists.
Julia source



Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=x³−x+3: from x₀=0 the iterates settle into a 4-cycle near 0.0074, 3.0005, 1.9619 and 1.1475 and never reach the real root at x≈−1.6717




Case 5 — Divergence to infinity, \(f(x) = xe^{-x}\), \(x_0 = 2.0\)
Behavior: The only root is \(x^* = 0\), but \(x_0 = 2\) lies beyond the maximum of \(f\) at \(x = 1\). There \(f > 0\) and \(f'(x) = (1-x)e^{-x} < 0\), so each tangent line meets the axis to the right: \(x_{n+1} = x_n^2/(x_n - 1) > x_n\). The iterates run off toward \(+\infty\) (2, 4, 5.33, 6.56, …, 10.02 after six steps) while \(f(x_n) \to 0\) — a small residual does not mean a root is near.
Julia source



Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=x·e⁻ˣ: from x₀=2.0 each tangent line meets the axis further right, and the iterates move away from the root at x=0 toward +∞




Case 6 — Divergent, \(f(x) = \arctan(x)\), \(x_0 = 1.4\)
Behavior: Same function as Case 3 but starting at \(x_0 = 1.4\) — just outside the critical convergence radius \(x_c \approx 1.3917\). The iterates do not converge to the root; they escape toward larger \(|x|\), illustrating the sensitivity of Newton-Raphson to the choice of starting point for flat-tailed functions.
Julia source



Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=arctan(x): divergent case starting just outside the critical radius at x₀=1.4

title: Newton-Cotes Integration
text:
Description
Newton-Cotes formulas approximate \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) from values of \(f\) at equally spaced nodes. On a panel of \(M\) subintervals of width \(h\), with nodes \(x_k=x_0+kh\) and \(f_k=f(x_k)\), they integrate the polynomial of degree \(M\) through the \(M+1\) nodes; the closed rules include both endpoints. Mathews states the first four with their error terms, for some \(c\) in the panel:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_{x_0}^{x_1} f(x)\,dx &= \frac{h}{2}\left(f_0+f_1\right) - \frac{h^3}{12}f^{(2)}(c) &&\text{(trapezoidal)}\\
\int_{x_0}^{x_2} f(x)\,dx &= \frac{h}{3}\left(f_0+4f_1+f_2\right) - \frac{h^5}{90}f^{(4)}(c) &&\text{(Simpson's 1/3)}\\
\int_{x_0}^{x_3} f(x)\,dx &= \frac{3h}{8}\left(f_0+3f_1+3f_2+f_3\right) - \frac{3h^5}{80}f^{(4)}(c) &&\text{(Simpson's 3/8)}\\
\int_{x_0}^{x_4} f(x)\,dx &= \frac{2h}{45}\left(7f_0+32f_1+12f_2+32f_3+7f_4\right) - \frac{8h^7}{945}f^{(6)}(c) &&\text{(Boole)}
\end{aligned}
\]
A composite rule splits \([a,b]\) into \(n\) subintervals, \(h=(b-a)/n\), and applies the panel rule to each of \(n/M\) panels, so \(n\) must be a multiple of \(M\); Cases 1 to 4 use \(M=1\), 2, 3 and 4.
Each error term needs \(f\) smooth on the panel: \(f\in C^2\) for the trapezoidal rule, \(C^4\) for both Simpson rules and \(C^6\) for Boole’s rule. The rules are exact for polynomials of degree 1, 3, 3 and 5, their degrees of precision; for even \(M\) the symmetric panel gains one degree. In general, if \(f\) has those continuous derivatives on \([a,b]\), the composite errors are \(O(h^2)\), \(O(h^4)\), \(O(h^4)\) and \(O(h^6)\).
The animations do not show these orders: every case uses \(f(x)=e^{-x}\sin(8x^{2/3})+1\) on \([0,2]\), which is not smooth at \(x=0\). The \(x^{2/3}\) term makes \(f'\) unbounded at \(x=0\) (\(f'(x)\approx \tfrac{16}{3}x^{-1/3}\) near \(0\)), so the textbook error order, which assumes smooth \(f\), does not hold for this integrand. The measured error of all four rules shrinks like \(O(h^{5/3})\) rather than \(O(h^2)\), \(O(h^4)\), \(O(h^4)\) and \(O(h^6)\): halving \(h\) (from 24 to 48 subintervals) divides it by about 3.14, 3.38, 3.55 and 3.15 for the trapezoidal, Simpson’s \(1/3\), Simpson’s \(3/8\) and Boole’s rules, tending to \(2^{5/3}\approx 3.17\) for each, instead of 4, 16, 16 and 64. So at equal \(h\) the higher-degree rules gain only a constant factor over the trapezoidal rule here, not extra powers of \(h\). At 121 sample points the panel at \(x=0\) contributes over 99% of the error of Simpson’s \(3/8\) and Boole’s rules (Case 3, Case 4). Adaptive Simpson’s Rule targets such errors by refining only panels whose error estimate is large. Raising \(M\) is no cure either: the closed rule on nine nodes (\(M=8\)) already has negative weights, which can amplify rounding errors in the \(f_k\).
Each rule has its own page (Trapezoidal, Simpson’s, Simpson’s 3/8, Boole’s); the panel polynomials are Lagrange interpolants, Romberg Integration recovers Simpson’s and Boole’s rules from trapezoidal sums, and Gauss-Legendre Quadrature drops equal spacing for degree of precision \(2N-1\) with \(N\) nodes.

title: Newton-Cotes Integration
text:
Derivation Notes
The four closed Newton-Cotes rules fit interpolants of degree 1, 2, 3 and 4 per panel, but their degrees of precision are 1, 3, 3 and 5: the rules with an even number of subintervals per panel (Simpson’s \(1/3\), Boole) are exact for one degree more than their interpolant. For smooth \(f\) (\(C^2\), \(C^4\), \(C^4\) and \(C^6\) on \([a,b]\) respectively) the composite errors are therefore \(O(h^2)\), \(O(h^4)\), \(O(h^4)\) and \(O(h^6)\). Simpson’s \(3/8\) rule is thus not higher order than Simpson’s \(1/3\) rule, and its composite error constant is larger: \(|E|=\tfrac{1}{80}(b-a)h^4|f^{(4)}(\xi)|\) against \(\tfrac{1}{180}(b-a)h^4|f^{(4)}(\xi)|\) for some \(\xi\in[a,b]\). Rules of very high degree on wide panels can become less robust.

title: Muller’s Method
text:
Animations
Each animation below shows Muller’s Method fitting a parabola through three successive approximations of a root. The parabola (dashed blue) passes through the current triple \((p_0, p_1, p_2)\), and the next iterate is found where the parabola crosses the x-axis (in Case 1 the parabola never reaches the axis; see that case). Each frame advances one iteration: the oldest point is dropped, and the new root estimate becomes \(p_2\) (red dot). The gray dots are \(p_0\) and \(p_1\).
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Convergent, \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2\), double root at \(p = 1\)
Behavior: The iterates converge to the double root \(p = 1\) of \(f(x) = (x-1)^2(x+2)\), starting from \(p_2 = 2.0\). None of the parabolas reaches the x-axis: at every step its roots are complex, so Muller’s next iterate would be complex (the first would be \(p_3 \approx 1.2873 + 0.3563i\)). This animation takes the real part of that complex root instead, which is the parabola’s vertex (open red circle). Each frame is zoomed to the current points, and the inset shows the vertex, whose height above the axis falls from 0.80 to \(5.4 \times 10^{-13}\) over the eight frames. The iterates \(1.2873, 1.1581, 1.0552, 1.0100, 1.0017, \ldots\) decrease to \(p = 1\) superlinearly (order \(\approx 1.32\) asymptotically for this real-part variant), faster than Newton’s method, which converges only linearly at a double root. Mathews’ own program (Mathew 2000-2019) handles the complex case differently: it drops the square root, so the step is \(p_3 = p_2 - 2f(p_2)/b\), where \(b\) is the parabola’s slope at \(p_2\). His program also keeps the two points nearest the new iterate rather than the two most recent, and its iterates \(1.1091, 1.4944, 1.0558, 0.9965, \ldots\) rise to 1.4944, drop below 1, and then approach 1 from both sides.

Muller’s Method animation for f(x) = x³ - 3x + 2 starting from p₂ = 2.0: the parabolas never reach the x-axis, so each new iterate is the parabola’s vertex (the real part of the complex root), and the iterates converge to the double root at p = 1; each frame is zoomed to the current points, and an inset shows the vertex just above the x-axis




Case 2 — Convergent, \(f(x) = \sin(x^2 - 2)(x^2 - 2)\), double root at \(p = \sqrt{2}\)
Behavior: The method converges to the double root \(p = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.4142\) starting from \(p_2 = 1.0\). The function has a double root where \(x^2 - 2 = 0\) since both factors vanish simultaneously, and Muller’s method locates it efficiently despite the flat tangent at the root. Each frame is zoomed to the current points, and the inset shows the step from \(p_2\) to the parabola’s axis crossing (open red circle), which is the next iterate; the step shrinks from 0.25 to \(3.6 \times 10^{-5}\) over the nine frames.

Case 3 — Convergent, \(f(x) = x^6 - 7x^4 + 15x^2 - 9\), double root at \(p = \sqrt{3}\)
Behavior: The function factors as \((x^2-1)(x^2-3)^2\), giving a double root at \(p = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.7321\). Starting from \(p_2 = 1.5\), Muller’s method converges to the double root. Newton’s method would converge linearly here; Muller’s method converges superlinearly, with order \(\approx 1.23\) at this double root (below the \(\approx 1.84\) it achieves at a simple root). Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Monte Carlo Integration
text:
Description
Monte Carlo integration approximates a definite integral \(I=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\), or an integral over a box in \(d\) dimensions, by random sampling instead of a fixed grid. The sample-mean estimator draws \(n\) independent points \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) uniformly from \([a,b]\), averages the function values and multiplies by the length of the interval (the volume of the box in \(d\) dimensions): \[
\hat I_n=(b-a)\,\hat f,\qquad \hat f=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i),\qquad
\text{error}\approx (b-a)\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{f^2}-\hat f^{\,2}}{n}},\quad \widehat{f^2}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i)^2 .
\] The estimate is the base times the “average height” of \(f\), which is the mean value theorem for integrals with the exact average replaced by a sample average.
The error is random. Its standard deviation, the standard error, is \((b-a)\,\sigma_f/\sqrt n\), where \(\sigma_f\) is the standard deviation of \(f\) over the interval, so the error falls like \(O(1/\sqrt n)\): a hundred times as many points buys one more correct digit. That rate does not depend on the dimension, whereas a product midpoint rule with \(n\) points in \(d\) dimensions has error \(O(n^{-2/d})\) for smooth integrands; for \(d>4\) the Monte Carlo rate is the faster one. Mathews’ module uses only the sample-mean estimator; the hit-or-miss variant, which counts the random points that land under the graph, is on the Monte Carlo Pi page. Every run gives a different estimate, so each single-run estimate on this page is one sample run, made with NumPy’s default_rng generator (PCG64) and the seed stated, and is quoted with its estimated standard error; the repeat studies give their seeds too, and Mathews’ own runs are quoted as his runs. A point in \(d\) dimensions takes \(d\) consecutive numbers from the stream (random((n, d))), one for each coordinate in the order \(x, y, z, u, w\), which is the order of the intervals in the box (outermost integral sign first), each scaled to that coordinate’s interval.

Animations

Case 1 — Example 3, \(\int_0^4\sqrt x\,dx=\tfrac{16}{3}\), \(n=2\) to \(10\,000\) (seed 3)
Behavior: The top panel puts each sampled point on the graph of \(\sqrt x\), newest points in red, under the rectangle of base 4 whose height is the mean of the sampled values \(f(x_i)\); its area is the estimate, and its height settles toward the exact average height \(\tfrac43\). In this run the estimate is \(6.846\) at \(n=2\), \(5.692\) at \(n=10\), \(5.444\pm0.05756\) at \(n=1000\) (error \(+0.1111\), 1.93 estimated standard errors) and \(5.343\pm0.01895\) at \(n=10\,000\) (error \(+0.009405\), 0.50 estimated standard errors). At \(n=2\) the two points happen to lie close together, so formula (4) gives an estimated error of only \(0.03967\) against a true standard deviation of \(1.333\), and the actual error, \(+1.513\), is 38 estimated standard errors: with very few points the error estimate is unreliable. From \(n=100\) on, the estimated standard error stays within 5.3% of the true value \(1.886/\sqrt n\), so in the bottom panel it runs along the dashed line of slope \(-\tfrac12\), and from \(n=10\) on the actual error is never more than 2.24 estimated standard errors (the largest is 2.23, at \(n=726\)).

title: Monte Carlo Integration
section: Background: The Average Value of a Function
text:
Background: The Average Value of a Function






TipTheorem — Mean Value Theorem for Integrals



If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), there is a number \(c\) with \(a<c<b\) such that \[
\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=f(c),
\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=(b-a)\,f(c).
\tag{1}
\]


The area under the curve equals the area of a rectangle with base \(b-a\) and height \(f(c)\), the average height of \(f\). Monte Carlo integration estimates that average height from random samples.

Example 1 — Average height of \(f(x)=\sin x+\tfrac13\sin 3x\) on \([0,\pi]\)
Find \(c\) so that \(\int_0^\pi f(x)\,dx=(\pi-0)\,f(c)\).
Step 1: Integrate. An antiderivative is \(-\cos x-\tfrac19\cos 3x\), so \[
\int_0^\pi\left(\sin x+\tfrac13\sin 3x\right)dx=\left(1+\tfrac19\right)-\left(-1-\tfrac19\right)=\frac{20}{9}\approx 2.222222.
\]
Step 2: The average height is \[
f(c)=\frac{1}{\pi}\cdot\frac{20}{9}=\frac{20}{9\pi}\approx 0.707355.
\]
Step 3: Solve \(\sin c+\tfrac13\sin 3c=\dfrac{20}{9\pi}\) on \((0,\pi)\). Since \(f'(x)=\cos x+\cos 3x=2\cos x\cos 2x\), the graph of \(f\) has two humps of height \(f(\pi/4)=f(3\pi/4)=2\sqrt2/3\approx0.9428\) with a dip to \(f(\pi/2)=2/3\) between them, so the horizontal line at height \(0.707355\) crosses it four times: \[
c\approx 0.405695,\qquad c\approx 1.364322,\qquad c\approx 1.777271,\qquad c\approx 2.735898 .
\] Because \(f(\pi-x)=f(x)\), the roots come in pairs \(c\) and \(\pi-c\). Mathews’ solution reports one of them, \(c=1.36432\).
Verification: each root satisfies \(f(c)-20/(9\pi)=0\) to the 30-digit working precision of the root finder, and \(\pi\,f(c)=\pi\cdot\dfrac{20}{9\pi}=\dfrac{20}{9}\). \(\checkmark\)

title: Monte Carlo Integration
text:
The Composite Midpoint Rule
The deterministic method to compare against samples \(f\) at the centres of equal subintervals instead of at random points.






TipTheorem — Composite Midpoint Rule



Divide \([a,b]\) into \(n\) subintervals of width \(h=(b-a)/n\) with midpoints \(x_i=a+\left(i-\tfrac12\right)h\), \(i=1,\dots,n\). Then \[
M(f,h)=h\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i)=(b-a)\,\hat f,\qquad \hat f=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i).
\tag{2}
\] If \(f''\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), there is a \(\xi\in(a,b)\) with \[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-M(f,h)=\frac{(b-a)\,f''(\xi)}{24}\,h^2=O(h^2).
\]


The midpoint rule and the Monte Carlo estimate have the same form, \((b-a)\) times an average of function values; they differ only in where the points are placed.

Example 2 — Midpoint rule for \(\int_0^4\sqrt x\,dx\)
The exact value is \(\int_0^4\sqrt x\,dx=\tfrac23\,4^{3/2}=\tfrac{16}{3}\approx5.333333\).
Step 1: With \(n=10\), \(h=0.4\) and the midpoints are \(0.2,0.6,\dots,3.8\): \[
M=0.4\left(\sqrt{0.2}+\sqrt{0.6}+\cdots+\sqrt{3.8}\right)\approx 5.3470707 .
\]

title: Monte Carlo Integration
section: Monte Carlo Integration in One Variable
text:
Monte Carlo Integration in One Variable
The name “Monte Carlo” was coined by Nicholas Metropolis, inspired by Stanislaw Ulam, after the gambling centre, because statistical simulation resembles games of chance.






ImportantAlgorithm — Monte Carlo integration in one variable



To approximate \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\):

Pick \(n\) independent points \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) uniformly distributed in \([a,b]\).
Compute the average value \(\hat f=\dfrac1n\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i)\).
Approximate the integral by \[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\approx(b-a)\,\hat f.
\tag{3}
\]
Estimate the error by \[
\text{error}\approx(b-a)\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{f^2}-\hat f^{\,2}}{n}},\qquad \widehat{f^2}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i)^2.
\tag{4}
\]









TipTheorem — Mean and spread of the estimate (general result)



Let \(\mu_f=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f\,dx\) and \(\sigma_f^2=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f^2\,dx-\mu_f^2\) be the mean and variance of \(f(X)\) for \(X\) uniform on \([a,b]\), and suppose \(\sigma_f\) is finite. Then the estimate \(\hat I_n=(b-a)\hat f\) satisfies \[
\mathbb E\big[\hat I_n\big]=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx,
\qquad
\operatorname{SD}\big[\hat I_n\big]=\frac{(b-a)\,\sigma_f}{\sqrt n}.
\tag{5}
\] By the central limit theorem the error \(\hat I_n-I\) is approximately normal for large \(n\), so it lies within one standard error about 68% of the time and within two about 95% of the time.


Formula (4) is the standard error (5) with \(\sigma_f\) replaced by its sample estimate. It is an estimate of the typical size of the error, not a bound: the actual error is sometimes larger.

Example 3 — Monte Carlo for \(\int_0^4\sqrt x\,dx\)
Step 1: The exact value is \(I=\tfrac{16}{3}\approx5.333333\), so \(\mu_f=\tfrac{16/3}{4}=\tfrac43\).
Step 2: The spread of \(f\). Since \(\frac14\int_0^4 x\,dx=2\), \[
\sigma_f^2=2-\left(\tfrac43\right)^2=\tfrac29,\qquad
\operatorname{SD}\big[\hat I_n\big]=\frac{4\sqrt{2/9}}{\sqrt n}=\frac{4\sqrt2}{3\sqrt n}\approx\frac{1.885618}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Step 3: One sample run (seed 2026). The first ten points drawn from \([0,4]\) are (rounded to four decimals) \[
0.7157,\ 2.5597,\ 1.8691,\ 1.4820,\ 1.4197,\ 3.1621,\ 3.6206,\ 0.7094,\ 2.6111,\ 1.1932,
\] with square roots summing to \(13.453433\). So \[
\hat f=\frac{13.453433}{10}=1.345343,\qquad \hat I_{10}=4\times1.345343=5.381373,
\] and formula (4) gives an estimated error of \(0.445971\).

title: Monte Carlo Integration
text:
Double Integrals
For a function of two variables on the rectangle \([a,b]\times[c,d]\), pick \(n\) independent uniform points \((x_i,y_i)\) in the rectangle and use the area \((b-a)(d-c)\) in place of the length: \[
\int_a^b\!\!\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx\approx(b-a)(d-c)\,\hat f,
\qquad
\text{error}\approx(b-a)(d-c)\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{f^2}-\hat f^{\,2}}{n}},
\tag{6}
\] with \(\hat f=\frac1n\sum f(x_i,y_i)\) and \(\widehat{f^2}=\frac1n\sum f(x_i,y_i)^2\).

Example 6 — \(\displaystyle\int_0^{5/4}\!\!\int_0^{5/4}\left(4-x^2-y^2\right)dy\,dx\)
Step 1: The exact value, by iterated integration: \[
\int_0^{5/4}\left(4-x^2-y^2\right)dy=\frac{835}{192}-\frac54x^2,
\qquad
\int_0^{5/4}\left(\frac{835}{192}-\frac54x^2\right)dx=\frac{1775}{384}\approx4.622396 .
\]
Step 2: The area is \(\tfrac{25}{16}\), so \(\mu_f=\tfrac{1775/384}{25/16}=\tfrac{71}{24}\approx2.958333\). Integrating \(f^2\) gives \(\tfrac{5291}{576}\) for its mean, hence \[
\sigma_f^2=\frac{5291}{576}-\left(\frac{71}{24}\right)^2=\frac{125}{288}\approx0.434028,
\qquad
\operatorname{SD}\big[\hat I_n\big]=\frac{25}{16}\sqrt{\frac{125}{288}}\Big/\sqrt n\approx\frac{1.029387}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Step 3: One run (seed 6) with \(n=10000\) points gives \(\hat f=2.967441\) and \(\widehat{f^2}=9.236689\), so \[
\hat I=\frac{25}{16}\times2.967441=4.636626,\qquad
\text{error}\approx\frac{25}{16}\sqrt{\frac{9.236689-2.967441^2}{10000}}=0.010258 .
\]

title: Monte Carlo Integration
text:
Multiple Integrals
The same recipe works in any number of dimensions. For \(f(\mathbf X)\) on the box \(V=[a_1,b_1]\times[a_2,b_2]\times\cdots\times[a_d,b_d]\), pick \(n\) independent uniform points \(\mathbf X_1,\dots,\mathbf X_n\) in \(V\): \[
\int\!\!\cdots\!\!\int_V f(\mathbf X)\,dV\approx(b_1-a_1)(b_2-a_2)\cdots(b_d-a_d)\,\hat f,
\qquad
\text{error}\approx(b_1-a_1)\cdots(b_d-a_d)\sqrt{\frac{\widehat{f^2}-\hat f^{\,2}}{n}} .
\tag{7}
\]






TipComparison of rates (general result)



A product midpoint rule with \(m\) points per axis uses \(n=m^d\) points and, for smooth \(f\), has error \(O(m^{-2})=O(n^{-2/d})\). The Monte Carlo standard error is \(O(n^{-1/2})\) in every dimension. The two rates are equal at \(d=4\), and \[
n^{-1/2}<n^{-2/d}\quad\text{for } d>4,
\] so for quintuple and higher integrals Monte Carlo has the faster rate. The constants still matter: the rate says which method wins for large enough \(n\), not for every \(n\).

title: Monte Carlo Integration
text:
Practical Notes

The error is set by \(\sigma_f\) and \(n\). Halving the standard error needs four times as many points. In Example 3, a standard error of \(0.01\) needs \(n\approx(1.885618/0.01)^2\approx35600\) points. A flatter integrand (smaller \(\sigma_f\), as in Example 7 against Example 6) gives a smaller error for the same \(n\).
The error estimate is random too. Formula (4) uses the same samples as the estimate. With very few points it can be far from the true standard deviation; in Example 3 with \(n=10\) only 63.7% of runs fell within one estimated error, against the nominal 68%.
Report the run. Quote the generator, seed and \(n\) with any Monte Carlo number, together with its estimated error, so the run can be reproduced and its uncertainty judged. Two runs with different seeds will not agree to more digits than the standard error allows.
Low dimensions favour deterministic rules. In one variable, the 10-point midpoint rule in Example 2 had error \(0.0137\), while 10-point Monte Carlo in Example 3 has RMS error \(0.593\). Monte Carlo becomes competitive as the dimension grows (Example 14) or when the integrand is too rough for the error formulas of deterministic rules.
\(n\) or \(n-1\). Formula (4) divides the sample variance by \(n\); dividing by \(n-1\) gives the unbiased sample variance. The two estimates differ by the factor \(\sqrt{n/(n-1)}\), which is negligible except for very small \(n\).

title: Midpoint Rule
text:
Description
The midpoint rule approximates a definite integral \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) by a sum of rectangles, like a Riemann sum, but it takes each rectangle’s height from \(f\) at the midpoint of its subinterval instead of at an endpoint. For a uniform partition of \([a,b]\) into \(n\) pieces with \(\Delta x=(b-a)/n\), the composite midpoint approximation is
\[
M_n = \Delta x \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} f\!\left(a + \left(i+\tfrac12\right)\Delta x\right).
\]
Each subinterval contributes a rectangle centered at its midpoint sample, the red dots in the animation.
As Riemann sums, the \(M_n\) converge to the integral for every \(f\) Riemann integrable on \([a,b]\). The error formula below needs more: \(f\) must be twice continuously differentiable on \([a,b]\), \(f\in C^2[a,b]\).
Each rectangle has the same area as the region under the tangent line to \(f\) at its midpoint, so the rule is exact for every linear \(f\), and the first term it misses involves \(f''\). The general result, as Mathews states it: if \(f\in C^2[a,b]\), there is a \(c\) with \(a<c<b\) such that
\[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx - M_n = \frac{(b-a)\,f''(c)}{24}\,\Delta x^2 .
\]
The error is therefore \(O(\Delta x^2)\), and halving \(\Delta x\) typically divides it by about 4. Under the same hypothesis the Trapezoidal Rule’s error is \(-(b-a)f''(c)\,\Delta x^2/12\), with its own \(c\), so when \(f'(a)\ne f'(b)\) the midpoint error is, for small \(\Delta x\), about half the trapezoidal error, of opposite sign. Left- and right-endpoint sums are in general only first order, \(O(\Delta x)\).
Case 1 shows what happens when the hypothesis fails. Its integrand \(f(x)=e^{-x}\sin(8x^{2/3})+1\) has \(f'\) unbounded at \(x=0\), so \(f\notin C^2[0,2]\), and the error shrinks only like \(\Delta x^{5/3}\): in the table below, halving \(\Delta x\) divides it by 2.86, 3.09 and then 3.14, approaching \(2^{5/3}\approx 3.17\), not 4. For \(n\) from 40 to 120 the midpoint error is also about \(-0.37\) times the trapezoidal error, not \(-1/2\).

In Case 1, with two subintervals both samples, at \(x=0.5\) and \(x=1.5\), fall near the two dips of \(f\), and \(M_2\approx 1.231\) is 0.79 below \(I\); with four, \(M_4\approx 2.0111\) happens to be closer to \(I\) than every frame from 6 to 28 sample points.
The midpoint rule is the one-point Gauss-Legendre rule applied on each subinterval and the simplest open Newton-Cotes formula; with \(T_n\) the trapezoidal sum, \(S_{2n}=(2M_n+T_n)/3\) is Simpson’s Rule on \(2n\) subintervals, the combination in which the two leading errors cancel for smooth \(f\).
