title: Damped Newton with Acceleration (Madsen-Reid Method)
text: ← Numerical Methods

title: Damped Newton with Acceleration (Madsen-Reid Method)
text:
Description
The Madsen-Reid method (Madsen and Reid 1975) is a robust, globally convergent Newton-based algorithm for finding all roots of a real-coefficient polynomial. This page follows Madsen’s method as implemented by Vestermark: the scripts port the iteration of newton_real (Newton_Real.cpp, Future Team ApS, 2002) with one correction (Stage 2, below), and the description below is of that implementation. It combines three complementary ideas into a single, practical solver:

1. Lengthened steps at multiple roots
Standard Newton-Raphson degrades to linear convergence at a root of multiplicity \(m > 1\) because \(f'(x^*) = 0\): near the root \(f/f' \approx (x-x^*)/m\), so each Newton step covers only \(1/m\) of the remaining distance and the error shrinks by the factor \((m-1)/m\) per step. Madsen-Reid counters this by taking multiple steps in the same direction: in Stage 1 (below), when the Newton point \(z - \Delta z\) does not increase \(|f|^2\), it also tries \(z - 2\Delta z,\ z - 3\Delta z, \dots\) (up to \(z - (n+1)\,\Delta z\) for a polynomial of degree \(n\)), stops at the first trial that does not lower \(|f|^2\), and keeps the trial before it. Near a root of multiplicity \(m\) that point is \(z - m\,\Delta z\), the multiplicity-corrected Newton step, so the convergence to a multiple root is quadratic while the iteration stays in Stage 1 (in Case 2, until rounding error takes over). Only Stage 1 searches, though: Stage 2 takes plain Newton steps, which are linear at a multiple root. Near a double root the two sides of the stage test (below) tend to equality, so whether a run stays in Stage 1 depends on the run. Case 2 stays in Stage 1 throughout. Started at \(x_0 = -0.7\) instead of 4, the same polynomial takes a plain Newton step past the root to \(x_1 \approx 1.7556\), then one Stage-2 step to \(x_2 \approx 1.4123\) (the error falls from 0.76 to 0.41). The stage test then fails (its left side is 1.24 times its right side), and three lengthened Stage-1 steps with \(k = 2\) take the error to \(2.3 \times 10^{-2}\), \(9.1 \times 10^{-5}\) and \(1.4 \times 10^{-9}\), where the computed \(|f|^2\) is exactly 0 and the run stops after 5 steps.
In general, at a simple root (\(f'(x^*) \neq 0\)) the trial point \(z - 2\Delta z\) lands about as far from the root as \(z\), on the other side, so near the root the search keeps \(k = 1\), no halving is needed, and the steps are plain Newton steps, which converge quadratically. Case 1 shows it: from step 3 on, each error divided by the square of the one before is 0.67, 0.74 and 0.74, approaching \(P''(x^*)/\bigl(2P'(x^*)\bigr) \approx 0.742\).
A separate safeguard limits the Newton step to length \(r_0\), which is reset after each Newton step to five times that step’s length before the cap:
\[r_0 \leftarrow 5\,|\Delta z|\]
A Newton step longer than \(r_0\) is cut to length \(r_0\) and rotated by \(53.13°\) by alterdirection (below); a rotation would take Cases 1 and 2 off the real axis, and their scripts stop with an error if one occurs. No Newton step in the three animations is longer than \(r_0\), so the cap never acts.


2. Safety — the two stages
Away from the saddle-point and rounding-error branches described below, every step moves from \(z\) to one of these points, where \(n\) is the polynomial’s degree and \(\Delta z\) is the Newton step, cut and rotated if it is longer than \(r_0\):
\[
\Delta z = \frac{f(z)}{f'(z)}, \qquad z - k\,\Delta z \ \ (k = 1, 2, \dots, n + 1), \qquad z - \tfrac12\,\Delta z, \qquad z - \tfrac{0.6 + 0.8i}{8}\,\Delta z
\]
The second are the plain (\(k = 1\)) and lengthened steps, the third is the halved step and the fourth is the rotated step; Stage 2 takes only \(k = 1\).
Each iteration computes the Newton step \(\Delta z = f(z)/f'(z)\), caps it at \(r_0\), and takes it in one of two stages:

Stage 1 (checked steps) compares \(|f|^2\) at trial points along the step. If \(z - \Delta z\) does not increase \(|f|^2\), the lengthening search above runs. If it does, the step is halved, and each halving is kept only while it lowers \(|f|^2\) below the previous trial. If two halvings both help, the iterate is taken to be near a saddle point: alterdirection rotates the step by \(53.13°\) and halves it once more (multiplication by \(0.5\,(0.6 + 0.8i)\)), and that point is accepted. The rotation makes the step complex, so it can only be shown in Case 3.
Stage 2 (plain Newton) takes \(z - \Delta z\) with no trial points, and ends the run once \(|f(z)|\) is no larger than Adams’ bound on the rounding error of \(f(z)\). It is used only when the previous step was a plain Newton step (the Stage-1 search left it unchanged) and the test \(2\,|f(z_k)|\,|w| \le |f'(z_k)|^2\,|z_{k-1} - z_k|\) passes. Here \(w = f'(z_{k-1}) - f'(z_k)\), so \(w/(z_{k-1} - z_k)\) estimates \(f''\) and the test estimates Kantorovich’s condition \(2|f|\,|f''| \le |f'|^2\) for Newton’s method to converge. The scripts follow newton_real except in one line: after each step they store the derivative \(f'(z_{k-1})\) for \(w\), as Madsen and Reid’s test (2.9) requires (Madsen and Reid 1975) and the reference’s own initial value \(f'(0)\) implies, where newton_real stores \(f(z_{k-1})\).

Two further branches handle a true saddle point (\(f'(z) = 0\): the previous step is rotated by \(53.13°\) and lengthened 5 times) and the rounding-error domain (when a Newton step shorter than \(2^{-26}|z|\) does not lower \(|f|^2\), it is retried from its starting point, rotated and halved). Neither is reached in the three animations.
The two-stage structure is designed to make \(|f(z)|^2\) decrease at every step, without requiring a full line search. It is not a guarantee: each halving is compared with the previous trial rather than with \(|f(z_k)|^2\), the rotated step is accepted without a check, and Stage-2 steps are not checked at all. In all three animations below \(|f|^2\) does decrease at every step.


3. Efficiency — minimizing function evaluations
Higher-order methods (Halley’s, Householder’s) achieve cubic or higher convergence but require evaluating \(f''\), \(f'''\), etc. Madsen-Reid achieves rapid convergence using only \(f\) and \(f'\) — the same derivatives as plain Newton, plus a few extra evaluations of \(f\) at the trial points — while the acceleration mechanism and dual-stage control make it far more reliable than unguarded Newton on difficult polynomials.
After each root is found, the polynomial is deflated (divided out), reducing the degree by 1 (real root) or 2 (complex conjugate pair), until the remaining linear or quadratic factor is solved analytically.

Note on generalization: Only part of this structure carries over to equations that are not polynomials. For a real equation \(f(x) = 0\), the descent test on \(|f|^2\), the lengthening and halving of the Newton step and the Kantorovich-style switch to plain Newton need only \(f\) and \(f'\) in real arithmetic; Cases 1 and 2 never leave the real axis. The lengthening bound \(n + 1\) and Adams’ stopping bound come from the polynomial’s degree and coefficients, so a general \(f\) needs its own. The \(53.13°\) rotation multiplies the step by the complex number \(0.6 + 0.8i\), so it needs an \(f\) that can be evaluated off the real axis, as a polynomial can (Case 3 uses it); it has no counterpart for a real equation on the real axis, and the method defines none for a system \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}\).

Newton-Raphson is the step every stage starts from, Accelerated and Modified Newton-Raphson restores quadratic convergence at a multiple root, in one of its two forms by multiplying the step by a known multiplicity \(m\) that the lengthening search here finds for itself, Halley’s Method uses \(f''\) to converge cubically at simple roots, and the Lin-Bairstow Method and Graeffe’s Method also find all the roots of a polynomial.

title: Damped Newton with Acceleration (Madsen-Reid Method)
text:
Animations
Each animation shows the iteration path of the Madsen-Reid method. Blue segments are plain Newton steps \(z - \Delta z\); green segments are lengthened steps \(z - k\,\Delta z\) with \(k \ge 2\), drawn as the tangent line down to the Newton point and then along the axis; orange segments are halved or rotated steps. The label of the current point names the stage of the step that reached it. Cases 1 and 2 start from their own \(x_0\) with \(r_0 = 5|x_0|\) rather than from the reference’s start-point rule; Case 3 starts where the reference does. In Case 3, star markers show the exact roots.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Simple root, \(P(x) = x^3 - 3x - 1\), \(x_0 = 3.0\)
Behavior: Three simple real roots exist. Starting from \(x_0 = 3.0\), the doubled step reduces \(|P|^2\) more than the Newton step does, and the tripled step does not (\(|P|^2\) = 17.3, 3.17 and 8.73 for \(\Delta x\), \(2\Delta x\) and \(3\Delta x\)), so the first move is the lengthened step \(x_1 = x_0 - 2\Delta x \approx 1.5833\) (green), which passes the root. Every later step is a plain Newton step (blue): step 2 is checked in Stage 1, and steps 3 to 6 are Stage-2 steps. No step is halved. Because \(P'(x^*) \neq 0\), the convergence to the root \(x^* \approx 1.8794\) is quadratic: the error falls \(9.8 \times 10^{-2}\), \(6.4 \times 10^{-3}\), \(3.0 \times 10^{-5}\), \(6.7 \times 10^{-10}\) over steps 2 to 5, and \(x_6\) equals \(x^*\) to double precision; there \(|P|\) is below Adams’ bound and the run stops.
Julia source



Madsen-Reid tangent-line animation on P(x)=x³−3x−1: a doubled first step from x₀=3.0 to x₁≈1.5833, then plain Newton steps, Stage 2 from step 3 on, converging quadratically to the simple root near x≈1.8794




Case 2 — Double root, \(P(x) = (x-1)^2(x+2)\), \(x_0 = 4.0\)
Behavior: \(P(x)\) has a double root at \(x^* = 1\) where \(P'(x^*) = 0\). Standard Newton-Raphson converges only linearly here: from \(x_0 = 4\) its error roughly halves each step and is still \(3.4 \times 10^{-4}\) after 14 steps. Madsen-Reid takes a lengthened step every time (all green, all in Stage 1: the run starts in Stage 1, and a lengthened step never leads to Stage 2): \(3\Delta x\) to \(x_1 = 0.4\), past the root, then \(2\Delta x\), the multiplicity-corrected step for \(m = 2\), four times. The errors \(8.6 \times 10^{-2}\), \(1.2 \times 10^{-3}\), \(2.3 \times 10^{-7}\) of \(x_2\) to \(x_4\) fall quadratically. The fifth step reaches \(x_5 \approx 0.99999999952\) (error \(4.8 \times 10^{-10}\)), where rounding makes the computed \(|P(x_5)|^2\) exactly 0 (its true value is about \(4.8 \times 10^{-37}\)), so the run stops. No step is halved. From \(x_2\) on, the window zooms in on each new step, because the steps shrink from \(0.69\) to \(2.3 \times 10^{-7}\) in \(x\); each zoomed frame shows the tangent reaching the axis halfway along the step, then the second \(\Delta x\) along the axis.
Julia source



Madsen-Reid animation on P(x)=(x−1)²(x+2): five lengthened steps (3Δx, then 2Δx four times) converging from x₀=4.0 to the double root at x=1, quadratically until rounding ends the run at x₅, the view zooming in on each step from x₂ on




Case 3 — Complex conjugate roots, \(P(z) = z^2 + 4\), \(z_0 = 1 + 0i\)
Behavior: The roots are \(z^* = \pm 2i\) — there are no real roots. The reference solves a quadratic in closed form, so this case runs its iteration loop on \(z^2 + 4\) directly, from the reference’s own start \(z_0 = 1\) with \(r_0 = 5\). The full Newton step to \(-1.5\) increases \(|P|^2\) (39.1 against 25), and one halving reaches \(z_1 = -0.25\) (a second halving, to \(0.375\), does not help). At \(z_1\) the full step to \(7.875\) increases \(|P|^2\) again, and two halvings both help (to \(3.8125\), then \(1.78125\)), so alterdirection rotates the step and halves it once more: \(z_2 = 0.359375 + 0.8125i\), off the real axis. Orange segments are the halved steps 1 and 3 and the rotated step 2. Step 4 is a plain Newton step checked in Stage 1, and steps 5 to 8 are Stage-2 plain Newton steps (blue), converging quadratically to \(z^* = +2i\); the run stops at \(z_8\), where \(|P| \approx 3.2 \times 10^{-30}\) is below Adams’ bound. No lengthened step occurs. The path is a polyline. This case illustrates how the algorithm handles polynomials with no real roots starting from a real initial guess.

Madsen-Reid animation in the complex plane on P(z)=z²+4: from z₀=1 a halved step, then a step rotated off the real axis after two helpful halvings, a further halved step, and plain Newton steps converging to the root at z=+2i

title: LU Factorization
text:
Background
LU factorization rewrites a matrix as a product of triangular matrices so that solving linear systems is reduced to forward and back substitution.






NoteDefinition - LU Factorization



For a nonsingular matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), an LU factorization is
\[
A = LU,
\]
where \(L\) is lower triangular and \(U\) is upper triangular.
In the Doolittle form, \(L\) has unit diagonal:
\[
\ell_{11}=\ell_{22}=\cdots=\ell_{nn}=1.
\]


The factorization is useful because once \(A=LU\) is known, each solve \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) needs only two triangular solves:
\[
L\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{b},\qquad U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}.
\tag{1}
\]






TipTheorem - LU without Pivoting



If Gaussian elimination can be performed without row exchanges (equivalently, each pivot is nonzero), then \(A\) admits a Doolittle factorization \(A=LU\).



Doolittle Recurrence
For \(k=1,2,\ldots,n\):
\[
u_{kj}=a_{kj}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}\ell_{ks}u_{sj},\qquad j=k,\ldots,n,
\tag{2}
\]
\[
\ell_{ik}=\frac{a_{ik}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}\ell_{is}u_{sk}}{u_{kk}},\qquad i=k+1,\ldots,n,
\tag{3}
\]
with \(\ell_{kk}=1\). Breakdown occurs when \(u_{kk}=0\).

title: LU Factorization
text:
Example 1 - Doolittle Factorization (No Pivoting)
From the source module, use
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
4 & 2 & 3\\
-3 & 1 & 4\\
2 & 4 & 5
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 1: First pivot \(u_{11}=4\), then
\[
\ell_{21}=-\frac{3}{4},\qquad \ell_{31}=\frac12.
\]
Step 2: Second-row entries of \(U\):
\[
u_{22}=1-\left(-\frac34\right)2=\frac52,
\qquad
u_{23}=4-\left(-\frac34\right)3=\frac{25}{4}.
\]
Step 3: Third multiplier and last pivot:
\[
\ell_{32}=\frac{4-(\frac12)2}{\frac52}=\frac65,
\qquad
u_{33}=5-\left(\frac12\right)3-\left(\frac65\right)\left(\frac{25}{4}\right)=-4.
\]
Hence
\[
L=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
-\frac34 & 1 & 0\\
\frac12 & \frac65 & 1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
U=
\begin{pmatrix}
4 & 2 & 3\\
0 & \frac52 & \frac{25}{4}\\
0 & 0 & -4
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Verification:



Row of \(LU\)
Computation
Result




1
\((1,0,0)U\)
\((4,2,3)\) \(\checkmark\)


2
\((-\tfrac34,1,0)U\)
\((-3,1,4)\) \(\checkmark\)


3
\((\tfrac12,\tfrac65,1)U\)
\((2,4,5)\) \(\checkmark\)



So \(LU=A\).

title: LU Factorization
section: Example 2 - Nonsingular Matrix That Fails Without Pivoting
text:
Example 2 - Nonsingular Matrix That Fails Without Pivoting
From the source module, consider
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2 & 6\\
4 & 8 & -1\\
-2 & 3 & 5
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The matrix is nonsingular (\(\det(A)=175\neq0\)), but no-pivot Doolittle breaks:
\[
u_{22}=8-\left(\frac{4}{1}\right)2=0.
\]
So nonsingularity alone does not guarantee an LU factorization without pivoting.
If we permute rows (equivalently, use a permutation matrix \(P\)), one valid reordered matrix is
\[
B=PA=
\begin{pmatrix}
4 & 8 & -1\\
-2 & 3 & 5\\
1 & 2 & 6
\end{pmatrix},
\]
which factors as
\[
L=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
-\frac12 & 1 & 0\\
\frac14 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
U=
\begin{pmatrix}
4 & 8 & -1\\
0 & 7 & \frac92\\
0 & 0 & \frac{25}{4}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Verification: \(LU=B=PA\).






TipTheorem - PA = LU with Pivoting



For every nonsingular matrix \(A\), there exists a permutation matrix \(P\) such that
\[
PA=LU.
\tag{4}
\]
Then solving \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) is equivalent to
\[
L\mathbf{y}=P\mathbf{b},\qquad U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}.
\tag{5}
\]

title: LU Factorization
section: Example 3 - Solving a System with PA = LU
text:
Example 3 - Solving a System with PA = LU
From the source module:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
2 & 4 & 1\\
4 & -10 & 2\\
1 & 2 & 4
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}5\\-8\\13\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Here no row swaps are needed, so \(P=I\). The LU factors are
\[
L=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
2 & 1 & 0\\
\frac12 & 0 & 1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
U=
\begin{pmatrix}
2 & 4 & 1\\
0 & -18 & 0\\
0 & 0 & \frac72
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 1: Solve \(L\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{b}\):
\[
y_1=5,
\qquad
2y_1+y_2=-8\Rightarrow y_2=-18,
\qquad
\frac12y_1+y_3=13\Rightarrow y_3=\frac{21}{2}.
\]
Step 2: Solve \(U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}\):
\[
\frac72x_3=\frac{21}{2}\Rightarrow x_3=3,
\qquad
-18x_2=-18\Rightarrow x_2=1,
\qquad
2x_1+4(1)+3=5\Rightarrow x_1=-1.
\]
The solution is
\[
\mathbf{x}=(-1,1,3)^T.
\]

title: LU Factorization
text:
Application - Least-Squares Polynomial Fitting
Given data \((x_i,y_i)\), the least-squares polynomial
\[
p_m(x)=c_1+c_2x+\cdots+c_{m+1}x^m
\]
is found from the normal equations
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{m+1} c_j\left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^{j+k-2}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^{k-1} y_i,
\qquad k=1,2,\ldots,m+1.
\tag{6}
\]
This is a linear system \(A\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{b}\) solved efficiently by LU.

title: Linear Programming-Simplex Method
text:
Linear Programming Background
Linear programming seeks to optimize a linear objective over a feasible region defined by linear inequalities. In standard maximization form:
\[
\text{maximize } f(\mathbf{x}) = c_1x_1 + c_2x_2 + \cdots + c_nx_n = \mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{x},
\tag{1}
\]
subject to
\[
A\mathbf{x} \le \mathbf{b}, \qquad \mathbf{x} \ge \mathbf{0}.
\tag{2}
\]






NoteDefinition - Convex Polytope



The feasible set \[
\mathcal{R} = \{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n : A\mathbf{x} \le \mathbf{b},\ \mathbf{x}\ge \mathbf{0}\}
\] is a convex polytope (or a convex polygon in two variables).








TipTheorem - Vertex Optimality



If a linear program has an optimal solution and the feasible set is nonempty and bounded, then at least one optimal solution occurs at a vertex (extreme point) of the feasible polytope.


This is why both graphical methods (in 2D) and the simplex method focus on moving among vertices.

title: Linear Programming-Simplex Method
text:
Standard Form and Tableau
For constraints of the type \(A\mathbf{x}\le\mathbf{b}\) with \(\mathbf{b}\ge\mathbf{0}\), introduce slack variables \(\mathbf{s}\ge\mathbf{0}\):
\[
A\mathbf{x} + I\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{b}.
\tag{3}
\]
For a maximization objective \(f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{x}\), the augmented objective equation is
\[
z - \mathbf{c}^T\mathbf{x} = 0.
\tag{4}
\]
The initial simplex tableau is built from the coefficients of (3) and (4):
\[
\left[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
A & I & \mathbf{b} \\
\hline
-\mathbf{c}^T & \mathbf{0}^T & 0
\end{array}
\right].
\tag{5}
\]






ImportantPivot Rules (Simplex Method)



At each iteration:

Choose the entering variable from the most negative coefficient in the bottom row.
Choose the leaving row by the minimum-ratio test \(b_i/a_{ij}\) over rows with \(a_{ij}>0\).
Pivot to make the entering column a unit vector.
Stop when there are no negative coefficients in the objective row.

title: Linear Programming-Simplex Method
text:
Example 1 - Student Work-Hour Optimization
Ann works \(x\) hours and Carl works \(y\) hours per week. The constraints from the source are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
80 &\le 4x+2y,\\
y &\le x+4,\\
x &\le y+8,\\
x+y &\le 40,\\
x &\ge 0,\ y\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Equivalent form for computation:
\[
\begin{aligned}
2x+y &\ge 40,\\
y &\le x+4,\\
y &\ge x-8,\\
x+y &\le 40,\\
x,y &\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
The four feasible vertices are obtained by intersecting boundary lines:
\[
(12,16),\ (18,22),\ (24,16),\ (16,8).
\]

Example 1(a)
Maximize \[
f(x,y)=15x+17y.
\]
Evaluate at vertices:

\]

\]

\]
Since maximizing \(16(x+y)\) is equivalent to maximizing \(x+y\), and the active top boundary is \(x+y=40\), every feasible point on that boundary segment is optimal.
In particular,

title: Linear Programming-Simplex Method
text:
Example 2 - Simplex Tableau Computation
From the source, maximize
\[
f(x,y)=10x+20y
\]
subject to
\[
\begin{aligned}
2x+y &\le 30,\\
x+4y &\le 64,\\
5x+6y &\le 110,\\
x,y &\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Introduce slack variables \(s_1,s_2,s_3\ge 0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
2x+y+s_1 &= 30,\\
x+4y+s_2 &= 64,\\
5x+6y+s_3 &= 110,\\
z-10x-20y &= 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Step 1: Initial Tableau
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc|c}
& x & y & s_1 & s_2 & s_3 & b \\
\hline
R_1 & 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 30 \\
R_2 & 1 & 4 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 64 \\
R_3 & 5 & 6 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 110 \\
\hline
R_z & -10 & -20 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0
\end{array}
\]
Entering variable: \(y\) (most negative bottom-row coefficient \(-20\)).
Minimum-ratio test:
\[
\frac{30}{1}=30,\quad \frac{64}{4}=16,\quad \frac{110}{6}=\frac{55}{3}.
\]
Leaving row: \(R_2\) (minimum ratio \(16\)). Pivot element: \(4\).


Step 2: First Pivot
After pivoting on row \(2\), column \(y\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc|c}
& x & y & s_1 & s_2 & s_3 & b \\
\hline
R_1 & \tfrac{7}{4} & 0 & 1 & -\tfrac14 & 0 & 14 \\
R_2 & \tfrac14 & 1 & 0 & \tfrac14 & 0 & 16 \\
R_3 & \tfrac72 & 0 & 0 & -\tfrac32 & 1 & 14 \\
\hline
R_z & -5 & 0 & 0 & 5 & 0 & 320
\end{array}
\]
Entering variable: \(x\) (bottom-row coefficient \(-5\)).
Minimum-ratio test (positive \(x\) entries):
\[
\frac{14}{7/4}=8,\quad \frac{16}{1/4}=64,\quad \frac{14}{7/2}=4.
\]
Leaving row: \(R_3\). Pivot element: \(\tfrac72\).


Step 3: Second Pivot (Optimal Tableau)
Pivoting on row \(3\), column \(x\) gives:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc|c}
& x & y & s_1 & s_2 & s_3 & b \\
\hline
R_1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & \tfrac12 & -\tfrac12 & 7 \\
R_2 & 0 & 1 & 0 & \tfrac{5}{14} & -\tfrac{1}{14} & 15 \\
R_3 & 1 & 0 & 0 & -\tfrac37 & \tfrac27 & 4 \\
\hline
R_z & 0 & 0 & 0 & \tfrac{20}{7} & \tfrac{10}{7} & 340
\end{array}
\]
No negative coefficients remain in the objective row, so this is optimal.
The solution is
\[
x_1=x=4,\qquad x_2=y=15,\qquad z_{\max}=340.
\]

\(\le 30\) \(\checkmark\)

\(4+4(15)=64\)
\(\le 64\) \(\checkmark\)


\(5x+6y\le 110\)
\(5(4)+6(15)=110\)
\(\le 110\) \(\checkmark\)

\[

title: Legendre Polynomials
text:
Animations
Each animation below illustrates Legendre polynomials \(P_n(x)\) on \([-1,1]\). The first animation reveals \(P_0\) through \(P_5\) one per frame; the second shows the Legendre series partial sums converging to \(f(x) = e^{x}\cos(\pi x/2)\).
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Successive polynomials \(P_0, P_1, \ldots, P_5\)
Properties: Each \(P_n\) is orthogonal to all lower-degree Legendre polynomials on \([-1,1]\). \(P_n(1)=1\), \(P_n(-1)=(-1)^n\), and \(P_n\) has exactly \(n\) zeros in \((-1,1)\). They are computed by the recurrence \((n+1)P_{n+1} = (2n+1)xP_n - nP_{n-1}\).
Julia source



Legendre polynomials P_0 through P_5 added one per frame on the interval [-1, 1], showing their oscillatory character




Case 2 — Legendre series for \(f(x) = e^{x}\cos(\pi x/2)\)
Behavior: The partial sum \(S_N(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{N} c_n P_n(x)\) with \(c_n = \tfrac{2n+1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1} f(x)P_n(x)\,dx\) converges to \(f\) as \(N\to\infty\). This \(f\) is the function of Mathews’ Example 8(b); it is neither even nor odd, and every coefficient \(c_0, \ldots, c_8\) is nonzero, so each frame adds a new term. Because \(S_N\) minimises the integrated squared error rather than the maximum error, the max error need not fall at every step: it rises from 0.699 for \(S_0\) to 1.09 for \(S_1\), then falls with each added term to \(7.74\times 10^{-6}\) for \(S_8\).

title: Least Squares Lines
text:
Description
A least-squares line fits a straight line \(y = b + a x\) to \(n\) data points \((x_k, y_k)\), \(k = 1, \ldots, n\). It chooses the coefficients \(a\) and \(b\) that minimize the sum of the squared residuals, the vertical distances from the points to the line:
\[
E(a, b) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \bigl(b + a x_k - y_k\bigr)^2 .
\]
Setting \(\partial E/\partial a\) and \(\partial E/\partial b\) to zero gives two linear equations, the normal equations, whose solution is
\[
a = \frac{n \sum x_k y_k - \sum x_k \sum y_k}{n \sum x_k^2 - \bigl(\sum x_k\bigr)^2},
\qquad
b = \frac{1}{n}\Bigl(\sum y_k - a \sum x_k\Bigr),
\]
with every sum over \(k = 1, \ldots, n\). The second normal equation says that the line passes through the centroid \((\bar x, \bar y)\) of the points and that the residuals sum to zero. Mathews’ power fit \(y = a x^m\), with \(m\) fixed, is linear in its one coefficient, so least squares gives
\[
a = \frac{\sum x_k^m y_k}{\sum x_k^{2m}} .
\]
The case \(m = 1\) is a line through the origin (Case 3), and \(m = 3/2\) is Kepler’s third law \(T = a r^{3/2}\) (Case 4).
The formulas for \(a\) and \(b\) need at least two distinct \(x_k\): the denominator equals \(n \sum (x_k - \bar x)^2\), which is zero when all the \(x_k\) are equal. The model treats the \(x_k\) as exact and puts all the error in the \(y_k\).
The method is direct, with no convergence order: when the \(x_k\) are not all equal, \(E\) has a unique minimum, and the formulas give it exactly, up to rounding. In general the minimum is \(E = (1 - r^2) \sum (y_k - \bar y)^2\), where \(r\) is the correlation coefficient, so for \(y_k\) not all equal the line passes through every point only when \(|r| = 1\). Adding a point never lowers the minimum: in Case 1 it rises from 0 with two points to \(39/28 \approx 1.3929\) with seven, and the eighth point lands on that line.
The line depends on which variable is treated as dependent: fitting \(x\) as a function of \(y\) minimizes horizontal residuals and gives a different line. In general, if \(x = c y + d\) is the fit of \(x\) on \(y\), then \(a c = r^2\), so the lines coincide only for collinear points, as in the first frame of Case 2; for all eight points \(r^2 \approx 0.9873\). A constraint the data do not satisfy biases the fit: Case 3’s free line is \(y \approx 0.3571 + 1.4762 x\), and forcing it through the origin raises the residual sum of squares from \(0.4762\) to \(0.6863\). In Case 4, \(a\) is the average of the ratios \(T_k / r_k^{3/2}\) weighted by \(r_k^3\), so Mars carries 71% of the weight and Mercury about 1%.
Least Squares Polynomials fits polynomials of higher degree through a larger system of normal equations, and Nonlinear Curve Fitting fits exponential and power curves by fitting a least-squares line to the logarithms of the data.

Case 1 - Standard Least-Squares Line, \(y = b + a x\)
Behavior: The unconstrained fit minimizes vertical residuals to a straight line. With all eight points the fit is \(a = -45/28 \approx -1.6071\) and \(b = 121/14 \approx 8.6429\). The eighth point \((6, -1)\) lies exactly on the seven-point line, so the last two frames show the same fit.

title: Lagrange Polynomial Interpolation and Approximation
text:
Description
Lagrange interpolation solves this problem: given \(n+1\) points \((x_i, y_i)\) with distinct nodes \(x_i\), find the polynomial of degree at most \(n\) that passes through all of them. That polynomial exists and is unique, and when \(y_i = f(x_i)\) it is used to approximate \(f\). Given nodes \((x_i, y_i)\), the interpolation polynomial is
\[
P_n(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n} y_i L_i(x), \qquad
L_i(x)=\prod_{j\ne i} \frac{x-x_j}{x_i-x_j}.
\]
Each \(L_i\) is 1 at \(x_i\) and 0 at the other nodes, so \(P_n(x_j) = y_j\). The animations evaluate it in the first barycentric form, \(P_n(x)=\ell(x)\sum_{i=0}^{n} \frac{w_i y_i}{x-x_i}\) with \(\ell(x)=\prod_{j=0}^{n}(x-x_j)\) and \(w_i=1/\prod_{j\ne i}(x_i-x_j)\). This is the same interpolant, and it stays accurate far outside the nodes, where the second barycentric form (a ratio of two such sums) gives values of the wrong sign in Cases 04 and 29.
Building \(P_n\) needs only distinct nodes; bounding its error needs a smooth \(f\). Mathews’ theorem: if \(f \in C^{n+1}[a, b]\) and the nodes lie in \([a, b]\), then for each \(x \in [a, b]\) there is a \(c\) in \([a, b]\) with
\[
f(x) - P_n(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}\,(x-x_0)(x-x_1)\cdots(x-x_n).
\]
In general, for fixed \(n\) and equally spaced nodes with spacing \(h\), the error on \([x_0, x_n]\) is therefore \(O(h^{n+1})\); for \(n = 1\) it is at most \(h^2 \max|f''|/8\). Raising \(n\) on a fixed interval need not help. For \(e^x\) on \([-2, 3]\) (Case 15) it does: the largest error on the node interval falls from \(9.65\) at degree 1 to \(3.05 \times 10^{-10}\) at degree 15.
For \(1/(1+10x^2)\) on \([-1, 1]\) (Case 08), smooth on the whole real line, the error falls to \(0.135\) with 8 nodes and then grows, to \(0.485\) with 16 nodes, in oscillations next to the end nodes: Runge’s phenomenon. In Case 04, \(\sqrt{x}\) is not in \(C^1[0, 2]\), and the largest error on \([0, 2]\) falls only to \(0.0485\) at degree 15, next to \(x = 0\). Outside \([a, b]\) the theorem says nothing: in Case 04 at degree 15 the interpolant is about \(64.5\) at \(x = 2.5\), where \(\sqrt{2.5} \approx 1.58\).
Newton Interpolation builds the same polynomial from divided differences, Neville’s algorithm evaluates it at a point, Hermite Interpolation also matches slopes, Chebyshev nodes avoid Runge’s phenomenon, and Cubic Splines use cubic pieces instead of one high-degree polynomial.
The 29 animations below follow the legacy Mathews case ordering. Each case heading gives the function and the node interval \([a, b]\); the nodes are equally spaced from \(a\) to \(b\), endpoints included. Where the plot window is wider than \([a, b]\) (Cases 01–11, 14, 18–20 and 24–29), the interpolant beyond the nodes is extrapolation. In Case 19, \(\arcsin x\) is undefined outside \([-1, 1]\), so there only the interpolant is drawn.

The degree in each title is the number of nodes minus one, the most the interpolant can have; its actual degree can be lower. With nodes symmetric about 0, the interpolant of an even \(f\) has only even powers of \(x\) and that of an odd \(f\) only odd powers, so in the even cases (08, 13, 17, 20 and 22) the frame titled degree 1 is a horizontal line and the frame titled degree 15 has degree 14. title: Iterative Refinement
text:
Residual-Correction Idea
Iterative refinement improves a computed solution of
\[
A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}
\tag{1}
\]
without recomputing a new factorization at every iteration.
If we have already computed
\[
PA=LU,
\tag{2}
\]
then each refinement step uses only triangular solves.
Refinement is most useful when the residual is computed in higher precision than the rest of the work; Mathews calls this the “signal feature” of the method. With residuals computed in working precision it can still remove a gross error in a starting vector (Example 2), but the residual stalls at roundoff level and further steps bring no steady gain.






NoteDefinition - Residual



For an approximation \(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\), the residual is \[
\mathbf{r}^{(k)}=\mathbf{b}-A\mathbf{x}^{(k)}.
\] It measures how far \(\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\) fails to satisfy the original equations.



Derivation of the Correction Equation
Suppose
\[
\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^{(k)}+\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(k)}.
\tag{3}
\]
Substitute into \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\):
\[
A\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(k)}=\mathbf{b}-A\mathbf{x}^{(k)}=\mathbf{r}^{(k)}.
\tag{4}
\]
So each iteration solves one correction system and updates
\[
\mathbf{x}^{(k+1)}=\mathbf{x}^{(k)}+\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(k)}.
\tag{5}
\]






TipAlgorithm - Iterative Refinement




Compute \(PA=LU\) once.
Compute an initial approximation \(\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\) from LU-solve.
For \(k=0,1,2,\dots\): \[
\mathbf{r}^{(k)}=\mathbf{b}-A\mathbf{x}^{(k)},
\qquad
A\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(k)}=\mathbf{r}^{(k)},
\qquad
\mathbf{x}^{(k+1)}=\mathbf{x}^{(k)}+\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(k)}.
\tag{6}
\] Compute \(\mathbf{r}^{(k)}\) in higher precision than the rest when possible. Stop when \(\|\mathbf{r}^{(k)}\|\) is sufficiently small or stops decreasing.

title: Iterative Refinement
section: Example 1 - One Refinement Step on a 4x4 System
text:
Example 1 - One Refinement Step on a 4x4 System
Use
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
1&-4&4&7\\
0&2&-1&0\\
2&1&1&4\\
2&-3&2&-5
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}x_1\\x_2\\x_3\\x_4\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}4\\5\\2\\9\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Take the initial guess
\[
\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=(-14,20,34,-6)^\top.
\]
Step 1: Residual
\[
\mathbf{r}^{(0)}=\mathbf{b}-A\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=
\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 2: Solve correction system
\[
A\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=\mathbf{r}^{(0)},
\qquad
\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-\tfrac{12}{25}\\
-\tfrac{11}{25}\\
\tfrac{3}{25}\\
\tfrac{8}{25}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 3: Update
\[
\mathbf{x}^{(1)}=\mathbf{x}^{(0)}+\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-\tfrac{362}{25}\\
\tfrac{489}{25}\\
\tfrac{853}{25}\\
-\tfrac{142}{25}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This is the exact solution. In exact arithmetic this always happens: (4) gives \(\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\), so one step from any \(\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\) lands on the solution. In floating point the correction is only approximate (Example 2).
Verification:



Row
Left-hand side
Right-hand side




1
\(x_1-4x_2+4x_3+7x_4=4\)
\(4\;\checkmark\)


2
\(2x_2-x_3=5\)
\(5\;\checkmark\)


3
\(2x_1+x_2+x_3+4x_4=2\)
\(2\;\checkmark\)


4
\(2x_1-3x_2+2x_3-5x_4=9\)
\(9\;\checkmark\)



The residual drops from \(\mathbf{r}^{(0)}=(4,-1,0,-1)^\top\) to
\[
\mathbf{r}^{(1)}=\mathbf{0}.
\]

title: Iterative Refinement
text:
Example 2 - Hilbert Matrix (Source Reconstruction)
The legacy module uses
\[
H_5\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},
\qquad
\mathbf{b}=(5,4,3,2,1)^\top,
\]
with
\[
H_5=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&\tfrac12&\tfrac13&\tfrac14&\tfrac15\\
\tfrac12&\tfrac13&\tfrac14&\tfrac15&\tfrac16\\
\tfrac13&\tfrac14&\tfrac15&\tfrac16&\tfrac17\\
\tfrac14&\tfrac15&\tfrac16&\tfrac17&\tfrac18\\
\tfrac15&\tfrac16&\tfrac17&\tfrac18&\tfrac19
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The true solution shown there is
\[
\mathbf{x}_{\text{true}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-95\\2160\\-10710\\17920\\-9450
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
(Mathews’ module also has a review \(PA=LU\) solve, a second \(5\times5\) system, and the same experiment for the Hilbert matrices \(H_6\) to \(H_{10}\), whose condition number \(\kappa_\infty\) grows from about \(2.9\times10^{7}\) to \(3.5\times10^{13}\); those examples are not reproduced here.)
The module then uses the pedagogical starting vector
\[
\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-100\\2000\\-10000\\18000\\-10000
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 1: Compute residual. In exact arithmetic
\[
\mathbf{r}^{(0)}=\mathbf{b}-H_5\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-\tfrac{185}{3}\\
-46\\
-\tfrac{737}{21}\\
-\tfrac{583}{21}\\
-\tfrac{1427}{63}
\end{pmatrix}
\approx
\begin{pmatrix}
-61.666666666666667\\
-46\\
-35.095238095238095\\
-27.761904761904762\\
-22.650793650793651
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Mathews’ Mathematica printout, which stores \(H_5\) in 16-digit floating point, shows this vector with errors of up to \(2.5\times10^{-13}\) in the last digits (for example \(-46.00000000000025\)).
Step 2: Solve correction system
\[
H_5\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=\mathbf{r}^{(0)}.
\]
Exactly, \(\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=\mathbf{x}_{\text{true}}-\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=(5,160,-710,-80,550)^\top\). A floating-point solve with the LU factors is only approximate; Mathews’ printed (Mathematica) values are
\[
\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
5.000000000190141\\
159.9999999968922\\
-709.9999999877721\\
-80.0000000172662\\
550.0000000080213
\end{pmatrix},
\]
off from the exact correction by up to about \(1.7\times10^{-8}\).
Step 3: Update. Mathews’ printed values are
\[
\mathbf{x}^{(1)}=\mathbf{x}^{(0)}+\Delta\mathbf{x}^{(0)}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-94.9999999998099\\
2159.999999996892\\
-10709.99999998777\\
17919.99999998273\\
-9449.99999999198
\end{pmatrix},
\]
about \(1.7\times10^{-8}\) from \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{true}}\). Substituting these printed digits exactly gives the residual
\[
\mathbf{r}^{(1)}=\mathbf{b}-H_5\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\approx
\begin{pmatrix}
7.3\\7.8\\2.5\\3.8\\4.8
\end{pmatrix}\times10^{-13},
\]
so the residual has fallen from \(\|\mathbf{r}^{(0)}\|_\infty=\tfrac{185}{3}\approx 61.7\) to below \(10^{-12}\) in one step. Mathews’ printout lists smaller residuals, about \(10^{-14}\), which cannot be reproduced from the 16 printed digits: at this level the residual depends on the last bits of \(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\) (one unit in the last place of \(x^{(1)}_4\), \(3.6\times10^{-12}\), changes it by up to about \(9\times10^{-13}\)) and on the order of the floating-point operations.
The step has not made \(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\) more accurate than a plain LU solve: Mathews’ LU-solve solution of \(H_5\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) is within \(3.5\times10^{-9}\) of \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{true}}\), against \(1.7\times10^{-8}\) for \(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\). The gain is relative to the artificial starting vector only. Mathews adds the caveat that if the iteration is done one more time the values will not get closer to the solution: his second step changes \(\mathbf{x}^{(1)}\) by at most about \(5\times10^{-10}\) and leaves it about \(1.7\times10^{-8}\) from \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{true}}\). Repeating the run in IEEE double precision (NumPy, LAPACK LU with partial pivoting) from the same \(\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\) shows the same stagnation: the errors after steps 1 to 5 are \(6.0\times10^{-8}\), \(2.7\times10^{-8}\), \(1.7\times10^{-9}\), \(8.9\times10^{-8}\) and \(3.6\times10^{-8}\) (the plain LU solve: \(3.4\times10^{-9}\)), while \(\|\mathbf{r}^{(k)}\|_\infty\) stays between \(4.5\times10^{-13}\) and \(6.8\times10^{-13}\). If instead each residual is computed exactly (rational arithmetic) and only the correction solves use the double-precision LU factors, the iterates reach the exact integer solution after two steps from \(\mathbf{x}^{(0)}\), and after one step from the LU-solve solution.

title: Iterative Refinement
text:
Conditioning and Accuracy Loss
For this Hilbert system, the module reports
\[
\operatorname{Cond}(A)=943656.
\]
This is the condition number in the \(\infty\)-norm, \(\kappa_\infty(H_5)=\|H_5\|_\infty\|H_5^{-1}\|_\infty\) (equal here to \(\kappa_1\); in the 2-norm, \(\kappa_2(H_5)\approx 476607.25\)).
Mathews’ error estimate comes from perturbation theory. Suppose every entry of \(A\) and \(\mathbf{b}\) is rounded to nearest in machine precision (relative error at most \(\varepsilon/2\)), and \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\) is the exact solution of the rounded system. Then, to first order in \(\varepsilon\),
\[
\|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_\infty\lesssim \|\mathbf{x}\|_\infty\,\kappa_\infty(A)\,\varepsilon.
\tag{7}
\]
For a solution computed by elimination, (7) is an estimate of the error, not a guaranteed bound, because elimination adds rounding errors of its own. With machine epsilon \(\varepsilon=2.22045\times10^{-16}\) and \(\|\mathbf{x}_{\text{true}}\|_\infty=17920\), it gives
\[
\|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_\infty
\lesssim
(17920)(943656)(2.22045\times10^{-16})
\approx 3.75\times10^{-6}.
\tag{8}
\]
Mathews’ printout gives \(4.82295\times10^{-6}\) instead, because it multiplies the \(\infty\)-norm condition number by the 2-norm \(\|\mathbf{x}_{\text{true}}\|_2=23017.6\). Using the 2-norm throughout gives \(\kappa_2\|\mathbf{x}_{\text{true}}\|_2\,\varepsilon\approx 2.44\times10^{-6}\). For example, the exact solution of the system with the entries of \(H_5\) rounded to double precision (solved in rational arithmetic) lies \(1.7\times10^{-8}\) from \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{true}}\), and the floating-point errors in Example 2 are at most \(8.9\times10^{-8}\): both are well inside these estimates. Mathews’ second refinement iterate \(\mathbf{x}^{(2)}\) agrees with that rounded-system solution to within \(6\times10^{-12}\) in every component (its error matches to 3 to 4 significant digits), so refinement with the rounded \(H_5\) has settled on the rounded system’s solution, not on \(\mathbf{x}_{\text{true}}\).






Iterative refinement can dramatically reduce residuals, but ill-conditioning still limits attainable accuracy. For this case, roughly \(\log_{10}(943656)\approx 5.97\) digits may be lost.

title: Numerical Methods
text:
My main intent with this “Numerical Methods” page is to capture the important points and intuitive animations that helped me build my intuition of numerical algorithms. I hope it helps you too. This page is not a math book, nor is it proof focused. There are many resources devoted to walking you through every detail. This page sticks to building your intuition of the algorithms without all the details. Each algorithm page is close to stand-alone.
This page was inspired by John H. Mathews’ website (Mathew 2000-2019). In 2019, his page was taken down. I tried contacting Cal State Fullerton, but they did not respond. Fast forward to April 2026: I realized I could pull it back, at least partially, from the Internet Archive (the Wayback Machine). That is why you will notice that much of this is modeled on his page.
The majority of these pages were AI generated, using Mathews’ site from the Internet Archive as a reference. Every page now has its text written, every page that gets an animation has one, and every animated page opens with a short overview of its method. Each page went through independent review-and-correction rounds with Claude Opus 5.5 until a round found no errors. Multiple rounds are what it took to get these highly technical numerical method examples right.
How the pages were checked (November 28, 2026). Every number, table entry and statement about how an animation behaves was recomputed independently in Python or Julia, and each one was recorded with the computation that confirmed it. Each page was then reviewed by a separate AI reviewer that had not seen how the page was written. Before trusting a round of reviews, I gave a reviewer a copy of a page with deliberately planted errors, to confirm that the review would catch them. Every serious finding was confirmed by another independent check before it was fixed, and every fix was checked by yet another reviewer who saw only the reported problem and the change. Review rounds were repeated until a round found no errors or misleading statements; the original animations went through nine such rounds. Each animation is made by a Julia script stored with its page, and the script reproduces the animation exactly. That is a lot of checking, but it is not a proof that nothing is wrong. As language models improve, I will use them to check these pages again, and I will keep reviewing the pages myself as I use them over time. If you find an error, please tell me through the contact page or by opening an issue on the site’s GitHub repository.

title: Householder Transformations
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).
Householder’s method takes a real symmetric \(n \times n\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) and, in exactly \(n - 2\) steps, produces a symmetric tridiagonal matrix with the same eigenvalues. Each step is an orthogonal similarity transformation \(\mathbf{A}_k = \mathbf{P}_k\mathbf{A}_{k-1}\mathbf{P}_k\) by a Householder matrix \(\mathbf{P}_k\), a reflection. Jacobi’s method also uses orthogonal similarity transformations, but each of its rotations makes only one symmetric pair of entries zero, and later rotations can make them nonzero again, so it needs many sweeps. A Householder step makes a whole column below the subdiagonal zero at once (and, by symmetry, the matching row), and later steps leave those zeros in place. The tridiagonal result is the starting point of the QR method, which then finds all the eigenvalues cheaply.
The QR method page shows the same reduction with the matrices \(\mathbf{P}_k\) written out, and its Case 2 animation shows the matrix of Example 1 below being reduced and then iterated to its eigenvalues. This page develops the reflection itself, the cheap way of applying it, and all of Mathews’ worked examples. For a matrix that is not symmetric the same steps give an upper Hessenberg matrix instead; see Hessenberg Factorization.

title: Homogeneous Linear Systems
text:
Background
A homogeneous linear system has the form
\[
A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
\tag{1}
\]
The vector \(\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\) always solves (1), so every homogeneous system has at least the trivial solution.






NoteDefinition - Reduced Row Echelon Form



A matrix is in reduced row echelon form (RREF) if:

Every nonzero row has leading entry \(1\).
Each leading \(1\) is the only nonzero entry in its column.
Leading \(1\) positions move to the right as you move down rows.
Any zero rows are grouped at the bottom.









NoteDefinition - Rank



The rank of a matrix \(A\), written \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\), is the number of nonzero rows in its RREF.


Because an augmented homogeneous matrix is
\[
M=[A\mid \mathbf{0}],
\tag{2}
\]
the last column is always zero, so
\[
\operatorname{rank}(A)=\operatorname{rank}(M).
\tag{3}
\]






TipTheorem - Solution Structure for \(n\times n\) Homogeneous Systems



For \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\):
\[
\operatorname{rank}(A)=n
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{the only solution is }\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0},
\tag{4}
\]
\[
\operatorname{rank}(A)<n
\Longleftrightarrow
\text{there are infinitely many nontrivial solutions}.
\tag{5}
\]


For square matrices, this is equivalent to:
\[
\det(A)\neq 0 \Rightarrow \text{unique trivial solution},
\qquad
\det(A)=0 \Rightarrow \text{infinitely many solutions}.
\tag{6}
\]

title: Homogeneous Linear Systems
text:
Algorithm

Form \([A\mid\mathbf{0}]\).
Row reduce to RREF.
Identify pivot variables and free variables.
Express pivot variables in terms of free variables.
Write the parametric vector form and verify by substitution into \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\).

title: Homogeneous Linear Systems
text:
Example 1 - Unique Trivial Solution
Solve
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1+x_2-2x_3&=0,\\
3x_1+2x_2+4x_3&=0,\\
4x_1+3x_2+3x_3&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Step 1: Build the coefficient matrix and row reduce.
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&1&-2\\
3&2&4\\
4&3&3
\end{pmatrix}
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{RREF}(A)=I_3.
\]
Step 2: Read off solution.
\[
x_1=x_2=x_3=0,
\qquad
\mathbf{x}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Verification:

\(0\ \checkmark\)



Since \(\det(A)=-1\neq0\), only the trivial solution exists.

title: Homogeneous Linear Systems
text:
Summary
Homogeneous systems are classified by comparing the rank with the number of unknowns \(n\) (for square systems, the determinant gives the same test):

\(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\) gives only the trivial solution.
\(\operatorname{rank}(A)<n\) gives \(n-\operatorname{rank}(A)\) free variables and infinitely many solutions. A system with fewer equations than unknowns always has \(\operatorname{rank}(A)<n\), so it always has nontrivial solutions; the propane system (\(3\) equations, \(4\) unknowns, rank \(3\)) is an example.
RREF exposes the null-space basis directly, which is useful both in algebra and in applications such as chemical equation balancing.

title: Hermite Polynomial Interpolation
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Hermite Polynomial Interpolation
text:
Description
Hermite polynomial interpolation builds a polynomial that matches both the values and the first derivatives of a function at the nodes. On one interval \([x_0, x_1]\) the data are the values \(y_0, y_1\) and the slopes \(y_0', y_1'\), and the interpolant is a cubic, which Mathews calls a “clamped cubic” because its slopes at the endpoints are fixed. With \(h = x_1 - x_0\) and \(t = (x - x_0)/h\), it is
\[
H(x)=y_0H_{00}(t)+hy_0'H_{10}(t)+y_1H_{01}(t)+hy_1'H_{11}(t),
\]
where the cubic Hermite basis functions are
\[
H_{00}(t)=2t^3-3t^2+1, \quad H_{10}(t)=t^3-2t^2+t, \quad H_{01}(t)=-2t^3+3t^2, \quad H_{11}(t)=t^3-t^2 .
\]
Each basis function has value or slope 1 for one of the four endpoint conditions and 0 for the other three, so each weighted term supplies one condition; the factor \(h\) converts a slope in \(x\) into a slope in \(t\). Case 2 adds the four terms one at a time.
The method needs \(x_0 \neq x_1\) and the derivatives at the nodes as well as the values. Given those four numbers, Mathews’ theorem states that exactly one cubic satisfies the four conditions. Applied on each subinterval of a mesh, the pieces join with matching value and slope, so the piecewise interpolant is \(C^1\) but in general not \(C^2\): in Case 1 with \(n = 2\), \(H''\) jumps from \(-2/\pi\) to \(2/\pi\) at \(x = \pi\).
The general error result, which Mathews’ module does not state: if \(f \in C^4[x_0, x_1]\), then for each \(x\) in the interval there is a \(\xi\) in \((x_0, x_1)\) with
\[
f(x)-H(x)=\frac{f^{(4)}(\xi)}{4!}\,(x-x_0)^2(x-x_1)^2 ,
\]
so \(|f(x) - H(x)| \le M_4 h^4/384\), where \(M_4\) bounds \(|f^{(4)}|\) on the interval. The piecewise interpolant’s error is therefore \(O(h^4)\), and every cubic is reproduced exactly. In Case 1, \(f = \sin x\) and \(M_4 = 1\), and the maximum error of every frame lies below \(h^4/384\): 0.425 against 4.06 for \(n = 1\), and 0.000906 against 0.000991 for \(n = 8\).
The \(O(h^4)\) rate is asymptotic, and coarse meshes can mislead: in Case 1 the three doublings of \(n\) divide the maximum error by 2.0, 19.9 and 11.9, not 16. Prescribed slopes can also push the cubic outside the range of the data: in Case 2, \(H\) rises to 2.098 near \(x = 1.205\) and dips to 0.654 near \(x = 2.629\), above the larger endpoint value and below the smaller. When derivatives are not known, they must be estimated, and their errors enter \(H\).
Hermite interpolation in general, matching derivatives of any order at any number of nodes, generalizes both the Taylor polynomial (one node) and the Lagrange polynomial (values only); Cubic Splines need only the values at the knots and two end conditions, and are \(C^2\), and Bézier Curves describe cubic Hermite pieces through control points.

title: Hermite Polynomial Interpolation
text:
Animations
These animations illustrate the cubic Hermite polynomial, which interpolates both function values and first derivatives at the endpoint nodes. Unlike ordinary (Lagrange) interpolation, which uses only function values, Hermite interpolation also matches the slope at each node.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.
Mathews’ Hermite polynomial module has no animation. Case 1, piecewise interpolation of \(\sin x\) on \([0, 2\pi]\), is this site’s own example; Case 2 uses the endpoint data of the module’s Example 1. The module’s Examples 2 and 3, a clamped and a natural cubic spline through given knots, are not animated here.

Case 1 — Piecewise cubic Hermite for \(\sin(x)\), refining the mesh
Behavior: Piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation uses \(n\) subintervals, each carrying a cubic polynomial that matches \(f\) and \(f'\) at its two endpoints. The maximum errors in the four frames are 0.425, 0.215, 0.0108 and 0.000906, so the doublings shown divide the error by about 2.0, 19.9 and 11.9. For smooth \(f\) the error is \(O(h^4)\), but these coarse meshes are not yet in the asymptotic range; the ratio approaches \(2^4 = 16\) only on finer meshes (15.0 for \(n = 8 \to 16\), 15.7 for \(16 \to 32\), 15.9 for \(32 \to 64\)).
Julia source



Piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation of sin(x) on 0 to 2pi, showing n=1,2,4,8 intervals; the maximum error falls from 0.425 at n=1 to 0.000906 at n=8




Case 2 — Hermite basis functions building the cubic with \(p(1)=2\), \(p'(1)=1\), \(p(3)=1\), \(p'(3)=2\)
Behavior: The four cubic Hermite basis functions \(H_{00}\), \(H_{10}\), \(H_{01}\), \(H_{11}\) each carry one degree of freedom (a value or derivative at an endpoint). Their weighted combination \(H(x) = y_0 H_{00} + h y_0' H_{10} + y_1 H_{01} + h y_1' H_{11}\) takes the prescribed values and slopes at both endpoints. Here \(h = 2\), so the slope weights are \(h y_0' = 2\) and \(h y_1' = 4\), and the result is \(H(x) = x^3 - \tfrac{23}{4}x^2 + \tfrac{19}{2}x - \tfrac{11}{4}\), the cubic of Mathews’ solution. The frames add the weighted terms one at a time and draw the running sum, with the prescribed tangent lines as short dotted segments; the first two partial sums fall to 0 with zero slope at \(x = 3\), because \(H_{00}\) and \(H_{10}\) have zero value and zero slope there.
Julia source



Running sum of the four weighted Hermite basis terms for the endpoint data p(1)=2, p’(1)=1, p(3)=1, p’(3)=2, adding one term per frame until it forms the complete cubic Hermite polynomial, which meets the dotted tangent segments at both endpoints

title: Halley’s Method
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Halley’s Method
text:
Description
Halley’s method, attributed to Edmond Halley (1656–1742), is a root-finding algorithm that extends Newton-Raphson by incorporating the second derivative \(f''\). Where Newton-Raphson fits a tangent line at each iterate and finds its \(x\)-intercept, Halley’s method fits an osculating hyperbola, a rational function \(y = \dfrac{a + b(x - x_n)}{1 + c(x - x_n)}\) that matches \(f\), \(f'\) and \(f''\) at \(x_n\), and takes its \(x\)-intercept as \(x_{n+1}\). (Taking the root of the second-order Taylor parabola instead gives a different iteration, Halley’s irrational method.) This extra curvature information yields cubic convergence at simple roots — the number of accurate digits roughly triples each iteration, compared to doubling for Newton-Raphson.

Iteration Formula
Given a smooth function \(f(x)\) with derivatives \(f'(x)\) and \(f''(x)\), the Halley iteration is:
\[x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{2\, f(x_n)\, f'(x_n)}{2\bigl[f'(x_n)\bigr]^2 - f(x_n)\, f''(x_n)}\]
This can be rewritten to make the Newton-Raphson correction explicit:
\[x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)} \cdot \frac{1}{\displaystyle 1 - \frac{f(x_n)\, f''(x_n)}{2\bigl[f'(x_n)\bigr]^2}}\]
The second factor, \(1\big/\bigl(1 - f(x_n)\, f''(x_n)/(2[f'(x_n)]^2)\bigr)\), is a multiplicative correction to the Newton step. When \(|f(x_n)\, f''(x_n)|\) is small compared with \(2[f'(x_n)]^2\), which always happens close to a simple root, this factor is close to 1 and the Halley step nearly coincides with the Newton step.


Convergence
For a simple root \(x^*\) (where \(f(x^*) = 0\) and \(f'(x^*) \neq 0\)), Halley’s method converges with order 3:
\[|e_{n+1}| \approx C\,|e_n|^3, \qquad e_n = x_n - x^*\]
where the asymptotic error constant is
\[C = \left|\frac{f'''(x^*)}{6\,f'(x^*)} - \frac{\bigl[f''(x^*)\bigr]^2}{4\bigl[f'(x^*)\bigr]^2}\right|.\]
Mathews’ theorem gives the hypotheses: \(f \in C^3[a, b]\), \(f(x^*) = 0\) with \(f'(x^*) \neq 0\), and \(x_0\) close enough to \(x^*\), so convergence is only local. Case 1b and Case 2 show the cubic rate: in extended precision, \(|e_{n+1}|/|e_n|^3\) settles at \(C = 1/8\) and \(C = 1/3\) by the third step.
At a multiple root of order \(m \geq 2\), the cubic rate is lost and the method reverts to linear convergence (as with Newton-Raphson).


Trade-offs
Each Halley step requires three function evaluations — \(f\), \(f'\), and \(f''\) — versus two for Newton-Raphson. Because its digits triple rather than double, Halley needs only about \(\log 2/\log 3 \approx 0.63\) times as many iterations for a high-precision result, but per function evaluation its efficiency index \(3^{1/3} \approx 1.442\) is barely above Newton’s \(2^{1/2} \approx 1.414\), so whether it saves time depends on how costly \(f''\) and the extra arithmetic are. Computing \(\sqrt{2}\) from \(x_0 = 2\) to 20,000 digits at fixed working precision with the first formula above, for example, Halley needs 10 iterations against Newton’s 15 but takes about as long or slightly longer (the second form, evaluated as written, does two more divisions per step and takes about twice as long as Newton).
Newton-Raphson is the method Halley’s corrects, the Secant Method needs no derivatives, and at multiple roots, where Halley’s is only linear, Accelerated and Modified Newton-Raphson and the Improved Newton Method restore quadratic convergence.

title: Halley’s Method
text:
Animations
Case 1a shows the Newton-Raphson tangent-line construction alone (tangent blue dashed) as a baseline. Cases 1b and 2 show the osculating-hyperbola construction of Halley’s method: at each step the current iterate \(x_n\) is marked on the curve, the tangent line (blue dotted) shows where Newton’s method would jump next, and the osculating hyperbola (orange dashed) crosses the \(x\)-axis at the Halley iterate \(x_{n+1}\) — yielding cubic rather than quadratic convergence at simple roots.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.
Cases 1a, 1b and 2 follow Examples 1(a), 1(b) and 2(b) of Mathews’ Halley’s Method module. The module’s Example 2(a), which applies Newton-Raphson iteration to the Case 2 function from the same starting value, is not animated here; Case 2’s blue diamond shows only the Newton step from the current Halley iterate.

Case 1a — Newton-Raphson baseline, \(f(x) = x^2 - 2\), \(x_0 = 2\)
Behavior: Starting at \(x_0 = 2\), the tangent at each iterate intersects the \(x\)-axis to produce the next iterate. The method converges quadratically to \(x^* = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.41421\), roughly doubling the number of correct digits per step (e.g., \(x_1 = 1.5\), \(x_2 \approx 1.4167\), \(x_3 \approx 1.4142\)).
Julia source



Newton-Raphson applied to f(x) = x² - 2 with x₀ = 2. Each frame advances one tangent-line step, showing the iterate converging quadratically to √2.




Case 1b — Halley’s Method, \(f(x) = x^2 - 2\), \(x_0 = 2\)
Behavior: Starting at the same \(x_0 = 2\), Halley’s iteration uses both \(f'\) and \(f''\) to correct the Newton step. The orange diamond marks the Halley iterate; the blue diamond shows where Newton would land for comparison. Halley achieves \(x_1 \approx 1.42857\) in one step (vs Newton’s \(x_1 = 1.5\)); from there the number of accurate digits roughly triples each iteration (about 1.8, 6.4 and 20 after steps 1, 2 and 3, in extended precision) because \(|g'''(x^*)| / 3!\) governs the asymptotic error rather than \(|g''(x^*)| / 2!\), where \(g\) is the iteration map, \(x_{n+1} = g(x_n)\).

Case 2 — Halley’s Method, \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2\), \(x_0 = -2.2\)
Behavior: \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2 = (x+2)(x-1)^2\) has a simple root at \(x = -2\) and a double root at \(x = 1\). Starting at \(x_0 = -2.2\) (near the simple root), Halley converges cubically: the first Halley step reaches \(x_1 \approx -2.002\), while Newton only reaches \(x_1 \approx -2.022\). In extended precision, Newton’s own iterates from \(x_0 = -2.2\) have errors of about \(2.2\times10^{-2}\), \(3.2\times10^{-4}\), \(6.9\times10^{-8}\) and \(3.2\times10^{-15}\) after steps 1–4, against Halley’s \(2.1\times10^{-3}\), \(2.9\times10^{-9}\) and \(8.2\times10^{-27}\) after steps 1–3; in double precision Newton first reaches \(-2\) exactly at \(x_5\), Halley at \(x_3\). Neither first step overshoots: both stay to the left of the root, on the same side as \(x_0\), and Halley’s lands within 0.0021 of it. The two first-step markers are only about 0.02 apart, so they overlap at this scale; the legend gives their values.

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and Pivoting
text:
Overview
Gauss-Jordan elimination is a direct method for solving linear systems
\[
A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},
\]
by applying elementary row operations to the augmented matrix
\[
\left[ A \mid \mathbf{b} \right].
\]
Unlike Gaussian elimination (which stops at upper-triangular form and then uses back substitution), Gauss-Jordan continues until the coefficient block is reduced all the way to the identity matrix.

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and Pivoting
text:
Existence and Uniqueness






NoteTheorem - Unique Solution Conditions



For an \(n \times n\) matrix \(A\), the following are equivalent:

For every right-hand side \(\mathbf{b}\), the system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) has a unique solution.
\(A\) is nonsingular.
\(\det(A) \neq 0\).
The homogeneous system \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}\) has only the trivial solution.



These conditions are exactly the setting where Gauss-Jordan elimination is guaranteed to succeed without encountering a truly zero pivot after proper pivoting.

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and Pivoting
text:
Augmented Matrix and Row Operations
Write the system
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij}x_j = b_i, \quad i=1,\dots,n
\]
as
\[
\left[ A \mid \mathbf{b} \right].
\]
Gauss-Jordan uses three elementary row operations:

Row interchange: \(R_i \leftrightarrow R_j\).
Row scaling: \(R_i \leftarrow cR_i\) with \(c \neq 0\).
Row replacement: \(R_i \leftarrow R_i + cR_j\) with \(j \neq i\).

Each operation preserves the solution set of the linear system.

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and Pivoting
text:
Pivot Elements and Pivoting
At step \(k\), a pivot element is the entry used to eliminate all other entries in column \(k\). In practice, we use partial pivoting:
\[
p = \operatorname*{arg\,max}_{i\in\{k,\dots,n\}} |a_{ik}|,
\]
then interchange rows \(k\) and \(p\) before elimination.






TipWhy Pivoting Matters



Pivoting avoids division by zero and reduces roundoff amplification when pivots are very small.

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and Pivoting
section: Algorithm I - Limited Gauss-Jordan (No Row Swaps)
text:
Algorithm I - Limited Gauss-Jordan (No Row Swaps)
This is the pedagogical version. It assumes that every pivot \(a_{kk}\) that arises during elimination is nonzero and reasonably sized; a nonzero diagonal in the original matrix is not enough (see Worked Example 3).

For \(k=1,\dots,n\):
Normalize pivot row: \(R_k \leftarrow R_k / a_{kk}\).
For each \(i \neq k\), eliminate column \(k\):

\[
R_i \leftarrow R_i - a_{ik}R_k.
\]

At termination, the left block is \(I\) and the last column is the solution vector.

This version is simple but fragile.

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and Pivoting
section: Algorithm II - Complete Gauss-Jordan with Partial Pivoting
text:
Algorithm II - Complete Gauss-Jordan with Partial Pivoting
This is the robust implementation pattern.
For \(k=1,\dots,n\):

Choose pivot row \(p\) with largest \(|a_{pk}|\) among rows \(k\) through \(n\) (if several rows tie, take the first of them).
If \(a_{pk}=0\), stop: the matrix is singular (or rank-deficient in exact arithmetic).
If \(p \neq k\), swap rows \(R_k\) and \(R_p\).
Normalize pivot row \(R_k\).
Eliminate column \(k\) from all rows \(i \neq k\).

After the final step, the matrix is in reduced row-echelon form (RREF).

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and Pivoting
text:
Worked Example 1
Solve
\[
\begin{aligned}
2x + y - z &= 8, \\
-3x - y + 2z &= -11, \\
-2x + y + 2z &= -3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Augmented matrix:
\[
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc|c}
2 & 1 & -1 & 8 \\
-3 & -1 & 2 & -11 \\
-2 & 1 & 2 & -3
\end{array}
\right].
\]
Applying Gauss-Jordan (with or without pivoting here) gives
\[
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & -1
\end{array}
\right],
\]
so the solution is
\[
(x,y,z) = (2,3,-1).
\]
This system is not Mathews’ Example 1; his system appears, with two equations interchanged, in Worked Example 3.

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and Pivoting
section: Worked Example 2 - Why Row Interchanges Are Needed
text:
Worked Example 2 - Why Row Interchanges Are Needed
Consider
\[
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc|c}
0 & 2 & 1 & 4 \\
1 & -2 & -3 & -6 \\
2 & 3 & 1 & 7
\end{array}
\right].
\]
If we attempt elimination starting at row 1, column 1, the pivot is zero and the method fails immediately. A row interchange (swap row 1 with row 2 or 3) fixes the issue and the elimination proceeds normally. The matrix is nonsingular (\(\det A = -7\)), so a unique solution exists.
Step 1: the candidates in column 1 are \(0, 1, 2\); Algorithm II swaps \(R_1 \leftrightarrow R_3\), divides by the pivot \(2\) and eliminates:
\[
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & \tfrac{3}{2} & \tfrac{1}{2} & \tfrac{7}{2} \\
0 & -\tfrac{7}{2} & -\tfrac{7}{2} & -\tfrac{19}{2} \\
0 & 2 & 1 & 4
\end{array}
\right].
\]
Step 2: the candidates in column 2 are \(-\tfrac{7}{2}, 2\), so no swap; the pivot is \(-\tfrac{7}{2}\):
\[
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 0 & -1 & -\tfrac{4}{7} \\
0 & 1 & 1 & \tfrac{19}{7} \\
0 & 0 & -1 & -\tfrac{10}{7}
\end{array}
\right].
\]
Step 3: the pivot is \(-1\):
\[
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc|c}
1 & 0 & 0 & \tfrac{6}{7} \\
0 & 1 & 0 & \tfrac{9}{7} \\
0 & 0 & 1 & \tfrac{10}{7}
\end{array}
\right],
\qquad
\mathbf{x} = \left(\tfrac{6}{7}, \tfrac{9}{7}, \tfrac{10}{7}\right).
\]
Verification:








Row

Right-hand side




1
\(0 + 2\cdot\tfrac{9}{7} + \tfrac{10}{7} = \tfrac{28}{7}\)
\(4\) \(\checkmark\)


2
\(\tfrac{6}{7} - 2\cdot\tfrac{9}{7} - 3\cdot\tfrac{10}{7} = -\tfrac{42}{7}\)
\(-6\) \(\checkmark\)


3
\(2\cdot\tfrac{6}{7} + 3\cdot\tfrac{9}{7} + \tfrac{10}{7} = \tfrac{49}{7}\)
\(7\) \(\checkmark\)



Here the zero pivot is visible in \(A\) itself. The failure that Mathews’ module emphasizes is subtler, and is the subject of the next example.

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and Pivoting
text:
Inverse Matrix via Gauss-Jordan
To compute \(A^{-1}\), augment with the identity:
\[
\left[ A \mid I \right].
\]
Use Gauss-Jordan elimination until the left block becomes \(I\):
\[
\left[ A \mid I \right]
\longrightarrow
\left[ I \mid A^{-1} \right].
\]






This works exactly when \(A\) is nonsingular. If at step \(k\) every candidate pivot \(a_{ik}\), \(i \ge k\), is zero, \(A\) is singular and has no inverse (entries above the pivot position may still be nonzero).




Worked Example 4 - Inverse of a \(4\times 4\) Matrix (Mathews’ Examples 4 and 5)
Find \(A^{-1}\) for
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix}
4 & 8 & 4 & 0 \\
1 & 4 & 7 & 2 \\
1 & 5 & 4 & -3 \\
1 & 3 & 0 & -2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Apply Algorithm II to \(\left[ A \mid I \right]\).
Step 1: the candidates in column 1 are \(4, 1, 1, 1\), so no swap; divide \(R_1\) by \(4\) and subtract it from \(R_2\), \(R_3\), \(R_4\):
\[
\left[
\begin{array}{cccc|cccc}
1 & 2 & 1 & 0 & \tfrac{1}{4} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 2 & 6 & 2 & -\tfrac{1}{4} & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & 3 & 3 & -3 & -\tfrac{1}{4} & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & -1 & -2 & -\tfrac{1}{4} & 0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}
\right].
\]
Step 2: the candidates in column 2 are \(2, 3, 1\); swap \(R_2 \leftrightarrow R_3\), divide by \(3\) and eliminate:
\[
\left[
\begin{array}{cccc|cccc}
1 & 0 & -1 & 2 & \tfrac{5}{12} & 0 & -\tfrac{2}{3} & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 1 & -1 & -\tfrac{1}{12} & 0 & \tfrac{1}{3} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 4 & 4 & -\tfrac{1}{12} & 1 & -\tfrac{2}{3} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -2 & -1 & -\tfrac{1}{6} & 0 & -\tfrac{1}{3} & 1
\end{array}
\right].
\]
Step 3: the candidates in column 3 are \(4, -2\), so no swap; divide by \(4\) and eliminate:
\[
\left[
\begin{array}{cccc|cccc}
1 & 0 & 0 & 3 & \tfrac{19}{48} & \tfrac{1}{4} & -\tfrac{5}{6} & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & -2 & -\tfrac{1}{16} & -\tfrac{1}{4} & \tfrac{1}{2} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & 1 & -\tfrac{1}{48} & \tfrac{1}{4} & -\tfrac{1}{6} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & -\tfrac{5}{24} & \tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{2}{3} & 1
\end{array}
\right].
\]
Step 4: the pivot is \(1\); eliminate column 4 from rows 1 to 3:
\[
\left[
\begin{array}{cccc|cccc}
1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & \tfrac{49}{48} & -\tfrac{5}{4} & \tfrac{7}{6} & -3 \\
0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & -\tfrac{23}{48} & \tfrac{3}{4} & -\tfrac{5}{6} & 2 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & \tfrac{3}{16} & -\tfrac{1}{4} & \tfrac{1}{2} & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 1 & -\tfrac{5}{24} & \tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{2}{3} & 1
\end{array}
\right],
\qquad
A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}
\tfrac{49}{48} & -\tfrac{5}{4} & \tfrac{7}{6} & -3 \\
-\tfrac{23}{48} & \tfrac{3}{4} & -\tfrac{5}{6} & 2 \\
\tfrac{3}{16} & -\tfrac{1}{4} & \tfrac{1}{2} & -1 \\
-\tfrac{5}{24} & \tfrac{1}{2} & -\tfrac{2}{3} & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Verification: multiplying out gives \(AA^{-1} = A^{-1}A = I\) (and \(\det A = -48 \neq 0\)). For example, \(A\) times the first column of \(A^{-1}\) is
\[
\left(\tfrac{196 - 184 + 36 + 0}{48},\ \tfrac{49 - 92 + 63 - 20}{48},\ \tfrac{49 - 115 + 36 + 30}{48},\ \tfrac{49 - 69 + 0 + 20}{48}\right) = (1, 0, 0, 0).
\]
Mathews’ Example 4 solves \(A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}\) for \(\mathbf{b} = (8, 10, -4, -4)^T\) with the same matrix. With \(A^{-1}\) in hand, \(\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b} = (3, -1, 1, 2)\), which checks:

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and Pivoting
section: Application - Polynomial Interpolation as a Linear System
text:
Application - Polynomial Interpolation as a Linear System
A degree-\(n\) polynomial
\[
p(x)=c_0 + c_1x + \cdots + c_nx^n
\]
through \(n+1\) data points leads to an \((n+1)\times(n+1)\) linear system for the coefficients. In matrix form:
\[
V\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{y},
\]
where \(V\) is a Vandermonde-type matrix built from sample locations. Gauss-Jordan provides a direct way to recover \(\mathbf{c}\) (or to solve the same system with pivoted elimination).

Worked Example 5 - Quintic Through Six Points (Mathews’ Example 6)
Find the polynomial \(p(x) = c_0 + c_1x + \cdots + c_5x^5\) through \((1,1)\), \((2,3)\), \((3,0)\), \((4,1)\), \((5,4)\), \((6,2)\).
Step 1: each point gives one equation \(p(x_i) = y_i\), so \(V\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{y}\) with
\[
\left[ V \mid \mathbf{y} \right] =
\left[
\begin{array}{cccccc|c}
1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\
1 & 2 & 4 & 8 & 16 & 32 & 3 \\
1 & 3 & 9 & 27 & 81 & 243 & 0 \\
1 & 4 & 16 & 64 & 256 & 1024 & 1 \\
1 & 5 & 25 & 125 & 625 & 3125 & 4 \\
1 & 6 & 36 & 216 & 1296 & 7776 & 2
\end{array}
\right],
\]
where row \(i\) is \((1, x_i, x_i^2, \dots, x_i^5 \mid y_i)\). The nodes are distinct, so \(V\) is nonsingular (\(\det V = 34560\)).
Step 2: Algorithm II reduces \(\left[ V \mid \mathbf{y} \right]\) to \(\left[ I \mid \mathbf{c} \right]\), with row interchanges at steps 2, 4 and 5 (the intermediate \(6\times 7\) matrices are not shown). The candidates tie at step 1 (all equal to \(1\)) and at step 3 (\(-6, -6, -4, -4\)); taking the first tied row, neither step swaps. Any other tie-break changes only the interchanges, not \(\mathbf{c}\):
\[
\mathbf{c} = \left(-32,\ \tfrac{3757}{60},\ -\tfrac{931}{24},\ \tfrac{31}{3},\ -\tfrac{29}{24},\ \tfrac{1}{20}\right).
\]
Step 3: the interpolating polynomial is
\[
p(x) = \frac{x^5}{20} - \frac{29x^4}{24} + \frac{31x^3}{3} - \frac{931x^2}{24} + \frac{3757x}{60} - 32.
\]
Verification: for example, \(p(2) = -32 + \tfrac{3757}{30} - \tfrac{931}{6} + \tfrac{248}{3} - \tfrac{58}{3} + \tfrac{8}{5} = \tfrac{-960 + 3757 - 4655 + 2480 - 580 + 48}{30} = \tfrac{90}{30} = 3\). Exact evaluation at all six nodes gives

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and Pivoting
text:
Practical Notes

Gauss-Jordan is excellent for teaching and for computing inverses, but it usually does more arithmetic than Gaussian elimination with back substitution.
Partial pivoting should be treated as standard practice in floating-point computation.
For large dense systems, LU factorization with pivoting is typically preferred computationally.
For sparse systems, specialized sparse solvers are often much more efficient.

title: Gauss-Jordan Elimination and Pivoting
text:
Summary
Gauss-Jordan elimination transforms \([A\mid b]\) directly to \([I\mid x]\) by row operations. The core ideas are:

Equivalent row operations preserve solutions.
Pivots drive elimination.
Row interchanges (partial pivoting) make the method robust.
The same machinery solves systems, exposes rank structure, and computes inverses.

title: Fixed Point Iteration
text:
Animations
Each animation below shows the cobweb (staircase) diagram for fixed point iteration. The diagram plots two curves — the identity line \(y = x\) and the iteration function \(y = g(x)\) — then traces the staircase path: from the current iterate \(x_n\) on the diagonal, vertical to the curve to get \(g(x_n) = x_{n+1}\), then horizontal back to the diagonal.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Convergent staircase, \(g(x) = \sqrt{2x}\), \(x_0 = 0.1\)
Behavior: The curve \(g(x) = \sqrt{2x}\) meets \(y = x\) at \(x = 0\) and at \(x^* = 2\). On \((0, 2)\) it is increasing and lies between \(y = x\) and \(y = 2\), so the iterates climb monotonically to \(x^* = 2\), even though \(g'(x) > 1\) for \(0 < x < \tfrac{1}{2}\), which includes \(x_0 = 0.1\). Near \(x^*\) the error is roughly halved at each step, since \(g'(2) = \tfrac{1}{2}\).
Julia source



Cobweb diagram: convergent fixed point iteration with g(x)=sqrt(2x), starting below the fixed point at x₀ = 0.1




Case 2 — Convergent staircase, \(g(x) = \sqrt{2x}\), \(x_0 = 4.0\)
Behavior: Same function as Case 1 but starting above the fixed point. The staircase descends monotonically to \(x^* = 2\), confirming convergence from both sides.
Julia source



Cobweb diagram: convergent fixed point iteration with g(x)=sqrt(2x), starting above the fixed point at x₀ = 4.0




Case 3 — Oscillating convergent, \(g(x) = \tfrac{8}{x+2}\), \(x_0 = 4.0\)
Behavior: The curve \(g(x) = \tfrac{8}{x+2}\) is strictly decreasing, with \(g'(x) = -\tfrac{8}{(x+2)^2}\), so \(g'(2) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\). Since \(|g'(2)| = \tfrac{1}{2} < 1\), iteration converges, but the staircase alternates sides of \(x^*\) on each step.
Julia source



Cobweb diagram: oscillating convergent fixed point iteration with g(x)=8/(x+2), starting at x₀ = 4.0




Case 4 — Repelled from \(x^* = 2\), converges to \(x = 0\), \(g(x) = \tfrac{x^2}{4} + \tfrac{x}{2}\), \(x_0 = 1.95\)
Behavior: The curve \(g(x) = \tfrac{x^2}{4} + \tfrac{x}{2}\) crosses \(y = x\) at \(x^* = 2\) (and again at \(x = 0\)); it lies below the diagonal for \(0 < x < 2\). Since \(g'(2) = \tfrac{3}{2} > 1\), the staircase walks away from \(x^* = 2\) toward the left and converges monotonically to the other fixed point \(x = 0\), where \(g'(0) = \tfrac{1}{2}\).
Julia source



Cobweb diagram: fixed point iteration with g(x)=x²/4+x/2, starting at x₀ = 1.95 just below the repelling fixed point x* = 2; the staircase walks left and converges to the fixed point x = 0




Case 5 — Divergent, \(g(x) = \tfrac{x^2}{4} + \tfrac{x}{2}\), \(x_0 = 2.03\)
Behavior: Same function as Case 4 but starting above the fixed point. The staircase moves monotonically rightward and diverges, showing instability from both sides. The animation stops at \(x_9 \approx 3.753\), the last iterate inside the window; the sequence keeps growing (\(x_{12} \approx 29.92\), \(x_{14} \approx 1.437 \times 10^4\)).
Julia source



Cobweb diagram: divergent fixed point iteration with g(x)=x²/4+x/2, starting just above the fixed point at x₀ = 2.03; the staircase climbs away from x* = 2 and reaches x₉ ≈ 3.753 at the right of the window




Case 6 — Oscillating, does not converge, \(g(x) = -\tfrac{x^2}{4} - \tfrac{x}{2} + 4\), \(x_0 = 1.97\)
Behavior: The curve \(g(x) = -\tfrac{x^2}{4} - \tfrac{x}{2} + 4\) is steeply decreasing at \(x^* = 2\). Since \(g'(2) = -\tfrac{3}{2}\) and \(|g'(2)| = \tfrac{3}{2} > 1\), the iteration does not converge to \(x^*\): the staircase moves away from \(x^* = 2\), alternating sides at every step, and settles onto a stable 4-cycle (≈ 4.25, −2.64, 3.58, −0.99).

title: Faddeev-Leverrier Method
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).
The eigenvalues of an \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\) are the roots of its characteristic polynomial (see Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors). Expanding \(\det(\lambda I - A)\) by cofactors gives a sum of \(n!\) terms, which is impractical beyond small \(n\). The Faddeev-Leverrier method finds every coefficient of the characteristic polynomial from a short recursion that uses only matrix products and traces. The same recursion also produces the inverse \(A^{-1}\) and the determinant \(\det A\) with almost no extra work.
The method is named after Urbain Le Verrier, who obtained the coefficients from the traces of the powers \(A^k\) through Newton’s identities, and D. K. Faddeev, who recast the computation as the matrix recursion below. It is an exact, finite algorithm and is well suited to hand computation and computer algebra. As a floating-point method for eigenvalues it is a poor choice for all but small matrices; the last section shows why.

title: Cubic Splines
text:
Description
A cubic spline interpolates data \((x_i, y_i)\), \(i = 0, \ldots, n\), at nodes \(a = x_0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n = b\) by a separate cubic \(S_i(x)\) on each panel \([x_i, x_{i+1}]\), with \(y_i = f(x_i)\) when the data sample a function \(f\). The panels are joined so that \(S(x)\), \(S'(x)\) and \(S''(x)\) are continuous at the interior nodes.
Write \(h_i = x_{i+1} - x_i\) and \(M_i = S''(x_i)\). Because \(S''\) is linear on each panel, each cubic is fixed by its end values and end second derivatives,
\[
S_i(x) = \frac{M_i (x_{i+1} - x)^3 + M_{i+1} (x - x_i)^3}{6 h_i} + \Bigl(\frac{y_i}{h_i} - \frac{M_i h_i}{6}\Bigr)(x_{i+1} - x) + \Bigl(\frac{y_{i+1}}{h_i} - \frac{M_{i+1} h_i}{6}\Bigr)(x - x_i),
\]
and continuity of \(S'\) at the interior nodes gives the tridiagonal system
\[
h_{i-1} M_{i-1} + 2 (h_{i-1} + h_i) M_i + h_i M_{i+1} = 6 \Bigl(\frac{y_{i+1} - y_i}{h_i} - \frac{y_i - y_{i-1}}{h_{i-1}}\Bigr), \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n-1.
\]
These are \(n-1\) equations in \(n+1\) unknowns, so two end conditions close the system. For a natural spline, the boundary conditions are
\[
S''(x_0)=0,\qquad S''(x_n)=0,
\]
that is, \(M_0 = M_n = 0\); a clamped spline instead prescribes the end slopes \(S'(a) = f'(a)\) and \(S'(b) = f'(b)\). Mathews shows that either choice gives a unique spline. The system is strictly diagonally dominant, so it is solved without pivoting in \(O(n)\) operations, and each cubic panel is then reconstructed.
In general, for \(f \in C^4[a, b]\) with clamped (exact \(f'\) at the ends) or not-a-knot end conditions, the maximum error scales like \(O(h^4)\), where \(h\) is the largest \(h_i\). With natural end conditions it is only \(O(h^2)\) unless \(f''(a) = f''(b) = 0\); that error sits near an end where \(f'' \neq 0\), and away from the ends the error is still \(O(h^4)\). Case 1 interpolates \(f(x) = \sin x\) on \([0, 2\pi]\), where \(\sin''(0) = \sin''(2\pi) = 0\), so the natural spline keeps the \(O(h^4)\) rate. Its frames, 3 to 9 nodes, are too coarse to show that rate cleanly, so the table continues it, beside \(f(x) = \cos x\), whose \(f''(0) = -1\):
