Each error is \(\max |S(x) - f(x)|\) over \([0, 2\pi]\) for the natural spline, and each ratio is the previous error over this one. Halving \(h\) divides the error by about 16 for \(\sin x\), the \(O(h^4)\) rate, but only by about 4 for \(\cos x\), the \(O(h^2)\) rate.
A spline knows only its data: in the first frame of Case 1 the three nodes \(0\), \(\pi\) and \(2\pi\) are all zeros of \(\sin x\), so \(S(x) \equiv 0\) and the maximum error is 1. The other trap is the natural end condition when \(f''(a)\) or \(f''(b)\) is not zero: the \(\cos x\) error falls only like \(h^2\), and its largest value always lies in the first or last panel.
Lagrange and Newton interpolation fit one polynomial whose degree grows with the number of nodes, Hermite interpolation also matches slopes, B-Splines and Bézier Curves shape curves from control points, Tri-Diagonal Matrices solves the system above, and Cubic Spline Quadrature integrates the natural spline.

title: Cubic Splines
text:
Animations
The animation below shows a natural cubic spline fitted to equally-spaced data from \(f(x) = \sin(x)\) on \([0, 2\pi]\), with the number of nodes increasing. The natural spline satisfies \(S''(a) = S''(b) = 0\) at the endpoints.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.
Mathews’ Cubic Splines module has no animation, and the \(\sin(x)\) example in Case 1 is new to this page rather than taken from that module. It is used because \(\sin(x)\) has a closed form, so each frame can report the spline’s maximum error; the module’s examples interpolate a table of data points with no underlying function. The module’s Examples 1–3, which construct a natural cubic spline (Examples 1 and 2, the second with Mathematica’s SplineFit procedure) and a clamped cubic spline (Example 3) through one shared set of data points, are not animated here.

Case 1 — Natural cubic spline convergence for \(\sin(x)\)
Behavior: Adding nodes shrinks the maximum error rapidly. For this \(f\) the natural end conditions are exact, since \(\sin''(0)=\sin''(2\pi)=0\), so the spline converges at \(O(h^4)\), where \(h\) is the maximum node spacing; for a smooth \(f\) with \(f''(a)\neq 0\) or \(f''(b)\neq 0\) the natural spline’s maximum error falls only as \(O(h^2)\). The 3 to 9 nodes shown are too few for this rate to show cleanly from frame to frame. Each frame uses a fully recomputed spline (solving the tridiagonal second-derivative system) for the new set of nodes.

title: Cholesky, Doolittle and Crout Factorizations
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Cholesky, Doolittle and Crout Factorizations
text:
LU-Factorization Background






NoteDefinition - LU Factorization



A nonsingular matrix \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) has an LU factorization if \[
A = LU,
\] where \(L\) is lower triangular and \(U\) is upper triangular.


An LU factorization, when it exists, is not unique: for any nonsingular diagonal matrix \(\Lambda\), \(A=(L\Lambda)(\Lambda^{-1}U)\) is another one. Common normalizations fix the choice:

Doolittle form: diagonal entries of \(L\) are all \(1\).
Crout form: diagonal entries of \(U\) are all \(1\).
Cholesky form (for symmetric positive definite \(A\)): \(A=R^\top R\), where \(R\) is upper triangular with positive diagonal entries (so \(L=R^\top\) and \(U=R\)).







TipTheorem - Solve via Factorization



If \(A=LU\) with \(A\) nonsingular (so every diagonal entry of \(L\) and of \(U\) is nonzero), then solving \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) is equivalent to \[
L\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{b},\qquad U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}.
\] So one forward substitution and one back substitution solve the original system.

title: Cholesky, Doolittle and Crout Factorizations
text:
Formulas
With \(L_D,U_D\) the Doolittle factors, \(L_C,U_C\) the Crout factors and \(R\) the Cholesky factor, the three forms are:
\[
A=L_DU_D \quad \text{(Doolittle)},
\tag{1}
\]
\[
A=L_CU_C \quad \text{(Crout)},
\tag{2}
\]
\[
A=R^\top R \quad \text{(Cholesky, SPD matrices)}.
\tag{3}
\]
Matching the entries of \(A\) with those of the product builds each factor one row or column at a time. Write \(l_{ij},u_{ij},r_{ij}\) for the entries of the factor being computed; for \(k=1,\dots,n\) (an empty sum is \(0\)):
Doolittle (row \(k\) of \(U\), then column \(k\) of \(L\); \(l_{kk}=1\)): \[
u_{kj}=a_{kj}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}l_{ks}u_{sj}\quad(j=k,\dots,n),\qquad
l_{ik}=\frac{1}{u_{kk}}\Bigl(a_{ik}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}l_{is}u_{sk}\Bigr)\quad(i=k+1,\dots,n).
\]
Crout (column \(k\) of \(L\), then row \(k\) of \(U\); \(u_{kk}=1\)): \[
l_{ik}=a_{ik}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}l_{is}u_{sk}\quad(i=k,\dots,n),\qquad
u_{kj}=\frac{1}{l_{kk}}\Bigl(a_{kj}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}l_{ks}u_{sj}\Bigr)\quad(j=k+1,\dots,n).
\]
Cholesky (row \(k\) of \(R\)): \[
r_{kk}=\sqrt{a_{kk}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}r_{sk}^2},\qquad
r_{kj}=\frac{1}{r_{kk}}\Bigl(a_{kj}-\sum_{s=1}^{k-1}r_{sk}r_{sj}\Bigr)\quad(j=k+1,\dots,n).
\]
Without pivoting, these recurrences succeed only while every divisor \(u_{kk}\), \(l_{kk}\) or \(r_{kk}\) is nonzero (and, for Cholesky, every quantity under the square root is positive).






TipTheorem - Cholesky Factorization



If \(A\) is real, symmetric and positive definite, then it has a Cholesky factorization \(A=R^\top R\) with \(R\) upper triangular and \(r_{kk}>0\); every quantity under the square root in the recurrence above is positive.

title: Cholesky, Doolittle and Crout Factorizations
text:
Example 1 - One Matrix, Three Factorizations
Factorize
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
2&1&1&3&2\\
1&2&2&1&1\\
1&2&9&1&5\\
3&1&1&7&1\\
2&1&5&1&8
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Doolittle (\(\operatorname{diag}(L_D)=1\))
\[
L_D=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0&0&0\\
\tfrac12&1&0&0&0\\
\tfrac12&1&1&0&0\\
\tfrac32&-\tfrac13&0&1&0\\
1&0&\tfrac47&-\tfrac67&1
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
U_D=
\begin{pmatrix}
2&1&1&3&2\\
0&\tfrac32&\tfrac32&-\tfrac12&0\\
0&0&7&0&4\\
0&0&0&\tfrac73&-2\\
0&0&0&0&2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]


Crout (\(\operatorname{diag}(U_C)=1\))
\[
L_C=
\begin{pmatrix}
2&0&0&0&0\\
1&\tfrac32&0&0&0\\
1&\tfrac32&7&0&0\\
3&-\tfrac12&0&\tfrac73&0\\
2&0&4&-2&2
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
U_C=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&\tfrac12&\tfrac12&\tfrac32&1\\
0&1&1&-\tfrac13&0\\
0&0&1&0&\tfrac47\\
0&0&0&1&-\tfrac67\\
0&0&0&0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]


Cholesky (\(A=R^\top R\))
The Cholesky factor (unique, since its diagonal must be positive) is
\[
R=
\begin{pmatrix}
\sqrt2&\tfrac1{\sqrt2}&\tfrac1{\sqrt2}&\tfrac3{\sqrt2}&\sqrt2\\
0&\sqrt{\tfrac32}&\sqrt{\tfrac32}&-\tfrac1{\sqrt6}&0\\
0&0&\sqrt7&0&\tfrac4{\sqrt7}\\
0&0&0&\sqrt{\tfrac73}&-2\sqrt{\tfrac37}\\
0&0&0&0&\sqrt2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Verification: \[
L_DU_D=A,\qquad L_CU_C=A,\qquad R^\top R=A.
\]
The Crout factors are the Doolittle factors rescaled by the pivots: \(L_C=L_D\operatorname{diag}(U_D)\) with \(\operatorname{diag}(U_D)=\operatorname{diag}(2,\tfrac32,7,\tfrac73,2)\), an instance of the non-uniqueness noted above.

title: Cholesky, Doolittle and Crout Factorizations
text:
Example 2 - Solve \(A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) with Doolittle Factors
Use the same \(A\) and
\[
\mathbf{b}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-2\\4\\3\\-5\\1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 1: Solve \(L_D\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{b}\).
\[
\mathbf{y}=
\begin{pmatrix}
-2\\5\\-1\\-\tfrac13\\\tfrac{23}{7}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 2: Solve \(U_D\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}\).
\[
\mathbf{x}=
\begin{pmatrix}

    frac{237}{49}\\[2pt]
-\tfrac{53}{49}\\[2pt]
    frac{62}{49}\\[2pt]
    frac{23}{14}
\end{pmatrix}
\approx
\begin{pmatrix}
-6.41837\\4.83673\\-1.08163\\1.26531\\1.64286
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

title: Catenary
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Catenary
text:
Animations
The animation below shows the catenary \(y = c\cosh(x/c) - c\), Mathews’ form with its lowest point at the origin, alongside its parabolic approximation \(y = x^2/(2c)\) as the catenary parameter \(c\) (the ratio of horizontal tension to weight per unit length; larger \(c\) means a tauter, flatter cable) increases from 0.5 to 4. The catenary is the curve formed by a flexible cable hanging under gravity; the parabola is the first nonzero term of its Maclaurin series.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.
Case 1 follows Exploration 2 (“Approximated by a parabola”) of Mathews’ Catenary module, which finds the Maclaurin series of the catenary. The module’s Exploration 1 (catenaries with different \(c\) are scaled copies of one shape), its arc-length Exploration 3, its catenary-fit section, and its Examples 1–2 (which solve numerically for the \(c\) of the catenary through the origin and two points at equal height on either side of the \(y\)-axis, compute its arc length with Simpson’s rule, and compare the catenary with the parabola through the same three points) are not animated here.

Case 1 — Catenary vs parabola approximation as \(c\) varies
Behavior: For large \(c\) (nearly taut cable), the two curves are nearly indistinguishable near \(x=0\). For small \(c\) (slack cable), the catenary climbs more steeply than the parabola and the two separate well inside the window: at \(c=0.5\) the gap passes 0.1 at \(|x|\approx0.73\), and the catenary leaves the top of the plot at \(|x|\approx1.94\), the parabola at \(|x|\approx3.39\). The catenary never lies below the parabola, since their difference \(x^4/(24c^3)+x^6/(720c^5)+\cdots\) is positive for every \(x\neq0\). The lowest point is always at \((0, 0)\). Every frame shows the same pair of shapes: the curves for parameter \(c\) are the \(c=1\) curves \(y=\cosh x-1\) and \(y=x^2/2\) scaled by the factor \(c\) about the origin, so the flattening as \(c\) grows comes from viewing ever larger copies through a fixed window.

title: Brent’s Method
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Brent’s Method
text:
Description
Brent’s method, developed by Richard Brent in 1971 based on earlier work by van Wijngaarden, Zonneveld, and Dijkstra (1963), Wilkinson (1967), Dekker (1969), and others, is a hybrid root-finding algorithm that guarantees convergence while achieving fast (superlinear) convergence whenever possible. It requires only that the function \(f\) be continuous on \([a, b]\) with \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) of opposite sign — no derivatives are needed.
The method maintains a bracket that always contains a root, and intelligently selects among three sub-methods at each step:

Inverse quadratic interpolation — fits \(x\) as a quadratic function of \(y\) through the three points \((a, f(a))\), \((b, f(b))\), \((c, f(c))\) (a sideways parabola) and evaluates it at \(y = 0\). Converges superlinearly near a simple root.
Secant method (regula falsi) — uses the chord through \((a, f(a))\) and \((b, f(b))\) as a fallback when inverse quadratic interpolation cannot be used (only two distinct points, \(a = c\)).
Bisection — used as a safeguard whenever interpolation is not making enough progress; guarantees the bracket shrinks by at least half.


State Variables
At a typical step, Brent’s method tracks three points — \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) — satisfying:
\[f(b) \cdot f(c) \leq 0, \qquad |f(b)| \leq |f(c)|\]
so that \(b\) is the current best approximation to the root and the root always lies between \(b\) and \(c\). The third point \(a\) is the previous value of \(b\) (or coincides with \(c\)) and supplies the extra point for interpolation.


Inverse Quadratic Interpolation Formula
Given function values \(y_a = f(a)\), \(y_b = f(b)\), \(y_c = f(c)\), the next estimate is:
\[s = \frac{y_b \, y_c}{(y_a - y_b)(y_a - y_c)}\,a + \frac{y_a \, y_c}{(y_b - y_a)(y_b - y_c)}\,b + \frac{y_a \, y_b}{(y_c - y_a)(y_c - y_b)}\,c\]
This step is accepted only if \(s\) falls inside the current bracket and the method is making adequate progress; otherwise a bisection step is taken instead.


Secant Method Formula
When only two distinct points are available (\(a = c\)), the method uses the secant step instead of IQI:
\[s = b - f(b) \cdot \frac{b - a}{f(b) - f(a)}\]


Convergence

Guaranteed: Brent’s method always keeps the root bracketed and converges. Its safeguards take a bisection instead of an interpolation step that would not stay within about three quarters of the way from \(b\) to \(c\), or that is not smaller than half the step before last. This does not make it at least as fast as bisection: for the very flat \(f(x) = x^9\) on \([-1, 2]\) it needs 96 function evaluations to shrink the bracket below \(10^{-10}\), where bisection needs 37.
Fast case: When IQI applies consistently near a simple root, convergence is superlinear with order approximately 1.839 (the positive real root of \(t^3 = t^2 + t + 1\)). Case 1 shows the superlinear phase: from step 4 to step 7 each step multiplies the error in \(b\) by a smaller factor (0.030, 0.017, then \(5.0\times10^{-4}\)), though, with secant and IQI steps mixed, the observed order does not settle at 1.839.
Robustness: Unlike the secant method or IQI alone, Brent’s method cannot fail to converge as long as the initial bracket is valid and \(f\) is continuous.

Case 1 — Polynomial root, \(f(x) = 4x^3 - 16x^2 + 17x - 4\), \([a_0, b_0] = [0, 1]\)
Behavior: \(f(0) = -4 < 0\) and \(f(1) = 1 > 0\), so the IVT guarantees a root in \([0, 1]\). The true root is \(x^* \approx 0.3285\). Brent’s method takes 8 steps: secant, bisection, IQI, secant, IQI, secant, secant, IQI. At step 3 the IQI point \(0.2276\) has the larger \(|f|\), so it becomes the other end of the bracket and \(b\) stays at \(0.4\). After the bisection at step 2 every step is an interpolation step, and at steps 5–8 the error in \(b\) falls to \(3.2\times10^{-4}\), \(5.5\times10^{-6}\), \(2.7\times10^{-9}\) and \(4.0\times10^{-19}\): at step 8 \(b\) is the double-precision number nearest the root, and \(f(b)\) evaluates to exactly 0. The run stops there because \(f(b) = 0\), with the bracket still \(3.2\times10^{-4}\) wide. To get within \(10^{-10}\) of the root on \([0, 1]\), bisection needs 32 iterations and regula falsi 24. The window also shows the cubic’s other two roots, \(x \approx 1.2647\) in \([1, 2]\) and \(x \approx 2.4068\) in \([2, 3]\); Mathews’ example also finds these with Brent’s method, but only the run on \([0, 1]\) is animated here.

Case 2 — Transcendental equation, \(f(x) = \tan(x) - 2x\), \([a_0, b_0] = [0.5, 1.5]\)

title: Bisection Method

Animations
Each animation below shows the bracket-halving diagram for the bisection method. The shaded region marks the current bracket \([a, b]\); when \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) and \(f(a)\), \(f(b)\) have opposite signs, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees that it contains a root. Each frame computes the midpoint \(c = \tfrac{a+b}{2}\), evaluates \(f(c)\), and narrows the bracket to the half that still contains the sign change. The top panel shows the full view; the bottom panel zooms in on the bracket from before the current step, so each halving stays visible after the bracket becomes narrower than a pixel in the full view (from step 9 on).
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Convergent, \(f(x) = x^3 + 4x^2 - 10\), \([a_0, b_0] = [-1, 2]\)
Behavior: \(f(-1) = -7 < 0\) and \(f(2) = 14 > 0\), so the IVT guarantees a root in \([-1, 2]\). The true root is \(x^* \approx 1.3652\). The bracket width halves each step, so the error bound \(|c_k - x^*| \le (b_0 - a_0)/2^k\) shrinks monotonically; the midpoints themselves are not monotone and fall on both sides of the root.
Julia source



Bisection animation on f(x)=x³+4x²−10: bracket narrows around the root at x≈1.3652 over 12 steps, with a lower panel zoomed on each halving




Case 2 — Spurious convergence (cautionary), \(f(x) = \tan(x)\), \([a_0, b_0] = [0, 2]\)
Behavior: \(f(0) = \tan(0) = 0\), so the starting bracket has a genuine root at its left end. The first midpoint is \(c_1 = 1\). This implementation moves \(b\) only when \(f(a)\,f(c) < 0\); since \(f(0)\,f(1) = 0\) is not negative, it keeps \([1, 2]\) and walks away from that root. (A variant testing \(f(a)\,f(c) \le 0\) would keep \([0, 1]\) and converge to the root at 0.) On \([1, 2]\), \(f(1) = \tan(1) > 0\) and \(f(2) = \tan(2) < 0\), but this sign change is caused by the vertical asymptote at \(x = \tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.5708\), not a root: \(\tan\) has no zero in \([1, 2]\). Bisection converges to the asymptote — illustrating that the IVT guarantee requires \(f\) to be continuous on \([a, b]\).

Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: B-Splines
text:
Description
A B-spline curve is a smooth parametric curve \(C(t)\) shaped by control points \(P_1,\ldots,P_n\): the points steer the curve, but it need not pass through them. A curve of order \(k\) (degree \(k-1\)) is a weighted sum of the control points and basis functions \(N_{i,k}(t)\) defined over a nondecreasing knot vector \(t_1\le t_2\le\cdots\le t_{n+k}\):
\[
C(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n} P_i\,N_{i,k}(t), \qquad t_k\le t\le t_{n+1}.
\]
The basis functions come from the Cox-de Boor recursion, starting from indicators of the knot spans:
\[
N_{i,1}(t)=\begin{cases}1, & t_i\le t<t_{i+1},\\ 0, & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}
\qquad
N_{i,k}(t)=\frac{t-t_i}{t_{i+k-1}-t_i}\,N_{i,k-1}(t)+\frac{t_{i+k}-t}{t_{i+k}-t_{i+1}}\,N_{i+1,k-1}(t),
\]
where a zero-denominator term (a repeated knot) is taken as zero, and the last non-empty span includes \(t_{n+1}\). Both animations use cubic B-splines (\(k=4\), basis functions \(N_{i,4}\)), \(n=7\) control points and the clamped knot vector \((0,0,0,0,1,2,3,4,4,4,4)\), so \(t\) runs over \([0,4]\).
The construction needs \(n\ge k\) control points and \(n+k\) knots. In general, each \(N_{i,k}\) is non-negative and zero outside \([t_i,t_{i+k}]\), and the basis functions sum to 1 on \([t_k,t_{n+1}]\) (partition of unity, Case 2). So on each knot span the curve lies in the convex hull of the \(k\) control points active there, and moving one control point changes the curve only where its basis function is non-zero (local support). At an interior knot of multiplicity \(m\le k-1\) the curve is at least \(C^{k-1-m}\), so a cubic with simple interior knots, as here, is \(C^2\). A clamped knot vector repeats its first and last knots \(k\) times, and the curve then starts at \(P_1\) and ends at \(P_n\), tangent there to the control polygon.
A B-spline curve has no convergence order, since it follows its control polygon rather than interpolating data. Used instead to interpolate equally spaced data, as in Mathews’ module, B-splines give a cubic spline, whose error is in general \(O(h^4)\) for \(f\in C^4[a,b]\) with clamped end conditions.
The control points are not points on the curve. In Case 1 the curve misses each interior control point by 0.68 to 1.21, and although \(P_3=(2,-1)\) and \(P_5=(4,-0.5)\) lie below the \(x\)-axis, the curve has \(y>0\) for all \(0<t<4\). Local support is weak with few knot spans: here \(N_{4,4}\) is non-zero on all of \((0,4)\), so moving \(P_4\) moves every point except the ends. Code that keeps every span half-open makes every basis function zero at \(t=4\), so direct evaluation gives \(C(4)=(0,0)\) instead of \(P_7=(6,0)\); the page’s scripts stop at \(t=4-10^{-9}\).
With four control points and knots \((0,0,0,0,1,1,1,1)\), a cubic B-spline curve is exactly the cubic Bézier curve, and Mathews’ B-spline construction is another route to the interpolating Cubic Splines.

Case 2 — Basis functions \(N_{1,4}, \ldots, N_{7,4}\) and the partition of unity
Behavior: Each cubic B-spline basis function \(N_{i,4}(t)\) is non-negative and is zero outside \([t_i, t_{i+4}]\), which is at most 4 knot spans. Their sum equals 1 everywhere in the domain (partition of unity), which is why the B-spline curve lies within the convex hull of the control polygon.

On this page the weights are the given control points, so no linear system is solved and the two animations concentrate on the curve and the basis functions that form it.

title: Aitken’s Method & Steffensen’s Acceleration
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Aitken’s Method & Steffensen’s Acceleration
text:
Description

The Problem: Linear Convergence at Multiple Roots
Newton–Raphson’s method converges quadratically at simple roots — the number of correct decimal digits roughly doubles each iteration. However, at a multiple root of order \(m \geq 2\), convergence degrades to linear: the error satisfies
\[
\lim_{k \to \infty} \frac{|x_{k+1} - p|}{|x_k - p|} = \frac{m - 1}{m}
\]
For a double root (\(m = 2\)) the ratio is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\), meaning each Newton step only halves the error, so about 50 iterations are needed to reduce an error of order 1 to \(10^{-16}\) (\(2^{-53} \approx 1.1 \times 10^{-16}\)). In double precision, rounding in \(f\) near a double root can stop progress earlier: for the expanded polynomials of Cases 1 and 3 below, \(f\) evaluates to exactly 0 after 28 and 25 Newton steps, at errors of \(1.5 \times 10^{-9}\) and \(2.6 \times 10^{-10}\).


Aitken’s \(\Delta^2\) Process
Given a sequence \(\{x_k\}\) converging to a limit \(p\) (not just Newton iterates) whose signed error ratios \((x_{k+1}-p)/(x_k-p)\) approach a constant \(A\) with \(|A| < 1\), as in the theorem below, Aitken’s process constructs an accelerated sequence \(\{\hat{x}_k\}\) that converges faster than the original. Define the forward difference operator \(\Delta x_k = x_{k+1} - x_k\) and the second difference \(\Delta^2 x_k = x_{k+2} - 2x_{k+1} + x_k\). Then
\[
\hat{x}_k = x_k - \frac{(\Delta x_k)^2}{\Delta^2 x_k} = x_k - \frac{(x_{k+1} - x_k)^2}{x_{k+2} - 2x_{k+1} + x_k}
\]
Theorem (Aitken Acceleration). If \(\{x_k\} \to p\) with \(x_k \neq p\) for all \(k\), and there is a real number \(A\) with \(|A| < 1\) such that
\[
\lim_{k \to \infty} \frac{x_{k+1} - p}{x_k - p} = A,
\]
then
\[
\lim_{k \to \infty} \frac{\hat{x}_k - p}{x_k - p} = 0
\]
i.e. \(\{\hat{x}_k\}\) converges to \(p\) faster than \(\{x_k\}\) in the sense that the ratio of errors goes to zero.


Steffensen’s Acceleration Method
Steffensen’s method applies Aitken’s \(\Delta^2\) process directly to the Newton iteration to create a self-contained algorithm that achieves superlinear convergence even at double roots. Starting from \(S_0 = x_0\):

Compute two Newton steps: \(\displaystyle q_1 = S_k - \frac{f(S_k)}{f'(S_k)}\), \(\quad q_2 = q_1 - \frac{f(q_1)}{f'(q_1)}\)
Apply Aitken’s formula: \(\displaystyle S_{k+1} = S_k - \frac{(q_1 - S_k)^2}{q_2 - 2q_1 + S_k}\)
Set \(k \leftarrow k+1\) and repeat.

Each outer iteration consumes two Newton steps but, once the iterates are close to the root and rounding in \(f\) does not dominate, produces a correction far more accurate than either step alone. The combined effect restores roughly quadratic convergence at roots where unaided Newton would only converge linearly.
In general, at a root \(p\) of multiplicity \(m\) the Newton map \(g(x) = x - f(x)/f'(x)\) has \(g'(p) = (m-1)/m \neq 1\), so if \(g\) is smooth enough near \(p\), Steffensen’s iteration converges at least quadratically from starts close enough to \(p\). Case 2 shows this rate: from \(S_1\) to \(S_3\) its Steffensen errors have exponents \(-2\), \(-4\) and \(-8\), doubling each step; that of \(S_4\) reaches rounding level.
Rounding limits both methods near a double root, where \(f\) is tiny and is computed with a large relative error. In Case 1 the expanded cubic rounds to exactly 0 at the third Steffensen iterate, so both Newton steps from it return the same point and the \(\Delta^2\) denominator is 0. In Case 3 the error stalls after three steps at a few times \(10^{-8}\).


Summary Comparison









Method

Convergence order
Notes

Steffensen’s method is Aitken’s process applied to a fixed-point iteration, here the Newton-Raphson map; Accelerated and Modified Newton-Raphson and the Improved Newton Method restore quadratic convergence at multiple roots in other ways, and the Power Method applies Aitken’s process to its eigenvalue estimates.

title: Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method
text:
Description
The Adams-Bashforth-Moulton (ABM) method is a predictor-corrector multistep scheme for the initial value problem \(y' = f(t,y)\), \(y(t_0) = y_0\), on a grid \(t_n = t_0 + nh\) in \([t_0, b]\). One-step methods such as Euler’s, Heun’s and Runge-Kutta step from the current point alone; ABM reuses the slopes \(f_k = f(t_k, y_k)\) at the four latest points. In the 4-step form, an explicit Adams-Bashforth predictor estimates \(y_{n+1}\) from this history, and an implicit Adams-Moulton corrector immediately refines it:
\[
p_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{h}{24}\bigl(55 f_n - 59 f_{n-1} + 37 f_{n-2} - 9 f_{n-3}\bigr),
\]
\[
y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{h}{24}\bigl(9 f(t_{n+1}, p_{n+1}) + 19 f_n - 5 f_{n-1} + f_{n-2}\bigr).
\]
Both formulas integrate a cubic that interpolates the slopes over \([t_n, t_{n+1}]\): the predictor’s cubic passes through the four past slopes, the corrector’s through three past slopes and the predicted one. With the past slopes stored, a step needs only two new evaluations of \(f\), at \(p_{n+1}\) and at \(y_{n+1}\).
Mathews’ theorem assumes that \(f\) is continuous and satisfies a Lipschitz condition in \(y\), and the coefficients assume a fixed step \(h\). ABM is not self-starting: \(y_1\), \(y_2\), \(y_3\) must come from a one-step method accurate to \(O(h^4)\), usually fourth-order Runge-Kutta.
In general (Mathews’ precision theorem), if \(y \in C^5[t_0, b]\), the local truncation error is \(O(h^5)\) and the global error \(|y(t_n) - y_n|\) is \(O(h^4)\), so halving a small enough \(h\) cuts the error about 16-fold. Since predictor and corrector have equal order, their difference estimates the local error, \(y(t_{n+1}) - y_{n+1} \approx -\tfrac{19}{270}(y_{n+1} - p_{n+1})\) for slowly varying \(y^{(5)}\), and can guide the step size. Case 1 does not show the \(h^4\) rate: up to \(m = 90\) instability sets the \(y(5)\) error, which falls 190-fold from \(m = 70\) to \(m = 80\), against 1.7 for \(h^4\). For \(m \ge 100\) the error does not grow after the frames’ shading begins; the largest error is truncation error near \(t \approx 3.3\), and the damped tail cuts the \(y(5)\) error faster than \(h^4\).
The pair is only conditionally stable: on \(y' = \lambda y\) with real \(\lambda < 0\) it damps errors only while \(h|\lambda| \le 1.285\). In Case 1, \(y' = 1 - t\sqrt[3]{y}\), \(y(0) = 1\), the solution decays to \(y(5) = 0.0081199\), and \(\partial f/\partial y = -t/(3y^{2/3})\) reaches \(-41.3\) at \(t = 5\), so by a frozen-coefficient analysis \(h\,|\partial f/\partial y|\) passes \(1.285\) before \(t = 5\) in every frame. For \(m = 12\) to \(60\) the run leaves the reference in the tail, its largest error is between \(0.096\) and \(0.74\), and \(y(5)\) jumps between \(-0.363\) and \(0.632\). The end value alone can also mislead: at \(m = 12\), \(y(5)\) is off by \(0.013\), while the run is off by \(0.74\) at \(t \approx 4.17\).
Predictor-Corrector Methods sets out the general framework, Milne-Simpson’s Method is the other fourth-order predictor-corrector pair, the Runge-Kutta Method supplies the starting values, and Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg is a one-step alternative with an adaptive step.

title: Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Method
text:
Animations
The animation below repeats the step-refinement sweep of Mathews’ animation for legacy Example 11 of the module: \(y' = 1 - t\sqrt[3]{y}\), \(y(0)=1\), over \(0 \le t \le 5\). Each frame is a complete ABM4 run with \(m\) subintervals (\(h=5/m\), the first three steps by RK4), for the 21 values of Mathews’ animation, \(m = 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48, 52, 56, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 120, 150\), labelled with the computed \(y(5)\) and its error.
The thick gray curve is a high-accuracy reference trajectory computed with fixed-step RK4 at \(h=10^{-4}\), since no closed-form exact solution is used for this case.

Case 1 - ABM4 predictor-corrector step-refinement sweep, \(y' = 1 - t\sqrt[3]{y}\), \(y(0)=1\), \(m = 12\) to \(150\) subintervals
Behavior: The reference solution rises from \(y(0)=1\) to about \(1.4498\) near \(t=0.88\), then decays to \(y(5)=0.0081199\). For \(m=12\) through \(52\) the computed curve visibly breaks away from the reference in the tail (from \(t\approx3.2\) to \(4.7\), depending on \(m\)), and each of these runs goes below zero somewhere (then \(\sqrt[3]{y}\) is the real cube root), at \(m=48\) only to \(-0.0049\), too little to see. For \(m=56\) and \(60\) the run stays on the reference until about \(t=4.8\) and \(4.9\) and then rises above it, by up to \(0.11\) and \(0.096\). Across \(m=12\) to \(60\) the end value jumps between \(y(5)\approx-0.363\) (\(m=20\)) and \(0.632\) (\(m=16\)), and a small absolute end error can hide a much worse run: at \(m=12\), \(y(5)=0.0214\) is off by only \(0.013\) (an error 1.6 times the exact value, so \(y(5)\) is 2.6 times it), while the run is off by \(0.74\) at \(t\approx4.17\). From \(m=60\) on, the error in \(y(5)\) falls at every refinement: \(9.6\times10^{-2}\) at \(m=60\), \(2.1\times10^{-3}\) at \(m=70\) (26% of \(y(5)\), but too small to see in the frame), \(1.1\times10^{-5}\) at \(m=80\), \(4.5\times10^{-9}\) at \(m=100\) and \(1.4\times10^{-10}\) at \(m=150\).
A frozen-coefficient linear stability analysis shows where this can start, not how large it gets. \(\partial f/\partial y=-t/(3y^{2/3})\) reaches \(-41.3\) at \(t=5\), and this ABM4 predictor-corrector is stable on \(y'=\lambda y\) with real \(\lambda<0\) only while \(h|\lambda|\le1.285\). So for every \(m\le160\) (\(h>0.0311\)), which includes every frame here, \(h\,|\partial f/\partial y|\) exceeds \(1.285\) before \(t=5\) (the shaded region, from \(t\approx2.83\) at \(m=12\) to \(t\approx4.89\) at \(m=150\)), and past that point the linear analysis no longer guarantees that errors are damped. For \(m=12\) to \(60\) the error at the last step before the shaded region is between \(5.6\times10^{-5}\) and \(2.2\times10^{-3}\), and after it the error reaches \(0.096\) to \(0.74\); for \(m=100\), \(120\) and \(150\) it is below \(10^{-8}\) there, and the error at \(t=5\) is smaller still. So \(h=0.0311\) is a linear stability bound, not an accuracy threshold. The module’s worked solution of Example 11 uses \(n=50\), \(100\) and \(150\) steps: the \(n=100\) and \(150\) runs (frames \(m=100\) and \(150\) here) end at \(y(5)=0.0081199\), while the \(n=50\) run (\(h=0.1\)) falls to \(y_{48}\approx-0.0018\) at \(t=4.8\) and ends at \(y(5)\approx0.138\), about 17 times the exact value.

title: 2D Trapezoidal and Simpson Rules
text:
Description
The 2D Trapezoidal and 2D Simpson rules approximate a double integral over a rectangle, \(\int_a^b\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx\), from values of \(f\) on a grid. Examples 1–6 of the archived module, and both animations, use \[
I = \int_0^1 \int_0^1 8e^{-x^2-y^4}\,dy\,dx,
\] the volume under the surface \(z=8e^{-x^2-y^4}\) over \(R=\{(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\ 0\le y\le 1\}\).
The rectangle \([a,b]\times[c,d]\) is divided into \(m\) panels of width \(h=(b-a)/m\) in \(x\) and \(n\) panels of width \(k=(d-c)/n\) in \(y\), with nodes \(x_i=a+ih\) and \(y_j=c+jk\). Each rule applies the 1D rule along \(y\) at every \(x_i\) and then along \(x\), so the weight of a node is the product of the 1D weights. The 2D Trapezoidal rule is \[
I_{T} = hk\sum_{i=0}^{m}\sum_{j=0}^{n} w_i w_j f(x_i,y_j),
\qquad
w_0=w_m=\tfrac{1}{2},\ w_i=1\ (1\le i\le m-1),
\] and the 2D Simpson rule is \[
I_{S} = \frac{hk}{9}\sum_{i=0}^{m}\sum_{j=0}^{n} a_i a_j f(x_i,y_j),
\qquad
a_0=a_m=1,\ a_i=4\ \text{(odd } i\text{)},\ a_i=2\ \text{(even } i,\ 0<i<m\text{)}.
\] The weights \(w_j\) and \(a_j\) are defined in the same way with \(n\) in place of \(m\). For Simpson’s rule \(m\) and \(n\) must be even. The general error results, as Mathews states them, are \[
\int_a^b\!\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx = I_T + O(h^2) + O(k^2) = I_S + O(h^4) + O(k^4).
\] They hold when \(f_{xx}\) and \(f_{yy}\) (for \(I_T\)), or \(f_{xxxx}\) and \(f_{yyyy}\) (for \(I_S\)), are continuous on \(R\). Halving both \(h\) and \(k\) then typically divides the error by about 4 for \(I_T\) and 16 for \(I_S\).
The animations use square meshes, \(m=n\) and \(h=k=1/n\). The table gives the frames that double \(n\); the ratio is the previous row’s error divided by this row’s.

The trapezoidal ratios in Case 1 are close to 4 from the start. The Simpson ratios in Case 2 swing between 13.8 and 21.7 on the coarse meshes and settle near 16 only on the fine ones (16.6 from \(n=10\) to \(n=20\)), so the rate cannot be read off two coarse frames. The coarse Simpson mesh also misleads visually: on the \(2\times2\) frame the quadratic along \(x=0\) peaks at about 8.30, above the largest value of \(f\), which is 8. Simpson’s higher order pays off quickly: its \(6\times6\) mesh, with 49 nodes, has error \(6.7\times10^{-4}\), smaller than the trapezoidal error \(0.0029\) on the \(20\times20\) mesh with 441 nodes. Both rules need a rectangle; when the inner limits depend on \(x\), as in the module’s Example 7, Simpson’s rule is applied in \(y\) at each \(x\) and then in \(x\).
These are the tensor-product forms of the 1D Trapezoidal Rule and Simpson’s Rule; Gauss-Legendre Quadrature chooses the nodes as well as the weights, and Monte Carlo Integration avoids the grid, which needs \((m+1)^d\) nodes in \(d\) dimensions with \(m\) panels per axis.

Case 1 - 2D Trapezoidal Rule, \(f(x,y)=8e^{-x^2-y^4}\)
Behavior: The coarse-to-fine tensor grid updates over the whole square each frame. The approximation converges toward the archived reference value, with visible second-order error decay under refinement. The black lines join the sample nodes with straight segments: they are the grid lines of the piecewise-bilinear interpolant, whose integral is the trapezoidal value \(I_T\).

Case 2 - 2D Simpson Rule, \(f(x,y)=8e^{-x^2-y^4}\)
Behavior: Simpson tensor-product weights are recomputed on each refined mesh. Compared with trapezoidal refinement, the Simpson estimate reaches high accuracy with fewer refinements. The black curves are the quadratics through the sample nodes over each pair of panels along every grid line: the grid lines of the piecewise-biquadratic interpolant (one patch per 2x2 block of panels), whose integral is the Simpson value \(I_S\). On the 2x2 mesh they differ from the trapezoidal straight lines by up to 0.51 in \(z\).

title: Accelerated & Modified Newton-Raphson
text:
Description
These methods find a root of \(f(x) = 0\) that has multiplicity \(m \ge 2\), where standard Newton-Raphson slows down. Mathews calls \(x^*\) a root of order \(m\) if \(f(x^*) = f'(x^*) = \cdots = f^{(m-1)}(x^*) = 0\) and \(f^{(m)}(x^*) \neq 0\), with \(f^{(m)}\) continuous near \(x^*\). Write \(e_n = x_n - x^*\). In general, standard Newton-Raphson converges quadratically at simple roots but degrades to linear convergence at multiple roots, \(e_{n+1} \approx \tfrac{m-1}{m}\,e_n\), because \(f'(x^*) = 0\) there. Two methods restore quadratic convergence.
Accelerated Newton-Raphson (Method A) multiplies the Newton step by the known root multiplicity \(m\): \[x_{n+1} = x_n - m \cdot \frac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\] This compensates for the vanishing derivative and recovers the quadratic rate. It requires knowing \(m\) in advance.
Modified Newton-Raphson (Method B) avoids needing \(m\) by reformulating the problem. If \(f\) has a root of multiplicity \(m\) at \(x^*\), then \(h(x) = f(x)/f'(x)\) has a simple root at \(x^*\). Applying Newton’s method to \(h\) gives: \[x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)\,f'(x_n)}{f'(x_n)^2 - f(x_n)\,f''(x_n)}\] This also converges quadratically, without knowing \(m\). It costs a second derivative at every step, and since \(h\) also has a simple root where \(f\) does, it works at simple roots too.
Both methods require that \(f\) be sufficiently smooth near the root and that the starting point \(x_0\) be close enough to \(x^*\). Under those hypotheses both converge quadratically in general, \(|e_{n+1}| \approx C\,|e_n|^2\) for large \(n\). All three cases start from \(x_0 = 1.2\) at the double root \(x^* = 1\) of \(f(x) = (x-1)^2(x+2)\). Case 1 shows standard Newton’s linear rate: \(e_n / e_{n-1}\) is 0.515, 0.508, 0.504, … and tends to \(1/2\). Case 2 and Case 3 show the quadratic rate: \(e_n / e_{n-1}^2\) tends to \(1/6\) for Method A and to \(-1/6\) for Method B, so Method B’s first step lands left of the root. The errors, in 50-digit arithmetic:

Method A fails if \(m\) is wrong: in general, a multiplier \(\mu \neq m\) is at best linear, \(e_{n+1} \approx (1 - \mu/m)\,e_n\), converging linearly only for \(0 < \mu < 2m\); standard Newton is \(\mu = 1\). With \(\mu = 2\) at the cubic’s simple root \(x = -2\) the ratio is the borderline \(-1\): from \(x_0 = -2.2\) the iterates alternate sides (\(-1.844444\), \(-2.193762\), …) and creep in sublinearly, still 0.17 away after ten steps. Rounding also limits both methods, because near the double root \(f(x_n) \approx 3e_n^2\) is small and computed with a large relative error. In double precision their third iterates already miss the table, with \(e_3 = 3.6 \times 10^{-12}\) and \(8.4 \times 10^{-12}\); there \(f\) evaluates to exactly 0, so later steps change nothing.
Both modify Newton-Raphson; the Improved Newton Method adds an adaptive method that needs no \(m\), Aitken’s and Steffensen’s acceleration speeds up the linear Newton sequence instead, and Halley’s Method uses \(f''\) to converge cubically at simple roots.

title: Accelerated & Modified Newton-Raphson
text:
Animations
The three animations below show a Newton-style line diagram for three methods, one per animation, applied to the same double root. At each iterate \(x_n\), the line from the plotted curve at \(x_n\) to the x-axis intercept traces the next approximation \(x_{n+1}\). In Cases 1 and 3 that line is the tangent to the plotted curve; in Case 2 it has half the tangent slope (see Case 2). Cases 1 and 2 both plot \(f(x)\); Case 3 plots \(h(x) = f(x)/f'(x)\), which has a simple root where \(f\) has a double root.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.
The three cases reproduce Examples 1(b), 2 and 4 of Mathews’ Accelerated and Modified Newton Methods module, all at the double root of the same cubic. The module’s Examples 1(a), 3, 5 and 6, which apply standard Newton-Raphson at the simple root of that cubic (Example 1(a)), the accelerated method (Example 3) and the modified method (Example 5) at a double and a triple root of a fifth-degree polynomial, and the standard, accelerated and modified methods at a root of higher multiplicity (Example 6), are not animated here.

Case 1 — Standard Newton-Raphson, linear convergence, \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2\), \(x_0 = 1.2\)
Behavior: \(f(x) = (x-1)^2(x+2)\) has a double root at \(x^* = 1\). Because \(f'(x^*) = 0\) at a multiple root, the asymptotic error constant is \((m-1)/m = 1/2\), meaning each step only halves the error. Near the root \(f(x) \approx 3(x-1)^2\), so the tangent at \(x_n\) meets the axis between \(x_n\) and \(x^*\), only about halfway there (\(x_{n+1} - 1 \approx (x_n - 1)/2\)). Each step covers just under half the remaining distance (1.2, 1.10303, 1.052356, 1.026401, …), so after 12 steps \(x_{12} = 1.000052\) is still about \(5.2 \times 10^{-5}\) from the root. At the scale of the plot only the first few steps can be told apart: from \(x_5\) on, the iterate is less than 0.007 from the root and its marker covers the root, so the remaining halvings show only in the legend value.
Julia source



Standard Newton-Raphson tangent-line animation on f(x)=x³−3x+2: slow linear convergence from x₀=1.2 toward the double root at x=1 over 12 iterations; from x₅ on the marker covers the root and the progress shows only in the legend value




Case 2 — Accelerated Newton-Raphson (Method A, \(m=2\)), quadratic convergence, \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2\), \(x_0 = 1.2\)
Behavior: The accelerated formula \(x_{n+1} = x_n - m \cdot \tfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}\) with \(m = 2\) enlarges each Newton step by the known multiplicity, compensating for the vanishing derivative at the double root. The orange line from \((x_n,\, f(x_n))\) is therefore not the tangent: its slope is \(f'(x_n)/2\), half the tangent slope, so it meets the axis twice as far from \(x_n\) as the Newton tangent would. This restores quadratic convergence: \(|e_{n+1}| \approx C |e_n|^2\). From the same starting point as Case 1, \(x_1 = 1.006061\), \(x_2 = 1.000006\), and \(x_3\) equals 1 to six decimals. Requires knowing \(m\) in advance.
Julia source



Accelerated Newton-Raphson (m=2) animation on f(x)=x³−3x+2: orange lines with half the tangent slope give steps twice the Newton step; quadratic convergence from x₀=1.2 to the double root at x=1, with x₃ equal to 1 to six decimals




Case 3 — Modified Newton-Raphson (Method B), quadratic convergence, \(f(x) = x^3 - 3x + 2\), \(x_0 = 1.2\)
Behavior: Define \(h(x) = f(x)/f'(x)\). At a double root of \(f\), \(h\) has a simple root — so standard Newton on \(h\) gives quadratic convergence. The iteration formula \[x_{n+1} = x_n - \frac{f(x_n)\,f'(x_n)}{f'(x_n)^2 - f(x_n)\,f''(x_n)}\] implements Newton on \(h(x)\) using \(f\), \(f'\), and \(f''\) directly. The animation plots \(h(x) = (x-1)(x+2)/(3(x+1))\) with the tangent lines dashed. \(h\) is nearly straight between the root and \(x_0\), so the first tangent lies almost on the curve and takes the iterate in one step to \(x_1 = 0.994152\), just left of the root. At this scale that overshoot and the later steps are too small to see, and the iterates are read from the legend: \(x_2 = 0.999994\), and, as in Case 2, \(x_3\) equals 1 to six decimals. Does not require knowing \(m\).
Julia source



Modified Newton-Raphson (Method B) tangent-line animation on h(x)=f(x)/f’(x): the dashed tangent from x₀=1.2 lies almost on the nearly straight curve and takes the iterate in one step to x₁=0.994152, just left of x=1 (double root of f); quadratic convergence, with x₃ equal to 1 to six decimals, without knowing the multiplicity

title: Adaptive Simpson’s Rule
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Adaptive Simpson’s Rule
text:
Description
Adaptive Simpson quadrature approximates \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) to a requested tolerance \(\varepsilon\) by recursively halving intervals until a local error estimate passes, so small subintervals appear only where \(f\) needs them. On an interval \([a,b]\) with midpoint \(m\), \[
S(a,b)=\frac{b-a}{6}\left[f(a)+4f(m)+f(b)\right],
\] and refinement compares \(S(a,b)\) against \(S(a,m)+S(m,b)\), which needs only two new values of \(f\), at the quarter-points.
The animation uses the acceptance test of Mathews’ routine: \([a,b]\) is accepted when \[
\left|S(a,m)+S(m,b)-S(a,b)\right| < \varepsilon_{[a,b]},
\] where the whole interval starts with \(\varepsilon\) and each half of a split interval gets half its tolerance, so refinement concentrates where curvature or oscillation is strongest. An accepted interval contributes \(S(a,m)+S(m,b)\) to the result. A common variant uses \(15\,\varepsilon_{[a,b]}\) on the right; for the example below it accepts 9 subintervals (the finest is \([0,1/32]\)) instead of 20 (the finest is \([0,1/2048]\)).
The test rests on a general result that needs \(f\in C^4\) on each interval. Simpson’s error on an interval of width \(w\) is \(-\tfrac{w^5}{2880}f^{(4)}(c)\) for some \(c\) in it, so halving the interval divides the error by about 16, and if \(f^{(4)}\) is nearly constant across \([a,b]\), \[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx-\bigl[S(a,m)+S(m,b)\bigr]\approx\frac{S(a,m)+S(m,b)-S(a,b)}{15}.
\] Under that assumption each accepted interval’s error is below about \(\varepsilon_{[a,b]}/15\), and because each split divides a tolerance between two halves, the accepted tolerances add up to exactly \(\varepsilon\); the total error is then at most about \(\varepsilon/15\), an estimate rather than a guaranteed bound. In Case 1 the routine’s value \(2.016273\) is within \(7.1\times10^{-6}\) of the integral, well inside \(\varepsilon=10^{-3}\), even though \(f\) is not \(C^4\) at \(x=0\). There the error on \([0,w]\) shrinks only like \(w^{5/3}\), and on \([0,1/2048]\) it is about 7 times the estimate, yet under its tolerance.
The test sees only five values of \(f\) per interval and can be fooled. For \(f(x)=\sin^2(4\pi x)\) on \([0,1]\), all five samples are \(0\), so the first test passes (at \(\varepsilon=10^{-3}\) or \(10^{-6}\)) and the routine returns \(0\) for an integral of \(1/2\). Mathews’ routine also has no limit on the depth of recursion. For the step \(f(x)=0\) on \([0,1/3)\) and \(1\) on \([1/3,1]\), the interval holding the jump fails the test at every level, since \(|S(a,m)+S(m,b)-S(a,b)|\) and the tolerance both shrink in proportion to its width; the recursion stops at depth 54 only when a floating-point midpoint rounds onto an endpoint.
Simpson’s Rule applies the same formula with one fixed step size; adding the error estimate to \(S(a,m)+S(m,b)\) is one Richardson Extrapolation step and gives Boole’s Rule on the interval, as in Romberg Integration.

title: Adaptive Simpson’s Rule
text:
Animations
Each animation below shows the adaptive Simpson refinement process for \(f(x)=1+e^{-x}\sin(8x^{2/3})\) on \([0,2]\) with tolerance \(\varepsilon=10^{-3}\). Starting from the single panel \([0,2]\), each frame splits the widest panel that fails the test (leftmost first, except that \([1/2,1]\) is split before \([0,1/2]\), as in Mathews’ trace) and marks the two new sample points in blue; “Approximation” is the composite Simpson sum of \(S(a,b)\) over the panels drawn.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Adaptive Refinement, \(f(x)=1+e^{-x}\sin(8x^{2/3})\), \([0,2]\), \(\varepsilon=10^{-3}\)
Behavior: Refinement stops when all 20 panels pass the test. The 41 points drawn are the nodes of the composite rule; the test also evaluates each panel’s two quarter-points, so reaching this partition samples \(f\) at 81 distinct points. \([1.5,2]\) is never split, while 19 of the 41 nodes lie in \([0,1/8]\). The last seven frames split \([0,1/16], [0,1/32], \dots, [0,1/1024]\) in turn, because \(f'\) is unbounded at \(x=0\) (\(f'(x)\approx \tfrac{16}{3}x^{-1/3}\) near \(0\)); the panels split in the last five frames are at most \(1/64\) wide (under 5 pixels at this scale), so the blue label names each one. The final estimate \(2.016252\) differs from the integral \(2.016280\) by \(-2.8\times10^{-5}\); summing \(S(a,m)+S(m,b)\) over the same panels, as the recursive routine returns, gives \(2.016273\).

title: Aitken’s and Neville’s Interpolation
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Aitken’s and Neville’s Interpolation
text:
Description
Neville’s interpolation algorithm evaluates the unique polynomial of degree at most \(n-1\) through data points \((x_i,y_i)\) without first converting to expanded polynomial coefficients. It uses a recursive tableau
\[
P_{i,i}(x)=y_i,
\qquad
P_{i,j}(x)=\frac{(x-x_i)P_{i+1,j}(x)-(x-x_j)P_{i,j-1}(x)}{x_j-x_i},
\quad i<j.
\]
Here \(P_{i,j}\) is the interpolant on the consecutive nodes \(x_i,\dots,x_j\), and the final interpolated value at a query point \(x\) is \(P_{0,n-1}(x)\). Aitken’s scheme is a different arrangement of the same idea, repeated linear interpolation. With \(Q_{0,j}=y_j\), and \(Q_{k,j}\) the interpolant on \(x_0,\dots,x_{k-1},x_j\), it computes
\[
Q_{k,j}(x)=\frac{(x-x_{k-1})\,Q_{k-1,j}(x)-(x-x_j)\,Q_{k-1,k-1}(x)}{x_j-x_{k-1}},
\qquad j\ge k.
\]
At stage \(k\) it combines the interpolant on \(x_0,\dots,x_{k-1}\) with the interpolant on \(x_0,\dots,x_{k-2},x_j\), so every entry in a column shares the same leading nodes, whereas Neville’s scheme combines interpolants on neighbouring runs of consecutive nodes. Entries built on different sets of nodes generally differ, but both schemes compute the interpolant on \(x_0,\dots,x_k\) for every \(k\), so they produce the same sequence \(Q_{k,k}=P_{0,k}\), \(k=0,\dots,n-1\) (the diagonal of Mathews’ two tableaux), and end with the same interpolated value. The animations below use Neville’s scheme.
Both recursions need only the values \(y_i\) and distinct nodes, since they divide by node differences; the nodes need not be equally spaced. Each query point costs \(n(n-1)/2\) new tableau entries.
In general, if \(y_i=f(x_i)\) and \(f\in C^{j+1}\) on an interval \(I\) that contains \(x\) and the nodes \(x_0,\dots,x_j\), the polynomial is the same as the Lagrange interpolant and has the same remainder term: for some \(c\in I\),
\[
f(x)-P_{0,j}(x)=\frac{f^{(j+1)}(c)}{(j+1)!}\prod_{i=0}^{j}(x-x_i).
\]
Since \(f-P_{0,j-1}=(P_{0,j}-P_{0,j-1})+(f-P_{0,j})\), the change between successive diagonal entries estimates the error of the earlier one, and Mathews tests convergence on these values. Case 2 shows both: each error at \(\hat x=1.8\) lies within the remainder bounds with \(e^1\le f^{(j+1)}(c)\le e^{\max(x_j,1.8)}\), and the changes 2.47, 0.772, 0.0877, \(1.25\times10^{-3}\), \(-5.66\times10^{-5}\) track the errors 3.33, 0.861, 0.0889, \(1.19\times10^{-3}\), \(-5.23\times10^{-5}\) of \(P_{0,0},\dots,P_{0,4}\).
Adding a node does not guarantee a smaller error. In Case 1, \(P_{0,2}\) uses only \(0,\pi/4,\pi/2\), so at \(x=\pi\) it extrapolates: the product \(\prod_i(x-x_i)\) is 11.6 there, against at most 0.19 between the nodes, and the largest error on \([0,\pi]\) rises from 0.90 to 1.66. The convergence test can also mislead: in Case 1, \(P_{0,4}=P_{0,3}\), so the last change is zero everywhere, yet \(P_{0,3}\) is in error by up to \(8.1\times10^{-3}\) on \([0,\pi]\).
The polynomial is the one the Lagrange and Newton forms give; Chebyshev Approximation chooses nodes that keep the product term small, Romberg Integration is Neville’s scheme in the variable \(h^2\), applied to trapezoidal sums and evaluated at \(h^2=0\), and Aitken’s interpolation is a different method from Aitken’s \(\Delta^2\) acceleration.

title: Aitken’s and Neville’s Interpolation
text:
Animations
The animations below illustrate Neville’s algorithm for polynomial interpolation. Each frame adds one node and shows \(P_{0,j}(x)\), the interpolant of degree at most \(j\) through the first \(j+1\) nodes: Case 1 uses \(f(x) = \cos(x)\) at 5 nodes \(x_0 = 0,\, \tfrac{\pi}{4},\, \tfrac{\pi}{2},\, \tfrac{3\pi}{4},\, \pi\) (\(j=0,\dots,4\)), and Case 2 uses \(f(x)=e^x\) at 6 nodes \(x_i = 1 + i/4\) (\(j=0,\dots,5\)).
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.
No archived animation GIF is available for this topic in the current snapshot; Mathews’ module has only static examples. Case 2 animates the module’s Example 3: \(e^x\) at the nodes \(x_i = 1 + i/4\), \(i=0,\dots,5\), evaluated at \(\hat x = 1.8\). Case 1 is the page’s own example, chosen to show that adding a node can increase the error and that symmetric nodes can make \(P_{0,4}=P_{0,3}\). The module’s other examples, 1, 2 and 4–7, are not animated here. Example 1 builds a quadratic through three nodes by recursion and plots the function with each linear interpolant and the quadratic. Examples 2–7 fill in Aitken’s and Neville’s tableaux at a single evaluation point, and Examples 3–5 also plot the function with the successive interpolants through the first one, two, three, … of their nodes (up to degree 3, 4 and 2 respectively), the kind of picture these animations build frame by frame, drawn there as one static plot; Case 2 carries Example 3’s picture on to degree 5. The explorations the module links to on its Theory and Proof page are not animated here either.

Case 1 — Neville’s algorithm: \(P_{0,0}\) through \(P_{0,4}\) for \(\cos(x)\)
Behavior: Neville’s algorithm builds the interpolating polynomial of degree at most \(n\) by combining two polynomials of degree at most \(n-1\): \(P_{i,j}(x) = \tfrac{(x-x_i)P_{i+1,j} - (x-x_j)P_{i,j-1}}{x_j - x_i}\). Adding a node does not always reduce the error: the largest error \(|P_{0,j}(x)-\cos x|\) on \([0,\pi]\) falls from 2.00 at \(j=0\) to 0.90 at \(j=1\), rises to 1.66 at \(j=2\) (at \(x=\pi\), where the quadratic reaches \(-2.66\)), then drops to \(8.1\times10^{-3}\) at \(j=3\). With these symmetric nodes the cubic \(P_{0,3}\) already passes through \((\pi,-1)\), because \(\cos\) is odd about \(\pi/2\), so the fifth node leaves the polynomial unchanged: \(P_{0,4}=P_{0,3}\), and the last two frames show the same curve.

Neville algorithm building successive polynomial interpolants of cos(x) at nodes 0, pi/4, pi/2, 3pi/4, pi, from the degree-0 constant to the five-node interpolant P_{0,4}, which is the same cubic as P_{0,3}




Case 2 — Mathews’ Example 3: \(P_{0,0}\) through \(P_{0,5}\) for \(e^x\) at \(\hat x = 1.8\)
Behavior: The nodes are \(x_i = 1 + i/4\) (\(1, 1.25, \dots, 2.25\)), and each frame marks \(P_{0,j}(1.8)\), the top-row entry of Neville’s tableau. The values 2.718282, 5.188877, 5.960761, 6.048454, 6.049700 and 6.049643 match the diagonal of Mathews’ Neville tableau and approach \(e^{1.8}=6.049647\). Here every added node helps: the error \(e^{1.8}-P_{0,j}(1.8)\) falls in size at each step, through 3.33, 0.861, 0.0889, \(1.19\times10^{-3}\), \(-5.23\times10^{-5}\) and \(4.34\times10^{-6}\) (negative only at \(j=4\)), and the largest error on \([1,2.25]\) also falls at each step, from 6.77 at \(j=0\) to \(3.2\times10^{-5}\) at \(j=5\). From \(j=4\) on, \(P_{0,j}\) and \(e^x\) are indistinguishable at the plot’s scale (at \(j=3\) they part only toward the right edge), so the legend carries the values at \(\hat x\).

title: Bézier Curves
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Bézier Curves
text:
Description
A Bézier curve solves a design problem, not an equation: it draws a smooth curve between two endpoints, shaped by control points that it does not, in general, pass through. With control points \(P_0,\ldots,P_n\), the degree-\(n\) curve is the Bernstein polynomial form
\[
B(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}\binom{n}{i}(1-t)^{n-i}t^iP_i,\qquad t\in[0,1].
\]
Mathews writes the cubic, with \(P_i=(x_i,y_i)\), in powers of \(t\); expanding the Bernstein form gives the same:
\[
x(t)=x_0+3t\,(x_1-x_0)+3t^2\,(x_0+x_2-2x_1)+t^3\,(x_3-x_0+3x_1-3x_2),
\]
and the same with \(y\) in place of \(x\). The animations evaluate the curve by the de Casteljau algorithm, which repeatedly interpolates linearly between adjacent points until one point remains:
\[
P_i^{(0)}=P_i,\qquad P_i^{(k)}(t)=(1-t)\,P_i^{(k-1)}(t)+t\,P_{i+1}^{(k-1)}(t),\qquad B(t)=P_0^{(n)}(t).
\]
Orange points are level 1, green level 2, and red is \(B(t)\). At \(t=1/2\) in Case 1, the levels are \((3/2,7/4)\), \((9/4,3/4)\), \((15/4,1/2)\), then \((15/8,5/4)\), \((3,5/8)\), and finally \(B(1/2)=(39/16,15/16)\).
The construction needs only the control points and \(t\in[0,1]\); there is no smoothness hypothesis. In general, the curve starts at \(P_0\), ends at \(P_n\), and is tangent there to its handles: \(B'(0)=n(P_1-P_0)\) and \(B'(1)=n(P_n-P_{n-1})\). The Bernstein weights are nonnegative and sum to 1, so the curve stays inside the convex hull of its control points, and the segment joining the two level-\((n-1)\) points (green) is tangent to it: \(B'(t)=n\bigl(P_1^{(n-1)}(t)-P_0^{(n-1)}(t)\bigr)\).
The curve is exactly the polynomial its control points define, so there is no truncation error, only rounding error. For \(0\le t\le 1\) every de Casteljau step is a convex combination, and in general its rounding error is at most a multiple, growing linearly with \(n\), of the unit roundoff times the size of the control points. Mathews’ power form is cheaper with Horner’s method, \(O(n)\) operations against \(O(n^2)\), but at high degree its coefficients can grow far larger than the control points and cancel, losing accuracy; for the cubics on this page both forms are accurate to about \(10^{-15}\).
Two features mislead readers expecting interpolation. The curve misses its handles: in Case 1 it passes no closer than 0.78 to \(P_1\) and 0.67 to \(P_2\). And control is global: every Bernstein weight is positive for \(0<t<1\), so moving one interior control point moves every point of the curve except the two ends. Case 2 doubles the handle lengths of Case 1, and the whole curve shifts, its leftmost point moving from \(x\approx 1.77\) to \(x\approx 1.33\).
A cubic Bézier curve is the Hermite clamped cubic with end values \(P_0\), \(P_3\) and end derivatives \(3(P_1-P_0)\), \(3(P_3-P_2)\); B-Splines join pieces with local control, while Cubic Splines and Lagrange interpolation pass through every given point.

title: Bézier Curves
text:
Animations
Each animation below demonstrates the de Casteljau algorithm for constructing a cubic Bézier curve. Tracing this point for all \(t \in [0,1]\) draws the full curve.

Case 1 — Mathews’ Example 3, \(P_0=(2,2)\), \(P_1=(1,1.5)\), \(P_2=(3.5,0)\), \(P_3=(4,1)\)
Behavior: The curve leaves \(P_0\) heading toward the handle \(P_1\), bends one way without an inflection, and arrives at \(P_3\) along the line from \(P_2\). Level-1 (orange), level-2 (green), and curve (red) points are shown at each \(t\). As \(t\) goes from 0 to 1, the red point traces the smooth cubic Bézier curve from \(P_0\) to \(P_3\).

De Casteljau construction for the cubic Bezier curve of Mathews’ Example 3, control points (2,2),(1,1.5),(3.5,0),(4,1): level-1 orange and level-2 green points locate the red point, which traces the smooth blue curve from P0 to P3




Case 2 — Mathews’ Example 4, handles twice as far out, \(P_0=(2,2)\), \(P_1=(0,1)\), \(P_2=(3,-1)\), \(P_3=(4,1)\)
Behavior: The endpoints and end-tangent directions are those of Case 1, but each handle sits twice as far from its endpoint. The de Casteljau construction proceeds identically. The curve stays closer to each end tangent and follows it farther before turning back, so its leftmost point is at \(x\approx 1.33\) instead of \(x\approx 1.77\) in Case 1. title: Boole’s Rule
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Boole’s Rule
text:
Description
Boole’s rule approximates a definite integral \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx\) from values of \(f\) at equally spaced points. It splits \([a,b]\) into \(n\) subintervals of width \(h=(b-a)/n\), with sample points \(x_i=a+ih\) and values \(f_i=f(x_i)\) for \(i=0,1,\dots,n\), and on each block of four subintervals \([x_{4k},x_{4k+4}]\) it replaces \(f\) by the quartic through the five nodes. Adding the areas under the quartics gives the composite rule \[
B_n = \frac{2h}{45}\sum_{k=0}^{n/4-1}\left(7f_{4k}+32f_{4k+1}+12f_{4k+2}+32f_{4k+3}+7f_{4k+4}\right).
\]
Each quartic spans four subintervals, so \(n\) must be a multiple of 4. The sums \(B_n\) converge to the integral for any continuous \(f\), but the error formula below needs more: \(f\) must be six times continuously differentiable on \([a,b]\), \(f\in C^6[a,b]\).
Although each panel uses a quartic, the rule is exact for every polynomial of degree 5, because the fifth-degree term’s error cancels by symmetry about the panel’s midpoint; the first term it misses involves \(f^{(6)}\). The general result, as Mathews states it: if \(f\in C^6[a,b]\), there is a \(c\) with \(a<c<b\) such that \[
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx - B_n = -\frac{2(b-a)\,f^{(6)}(c)}{945}\,h^6 .
\] The error is therefore \(O(h^6)\), the highest order of the four closed Newton-Cotes rules on this site, and halving \(h\) typically divides it by about 64. Closed rules with seven or more nodes per panel are exact to higher degree (the seven-node rule to degree 7). The animation on this page does not show the \(O(h^6)\) rate, because its integrand is not in \(C^6[0,2]\).
Case 1 shows what happens when that hypothesis fails. Its integrand \(f(x)=1+e^{-x}\sin(8x^{2/3})\) has \(f'\) unbounded at \(x=0\), and the error shrinks only like \(h^{5/3}\): in the last two rows of the table below, halving \(h\) divides it by 3.10 and then 3.17, close to \(2^{5/3}\approx 3.17\), not 64. The higher order then buys little: for \(n\) from 48 to 120, Boole’s error is about 0.85 times that of Simpson’s Rule at the same \(n\). A coarse partition misleads too: on the first quadrature frame (\(n=4\)) the single quartic misses the peak \(f\approx 1.92\) near \(x\approx 0.08\), and its error, \(-0.463\), is more than twice the Trapezoidal Rule’s \(-0.214\) on the same five points.

← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Broyden’s Method
text:
Description
Solving a nonlinear system \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{0}\) in \(n\) dimensions by Newton’s method is powerful but expensive: every iteration requires computing all \(n^2\) partial derivatives that form the Jacobian matrix \(J(\mathbf{X}^{(k)})\). In large problems this cost can dominate the computation. Broyden’s method eliminates that bottleneck by maintaining an approximate Jacobian that is cheaply updated at each step using only the change in function values — no additional derivative or finite-difference evaluations are needed after the first iteration.

Newton’s Method for Systems (the baseline)
For a vector function \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}) = \bigl(f_1(\mathbf{X}),\dots,f_n(\mathbf{X})\bigr)^T\) Newton’s method linearizes \(\mathbf{F}\) at the current iterate and solves the resulting \(n \times n\) linear system:
\[J\!\left(\mathbf{X}^{(k)}\right)\Delta\mathbf{X}^{(k)} = -\mathbf{F}\!\left(\mathbf{X}^{(k)}\right), \qquad \mathbf{X}^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{X}^{(k)} + \Delta\mathbf{X}^{(k)}.\]
It converges quadratically near a simple root but demands \(n^2\) new partial-derivative evaluations each step. See Nonlinear Systems for the full treatment.


Reducing Cost with a Finite-Difference Jacobian
One obvious improvement replaces every partial derivative with a finite-difference quotient. For two dimensions:
\[M_{ij} \approx \frac{F_i(\mathbf{X} + h\,\mathbf{e}_j) - F_i(\mathbf{X} - h\,\mathbf{e}_j)}{2h},\]
where \(\mathbf{e}_j\) is the \(j\)-th unit vector and \(h\) is a small step size. This “Pseudo-Newton” or finite-difference Newton approach trades symbolic derivatives for \(2n^2\) additional function evaluations per iteration. For large \(n\) this is still expensive.


The Broyden Update: A Quasi-Newton Method
Broyden’s method goes further: instead of recomputing (or re-approximating) the full Jacobian at every step, it updates the previous approximate Jacobian \(B_k\) using only the information gained in the last iteration. The key requirement is the quasi-Newton (secant) condition — the new approximate Jacobian must satisfy
\[B_{k+1}\,\mathbf{s}_k = \mathbf{y}_k,\]
where \(\mathbf{s}_k = \mathbf{X}^{(k+1)} - \mathbf{X}^{(k)}\) is the step taken and \(\mathbf{y}_k = \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}^{(k+1)}) - \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}^{(k)})\) is the corresponding change in function values. This is the multidimensional analogue of the scalar secant equation \(f'(x) \approx (f(x_1) - f(x_0))/(x_1 - x_0)\).
The secant condition alone does not uniquely determine \(B_{k+1}\) when \(n > 1\). Broyden’s rank-1 update resolves the ambiguity by choosing the matrix closest to \(B_k\) (in the Frobenius sense) that satisfies the secant condition:
\[B_{k+1} = B_k + \frac{\left(\mathbf{y}_k - B_k\,\mathbf{s}_k\right)\mathbf{s}_k^T}{\mathbf{s}_k^T\,\mathbf{s}_k}.\]
This is a least-change secant update: the correction to \(B_k\) has rank 1, so only \(O(n^2)\) arithmetic operations are needed to update the approximate Jacobian, and no new function evaluations are required beyond computing \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}^{(k+1)})\).


Algorithm
Step 0. Compute the exact Jacobian \(B_0 = J(\mathbf{X}^{(0)})\). Apply one Newton step to obtain the first iterate:
\[\mathbf{X}^{(1)} = \mathbf{X}^{(0)} - B_0^{-1}\,\mathbf{F}\!\left(\mathbf{X}^{(0)}\right).\]
For \(k = 1, 2, \dots\):

Evaluate \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}^{(k)})\).
Update the approximate Jacobian: \[B_k = B_{k-1} + \frac{\left(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}^{(k)}) - \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}^{(k-1)}) - B_{k-1}\,\mathbf{s}_{k-1}\right)\mathbf{s}_{k-1}^T}{\mathbf{s}_{k-1}^T\,\mathbf{s}_{k-1}}.\]
Solve \(B_k\,\Delta\mathbf{X} = -\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}^{(k)})\) for the step \(\Delta\mathbf{X}\).
Update: \(\mathbf{X}^{(k+1)} = \mathbf{X}^{(k)} + \Delta\mathbf{X}\).



Convergence
Broyden’s method converges superlinearly near a simple root — faster than linear, but slower than Newton’s quadratic rate. As a general result, this needs \(\mathbf{F}\) continuously differentiable with a Lipschitz-continuous Jacobian near the root \(\mathbf{X}^*\), \(J(\mathbf{X}^*)\) nonsingular (a simple root), and \(\mathbf{X}^{(0)}\) and \(B_0\) close enough to \(\mathbf{X}^*\) and \(J(\mathbf{X}^*)\); with \(B_0 = J(\mathbf{X}^{(0)})\), as here, \(B_0\) is close whenever \(\mathbf{X}^{(0)}\) is. The ratio of successive errors \(\|\mathbf{X}^{(k+1)} - \mathbf{X}^*\| / \|\mathbf{X}^{(k)} - \mathbf{X}^*\|\) then tends to zero: in Case A it is between 0.02 and 0.04 for each of the first four steps and about \(8\times10^{-4}\) for the fifth, where the log-scale residual plot steepens. Each iteration after the first avoids the \(n^2\) derivative evaluations, so when evaluating the Jacobian dominates the cost, Broyden’s method can reach a given accuracy in less total work than Newton’s method. As written, step 3 still solves a linear system, which costs \(O(n^3)\) for a dense matrix, the same order as the solve in Newton’s method; the arithmetic per iteration falls to \(O(n^2)\) when \(B_k^{-1}\) or a factorization of \(B_k\) is updated instead, for example with the Sherman–Morrison formula. Convergence can fail if the starting point is far from a root or if the approximate Jacobian becomes ill-conditioned.

title: Broyden’s Method
text:
Animations
Each animation below shows Broyden’s method converging on the nonlinear system
\[f_1(x,y) = 1 - 4x + 2x^2 - 2y^3 = 0, \qquad f_2(x,y) = -4 + x^4 + 4y + 4y^4 = 0.\]
The blue curve is \(f_1 = 0\) and the red curve is \(f_2 = 0\); their intersections are the solutions. The system has exactly two real solutions, near \((0.062,\,0.724)\) and \((1.556,\,-0.576)\), and both lie inside the plotted window. In the left panel each frame adds the next iterate \(\mathbf{X}^{(k)}\), connected to the earlier ones by a line; after the first (Newton) step the iterates are too close to the root to separate at this scale. The right panel plots \(\|\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}^{(k)})\|\) on a log scale, which is where the Broyden steps show.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.
The system and both starting points follow Mathews’ Broyden’s Method module: Example 5 poses this system for Broyden’s method, but its archived copy is missing the starting-point, result and graph images, so the starting points are those of the standard Broyden runs in Example 8, whose printed iterates these animations reproduce. The module’s Newton’s-method and pseudo-Newton examples (Examples 1 and 3), its improved Broyden method based on the Sherman–Morrison formula (Example 8), and its exercises in three and four dimensions are not animated here.

Case A — Convergent, \(\mathbf{X}^{(0)} = (0.1,\,0.7)\), root \(\approx (0.062,\, 0.724)\)
Behavior: Starting close to the upper intersection, the initial exact Newton step moves the iterate by about 0.05 and reduces \(\|\mathbf{F}\|\) from \(2.5\times10^{-1}\) to \(7.8\times10^{-3}\). The Broyden steps that follow update the approximate Jacobian by the rank-1 formula, with no new derivative evaluations, and bring \(\|\mathbf{F}\|\) down to about \(10^{-15}\) (machine precision) at \(\mathbf{X}^{(6)}\). From \(\mathbf{X}^{(0)}\) to \(\mathbf{X}^{(4)}\), \(\|\mathbf{F}\|\) shrinks by between 24 and 43 times per step, and over each of the last two steps by more than 1000 times, consistent with the superlinear convergence described above.

This case illustrates that the method is starting-point dependent: a different initial guess finds a different root.

title: Chebyshev Approximation Polynomial
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Chebyshev Approximation Polynomial
text:
Description
A Chebyshev approximation polynomial approximates a function \(f\) on an interval \([a,b]\) by the polynomial \(P_{n-1}\) of degree at most \(n-1\) that interpolates \(f\) at \(n\) Chebyshev nodes, \(P_{n-1}(x_k)=f(x_k)\). Chebyshev-node interpolation uses clustered nodes near interval endpoints to reduce oscillation compared with equally spaced interpolation at the same degree. This is why Chebyshev-based polynomial approximation is a standard remedy for Runge-type endpoint blow-up.
On an interval \([a,b]\), the \(n\) Chebyshev nodes are the roots \(t_k=\cos\bigl((2k-1)\pi/(2n)\bigr)\) of the Chebyshev polynomial \(T_n(t)=\cos(n\arccos t)\), mapped from \([-1,1]\) to \([a,b]\):
\[
x_k = \frac{a+b}{2} + \frac{b-a}{2}\cos\!\left(\frac{(2k-1)\pi}{2n}\right),\qquad k=1,\ldots,n.
\]
Mathews writes the interpolant as a sum of Chebyshev polynomials in \(t\), where \(x=\frac{a+b}{2}+\frac{b-a}{2}t\), with coefficients computed from the node values:
\[
P_{n-1}(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_j\,T_j(t),\qquad
c_0=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(x_k),\qquad
c_j=\frac2n\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(x_k)\cos\!\left(\frac{j(2k-1)\pi}{2n}\right).
\]
The animations evaluate the same polynomial in barycentric Lagrange form.
Building \(P_{n-1}\) needs only the values \(f(x_k)\). The error bound needs more: in general, Mathews’ Lagrange–Chebyshev theorem states that if \(f\in C^{n}[a,b]\), then for every \(x\in[a,b]\)
\[
|f(x)-P_{n-1}(x)| \le \frac{2\,(b-a)^{n}}{4^{n}\,n!}\max_{a\le x\le b}\bigl|f^{(n)}(x)\bigr|.
\]
Its factor \(2(b-a)^n/4^n\) is the largest value of \(\bigl|\prod_{k=1}^{n}(x-x_k)\bigr|\) on \([a,b]\), and no other choice of \(n\) nodes in \([a,b]\) makes that largest value smaller; for 16 nodes on \([-1,1]\), equally spaced nodes make it 44 times larger. For \(e^x\) on \([-2,3]\) (Case 15), the largest error with 16 nodes is \(7.1\times10^{-12}\), within the bound’s \(6.8\times10^{-11}\). For \(1/(1+10x^2)\) on \([-1,1]\) (Case 08), the error falls by a factor of about 3.47 for every four nodes added, from \(1.4\times10^{-2}\) at 16 nodes to \(9.5\times10^{-5}\) at 32, while 16 equally spaced nodes leave an error of 0.48. There the bound misleads: it is about 3050 at 16 nodes and grows with \(n\), so it says nothing although the error shrinks.
Two failures matter in the cases below. The bound covers only \([a,b]\): beyond it the interpolant is extrapolation and leaves \(f\) quickly, as in Case 04, where 16 nodes on \([0,2]\) give \(P_{15}(3)\approx 5.0\times10^{4}\) against \(\sqrt3\approx1.73\). And when \(f\) has an infinite derivative at an endpoint, the theorem does not apply and convergence is slow: for \(\sqrt{x}\) on \([0,2]\) (Case 04) and \(\arcsin x\) on \([-1,1]\) (Case 19), the largest error sits at an endpoint and only halves when the number of nodes doubles from 8 to 16.
The same interpolation with equally spaced nodes is on the Lagrange and Newton pages, and Newton’s Case 08 shows the Runge oscillation of \(1/(1+10x^2)\); Rational Approximation also uses Chebyshev nodes, and Least-Squares Polynomials and Legendre Polynomials fit by least squares instead.

title: Circle of Curvature
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Circle of Curvature
text:
Curvature for y = f(x)






NoteDefinition - Curvature and Radius



For a twice-differentiable curve \(y=f(x)\),
\[
\kappa(x)=\frac{f''(x)}{\left(1+\left(f'(x)\right)^2\right)^{3/2}},
\qquad
\rho(x)=\frac{\left(1+\left(f'(x)\right)^2\right)^{3/2}}{f''(x)}.
    ag{1}
\]
Geometrically, \(|\rho(x)|\) is the radius of the osculating circle.


Given \(y=f(x)\), the unit tangent and unit normal vectors are
\[
\widehat{\mathbf{u}}(x)=\frac{(1,f'(x))}{\sqrt{1+\left(f'(x)\right)^2}},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf{n}}(x)=\frac{(-f'(x),1)}{\sqrt{1+\left(f'(x)\right)^2}}.
    ag{2}
\]






TipTheorem - Center of Curvature for y = f(x)



At the point \((x,f(x))\), the center \((a,b)\) of the osculating circle is
\[
a(x)=x-\frac{f'(x)}{f''(x)}-\frac{\left(f'(x)\right)^3}{f''(x)},
    ag{3}
\]
\[
b(x)=f(x)+\frac{1}{f''(x)}+\frac{\left(f'(x)\right)^2}{f''(x)}.
    ag{4}
\]








ImportantOsculating Circle Equation



Once \((a,b)\) and \(r=|\rho(x)|\) are known, the osculating circle is
\[
(X-a)^2+(Y-b)^2=r^2.
    ag{5}
\]



Example 1 - Parabola at the origin
Use \(y=f(x)=x^2\) at \((0,0)\).
Step 1: Compute derivatives.
\[
f'(x)=2x,\qquad f''(x)=2.
\]
Step 2: Curvature and radius.
\[
\kappa(0)=\frac{2}{(1+0)^{3/2}}=2,
\qquad
\rho(0)=\frac{(1+0)^{3/2}}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.
\]
Step 3: Center of curvature.
\[
a(0)=0-0-0=0,
\qquad
b(0)=0+\frac{1}{2}+0=\frac{1}{2}.
\]
The osculating circle is
\[
X^2+\left(Y-\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2.
\]
Verification:







Check
Result

\((0,0)\) gives \(0+(-\tfrac{1}{2})^2=\tfrac{1}{4}\)

Distance from \((0,\tfrac{1}{2})\) to \((0,0)\) is \(\tfrac{1}{2}\)





Example 2 - Tangent, normal, and osculating circle at (1,1)
For \(y=x^2\) at \((1,1)\):
Step 1: Tangent and normal vectors.
\[
f'(1)=2,
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf{u}}(1)=\frac{(1,2)}{\sqrt{5}},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf{n}}(1)=\frac{(-2,1)}{\sqrt{5}}.
\]
Step 2: Radius and center.
\[
\rho(1)=\frac{(1+2^2)^{3/2}}{2}=\frac{5\sqrt{5}}{2}.
\]
\[
a(1)=1-\frac{2}{2}-\frac{2^3}{2}=-4,
\qquad
b(1)=1+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2^2}{2}=\frac{7}{2}.
\]
So the osculating circle is
\[
(X+4)^2+\left(Y-\frac{7}{2}\right)^2=\left(\frac{5\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^2=\frac{125}{4}.
\]

Example 3 - Collocation circle and limit
For \(y=x^2\) at \((0,0)\), use the three points
\[
(-h,f(-h)),\ (0,f(0)),\ (h,f(h)).
\]
Step 1: Write a circle equation.
\[
(X-a)^2+(Y-b)^2=r^2.
\]
By symmetry, \(a=0\).
Step 2: Use \((0,0)\) and \((h,h^2)\).
\[
r^2=b^2,
\]
\[
h^2+(h^2-b)^2=b^2.
\]
Solve for \(b\):
\[
b=\frac{1+h^2}{2},
\qquad
r=\frac{1+h^2}{2}.
\]
Step 3: Take the limit.
\[
\lim_{h\to 0} b = \frac{1}{2},
\qquad
\lim_{h\to 0} r = \frac{1}{2}.
\]
So the collocation circle converges to the osculating circle from Example 1.

title: Circle of Curvature
text:
Generalization to Parametric Curves
For a planar parametric curve
\[
x=f(t),\qquad y=g(t),
\]
the radius is
\[
r(t)=\frac{\left(f'(t)^2+g'(t)^2\right)^{3/2}}{\left|f'(t)g''(t)-g'(t)f''(t)\right|}.
    ag{6}
\]
and the center is
\[
\mathbf{c}(t)=\left\{
f(t)-\frac{g'(t)\left(f'(t)^2+g'(t)^2\right)}{f'(t)g''(t)-g'(t)f''(t)},
\ g(t)+\frac{f'(t)\left(f'(t)^2+g'(t)^2\right)}{f'(t)g''(t)-g'(t)f''(t)
}\right\}.
    ag{7}
\]






WarningOrientation Caveat



Without absolute values in the radius formula, reversing orientation can produce a negative signed radius. The geometric radius is always nonnegative.



Example 4 - Cardioid with counterclockwise orientation
Use
\[

title: Conic Fit
text:
Determinant-Based Conic Fitting
Given data points \((x_i,y_i)\) in the plane, we fit an implicit curve
\[
F(x,y)=0
\]
so every data point satisfies the equation exactly.






NoteDefinition - General Conic



A planar conic can be written as \[
Ax^2+Bxy+Cy^2+Dx+Ey+F=0,
\tag{1}
\] with \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) not all zero.








TipTheorem - Uniqueness Through Five Points



Through any five distinct points passes at least one conic. It is unique (up to a nonzero scale factor) exactly when no four of the points are collinear, which is when the \(5\times 6\) fitting system has rank 5. If in addition no three are collinear, the conic is nondegenerate.

title: Conic Fit
text:
Core Determinant Formulas
For a symbolic point \((x,y)\) and data points \((x_i,y_i)\), the legacy module uses determinants so that replacing the first row by a point row forces that point onto the curve.






ImportantKey Implicit Forms



Line through two points: \[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
x & y & 1\\
x_1 & y_1 & 1\\
x_2 & y_2 & 1
\end{pmatrix}=0.
\tag{2}
\]
Circle through three points: \[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
x^2+y^2 & x & y & 1\\
x_1^2+y_1^2 & x_1 & y_1 & 1\\
x_2^2+y_2^2 & x_2 & y_2 & 1\\
x_3^2+y_3^2 & x_3 & y_3 & 1
\end{pmatrix}=0.
\tag{3}
\]
Standard parabola model \(y=ax^2+bx+c\): \[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
x^2 & x & 1 & y\\
x_1^2 & x_1 & 1 & y_1\\
x_2^2 & x_2 & 1 & y_2\\
x_3^2 & x_3 & 1 & y_3
\end{pmatrix}=0.
\tag{4}
\]
Alternate parabola model \(x=ay^2+by+c\): \[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
y^2 & y & 1 & x\\
y_1^2 & y_1 & 1 & x_1\\
y_2^2 & y_2 & 1 & x_2\\
y_3^2 & y_3 & 1 & x_3
\end{pmatrix}=0.
\tag{5}
\]
Standard ellipse model \(Ax^2+Cy^2+Dx+Ey+F=0\): \[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
x^2 & y^2 & x & y & 1\\
x_1^2 & y_1^2 & x_1 & y_1 & 1\\
x_2^2 & y_2^2 & x_2 & y_2 & 1\\
x_3^2 & y_3^2 & x_3 & y_3 & 1\\
x_4^2 & y_4^2 & x_4 & y_4 & 1
\end{pmatrix}=0.
\tag{6}
\]
General five-point conic: \[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
x^2 & xy & y^2 & x & y & 1\\
x_1^2 & x_1y_1 & y_1^2 & x_1 & y_1 & 1\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\
x_5^2 & x_5y_5 & y_5^2 & x_5 & y_5 & 1
\end{pmatrix}=0.
\tag{7}
\]

Example 1 - Line Through Two Points
Find the line through \((1,4)\) and \((5,3)\).
Step 1: Use the two-point form.
\[
\frac{y-4}{x-1}=\frac{3-4}{5-1}=-\frac14.
\]
Step 2: Rearrange to implicit form.
\[
y=-\frac14x+\frac{17}{4}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
x+4y-17=0.
\]
The fitted line is
\[
\boxed{x+4y-17=0}.
\]

Vertical and horizontal lines (legacy Examples 2 and 3)
The two-point slope form fails for the line through \((3,1)\) and \((3,4)\), because its slope \(\tfrac{4-1}{3-3}\) divides by zero. The determinant (2) has no division.
Step 1: Expand (2) along the first row for \((3,1)\) and \((3,4)\).
\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
x & y & 1\\
3 & 1 & 1\\
3 & 4 & 1
\end{pmatrix}
=x(1-4)-y(3-3)+(12-3)=-3x+9=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{x=3}.
\]
Step 2: Do the same for the horizontal line through \((1,4)\) and \((5,4)\).
\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
x & y & 1\\
1 & 4 & 1\\
5 & 4 & 1
\end{pmatrix}
=x(4-4)-y(1-5)+(4-20)=4y-16=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\boxed{y=4}.
\]
Verification: \(-3x+9\) is \(0\) at \((3,1)\) and at \((3,4)\) (both have \(x=3\)), and \(4y-16\) is \(0\) at \((1,4)\) and at \((5,4)\) (both have \(y=4\)).

title: Conic Fit
text:
Classification by Discriminant
For
\[
Ax^2+Bxy+Cy^2+Dx+Ey+F=0,
\]
the discriminant is
\[
\Delta=B^2-4AC.
\tag{8}
\]






ImportantQuick Classification Rule



Call the conic nondegenerate when \[
\det\begin{pmatrix}
A & B/2 & D/2\\
B/2 & C & E/2\\
D/2 & E/2 & F
\end{pmatrix}\ne 0
\tag{9}
\] and the curve has real points. For a nondegenerate conic:

If \(\Delta<0\): ellipse (or circle as a special case).
If \(\Delta=0\): parabola.
If \(\Delta>0\): hyperbola.

When the determinant (9) is zero or the curve has no real points, the conic is degenerate: a pair of intersecting lines (\(\Delta>0\)); two parallel lines, one double line, or no real points (\(\Delta=0\)); a single point or no real points (\(\Delta<0\)).
