title: Newton’s Search Method
text:
Description
Newton’s search method looks for a local minimum of a function \(f(\mathbf{X})\) of several variables, \(\mathbf{X} = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)\), whose first and second partial derivatives can be evaluated. At the current point \(\mathbf{P}_k\) it replaces \(f\) by its second-degree Taylor polynomial, which is built from the gradient \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) and the Hessian matrix \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\) of second partial derivatives, and moves to the point where the gradient of that quadratic is zero:
\[
\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + \Delta\mathbf{P}_k, \qquad \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\,\Delta\mathbf{P}_k = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k).
\]
This is the Newton-Raphson method applied to the system \(\nabla f(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{0}\), with the Hessian playing the part of the Jacobian. With one variable it reduces to \(p_{k+1} = p_k - f'(p_k)/f''(p_k)\). Near a minimum where the Hessian is positive definite the iteration converges quadratically, and a quadratic \(f\) with a positive definite Hessian is minimised in a single step. But the method only looks for a zero of the gradient, so it converges just as readily to a saddle point or a maximum, and from a poor starting point it can run away altogether. Mathews works in two variables, \(\mathbf{P}_k = (x_k, y_k)\), so every run below is a path of points on the surface \(z = f(x, y)\), and every one has been recomputed in 60-digit arithmetic.

title: Newton’s Search Method
text:
Gradient and Hessian






NoteDefinition — Gradient



If \(f(x, y)\) has partial derivatives \(f_x\) and \(f_y\), its gradient is the vector function
\[
\nabla f(x, y) = \bigl(f_x(x, y),\ f_y(x, y)\bigr).
\]








NoteDefinition — Jacobian matrix



If \(f_1(x, y)\) and \(f_2(x, y)\) have partial derivatives, their Jacobian matrix is
\[
\mathbf{J}(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial y} \\[2mm] \dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial y} \end{pmatrix}.
\]








NoteDefinition — Hessian matrix



If \(f(x, y)\) has partial derivatives up to order two, its Hessian matrix is
\[
\mathbf{H}(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} f_{xx}(x, y) & f_{xy}(x, y) \\ f_{yx}(x, y) & f_{yy}(x, y) \end{pmatrix}.
\]








TipLemma 1 and Lemma 2




The Hessian of \(f\) is the Jacobian of the two components of its gradient, \(f_1 = f_x\) and \(f_2 = f_y\): \(\ \mathbf{H}(x, y) = \mathbf{J}\bigl(f_x, f_y\bigr)\).
If the second partial derivatives of \(f\) are continuous, then \(f_{xy} = f_{yx}\) and the Hessian is symmetric.




Example 1 — Gradient and Hessian of \(f(x, y) = (x - y)/(x^2 + y^2 + 2)\) at \((-3, -2)\)
Step 1 (first derivatives): by the quotient rule,
\[
f_x = -\frac{x^2 - 2xy - y^2 - 2}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^2}, \qquad
f_y = -\frac{x^2 + 2xy - y^2 + 2}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^2}.
\]
At \((-3, -2)\) the denominator is \(15^2 = 225\), and
\[
\nabla f(-3, -2) = \left(\frac{9}{225},\ -\frac{19}{225}\right) = \left(\frac{1}{25},\ -\frac{19}{225}\right) \approx (0.04,\ -0.084444).
\]
Step 2 (second derivatives):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_{xx} &= \frac{2\,(x^3 - 3x^2 y - 3x y^2 + y^3 - 6x + 2y)}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^3}, \\
f_{xy} &= \frac{2\,(x^3 + 3x^2 y - 3x y^2 - y^3 + 2x - 2y)}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^3}, \\
f_{yy} &= -\frac{2\,(x^3 - 3x^2 y - 3x y^2 + y^3 + 2x - 6y)}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Step 3 (Hessian at the point): the denominator is \(15^3 = 3375\) and the three numerators are \(138\), \(-78\) and \(-122\), so
\[
\boxed{\ \mathbf{H}(-3, -2) = \frac{1}{3375}\begin{pmatrix} 138 & -78 \\ -78 & -122 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac{46}{1125} & -\tfrac{26}{1125} \\[1mm] -\tfrac{26}{1125} & -\tfrac{122}{3375} \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0.040889 & -0.023111 \\ -0.023111 & -0.036148 \end{pmatrix}\ }
\]
The Hessian agrees with Mathews’ output. Verification: the derivatives above were checked symbolically against direct differentiation (the differences simplify to \(0\)). The Hessian here is indefinite: \(\det \mathbf{H}(-3, -2) = -1528/759375 < 0\), and its eigenvalues are \(-0.042550\) and \(0.047290\). Near \((-3, -2)\) the surface curves up in one direction and down in another, which matters in Example 2.

title: Newton’s Search Method
text:
The Quadratic Taylor Polynomial
Expand \(f\) about the point \(\mathbf{P} = (p, q)\) and write \(\Delta p = x - p\), \(\Delta q = y - q\). In series notation the second-degree Taylor polynomial is
\[
Q(x, y) = f(p, q) + f_x(p, q)\,\Delta p + f_y(p, q)\,\Delta q + \tfrac12\Bigl(f_{xx}(p, q)\,\Delta p^2 + 2 f_{xy}(p, q)\,\Delta p\,\Delta q + f_{yy}(p, q)\,\Delta q^2\Bigr).
\tag{1}
\]
With \(\mathbf{X} = (x, y)\) and \(\Delta\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{X} - \mathbf{P} = (\Delta p, \Delta q)\), the same polynomial in vector and matrix notation is
\[
Q(\mathbf{X}) = f(\mathbf{P}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \cdot \Delta\mathbf{P} + \tfrac12\, \Delta\mathbf{P}\, \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P})\, \Delta\mathbf{P}^{T}.
\tag{2}
\]
Form (2) holds unchanged for \(n\) variables, with \(\nabla f\) a vector of \(n\) first partial derivatives and \(\mathbf{H}\) the \(n \times n\) matrix of second partial derivatives.

Example 2 — Taylor polynomials of \(f(x, y) = (x - y)/(x^2 + y^2 + 2)\)
(a) Centre \(\mathbf{P} = (-3, -2)\). From Example 1, \(f(-3, -2) = -\tfrac{1}{15}\), so by (1)
\[
Q(x, y) = -\frac{1}{15} + \frac{x + 3}{25} - \frac{19\,(y + 2)}{225} + \frac{23\,(x + 3)^2}{1125} - \frac{26\,(x + 3)(y + 2)}{1125} - \frac{61\,(y + 2)^2}{3375},
\]
and expanding,
\[
\boxed{\ Q(x, y) = \frac{-481 + 393x + 69x^2 - 763y - 78xy - 61y^2}{3375}\ }
\]
which is Mathews’ simplified form. Because \(\mathbf{H}(-3, -2)\) is indefinite, this quadratic is a saddle surface: it has no minimum. Its only stationary point is at \((-\tfrac{1791}{382}, -\tfrac{622}{191}) \approx (-4.688482, -3.256545)\), where \(f = -0.041401\), higher than \(f(-3, -2) = -0.066667\). A Newton step from \((-3, -2)\) would go there.
(b) Centre \(\mathbf{P} = (-0.3, 0.2)\), closer to the minimum. Here
\[
f(-0.3, 0.2) = -\frac{50}{213} \approx -0.234742, \qquad \nabla f(-0.3, 0.2) \approx (0.403359,\ -0.425401),
\]
\[
\mathbf{H}(-0.3, 0.2) \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0.447659 & -0.195579 \\ -0.195579 & 0.380190 \end{pmatrix},
\]
and
\[
Q(x, y) \approx 0.010829 + 0.576773\,x - 0.560112\,y + 0.223830\,x^2 - 0.195579\,xy + 0.190095\,y^2 .
\]
This Hessian is positive definite (eigenvalues \(0.215457\) and \(0.612392\)), so \(Q\) is a bowl. Its minimum is at \((-0.831690,\ 1.045402)\), with \(Q = -0.521790\) and \(f = -0.495985\) there. The true minimum of \(f\) is at \((-1, 1)\), where \(f = -\tfrac12\).
Verification: both expansions were recomputed symbolically from (2), and the stationary points of \(Q\) were found by solving \(\nabla Q = \mathbf{0}\) exactly. The two stationary points of \(f\) itself are \((-1, 1)\), a minimum with \(\mathbf{H} = \tfrac14 \mathbf{I}\), and \((1, -1)\), a maximum with \(f = \tfrac12\). As Mathews observes, when the centre is close to the minimum, the minimum of the quadratic is close to the minimum of the surface. That is the idea of Newton’s method, and the minimiser of \(Q\) in (b) is exactly the first Newton step \(\mathbf{P}_1\) of Example 6.

title: Newton’s Search Method
section: Newton’s Method for Finding a Minimum
text:
Newton’s Method for Finding a Minimum
Assume that the first and second partial derivatives of \(f\) are continuous near a minimum \(\mathbf{P}^*\) and that \(\mathbf{P}_0\) is close to it. The minimum of the quadratic approximation (2), centred at \(\mathbf{P}_0\), is where \(\nabla Q(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{0}\). Since \(\mathbf{H}\) is symmetric,
\[
\nabla Q(\mathbf{X}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0) + \Delta\mathbf{P}\, \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_0),
\]
so setting \(\nabla Q(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{0}\) gives \(\Delta\mathbf{P}\, \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_0) = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0)\). If \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_0)\) is invertible,
\[
\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{P}_0 - \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0)\, \bigl(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_0)\bigr)^{-1}.
\]
This \(\mathbf{X}\) is the next approximation \(\mathbf{P}_1\). Repeating the construction at each new point gives Newton’s method for finding a minimum:






ImportantNewton search formula



\[
\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k - \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\, \bigl(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\bigr)^{-1} \qquad \text{(row vectors)},
\tag{3}
\]
\[
\mathbf{P}_{k+1}^{T} = \mathbf{P}_k^{T} - \bigl(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\bigr)^{-1} \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)^{T} \qquad \text{(column vectors)}.
\tag{4}
\]


The two forms agree because \(\mathbf{H}\) is symmetric. Form (4) is the Newton-Raphson formula \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1}^{T} = \mathbf{P}_k^{T} - \mathbf{J}(\mathbf{P}_k)^{-1} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{P}_k)^{T}\) for a root of the vector function \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{X})\), since by Lemma 1 its Jacobian is \(\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{H}\). For a function of one variable, (3) is \(p_{k+1} = p_k - f'(p_k)/f''(p_k)\): Newton-Raphson applied to \(f'(x) = 0\).
The theory of Newton-Raphson therefore carries over. The following is a general result, not a claim about any one example:






TipTheorem — Local quadratic convergence (general)



Suppose the second partial derivatives of \(f\) are continuous near \(\mathbf{P}^*\) and satisfy a Lipschitz condition there, that \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}^*) = \mathbf{0}\), and that \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}^*)\) is nonsingular. Then there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that for every \(\mathbf{P}_0\) with \(\lVert \mathbf{P}_0 - \mathbf{P}^* \rVert < \delta\) the iterates (3) are defined, converge to \(\mathbf{P}^*\), and satisfy
\[
\lVert \mathbf{P}_{k+1} - \mathbf{P}^* \rVert \le C\, \lVert \mathbf{P}_k - \mathbf{P}^* \rVert^2
\]
for some constant \(C\). The point \(\mathbf{P}^*\) is a strict local minimum if \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}^*)\) is positive definite, a strict local maximum if it is negative definite, and a saddle point if it is indefinite.


The theorem does not require \(\mathbf{P}^*\) to be a minimum. Newton’s method treats every nondegenerate stationary point alike. Examples 5 and 6 show it converging quadratically to two saddle points and to a maximum, so the type of the limit has to be checked afterwards with the Hessian. Nor does the theorem say how small \(\delta\) is: Example 6 shows a starting point from which the iterates go off to infinity.

Algorithm






ImportantAlgorithm — Newton’s method for finding a minimum



Start with an approximation \(\mathbf{P}_0\) to the minimum point \(\mathbf{P}^*\). Set \(k = 0\).

Evaluate the gradient vector \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) and the Hessian matrix \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\).
Solve the linear system \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\, \Delta\mathbf{P}_k^{T} = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)^{T}\) and set \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + \Delta\mathbf{P}_k\).
Perform the termination test: stop when \(\lVert \Delta\mathbf{P}_k \rVert\) and \(\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1}) \rVert\) are small enough. Otherwise set \(k = k + 1\) and repeat.
Check the Hessian at the final point. If it is not positive definite, the point is not a local minimum.



Mathews’ formula (3) is written with the inverse of the Hessian, but as he notes, it is better to solve the linear system in step 2 with a linear system solver: the inverse is a theoretical tool, and computing it is inefficient. His program NewtonSearch runs a fixed number of iterations of (3) and prints each point and the value of \(f\) there; the tables below do the same.

text:
Example 3 — A quadratic function: one step is exact
Use Newton’s method to find the minimum of
\[
f(x, y) = x^2 - 4x + y^2 - y - xy
\]
starting from \(\mathbf{P}_0 = (0, 0)\).
Step 1: the gradient and Hessian are
\[
\nabla f(x, y) = (2x - y - 4,\ 2y - x - 1), \qquad \mathbf{H} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The Hessian is constant, with eigenvalues \(1\) and \(3\), so it is positive definite everywhere.
Step 2: at \(\mathbf{P}_0\), \(\nabla f(0, 0) = (-4, -1)\). Solve
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \Delta x \\ \Delta y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Delta\mathbf{P}_0 = (3,\ 2).
\]
Step 3: \(\mathbf{P}_1 = (0, 0) + (3, 2) = (3, 2)\), and \(\nabla f(3, 2) = (6 - 2 - 4,\ 4 - 3 - 1) = (0, 0)\).

section: Example 6 — Iterating to the minimum, and a starting point that fails
text:
Example 6 — Iterating to the minimum, and a starting point that fails
Given \(f(x, y) = \dfrac{x - y}{x^2 + y^2 + 2}\) (the function of Examples 1 and 2) and the initial point \(\mathbf{P}_0 = (-0.3, 0.2)\), use Newton’s method to find \(\mathbf{P}_1\) and \(\mathbf{P}_2\).
The plots of the gradient components show the two curves \(f_x = 0\) and \(f_y = 0\) crossing at \((-1, 1)\). Since \(f_x = 0\) means \(x^2 - 2xy - y^2 = 2\) and \(f_y = 0\) means \(x^2 + 2xy - y^2 = -2\), adding gives \(x^2 = y^2\) and subtracting gives \(xy = -1\), so the only stationary points are \((-1, 1)\) and \((1, -1)\).
Step 1 (find \(\mathbf{P}_1\)): the gradient and Hessian at \(\mathbf{P}_0\) are those of Example 2(b),
\[
\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0) \approx (0.403359,\ -0.425401), \qquad
\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_0) \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0.447659 & -0.195579 \\ -0.195579 & 0.380190 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Solving \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_0)\,\Delta\mathbf{P}_0^T = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0)^T\) gives \(\Delta\mathbf{P}_0 \approx (-0.531690,\ 0.845402)\), so
\[
\mathbf{P}_1 = \left(-\tfrac{120279}{144620},\ \tfrac{10799}{10330}\right) \approx (-0.831690,\ 1.045402), \qquad f(\mathbf{P}_1) = -0.495985 .
\]

\[
\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_1) \approx (0.0462373,\ 0.00977846), \qquad

After Mathews’ ten iterations the point is \((-241.019696,\ 145.628489)\), with \(f = -0.004876\). Newton’s method is “diverging to the point at infinity”, in Mathews’ words. Far from the origin the surface flattens out and its gradient tends to zero, and the iteration chases that flat region instead of a stationary point. The Hessian is indefinite at every iterate computed (\(k = 0\) to \(12\)), and at each of them the Newton step points uphill (\(\nabla f \cdot \Delta\mathbf{P}_k > 0\)).


Convergence to a maximum
Because \(f(-x, -y) = -f(x, y)\), the gradient satisfies \(\nabla f(-\mathbf{X}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{X})\) and the Hessian \(\mathbf{H}(-\mathbf{X}) = -\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{X})\), so the Newton step from \(-\mathbf{P}\) is exactly the negative of the step from \(\mathbf{P}\). Started at \((0.3, -0.2)\), Newton’s method therefore produces the negatives of the iterates in the table above, \((0.831690, -1.045402)\), \((0.988071, -0.993270)\), \(\ldots\), and converges just as quickly to \((1, -1)\), where \(f = \tfrac12\) is the maximum (\(\mathbf{H}(1, -1) = -\tfrac14 \mathbf{I}\)). In one variable the same holds in general: by the theorem with \(n = 1\), \(p_{k+1} = p_k - f'(p_k)/f''(p_k)\) started close enough to a maximum, where \(f'' < 0\), converges to that maximum.

title: Newton’s Search Method
section: Enhanced Newton Method for Finding a Minimum
text:
Enhanced Newton Method for Finding a Minimum
Newton’s method can be modified by treating \(\mathbf{S}_k = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\,\bigl(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\bigr)^{-1}\) as a search direction, as the gradient method uses the direction \(-\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\), and doing a one-parameter minimisation (line search) along it:

Evaluate the gradient vector \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) and the Hessian matrix \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\).
Compute the search direction \(\mathbf{S}_k = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\,\bigl(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\bigr)^{-1}\).
Minimise the function of one variable \(\phi(t) = f(\mathbf{P}_k + t\,\mathbf{S}_k)\), for instance with a golden ratio or quadratic interpolative search, giving a value \(t_k\). This is a minimum of \(f\) along the search line; at an interior minimum \(\phi'(t_k) = \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k + t_k\,\mathbf{S}_k) \cdot \mathbf{S}_k = 0\), so the gradient at the new point is perpendicular to the line.
Set \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + t_k\,\mathbf{S}_k\).
Perform the termination test: are \(f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) and \(f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1})\) sufficiently close, and is \(\lVert \mathbf{P}_{k+1} - \mathbf{P}_k \rVert\) small enough? If not, set \(k = k + 1\) and repeat.

With \(t_k = 1\) this is the plain method (3). In general, Mathews says, the modified method is more reliable, and he leaves its investigation to the reader. Two of the runs above show what the line search can and cannot fix:

In the Example 4 variant from \((1.8, 1.2)\), the direction at \(k = 1\) points downhill but the full step overshoots and raises \(f\) from \(0.637\) to \(40.4\). A line search along that direction would pick a step that lowers \(f\).
From \((-3, 2)\) in Example 6, \(\mathbf{S}_k\) points uphill at every iterate. If \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\) is positive definite, then \(\nabla f \cdot \mathbf{S}_k = -\nabla f\, \mathbf{H}^{-1} \nabla f^{T} < 0\) and \(\mathbf{S}_k\) is a descent direction, but here \(\mathbf{H}\) is indefinite. A line search over \(t > 0\) along an uphill direction cannot lower \(f\). The direction itself has to be changed, for example to \(-\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) or to the Newton direction of a modified, positive definite Hessian.

title: Newton’s Search Method
text:
Implementation Notes

Solve, don’t invert. Compute \(\Delta\mathbf{P}_k\) from \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\,\Delta\mathbf{P}_k^T = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)^T\) with a linear solver (for example a Cholesky factorisation, which also reports whether \(\mathbf{H}\) is positive definite).
Cost per step. Each iteration needs the \(n\) first partial derivatives, the \(n(n+1)/2\) distinct second partial derivatives and the solution of an \(n \times n\) system. The gradient method needs only the first derivatives but generally converges much more slowly.
Check what was found. The iteration stops where \(\nabla f = \mathbf{0}\), and that can be a saddle point (Example 5) or a maximum (Example 6). Test the Hessian at the final point.
Watch the starting point. Convergence is guaranteed only from close enough to \(\mathbf{P}^*\). Signs of trouble are a Hessian that is not positive definite and a step that increases \(f\) (Example 6 from \((-3, 2)\)). A safeguarded version takes a line search along the Newton direction, and falls back to \(-\nabla f\) when that direction is not downhill.
Termination. Use \(\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) \rVert\) and \(\lVert \Delta\mathbf{P}_k \rVert\), not only the change in \(f\). Near a minimum \(f(\mathbf{P}) - f(\mathbf{P}^*) \approx \tfrac12 (\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{P}^*)\,\mathbf{H}\,(\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{P}^*)^T\) is quadratic in the error, so the values of \(f\) settle long before the point does. In Example 6 the printed \(f(\mathbf{P}_4)\) is already \(-0.500000000000\) while \(\mathbf{P}_4\) is still \(3.7 \times 10^{-8}\) from \((-1, 1)\).
Flat valleys. When the Hessian at the minimum is badly conditioned (eigenvalues \(0.40\) and \(1002\) for Rosenbrock’s function), function values alone locate the minimum poorly along the valley. Newton’s method still converges quickly there, because it uses the curvature in each direction.

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Description
Golden ratio search finds the minimum of a function \(f\) on an interval \([a_0, b_0]\) using only function values, no derivatives. It needs \(f\) to be unimodal on the interval: decreasing up to a single minimiser \(p\) and increasing after it. Each step evaluates \(f\) at two interior points \(c_k < d_k\) and throws away the part of the interval that cannot contain \(p\). If \(f(c_k) \le f(d_k)\) the minimiser lies in \([a_k, d_k]\), otherwise it lies in \([c_k, b_k]\).
The interior points divide every interval in the same proportions:
\[
c_k = a_k + (1 - \rho)(b_k - a_k), \qquad d_k = a_k + \rho\,(b_k - a_k), \qquad \rho = \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{2} \approx 0.618034.
\]
Because \(\rho^2 = 1 - \rho\), the interior point that survives a step is exactly an interior point of the next interval, so every step after the first costs one new function evaluation, and every step shrinks the interval by the same factor: \(b_k - a_k = \rho^k (b_0 - a_0)\). Unlike Fibonacci search, which fixes the number of steps in advance and changes the ratio at every step, the golden ratio search can simply run until the interval is shorter than a tolerance \(\delta\).

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Unimodal Functions and Bracketing






NoteDefinition — Unimodal function



The function \(f\) is unimodal on \(I = [a, b]\) if there is a unique number \(p \in I\) such that \(f\) is decreasing on \([a, p]\) and increasing on \([p, b]\).


A bracketing search keeps an interval \([a_k, b_k]\) that is known to contain \(p\) and shrinks it by comparing \(f\) at two interior points \(c_k < d_k\):

If \(f(c_k) \le f(d_k)\), the minimum cannot lie to the right of \(d_k\). Squeeze from the right: set \(a_{k+1} = a_k\), \(b_{k+1} = d_k\).
If \(f(c_k) > f(d_k)\), the minimum cannot lie to the left of \(c_k\). Squeeze from the left: set \(a_{k+1} = c_k\), \(b_{k+1} = b_k\).

A tie \(f(c_k) = f(d_k)\) puts \(p\) between \(c_k\) and \(d_k\), so either choice is safe; the rule above keeps \([a_k, d_k]\). Mathews’ programs keep \([c_k, b_k]\) in a tie. No comparison in the examples below is a tie, so both rules give the same steps. The method uses only comparisons of function values, so it also works when \(f\) is not differentiable.

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Derivation of the Golden Ratio
Place the interior points of \([a, b]\) symmetrically, so that \(c - a = b - d\):
\[
c = a + (1 - r)(b - a), \qquad d = a + r\,(b - a), \qquad \tfrac12 < r < 1,
\tag{1}
\]
where \(r > \tfrac12\) keeps \(c < d\). We want the same \(r\) on every interval, and one of the old interior points must become an interior point of the new interval, so that each step needs only one new function value.
Suppose \(f(c) \le f(d)\), so the new interval is \([a, d]\), of length \(r(b - a)\). Its right interior point is \(a + r(d - a)\), and for this to be the old point \(c\) we need \(c - a = r(d - a)\), that is
\[
(1 - r)(b - a) = r \cdot r\,(b - a)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
r^2 + r - 1 = 0.
\tag{2}
\]
If instead \(f(c) > f(d)\), the new interval is \([c, b]\), also of length \(r(b - a)\), and its left interior point \(c + (1 - r)(b - c)\) must be the old point \(d\). Since \(d - c = (2r - 1)(b - a)\) and \(b - c = r(b - a)\), this gives \(2r - 1 = (1 - r)\,r\), which is the same equation (2). Its roots are \(r = (-1 \pm \sqrt5)/2\), and the root in \((\tfrac12, 1)\) is
\[
\rho = \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{2} = 0.6180339887\ldots, \qquad \rho^2 = 1 - \rho = 0.3819660113\ldots
\tag{3}
\]
Mathews calls \(\rho\) the golden ratio. The name is more often given to its reciprocal \(\phi = 1/\rho = (1 + \sqrt5)/2 = 1.6180339887\ldots\); either way, \(\rho\) is the factor by which the interval shrinks. Equation (2) is the special case \(r_1 = r_0\) of the equation \(r_1 = (1 - r_0)/r_0\) on the Fibonacci search page.






TipTheorem — Interval lengths in golden ratio search



If \(f\) is unimodal on \([a_0, b_0]\) (and the comparisons are exact), every interval \([a_k, b_k]\) contains the minimiser \(p\), and
\[
b_k - a_k = \rho^k\,(b_0 - a_0).
\tag{4}
\]
The midpoint \((a_k + b_k)/2\) is within \(\tfrac12 \rho^k (b_0 - a_0)\) of \(p\). The interval is shorter than a tolerance \(\delta\) once
\[
k \ge \frac{\ln\bigl(\delta / (b_0 - a_0)\bigr)}{\ln \rho}.
\tag{5}
\]


This is a general result. The interval shrinks by the same factor \(\rho \approx 0.618\) at every step whatever \(f\) is, so the convergence is linear, and each extra decimal digit of accuracy costs \(\ln 10 / \ln \phi \approx 4.78\) steps.

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Algorithm






ImportantAlgorithm — Golden ratio search for a minimum



Given \(f\) unimodal on \([a_0, b_0]\) and a tolerance \(\delta\) (or a number of steps):

Compute \(c_0 = a_0 + (1 - \rho)(b_0 - a_0)\) and \(d_0 = a_0 + \rho(b_0 - a_0)\), and evaluate \(f(c_0)\), \(f(d_0)\).
For \(k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\) until \(b_k - a_k \le \delta\):

if \(f(c_k) \le f(d_k)\): set \(a_{k+1} = a_k\), \(b_{k+1} = d_k\), \(d_{k+1} = c_k\), and compute the new point \(c_{k+1} = a_{k+1} + (1 - \rho)(b_{k+1} - a_{k+1})\);
otherwise: set \(a_{k+1} = c_k\), \(b_{k+1} = b_k\), \(c_{k+1} = d_k\), and compute the new point \(d_{k+1} = a_{k+1} + \rho(b_{k+1} - a_{k+1})\);
evaluate \(f\) at the one new point.

Return an approximation to \(p\) from the last interval, for example its midpoint.



After \(K\) steps the method has used \(K + 2\) function evaluations and the interval has length \(\rho^K (b_0 - a_0)\). The values \(f(c_K)\) and \(f(d_K)\) are already known, so one more comparison shrinks the interval to \(\rho^{K+1}(b_0 - a_0)\) for free. With \(N = K + 2\) evaluations the bracket is therefore \(\rho^{N-1}(b_0 - a_0)\), the figure used on the Fibonacci search page.
Mathews gives two programs:

GoldenSearch[a0, b0, max] makes exactly max steps.
GoldenSearch[a0, b0, δ, ε] continues while \(\lvert f(b_k) - f(a_k) \rvert > \varepsilon\) or \(b_k - a_k > \delta\), so it stops once both \(b_k - a_k \le \delta\) and \(\lvert f(b_k) - f(a_k) \rvert \le \varepsilon\).

Both also evaluate \(f(a_0)\) and \(f(b_0)\) (so \(K + 4\) evaluations in all), keep \([c_k, b_k]\) in a tie, print the list \(\{a_k, c_k, d_k, b_k\}\) at every step, and return whichever endpoint, \(a_k\) or \(b_k\), has the smaller function value. The returned endpoint is within \(b_k - a_k\) of \(p\). The midpoint has half that error bound.

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Example 1 — Minimise \(x^2 - \sin x\) on \([0, 1]\)
Find the minimum of the unimodal function
\[
f(x) = x^2 - \sin x

on \([0, 1]\). Mathews runs this example for \(25\) steps. The function is unimodal on \([0, 1]\) because \(f''(x) = 2 + \sin x \ge 2 > 0\) there.

\[
c_0 = 0 + (1 - \rho)(1 - 0) = \frac{3 - \sqrt5}{2} \approx 0.3819660, \qquad d_0 = 0 + \rho\,(1 - 0) = \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{2} \approx 0.6180340,
\]

c_1 = 0 + (1 - \rho)(0.6180340 - 0) = 0.2360680, \qquad f(c_1) = -0.1781533860.

d_2 = 0.2360680 + \rho\,(0.6180340 - 0.2360680) = 0.4721360, \qquad f(d_2) = -0.2318772406.

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Fibonacci Versus Golden Ratio Search
Both methods use the same squeeze rule and one new function evaluation per step. The Fibonacci ratios \(r_k = F_{n-1-k}/F_{n-k}\) tend to \(\rho\), and on the two functions both pages use, the two searches keep the same side at every comparison the Fibonacci search makes: \(18\) of them in Example 1 and \(9\) in Example 6. The differences are:

Planning. Fibonacci search fixes the number of evaluations before it starts, and a tighter tolerance means starting again. The golden ratio search uses the same ratio at every step, so it can be stopped by a tolerance, or continued, at any time.
Efficiency. With \(N\) evaluations the golden ratio search leaves a bracket of length \(\rho^{N-1}(b_0 - a_0)\), and Fibonacci search, with Mathews’ final split (\(e = 0.01\)), leaves one about \(0.871\) times as long (the ratio tends to \((1 + 2e)\sqrt5/\phi^2\) as \(N\) grows; see the Fibonacci search page). Apart from the last few Fibonacci steps, both shrink the bracket by a factor close to \(0.618\) per evaluation.

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Implementation Notes

Reuse the surviving point. Keep the surviving interior point and its function value, and evaluate \(f\) only at the new point. This is what makes each step cost one evaluation.
Choosing the stopping rule. The width test \(b_k - a_k \le \delta\) fixes the number of steps in advance through (5). A test on function values alone can be met while the interval is still wide, because \(f\) is flat near \(p\) and because \(f(a_k)\) and \(f(b_k)\) can be close when \(p\) is near the middle of the interval. In Example 1, \(\lvert f(b_k) - f(a_k) \rvert \le 10^{-6}\) already holds at \(k = 14\), when the interval is still \(1.19 \times 10^{-3}\) wide. Mathews’ second program requires both tests.
Precision limit. Near \(p\) the compared values differ by roughly \(\tfrac12 f''(p)\) times the square of the spacing of the points, so in floating point the comparisons eventually fail. For Example 1 in double precision, from \(k = 37\) (interval \(1.9 \times 10^{-8}\)) every computed difference \(f(c_k) - f(d_k)\) is at most two units of the spacing \(2.8 \times 10^{-17}\) of double-precision numbers near \(f(p)\), so its sign is decided by rounding. The first wrong comparison comes at \(k = 42\), and from \(k = 43\) (interval \(1.0 \times 10^{-9}\)) the interval no longer contains \(p\). As a general rule of thumb, an interval much shorter than about \(\sqrt{u} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-8}\) times the size of \(p\), where \(u = 2^{-52}\), cannot be trusted in double precision.
Unimodality is required. If \(f\) has several local minima in \([a_0, b_0]\), the comparisons can discard the part containing the minimum wanted. The method still returns a point, but there is no guarantee which minimum it approaches (Example 2 started on \([-1, 1]\) works only because the first comparison happens to discard the local maximum).
Maxima. To find a maximum of \(f\), minimise \(-f\), as in Examples 3 and 4.

title: Quadratic Interpolative Search
text:
Description
Quadratic interpolative search finds the minimum of a unimodal function \(f\) on an interval \([a, b]\) by fitting a parabola through three function values and moving to the parabola’s lowest point. The version on this page is the one in Mathews’ module and Mathematica subroutine, which uses three equally spaced points \(p_0\), \(p_1 = p_0 + h\), \(p_2 = p_0 + 2h\). It starts from \(p_0 = a\) with \(h = (b - a)/2\) and steps to the right when \(f'(p_0) < 0\), to the left when \(f'(p_0) > 0\). It then halves \(h\) while \(f(p_0) \le f(p_1)\) and doubles it while \(f(p_2) < f(p_1)\), until the middle value is the lowest, \(f(p_0) > f(p_1) \le f(p_2)\). With \(y_i = f(p_i)\), the vertex of the interpolating quadratic is
\[
p_{\min} = p_0 + h_{\min}, \qquad h_{\min} = \frac{h\,(4y_1 - 3y_0 - y_2)}{2\,(2y_1 - y_0 - y_2)}.
\]
The search restarts from \(p_0 = p_{\min}\), with \(h\) equal to the distance from \(p_{\min}\) to the nearest of the three old points. It stops when one of \(y_0, y_1, y_2\) agrees with \(f(p_{\min})\) to within a tolerance \(\varepsilon\).
The module also covers cubic interpolative search, which uses derivative values explicitly. It fits a cubic \(P\) to the values of \(f\) and \(f'\) at two points \(p_0\) and \(p_1 = p_0 + h\), and moves to the local minimum of the cubic, \(p_2 = p_0 + \gamma h\), where
\[
\gamma = \frac{-2h f'(p_0)}{(G - 3\alpha) + \sqrt{(G - 3\alpha)^2 - 12 h \alpha f'(p_0)}}, \qquad
F = f(p_1) - f(p_0), \quad G = h\bigl(f'(p_1) - f'(p_0)\bigr), \quad \alpha = G - 2\bigl(F - h f'(p_0)\bigr).
\]
Then \((p_0, p_1)\) is replaced by \((p_1, p_2)\) and the step repeats. The cubic search does not keep a bracket: in both of Mathews’ examples its first point \(p_1\) lies outside \([a, b]\). The examples below keep Mathews’ numbers. Examples 1 and 3 use the quadratic search and Examples 2 and 4 the cubic search. Examples 1 and 2 minimise the same function, and so do Examples 3 and 4.

title: Quadratic Interpolative Search
section: Unimodal Functions and the Derivative Test
text:
Unimodal Functions and the Derivative Test






NoteDefinition — Unimodal function



The function \(f\) is unimodal on \(I = [a, b]\) if there is a unique number \(p \in I\) such that \(f\) is decreasing on \([a, p]\) and increasing on \([p, b]\).


Bracketing searches such as the golden ratio and Fibonacci searches need only this condition. The two methods on this page also use the derivative. Suppose \(f\) is unimodal on \([a, b]\) with minimum at \(p\), \(f'\) exists on \((a, b)\), and \(p_0 \in (a, b)\). If \(f'(p_0) < 0\) the minimum lies to the right of \(p_0\), and if \(f'(p_0) > 0\) it lies to the left.
Both of Mathews’ functions are unimodal on \([0, 1]\):

\(f(x) = x^2 - \sin x\) has \(f''(x) = 2 + \sin x \ge 2 > 0\) on \([0, 1]\), \(f'(0) = -1 < 0\) and \(f'(1) = 2 - \cos 1 = 1.4597 > 0\). The minimiser is the root of \(2x = \cos x\), \(p = 0.4501836113\), with \(f(p) = -0.2324655752\).
\(f(x) = \tfrac12 + x^5 - \tfrac45 x\) has \(f''(x) = 20x^3 > 0\) on \((0, 1]\), \(f'(0) = -0.8\) and \(f'(1) = 4.2\). The minimiser is exact: \(5p^4 = \tfrac45\) gives \(p = (4/25)^{1/4} = \sqrt{10}/5 = 0.6324555320\), with \(f(p) = 0.0952284595\).

title: Quadratic Interpolative Search
text:
Quadratic Interpolative Search

Bracketing the minimum
The first task is to find three test values
\[
p_0, \qquad p_1 = p_0 + h, \qquad p_2 = p_0 + 2h
\tag{1}
\]
such that
\[
f(p_0) > f(p_1) \qquad\text{and}\qquad f(p_1) < f(p_2).
\tag{2}
\]
Suppose \(f'(p_0) < 0\), so that \(p_0 < p\) and \(h\) is chosen positive. One pass of the bracketing loop does one of three things:

Case (i): if (2) holds, the bracket is found.
Case (ii): if \(f(p_0) > f(p_1)\) and \(f(p_1) > f(p_2)\), then \(p_2 < p\) and the points must reach farther right. Double the step: \(p_1 \leftarrow p_2\), \(h \leftarrow 2h\), \(p_2 \leftarrow p_0 + 2h\).
Case (iii): if \(f(p_0) \le f(p_1)\), the step has jumped over \(p\) and is too large. Halve the step: \(p_2 \leftarrow p_1\), \(h \leftarrow h/2\), \(p_1 \leftarrow p_0 + h\).

Each pass of cases (ii) and (iii) evaluates \(f\) at one new point. When \(f'(p_0) > 0\) the step \(h\) is negative and the same three cases apply. Mathews’ subroutine accepts the bracket when \(f(p_0) > f(p_1)\) and \(f(p_2) \ge f(p_1)\), so a tie between \(f(p_1)\) and \(f(p_2)\) also ends the loop. The loop also stops if \(|h|\) falls to a minimum step \(\delta\). Mathews’ text starts with \(h = 1\), or \(h = \tfrac12\) if \(a + 1 < b\) fails. His subroutine starts with \(h = (b - a)/2\), which for the interval \([0, 1]\) of both examples is the same \(h = \tfrac12\).


The vertex of the interpolating quadratic
With \(y_i = f(p_i)\) for \(i = 0, 1, 2\), the Lagrange polynomial through the three points (1) is
\[
Q(x) = y_0\,\frac{(x - p_1)(x - p_2)}{2h^2} - y_1\,\frac{(x - p_0)(x - p_2)}{h^2} + y_2\,\frac{(x - p_0)(x - p_1)}{2h^2},
\tag{3}
\]
and its derivative is
\[
Q'(x) = y_0\,\frac{2x - p_1 - p_2}{2h^2} - y_1\,\frac{2x - p_0 - p_2}{h^2} + y_2\,\frac{2x - p_0 - p_1}{2h^2}.
\tag{4}
\]
Write the critical point as \(x = p_0 + h_{\min}\), set \(Q'(p_0 + h_{\min}) = 0\), multiply by \(2h^2\) and collect the terms in \(h_{\min}\):
\[
0 = h_{\min}(2y_0 - 4y_1 + 2y_2) + y_0(2p_0 - p_1 - p_2) - y_1(4p_0 - 2p_0 - 2p_2) + y_2(2p_0 - p_0 - p_1).
\]
With \(p_1 = p_0 + h\) and \(p_2 = p_0 + 2h\) the last three terms are \(-3hy_0 + 4hy_1 - hy_2\), so
\[
h_{\min} = \frac{h\,(4y_1 - 3y_0 - y_2)}{2\,(2y_1 - y_0 - y_2)}, \qquad p_{\min} = p_0 + h_{\min}.
\tag{5}
\]
Subtracting \(h\) gives the position of the vertex relative to the middle point:
\[
p_{\min} - p_1 = h_{\min} - h = \frac{h\,(y_0 - y_2)}{2\,(y_0 - 2y_1 + y_2)}.
\tag{6}
\]






TipProperty of the vertex step (general)



The second derivative of \(Q\) is \(Q'' = (y_0 - 2y_1 + y_2)/h^2\). If the triple is bracketed, \(y_0 > y_1\) and \(y_2 \ge y_1\), then \(Q'' > 0\), so \(p_{\min}\) is the minimum of \(Q\), and
\[
-\tfrac12 |h| < \operatorname{sign}(h)\,(p_{\min} - p_1) \le \tfrac12 |h|,
\]
with equality only when \(y_2 = y_1\). So \(p_{\min}\) lies within half a step of \(p_1\), strictly between \(p_0\) and \(p_2\). To see this, put \(u = y_0 - y_1 > 0\) and \(v = y_2 - y_1 \ge 0\); then (6) reads \((p_{\min} - p_1)/h = (u - v)/\bigl(2(u + v)\bigr)\), and \(|u - v| < u + v\) unless \(v = 0\).


In the seven vertex steps of Examples 1 and 3, \(|p_{\min} - p_1|/|h|\) takes the values \(0.128\), \(0.105\), \(0.418\) and \(0.107\), \(0.270\), \(0.490\), \(0.165\), all below \(\tfrac12\).






WarningWhen the vertex formula fails (general)



The denominator \(2(2y_1 - y_0 - y_2)\) of (5) is zero when the three points are collinear, \(y_1 = (y_0 + y_2)/2\). If the triple is not bracketed, for instance because the bracketing loop stopped at \(|h| \le \delta\), then \(Q\) can be concave, and (5) then gives its maximum, or \(p_{\min}\) can lie far outside the triple. In Examples 1 and 3 every bracketing loop ends in case (i), so neither problem arises.




Restarting and stopping
Mathews notes that \(p_{\min}\) is a better approximation to \(p\) than \(p_0\), so the search replaces \(p_0\) by \(p_{\min}\) and repeats both processes with a new \(h\). His subroutine takes the new step to be the distance from \(p_{\min}\) to the nearest point of the old triple,
\[
h_{\text{new}} = \min\bigl\{\,|h_{\min}|,\ |h_{\min} - h|,\ |h_{\min} - 2h|\,\bigr\},
\tag{7}
\]
and uses \(h_{\text{new}} = h_{\min}\) if this minimum is zero. The sign of \(f'(p_{\min})\) then sets the direction of the next step. (The subroutine evaluates (7) after replacing \(h\) by \(|h|\), so the three numbers are the distances to \(p_0\), \(p_1\), \(p_2\) only for a step to the right. Every outer step of Examples 1 and 3 goes to the right.)
The subroutine stops on function values, not on the distance to \(p\). After each vertex it computes \(e_i = |y_i - f(p_{\min})|\) for \(i = 0, 1, 2\). \(\mathrm{Err}\) is the smallest nonzero \(e_i\) found so far, starting from \(\mathrm{Err} = 1\), and the search stops when \(\mathrm{Err} \le \varepsilon\). It also stops after 50 outer steps, and each bracketing loop is limited to 50 passes.
Mathews writes that the method uses the derivative only implicitly, through (4), and makes no explicit use of \(f'\). His subroutine does evaluate \(f'(p_0)\) once per outer step, but uses only its sign, to choose the direction.






ImportantAlgorithm — Quadratic search for a minimum (Mathews’ subroutine)



Given \(f\) unimodal on \([a, b]\), a minimum step \(\delta\) and a tolerance \(\varepsilon\): set \(p_0 = a\), \(h = (b - a)/2\), \(\mathrm{Err} = 1\), \(k = 0\).

If \(f'(p_0) > 0\), set \(h = -|h|\). Evaluate \(y_i = f(p_i)\) at the triple (1).
While \(|h| > \delta\) and the triple is not bracketed: if \(y_0 \le y_1\), halve (case iii); otherwise, if \(y_2 < y_1\), double (case ii).
Compute \(h_{\min}\) and \(p_{\min} = p_{3k+3}\) from (5), and \(f(p_{\min})\).
Update \(\mathrm{Err}\) from the \(e_i\) and set the new \(h\) from (7).
Set \(p_0 = p_{\min}\) and \(k \leftarrow k + 1\). Repeat from step 1 while \(\mathrm{Err} > \varepsilon\).



The tables label the points as Mathews does. The bracketing triple of outer step \(k\) is \(p_{3k}, p_{3k+1}, p_{3k+2}\), its vertex is \(p_{3k+3}\), and the trial points of the bracketing loop are \(q_{3k+2,j}\), \(j = 0, 1, \ldots\)


Example 1 — Minimise \(x^2 - \sin x\) on \([0, 1]\)
Find the minimum of
\[
f(x) = x^2 - \sin x
\]
on \([0, 1]\) with the quadratic search. Mathews calls his subroutine with \(\delta = \varepsilon = 10^{-6}\).
Step 1 (first triple): \(p_0 = 0\) and \(f'(0) = -1 < 0\), so \(h = (1 - 0)/2 = 0.5\) is positive. The triple is
\[
p_0 = 0,\quad p_1 = 0.5,\quad p_2 = 1, \qquad y_0 = 0,\quad y_1 = -0.2294255386,\quad y_2 = 0.1585290152 .
\]
Since \(y_0 > y_1 < y_2\), this triple is already bracketed (case i).
Step 2 (first vertex): from (5),
\[
h_{\min} = \frac{0.5\,(4y_1 - 3y_0 - y_2)}{2\,(2y_1 - y_0 - y_2)} = \frac{0.5\,(-1.0762311696)}{-1.2347601848} = 0.4358057471,
\]
so \(p_3 = 0.4358057471\) and \(f(p_3) = -0.2322143232\).
Step 3 (restart): the distances from \(p_3\) to the old points are \(0.4358057471\), \(0.0641942529\) and \(0.5641942529\), so by (7) the new step is \(h = 0.0641942529\), the distance to \(p_1 = 0.5\). The differences \(e_i\) are \(0.232\), \(2.79 \times 10^{-3}\) and \(0.391\), so \(\mathrm{Err} = 2.79 \times 10^{-3} > 10^{-6}\) and the search continues. Since \(f'(p_3) = -0.0349 < 0\), the step stays positive.
Step 4 (second bracket): the new triple is \(0.4358057471\), \(0.5\), \(0.5641942529\), with values \(-0.2322143232\), \(-0.2294255386\), \(-0.2164199625\). Since \(y_0 \le y_1\), halve: \(q_{5,0} = 0.4679028735\), with \(f = -0.2320824604\), is still above \(y_0\), so halve again: \(q_{5,1} = 0.4518543103\), with \(f = -0.2324621759\). Now \(y_0 > y_1\) and \(y_2 = f(0.4679028735) > y_1\), so the bracket is \((0.4358057471, 0.4518543103, 0.4679028735)\) with \(h = 0.0160485632\).
Step 5 (second vertex): (5) gives \(h_{\min} = 0.0143625245\), so \(p_6 = 0.4501682715\) and \(f(p_6) = -0.232465574872\). The new step is \(h = 0.0016860388\), the distance to \(0.4518543103\), and \(\mathrm{Err} = 3.40 \times 10^{-6}\).
Step 6 (third bracket and vertex): six halvings bring the step down to \(h = 2.63444 \times 10^{-5}\), and the vertex is \(p_9 = 0.4501836113\). Now \(\mathrm{Err} = 1.47 \times 10^{-10} \le 10^{-6}\), and the search stops.

Example 3 — Minimise \(\tfrac12 + x^5 - \tfrac45 x\) on \([0, 1]\)

\[
f(x) = \frac12 + x^5 - \frac45\,x
\]
on \([0, 1]\) with the quadratic search, again with \(\delta = \varepsilon = 10^{-6}\). This is the example of Mathews’ quadratic-search animation. His solution prints the points in the order of the table below and interleaves the printed lines with graphs of \(f\) that mark the current points. This example uses all three cases of the bracketing loop.
Step 1 (first triple and vertex): \(f'(0) = -0.8 < 0\) and \(h = 0.5\). The triple \(0, 0.5, 1\) has values \(0.5\), \(0.13125\), \(0.7\), so it is bracketed. Here \(4y_1 - 3y_0 - y_2 = -1.675\) and \(2(2y_1 - y_0 - y_2) = -1.875\), so
\[
h_{\min} = \frac{0.5\,(-1.675)}{-1.875} = 0.4466666667 = \tfrac{67}{150}, \qquad p_3 = 0.4466666667, \qquad f(p_3) = 0.1604460919.
\]
The new step is the distance to \(0.5\), \(h = 0.0533333333\), and \(\mathrm{Err} = 2.92 \times 10^{-2}\).
Step 2 (doubling, case ii): the triple \(0.4466666667\), \(0.5\), \(0.5533333333\) has values \(0.1604460919\), \(0.13125\), \(0.1092054735\), which decrease, so double: \(q_{5,0} = p_0 + 2(0.1066666667) = 0.66\), with \(f = 0.0972332576\), is lower again, so double once more: \(q_{5,1} = 0.8733333333\), with \(f = 0.3093759954\). The bracket is \((0.4466666667, 0.66, 0.8733333333)\) with \(h = 0.2133333333\). Its vertex is \(p_6 = 0.6023078449\), with \(f(p_6) = 0.0974207564\). This value is higher than \(f(0.66) = 0.0972332576\), and \(p_6\) is farther from \(p\) (\(0.0302\)) than \(0.66\) is (\(0.0275\)). The vertex is not always the best point found so far. The new step is \(h = 0.0576921551\), the distance to \(0.66\), and \(\mathrm{Err} = 1.87 \times 10^{-4}\).
Step 3 (bracketed at once): the triple \(0.6023078449\), \(0.66\), \(0.7176921551\) is bracketed without halving or doubling, and its vertex is \(p_9 = 0.6317169944\). None of its \(e_i\) is below \(1.87 \times 10^{-4}\), so \(\mathrm{Err}\) does not change.

title: Quadratic Interpolative Search
text:
Cubic Interpolative Search

The starting step
Assume \(f\) is unimodal and differentiable on \([a, b]\), with minimum at \(p\), and let \(p_0 = a\). Any reasonable step \(h\) can start the iteration. Mathews estimates one from the mean value theorem, \(f(a + h) - f(a) = h f'(c)\) for some \(c\) between \(a\) and \(a + h\). If \(a + h\) were just to the right of the minimum, the average slope \(f'(c)\) might be about \(\tfrac12 f'(a)\). Since the position of \(a + h\) is unknown, he takes \(f(a + h) \approx f(b)\) and obtains
\[
h_0 = \frac{2\bigl(f(b) - f(a)\bigr)}{f'(a)}, \qquad p_1 = p_0 + h_0.
\tag{8}
\]
When \(f'(a) < 0\), this \(h_0\) is positive only if \(f(b) < f(a)\). In both of Mathews’ examples \(f(b) > f(a)\), so \(h_0 < 0\) and \(p_1\) lies to the left of \(a\), outside the interval.


The interpolating cubic
Let \(h = p_1 - p_0\). The cubic \(P\) is written about the abscissa \(p_2\) of its minimum:
\[
P(x) = \frac{\alpha}{h^3}(x - p_2)^3 + \frac{\beta}{h^2}(x - p_2)^2 + f(p_2),
\qquad
P'(x) = \frac{3\alpha}{h^3}(x - p_2)^2 + \frac{2\beta}{h^2}(x - p_2).
\tag{9}
\]
It must satisfy \(P(p_0) = f(p_0)\), \(P(p_1) = f(p_1)\), \(P'(p_0) = f'(p_0)\) and \(P'(p_1) = f'(p_1)\). (The powers of \(h\) in the denominators make the following algebra simpler.) Put
\[
p_2 = p_0 + \gamma h,
\tag{10}
\]
so that \(p_1 - p_2 = (1 - \gamma)h\) and \(p_0 - p_2 = -\gamma h\). Substituting into (9) gives three equations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
F &= f(p_1) - f(p_0) = \alpha(3\gamma^2 - 3\gamma + 1) + \beta(1 - 2\gamma), \\
G &= h\bigl(f'(p_1) - f'(p_0)\bigr) = 3\alpha(1 - 2\gamma) + 2\beta, \\
h f'(p_0) &= 3\alpha\gamma^2 - 2\beta\gamma.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
The book section linked from Mathews’ module gives the middle equation as \(G = f'(p_1) - f'(p_0)\), without the factor \(h\). The module and the subroutine include the factor, and it is needed. The combination \(G - 2(F - h f'(p_0))\) cancels both \(\beta\) and every \(\gamma\):
\[
\alpha = G - 2\bigl(F - h f'(p_0)\bigr).
\tag{12}
\]
Multiplying the second equation of (11) by \(\gamma\) and adding the third eliminates \(\beta\):
\[
3\alpha\gamma^2 + (G - 3\alpha)\gamma + h f'(p_0) = 0.
\tag{13}
\]
The quadratic formula, with the numerator rationalised, gives the root Mathews uses:
\[
\gamma = \frac{-2h f'(p_0)}{(G - 3\alpha) + \sqrt{(G - 3\alpha)^2 - 12 h \alpha f'(p_0)}}.
\tag{14}
\]






TipWhich root (general)



From (9), \(P''(p_2) = 2\beta/h^2\), so \(p_2\) is a local minimum of \(P\) when \(\beta > 0\). Each critical point of the cubic through the four conditions gives a representation (9) about that point, so the two roots of (13) are the cubic’s two critical points. Form (14) is the root that stays finite as \(\alpha \to 0\). In that limit \(P\) is a quadratic and \(\gamma = -h f'(p_0)/G\), so
\[
p_2 = p_0 - f'(p_0)\,\frac{p_1 - p_0}{f'(p_1) - f'(p_0)},
\]
the secant step for \(f'(x) = 0\). If the discriminant in (14) is negative, the cubic has no critical point and the step is undefined.


In every step of Examples 2 and 4 the discriminant is positive and \(\beta > 0\), so (14) picks the local minimum of the cubic.
To continue, set \(h = p_2 - p_1\) and replace \(p_0, p_1\) by \(p_1, p_2\) in (11)–(14). The method does not keep a bracket, so a stopping rule is harder to choose. Mathews suggests \(|f'(p_k)| < \varepsilon\), since \(f'(p) = 0\). His subroutine simply runs a fixed number of steps.






ImportantAlgorithm — Cubic search for a minimum (Mathews’ subroutine)



Given \(f\) unimodal and differentiable on \([a, b]\) and a number of steps \(m_{\max}\): set \(p_0 = a\), \(h_0 = 2(f(b) - f(a))/f'(a)\), \(p_1 = p_0 + h_0\). For \(k = 0, 1, \ldots, m_{\max} - 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
F &= f(p_{k+1}) - f(p_k), \qquad G = h_k\bigl(f'(p_{k+1}) - f'(p_k)\bigr), \qquad \alpha = G - 2\bigl(F - h_k f'(p_k)\bigr), \\
\gamma &= \frac{-2h_k f'(p_k)}{(G - 3\alpha) + \sqrt{(G - 3\alpha)^2 - 12 h_k \alpha f'(p_k)}}, \qquad
p_{k+2} = p_k + \gamma h_k, \qquad h_{k+1} = p_{k+2} - p_{k+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]


Mathews’ algorithm statement lists \(p_1 = b\) among the starting values. In his subroutine \(b\) enters only through \(f(b)\) in \(h_0\), and the iteration starts from \(p_1 = p_0 + h_0\).

Examples 1 and 2 minimise the same function, so the methods can be compared directly.

Cubic search (Example 2)

Secant method on \(f'\)

To see the rate of convergence without the limit of double precision, the three iterations were repeated in 400-digit arithmetic. The ratio \(\log e_{k+1} / \log e_k\) of successive errors measures the order:

Cubic search: the ratios settle near \(2\). The last ratios before the 400-digit limit are \(2.10\), \(1.98\), \(2.02\) in Example 2 and \(2.09\), \(1.95\), \(2.02\) in Example 4. This is consistent with the order \(2\) of cubic interpolation using function and derivative values (a general result).
Secant method on \(f'\): the ratios fall to \(1.62\), the golden ratio \((1 + \sqrt5)/2 \approx 1.618\) that is the general order of the secant method.
Mathews’ quadratic search: each outer step roughly squares the error. The ratios are \(2.61\), \(2.22\), \(2.11\), \(2.05\), \(2.02\), \(2.01\) in Example 1 and \(2.08\), \(2.06\), \(2.00\), \(2.02\), \(2.00\), \(2.00\), \(2.00\), \(2.00\) in Example 3. But the bracketing loops of the successive outer steps need more and more halvings or doublings: \(2, 6, 19, 34, 76, 156\) in Example 1 and \(2, 0, 5, 8, 13, 39, 82, 164\) in Example 3. In the last three steps of each run that is \(1.4\) to \(1.7\) passes, each costing one evaluation of \(f\), per decimal digit gained. Counted per function evaluation, the quadratic search therefore converges far more slowly than the squaring per step suggests.

This variant is not the textbook successive parabolic interpolation, which keeps the three most recent points, unequally spaced, and needs no bracketing loop.

title: Quadratic Interpolative Search
text:
Implementation Notes

Quadratic search, direction. The subroutine evaluates \(f'(p_0)\) once per outer step and uses only its sign. A version without derivatives must choose the direction from function values instead.
Quadratic search, step rule. Rule (7) gives the distance from \(p_{\min}\) to the nearest old point only when \(h > 0\), because the subroutine replaces \(h\) by \(|h|\) first. Every outer step in Examples 1 and 3 has \(f'(p_0) < 0\) and therefore \(h > 0\).
Quadratic search, bracketing. Check that the triple really is bracketed before using (5). The loop can also end because \(|h| \le \delta\), and the vertex of an unbracketed or collinear triple is meaningless or undefined.
Quadratic search, stopping. \(\mathrm{Err}\) compares function values, which agree to about the square of the distance to \(p\) (Example 3: \(8.1 \times 10^{-13}\) in \(f\) against \(5.7 \times 10^{-7}\) in \(x\)). A tolerance \(\varepsilon\) on \(f\) therefore corresponds to a distance of roughly \(\sqrt{2\varepsilon / f''(p)}\) (general).
Cubic search, starting step. Formula (8) needs \(f'(a) \ne 0\), and with \(f(b) > f(a)\) it sends \(p_1\) outside \([a, b]\) (both examples). The method does not keep a bracket, and \(p_1\) can land where \(f\) is not convex, as in Example 4.
Cubic search, stopping. Use a test such as \(|f'(p_k)| < \varepsilon\) rather than a fixed number of steps. Once the iterates agree to rounding, \(F\), \(G\) and \(\alpha\) are pure rounding noise. Continued in double precision, both examples eventually reach \(0/0\) in (14): Example 2 at \(p_9\), after \(p_7 = p_8\) exactly, and Example 4 also at \(p_9\), where \(f'(p_7) = 0\) exactly. Mathews’ runs stop before this.
Unimodality. Neither method can tell a local minimum from the global one. If \(f\) has several minima in \([a, b]\), the result depends on the start.

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Description
Golden ratio search finds the minimum of a function \(f\) on an interval \([a_0, b_0]\) using only function values, no derivatives. It needs \(f\) to be unimodal on the interval: decreasing up to a single minimiser \(p\) and increasing after it. Each step evaluates \(f\) at two interior points \(c_k < d_k\) and throws away the part of the interval that cannot contain \(p\). If \(f(c_k) \le f(d_k)\) the minimiser lies in \([a_k, d_k]\), otherwise it lies in \([c_k, b_k]\).
The interior points divide every interval in the same proportions:
\[
c_k = a_k + (1 - \rho)(b_k - a_k), \qquad d_k = a_k + \rho\,(b_k - a_k), \qquad \rho = \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{2} \approx 0.618034.
\]
Because \(\rho^2 = 1 - \rho\), the interior point that survives a step is exactly an interior point of the next interval, so every step after the first costs one new function evaluation, and every step shrinks the interval by the same factor: \(b_k - a_k = \rho^k (b_0 - a_0)\). Unlike Fibonacci search, which fixes the number of steps in advance and changes the ratio at every step, the golden ratio search can simply run until the interval is shorter than a tolerance \(\delta\).

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Animations
Each animation below shows the shrinking bracket of a golden ratio search. The top panel keeps the picture of Mathews’ plotting program: the graph of \(f\) in magenta, the current interval \([a_k, b_k]\) as a red arc with pink fill, red dots at \(a_k\) and \(b_k\), blue dots at the interior points \(c_k\) and \(d_k\), and the list \(\{a_k, c_k, d_k, b_k\}\) in the title. The bottom panel is new. It zooms on \([a_k, b_k]\) and plots \(f(x) - f(p)\), where \(p\) is the true minimiser (the dashed green line in both panels), so the comparison of \(f(c_k)\) with \(f(d_k)\) stays visible after the bracket has become too narrow to see in the top panel. Its title gives the step \(k\), the width \(b_k - a_k\), the sign of \(f(c_k) - f(d_k)\) and the part that is kept, which a green bar marks. In Cases 1 and 2, frame \(k\) shows row \(k\) of the example’s table. The last frame gives the endpoint that Mathews’ program returns and the midpoint of the last interval, and it is held. Points are labelled with enough significant figures to tell them apart, so the labels gain digits as the bracket shrinks. The differences in the titles and the curve in the bottom panel are evaluated in high precision at the double-precision points. Every double-precision comparison has the same sign as that high-precision difference, and a 50-digit run of each search keeps the same side at every step.
Mathews’ module has one animation, linked from the solution of Example 6. Its GIF is lost (the archive keeps only the animation’s HTML page), and so are the ten pictures of his Example 6 solution. Case 1 rebuilds it from his plotting program, which survives, and from the Example 6 text: the same function, interval, window and picture elements, and the ten pictures of his solution, the start and nine steps (how many frames his GIF had is not recorded). Cases 2 and 3 are new, with no Mathews original. Example 2’s search on \([0, 1]\), Example 3, Examples 4 and 5 (his Exercises 4 and 5) and the secant-method comparison in Example 1 are not animated. The scripts squeeze with the rule of the Description and of the algorithm below, which keeps \([a_k, d_k]\) when \(f(c_k) \le f(d_k)\); Mathews’ program keeps \([c_k, b_k]\) in a tie, but no comparison in the three runs is a tie, so both rules give the same steps. Like Mathews’ program, the scripts compute \(1 - \rho\) as \(\rho^2\) and return the endpoint with the smaller function value.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Mathews’ animation, Example 6, \(f(x) = \tfrac12 + x^5 - \tfrac45 x\) on \([0, 1]\), \(9\) steps
Behavior: Mathews’ plotting program draws the starting interval and then makes max − 1 steps. His Example 6 solution has ten pictures, so max = 10, and the animation shows \(k = 0, \ldots, 9\), the rows of the Example 6 table, in his window \([-0.05, 1.05] \times [0, 0.72]\). The bracket is squeezed from the left (keep \([c_k, b_k]\)) at \(k = 0, 2, 4, 5, 8\) and from the right (keep \([a_k, d_k]\)) at \(k = 1, 3, 6, 7\), and every bracket contains \(p = \sqrt{10}/5 \approx 0.6325\). By \(k = 9\) the four dots overlap at Mathews’ scale, and the zoom panel separates them. The last interval is \([0.6262, 0.6393]\), of width \(\rho^9 = 0.01316\). Mathews’ program returns \(a_9 = 0.6262\), which is \(6.29 \times 10^{-3}\) from \(p\); the midpoint \(0.6327\) is \(2.9 \times 10^{-4}\) from \(p\).

Case 2 — Example 1, \(f(x) = x^2 - \sin x\) on \([0, 1]\), \(25\) steps (new)

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Unimodal Functions and Bracketing






NoteDefinition — Unimodal function



The function \(f\) is unimodal on \(I = [a, b]\) if there is a unique number \(p \in I\) such that \(f\) is decreasing on \([a, p]\) and increasing on \([p, b]\).


A bracketing search keeps an interval \([a_k, b_k]\) that is known to contain \(p\) and shrinks it by comparing \(f\) at two interior points \(c_k < d_k\):

If \(f(c_k) \le f(d_k)\), the minimum cannot lie to the right of \(d_k\). Squeeze from the right: set \(a_{k+1} = a_k\), \(b_{k+1} = d_k\).
If \(f(c_k) > f(d_k)\), the minimum cannot lie to the left of \(c_k\). Squeeze from the left: set \(a_{k+1} = c_k\), \(b_{k+1} = b_k\).

A tie \(f(c_k) = f(d_k)\) puts \(p\) between \(c_k\) and \(d_k\), so either choice is safe; the rule above keeps \([a_k, d_k]\). Mathews’ programs keep \([c_k, b_k]\) in a tie. No comparison in the examples below is a tie, so both rules give the same steps. The method uses only comparisons of function values, so it also works when \(f\) is not differentiable.

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Derivation of the Golden Ratio
Place the interior points of \([a, b]\) symmetrically, so that \(c - a = b - d\):
\[
c = a + (1 - r)(b - a), \qquad d = a + r\,(b - a), \qquad \tfrac12 < r < 1,
\tag{1}
\]
where \(r > \tfrac12\) keeps \(c < d\). We want the same \(r\) on every interval, and one of the old interior points must become an interior point of the new interval, so that each step needs only one new function value.
Suppose \(f(c) \le f(d)\), so the new interval is \([a, d]\), of length \(r(b - a)\). Its right interior point is \(a + r(d - a)\), and for this to be the old point \(c\) we need \(c - a = r(d - a)\), that is
\[
(1 - r)(b - a) = r \cdot r\,(b - a)
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
r^2 + r - 1 = 0.
\tag{2}
\]
If instead \(f(c) > f(d)\), the new interval is \([c, b]\), also of length \(r(b - a)\), and its left interior point \(c + (1 - r)(b - c)\) must be the old point \(d\). Since \(d - c = (2r - 1)(b - a)\) and \(b - c = r(b - a)\), this gives \(2r - 1 = (1 - r)\,r\), which is the same equation (2). Its roots are \(r = (-1 \pm \sqrt5)/2\), and the root in \((\tfrac12, 1)\) is
\[
\rho = \frac{\sqrt5 - 1}{2} = 0.6180339887\ldots, \qquad \rho^2 = 1 - \rho = 0.3819660113\ldots
\tag{3}
\]
Mathews calls \(\rho\) the golden ratio. The name is more often given to its reciprocal \(\phi = 1/\rho = (1 + \sqrt5)/2 = 1.6180339887\ldots\); either way, \(\rho\) is the factor by which the interval shrinks. Equation (2) is the special case \(r_1 = r_0\) of the equation \(r_1 = (1 - r_0)/r_0\) on the Fibonacci search page.






TipTheorem — Interval lengths in golden ratio search



If \(f\) is unimodal on \([a_0, b_0]\) (and the comparisons are exact), every interval \([a_k, b_k]\) contains the minimiser \(p\), and
\[
b_k - a_k = \rho^k\,(b_0 - a_0).
\tag{4}
\]
The midpoint \((a_k + b_k)/2\) is within \(\tfrac12 \rho^k (b_0 - a_0)\) of \(p\). The interval is shorter than a tolerance \(\delta\) once
\[
k \ge \frac{\ln\bigl(\delta / (b_0 - a_0)\bigr)}{\ln \rho}.
\tag{5}
\]


This is a general result. The interval shrinks by the same factor \(\rho \approx 0.618\) at every step whatever \(f\) is, so the convergence is linear, and each extra decimal digit of accuracy costs \(\ln 10 / \ln \phi \approx 4.78\) steps.

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Algorithm






ImportantAlgorithm — Golden ratio search for a minimum



Given \(f\) unimodal on \([a_0, b_0]\) and a tolerance \(\delta\) (or a number of steps):

Compute \(c_0 = a_0 + (1 - \rho)(b_0 - a_0)\) and \(d_0 = a_0 + \rho(b_0 - a_0)\), and evaluate \(f(c_0)\), \(f(d_0)\).
For \(k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\) until \(b_k - a_k \le \delta\):

if \(f(c_k) \le f(d_k)\): set \(a_{k+1} = a_k\), \(b_{k+1} = d_k\), \(d_{k+1} = c_k\), and compute the new point \(c_{k+1} = a_{k+1} + (1 - \rho)(b_{k+1} - a_{k+1})\);
otherwise: set \(a_{k+1} = c_k\), \(b_{k+1} = b_k\), \(c_{k+1} = d_k\), and compute the new point \(d_{k+1} = a_{k+1} + \rho(b_{k+1} - a_{k+1})\);
evaluate \(f\) at the one new point.

Return an approximation to \(p\) from the last interval, for example its midpoint.



After \(K\) steps the method has used \(K + 2\) function evaluations and the interval has length \(\rho^K (b_0 - a_0)\). The values \(f(c_K)\) and \(f(d_K)\) are already known, so one more comparison shrinks the interval to \(\rho^{K+1}(b_0 - a_0)\) for free. With \(N = K + 2\) evaluations the bracket is therefore \(\rho^{N-1}(b_0 - a_0)\), the figure used on the Fibonacci search page.
Mathews gives two programs:

GoldenSearch[a0, b0, max] makes exactly max steps.
GoldenSearch[a0, b0, δ, ε] continues while \(\lvert f(b_k) - f(a_k) \rvert > \varepsilon\) or \(b_k - a_k > \delta\), so it stops once both \(b_k - a_k \le \delta\) and \(\lvert f(b_k) - f(a_k) \rvert \le \varepsilon\).

Both also evaluate \(f(a_0)\) and \(f(b_0)\) (so \(K + 4\) evaluations in all), keep \([c_k, b_k]\) in a tie, print the list \(\{a_k, c_k, d_k, b_k\}\) at every step, and return whichever endpoint, \(a_k\) or \(b_k\), has the smaller function value. The returned endpoint is within \(b_k - a_k\) of \(p\). The midpoint has half that error bound.

Example 1 — Minimise \(x^2 - \sin x\) on \([0, 1]\)
Find the minimum of the unimodal function
\[
f(x) = x^2 - \sin x

on \([0, 1]\). Mathews runs this example for \(25\) steps. The function is unimodal on \([0, 1]\) because \(f''(x) = 2 + \sin x \ge 2 > 0\) there.

\[

\]

d_2 = 0.2360680 + \rho\,(0.6180340 - 0.2360680) = 0.4721360, \qquad f(d_2) = -0.2318772406.

Example 2 — Local minimum of \(e^x - \sin 2x\) over \([-1, 1]\)

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Fibonacci Versus Golden Ratio Search
Both methods use the same squeeze rule and one new function evaluation per step. The Fibonacci ratios \(r_k = F_{n-1-k}/F_{n-k}\) tend to \(\rho\), and on the two functions both pages use, the two searches keep the same side at every comparison the Fibonacci search makes: \(18\) of them in Example 1 and \(9\) in Example 6. The differences are:

Planning. Fibonacci search fixes the number of evaluations before it starts, and a tighter tolerance means starting again. The golden ratio search uses the same ratio at every step, so it can be stopped by a tolerance, or continued, at any time.
Efficiency. With \(N\) evaluations the golden ratio search leaves a bracket of length \(\rho^{N-1}(b_0 - a_0)\), and Fibonacci search, with Mathews’ final split (\(e = 0.01\)), leaves one about \(0.871\) times as long (the ratio tends to \((1 + 2e)\sqrt5/\phi^2\) as \(N\) grows; see the Fibonacci search page). Apart from the last few Fibonacci steps, both shrink the bracket by a factor close to \(0.618\) per evaluation.

title: Golden Ratio Search
text:
Implementation Notes

Reuse the surviving point. Keep the surviving interior point and its function value, and evaluate \(f\) only at the new point. This is what makes each step cost one evaluation.
Choosing the stopping rule. The width test \(b_k - a_k \le \delta\) fixes the number of steps in advance through (5). A test on function values alone can be met while the interval is still wide, because \(f\) is flat near \(p\) and because \(f(a_k)\) and \(f(b_k)\) can be close when \(p\) is near the middle of the interval. In Example 1, \(\lvert f(b_k) - f(a_k) \rvert \le 10^{-6}\) already holds at \(k = 14\), when the interval is still \(1.19 \times 10^{-3}\) wide. Mathews’ second program requires both tests.
Precision limit. Near \(p\) the compared values differ by roughly \(\tfrac12 f''(p)\) times the square of the spacing of the points, so in floating point the comparisons eventually fail. For Example 1 in double precision, from \(k = 37\) (interval \(1.9 \times 10^{-8}\)) every computed difference \(f(c_k) - f(d_k)\) is at most two units of the spacing \(2.8 \times 10^{-17}\) of double-precision numbers near \(f(p)\), so its sign is decided by rounding. The first wrong comparison comes at \(k = 42\), and from \(k = 43\) (interval \(1.0 \times 10^{-9}\)) the interval no longer contains \(p\). As a general rule of thumb, an interval much shorter than about \(\sqrt{u} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-8}\) times the size of \(p\), where \(u = 2^{-52}\), cannot be trusted in double precision.
Unimodality is required. If \(f\) has several local minima in \([a_0, b_0]\), the comparisons can discard the part containing the minimum wanted. The method still returns a point, but there is no guarantee which minimum it approaches (Example 2 started on \([-1, 1]\) works only because the first comparison happens to discard the local maximum).
Maxima. To find a maximum of \(f\), minimise \(-f\), as in Examples 3 and 4.

title: Quadratic Interpolative Search
text:
Description
Quadratic interpolative search finds the minimum of a unimodal function \(f\) on an interval \([a, b]\) by fitting a parabola through three function values and moving to the parabola’s lowest point. The version on this page is the one in Mathews’ module and Mathematica subroutine, which uses three equally spaced points \(p_0\), \(p_1 = p_0 + h\), \(p_2 = p_0 + 2h\). It starts from \(p_0 = a\) with \(h = (b - a)/2\) and steps to the right when \(f'(p_0) < 0\), to the left when \(f'(p_0) > 0\). It then halves \(h\) while \(f(p_0) \le f(p_1)\) and doubles it while \(f(p_2) < f(p_1)\), until the middle value is the lowest, \(f(p_0) > f(p_1) \le f(p_2)\). With \(y_i = f(p_i)\), the vertex of the interpolating quadratic is
\[
p_{\min} = p_0 + h_{\min}, \qquad h_{\min} = \frac{h\,(4y_1 - 3y_0 - y_2)}{2\,(2y_1 - y_0 - y_2)}.
\]
The search restarts from \(p_0 = p_{\min}\), with \(h\) equal (after a step to the right) to the distance from \(p_{\min}\) to the nearest of the three old points. It stops when one of \(y_0, y_1, y_2\) agrees with \(f(p_{\min})\) to within a tolerance \(\varepsilon\).
The module also covers cubic interpolative search, which uses derivative values explicitly. It fits a cubic \(P\) to the values of \(f\) and \(f'\) at two points \(p_0\) and \(p_1 = p_0 + h\), and moves to the local minimum of the cubic, \(p_2 = p_0 + \gamma h\), where
\[
\gamma = \frac{-2h f'(p_0)}{(G - 3\alpha) + \sqrt{(G - 3\alpha)^2 - 12 h \alpha f'(p_0)}}, \qquad
F = f(p_1) - f(p_0), \quad G = h\bigl(f'(p_1) - f'(p_0)\bigr), \quad \alpha = G - 2\bigl(F - h f'(p_0)\bigr).
\]
Then \((p_0, p_1)\) is replaced by \((p_1, p_2)\) and the step repeats. The cubic search does not keep a bracket: in both of Mathews’ examples its first point \(p_1\) lies outside \([a, b]\). The examples below keep Mathews’ numbers. Examples 1 and 3 use the quadratic search and Examples 2 and 4 the cubic search. Examples 1 and 2 minimise the same function, and so do Examples 3 and 4.

title: Quadratic Interpolative Search
text:
Animations
Both animations run Mathews’ examples on \(f(x) = \tfrac12 + x^5 - \tfrac45 x\), whose minimiser is \(p = \sqrt{10}/5 \approx 0.6325\) (the dashed green line, also in the bottom panel whenever \(p\) lies in its window). The top panel keeps the picture of the graphs in Mathews’ solutions of Examples 3 and 4: the graph of \(f\) in magenta, red dots on the points the current step works from and a blue dot on the newest point. The bottom panel is new. It zooms on the current points and plots \(f(x) - f(p)\), evaluated in high precision, so the steps stay visible after they have become too small to see in the top panel. Points are labelled with enough significant figures to tell them apart, so the labels gain digits as the steps shrink, and the last frame is held. The scripts run Mathews’ two subroutines line by line in double precision, and every point they compute agrees with the Example 3 and Example 4 tables.
Mathews’ module has two animations, a quadratic search linked from Example 3 and a cubic search linked from Example 4. Both GIFs are lost: the archive keeps only their HTML pages. Cases 1 and 2 rebuild them from his subroutines and from the graphs of his Example 3 and Example 4 solutions, which survive (twelve graphs for Example 3, eight for Example 4); how many frames his GIFs had is not recorded. The parabola, the cubic, the slopes and the zoom panel are new. Examples 1 and 2, which run the same two searches on \(x^2 - \sin x\), and the secant-method comparison in Example 2 are not animated.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Mathews’ quadratic search animation, Example 3, \(f(x) = \tfrac12 + x^5 - \tfrac45 x\) on \([0, 1]\), \(\delta = \varepsilon = 10^{-6}\)
Behavior: There is one frame for each event of Mathews’ subroutine, \(15\) in all: each new triple \(p_0,\ p_0 + h,\ p_0 + 2h\), each halving or doubling of \(h\), and each vertex. These are the \(23\) rows of the Example 3 table, with the three points of a new triple shown together. The pink span with the red arc is the interval of the current triple, and the bottom title gives the test that decides the next move. In a vertex frame the dashed parabola \(Q\) through the triple is drawn with its vertex (open circle) and the new point \(p_{3k+3}\) on \(f\) (blue). The run uses all three cases of the bracketing loop: the triples of outer steps \(k = 0\) and \(k = 2\) are bracketed at once, step \(k = 1\) doubles twice, to \(0.66\) and \(0.8733\), and step \(k = 3\) halves five times, down to \(h = 8.838 \times 10^{-4}\). During those halvings the triple shrinks to a width of \(1.77 \times 10^{-3}\), and its dots overlap in the top panel while the zoom keeps them apart. In the last frame \(Q\) and \(f\) differ by at most \(1.1 \times 10^{-9}\) over the zoom window, less than \(0.03\%\) of its height, so the two curves coincide there. The search stops after four vertex steps and \(23\) calls of \(f\), when \(\mathrm{Err} = 5.34 \times 10^{-8} \le 10^{-6}\), at \(p_{12} = 0.63245496\), which is \(5.67 \times 10^{-7}\) from \(p\).

title: Quadratic Interpolative Search
section: Unimodal Functions and the Derivative Test
text:
Unimodal Functions and the Derivative Test






NoteDefinition — Unimodal function



The function \(f\) is unimodal on \(I = [a, b]\) if there is a unique number \(p \in I\) such that \(f\) is decreasing on \([a, p]\) and increasing on \([p, b]\).


Bracketing searches such as the golden ratio and Fibonacci searches need only this condition. The two methods on this page also use the derivative. Suppose \(f\) is unimodal on \([a, b]\) with minimum at \(p\), \(f'\) exists on \((a, b)\), and \(p_0 \in (a, b)\). If \(f'(p_0) < 0\) the minimum lies to the right of \(p_0\), and if \(f'(p_0) > 0\) it lies to the left.
Both of Mathews’ functions are unimodal on \([0, 1]\):

\(f(x) = x^2 - \sin x\) has \(f''(x) = 2 + \sin x \ge 2 > 0\) on \([0, 1]\), \(f'(0) = -1 < 0\) and \(f'(1) = 2 - \cos 1 = 1.4597 > 0\). The minimiser is the root of \(2x = \cos x\), \(p = 0.4501836113\), with \(f(p) = -0.2324655752\).
\(f(x) = \tfrac12 + x^5 - \tfrac45 x\) has \(f''(x) = 20x^3 > 0\) on \((0, 1]\), \(f'(0) = -0.8\) and \(f'(1) = 4.2\). The minimiser is exact: \(5p^4 = \tfrac45\) gives \(p = (4/25)^{1/4} = \sqrt{10}/5 = 0.6324555320\), with \(f(p) = 0.0952284595\).

title: Quadratic Interpolative Search
text:
Quadratic Interpolative Search

Bracketing the minimum
The first task is to find three test values
\[
p_0, \qquad p_1 = p_0 + h, \qquad p_2 = p_0 + 2h
\tag{1}
\]
such that
\[
f(p_0) > f(p_1) \qquad\text{and}\qquad f(p_1) < f(p_2).
\tag{2}
\]
Suppose \(f'(p_0) < 0\), so that \(p_0 < p\) and \(h\) is chosen positive. One pass of the bracketing loop does one of three things:

Case (i): if (2) holds, the bracket is found.
Case (ii): if \(f(p_0) > f(p_1)\) and \(f(p_1) > f(p_2)\), then \(p_1 < p\): the minimum lies to the right of \(p_1\), so the points must reach farther right. (Mathews writes \(p_2 < p\), which need not hold: in Example 3 the triple \((0.4467, 0.5533, 0.66)\) is doubled although \(0.66 > p\).) Double the step: \(p_1 \leftarrow p_2\), \(h \leftarrow 2h\), \(p_2 \leftarrow p_0 + 2h\).
Case (iii): if \(f(p_0) \le f(p_1)\), the step has jumped over \(p\) and is too large. Halve the step: \(p_2 \leftarrow p_1\), \(h \leftarrow h/2\), \(p_1 \leftarrow p_0 + h\).

Each pass of cases (ii) and (iii) evaluates \(f\) at one new point. When \(f'(p_0) > 0\) the step \(h\) is negative and the same three cases apply. Mathews’ subroutine accepts the bracket when \(f(p_0) > f(p_1)\) and \(f(p_2) \ge f(p_1)\), so a tie between \(f(p_1)\) and \(f(p_2)\) also ends the loop. The loop also stops if \(|h|\) falls to a minimum step \(\delta\). Mathews’ text starts with \(h = 1\), or \(h = \tfrac12\) if \(a + 1 < b\) fails. His subroutine starts with \(h = (b - a)/2\), which for the interval \([0, 1]\) of both examples is the same \(h = \tfrac12\).


The vertex of the interpolating quadratic
With \(y_i = f(p_i)\) for \(i = 0, 1, 2\), the Lagrange polynomial through the three points (1) is
\[
Q(x) = y_0\,\frac{(x - p_1)(x - p_2)}{2h^2} - y_1\,\frac{(x - p_0)(x - p_2)}{h^2} + y_2\,\frac{(x - p_0)(x - p_1)}{2h^2},
\tag{3}
\]
and its derivative is
\[
Q'(x) = y_0\,\frac{2x - p_1 - p_2}{2h^2} - y_1\,\frac{2x - p_0 - p_2}{h^2} + y_2\,\frac{2x - p_0 - p_1}{2h^2}.
\tag{4}
\]
Write the critical point as \(x = p_0 + h_{\min}\), set \(Q'(p_0 + h_{\min}) = 0\), multiply by \(2h^2\) and collect the terms in \(h_{\min}\):
\[
0 = h_{\min}(2y_0 - 4y_1 + 2y_2) + y_0(2p_0 - p_1 - p_2) - y_1(4p_0 - 2p_0 - 2p_2) + y_2(2p_0 - p_0 - p_1).
\]
With \(p_1 = p_0 + h\) and \(p_2 = p_0 + 2h\) the last three terms are \(-3hy_0 + 4hy_1 - hy_2\), so
\[
h_{\min} = \frac{h\,(4y_1 - 3y_0 - y_2)}{2\,(2y_1 - y_0 - y_2)}, \qquad p_{\min} = p_0 + h_{\min}.
\tag{5}
\]
Subtracting \(h\) gives the position of the vertex relative to the middle point:
\[
p_{\min} - p_1 = h_{\min} - h = \frac{h\,(y_0 - y_2)}{2\,(y_0 - 2y_1 + y_2)}.
\tag{6}
\]






TipProperty of the vertex step (general)



The second derivative of \(Q\) is \(Q'' = (y_0 - 2y_1 + y_2)/h^2\). If the triple is bracketed, \(y_0 > y_1\) and \(y_2 \ge y_1\), then \(Q'' > 0\), so \(p_{\min}\) is the minimum of \(Q\), and
\[
-\tfrac12 |h| < \operatorname{sign}(h)\,(p_{\min} - p_1) \le \tfrac12 |h|,
\]
with equality only when \(y_2 = y_1\). So \(p_{\min}\) lies within half a step of \(p_1\), strictly between \(p_0\) and \(p_2\). To see this, put \(u = y_0 - y_1 > 0\) and \(v = y_2 - y_1 \ge 0\); then (6) reads \((p_{\min} - p_1)/h = (u - v)/\bigl(2(u + v)\bigr)\), and \(|u - v| < u + v\) unless \(v = 0\).


In the seven vertex steps of Examples 1 and 3, \(|p_{\min} - p_1|/|h|\) takes the values \(0.128\), \(0.105\), \(0.418\) and \(0.107\), \(0.270\), \(0.490\), \(0.165\), all below \(\tfrac12\).






WarningWhen the vertex formula fails (general)



The denominator \(2(2y_1 - y_0 - y_2)\) of (5) is zero when the three points are collinear, \(y_1 = (y_0 + y_2)/2\). If the triple is not bracketed, for instance because the bracketing loop stopped at \(|h| \le \delta\), then \(Q\) can be concave, and (5) then gives its maximum, or \(p_{\min}\) can lie far outside the triple. In Examples 1 and 3 every bracketing loop ends in case (i), so neither problem arises.




Restarting and stopping
Mathews notes that \(p_{\min}\) is a better approximation to \(p\) than \(p_0\), so the search replaces \(p_0\) by \(p_{\min}\) and repeats both processes with a new \(h\). His subroutine computes the new step as
\[
h_{\text{new}} = \min\bigl\{\,|h|,\ |h_{\min}|,\ \bigl|h_{\min} - |h|\bigr|,\ \bigl|h_{\min} - 2|h|\bigr|\,\bigr\},
\tag{7}
\]
and uses \(h_{\text{new}} = h_{\min}\) if this minimum is zero. The sign of \(f'(p_{\min})\) then sets the direction of the next step. (For a step to the right, \(h > 0\), the last three numbers are the distances to \(p_0\), \(p_1\), \(p_2\), and for a bracketed triple the cap \(|h|\) never binds, because \(p_{\min}\) lies within \(|h|/2\) of \(p_1\); so \(h_{\text{new}}\) is the distance from \(p_{\min}\) to the nearest point of the old triple. For a bracketed step to the left, (7) gives \(\min\{|h|, |h_{\min}|\}\) instead. Every outer step of Examples 1 and 3 goes to the right.)
The subroutine stops on function values, not on the distance to \(p\). After each vertex it computes \(e_i = |y_i - f(p_{\min})|\) for \(i = 0, 1, 2\). \(\mathrm{Err}\) is the smallest nonzero \(e_i\) found so far, starting from \(\mathrm{Err} = 1\) (or \(\mathrm{Err} = 0\) if all three \(e_i\) are zero), and the search stops when \(\mathrm{Err} \le \varepsilon\). It also stops after 50 outer steps, and each bracketing loop is limited to 50 passes.
Mathews writes that the method uses the derivative only implicitly, through (4), and makes no explicit use of \(f'\). His subroutine does evaluate \(f'(p_0)\) once per outer step, but uses only its sign, to choose the direction.






ImportantAlgorithm — Quadratic search for a minimum (Mathews’ subroutine)



Given \(f\) unimodal on \([a, b]\), a minimum step \(\delta\) and a tolerance \(\varepsilon\): set \(p_0 = a\), \(h = (b - a)/2\), \(\mathrm{Err} = 1\), \(k = 0\).

If \(f'(p_0) > 0\), set \(h = -|h|\). Evaluate \(y_i = f(p_i)\) at the triple (1).
While \(|h| > \delta\) and the triple is not bracketed: if \(y_0 \le y_1\), halve (case iii); otherwise, if \(y_2 < y_1\), double (case ii).
Compute \(h_{\min}\) and \(p_{\min} = p_{3k+3}\) from (5), and \(f(p_{\min})\).
Update \(\mathrm{Err}\) from the \(e_i\) and set the new \(h\) from (7).
Set \(p_0 = p_{\min}\) and \(k \leftarrow k + 1\). Repeat from step 1 while \(\mathrm{Err} > \varepsilon\).



The tables label the points as Mathews does. The bracketing triple of outer step \(k\) is \(p_{3k}, p_{3k+1}, p_{3k+2}\), its vertex is \(p_{3k+3}\), and the trial points of the bracketing loop are \(q_{3k+2,j}\), \(j = 0, 1, \ldots\)


Example 1 — Minimise \(x^2 - \sin x\) on \([0, 1]\)
Find the minimum of
\[
f(x) = x^2 - \sin x
\]
on \([0, 1]\) with the quadratic search. Mathews calls his subroutine with \(\delta = \varepsilon = 10^{-6}\).
Step 1 (first triple): \(p_0 = 0\) and \(f'(0) = -1 < 0\), so \(h = (1 - 0)/2 = 0.5\) is positive. The triple is
\[
p_0 = 0,\quad p_1 = 0.5,\quad p_2 = 1, \qquad y_0 = 0,\quad y_1 = -0.2294255386,\quad y_2 = 0.1585290152 .
\]
Since \(y_0 > y_1 < y_2\), this triple is already bracketed (case i).
Step 2 (first vertex): from (5),
\[
h_{\min} = \frac{0.5\,(4y_1 - 3y_0 - y_2)}{2\,(2y_1 - y_0 - y_2)} = \frac{0.5\,(-1.0762311696)}{-1.2347601848} = 0.4358057471,
\]
so \(p_3 = 0.4358057471\) and \(f(p_3) = -0.2322143232\).
Step 3 (restart): the distances from \(p_3\) to the old points are \(0.4358057471\), \(0.0641942529\) and \(0.5641942529\), so by (7) the new step is \(h = 0.0641942529\), the distance to \(p_1 = 0.5\). The differences \(e_i\) are \(0.232\), \(2.79 \times 10^{-3}\) and \(0.391\), so \(\mathrm{Err} = 2.79 \times 10^{-3} > 10^{-6}\) and the search continues. Since \(f'(p_3) = -0.0349 < 0\), the step stays positive.
Step 4 (second bracket): the new triple is \(0.4358057471\), \(0.5\), \(0.5641942529\), with values \(-0.2322143232\), \(-0.2294255386\), \(-0.2164199625\). Since \(y_0 \le y_1\), halve: \(q_{5,0} = 0.4679028735\), with \(f = -0.2320824604\), is still above \(y_0\), so halve again: \(q_{5,1} = 0.4518543103\), with \(f = -0.2324621759\). Now \(y_0 > y_1\) and \(y_2 = f(0.4679028735) > y_1\), so the bracket is \((0.4358057471, 0.4518543103, 0.4679028735)\) with \(h = 0.0160485632\).
Step 5 (second vertex): (5) gives \(h_{\min} = 0.0143625245\), so \(p_6 = 0.4501682715\) and \(f(p_6) = -0.232465574872\). The new step is \(h = 0.0016860388\), the distance to \(0.4518543103\), and \(\mathrm{Err} = 3.40 \times 10^{-6}\).
Step 6 (third bracket and vertex): six halvings bring the step down to \(h = 2.63444 \times 10^{-5}\), and the vertex is \(p_9 = 0.4501836113\). Now \(\mathrm{Err} = 1.47 \times 10^{-10} \le 10^{-6}\), and the search stops.

\[
f(x) = \frac12 + x^5 - \frac45\,x
