It does not print a starting triple that still needs halving or doubling. It interleaves the printed lines with graphs of \(f\) that mark the current points. This example uses all three cases of the bracketing loop.
Step 1 (first triple and vertex): \(f'(0) = -0.8 < 0\) and \(h = 0.5\). The triple \(0, 0.5, 1\) has values \(0.5\), \(0.13125\), \(0.7\), so it is bracketed. Here \(4y_1 - 3y_0 - y_2 = -1.675\) and \(2(2y_1 - y_0 - y_2) = -1.875\), so
\[
h_{\min} = \frac{0.5\,(-1.675)}{-1.875} = 0.4466666667 = \tfrac{67}{150}, \qquad p_3 = 0.4466666667, \qquad f(p_3) = 0.1604460919.
\]
The new step is the distance to \(0.5\), \(h = 0.0533333333\), and \(\mathrm{Err} = 2.92 \times 10^{-2}\).
Step 2 (doubling, case ii): the triple \(0.4466666667\), \(0.5\), \(0.5533333333\) has values \(0.1604460919\), \(0.13125\), \(0.1092054735\), which decrease, so double: \(q_{5,0} = p_0 + 2(0.1066666667) = 0.66\), with \(f = 0.0972332576\), is lower again, so double once more: \(q_{5,1} = 0.8733333333\), with \(f = 0.3093759954\). This value is higher than \(f(0.66) = 0.0972332576\), and \(p_6\) is farther from \(p\) (\(0.0301\)) than \(0.66\) is (\(0.0275\)). The vertex is not always the best point found so far. The new step is \(h = 0.0576921551\), the distance to \(0.66\), and \(\mathrm{Err} = 1.87 \times 10^{-4}\).
Step 3 (bracketed at once): the triple \(0.6023078449\), \(0.66\), \(0.7176921551\) is bracketed without halving or doubling, and its vertex is \(p_9 = 0.6317169944\). None of its \(e_i\) is below \(1.87 \times 10^{-4}\), so \(\mathrm{Err}\) does not change.

title: Quadratic Interpolative Search
text:
Cubic Interpolative Search

The starting step
Assume \(f\) is unimodal and differentiable on \([a, b]\), with minimum at \(p\), and let \(p_0 = a\). Any reasonable step \(h\) can start the iteration. Mathews estimates one from the mean value theorem, \(f(a + h) - f(a) = h f'(c)\) for some \(c\) between \(a\) and \(a + h\). If \(a + h\) were just to the right of the minimum, the average slope \(f'(c)\) might be about \(\tfrac12 f'(a)\). Since the position of \(a + h\) is unknown, he takes \(f(a + h) \approx f(b)\) and obtains
\[
h_0 = \frac{2\bigl(f(b) - f(a)\bigr)}{f'(a)}, \qquad p_1 = p_0 + h_0.
\tag{8}
\]
When \(f'(a) < 0\), this \(h_0\) is positive only if \(f(b) < f(a)\). In both of Mathews’ examples \(f(b) > f(a)\), so \(h_0 < 0\) and \(p_1\) lies to the left of \(a\), outside the interval.


The interpolating cubic
Let \(h = p_1 - p_0\). The cubic \(P\) is written about the abscissa \(p_2\) of its minimum:
\[
P(x) = \frac{\alpha}{h^3}(x - p_2)^3 + \frac{\beta}{h^2}(x - p_2)^2 + f(p_2),
\qquad
P'(x) = \frac{3\alpha}{h^3}(x - p_2)^2 + \frac{2\beta}{h^2}(x - p_2).
\tag{9}
\]
It must satisfy \(P(p_0) = f(p_0)\), \(P(p_1) = f(p_1)\), \(P'(p_0) = f'(p_0)\) and \(P'(p_1) = f'(p_1)\). (The powers of \(h\) in the denominators make the following algebra simpler.) Put
\[
p_2 = p_0 + \gamma h,
\tag{10}
\]
so that \(p_1 - p_2 = (1 - \gamma)h\) and \(p_0 - p_2 = -\gamma h\). Substituting into (9) gives three equations:
\[
\begin{aligned}
F &= f(p_1) - f(p_0) = \alpha(3\gamma^2 - 3\gamma + 1) + \beta(1 - 2\gamma), \\
G &= h\bigl(f'(p_1) - f'(p_0)\bigr) = 3\alpha(1 - 2\gamma) + 2\beta, \\
h f'(p_0) &= 3\alpha\gamma^2 - 2\beta\gamma.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
The book section linked from Mathews’ module gives the middle equation as \(G = f'(p_1) - f'(p_0)\), without the factor \(h\). The module and the subroutine include the factor, and it is needed. The combination \(G - 2(F - h f'(p_0))\) cancels both \(\beta\) and every \(\gamma\):
\[
\alpha = G - 2\bigl(F - h f'(p_0)\bigr).
\tag{12}
\]
Multiplying the second equation of (11) by \(\gamma\) and adding the third eliminates \(\beta\):
\[
3\alpha\gamma^2 + (G - 3\alpha)\gamma + h f'(p_0) = 0.
\tag{13}
\]
The quadratic formula, with the numerator rationalised, gives the root Mathews uses:
\[
\gamma = \frac{-2h f'(p_0)}{(G - 3\alpha) + \sqrt{(G - 3\alpha)^2 - 12 h \alpha f'(p_0)}}.
\tag{14}
\]






TipWhich root (general)



From (9), \(P''(p_2) = 2\beta/h^2\), so \(p_2\) is a local minimum of \(P\) when \(\beta > 0\). Each critical point of the cubic through the four conditions gives a representation (9) about that point, so the two roots of (13) are the cubic’s two critical points. When \(G > 0\), form (14) is the root that stays finite as \(\alpha \to 0\) (for \(G < 0\) it is unbounded). In that limit \(P\) is a quadratic and \(\gamma = -h f'(p_0)/G\), so
\[
p_2 = p_0 - f'(p_0)\,\frac{p_1 - p_0}{f'(p_1) - f'(p_0)},
\]
the secant step for \(f'(x) = 0\). If the discriminant in (14) is negative, the cubic has no critical point and the step is undefined.


In every step of Examples 2 and 4 the discriminant is positive and \(\beta > 0\), so (14) picks the local minimum of the cubic.
To continue, set \(h = p_2 - p_1\) and replace \(p_0, p_1\) by \(p_1, p_2\) in (11)–(14). The method does not keep a bracket, so a stopping rule is harder to choose. Mathews suggests \(|f'(p_k)| < \varepsilon\), since \(f'(p) = 0\). His subroutine simply runs a fixed number of steps.






ImportantAlgorithm — Cubic search for a minimum (Mathews’ subroutine)



Given \(f\) unimodal and differentiable on \([a, b]\) and a number of steps \(m_{\max}\): set \(p_0 = a\), \(h_0 = 2(f(b) - f(a))/f'(a)\), \(p_1 = p_0 + h_0\). For \(k = 0, 1, \ldots, m_{\max} - 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
F &= f(p_{k+1}) - f(p_k), \qquad G = h_k\bigl(f'(p_{k+1}) - f'(p_k)\bigr), \qquad \alpha = G - 2\bigl(F - h_k f'(p_k)\bigr), \\
\gamma &= \frac{-2h_k f'(p_k)}{(G - 3\alpha) + \sqrt{(G - 3\alpha)^2 - 12 h_k \alpha f'(p_k)}}, \qquad
p_{k+2} = p_k + \gamma h_k, \qquad h_{k+1} = p_{k+2} - p_{k+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]


Mathews’ algorithm statement lists \(p_1 = b\) among the starting values. In his subroutine \(b\) enters only through \(f(b)\) in \(h_0\), and the iteration starts from \(p_1 = p_0 + h_0\).

To see the rate of convergence without the limit of double precision, the three iterations were repeated in 400-digit arithmetic. The ratio \(\log e_{k+1} / \log e_k\) of successive errors measures the order:

Cubic search: the ratios settle near \(2\). The last ratios before the 400-digit limit are \(2.10\), \(1.98\), \(2.02\) in Example 2 and \(2.09\), \(1.95\), \(2.02\) in Example 4. This is consistent with the order \(2\) of cubic interpolation using function and derivative values (a general result).
Secant method on \(f'\): the ratios fall to \(1.62\), the golden ratio \((1 + \sqrt5)/2 \approx 1.618\) that is the general order of the secant method.
Mathews’ quadratic search: with \(\delta\), \(\varepsilon\) and the 50-pass limit removed, each outer step roughly squares the error. The ratios are \(2.61\), \(2.22\), \(2.11\), \(2.05\), \(2.02\), \(2.01\) in Example 1 and \(2.08\), \(2.06\), \(1.99\), \(2.02\), \(2.00\), \(2.00\), \(2.00\), \(2.00\) in Example 3. But the bracketing loops of the successive outer steps need more and more halvings or doublings: \(2, 6, 19, 34, 76, 156\) in Example 1 and \(2, 0, 5, 8, 13, 39, 82, 164\) in Example 3. In the last three steps of each run that is \(1.4\) to \(1.7\) passes, each costing one evaluation of \(f\), per decimal digit gained. Counted per function evaluation, the quadratic search therefore converges far more slowly than the squaring per step suggests.

This variant is not the textbook successive parabolic interpolation, which keeps the three most recent points, unequally spaced, and needs no bracketing loop.

title: Quadratic Interpolative Search
text:
Implementation Notes

Quadratic search, direction. The subroutine evaluates \(f'(p_0)\) once per outer step and uses only its sign. A version without derivatives must choose the direction from function values instead.
Quadratic search, step rule. Rule (7) gives the distance from \(p_{\min}\) to the nearest old point for every bracketed step with \(h > 0\). Because the subroutine replaces \(h\) by \(|h|\) first, a bracketed step to the left gets \(\min\{|h|, |h_{\min}|\}\) instead. Every outer step in Examples 1 and 3 has \(f'(p_0) < 0\) and therefore \(h > 0\).
Quadratic search, bracketing. Check that the triple really is bracketed before using (5). The loop can also end because \(|h| \le \delta\), and the vertex of an unbracketed or collinear triple is meaningless or undefined.
Quadratic search, stopping. \(\mathrm{Err}\) compares function values, which agree to about the square of the distance to \(p\) (Example 3: \(8.1 \times 10^{-13}\) in \(f\) against \(5.7 \times 10^{-7}\) in \(x\)). A tolerance \(\varepsilon\) on \(f\) therefore corresponds to a distance of roughly \(\sqrt{2\varepsilon / f''(p)}\) (general).
Cubic search, starting step. Formula (8) needs \(f'(a) \ne 0\), and with \(f(b) > f(a)\) it sends \(p_1\) outside \([a, b]\) (both examples). The method does not keep a bracket, and \(p_1\) can land where \(f\) is not convex, as in Example 4.
Cubic search, stopping. Use a test such as \(|f'(p_k)| < \varepsilon\) rather than a fixed number of steps. Once the iterates agree to rounding, \(F\), \(G\) and \(\alpha\) are pure rounding noise. Continued in double precision, both examples eventually reach \(0/0\) in (14): Example 2 at \(p_9\), after \(p_7 = p_8\) exactly, and Example 4 also at \(p_9\), where \(f'(p_7) = 0\) exactly. Mathews’ runs stop before this.
Unimodality. Neither method can tell a local minimum from the global one. If \(f\) has several minima in \([a, b]\), the result depends on the start.

title: Newton’s Search Method
text:
Description
Newton’s search method looks for a local minimum of a function \(f(\mathbf{X})\) of several variables, \(\mathbf{X} = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)\), whose first and second partial derivatives can be evaluated. At the current point \(\mathbf{P}_k\) it replaces \(f\) by its second-degree Taylor polynomial, which is built from the gradient \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) and the Hessian matrix \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\) of second partial derivatives, and moves to the point where the gradient of that quadratic is zero:
\[
\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + \Delta\mathbf{P}_k, \qquad \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\,\Delta\mathbf{P}_k = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k).
\]
This is the Newton-Raphson method applied to the system \(\nabla f(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{0}\), with the Hessian playing the part of the Jacobian. With one variable it reduces to \(p_{k+1} = p_k - f'(p_k)/f''(p_k)\). Near a minimum where the Hessian is positive definite the iteration converges quadratically, and a quadratic \(f\) with a positive definite Hessian is minimised in a single step. But the method only looks for a zero of the gradient, so it converges just as readily to a saddle point or a maximum, and from a poor starting point it can run away altogether. Mathews works in two variables, \(\mathbf{P}_k = (x_k, y_k)\), so every run below is a path of points on the surface \(z = f(x, y)\), and every one has been recomputed in 60-digit arithmetic.

title: Newton’s Search Method
text:
Animations
Each animation below draws Newton’s search method on a contour map of \(f\). The iterates \(\mathbf{P}_0, \mathbf{P}_1, \ldots\) are joined in order, and the stationary points are marked by type, found from the eigenvalues of the Hessian there: a star for a minimum, a cross for a saddle point, a triangle for a maximum. The titles give \(\mathbf{P}_k\), \(f(\mathbf{P}_k)\), the distance to the limit and whether \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\) is positive definite or indefinite, and frame \(k\) shows row \(k\) of the example’s table further down this page; Case 2 goes on to \(k = 10\), Mathews’ ten iterations, past the end of the table for \((-3, 2)\). The scripts iterate in 256-bit (about 77-digit) arithmetic, so every computed value in a title is correctly rounded to four significant figures. Cases 2 and 3 keep trailing zeros; Case 1 drops them; for example, its \(0.045\) stands for \(0.04500\) and its \(0.721\) for \(0.7210\). An independent run in 80-digit arithmetic produces the same title text in every frame.
Mathews’ module has no animation for this method. Neither the module page nor its notebook links to one, and the archive’s optimization animations (a2001/Animations/Optimization/) have none for Newton’s search, so all three animations are new, with no Mathews original. They use his examples and starting points, and the windows of his contour plots where the notebook gives one: \([-3, 3] \times [-0.5, 2]\) for Example 5 and \([-4, 4] \times [-4, 4]\) for Example 6. Examples 1 and 2 (a gradient, a Hessian and a Taylor polynomial at one point, with no iteration), Example 3 (a quadratic, minimised exactly in one step), Mathews’ comparison of \(f\) at four neighbours of \((1.0, 0.8)\) in Example 5, his FindMinimum comparisons (Examples 3 to 6), his plots of the vector field \(-\nabla f\) (Examples 5 and 6) and the enhanced method with a line search are not animated.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Example 5, three minima and two saddle points, \(f(x, y) = 5x^2 + x^4 - 9x^2 y + 3y^2 + 2y^4 + \tfrac14 x\) (new)
Behavior: The five runs of Example 5 follow one another, \(25\) frames in all: the three minima from \((0, 0)\), \((2, 1.5)\) and \((-2, 1.5)\), with \(4\), \(5\) and \(5\) steps as in Mathews’ tables, then the two runs from \((1.0, 0.8)\) and \((-1.0, 0.8)\), with \(3\) steps each (Mathews runs \(5\) steps from \((1.0, 0.8)\), but steps \(4\) and \(5\) repeat \(\mathbf{P}_3\) to \(12\) decimals). The left panel keeps Mathews’ contour window and adds the two curves he plots separately, \(f_x = 0\) (dashed orange) and \(f_y = 0\) (dash-dot purple), whose five crossings are the stationary points. The right panel zooms on \(\mathbf{P}_j\), with axes in units of a power of ten that shrinks within each run (overall from \(10^{-1}\) down to \(10^{-29}\)), and draws the contours of \(f\) (grey) over those of the quadratic model \(Q\) at \(\mathbf{P}_j\) (dashed). The next iterate \(\mathbf{P}_{j+1}\) is the stationary point of \(Q\), at the end of the black arrow. In the three runs to a minimum, \(\mathbf{H}\) is positive definite at every iterate, the model’s contours are blue ellipses and each step goes to their centre. From \((1.0, 0.8)\) and \((-1.0, 0.8)\), \(\mathbf{H}\) is indefinite at every iterate (eigenvalues \(-4.79\) and \(33.75\) at both starts), the model’s contours are red hyperbolas, and each step goes to the saddle point of the model. Newton’s method converges just as fast to the saddle points \((0.9685, 0.7784)\) and \((-0.9021, 0.7210)\) of \(f\), and \(f\) goes up on the first step of both runs. At \(\mathbf{P}_0\) the contours of \(f\) and \(Q\) differ by up to \(5.6\%\) of the spread of \(Q\) across the zoom; from \(\mathbf{P}_2\) on they differ by less than \(0.1\%\) and the two sets of curves coincide. Each new iterate lands much closer to the limit than the last: in case (ii) the distances are \(0.172\), \(0.0450\), \(0.00203\), \(4.39 \times 10^{-6}\), \(2.07 \times 10^{-11}\) and \(4.59 \times 10^{-22}\).

title: Newton’s Search Method
text:
Gradient and Hessian






NoteDefinition — Gradient



If \(f(x, y)\) has partial derivatives \(f_x\) and \(f_y\), its gradient is the vector function
\[
\nabla f(x, y) = \bigl(f_x(x, y),\ f_y(x, y)\bigr).
\]








NoteDefinition — Jacobian matrix



If \(f_1(x, y)\) and \(f_2(x, y)\) have partial derivatives, their Jacobian matrix is
\[
\mathbf{J}(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial y} \\[2mm] \dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial f_2}{\partial y} \end{pmatrix}.
\]








NoteDefinition — Hessian matrix



If \(f(x, y)\) has partial derivatives up to order two, its Hessian matrix is
\[
\mathbf{H}(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} f_{xx}(x, y) & f_{xy}(x, y) \\ f_{yx}(x, y) & f_{yy}(x, y) \end{pmatrix}.
\]








TipLemma 1 and Lemma 2




The Hessian of \(f\) is the Jacobian of the two components of its gradient, \(f_1 = f_x\) and \(f_2 = f_y\): \(\ \mathbf{H}(x, y) = \mathbf{J}\bigl(f_x, f_y\bigr)\).
If the second partial derivatives of \(f\) are continuous, then \(f_{xy} = f_{yx}\) and the Hessian is symmetric.




Example 1 — Gradient and Hessian of \(f(x, y) = (x - y)/(x^2 + y^2 + 2)\) at \((-3, -2)\)
Step 1 (first derivatives): by the quotient rule,
\[
f_x = -\frac{x^2 - 2xy - y^2 - 2}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^2}, \qquad
f_y = -\frac{x^2 + 2xy - y^2 + 2}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^2}.
\]
At \((-3, -2)\) the denominator is \(15^2 = 225\), and
\[
\nabla f(-3, -2) = \left(\frac{9}{225},\ -\frac{19}{225}\right) = \left(\frac{1}{25},\ -\frac{19}{225}\right) \approx (0.04,\ -0.084444).
\]
Step 2 (second derivatives):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_{xx} &= \frac{2\,(x^3 - 3x^2 y - 3x y^2 + y^3 - 6x + 2y)}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^3}, \\
f_{xy} &= \frac{2\,(x^3 + 3x^2 y - 3x y^2 - y^3 + 2x - 2y)}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^3}, \\
f_{yy} &= -\frac{2\,(x^3 - 3x^2 y - 3x y^2 + y^3 + 2x - 6y)}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Step 3 (Hessian at the point): the denominator is \(15^3 = 3375\) and the three numerators are \(138\), \(-78\) and \(-122\), so
\[
\boxed{\ \mathbf{H}(-3, -2) = \frac{1}{3375}\begin{pmatrix} 138 & -78 \\ -78 & -122 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \tfrac{46}{1125} & -\tfrac{26}{1125} \\[1mm] -\tfrac{26}{1125} & -\tfrac{122}{3375} \end{pmatrix} \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0.040889 & -0.023111 \\ -0.023111 & -0.036148 \end{pmatrix}\ }
\]
The Hessian agrees with Mathews’ output. Verification: the derivatives above were checked symbolically against direct differentiation (the differences simplify to \(0\)). The Hessian here is indefinite: \(\det \mathbf{H}(-3, -2) = -1528/759375 < 0\), and its eigenvalues are \(-0.042550\) and \(0.047290\). Near \((-3, -2)\) the surface curves up in one direction and down in another, which matters in Example 2.

title: Newton’s Search Method
text:
The Quadratic Taylor Polynomial
Expand \(f\) about the point \(\mathbf{P} = (p, q)\) and write \(\Delta p = x - p\), \(\Delta q = y - q\). In series notation the second-degree Taylor polynomial is
\[
Q(x, y) = f(p, q) + f_x(p, q)\,\Delta p + f_y(p, q)\,\Delta q + \tfrac12\Bigl(f_{xx}(p, q)\,\Delta p^2 + 2 f_{xy}(p, q)\,\Delta p\,\Delta q + f_{yy}(p, q)\,\Delta q^2\Bigr).
\tag{1}
\]
With \(\mathbf{X} = (x, y)\) and \(\Delta\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{X} - \mathbf{P} = (\Delta p, \Delta q)\), the same polynomial in vector and matrix notation is
\[
Q(\mathbf{X}) = f(\mathbf{P}) + \nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \cdot \Delta\mathbf{P} + \tfrac12\, \Delta\mathbf{P}\, \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P})\, \Delta\mathbf{P}^{T}.
\tag{2}
\]
Form (2) holds unchanged for \(n\) variables, with \(\nabla f\) a vector of \(n\) first partial derivatives and \(\mathbf{H}\) the \(n \times n\) matrix of second partial derivatives.

Example 2 — Taylor polynomials of \(f(x, y) = (x - y)/(x^2 + y^2 + 2)\)
(a) Centre \(\mathbf{P} = (-3, -2)\). From Example 1, \(f(-3, -2) = -\tfrac{1}{15}\), so by (1)
\[
Q(x, y) = -\frac{1}{15} + \frac{x + 3}{25} - \frac{19\,(y + 2)}{225} + \frac{23\,(x + 3)^2}{1125} - \frac{26\,(x + 3)(y + 2)}{1125} - \frac{61\,(y + 2)^2}{3375},
\]
and expanding,
\[
\boxed{\ Q(x, y) = \frac{-481 + 393x + 69x^2 - 763y - 78xy - 61y^2}{3375}\ }
\]
which is Mathews’ simplified form. Because \(\mathbf{H}(-3, -2)\) is indefinite, this quadratic is a saddle surface: it has no minimum. Its only stationary point is at \((-\tfrac{1791}{382}, -\tfrac{622}{191}) \approx (-4.688482, -3.256545)\), where \(f = -0.041401\), higher than \(f(-3, -2) = -0.066667\). A Newton step from \((-3, -2)\) would go there.
(b) Centre \(\mathbf{P} = (-0.3, 0.2)\), closer to the minimum. Here
\[
f(-0.3, 0.2) = -\frac{50}{213} \approx -0.234742, \qquad \nabla f(-0.3, 0.2) \approx (0.403359,\ -0.425401),
\]
\[
\mathbf{H}(-0.3, 0.2) \approx \begin{pmatrix} 0.447659 & -0.195579 \\ -0.195579 & 0.380190 \end{pmatrix},
\]
and
\[
Q(x, y) \approx 0.010829 + 0.576773\,x - 0.560112\,y + 0.223830\,x^2 - 0.195579\,xy + 0.190095\,y^2 .
\]
This Hessian is positive definite (eigenvalues \(0.215457\) and \(0.612392\)), so \(Q\) is a bowl. Its minimum is at \((-0.831690,\ 1.045402)\), with \(Q = -0.521790\) and \(f = -0.495985\) there. The true minimum of \(f\) is at \((-1, 1)\), where \(f = -\tfrac12\).
Verification: both expansions were recomputed symbolically from (2), and the stationary points of \(Q\) were found by solving \(\nabla Q = \mathbf{0}\) exactly. The two stationary points of \(f\) itself are \((-1, 1)\), a minimum with \(\mathbf{H} = \tfrac14 \mathbf{I}\), and \((1, -1)\), a maximum with \(f = \tfrac12\). As Mathews observes, when the centre is close to the minimum, the minimum of the quadratic is close to the minimum of the surface. That is the idea of Newton’s method, and the minimiser of \(Q\) in (b) is exactly the first Newton step \(\mathbf{P}_1\) of Example 6.

title: Newton’s Search Method
section: Newton’s Method for Finding a Minimum
text:
Newton’s Method for Finding a Minimum
Assume that the first and second partial derivatives of \(f\) are continuous near a minimum \(\mathbf{P}^*\) and that \(\mathbf{P}_0\) is close to it. The minimum of the quadratic approximation (2), centred at \(\mathbf{P}_0\), is where \(\nabla Q(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{0}\). Since \(\mathbf{H}\) is symmetric,
\[
\nabla Q(\mathbf{X}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0) + \Delta\mathbf{P}\, \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_0),
\]
so setting \(\nabla Q(\mathbf{X}) = \mathbf{0}\) gives \(\Delta\mathbf{P}\, \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_0) = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0)\). If \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_0)\) is invertible,
\[
\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{P}_0 - \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0)\, \bigl(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_0)\bigr)^{-1}.
\]
This \(\mathbf{X}\) is the next approximation \(\mathbf{P}_1\). Repeating the construction at each new point gives Newton’s method for finding a minimum:






ImportantNewton search formula



\[
\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k - \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\, \bigl(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\bigr)^{-1} \qquad \text{(row vectors)},
\tag{3}
\]
\[
\mathbf{P}_{k+1}^{T} = \mathbf{P}_k^{T} - \bigl(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\bigr)^{-1} \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)^{T} \qquad \text{(column vectors)}.
\tag{4}
\]


The two forms agree because \(\mathbf{H}\) is symmetric. Form (4) is the Newton-Raphson formula \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1}^{T} = \mathbf{P}_k^{T} - \mathbf{J}(\mathbf{P}_k)^{-1} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{P}_k)^{T}\) for a root of the vector function \(\mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{X})\), since by Lemma 1 its Jacobian is \(\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{H}\). For a function of one variable, (3) is \(p_{k+1} = p_k - f'(p_k)/f''(p_k)\): Newton-Raphson applied to \(f'(x) = 0\).
The theory of Newton-Raphson therefore carries over. The following is a general result, not a claim about any one example:






TipTheorem — Local quadratic convergence (general)



Suppose the second partial derivatives of \(f\) are continuous near \(\mathbf{P}^*\) and satisfy a Lipschitz condition there, that \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}^*) = \mathbf{0}\), and that \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}^*)\) is nonsingular. Then there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that for every \(\mathbf{P}_0\) with \(\lVert \mathbf{P}_0 - \mathbf{P}^* \rVert < \delta\) the iterates (3) are defined, converge to \(\mathbf{P}^*\), and satisfy
\[
\lVert \mathbf{P}_{k+1} - \mathbf{P}^* \rVert \le C\, \lVert \mathbf{P}_k - \mathbf{P}^* \rVert^2
\]
for some constant \(C\). The point \(\mathbf{P}^*\) is a strict local minimum if \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}^*)\) is positive definite, a strict local maximum if it is negative definite, and a saddle point if it is indefinite.


The theorem does not require \(\mathbf{P}^*\) to be a minimum. Newton’s method treats every nondegenerate stationary point alike. Examples 5 and 6 show it converging quadratically to two saddle points and to a maximum, so the type of the limit has to be checked afterwards with the Hessian. Nor does the theorem say how small \(\delta\) is: Example 6 shows a starting point from which the iterates go off to infinity.

Algorithm






ImportantAlgorithm — Newton’s method for finding a minimum



Start with an approximation \(\mathbf{P}_0\) to the minimum point \(\mathbf{P}^*\). Set \(k = 0\).

Evaluate the gradient vector \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) and the Hessian matrix \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\).
Solve the linear system \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\, \Delta\mathbf{P}_k^{T} = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)^{T}\) and set \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + \Delta\mathbf{P}_k\).
Perform the termination test: stop when \(\lVert \Delta\mathbf{P}_k \rVert\) and \(\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1}) \rVert\) are small enough. Otherwise set \(k = k + 1\) and repeat.
Check the Hessian at the final point. If it is not positive definite, the point is not a local minimum.



Mathews’ formula (3) is written with the inverse of the Hessian, but as he notes, it is better to solve the linear system in step 2 with a linear system solver: the inverse is a theoretical tool, and computing it is inefficient. His program NewtonSearch runs a fixed number of iterations of (3) and prints each point and the value of \(f\) there; the tables below do the same.

section: Example 3 — A quadratic function: one step is exact
text:
Example 3 — A quadratic function: one step is exact
Use Newton’s method to find the minimum of
\[
f(x, y) = x^2 - 4x + y^2 - y - xy
\]
starting from \(\mathbf{P}_0 = (0, 0)\).
Step 1: the gradient and Hessian are
\[
\nabla f(x, y) = (2x - y - 4,\ 2y - x - 1), \qquad \mathbf{H} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The Hessian is constant, with eigenvalues \(1\) and \(3\), so it is positive definite everywhere.
Step 2: at \(\mathbf{P}_0\), \(\nabla f(0, 0) = (-4, -1)\). Solve
\[
\begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \Delta x \\ \Delta y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Delta\mathbf{P}_0 = (3,\ 2).
\]
Step 3: \(\mathbf{P}_1 = (0, 0) + (3, 2) = (3, 2)\), and \(\nabla f(3, 2) = (6 - 2 - 4,\ 4 - 3 - 1) = (0, 0)\).

title: Newton’s Search Method

Example 4 — Rosenbrock’s parabolic valley
Use Newton’s method to find the minimum of Rosenbrock’s function (circa 1960)
\[
f(x, y) = 100\,(y - x^2)^2 + (1 - x)^2
\]
starting from \(\mathbf{P}_0 = (0.99, 1.01)\). The minimum is at \((1, 1)\), where \(f = 0\). It lies in a long, curved valley along the parabola \(y = x^2\).
Step 1: the gradient and Hessian are
\[
\nabla f = \bigl(-400x(y - x^2) - 2(1 - x),\ \ 200(y - x^2)\bigr), \qquad
\mathbf{H} = \begin{pmatrix} 1200x^2 - 400y + 2 & -400x \\ -400x & 200 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 2: at \(\mathbf{P}_0 = (0.99, 1.01)\), \(y - x^2 = 0.0299\) and \(f(\mathbf{P}_0) = 0.089501\), so
\[
\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0) = (-11.8604,\ 5.98), \qquad
\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_0) = \begin{pmatrix} 774.12 & -396 \\ -396 & 200 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 3: solving \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_0)\,\Delta\mathbf{P}_0^T = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0)^T\) gives \(\Delta\mathbf{P}_0 = \bigl(-\tfrac{1}{498},\ -\tfrac{28117}{830000}\bigr) \approx (-0.002008,\ -0.033876)\), so
\[
\mathbf{P}_1 \approx (0.987992,\ 0.976124), \qquad f(\mathbf{P}_1) = 1.441945 \times 10^{-4}.
\]

Example 5 — Three minima and two saddle points
Use Newton’s method to find the minima of
\[
f(x, y) = 5x^2 + x^4 - 9x^2 y + 3y^2 + 2y^4 + \tfrac14 x .
\]
Mathews asks the reader to estimate the local minima from graphs of the surface and its contours on \(-3 \le x \le 3\), \(-0.5 \le y \le 2\), and then to plot the curves where each component of the gradient is zero:
\[
\nabla f = \bigl(4x^3 + 10x - 18xy + \tfrac14,\ \ -9x^2 + 6y + 8y^3\bigr), \qquad
\mathbf{H} = \begin{pmatrix} 12x^2 - 18y + 10 & -18x \\ -18x & 24y^2 + 6 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The curve \(f_x = 0\) can be written \(y = (4x^3 + 10x + \tfrac14)/(18x)\), which has a vertical asymptote at \(x = 0\). The stationary points are the intersections of the two curves. Example 6 — Iterating to the minimum, and a starting point that fails
Given \(f(x, y) = \dfrac{x - y}{x^2 + y^2 + 2}\) (the function of Examples 1 and 2) and the initial point \(\mathbf{P}_0 = (-0.3, 0.2)\), use Newton’s method to find \(\mathbf{P}_1\) and \(\mathbf{P}_2\).
The plots of the gradient components show the two curves \(f_x = 0\) and \(f_y = 0\) crossing at \((-1, 1)\). Since \(f_x = 0\) means \(x^2 - 2xy - y^2 = 2\) and \(f_y = 0\) means \(x^2 + 2xy - y^2 = -2\), adding gives \(x^2 = y^2\) and subtracting gives \(xy = -1\), so the only stationary points are \((-1, 1)\) and \((1, -1)\).

Far from the origin the surface flattens out and its gradient tends to zero, and the iteration chases that flat region instead of a stationary point. The Hessian is indefinite at every iterate computed (\(k = 0\) to \(12\)), and at each of them the Newton step points uphill (\(\nabla f \cdot \Delta\mathbf{P}_k > 0\)).


Convergence to a maximum
Because \(f(-x, -y) = -f(x, y)\), the gradient satisfies \(\nabla f(-\mathbf{X}) = \nabla f(\mathbf{X})\) and the Hessian \(\mathbf{H}(-\mathbf{X}) = -\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{X})\), so the Newton step from \(-\mathbf{P}\) is exactly the negative of the step from \(\mathbf{P}\). Started at \((0.3, -0.2)\), Newton’s method therefore produces the negatives of the iterates in the table above, \((0.831690, -1.045402)\), \((0.988071, -0.993270)\), \(\ldots\), and converges just as quickly to \((1, -1)\), where \(f = \tfrac12\) is the maximum (\(\mathbf{H}(1, -1) = -\tfrac14 \mathbf{I}\)). In one variable the same holds in general: by the theorem with \(n = 1\), \(p_{k+1} = p_k - f'(p_k)/f''(p_k)\) started close enough to a maximum, where \(f'' < 0\), converges to that maximum.

title: Newton’s Search Method
section: Enhanced Newton Method for Finding a Minimum
text:
Enhanced Newton Method for Finding a Minimum
Newton’s method can be modified by treating \(\mathbf{S}_k = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\,\bigl(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\bigr)^{-1}\) as a search direction, as the gradient method uses the direction \(-\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\), and doing a one-parameter minimisation (line search) along it:

Evaluate the gradient vector \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) and the Hessian matrix \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\).
Compute the search direction \(\mathbf{S}_k = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\,\bigl(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\bigr)^{-1}\).
Minimise the function of one variable \(\phi(t) = f(\mathbf{P}_k + t\,\mathbf{S}_k)\), for instance with a golden ratio or quadratic interpolative search, giving a value \(t_k\). This is a minimum of \(f\) along the search line; at an interior minimum \(\phi'(t_k) = \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k + t_k\,\mathbf{S}_k) \cdot \mathbf{S}_k = 0\), so the gradient at the new point is perpendicular to the line.
Set \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + t_k\,\mathbf{S}_k\).
Perform the termination test: are \(f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) and \(f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1})\) sufficiently close, and is \(\lVert \mathbf{P}_{k+1} - \mathbf{P}_k \rVert\) small enough? If not, set \(k = k + 1\) and repeat.

With \(t_k = 1\) this is the plain method (3). In general, Mathews says, the modified method is more reliable, and he leaves its investigation to the reader. Two of the runs above show what the line search can and cannot fix:

In the Example 4 variant from \((1.8, 1.2)\), the direction at \(k = 1\) points downhill but the full step overshoots and raises \(f\) from \(0.637\) to \(40.4\). A line search along that direction would pick a step that lowers \(f\).
From \((-3, 2)\) in Example 6, \(\mathbf{S}_k\) points uphill at every iterate. If \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\) is positive definite, then \(\nabla f \cdot \mathbf{S}_k = -\nabla f\, \mathbf{H}^{-1} \nabla f^{T} < 0\) and \(\mathbf{S}_k\) is a descent direction, but here \(\mathbf{H}\) is indefinite. A line search over \(t > 0\) along an uphill direction cannot lower \(f\). The direction itself has to be changed, for example to \(-\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) or to the Newton direction of a modified, positive definite Hessian.

title: Newton’s Search Method
text:
Implementation Notes

Solve, don’t invert. Compute \(\Delta\mathbf{P}_k\) from \(\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}_k)\,\Delta\mathbf{P}_k^T = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)^T\) with a linear solver (for example a Cholesky factorisation, which also reports whether \(\mathbf{H}\) is positive definite).
Cost per step. Each iteration needs the \(n\) first partial derivatives, the \(n(n+1)/2\) distinct second partial derivatives and the solution of an \(n \times n\) system. The gradient method needs only the first derivatives but generally converges much more slowly.
Check what was found. The iteration stops where \(\nabla f = \mathbf{0}\), and that can be a saddle point (Example 5) or a maximum (Example 6). Test the Hessian at the final point.
Watch the starting point. Convergence is guaranteed only from close enough to \(\mathbf{P}^*\). Signs of trouble are a Hessian that is not positive definite and a step that increases \(f\) (Example 6 from \((-3, 2)\)). A safeguarded version takes a line search along the Newton direction, and falls back to \(-\nabla f\) when that direction is not downhill.
Termination. Use \(\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) \rVert\) and \(\lVert \Delta\mathbf{P}_k \rVert\), not only the change in \(f\). Near a minimum \(f(\mathbf{P}) - f(\mathbf{P}^*) \approx \tfrac12 (\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{P}^*)\,\mathbf{H}\,(\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{P}^*)^T\) is quadratic in the error, so the values of \(f\) settle long before the point does. In Example 6 the printed \(f(\mathbf{P}_4)\) is already \(-0.500000000000\) while \(\mathbf{P}_4\) is still \(3.7 \times 10^{-8}\) from \((-1, 1)\).
Flat valleys. When the Hessian at the minimum is badly conditioned (eigenvalues \(0.40\) and \(1002\) for Rosenbrock’s function), function values alone locate the minimum poorly along the valley. Newton’s method still converges quickly there, because it uses the curvature in each direction.

title: Shooting Methods for ODE’s
text:
Description
A boundary value problem asks for a solution of a second-order differential equation \(x'' = f(t, x, x')\) on an interval \(a \le t \le b\) whose values are prescribed at both ends, \(x(a) = \alpha\) and \(x(b) = \beta\). The numerical methods for initial value problems cannot be used directly, because they need \(x(a)\) and the slope \(x'(a)\), and the slope is unknown. A shooting method guesses the missing slope \(s = x'(a)\), solves the initial value problem from \(t = a\) like firing a shot from a cannon at angle \(s\), sees where the shot lands at \(t = b\), and corrects \(s\) until it lands on the target value \(\beta\).
For a linear equation \(x'' = p(t)\,x' + q(t)\,x + r(t)\) no trial and error is needed. Two initial value problems are solved, one for \(u(t)\) with \(u(a) = \alpha\), \(u'(a) = 0\) and one for \(v(t)\) (without the term \(r(t)\)) with \(v(a) = 0\), \(v'(a) = 1\). Every solution that starts at \(\alpha\) is then \(u(t) + s\,v(t)\), and the one that ends at \(\beta\) is
\[
x(t) = u(t) + \frac{\beta - u(b)}{v(b)}\, v(t), \qquad v(b) \ne 0 .
\]
Mathews solves both initial value problems with the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method and works one example from start to finish: \(x'' + \tfrac{1}{t} x' + \bigl(1 - \tfrac{1}{4t^2}\bigr) x = \sqrt{t}\cos t\) on \([1, 6]\) with \(x(1) = 1\) and \(x(6) = -0.5\). That equation can also be solved in closed form, so every number below is checked against the exact solution.

title: Shooting Methods for ODE’s
text:
Boundary Value Problems






NoteDefinition — Boundary value problem



A boundary value problem is a differential equation
\[
x'' = f(t, x, x') \qquad \text{for } a \le t \le b
\tag{1}
\]
together with the boundary conditions
\[
x(a) = \alpha \qquad \text{and} \qquad x(b) = \beta .
\tag{2}
\]


Before any numerical scheme is applied, it should be checked that a solution exists; otherwise the program prints a list of meaningless numbers. The notation \(y = x'(t)\) is used below to name the third variable of \(f(t, x, x')\).






TipTheorem — Boundary value problem



Assume that \(f(t, x, y)\) is continuous on the region \(R = \{(t, x, y) : a \le t \le b,\ -\infty < x < \infty,\ -\infty < y < \infty\}\) and that \(\partial f/\partial x = f_x(t, x, y)\) and \(\partial f/\partial y = f_y(t, x, y)\) are continuous on \(R\). If there is a constant \(M > 0\) for which
\[
f_x(t, x, y) > 0 \quad \text{and} \quad |f_y(t, x, y)| \le M \qquad \text{for all } (t, x, y) \in R,
\]
then the boundary value problem \(x'' = f(t, x, x')\) with \(x(a) = \alpha\) and \(x(b) = \beta\) has a unique solution \(x = x(t)\) for \(a \le t \le b\).


The special case of a linear differential equation deserves its own statement.






TipCorollary — Linear boundary value problem



Assume that \(f\) in the theorem has the form \(f(t, x, y) = p(t)\,y + q(t)\,x + r(t)\) and that \(f\) and its partial derivatives \(f_x = q(t)\) and \(f_y = p(t)\) are continuous on \(R\). If
\[
q(t) > 0 \qquad \text{for all } t \in [a, b],
\]
then the linear boundary value problem
\[
x'' = p(t)\,x'(t) + q(t)\,x(t) + r(t) \qquad \text{with } x(a) = \alpha \text{ and } x(b) = \beta
\tag{3}
\]
has a unique solution \(x = x(t)\) over \(a \le t \le b\).


The bound on \(f_y = p(t)\) needs no separate check in the corollary: a continuous \(p\) on the closed interval \([a, b]\) is bounded, with \(M = \max_{a \le t \le b} |p(t)|\).






WarningThe conditions are sufficient, not necessary



Take \(x'' = -x\), whose general solution is \(x(t) = c_1 \cos t + c_2 \sin t\), with the boundary conditions \(x(0) = \alpha\) and \(x(\pi) = \beta\). The first condition gives \(c_1 = \alpha\) and the second gives \(-c_1 = \beta\), so the problem can be solved only if \(\beta = -\alpha\), and then it has infinitely many solutions \(\alpha\cos t + c_2 \sin t\). (Mathews writes the condition as \(\alpha = \beta\); since \(\cos \pi = -1\) it is \(\beta = -\alpha\).) Here \(q(t) = -1 < 0\), and this counterexample is why the theory is phrased with \(q(t) > 0\). But the condition is only sufficient. Many problems with \(q(t) < 0\) have exactly one solution and can be solved by shooting, Mathews’ example below among them; the method just has to be used with care, because it may fail.

title: Shooting Methods for ODE’s
section: Reduction to Two Initial Value Problems: Linear Shooting
text:
Reduction to Two Initial Value Problems: Linear Shooting
The linear structure of (3) lets the boundary value problem be split into two initial value problems. Let \(u(t)\) be the unique solution of
\[
u'' = p(t)\,u'(t) + q(t)\,u(t) + r(t) \qquad \text{with } u(a) = \alpha \text{ and } u'(a) = 0,
\tag{4}
\]
and let \(v(t)\) be the unique solution of the homogeneous problem
\[
v'' = p(t)\,v'(t) + q(t)\,v(t) \qquad \text{with } v(a) = 0 \text{ and } v'(a) = 1.
\tag{5}
\]
For any constant \(C\) the combination \(x(t) = u(t) + C\,v(t)\) solves the differential equation in (3), because
\[
x'' = u'' + C v'' = p(t)\,u' + q(t)\,u + r(t) + p(t)\,C v' + q(t)\,C v = p(t)\,x' + q(t)\,x + r(t).
\]
It also satisfies \(x(a) = u(a) + C\,v(a) = \alpha\) for every \(C\). Choosing \(C\) so that \(x(b) = u(b) + C\,v(b) = \beta\) gives the solution of the boundary value problem.






ImportantLinear shooting formula



If \(v(b) \ne 0\), the solution of (3) is
\[
x(t) = u(t) + \frac{\beta - u(b)}{v(b)}\, v(t).
\tag{6}
\]



Why it is called shooting
The solution of (3) with initial values \(x(a) = \alpha\) and \(x'(a) = s\) is \(x(t; s) = u(t) + s\,v(t)\), since both sides solve the same initial value problem. So the constant \(C\) in (6) is the initial slope, \(x'(a) = C\). A shot fired with slope \(s = 0\) is \(u(t)\) and lands at \(u(b)\); a shot with slope \(s = 1\) lands at \(u(b) + v(b)\). Because the landing point \(x(b; s) = u(b) + s\,v(b)\) is a straight-line function of \(s\), the straight line through these two shots hits the target \(\beta\) exactly, at \(s = (\beta - u(b))/v(b)\). When \(f\) is not linear, \(x(b; s)\) is no longer a straight-line function of \(s\), and in general the slope must be found by solving \(x(b; s) - \beta = 0\) iteratively, for instance with the secant method, one initial value problem per shot. Mathews’ module treats only the linear case.


When linear shooting works
What a computation really needs is that two linearly independent solutions \(u\) and \(v\) can be computed and that \(v(b) \ne 0\). (Mathews states this with \(\alpha \ne \beta\) as a premise; formula (6) needs \(v(b) \ne 0\) whatever \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) are.) The following general fact, which follows from the argument above, explains the role of \(v(b)\).






TipTheorem — Existence and uniqueness through \(v(b)\)



Let \(p\), \(q\) and \(r\) be continuous on \([a, b]\), and let \(u\) and \(v\) be the solutions of (4) and (5). Every solution of the differential equation in (3) with \(x(a) = \alpha\) has the form \(u(t) + s\,v(t)\) with \(s = x'(a)\). Hence

if \(v(b) \ne 0\), the boundary value problem (3) has exactly one solution, given by (6);
if \(v(b) = 0\), it has no solution when \(\beta \ne u(b)\) and infinitely many when \(\beta = u(b)\).



The counterexample above is the case \(v(b) = 0\): for \(x'' = -x\) on \([0, \pi]\), \(v(t) = \sin t\) and \(v(\pi) = 0\), while \(u(t) = \alpha \cos t\) and \(u(\pi) = -\alpha\).






WarningA small \(v(b)\)



In general, formula (6) divides by \(v(b)\), and when \(v(b)\) is close to zero, the errors made in computing \(u(b)\) and \(v(b)\) are magnified in \(C\) and in the whole computed solution, so a small \(|v(b)|\) is a warning that the problem is close to one without a unique solution.




Algorithm
To approximate the solution of (3) over \([a, b]\) with the Runge–Kutta method of order 4, write each initial value problem as a system of two first-order equations.
Step 1. Solve for \(u\) with \(y = u'\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
u' &= y(t), & u(a) &= \alpha, \\
y' &= p(t)\,y(t) + q(t)\,u(t) + r(t), & y(a) &= u'(a) = 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]
Step 2. Solve for \(v\) with \(z = v'\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
v' &= z(t), & v(a) &= 0, \\
z' &= p(t)\,z(t) + q(t)\,v(t), & z(a) &= v'(a) = 1 .
\end{aligned}
\]
Mathews’ subroutine Runge2D solves a system \(\mathbf{Z}' = \mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z})\) with \(\mathbf{Z} = (x, y)\) using \(m\) steps of size \(h = (b - a)/m\) at the nodes \(t_j = a + jh\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{k}_1 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j, \mathbf{Z}_j), &
\mathbf{k}_2 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2}, \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac12\mathbf{k}_1\bigr), \\
\mathbf{k}_3 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2}, \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac12\mathbf{k}_2\bigr), &
\mathbf{k}_4 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j + h, \mathbf{Z}_j + \mathbf{k}_3),
\end{aligned}
\qquad
\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} = \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac16(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4).
\]
Step 3. With \(u_j \approx u(t_j)\) and \(v_j \approx v(t_j)\) from the two runs on the same nodes, form
\[
x_j = u_j + \frac{\beta - u_m}{v_m}\, v_j, \qquad j = 0, 1, \ldots, m .
\]
The points \((t_j, x_j)\) approximate the solution. By construction \(x_0 = \alpha\) and \(x_m = \beta\) (up to rounding), whatever the accuracy of the runs; the error shows in the interior.

title: Shooting Methods for ODE’s
text:
Worked Examples
All six of Mathews’ examples treat the same boundary value problem,
\[
x'' + \frac{1}{t}\,x' + \left(1 - \frac{1}{4t^2}\right) x = \sqrt{t}\,\cos t \qquad \text{over } [1, 6], \qquad x(1) = 1.0, \quad x(6) = -0.5 .
\tag{7}
\]

Example 1 — Is the equation linear?
Problem. Is (7) a linear differential equation? Identify \(p(t)\), \(q(t)\) and \(r(t)\).
Solution. Solving (7) for \(x''\) gives
\[
x'' = -\frac{1}{t}\,x'(t) - \left(1 - \frac{1}{4t^2}\right) x(t) + \sqrt{t}\,\cos t .
\]
It is linear: \(x\) and \(x'\) appear only to the first power, multiplied by functions of \(t\) alone. In the form (3),
\[
\boxed{\ p(t) = -\frac{1}{t}, \qquad q(t) = -\left(1 - \frac{1}{4t^2}\right), \qquad r(t) = \sqrt{t}\,\cos t\ }
\]
All three are continuous on \([1, 6]\). But \(q(t) < 0\) on the whole interval: \(1/(4t^2) \le 1/4\) for \(t \ge 1\), and \(q\) decreases from \(q(1) = -3/4\) to \(q(6) = -143/144 \approx -0.993056\). So the corollary does not apply. That does not matter for the computation: as Mathews notes, the solution can still be computed provided \(v(6) \ne 0\), and Example 3 finds that it is.


Example 2 — The first function \(u(t)\)
Problem. Use linear shooting on (7) and solve for \(u(t)\).
Step 1 (the system): with \(y = u'\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
u' &= y, & u(1) &= 1, \\
y' &= \left(-1 + \frac{1}{4t^2}\right) u - \frac{y}{t} + \sqrt{t}\,\cos t, & y(1) &= u'(1) = 0 .
\end{aligned}
\]
Step 2 (Runge–Kutta): Mathews runs Runge2D with \(m = 100\) steps, so \(h = (6 - 1)/100 = 0.05\), from \((u, y) = (1, 0)\) at \(t = 1\).
Result. The last node gives
\[
u(6) \approx u_{100} = -0.370482 .
\]
This agrees with Mathews’ output. The exact value, from the closed form in Example 6, is \(u(6) = -0.3704820481\); the Runge–Kutta value is \(-0.3704824638\), and over all 101 nodes \(|u_j - u(t_j)| \le 4.2 \times 10^{-7}\).


Example 3 — The second function \(v(t)\)
Problem. Use linear shooting on (7) and solve for \(v(t)\).
Step 1 (the system): with \(z = v'\) and no \(r(t)\) term,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v' &= z, & v(1) &= 0, \\
z' &= \left(-1 + \frac{1}{4t^2}\right) v - \frac{z}{t}, & z(1) &= v'(1) = 1 .
\end{aligned}
\]
Step 2 (Runge–Kutta): Runge2D with the same \(m = 100\) and \(h = 0.05\), from \((v, z) = (0, 1)\).
Result.
\[
v(6) \approx v_{100} = -0.391479 \ne 0,
\]
in agreement with Mathews’ output, so (6) can be used: “we are in luck”, as Mathews says.
Verification. For this equation \(v\) is known exactly. The functions \(\cos t/\sqrt{t}\) and \(\sin t/\sqrt{t}\) solve the homogeneous equation (see Example 6), and the combination with \(v(1) = 0\), \(v'(1) = 1\) is
\[
v(t) = \frac{\sin(t - 1)}{\sqrt{t}}, \qquad v(6) = \frac{\sin 5}{\sqrt 6} = -0.3914791958 .
\]
The Runge–Kutta value is \(-0.3914792683\), and over all 101 nodes \(|v_j - v(t_j)| \le 7.3 \times 10^{-8}\). The exact form also shows where the luck lies: \(v(b) = \sin(b - 1)/\sqrt{b}\) vanishes exactly when \(b - 1\) is a multiple of \(\pi\). On \([1, 6]\), \(v\) changes sign once, at \(t = 1 + \pi \approx 4.1416\), but \(v(6) \ne 0\) because \(5\) is not a multiple of \(\pi\). Had the right end been \(b = 1 + \pi\), linear shooting would have failed.


Example 4 — Neither \(u\) nor \(v\) solves the boundary value problem
Problem. Show that neither of the solutions in Examples 2 and 3 satisfies the boundary conditions, although each satisfies its own initial conditions \(u(1) = 1\), \(u'(1) = 0\) and \(v(1) = 0\), \(v'(1) = 1\).
Solution. Mathews graphs the two functions to see this. The Runge–Kutta values at the integer nodes are:

Example 5 — The solution of the boundary value problem
Problem. Form the solution of (7).
Step 1 (the constant): with \(\beta = -0.5\), \(u(b) \approx u_{100}\) and \(v(b) \approx v_{100}\),
\[
C = \frac{\beta - u_{100}}{v_{100}} = \frac{-0.5 - (-0.3704824638)}{-0.3914792683} = 0.3308413669 .

x_j = u_j + 0.3308413669\, v_j , \qquad j = 0, 1, \ldots, 100 .
\]

The solution rises from \(1\) to a maximum of \(1.0861\) near \(t = 1.4828\), crosses zero near \(t = 2.8711\), falls to a minimum of \(-2.9057\) near \(t = 4.7825\), and then climbs to \(-0.5\) at \(t = 6\) (the extrema and the zero are those of the exact solution of Example 6).

Example 6 — The analytic solution
Problem. Find the analytic solution of (7).
Step 1 (a substitution): put \(x(t) = w(t)/\sqrt{t}\). A direct computation gives
\[
x'' + \frac{1}{t}\,x' + \left(1 - \frac{1}{4t^2}\right) x = \frac{w'' + w}{\sqrt{t}},
\]
so (7) becomes \(w'' + w = t \cos t\). (Equation (7) is Bessel’s equation of order \(\tfrac12\) with a forcing term, which is why this substitution works.)
Step 2 (general solution): the homogeneous equation \(w'' + w = 0\) has the solutions \(\cos t\) and \(\sin t\), and \(w_p = \tfrac14\left(t\cos t + t^2 \sin t\right)\) satisfies \(w_p'' + w_p = t\cos t\). Hence
\[
x(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}\left( c_1 \cos t + c_2 \sin t + \frac{t \cos t + t^2 \sin t}{4} \right).
\tag{8}
\]
Mathematica’s DSolve returns the same family written with the complex exponentials \(e^{\pm i t}/\sqrt{t}\), which is why, as Mathews remarks, this real equation appears to have a solution “involving complex numbers”; by Euler’s formula it is the real family (8), and its particular part differs from \(w_p/\sqrt{t}\) only by the homogeneous term \(-\sin t/(8\sqrt{t})\).
Step 3 (boundary conditions): \(x(1) = 1\) and \(\sqrt{6}\,x(6) = -\sqrt{6}/2\) give the linear system
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_1 \cos 1 + c_2 \sin 1 &= 1 - \tfrac14(\cos 1 + \sin 1) = 0.654556677, \\
c_1 \cos 6 + c_2 \sin 6 &= -\tfrac{\sqrt 6}{2} - \tfrac14(6\cos 6 + 36 \sin 6) = -0.150260818 .
\end{aligned}
\]
Its determinant is \(\cos 1 \sin 6 - \sin 1 \cos 6 = \sin 5 = -0.958924 \ne 0\), the same \(\sin 5\) that makes \(v(6) = \sin 5/\sqrt{6}\) nonzero in Example 3. By Cramer’s rule,
\[
\boxed{\ c_1 = 0.0588713452, \qquad c_2 = 0.7400710958\ }
\]
and the exact solution of (7) is (8) with these constants. Its slope at the left end is \(x'(1) = 0.3308424899\), the slope \(C\) that linear shooting approximates in Example 5.
Verification. Substituting (8) into (7) symbolically leaves a residual of \(0\) for every \(c_1\) and \(c_2\); with the constants above, \(x(1) = 1\) and \(x(6) = -0.5\). The functions \(u\) and \(v\) of Examples 2 and 3 come from the same formula: \(v(t) = \sin(t - 1)/\sqrt{t}\), and \(u\) is (8) with \(c_1 = 0.3372657010\) and \(c_2 = 0.5613161356\), which give \(u(1) = 1\), \(u'(1) = 0\) and \(u(6) = -0.3704820481\). The exact solution also satisfies \(x = u + C v\) with the exact \(C = (-0.5 - u(6))/v(6) = 0.3308424899\), which confirms formula (6) on this problem.

title: Finite Difference Method for ODE’s
text:
Description
A second-order boundary value problem asks for a function \(x(t)\) on an interval \([a, b]\) that satisfies a differential equation inside the interval and prescribed values at both ends. For the linear equation
\[
x'' = p(t)\,x' + q(t)\,x + r(t), \qquad x(a) = \alpha, \quad x(b) = \beta,
\]
the finite difference method divides \([a, b]\) into \(n\) equal subintervals of width \(h = (b - a)/n\), with mesh points \(t_j = a + jh\), and looks for numbers \(x_j \approx x(t_j)\). At every interior mesh point it replaces \(x'\) and \(x''\) by central difference quotients, which turns the differential equation into one linear equation linking \(x_{j-1}\), \(x_j\) and \(x_{j+1}\):
\[
\Bigl(-\frac{h}{2}p_j - 1\Bigr)x_{j-1} + \bigl(2 + h^2 q_j\bigr)x_j + \Bigl(\frac{h}{2}p_j - 1\Bigr)x_{j+1} = -h^2 r_j, \qquad j = 1, 2, \ldots, n-1,
\]
where \(p_j = p(t_j)\), \(q_j = q(t_j)\), \(r_j = r(t_j)\), \(x_0 = \alpha\) and \(x_n = \beta\). These \(n - 1\) equations form a tridiagonal linear system, which tridiagonal elimination solves in \(O(n)\) operations, and the solution values together with the two boundary values give the approximate solution curve.
Both difference quotients are accurate to \(O(h^2)\). Under the conditions stated below, and for a smooth solution, the error of the method is then \(O(h^2)\), so halving \(h\) cuts it by about a factor of four, and two runs with \(h\) and \(h/2\) can be combined by Richardson extrapolation into a much more accurate answer. Mathews’ examples do exactly this for one equation on \([1, 6]\) with \(25\) and \(50\) subintervals; every number below has been recomputed (the example tables in 40-digit arithmetic), and the computed solutions are compared with the exact solution.

title: Finite Difference Method for ODE’s
text:
Boundary Value Problems
The boundary value problem \(x'' = f(t, x, x')\), \(x(a) = \alpha\), \(x(b) = \beta\) need not have a solution, and when it has one it need not be unique. The following theorem gives a sufficient condition. In it, \(y\) stands for the third argument of \(f\), the slot where \(x'(t)\) goes, so that the partial derivatives \(f_x\) and \(f_y\) can be written down.






TipTheorem — Boundary value problem



Assume that \(f(t, x, y)\) is continuous on the region \(R = \{(t, x, y) : a \le t \le b,\ -\infty < x < \infty,\ -\infty < y < \infty\}\) and that \(f_x\) and \(f_y\) are continuous on \(R\). If there is a constant \(M > 0\) for which
\[
f_x(t, x, y) > 0 \quad\text{and}\quad |f_y(t, x, y)| \le M \qquad \text{for all } (t, x, y) \in R,
\]
then the boundary value problem
\[
x'' = f(t, x, x'), \qquad x(a) = \alpha, \quad x(b) = \beta
\]
has a unique solution \(x = x(t)\) for \(a \le t \le b\).


For a linear equation, \(f(t, x, y) = p(t)\,y + q(t)\,x + r(t)\), so \(f_x = q(t)\) and \(f_y = p(t)\), and the theorem becomes:






TipCorollary — Linear boundary value problem



Assume that \(p\), \(q\) and \(r\) are continuous on \([a, b]\) and that
\[
q(t) > 0 \qquad \text{for all } t \in [a, b].
\]
Then the linear boundary value problem
\[
x'' = p(t)\,x'(t) + q(t)\,x(t) + r(t), \qquad x(a) = \alpha, \quad x(b) = \beta
\tag{1}
\]
has a unique solution \(x = x(t)\) over \(a \le t \le b\). (A bound \(|p(t)| \le M\) is automatic here, with \(M = \max_{a \le t \le b} |p(t)|\), because \(p\) is continuous on a closed interval.)








WarningThe condition \(q(t) > 0\) is sufficient, not necessary



The equation \(x'' = -x\) has \(q(t) = -1 < 0\), and its general solution is \(x(t) = c_1 \cos t + c_2 \sin t\). With the boundary conditions \(x(0) = \alpha\) and \(x(\pi) = \beta\), the first condition gives \(c_1 = \alpha\) and the second gives \(x(\pi) = -c_1 = -\alpha\), so the problem can be solved only when \(\beta = -\alpha\), and then \(c_2\) is arbitrary and there are infinitely many solutions. (Mathews’ footnote states the condition as \(\alpha = \beta\); the general solution gives \(\beta = -\alpha\).) This counterexample is why the theory is phrased with \(q(t) > 0\). But the condition is only sufficient: many problems with \(q(t) < 0\) somewhere, including the one solved on this page, still have exactly one solution, and they can be solved by finite differences or by the shooting method with some care.

title: Finite Difference Method for ODE’s
text:
The Finite-Difference Method

Derivation
Consider the linear equation (1) over \([a, b]\) with \(x(a) = \alpha\) and \(x(b) = \beta\). Form a partition of \([a, b]\) using the points \(a = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = b\), where
\[
h = \frac{b - a}{n} \qquad\text{and}\qquad t_j = a + jh \quad\text{for } j = 0, 1, \ldots, n.
\]
The central difference formulas approximate the derivatives at an interior point \(t_j\):
\[
x'(t_j) = \frac{x(t_{j+1}) - x(t_{j-1})}{2h} + O(h^2),
\tag{2}
\]
\[
x''(t_j) = \frac{x(t_{j+1}) - 2x(t_j) + x(t_{j-1})}{h^2} + O(h^2).
\tag{3}
\]
For a solution with continuous fourth derivative the two error terms are \(-\tfrac{h^2}{6}x'''(c_1)\) and \(-\tfrac{h^2}{12}x^{(4)}(c_2)\) for some \(c_1, c_2\) in \((t_{j-1}, t_{j+1})\); Taylor expansion of the quotients gives \(x' + \tfrac{h^2}{6}x''' + \cdots\) and \(x'' + \tfrac{h^2}{12}x^{(4)} + \cdots\).
Write \(x_j\) for the approximation to \(x(t_j)\), drop the two \(O(h^2)\) terms, and use the notation \(p_j = p(t_j)\), \(q_j = q(t_j)\) and \(r_j = r(t_j)\). Equation (1) at \(t = t_j\) becomes the difference equation
\[
\frac{x_{j+1} - 2x_j + x_{j-1}}{h^2} = p_j\,\frac{x_{j+1} - x_{j-1}}{2h} + q_j x_j + r_j.
\tag{4}
\]
Multiply each side by \(h^2\) and collect the terms involving \(x_{j-1}\), \(x_j\) and \(x_{j+1}\):






ImportantThe finite difference equations



\[
\Bigl(-\frac{h}{2}p_j - 1\Bigr)x_{j-1} + \bigl(2 + h^2 q_j\bigr)x_j + \Bigl(\frac{h}{2}p_j - 1\Bigr)x_{j+1} = -h^2 r_j
\tag{5}
\]
for \(j = 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1\), where \(x_0 = \alpha\) and \(x_n = \beta\).


(Mathews’ module prints the left boundary value as \(x_0 = \beta\); it is \(x_0 = x(a) = \alpha\).)


The tridiagonal system
Equation (5) for \(j = 1\) contains the known value \(x_0 = \alpha\), and for \(j = n - 1\) the known value \(x_n = \beta\); moving these to the right-hand side leaves \(n - 1\) equations in the \(n - 1\) unknowns \(x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}\). Write
\[
d_j = 2 + h^2 q_j, \qquad a_j = -\frac{h}{2}p_j - 1, \qquad c_j = \frac{h}{2}p_j - 1, \qquad e_j = -h^2 r_j.
\]
Then the system is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
d_1 & c_1 & & & \\
a_2 & d_2 & c_2 & & \\
& \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\
& & a_{n-2} & d_{n-2} & c_{n-2} \\
& & & a_{n-1} & d_{n-1}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_{n-2} \\ x_{n-1} \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} e_1 - a_1\alpha \\ e_2 \\ \vdots \\ e_{n-2} \\ e_{n-1} - c_{n-1}\beta \end{pmatrix},
\tag{6}
\]
which has the familiar tridiagonal form and is solved by elimination in \(O(n)\) operations.






TipWhen the system has a unique solution (general result)



Suppose \(q(t_j) > 0\) at every interior mesh point and \(h\,|p(t_j)| \le 2\) there (for instance \(h \le 2/M\) with \(M = \max_{a \le t \le b}|p(t)|\)). Then \(a_j \le 0\) and \(c_j \le 0\), so \(|a_j| + |c_j| = \bigl(1 + \tfrac{h}{2}p_j\bigr) + \bigl(1 - \tfrac{h}{2}p_j\bigr) = 2 < 2 + h^2 q_j = d_j\). Every row of (6) is strictly diagonally dominant, so the matrix is nonsingular and the tridiagonal elimination needs no pivoting.


When \(q\) is negative, as in the example below, the matrix is not diagonally dominant and nonsingularity has to be checked another way; it does not follow from this result.
The finite difference solution also converges to \(x(t)\) as \(h \to 0\): under the conditions of the corollary, with \(h \le 2/M\), and for a solution with continuous fourth derivative, the error at the mesh points is \(O(h^2)\). This is a standard general result. The example below does not satisfy these conditions, but it shows the factor of four per halving of \(h\) numerically all the same.


Algorithm
To approximate the solution of \(x'' = p(t)x'(t) + q(t)x(t) + r(t)\) with \(x(a) = \alpha\) and \(x(b) = \beta\) over \([a, b]\) by the finite difference method of order \(O(h^2)\), Mathews’ program uses the mesh \(a = t_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_{n+1} = b\) (numbered from \(1\), so it has \(n + 1\) points for \(n\) subintervals) and returns the solution points \(\{(t_j, x_j)\}_{j=1}^{n+1}\). Its three steps are:

Construct the tridiagonal matrix and the right-hand-side vector of (6).
Solve the system in step 1 for the ordinates strictly inside the interval.
Join the mesh points and the solution vector from step 2 into points, and put the boundary points \((a, \alpha)\) and \((b, \beta)\) at the two ends.

title: Finite Difference Method for ODE’s
text:
Worked Examples
All six of Mathews’ examples use the same boundary value problem,
\[
x'' + \frac{1}{t}\,x' + \Bigl(1 - \frac{1}{4t^2}\Bigr)x = \sqrt{t}\,\cos t, \qquad x(1) = 1, \quad x(6) = -0.5,
\tag{7}
\]
over \([1, 6]\). In the form (1) it has
\[
p(t) = -\frac{1}{t}, \qquad q(t) = \frac{1}{4t^2} - 1, \qquad r(t) = \sqrt{t}\,\cos t.
\]
Here \(q(t)\) decreases from \(q(1) = -0.75\) to \(q(6) = -0.993056\), so it is negative on the whole interval and the corollary does not apply. The problem nevertheless has exactly one solution, which can be written down.

The exact solution
The homogeneous equation \(x'' + \tfrac{1}{t}x' + \bigl(1 - \tfrac{1}{4t^2}\bigr)x = 0\) is Bessel’s equation of order \(\tfrac12\). The substitution \(x = u/\sqrt{t}\) turns (7) into
\[
u'' + u = t\cos t,
\]
whose general solution is \(u = c_1\cos t + c_2\sin t + \tfrac14 t\cos t + \tfrac14 t^2\sin t\). Hence
\[
x(t) = \frac{c_1\cos t + c_2\sin t}{\sqrt{t}} + \frac14\sqrt{t}\,\cos t + \frac14\,t^{3/2}\sin t.
\tag{8}
\]
The boundary conditions give two linear equations for \(c_1\) and \(c_2\), whose determinant is \(\cos 1\,\sin 6 - \sin 1\,\cos 6 = \sin 5 = -0.958924 \neq 0\), so there is exactly one solution:
\[
c_1 = 0.0588713451552886, \qquad c_2 = 0.740071095780206,
\]
the same constants that Mathews uses in Example 6. The same determinant shows that the homogeneous problem with \(x(1) = x(6) = 0\) has only the zero solution. Formula (8) satisfies (7) and both boundary conditions to 40-digit precision, and an independent numerical solution of (7) with SciPy’s solve_bvp agrees with it to within \(9 \times 10^{-16}\) on \([1, 6]\). Its minimum on \([1, 6]\) is about \(-2.9057\), near \(t = 4.78\).


Example 1 — \(25\) subintervals, step by step
Solve (7) over \([1, 6]\) with the finite difference method and \(n = 25\) subintervals (\(26\) points).
Step 1: The mesh. With \(h = (6 - 1)/25 = 0.2\),
\[
t_j = 1 + 0.2j, \qquad j = 0, 1, \ldots, 25,
\]
and the unknowns are \(x_1, \ldots, x_{24}\) at \(t = 1.2, 1.4, \ldots, 5.8\).
Step 2: The coefficient functions at the mesh points. At \(t_1 = 1.2\),
\[
p_1 = -\frac{1}{1.2} = -0.833333, \qquad q_1 = \frac{1}{4(1.44)} - 1 = -0.826389, \qquad r_1 = \sqrt{1.2}\,\cos 1.2 = 0.396943.
\]
Step 3: The first row of (6). With \(h/2 = 0.1\) and \(h^2 = 0.04\),
\[
d_1 = 2 + 0.04\,q_1 = 1.966944, \qquad c_1 = 0.1\,p_1 - 1 = -1.083333,
\]
\[
e_1 - a_1\alpha = -0.04\,r_1 + (1 + 0.1\,p_1)(1) = -0.015878 + 0.916667 = 0.900789.
\]
The second row, at \(t_2 = 1.4\), is the first full one: \(a_2 = -0.928571\), \(d_2 = 1.965102\), \(c_2 = -1.071429\) and right-hand side \(e_2 = -0.04\,r_2 = -0.008044\).
Step 4: The last row, at \(t_{24} = 5.8\), where \(p_{24} = -0.172414\), \(q_{24} = -0.992568\) and \(r_{24} = 2.132613\):
\[
a_{24} = -0.1\,p_{24} - 1 = -0.982759, \qquad d_{24} = 2 + 0.04\,q_{24} = 1.960297,
\]
\[
e_{24} - c_{24}\beta = -0.04\,r_{24} + (1 - 0.1\,p_{24})(-0.5) = -0.085305 - 0.508621 = -0.593925.
\]
These are the first and last entries of the four vectors Mathews prints (sub-diagonal, diagonal, super-diagonal, right-hand side), and all four agree with the recomputation to the six figures he shows.
Step 5: Solve the \(24 \times 24\) tridiagonal system. Because \(q < 0\), the diagonal entries run from \(d_1 = 1.966944\) down to \(d_{24} = 1.960297\), all below \(2\), while \(|a_j| + |c_j| = 2\) in rows \(2\) to \(23\); so the matrix is not diagonally dominant and the general result above does not apply. It is nonsingular all the same: its determinant is \(-4.903642\) and its condition number (2-norm) is about \(225\).
Step 6: Put the boundary points \((1, 1)\) and \((6, -0.5)\) at the ends of the list of points \((t_j, x_j)\). The finite difference solution, compared with the exact solution (8), is:

Example 2 — the same problem with the program
Mathews repeats Example 1 with his finite difference program, which carries out the three steps of the algorithm in one call with \(a = 1\), \(b = 6\), \(\alpha = 1\), \(\beta = -0.5\) and \(25\) subintervals, skipping the details. The program returns the same \(26\) points as the table in Example 1; the list he calls points1 and prints again in Example 4 is identical to his Example 1 list. Call these values \(X_1\).


Example 3 — \(50\) subintervals
Solve (7) again with \(n = 50\) subintervals (\(51\) points), so \(h = 0.1\) and the system has \(49\) unknowns. Call the result \(X_2\). Its first and last interior values are \(x(1.1) \approx 1.03057\) and \(x(5.9) \approx -0.868321\), as in Mathews’ output; the values at the \(26\) points \(t = 1.0, 1.2, \ldots, 6.0\) that it shares with \(X_1\) are listed in the table under Example 5.


Example 4 — how much do the two solutions differ?
The two solutions cannot be subtracted directly: \(X_1\) has \(26\) points and \(X_2\) has \(51\). The mesh of \(X_1\) is every other point of the mesh of \(X_2\), so Mathews takes points \(1, 3, 5, \ldots, 51\) of \(X_2\) (numbering from \(1\)), which lie at \(t = 1.0, 1.2, \ldots, 6.0\), and forms the difference \(X_2 - X_1\) there. It appears in the table under Example 5. The difference is negative from \(t = 1.2\) to \(t = 3.4\), positive from \(t = 3.6\) to \(t = 5.8\), and largest in size at \(t = 4.8\), where \(X_2 - X_1 = 0.01100\).
Is that small or large? Since the method is of order \(O(h^2)\), the error of \(X_2\) should be about a quarter of the error of \(X_1\), so \(X_2 - X_1 \approx -\tfrac34(X_1 - x)\), and the difference itself estimates the error: \(X_1 - x \approx -\tfrac43(X_2 - X_1)\), which at \(t = 4.8\) is \(-\tfrac43(0.01100) = -0.01467\), close to the actual error \(-0.01464\). The improvement scheme of the next example removes most of it.


Example 5 — Richardson extrapolation
Use Richardson extrapolation and the results of Examples 2 and 3 to construct a more accurate solution at the \(26\) points of the \(25\)-subinterval mesh.
If the error of the method behaves like \(C h^2\) at a fixed point \(t\), then \(X_1 \approx x + Ch^2\) and \(X_2 \approx x + C h^2/4\). Eliminating \(C\) gives the extrapolated values
\[
X_3 = \frac{4X_2 - X_1}{3} = X_2 + \frac{X_2 - X_1}{3}.
\tag{9}
\]
(The output of this example is missing from Mathews’ archive; formula (9) is the one he uses in Example 6.) At \(t = 4.8\), for instance, \(X_3 = (4(-2.908846) - (-2.919846))/3 = -2.905179\), compared with the exact value \(-2.905208\).

The extrapolated values improve faster. Applying (9) to the pairs \((25, 50)\), \((50, 100)\) and \((100, 200)\) gives largest errors \(2.869 \times 10^{-5}\), \(1.788 \times 10^{-6}\) and \(1.115 \times 10^{-7}\), with ratios \(0.0623\) and \(0.0624\), close to \(\tfrac{1}{16}\): for this problem the extrapolated solution behaves like a method of order \(O(h^4)\).

title: Predictor-Corrector Methods
text:
Description
A predictor-corrector method approximates the solution of an initial value problem \(y' = f(t, y)\), \(y(t_0) = y_0\), on a grid \(t_n = t_0 + nh\). It pairs two multistep formulas. The corrector is implicit: the new value \(y_{n+1}\) appears on both sides, inside \(f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1})\). Implicit formulas typically have smaller error constants and better stability than explicit ones of the same order, but solving them exactly at every step means solving a nonlinear equation. The predictor is explicit and supplies a first estimate \(p_{n+1}\); the corrector is then applied once, or a few times, with the unknown slope replaced by the slope at the latest estimate. One step of the basic scheme, called PECE, is
\[
\underbrace{p_{n+1} = \text{explicit formula}}_{\text{P}}, \quad
\underbrace{f^{*}_{n+1} = f(t_{n+1}, p_{n+1})}_{\text{E}}, \quad
\underbrace{y_{n+1} = \text{implicit formula with } f^{*}_{n+1}}_{\text{C}}, \quad
\underbrace{f_{n+1} = f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1})}_{\text{E}}.
\]
Repeating the correct-evaluate pair \(m\) times gives the mode P(EC)\(^m\)E. The two estimates \(p_{n+1}\) and \(y_{n+1}\) come for free at every step, and when the two formulas have the same order their difference estimates the local error of the step (Milne’s device). That estimate drives step-size control, and it can also be added back to the computed values (a modifier). Two fourth-order pairs have their own pages: Adams-Bashforth-Moulton and Milne-Simpson. This page sets out the general framework and works it through the simplest Adams pair, the two-step Adams-Bashforth predictor with the trapezoidal corrector, on \(y' = 1 + y^2\), \(y(0) = 0\), whose exact solution is \(y = \tan t\).
Mathews’ module for this topic was never written: the archive’s page for it is an “under construction” placeholder, with only a bibliography page beside it. This page is therefore written from standard sources, in particular the chapter on predictor-corrector methods in J. D. Lambert, Numerical Methods for Ordinary Differential Systems (Wiley, 1991). Every number on this page was computed for it: the runs of the examples in 50-digit arithmetic, each reproduced by an independent 200-bit implementation, the error constants by symbolic Taylor expansion, and the stability intervals from the roots of the characteristic polynomials.

title: Predictor-Corrector Methods
text:
Linear Multistep Formulas






NoteDefinition — Linear multistep formula



A \(k\)-step linear multistep formula for \(y' = f(t, y)\) computes \(y_{n+1}\) from the \(k\) previous values and slopes \(f_j = f(t_j, y_j)\):
\[
y_{n+1} = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} a_j\, y_{n-j} + h \sum_{j=-1}^{k-1} b_j\, f_{n-j}.
\tag{1}
\]
It is explicit if \(b_{-1} = 0\), so that \(y_{n+1}\) is given directly, and implicit if \(b_{-1} \neq 0\), so that \(y_{n+1}\) also appears on the right in \(f_{n+1} = f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1})\).








NoteDefinition — Order and error constant



Replace every \(y_j\) in (1) by the exact value \(y(t_j)\) and every \(f_j\) by \(y'(t_j)\). The local truncation error is the amount by which \(y(t_{n+1})\) then fails to satisfy (1). The formula has order \(p\) and error constant \(C_{p+1}\) if, for every smooth \(y\),
\[
y(t_{n+1}) - \Bigl[\sum_{j=0}^{k-1} a_j\, y(t_{n-j}) + h \sum_{j=-1}^{k-1} b_j\, y'(t_{n-j})\Bigr] = C_{p+1}\, h^{p+1}\, y^{(p+1)}(t_n) + O(h^{p+2}).
\tag{2}
\]
The leading term \(C_{p+1} h^{p+1} y^{(p+1)}\) is the principal local truncation error. Errors on this page are always exact minus computed.


The formulas used on this page and on the two linked pages are listed below; each order and error constant was obtained by expanding (2) in a Taylor series about \(t_n\).

In both Adams pairs of the same order, the implicit formula’s error constant is much smaller in size than the explicit one’s: \(-\tfrac{1}{12}\) against \(\tfrac{5}{12}\) (5 times smaller), and \(-\tfrac{19}{720}\) against \(\tfrac{251}{720}\) (about 13 times smaller).

Solving the corrector by iteration
An implicit formula (1) can be written \(y_{n+1} = h\, b_{-1}\, f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) + g_n\), where \(g_n\) collects the known terms. The natural way to solve it is fixed-point iteration, \(y^{[s+1]}_{n+1} = h\, b_{-1}\, f\bigl(t_{n+1}, y^{[s]}_{n+1}\bigr) + g_n\).






TipTheorem — Convergence of the corrector iteration (general)



Suppose \(f\) satisfies a Lipschitz condition \(|f(t, u) - f(t, v)| \le L\,|u - v|\) in \(y\). If
\[
h\, |b_{-1}|\, L < 1,
\tag{3}
\]
then the implicit formula has exactly one solution \(y_{n+1}\), and the iteration converges to it from any starting value; each iteration multiplies the distance to the solution by at most \(h |b_{-1}| L\). This is the contraction mapping theorem. Near the solution the factor per iteration is about \(h\,|b_{-1}|\,|\partial f / \partial y|\).


A predictor-corrector method uses an explicit formula to start this iteration close to the solution, and then stops after a fixed number of iterations instead of iterating to convergence.

title: Predictor-Corrector Methods
text:
The Predictor-Corrector Framework

Modes
Take an explicit predictor and an implicit corrector, both of the form (1). Write \(f^{[s]}_{n+1} = f\bigl(t_{n+1}, y^{[s]}_{n+1}\bigr)\). One step in the mode P(EC)\(^m\)E is:

P (predict): \(y^{[0]}_{n+1} = p_{n+1}\) from the explicit formula, using the stored values \(y_n, y_{n-1}, \ldots\) and \(f_n, f_{n-1}, \ldots\)
For \(s = 0, 1, \ldots, m-1\):

E (evaluate): \(f^{[s]}_{n+1} = f\bigl(t_{n+1}, y^{[s]}_{n+1}\bigr)\);
C (correct): \(y^{[s+1]}_{n+1}\) from the implicit formula with \(f^{[s]}_{n+1}\) in place of \(f_{n+1}\).

E (final evaluation): \(y_{n+1} = y^{[m]}_{n+1}\) and \(f_{n+1} = f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1})\), which is stored for the next steps.

In the mode P(EC)\(^m\) the last evaluation is skipped, and the slope stored for later steps is \(f^{[m-1]}_{n+1}\), the slope at the previous iterate. The common modes are:

A multistep predictor needs several back values, so the method is not self-starting: the first few values come from a one-step method, usually a Runge-Kutta method of at least the same order (the Runge-Kutta page covers RK4). Heun’s method, Euler’s method as predictor and the trapezoidal rule as corrector in PECE mode, is itself a one-step predictor-corrector method:
\[
p_{n+1} = y_n + h f_n, \qquad y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{h}{2}\bigl(f_n + f(t_{n+1}, p_{n+1})\bigr).
\tag{4}
\]
It is not the modified Euler method of Euler’s method, which takes its slope at the midpoint of the step.


Order of a predictor-corrector method






TipTheorem — Order of P(EC)\(^m\)E and P(EC)\(^m\) (general; Lambert, 1991)



Let the predictor have order \(p^*\) and the corrector order \(p\), and let \(f\) be smooth.

If \(p^* \ge p\), or if \(p^* < p\) and \(m > p - p^*\), the predictor-corrector method has the order \(p\) and the principal local truncation error of the corrector.
If \(p^* < p\) and \(m = p - p^*\), it has the order \(p\) of the corrector, but a different principal local truncation error.
If \(p^* < p\) and \(m < p - p^*\), its order is \(p^* + m\), lower than \(p\).



So a predictor one order below the corrector costs nothing in order with a single correction, and a predictor of the same order makes the PECE method’s leading error term the corrector’s own. For the AB2-trapezoid pair (\(p^* = p = 2\)), case 1 applies for every \(m \ge 1\); Heun’s method (4) (\(p^* = 1\), \(p = 2\), \(m = 1\)) is case 2. Example 3 measures both orders.






WarningMore corrections approach the corrector, not the solution



Iterating the corrector further moves \(y_{n+1}\) toward the solution of the implicit formula, which still carries the corrector’s own truncation error. Under the condition (3), P(EC)\(^m\)E tends to the corrector solved exactly as \(m \to \infty\). Extra corrections do not, in general, make the result more accurate, and each one costs another evaluation of \(f\). In Example 2, every correction beyond the first makes the error at \(t = 1\) larger.




Milne’s device: estimating the local error
Suppose the predictor and the corrector have the same order \(p\), with error constants \(C^*_{p+1}\) and \(C_{p+1}\), and that the mode satisfies case 1 of the theorem (for example PECE). If the back values are exact and \(y^{(p+1)}\) is nearly constant over the few steps involved, then by (2)
\[
y(t_{n+1}) - p_{n+1} \approx C^*_{p+1} h^{p+1} y^{(p+1)}, \qquad
y(t_{n+1}) - y_{n+1} \approx C_{p+1} h^{p+1} y^{(p+1)}.
\]
Subtracting eliminates the unknown \(y(t_{n+1})\): \(y_{n+1} - p_{n+1} \approx (C^*_{p+1} - C_{p+1})\, h^{p+1} y^{(p+1)}\). Substituting back gives estimates of both local errors from computed quantities alone.






ImportantMilne’s device



\[
y(t_{n+1}) - y_{n+1} \approx \frac{C_{p+1}}{C^*_{p+1} - C_{p+1}}\,\bigl(y_{n+1} - p_{n+1}\bigr), \qquad
y(t_{n+1}) - p_{n+1} \approx \frac{C^*_{p+1}}{C^*_{p+1} - C_{p+1}}\,\bigl(y_{n+1} - p_{n+1}\bigr).
\tag{5}
\]

The estimate costs no extra evaluations of \(f\). In a variable-step code it is compared with a tolerance at every step: the step is rejected and repeated with a smaller \(h\) when the estimate is too large, and \(h\) may be increased when it is much smaller. The estimate is only as good as its assumptions; the back values in a real computation are not exact, and \(y^{(p+1)}\) is not constant, which Example 1 shows at \(h = 0.1\).


Modifiers
Because (5) estimates the errors, it can also be used to improve the values. This is called local extrapolation, or applying a modifier. There are two kinds.

Corrector modifier (PECLE, with L for local extrapolation): after the correction, replace \(y_{n+1}\) by \[
\hat{y}_{n+1} = y_{n+1} + \frac{C_{p+1}}{C^*_{p+1} - C_{p+1}}\,\bigl(y_{n+1} - p_{n+1}\bigr),
\tag{6}
\] then evaluate \(f\) at \(\hat{y}_{n+1}\). For a pair of equal order this cancels the principal local truncation error, so in general the order goes up by one.
Predictor modifier (PMECE): the difference \(y_{n+1} - p_{n+1}\) of the current step is not known when predicting, so the previous step’s difference is used: \[
\hat{p}_{n+1} = p_{n+1} + \frac{C^*_{p+1}}{C^*_{p+1} - C_{p+1}}\,\bigl(y_n - p_n\bigr),
\tag{7}
\] and \(\hat{p}_{n+1}\) replaces \(p_{n+1}\) in the corrector. The unmodified \(p_n\) is used in the difference. For Milne’s pair this is the modifier \(p_{k+1} + \tfrac{28}{29}(y_k - p_k)\) quoted on the Milne-Simpson page.

For the AB2-trapezoid pair the corrector modifier gives an exact identity. With \(f^*_{n+1} = f(t_{n+1}, p_{n+1})\), the extrapolated value is
\[
y_{n+1} - \tfrac16\bigl(y_{n+1} - p_{n+1}\bigr)
= \tfrac56\Bigl[y_n + \tfrac{h}{2}\bigl(f_n + f^*_{n+1}\bigr)\Bigr] + \tfrac16\Bigl[y_n + \tfrac{h}{2}\bigl(3f_n - f_{n-1}\bigr)\Bigr]
= y_n + \frac{h}{12}\bigl(5f^*_{n+1} + 8f_n - f_{n-1}\bigr),
\]
which is the third-order Adams-Moulton formula AM3 with the predicted slope. So PECLE for this pair is the PECE method with predictor AB2 (\(p^* = 2\)) and corrector AM3 (\(p = 3\)), which by case 2 of the theorem has order 3.
A modifier changes the method, and with it the stability (see the table below). With the corrector modifier, (5) estimates the error of the unmodified value, not of the value carried forward.


Stability
Applied to the test equation \(y' = \lambda y\), a predictor-corrector method is a linear recurrence whose characteristic polynomial depends on \(z = h\lambda\), on the mode and on any modifier. Its stability region is in general that of neither the predictor nor the corrector. For the AB2-trapezoid pair in PECE mode, for example, one step gives \(y_{n+1} = \bigl(1 + z + \tfrac34 z^2\bigr) y_n - \tfrac14 z^2 y_{n-1}\), with characteristic polynomial
\[
4\zeta^2 - \bigl(4 + 4z + 3z^2\bigr)\zeta + z^2 = 0.
\tag{8}
\]
Solving these polynomials numerically for real \(z < 0\) (a decaying solution) gives the intervals of absolute stability, where every root lies inside the unit circle:

At \(z = -2\) the PECE polynomial (8) becomes \(4(\zeta - 1)^2\), a double root on the unit circle. The trapezoidal rule alone is A-stable, stable for every \(z\) with \(\operatorname{Re} z < 0\), but no mode with a fixed \(m\) in this table keeps that property, and adding corrections does not enlarge the interval steadily (\(-2\), then \(-1.478\), then \(-2\)). This is why stiff problems are solved with the implicit formula solved by Newton’s method rather than by a predictor-corrector pair. In the examples below \(\partial f / \partial y = 2y > 0\), so the solution grows and these intervals on the negative real axis do not limit the step.

title: Predictor-Corrector Methods
text:
Worked Examples
All three examples use the same problem:
\[
y' = 1 + y^2, \qquad y(0) = 0, \qquad 0 \le t \le 1,
\]
with the exact solution \(y = \tan t\), since \((\tan t)' = \sec^2 t = 1 + \tan^2 t\) and \(\tan 0 = 0\). The predictor is AB2 and the corrector the trapezoidal rule:
\[
p_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{h}{2}\bigl(3f_n - f_{n-1}\bigr), \qquad
y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac{h}{2}\bigl(f_n + f(t_{n+1}, p_{n+1})\bigr), \qquad f_n = 1 + y_n^2.
\tag{9}
\]
AB2 needs two back values, so \(y_1\) comes from one step of Heun’s method (4). The error is \(e_n = \tan t_n - y_n\).

Example 1 — PECE with \(h = 0.1\), step by step
Step 0 (starting value by Heun’s method): \(f_0 = 1\), so \(p_1 = 0 + 0.1(1) = 0.1\) and \(f(t_1, p_1) = 1 + 0.1^2 = 1.01\). Then
\[
y_1 = 0 + 0.05\,(1 + 1.01) = 0.1005, \qquad f_1 = 1 + 0.1005^2 = 1.01010025.
\]
The exact value is \(\tan 0.1 = 0.1003346721\), so \(e_1 = -1.65 \times 10^{-4}\).
Step 1 (first predictor, \(n = 1\)): \(3f_1 - f_0 = 2.03030075\), so
\[
p_2 = 0.1005 + 0.05\,(2.03030075) = 0.2020150375.
\]
Step 2 (evaluate and correct): \(f(t_2, p_2) = 1 + 0.2020150375^2 = 1.0408100754\), and
\[
y_2 = 0.1005 + 0.05\,(1.01010025 + 1.0408100754) = 0.1005 + 0.05\,(2.0509103254) = 0.2030455163.
\]
Step 3 (evaluate): \(f_2 = 1 + y_2^2 = 1.0412274817\). The exact value is \(\tan 0.2 = 0.2027100355\), so \(e_2 = -3.35 \times 10^{-4}\). The predictor was low and the corrector high: \(\tan 0.2 - p_2 = 6.95 \times 10^{-4}\).
Step 4 (error estimate): the difference is \(y_2 - p_2 = 0.0010304788\), so Milne’s device (5) estimates the local error of the step as
\[
-\tfrac16\,(0.0010304788) = -1.72 \times 10^{-4}.
\]
The true local error of this step, the error of one PECE step from the exact values \(\tan 0\) and \(\tan 0.1\), is \(-1.65 \times 10^{-4}\).
Step 5 (next step, \(n = 2\)): \(3f_2 - f_1 = 2.1135821950\), \(p_3 = 0.2030455163 + 0.05\,(2.1135821950) = 0.3087246260\), \(f(t_3, p_3) = 1.0953108947\), and
\[
y_3 = 0.2030455163 + 0.05\,(1.0412274817 + 1.0953108947) = 0.3098724351,
\]
against \(\tan 0.3 = 0.3093362496\). The run continues in the same way to \(t = 1\).
