title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
text:
Description
The gradient method, also called the method of steepest descent, looks for a local minimum of a function \(f(\mathbf{X})\) of \(n\) variables, \(\mathbf{X} = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)\), whose first partial derivatives can be evaluated. At the current point \(\mathbf{P}_k\) the gradient \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) points in the direction in which \(f\) increases fastest, so the unit vector opposite to it is the direction of steepest descent. The method searches along the line through \(\mathbf{P}_k\) in that direction for the lowest value of \(f\) and moves there:
\[
\mathbf{S}_k = -\frac{\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)}{\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) \rVert}, \qquad
\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + h_k\,\mathbf{S}_k, \qquad
h_k \approx \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\gamma \ge 0}\, f(\mathbf{P}_k + \gamma\,\mathbf{S}_k).
\]
Each iteration needs only the gradient and a one-variable minimisation along a line. When that line minimisation is exact, \(f\) decreases at every step and each new search direction is perpendicular to the previous one, so the path to the minimum is a zigzag. In a long, narrow valley the zigzag steps are short and the method is slow. Mathews carries out the line search with a single quadratic interpolation per step (the quadratic interpolative search idea), and his examples work in two variables, \(\mathbf{P}_k = (x_k, y_k)\): a quadratic, Rosenbrock’s banana-shaped valley, a quartic with three local minima and a rational function. Every run below was recomputed with his line search and stopping rule in 60-digit arithmetic and agrees with a 120-digit run to more than 50 digits.

title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
section: The Gradient and the Direction of Steepest Descent
text:
The Gradient and the Direction of Steepest Descent






NoteDefinition — Gradient



Let \(z = f(\mathbf{X})\) be a function of \(\mathbf{X} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)\) such that \(\partial f(\mathbf{X})/\partial x_k\) exists for \(k = 1, 2, \ldots, n\). The gradient of \(f\) is the vector
\[
\nabla f(\mathbf{X}) = \left( \frac{\partial f(\mathbf{X})}{\partial x_1},\ \frac{\partial f(\mathbf{X})}{\partial x_2},\ \ldots,\ \frac{\partial f(\mathbf{X})}{\partial x_n} \right).
\tag{1}
\]








TipTheorem — Direction of steepest descent (general)



Let \(f\) be differentiable at \(\mathbf{P}\) with \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \neq \mathbf{0}\). The rate of change of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{P}\) in the direction of a unit vector \(\mathbf{u}\) is \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \cdot \mathbf{u}\). By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality it lies between \(-\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \rVert\) and \(\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \rVert\), with the largest value for \(\mathbf{u} = \nabla f(\mathbf{P}) / \lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \rVert\) and the smallest for
\[
\mathbf{u} = -\frac{\nabla f(\mathbf{P})}{\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \rVert}.
\]


So locally \(f\) increases fastest along \(\nabla f\) and decreases fastest along \(-\nabla f\). The decrease is local only: a long step in the direction \(-\nabla f\) can overshoot, which is why the method looks for the best step length along the line.

Illustrations — two gradients
Mathews starts by finding the gradients of two functions that reappear in the examples.
For the quartic of Example 3,
\[
f(x, y) = 5x^2 + x^4 - 9x^2 y + 3y^2 + 2y^4 + \tfrac14 x, \qquad
\nabla f(x, y) = \bigl(10x + 4x^3 - 18xy + \tfrac14,\ \ -9x^2 + 6y + 8y^3\bigr).
\]
For the rational function of Example 4, the quotient rule gives
\[
f(x, y) = \frac{x - y}{x^2 + y^2 + 2}, \qquad
\nabla f(x, y) = \left( \frac{-x^2 + 2xy + y^2 + 2}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^2},\ \ \frac{-x^2 - 2xy + y^2 - 2}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^2} \right),
\]
and at the point \((-3, -2)\), where \(x^2 + y^2 + 2 = 15\),
\[
\nabla f(-3, -2) = \left( \frac{9}{225},\ -\frac{19}{225} \right) = \left( \frac{1}{25},\ -\frac{19}{225} \right) \approx (0.04,\ -0.0844444).
\]
Verification: both gradients were checked symbolically against direct differentiation (the differences simplify to \(0\)), and the value at \((-3, -2)\) was computed in exact rational arithmetic.

title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
text:
The Gradient Method
Start at \(\mathbf{P}_0\) and search along the line through \(\mathbf{P}_0\) in the direction \(\mathbf{S}_0 = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0)/\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0) \rVert\). The point \(\mathbf{P}_1\) is where \(f\), restricted to the line \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{P}_0 + \gamma\,\mathbf{S}_0\), has a local minimum. Then compute \(\mathbf{S}_1\) from \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_1)\), search along the line through \(\mathbf{P}_1\), and so on.






ImportantOutline of the gradient method



Suppose \(\mathbf{P}_k\) has been found.

Evaluate the gradient vector \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\).
Compute the search direction \(\mathbf{S}_k = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) / \lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) \rVert\).
Minimise the function of one variable \[\varphi_k(\gamma) = f(\mathbf{P}_k + \gamma\,\mathbf{S}_k) \tag{2}\] on an interval \([0, b]\), where \(b\) is large. This gives a value \(\gamma = h_k\) at which \(\varphi_k\) has a local minimum, so \(f(\mathbf{P}_k + h_k \mathbf{S}_k)\) is a minimum of \(f\) along the search line.
Construct the next point \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + h_k\,\mathbf{S}_k\).
Termination test: are \(f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) and \(f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1})\) close enough, and is the distance \(\lVert \mathbf{P}_{k+1} - \mathbf{P}_k \rVert\) small enough? If not, repeat.









TipTheorem — Properties with an exact line search (general)



Let \(f\) be continuously differentiable and let each \(h_k > 0\) be an exact local minimiser of \(\varphi_k\) in (2), with \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) \neq \mathbf{0}\).

Descent. \(\varphi_k'(0) = \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) \cdot \mathbf{S}_k = -\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) \rVert < 0\), so \(f\) decreases strictly: \(f(\mathbf{P}_0) > f(\mathbf{P}_1) > \cdots > f(\mathbf{P}_k) > \cdots\).
Zigzag. \(\varphi_k'(h_k) = \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1}) \cdot \mathbf{S}_k = 0\), and \(\mathbf{S}_{k+1}\) is a negative multiple of \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1})\), so \(\mathbf{S}_{k+1} \cdot \mathbf{S}_k = 0\): consecutive search directions are perpendicular.
Limit. Every limit point \(\mathbf{P}\) of the sequence \(\{\mathbf{P}_k\}\) satisfies \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}) = \mathbf{0}\).



Mathews states that if \(\mathbf{P}_k \to \mathbf{P}\) then \(f(\mathbf{P})\) is a local minimum. That is what happens in every run on this page, but in general the theory guarantees only a stationary point. Because \(f\) decreases at every step, the limit cannot be a strict local maximum, but a saddle point can be reached from special starting points: for \(f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2\) from \((1, 0)\), the first exact line search lands on the saddle point \((0, 0)\), where the gradient is zero and the method stops. With an approximate line search such as Mathews’ single quadratic fit, properties 1 and 2 hold exactly only when \(\varphi_k\) is a quadratic, as in Example 1. In the other examples they hold approximately, and each case says how closely.






TipTheorem — Rate on a quadratic (general)



Let \(f(\mathbf{X}) = f^{*} + \tfrac12 (\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X}^{*})\,\mathbf{A}\,(\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X}^{*})^{T}\), where \(\mathbf{A}\) is symmetric positive definite with smallest and largest eigenvalues \(\lambda_{\min}\) and \(\lambda_{\max}\), and let \(\kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\). With exact line searches the gradient method satisfies
\[
f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1}) - f^{*} \le \left( \frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1} \right)^{2} \bigl( f(\mathbf{P}_k) - f^{*} \bigr).
\]


When \(\kappa\) is large, the level curves of \(f\) are long, thin ellipses and the factor is close to \(1\).






WarningSlow convergence



Convergence to a minimum can be slow. In Mathews’ words, the geometry of a minimum often makes \(h_k\) small, so the method returns to the line search (step 3) many times. In four of the six runs below (Examples 1, 2, 3(ii) and 3(iii)) Mathews’ program reaches its work limit before its tolerance.

title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
text:
Mathews’ Implementation
Mathews’ Mathematica program has two parts: a line search that takes one step along \(\mathbf{S}_k\), and an outer loop that repeats it.
Line search. It carries a trial step \(h\) from one iteration to the next (\(h = 1\) at the start of a run). With \(Y_0 = \varphi_k(0)\), \(Y_1 = \varphi_k(h)\) and \(Y_2 = \varphi_k(2h)\) it repeats, at most \(15\) times:

if \(Y_0 \le Y_1\), the step is too long: halve \(h\) (the old middle point becomes the new right point) and evaluate the new middle point;
otherwise, if \(Y_2 < Y_1\), \(\varphi_k\) is still falling at \(2h\): double \(h\) (the old right point becomes the middle point) and evaluate the new right point;
otherwise \(Y_1 < Y_0\) and \(Y_1 \le Y_2\), so the points \(0\), \(h\), \(2h\) bracket a minimum: stop.

The step is the vertex of the parabola through \((0, Y_0)\), \((h, Y_1)\), \((2h, Y_2)\),
\[
h_k = \frac{h\,(4Y_1 - 3Y_0 - Y_2)}{2\,(2Y_1 - Y_0 - Y_2)},
\tag{3}
\]
and \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + h_k \mathbf{S}_k\). This is one quadratic fit, not repeated: \(h_k\) is the exact minimiser of \(\varphi_k\) only when \(\varphi_k\) is itself a quadratic. The trial step for the next iteration is the smallest of \(h\), \(|h_k|\), \(|h_k - h|\) and \(|h_k - 2h|\).
Outer loop and stopping rule. The program keeps \(\mathrm{Err}\), the smallest nonzero difference \(|Y_i - f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1})|\) (\(i = 0, 1, 2\)) met so far in the run, starting from \(\mathrm{Err} = 1\). It stops as soon as both \(h \le \delta\) and \(\mathrm{Err} \le \varepsilon\), or when a work counter reaches \(60\); each iteration adds \(j + 1\) to the counter, where \(j\) is the number of passes through the bracketing loop. Mathews uses \(\delta = \varepsilon = 10^{-10}\) in Examples 1, 2, 3(i) and 4, and \(\delta = \varepsilon = 10^{-14}\) in Examples 3(ii) and 3(iii).
In the tables below \(h_k\) is the step taken from \(\mathbf{P}_k\); since \(\lVert \mathbf{S}_k \rVert = 1\) it is also the distance from \(\mathbf{P}_k\) to \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1}\). \(\mathbf{P}^{*}\) is the minimum the run approaches. Mathews’ own tables, computed in machine arithmetic, print \(12\) decimal places (in scientific notation for the smallest values). Each example says how far they agree with the recomputation. In every one of his tables the first line pairs \(\mathbf{P}_0\) with a function value left over from the previous computation (his program prints \(f(\mathbf{P}_0)\) before evaluating it), so the tables here give the correct \(f(\mathbf{P}_0)\).

title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
section: Example 1 — A quadratic, \(f(x, y) = x^2 - 4x + y^2 - y - xy\), from \((0.99, 1.01)\)

title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
section: Example 2 — Rosenbrock’s parabolic valley, \(f(x, y) = 100(y - x^2)^2 + (1 - x)^2\), from \((0.99, 1.01)\)
text:
Example 2 — Rosenbrock’s parabolic valley, \(f(x, y) = 100(y - x^2)^2 + (1 - x)^2\), from \((0.99, 1.01)\)
Use the gradient method to find the minimum of Rosenbrock’s function (circa 1960),
\[
f(x, y) = 100\,(y - x^2)^2 + (1 - x)^2, \qquad \mathbf{P}_0 = (0.99,\ 1.01).
\]
Step 0 (gradient and minimum):
\[
\nabla f(x, y) = \bigl(-400x\,(y - x^2) - 2(1 - x),\ \ 200\,(y - x^2)\bigr).
\]
The minimum is \(f(1, 1) = 0\), at the end of the curved valley floor \(y = x^2\). There
\[
\mathbf{H}(1, 1) = \begin{pmatrix} 802 & -400 \\ -400 & 200 \end{pmatrix}
\]
has eigenvalues \(0.3993608\) and \(1001.601\), a ratio \(\kappa \approx 2508\): the valley is very narrow.

title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
text:
Example 4 — \(f(x, y) = (x - y)/(x^2 + y^2 + 2)\) from \((-3, -2)\)
Use the gradient method to find the minimum of
\[
f(x, y) = \frac{x - y}{x^2 + y^2 + 2}, \qquad \mathbf{P}_0 = (-3,\ -2).
\]
Step 0 (the minimum): \(\nabla f(-1, 1) = (0, 0)\), \(f(-1, 1) = -\tfrac12\) and \(\mathbf{H}(-1, 1) = \tfrac14 \mathbf{I}\). The minimum is round: near it the level curves are almost circles. The function is also symmetric about the line \(y = -x\), since \(f(-y, -x) = f(x, y)\).
Step 1 (first iteration): from the illustration above, \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0) = (0.04,\ -0.0844444)\) and \(\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0) \rVert = 0.09343909\), so
\[
\mathbf{S}_0 = (-0.4280863,\ 0.9037378), \qquad
\varphi_0(\gamma) = \frac{-1 - 1.331824\,\gamma}{2 + (-3 - 0.4280863\,\gamma)^2 + (-2 + 0.9037378\,\gamma)^2}.
\]
The line search starts with \(h = 1\): \(Y_0 = -0.06666667\), \(Y_1 = \varphi_0(1) = -0.1559377\) and \(Y_2 = \varphi_0(2) = -0.2166925\). It doubles \(h\) twice, to \(4\), where \(Y_1 = \varphi_0(4) = -0.2359675\) and \(Y_2 = \varphi_0(8) = -0.1650125\). Formula (3) gives
\[
h_0 = 4.818676, \qquad \mathbf{P}_1 = (-5.062809,\ 2.354820), \qquad f(\mathbf{P}_1) = -0.2235760 .
\]
The exact minimum of \(\varphi_0\) is at \(\gamma = 3.292600\), where \(\varphi_0 = -0.2404550\): the parabola through \(\gamma = 0, 4, 8\) overshoots it. Mathews’ textbook works this same iteration (its Example 8.9), and there \(4.8186760\) is called the minimum of \(\varphi_0\). It is the single quadratic-interpolation estimate, not the minimum.
Step 2 (second iteration): \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_1) = (-0.03809377,\ 0.001596349)\) and \(\mathbf{S}_1 = (0.9991231,\ -0.04186903)\), at \(117.75^\circ\) to \(\mathbf{S}_0\). The trial step \(0.8186760\) is doubled twice, to \(3.274704\), and
\[
h_1 = 2.770828, \qquad \mathbf{P}_2 = (-2.294411,\ 2.238808), \qquad f(\mathbf{P}_2) = -0.3692574,
\]
while the exact minimum of \(\varphi_1\) is at \(\gamma = 3.891620\). The textbook’s \(\mathbf{P}_1\), \(\mathbf{S}_1\), \(h_1\) and \(\mathbf{P}_2\) agree with these values.
Step 3 (the full run): the run ends after \(8\) iterations because the tolerances are met (the counter stands at \(47\)).

The first step lowers \(f\) but moves away from the minimum, from a distance of \(3.606\) to \(4.283\), and the first directions are far from perpendicular (\(117.75^\circ\) and \(40.86^\circ\)). Near the round minimum \(-\nabla f\) points almost straight at \((-1, 1)\), so there is no zigzag. Each step lands much closer than the last: the distances fall by factors \(0.31\), \(0.19\), \(0.049\), \(0.0026\), \(5.0 \times 10^{-6}\) and \(8.2 \times 10^{-10}\).

Mathews’ table agrees with rows \(1\) to \(7\) to within \(9.1 \times 10^{-13}\), but it has a ninth iteration and prints \((-0.999999998992,\ 0.999999998992)\) for both \(\mathbf{P}_8\) and \(\mathbf{P}_9\). That is rounding error: so close to the minimum, \(f\) differs from \(-\tfrac12\) by less than machine arithmetic can resolve, and the quadratic fit (3) divides one rounding error by another.

text:
Example 5 — Drawing the iterations
Mathews’ last example returns to the quadratic of Example 1 with a version of the program that draws each step. On a contour plot of \(f\) over \([2.5, 3.05] \times [1.6, 2.15]\) it draws the level curve of \(f\) through \(\mathbf{P}_k\), the search line from \(\mathbf{P}_k\) in the direction \(\mathbf{S}_k\), and the three trial points \(\mathbf{P}_k\), \(\mathbf{P}_k + h\mathbf{S}_k\) and \(\mathbf{P}_k + 2h\mathbf{S}_k\), then marks the new point. This version also differs in detail from the program above: it starts with \(h = 0.2\), stops when the counter reaches \(20\), and takes \(h_k = h/3\) when the three trial values do not lie on an upward parabola. The starting point and the output of this example survive only in images that are missing from the archive, so the run cannot be reproduced. Its plotting window contains \((3, 2)\), the minimum of Example 1, whose run is tabulated in full above.

title: Pendulum
text:
Description
A simple pendulum is a point mass \(m\) on a rigid rod of length \(l\) and negligible weight, swinging about a fixed pivot. If \(\theta(t)\) is the angle of the rod measured from the downward vertical, Newton’s second law for rotation gives the nonlinear pendulum equation
\[
\theta'' + \frac{g}{l}\sin\theta = 0 .
\]
For small swings \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\), and the equation becomes the linear equation of simple harmonic motion, whose solutions are sines and cosines with period \(2\pi\sqrt{l/g}\) whatever the amplitude. The nonlinear equation has no solution in elementary functions, so Mathews solves it numerically: the substitution \(y = x'\) turns the second-order equation \(x'' = f(t, x, x')\) into the first-order system \(x' = y\), \(y' = f(t, x, y)\), and the classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method is applied to that system in vector form, \(\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} = \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac16(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4)\) with \(\mathbf{Z}_j = (x_j, y_j)\). With a damping term \(\tfrac{1}{10}x'\) added, the module compares the linear and the nonlinear model in the \((t, x)\) plane (Examples 1 to 4).
The second half of the module draws phase portraits: curves \((x(t), y(t))\) in the plane of angle and angular velocity. Without damping (Examples 5 and 6) the energy \(E = \tfrac12 y^2 + \tfrac{g}{l}(1 - \cos x)\) is constant along every solution, so small swings are closed loops around the rest positions \(x = 2k\pi\), and swings with enough energy run over the top, round and round the pivot. With damping (Example 7) the energy decreases, the loops become spirals, and every curve of Example 7 tends to rest at one of the points \((2k\pi, 0)\). Every number on this page was recomputed: the Runge-Kutta runs with Mathews’ own step counts, and the reference solutions with an adaptive eighth-order integrator at a tolerance of \(10^{-13}\).

title: Pendulum
text:
The Pendulum Equation

The nonlinear pendulum
The torque of gravity about the pivot is
\[
\tau = -m g l \sin\theta,
\tag{1}
\]
where \(\theta\) is the angle of the rod measured downward from the vertical; the minus sign says the torque turns the mass back toward \(\theta = 0\). The moment of inertia of the point mass is \(I = m l^2\), and Newton’s second law for rotation, \(\tau = I\alpha\) with angular acceleration \(\alpha = \theta''\), gives
\[
\tau = I \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}.
\tag{2}
\]
Equating (1) and (2):






ImportantThe nonlinear pendulum equation



\[
\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{m g l}{I}\sin\theta = 0,
\qquad\text{and with } I = m l^2:\qquad
\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{g}{l}\sin\theta = 0 .
\tag{3}
\]


The mass cancels: the motion depends only on \(g/l\).


The linear pendulum
If the angle stays small, the approximation \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\) in (3) gives the familiar linear equation of simple harmonic motion,
\[
\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{m g l}{I}\,\theta = 0 .
\tag{4}
\]
With \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{m g l / I} = \sqrt{g/l}\) its general solution is
\[
\theta(t) = a_1 \cos(\omega_0 t) + a_2 \sin(\omega_0 t),
\tag{5}
\]
which has period \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(g l m)} = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}\). Written with a phase shift, the solution is
\[
\theta(t) = A \cos(\omega_0 t + \delta).
\tag{6}
\]






WarningThe linear period does not depend on the amplitude; the nonlinear one does



In (5) the period \(2\pi/\omega_0\) is the same for every swing. For the nonlinear equation (3) with amplitude \(\theta_{\max} < \pi\) the period is (a general result, derived from the energy below)
\[
T = \frac{4}{\omega_0} K(k), \qquad k = \sin\frac{\theta_{\max}}{2}, \qquad K(k) = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{d\phi}{\sqrt{1 - k^2 \sin^2\phi}},
\]
and \(K(k)\) grows from \(\pi/2\) at \(k = 0\) to \(\infty\) as \(k \to 1\). A swing to \(29°\) takes \(1.6\%\) longer than the linear period, a swing to \(60°\) \(7.3\%\) longer, and a swing to \(143.6°\) \(65\%\) longer (Example 5).




Energy and the phase plane
With \(x = \theta\) and \(y = \theta'\), equation (3) is the system \(x' = y\), \(y' = -\omega_0^2 \sin x\). A solution traced in the \(xy\)-plane is a phase curve, and a set of phase curves is a phase portrait. Mathews puts the angle \(x\) on the horizontal axis and the angular velocity \(y\) on the vertical axis; since \(x\) increases where \(y > 0\), curves are traversed clockwise.






NoteDefinition — Energy of the pendulum



For \(x'' + c\,x' + \omega_0^2 \sin x = 0\) with \(c \ge 0\), the energy (per unit \(m l^2\)) of the state \((x, y) = (x, x')\) is
\[
E(x, y) = \tfrac12 y^2 + \omega_0^2 (1 - \cos x),
\]
kinetic energy plus potential energy, with \(E = 0\) at rest at the bottom and \(E = 2\omega_0^2\) at rest at the top.








TipTheorem — Energy is conserved without damping and decreases with damping



Along any solution of \(x' = y\), \(y' = -c\,y - \omega_0^2 \sin x\),
\[
\frac{d}{dt} E\bigl(x(t), y(t)\bigr) = y\,y' + \omega_0^2 \sin x \; x' = -c\, y^2 .
\]
So for \(c = 0\) every phase curve lies on a level curve \(E = E_0\), and for \(c > 0\) the energy never increases.


For \(c = 0\) the level curves give the whole picture. The equilibria are \((k\pi, 0)\). If \(E_0 < 2\omega_0^2\) and the start has \(|x_0| < \pi\), the pendulum swings back and forth, \(|x|\) never reaches \(\pi\), and the phase curve is a closed loop around \((0, 0)\) (and, since the equation is \(2\pi\)-periodic in \(x\), the same loops appear around every \((2k\pi, 0)\)). If \(E_0 > 2\omega_0^2\), \(y\) never vanishes and the pendulum runs over the top and round the pivot forever, \(y = \pm\sqrt{2E_0 - 2\omega_0^2(1-\cos x)}\). The level \(E_0 = 2\omega_0^2\) is the separatrix \(y = \pm 2\omega_0 \cos(x/2)\), which separates the two kinds of motion: a pendulum started on it at the bottom with speed exactly \(2\omega_0\) creeps toward the top \((\pi, 0)\) and never reaches it in finite time. Starting at \(x = 0\) with speed \(y_0\), the energy is \(E_0 = \tfrac12 y_0^2\), so the swing is a closed loop when \(y_0 < 2\omega_0\), a rotation when \(y_0 > 2\omega_0\), and the modulus in the period formula is \(k = y_0/(2\omega_0)\).
For \(c > 0\) the energy leaks away. The rest positions at the bottom, \((2k\pi, 0)\), attract nearby curves: there the linearised equation is \(u'' + c\,u' + \omega_0^2 u = 0\), and when \(c < 2\omega_0\) (as in Example 7, where \(c = \tfrac{1}{10}\) and \(2\omega_0 = 2.83\)) its solutions oscillate as they decay, so the curves spiral in. The tops \(((2k+1)\pi, 0)\) are saddle points. A curve with enough energy still runs over one or more tops, but each pass costs energy, and once the energy is below \(2\omega_0^2\) the curve is trapped in one well between two tops and tends to the rest position at its bottom.

title: Pendulum
text:
Runge-Kutta Method for Second-Order Equations
To approximate the solution of the initial value problem
\[
x'' = f(t, x, x'), \qquad x(a) = \alpha, \qquad x'(a) = \beta, \qquad a \le t \le b,
\]
substitute \(y = x'\). The second-order problem becomes the first-order system
\[
x' = y, \qquad y' = f(t, x, y), \qquad x(a) = \alpha, \quad y(a) = \beta .
\tag{7}
\]
More generally, the module’s two-dimensional solver handles any system \(x' = f_1(t, x, y)\), \(y' = f_2(t, x, y)\) with \(x(a) = \alpha\), \(y(a) = \beta\). It is the one-dimensional Runge-Kutta method in vector form, with the scalar \(f\) replaced by \(\mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z}) = \bigl(f_1(t, x, y), f_2(t, x, y)\bigr)\), \(\mathbf{Z} = (x, y)\).






NoteAlgorithm — Runge-Kutta method in two dimensions (Mathews’ Runge2D)



Given \(a\), \(b\), \(\mathbf{Z}_0 = (\alpha, \beta)\) and a number of steps \(m\), set \(h = (b - a)/m\) and \(t_j = a + j h\). For \(j = 0, 1, \ldots, m - 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{k}_1 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j, \mathbf{Z}_j), &
\mathbf{k}_2 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2}, \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac12 \mathbf{k}_1\bigr), \\
\mathbf{k}_3 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2}, \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac12 \mathbf{k}_2\bigr), &
\mathbf{k}_4 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j + h, \mathbf{Z}_j + \mathbf{k}_3),
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} = \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac16\bigl(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4\bigr).
\tag{8}
\]
The output is the list of points \(\mathbf{Z}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{Z}_m\). The first coordinates \(x_j\) approximate the solution \(x(t_j)\) of the second-order problem; plotting \((t_j, x_j)\) gives the solution curve, and plotting \((x_j, y_j)\) gives the phase curve.


The global error of the method is \(O(h^4)\) for a smooth \(\mathbf{F}\) (a general result), so halving the step should divide the error by about \(16\); Example 1 checks this.

title: Pendulum
text:
Example 1 — Runge-Kutta solution of \(x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2x = 0\)
Solve
\[
x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2x = 0, \qquad x(0) = 1, \qquad x'(0) = 2,
\]
over \([0, 20]\) with the Runge-Kutta method. This is a linear pendulum (or a mass on a spring) with \(\omega_0^2 = 2\) and a light damping term.
Step 1: Write the equation as \(x'' = f(t, x, x')\) with
\[
f(t, x, x') = -\tfrac{1}{10}x' - 2x .
\]
Step 2: With \(y = x'\) the system (7) is
\[
x' = y, \qquad y' = -\tfrac{1}{10}y - 2x, \qquad x(0) = 1, \quad y(0) = 2,
\qquad \mathbf{F}(t, (x, y)) = \bigl(y,\ -2x - \tfrac{y}{10}\bigr).
\]
Step 3: Mathews takes \(m = 100\) steps on \([0, 20]\), so \(h = 0.2\). The first step, from \(\mathbf{Z}_0 = (1, 2)\), is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{k}_1 &= 0.2\,\mathbf{F}(0, (1, 2)) = (0.4,\ -0.44), \\
\mathbf{k}_2 &= 0.2\,\mathbf{F}(0.1, (1.2, 1.78)) = (0.356,\ -0.5156), \\
\mathbf{k}_3 &= 0.2\,\mathbf{F}(0.1, (1.178, 1.7422)) = (0.34844,\ -0.506044), \\
\mathbf{k}_4 &= 0.2\,\mathbf{F}(0.2, (1.34844, 1.493956)) = (0.2987912,\ -0.56925512),
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\mathbf{Z}_1 = (1, 2) + \tfrac16(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4) = (1.3512785,\ 1.4912428).
\]
The exact values (from Example 2) are \(x(0.2) = 1.3512965\) and \(x'(0.2) = 1.4912143\), so the first step is off by \(-1.8 \times 10^{-5}\) in \(x\).
Step 4: The remaining 99 steps are the same computation. The solution we want is the first coordinate \(x_j\); Mathews plots the points \((t_j, x_j)\) joined by line segments. The computed \(x_j\) range from \(-1.5140\) to \(1.6976\).

title: Pendulum
text:
Example 2 — The analytic solution of \(x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2x = 0\)
Find the analytic solution of the initial value problem of Example 1,
\[
x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2x = 0, \qquad x(0) = 1, \qquad x'(0) = 2,
\]
and plot it over \([0, 20]\).
Step 1: The characteristic equation \(r^2 + \tfrac{1}{10} r + 2 = 0\) has the complex roots
\[
r = -\frac{1}{20} \pm \frac{\sqrt{799}}{20}\, i .
\]
Mathematica’s DSolve returns the solution in terms of the complex exponentials \(e^{\frac{1}{20}(-1 \pm i\sqrt{799})t}\), divided by \(1598\).
Step 2: In terms of real functions, with \(\omega = \sqrt{799}/20 = 1.413329\),
\[
x(t) = e^{-t/20}\cos\!\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt{799}}{20}\,t\Bigr) + \frac{41}{\sqrt{799}}\, e^{-t/20}\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt{799}}{20}\,t\Bigr).
\]
Step 3: In the phase-shift form (6), with a decaying amplitude,
\[
x(t) = A\, e^{-t/20} \cos(\omega t + \delta), \qquad A = \sqrt{\tfrac{2480}{799}} = 1.761783, \qquad \delta = -\arctan\frac{41}{\sqrt{799}} = -0.967200 .
\]
The solution oscillates with the constant quasi-period \(2\pi/\omega = 4.445662\) inside the envelope \(\pm A e^{-t/20}\). On \([0, 20]\) its largest value is \(1.703585\) at \(t = 0.6593\) and its smallest is \(-1.524389\) at \(t = 2.8822\).
Verification: Substituting \(x(t)\) into the equation gives \(x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2x = 0\) identically, \(x(0) = 1\), and \(x'(0) = -\tfrac{1}{20} + \tfrac{41}{\sqrt{799}}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt{799}}{20} = 2\). The phase form agrees: \(A\cos\delta = 1\) and \(-A\sin\delta = 41/\sqrt{799} = 1.450476\).

text:
Example 3 — The nonlinear pendulum \(x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2\sin x = 0\)
Solve
\[
x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2\sin x = 0, \qquad x(0) = 1, \qquad x'(0) = 2,
\]
the damped nonlinear pendulum with \(g/l = 2\) and the same damping and starting values as Example 1.
Step 1: \(f(t, x, x') = -\tfrac{1}{10}x' - 2\sin x\), so the system is
\[
x' = y, \qquad y' = -\tfrac{1}{10}y - 2\sin x, \qquad x(0) = 1, \quad y(0) = 2 .
\]
Step 2: As in Example 1, Mathews runs the Runge-Kutta method on \([0, 20]\) with \(m = 100\) steps, \(h = 0.2\), and plots \((t_j, x_j)\). The computed \(x_j\) range from \(-1.6613\) to \(1.9766\).

So the pendulum swings back and forth and never goes over the top: the largest angle, \(x = 1.976621\) at \(t = 0.9963\), is \(113.25°\), below \(\pi\). By \(t = 20\) the energy has fallen to \(0.448391\).

Example 4 — Linear or nonlinear: comparing the two models

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
Description
The Lotka-Volterra equations are two coupled nonlinear differential equations for a prey population \(x(t)\) and a predator population \(y(t)\):
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = k_1 x - k_2 x y, \qquad \frac{dy}{dt} = -k_3 y + k_4 x y, \qquad k_1, k_2, k_3, k_4 > 0 .
\]
Without predators the prey grow at the rate \(k_1\), and without prey the predators die out at the rate \(k_3\); the products \(x y\) count the encounters between the two species, which cost the prey and feed the predators. Mathews does not try to write \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) as formulas. He computes them with the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method in vector form: with \(\mathbf{Z} = (x, y)\), \(\mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z}) = (k_1 x - k_2 x y,\ -k_3 y + k_4 x y)\) and step \(h = (b - a)/m\),
\[
\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} = \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac16\left(\mathbf{K}_1 + 2\mathbf{K}_2 + 2\mathbf{K}_3 + \mathbf{K}_4\right),
\]
where \(\mathbf{K}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{K}_4\) are \(h\) times \(\mathbf{F}\) evaluated at the start, twice at the midpoint and at the end of the step. The computed points \(\mathbf{Z}_0, \mathbf{Z}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{Z}_m\) trace a curve in the \(xy\)-plane, the phase plane.
For positive starting values other than the equilibrium, the exact curves are closed. Dividing the two equations gives a separable equation for \(dy/dx\), whose solution says that the quantity \(V(x, y) = k_4 x - k_3 \ln x + k_2 y - k_1 \ln y\) keeps its initial value along every solution in the first quadrant. Its level curves are closed loops around the equilibrium \((k_3/k_4,\ k_1/k_2)\), so the populations rise and fall periodically, the predators peaking after the prey. After a scalar warm-up (Example 1), the examples solve the case \(k_1 = k_2 = k_3 = k_4 = 1\) from \((x_0, y_0) = (2, 1)\) numerically and analytically and compare the two, and then follow a population of \(5000\) rabbits and \(100\) foxes.

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
The Lotka-Volterra Equations






NoteDefinition — Lotka-Volterra equations



For constants \(k_1, k_2, k_3, k_4 > 0\) the Lotka-Volterra equations are
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = k_1 x - k_2 x y, \qquad \frac{dy}{dt} = -k_3 y + k_4 x y,
\tag{1}
\]
solved with initial values \(x(0) = x_0 > 0\) and \(y(0) = y_0 > 0\).



Equilibrium points
An equilibrium (critical point) is a point where \(dx/dt = 0\) and \(dy/dt = 0\) at once. Writing (1) as \(x(k_1 - k_2 y) = 0\) and \(y(-k_3 + k_4 x) = 0\) shows there are exactly two:
\[
(0, 0) \qquad \text{and} \qquad (x_e, y_e) = \left(\frac{k_3}{k_4},\ \frac{k_1}{k_2}\right).
\tag{2}
\]
Mathews states that there is one critical point, \((k_3/k_4,\ k_1/k_2)\); that is the only one with both populations positive, but the origin is an equilibrium too.
The Jacobian matrix of the right-hand side of (1) is
\[
J(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} k_1 - k_2 y & -k_2 x \\ k_4 y & -k_3 + k_4 x \end{pmatrix}.
\]
At the origin \(J = \operatorname{diag}(k_1, -k_3)\), with one positive and one negative eigenvalue: the origin is a saddle point, repelling along the \(x\)-axis (prey alone grow) and attracting along the \(y\)-axis (predators alone die out). At \((x_e, y_e)\)
\[
J(x_e, y_e) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -k_2 k_3/k_4 \\ k_1 k_4/k_2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \lambda = \pm\, i\sqrt{k_1 k_3},
\tag{3}
\]
so the linearised system rotates around \((x_e, y_e)\) with angular frequency \(\sqrt{k_1 k_3}\), that is with period \(2\pi/\sqrt{k_1 k_3}\). Purely imaginary eigenvalues alone do not decide what the nonlinear system does near the equilibrium; the conserved quantity below does.


A conserved quantity and closed orbits






TipTheorem — Conserved quantity (general, for \(k_1, \ldots, k_4 > 0\) and \(x, y > 0\))



Along every solution of (1) with \(x_0, y_0 > 0\) the function
\[
V(x, y) = k_4 x - k_3 \ln x + k_2 y - k_1 \ln y
\tag{4}
\]
is constant. Equivalently, \(x^{k_3}\, y^{k_1}\, e^{-k_4 x - k_2 y}\) is constant.


Proof. The two axes are solution curves of (1) (\(x = 0\) gives \(dx/dt = 0\), \(y = 0\) gives \(dy/dt = 0\)), so a solution that starts in the open first quadrant stays in it and \(\ln x\), \(\ln y\) are defined. By the chain rule
\[
\frac{dV}{dt} = \left(k_4 - \frac{k_3}{x}\right)(k_1 x - k_2 x y) + \left(k_2 - \frac{k_1}{y}\right)(-k_3 y + k_4 x y)
= (k_4 x - k_3)(k_1 - k_2 y) + (k_2 y - k_1)(k_4 x - k_3) = 0. \qquad \blacksquare
\]






TipTheorem — Periodic orbits (general, for \(k_1, \ldots, k_4 > 0\))



Every solution of (1) that starts at a point \((x_0, y_0)\) with \(x_0, y_0 > 0\), other than the equilibrium \((x_e, y_e)\), is periodic: its orbit in the phase plane is a closed curve around \((x_e, y_e)\), traversed counterclockwise.


Why. The gradient of \(V\) is \((k_4 - k_3/x,\ k_2 - k_1/y)\), which vanishes only at \((x_e, y_e)\), and its Hessian \(\operatorname{diag}(k_3/x^2,\ k_1/y^2)\) is positive definite, so \(V\) is strictly convex on the quadrant with its only minimum at the equilibrium. Since \(V \to \infty\) as \(x\) or \(y\) tends to \(0\) or to \(\infty\), each level set \(V = V(x_0, y_0)\) above the minimum is a single closed curve around \((x_e, y_e)\). The solution stays on that curve, and the curve holds no equilibrium, so the solution keeps moving round it and returns to its starting point after a finite time \(T\). Below the equilibrium (\(y < y_e\)) the prey increase, so the motion is counterclockwise.






TipTheorem — Average populations (general)



For a periodic solution of (1) with period \(T\),
\[
\frac1T \int_0^T x(t)\,dt = \frac{k_3}{k_4} = x_e, \qquad \frac1T \int_0^T y(t)\,dt = \frac{k_1}{k_2} = y_e .
\tag{5}
\]


Proof. From (1), \(\dfrac{d}{dt}\ln y = -k_3 + k_4 x\). Integrating over one period, the left side gives \(\ln y(T) - \ln y(0) = 0\), so \(0 = -k_3 T + k_4 \int_0^T x\,dt\). The same argument with \(\dfrac{d}{dt}\ln x = k_1 - k_2 y\) gives the average of \(y\). \(\blacksquare\)
The period itself depends on the orbit. For small orbits around \((x_e, y_e)\) it approaches the linearised value \(2\pi/\sqrt{k_1 k_3}\) from (3); in Example 2 and Example 6 the computed periods of the larger orbits exceed it.

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
Predator-Prey Model
The study of interacting populations goes back to two independently published works by Alfred James Lotka (1880–1949) and Vito Volterra (1860–1940). Let \(x(t)\) be the number of prey (rabbits) and \(y(t)\) the number of predators (foxes). The prey have ample food and reproduce with birth rate \(c_1\) and death rate \(c_2\); successful hunting by the predators removes a further \(k_2\, y x\) prey per unit time, proportional to the number of encounters. Combining the three terms,
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = c_1 x - c_2 x - k_2\, y x = (c_1 - c_2)\,x - k_2\, x y,
\]
and the substitution \(k_1 = c_1 - c_2\) (the net growth rate of the prey) gives
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = k_1 x - k_2 x y .
\]
The predators’ birth rate is proportional to their food supply, \(k_4 x\), and their death rate is \(k_3\), so
\[
\frac{dy}{dt} = -k_3 y + k_4 x y .
\]
These are the Lotka-Volterra equations (1). In this setting the equilibrium (2) is the pair of population sizes at which neither species changes, and (5) says that over each cycle the populations average exactly those sizes.

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
The Runge-Kutta Method

One equation
Mathews solves the equations with the classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method. For the initial value problem \(y' = f(t, y)\), \(y(a) = \alpha\), on \(a \le t \le b\), divide \([a, b]\) into \(m\) steps of length \(h = (b - a)/m\), set \(t_j = a + jh\) and \(y_0 = \alpha\), and compute






ImportantRunge-Kutta method of order 4



\[
\begin{aligned}
K_1 &= h\, f(t_j,\ y_j), \\
K_2 &= h\, f\!\left(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2},\ y_j + \tfrac{K_1}{2}\right), \\
K_3 &= h\, f\!\left(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2},\ y_j + \tfrac{K_2}{2}\right), \\
K_4 &= h\, f(t_j + h,\ y_j + K_3), \\
y_{j+1} &= y_j + \tfrac16\left(K_1 + 2K_2 + 2K_3 + K_4\right),
\end{aligned}
\qquad j = 0, 1, \ldots, m - 1.
\tag{6}
\]


Mathews names the four slopes \(k_1, \ldots, k_4\), the same letters as the model constants in (1); this page writes them as capitals. The result is a discrete set of points \((t_j, y_j)\) that approximate the solution, not a formula. For a smooth solution the error at a fixed \(t\) is \(O(h^4)\), so halving \(h\) divides it by about \(16\) (a general result for sufficiently smooth \(f\); Example 1 checks it). The Runge-Kutta method page treats the method in detail.


Systems of two equations
The method extends to a system
\[
x' = f_1(t, x, y),\quad x(a) = \alpha, \qquad y' = f_2(t, x, y),\quad y(a) = \beta, \qquad a \le t \le b,
\]
by applying (6) to the vector \(\mathbf{Z} = (x, y)\) and the vector function \(\mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z}) = \bigl(f_1(t, x, y),\ f_2(t, x, y)\bigr)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{K}_1 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j,\ \mathbf{Z}_j), &
\mathbf{K}_2 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\!\left(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2},\ \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac{\mathbf{K}_1}{2}\right), \\
\mathbf{K}_3 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\!\left(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2},\ \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac{\mathbf{K}_2}{2}\right), &
\mathbf{K}_4 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j + h,\ \mathbf{Z}_j + \mathbf{K}_3),
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} = \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac16\left(\mathbf{K}_1 + 2\mathbf{K}_2 + 2\mathbf{K}_3 + \mathbf{K}_4\right), \qquad \mathbf{Z}_0 = (\alpha, \beta).
\tag{7}
\]
This is the one-dimensional method in “vector form”: \(f\) is replaced by \(\mathbf{F}\), and both components of each \(\mathbf{K}_i\) are computed before the next one. A negative \(b\) (with \(a = 0\)) gives a negative \(h\) and integrates backward in time. Mathews’ subroutine returns only the points \(\mathbf{Z}_j\), which are joined by straight segments to draw the orbit.


Example 1 — A single equation, \(y' = t^2 - y\)
Problem. Solve \(y' = t^2 - y\), \(y(0) = 1\), over \([0, 10]\) with the Runge-Kutta method.
Only the text of this example’s solution page survives: the images holding Mathews’ program, output and graph are lost. Whether Mathews compared with the exact solution cannot be told from what survives; this page does. The equation is linear, and
\[
y(t) = t^2 - 2t + 2 - e^{-t}
\]
satisfies it: \(y' = 2t - 2 + e^{-t} = t^2 - y\), and \(y(0) = 2 - 1 = 1\).
Step 1 (\(t_0 = 0\), \(y_0 = 1\), \(h = 0.2\)):
\[

K_1 &= 0.2\,(0^2 - 1) = -0.2, \\

K_4 &= 0.2\,\bigl(0.2^2 - (1 - 0.1802)\bigr) = -0.15596, \\
y_1 &= 1 + \tfrac16\bigl(-0.2 - 0.356 - 0.3604 - 0.15596\bigr) = 0.8212733,
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
section: Example 2 — The Lotka-Volterra system with \(k_1 = k_2 = k_3 = k_4 = 1\)
text:
Example 2 — The Lotka-Volterra system with \(k_1 = k_2 = k_3 = k_4 = 1\)
Problem. Solve
\[
x' = x - xy, \quad x(0) = 2, \qquad y' = -y + xy, \quad y(0) = 1,
\tag{8}
\]
with the Runge-Kutta method over (a) \(0 \le t \le 3.3\), (b) \(-3.3 \le t \le 0\), (c) \(0 \le t \le 6.6\). Does the solution form an orbit?
Here \(\mathbf{F}(t, x, y) = (x - xy,\ -y + xy)\), the equilibria are \((0, 0)\) and \((1, 1)\), and the conserved quantity (4) is \(V(x, y) = x - \ln x + y - \ln y\), with \(V(2, 1) = 3 - \ln 2 = 2.306853\). Mathews uses \(m = 50\) steps in (a) and (b) and \(m = 100\) in (c), so \(h = \pm 0.066\) throughout, and plots the orbits in the window \([0, 2] \times [0, 2]\).
Step 1 of (a) (\(h = 3.3/50 = 0.066\), \(\mathbf{Z}_0 = (2, 1)\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{K}_1 &= 0.066\,\mathbf{F}(2, 1) = (0,\ 0.066), \\
\mathbf{K}_2 &= 0.066\,\mathbf{F}(2,\ 1.033) = (-0.004356,\ 0.068178), \\
\mathbf{K}_3 &= 0.066\,\mathbf{F}(1.997822,\ 1.034089) = (-0.0044948,\ 0.0681012), \\
\mathbf{K}_4 &= 0.066\,\mathbf{F}(1.9955052,\ 1.0681012) = (-0.0089692,\ 0.0701778), \\
\mathbf{Z}_1 &= (2, 1) + \tfrac16\bigl(\mathbf{K}_1 + 2\mathbf{K}_2 + 2\mathbf{K}_3 + \mathbf{K}_4\bigr) = (1.9955549,\ 1.0681227).
\end{aligned}
\]
A reference solution (an adaptive eighth-order integrator with tolerance \(10^{-13}\)) gives \((1.9955549,\ 1.0681228)\) at \(t = 0.066\). The prey begin to fall and the predators to rise, since \(y_0 = 1\) sits exactly at the level where \(x' = 0\).

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
section: Example 3 — The orbit as a separable equation
text:
Example 3 — The orbit as a separable equation
Problem. For the system (8), combine the two differential equations into a separable first-order equation and solve it.
Step 1. In Leibniz notation, \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = x - xy\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -y + xy\). Divide the second by the first, using \(\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \dfrac{dy}{dx}\):
\[
\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-y + xy}{x - xy} = \frac{y\,(x - 1)}{x\,(1 - y)} .
\]
Step 2. Separate the variables:
\[
\frac{1 - y}{y}\,dy = \frac{x - 1}{x}\,dx .
\]
Step 3. Integrate both sides, writing the constant of integration as \(\ln c\):
\[
\ln y - y = x - \ln x + \ln c .
\]
Step 4. Collect the logarithms, \(\ln x + \ln y - x - y = \ln c\), and exponentiate:
\[
x\,y\,e^{-x-y} = c .
\]
Step 5. The curve passes through the initial point \((2, 1)\), so \(c = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot e^{-3} = 2/e^3 = 0.0995741\). The orbit is the curve
\[
x\,y\,e^{-x-y} = \frac{2}{e^3}.
\tag{9}
\]
Mathews graphs (9) with an implicit plot in the window \([0, 2] \times [0, 2]\); it is the closed loop of Example 2.
Verification. Equation (9) is (4) with every \(k_i = 1\): \(V(x, y) = x - \ln x + y - \ln y = -\ln\bigl(x y e^{-x-y}\bigr)\), so (9) says \(V(x, y) = 3 - \ln 2\). The general separation, with arbitrary \(k_i\), gives the constant \(x^{k_3} y^{k_1} e^{-k_4 x - k_2 y}\) of (4) in the same way.

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
section: Example 4 — The numerical and analytic solutions agree
text:
Example 4 — The numerical and analytic solutions agree
Problem. For the system (8), show that the numerical solution of Example 2 and the analytic solution of Example 3 agree. (Mathews’ statement says “the numerical solution in Example 3 and the analytic solution in Example 4”; the numerical solution is the one of Example 2 and the implicit curve the one of Example 3.)
Mathews places the Runge-Kutta orbit with \(m = 200\) steps over \([0,\ 6.6084827203]\) beside the implicit plot of (9), both in \([0, 2] \times [0, 2]\), and then draws one over the other, where the two curves coincide.
Verification. Substituting the \(201\) Runge-Kutta points into the left side of (9):
\[
\max_{0 \le j \le 200} \bigl|\, x_j y_j e^{-x_j - y_j} - 2/e^3 \bigr| = 1.4 \times 10^{-9},
\]
a relative deviation of \(1.4 \times 10^{-8}\). For the coarser runs of Example 2 the largest deviation is \(2.3 \times 10^{-8}\) (runs (a) and (c)) and \(8.3 \times 10^{-9}\) (run (b)). The numerical points lie on the analytic curve to far better than plotting accuracy.
Mathews also draws a contour plot of \(G(x, y) = x y e^{-x-y}\) over \([0, 2] \times [0, 2]\). Each level curve \(G = c\) with \(0 < c < e^{-2}\) is an orbit of (8); \(G\) takes its largest value \(e^{-2} = 0.135335\) at the equilibrium \((1, 1)\), and the orbit of Examples 2 and 3 is the level \(c = 2/e^3 = 0.0995741\).

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
Example 5 — Solving the orbit for \(y\)
Problem. For the system (8) the implicit solution is \(x y e^{-x-y} = 2/e^3\). Can \(y\) be solved as a function of \(x\)?
Step 1. Write (9) as \(y e^{-y} = \dfrac{2 e^{x-3}}{x}\), that is \((-y)\,e^{-y} = -\dfrac{2 e^{x-3}}{x}\). The equation \(w e^{w} = z\) is solved by the Lambert \(W\) function, \(w = W(z)\) (Mathematica’s ProductLog), so
\[
y = -W\!\left(-\frac{2e^{x-3}}{x}\right).
\tag{10}
\]
Step 2. For real \(w\), \(w e^w = z\) has real solutions only when \(z \ge -1/e\), and two of them when \(-1/e < z < 0\): the principal branch \(W_0(z) \in (-1, 0)\) and the lower branch \(W_{-1}(z) < -1\). Here \(z = -2e^{x-3}/x \ge -1/e\) exactly when \(x e^{-x} \ge 2/e^2\), that is for
\[
0.40638 \le x \le 2 .
\]
At both ends \(z = -1/e\) and \(W = -1\), so \(y = 1\): these are the leftmost and rightmost points \((0.40638, 1)\) and \((2, 1)\) of the orbit.
Step 3. Mathematica’s Solve returns the principal branch, \(y = -W_0\bigl(-2e^{x-3}/x\bigr)\), which Mathews plots for \(0.40638 \le x \le 2\). Since \(W_0 \in [-1, 0)\), this gives \(y \le 1\): the lower half of the orbit. Mathews concludes that only the lower half of the curve can be solved explicitly. In fact the upper half is the other branch, \(y = -W_{-1}\bigl(-2e^{x-3}/x\bigr) \ge 1\), which Solve does not return:

Step 4. Solving (9) for \(x\) instead gives, by the symmetry of (9), \(x = -W\bigl(-2e^{y-3}/y\bigr)\) for \(0.40638 \le y \le 2\). Mathews plots the principal branch, which is the left half of the orbit (\(x \le 1\)); the branch \(W_{-1}\) gives the right half.

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
Numerical Notes

Monitor the conserved quantity. Because \(V\) in (4) is constant along exact solutions, the change of \(V\) along the computed points measures the accuracy of a run without knowing the exact solution.
The Runge-Kutta method does not conserve \(V\). Over many periods the computed orbit slowly drifts off its level curve. For the system (8) from \((2, 1)\) with \(h = 0.066\), the change in \(V\) after \(100\), \(1001\) and \(10013\) steps (about \(1\), \(10\) and \(100\) periods) is \(-1.9 \times 10^{-8}\), \(-2.1 \times 10^{-7}\) and \(-2.1 \times 10^{-6}\), growing in proportion to the number of periods.
Stopping at a fixed time does not close the curve. A computed orbit closes only if the time interval is a whole number of periods. The gaps in Example 2 and the overlaps in its aside come from the interval length, not from the Runge-Kutta error.

title: Spring-Mass Systems
text:
Description
Two masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) slide without friction along a line and are joined to each other, and to one or two walls, by springs with constants \(k_1, k_2\) (and \(k_3\)). Let \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) be the displacements of \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) from their equilibrium positions. Newton’s second law and Hooke’s law give a linear system of two second-order differential equations, which in matrix form is
\[
\begin{pmatrix} x'' \\ y'' \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{A} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac{k_1 + k_2}{m_1} & \dfrac{k_2}{m_1} \\[2mm] \dfrac{k_2}{m_2} & -\dfrac{k_2 + k_3}{m_2} \end{pmatrix},
\]
with \(k_3 = 0\) when \(m_2\) has a free end. Mathews solves these systems exactly, not numerically: there is no integration method and no step size on this page. He eliminates \(y\) to get a fourth-order equation for \(x\), whose characteristic roots are two pairs of purely imaginary numbers \(\pm i\omega_1\), \(\pm i\omega_2\). The \(\omega_j\) are the natural frequencies (eigenfrequencies), and \(-\omega_1^2\), \(-\omega_2^2\) are the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{A}\). Every motion is a superposition of two natural modes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x(t) &= a_1 \cos\omega_1 t + a_2 \sin\omega_1 t + b_1 \cos\omega_2 t + b_2 \sin\omega_2 t, \\
y(t) &= \rho_1\,(a_1 \cos\omega_1 t + a_2 \sin\omega_1 t) + \rho_2\,(b_1 \cos\omega_2 t + b_2 \sin\omega_2 t),
\end{aligned}
\qquad \rho_j = \frac{k_1 + k_2 - m_1\omega_j^2}{k_2}.
\]
In each mode both masses oscillate at the same frequency with fixed amplitude ratio \(y/x = \rho_j\): in the faster mode (\(\omega_1\), with \(\rho_1 < 0\)) the masses move in opposite directions, and in the slower mode (\(\omega_2\), with \(\rho_2 > 0\)) in the same direction. Mathews works ten examples, five with one wall and five with two walls, and plots each mode against time and as a space-time picture with time running up the page. Every frequency, mode ratio and eigenvalue below has been recomputed symbolically, and each general solution has been substituted back into its system.

title: Spring-Mass Systems
text:
Two Masses and Two Springs






NoteDefinition — One-wall spring-mass system



A spring with constant \(k_1\) joins a wall on the left to mass \(m_1\), and a spring with constant \(k_2\) joins \(m_1\) to mass \(m_2\), whose right side is free. The masses slide on a frictionless surface with no external force, and \(x(t)\), \(y(t)\) are the displacements of \(m_1\), \(m_2\) from static equilibrium (positive to the right).


The first spring is stretched by \(x\) and the second by \(y - x\), so Newton’s second law and Hooke’s law give
\[
\begin{aligned}
m_1 x'' &= -k_1 x + k_2 (y - x), \\
m_2 y'' &= -k_2 (y - x).
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
\]
Dividing by the masses puts (1) in the form \(\mathbf{X}'' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}\) with \(\mathbf{X} = (x, y)^T\) and
\[
\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac{k_1 + k_2}{m_1} & \dfrac{k_2}{m_1} \\[2mm] \dfrac{k_2}{m_2} & -\dfrac{k_2}{m_2} \end{pmatrix}.
\tag{2}
\]

Solving by elimination
Write \(D = d/dt\). In operator form (1) is
\[
(m_1 D^2 + k_1 + k_2)\,x - k_2\,y = 0, \qquad -k_2\,x + (m_2 D^2 + k_2)\,y = 0 .
\]
Applying \(m_2 D^2 + k_2\) to the first equation and adding \(k_2\) times the second eliminates \(y\) and leaves a fourth-order equation for \(x\) alone, \(\bigl[(m_1 D^2 + k_1 + k_2)(m_2 D^2 + k_2) - k_2^2\bigr]x = 0\). Its characteristic equation is
\[
p(r) = (m_1 r^2 + k_1 + k_2)(m_2 r^2 + k_2) - k_2^2 = 0,
\tag{3}
\]
a quadratic in \(r^2\). (Mathews’ Mathematica printout gives (3) divided by a constant; where his printout survives, the reduced forms in the examples below match it.) With roots \(r = \pm i\omega_1\), \(\pm i\omega_2\), the general solution for \(x\) is the first line of (4). Mathews then recovers \(y\) from the first equation of (1), \(y = \bigl(m_1 x'' + (k_1 + k_2)\,x\bigr)/k_2\), which multiplies the \(\omega_j\) terms by \(\rho_j\):






ImportantGeneral solution



\[
\begin{aligned}
x(t) &= a_1 \cos\omega_1 t + a_2 \sin\omega_1 t + b_1 \cos\omega_2 t + b_2 \sin\omega_2 t, \\
y(t) &= \rho_1\,(a_1 \cos\omega_1 t + a_2 \sin\omega_1 t) + \rho_2\,(b_1 \cos\omega_2 t + b_2 \sin\omega_2 t),
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]
\[
\rho_j = \frac{k_1 + k_2 - m_1 \omega_j^2}{k_2}, \qquad j = 1, 2,
\tag{5}
\]
with \(\omega_1 > \omega_2 > 0\) and four arbitrary constants \(a_1, a_2, b_1, b_2\).


Remark (eigenfrequencies). Substituting \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{v}\cos\omega t\) into \(\mathbf{X}'' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}\) gives \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{v} = -\omega^2\mathbf{v}\), so the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{A}\) are \(\lambda_j = -\omega_j^2\), and the eigenfrequencies are \(\omega_j = \sqrt{-\lambda_j}\); Mathews computes them as the imaginary parts of \(\sqrt{\lambda_j}\). The eigenvector for \(\lambda_j\) is \((1, \rho_j)^T\), and \(\det(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I}) = 0\) is (3) with \(r^2 = \lambda\), divided by \(m_1 m_2\).


Natural modes






NoteDefinition — Natural mode



A natural mode is a solution in which both masses oscillate at a single frequency. Taking \(b_1 = b_2 = 0\) in (4) gives the first mode, \(x = a_1\cos\omega_1 t + a_2 \sin\omega_1 t\), \(y = \rho_1 x\); taking \(a_1 = a_2 = 0\) gives the second, \(y = \rho_2 x\) at frequency \(\omega_2\).


The following holds for every system of this page, not only for the examples:






TipTheorem — Two distinct frequencies, one in-phase and one anti-phase mode (general)



Let \(m_1, m_2, k_1, k_2 > 0\) and \(k_3 \ge 0\) (with \(k_3 = 0\) for the one-wall system). Then

the two roots \(s = r^2\) of the characteristic equation are real, distinct and negative, so the roots of (3) are \(\pm i\omega_1\), \(\pm i\omega_2\) with \(\omega_1 > \omega_2 > 0\);
\(\rho_1 \rho_2 = -m_1/m_2\), so \(\rho_1 < 0 < \rho_2\): in the faster mode the masses move in opposite directions, in the slower mode in the same direction;
the energy \(E = \tfrac12 m_1 x'^2 + \tfrac12 m_2 y'^2 + \tfrac12 k_1 x^2 + \tfrac12 k_2 (y - x)^2 + \tfrac12 k_3 y^2\) is constant along every solution.



Why. As a quadratic in \(s = r^2\), the characteristic equation \(m_1 m_2 s^2 + \bigl(m_1(k_2 + k_3) + m_2(k_1 + k_2)\bigr)s + (k_1 k_2 + k_1 k_3 + k_2 k_3) = 0\) has discriminant \(\bigl(m_1(k_2 + k_3) - m_2(k_1 + k_2)\bigr)^2 + 4 m_1 m_2 k_2^2 > 0\), and all its coefficients are positive, so both roots are real, distinct and negative. The product \(\rho_1\rho_2 = -m_1/m_2\) is the orthogonality of the two eigenvectors with respect to the mass matrix, \(m_1 + m_2\rho_1\rho_2 = 0\), and (5) shows that \(\rho_j\) decreases as \(\omega_j\) increases, so the faster mode has the negative ratio. Differentiating \(E\) and using the equations of motion gives \(E' = 0\). All three statements were checked symbolically for general parameters.
A natural mode with \(a_1 = 1\), \(a_2 = 0\) (or \(b_1 = 1\), \(b_2 = 0\)) is the solution with initial conditions \(x(0) = 1\), \(y(0) = \rho_j\), \(x'(0) = y'(0) = 0\). In general, the initial values \(x(0) = x_0\), \(y(0) = y_0\), \(x'(0) = v_0\), \(y'(0) = u_0\) fix the constants:
\[
a_1 = \frac{\rho_2 x_0 - y_0}{\rho_2 - \rho_1}, \quad
b_1 = \frac{y_0 - \rho_1 x_0}{\rho_2 - \rho_1}, \quad
a_2 = \frac{\rho_2 v_0 - u_0}{\omega_1(\rho_2 - \rho_1)}, \quad
b_2 = \frac{u_0 - \rho_1 v_0}{\omega_2(\rho_2 - \rho_1)}.
\tag{6}
\]


How Mathews presents each example
Every example follows the same steps: the characteristic equation and its roots, the natural frequencies, the general solution (4), the eigenvalues of \(\mathbf{A}\), the two natural modes, and a check that each mode satisfies the system. He then draws each mode with \(a_1 = 1\), \(a_2 = 0\) (first mode) or \(b_1 = 1\), \(b_2 = 0\) (second mode) in two ways:

Against time: \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) on one set of axes.
Space-time picture: time on the vertical axis, \(m_1\) drawn at horizontal position \(2 + x(t)\) and \(m_2\) at \(6 + y(t)\), with vertical lines at the equilibrium positions \(2\) and \(6\). In every example whose plots survive, the first picture shows the masses moving in opposite directions at frequency \(\omega_1\), the second in the same direction at \(\omega_2\).

The time windows and vertical ranges of these plots are listed with each example. For Examples 1 and 4 the archive’s images of Mathews’ notebook are lost; their results below are computed from the equations in the module’s problem statements, and their plot windows are unknown.


Verification method
To check a mode, substitute \(x = \cos\omega_j t\), \(y = \rho_j \cos\omega_j t\) into (1) and divide by \(\cos\omega_j t\). The two equations become
\[
\underbrace{-m_1\omega_j^2}_{\text{row 1, left}} = \underbrace{-(k_1 + k_2) + k_2\rho_j}_{\text{row 1, right}}, \qquad
\underbrace{-m_2\omega_j^2\rho_j}_{\text{row 2, left}} = \underbrace{k_2 - (k_2 + k_3)\rho_j}_{\text{row 2, right}}.
\]
The \(\sin\omega_j t\) terms give the same two equations, so a mode passes when both rows balance. Each example’s verification table lists these four numbers for both modes. In addition, the full general solution (4) of every example was substituted into its system symbolically (both residuals simplify to \(0\)), and each mode was integrated numerically from \(x(0) = 1\), \(y(0) = \rho_j\), \(x'(0) = y'(0) = 0\) over \(0 \le t \le 10\pi\) with an adaptive Runge-Kutta solver (relative tolerance \(10^{-11}\)); the numerical and closed-form solutions differ by at most \(2 \times 10^{-10}\).


Example 1 — Equal masses, unequal spring constants
Find the general solution of (1) with
\[
m_1 = 6, \quad m_2 = 6, \quad k_1 = 3, \quad k_2 = 2:
\qquad
\begin{aligned}
6x'' &= -3x + 2(y - x), \\
6y'' &= -2(y - x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Step 1 (characteristic equation): from (3), \((6r^2 + 5)(6r^2 + 2) - 4 = 36r^4 + 42r^2 + 6\), and dividing by \(6\),
\[
6r^4 + 7r^2 + 1 = (6r^2 + 1)(r^2 + 1) = 0, \qquad r = \pm i, \ \pm \frac{i}{\sqrt 6}.
\]
Step 2 (frequencies and eigenvalues): \(\omega_1 = 1\) and \(\omega_2 = 1/\sqrt6 \approx 0.408248\). The matrix (2) is
\[
\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} -\tfrac56 & \tfrac13 \\[1mm] \tfrac13 & -\tfrac13 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \lambda_1 = -1, \quad \lambda_2 = -\tfrac16,
\]
and \(\sqrt{-\lambda_j}\) gives the same frequencies.
Step 3 (mode ratios): by (5), \(\rho_1 = (5 - 6)/2 = -\tfrac12\) and \(\rho_2 = (5 - 1)/2 = 2\).
\[
\boxed{\
\begin{aligned}
x(t) &= a_1 \cos t + a_2 \sin t + b_1 \cos\tfrac{t}{\sqrt6} + b_2 \sin\tfrac{t}{\sqrt6}, \\
y(t) &= -\tfrac12\,(a_1 \cos t + a_2 \sin t) + 2\,\bigl(b_1 \cos\tfrac{t}{\sqrt6} + b_2 \sin\tfrac{t}{\sqrt6}\bigr)
\end{aligned}\ }
\]
In the first mode (\(\omega_1 = 1\)) the masses move in opposite directions and \(m_2\) moves half as far as \(m_1\); in the second mode (\(\omega_2 = 1/\sqrt6\)) they move in the same direction and \(m_2\) moves twice as far.

title: Spring-Mass Systems
text:
Two Masses and Three Springs






NoteDefinition — Two-wall spring-mass system



As before, but a third spring with constant \(k_3\) joins \(m_2\) to a wall on the right: wall, spring \(k_1\), mass \(m_1\), spring \(k_2\), mass \(m_2\), spring \(k_3\), wall.


The third spring is compressed by \(y\), which adds \(-k_3 y\) to the force on \(m_2\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
m_1 x'' &= -k_1 x + k_2 (y - x), \\
m_2 y'' &= -k_2 (y - x) - k_3 y,
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]
\[
\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} -\dfrac{k_1 + k_2}{m_1} & \dfrac{k_2}{m_1} \\[2mm] \dfrac{k_2}{m_2} & -\dfrac{k_2 + k_3}{m_2} \end{pmatrix}.
\tag{8}
\]
Elimination now gives the characteristic equation
\[
(m_1 r^2 + k_1 + k_2)(m_2 r^2 + k_2 + k_3) - k_2^2 = 0,
\tag{9}
\]
and the general solution is again (4) with the ratios (5), because \(y\) is still recovered from the first equation, which has not changed. The eigenfrequencies are again \(\sqrt{-\lambda_j}\) for the eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) of (8), and the theorem above applies.
In the space-time pictures of Examples 6, 7 and 9, Mathews draws a third vertical line at \(8\), the right edge of the picture; in Example 10 the equilibrium positions are \(2\) and \(7\) and the extra line is at \(11\).






WarningThe captions of the space-time pictures



In Examples 6–10 the sentences that introduce the two space-time pictures say that the first shows the masses moving in the same direction and the second in opposite directions; in Examples 6, 7, 9 and 10 they also give the frequencies as \(1\) and \(3\), the values of Example 6. In Examples 6, 7, 9 and 10, whose plots survive, the pictures themselves show the first mode (opposite directions, \(\omega_1\)) and then the second (same direction, \(\omega_2\)), as described below.


When \(m_1 = m_2\) and \(k_1 = k_3\) (Examples 6, 7 and 8) the system is symmetric: \(\rho_1 = -1\) and \(\rho_2 = 1\). In the slow mode the masses move together and the middle spring is never stretched (\(y - x = 0\)), so \(\omega_2^2 = k_1/m_1\); in the fast mode they are mirror images and \(\omega_1^2 = (k_1 + 2k_2)/m_1\).

title: Spring-Mass Systems
text:
Long-Term Behaviour: Energy and Periodicity
There is no friction, so no motion of these systems decays: by part 3 of the theorem the energy \(E\) is constant, and the amplitudes \(a_j\), \(b_j\) in (4) never change. Substituting each general solution into \(E\) confirms \(E' = 0\) symbolically in all ten examples.
Whether a motion repeats depends on the ratio of the frequencies. A single mode is always periodic, with period \(2\pi/\omega_j\). The following is a general fact about sums of two sinusoids, not a claim about one example: when both modes are present, the motion is periodic if and only if \(\omega_1/\omega_2\) is rational; otherwise it is quasi-periodic: it never repeats exactly, although it comes back arbitrarily close to any state it has passed through.

title: van der Pol System
text:
Description
The van der Pol equation \(x'' - \mu (1 - x^2)\, x' + x = 0\), with a constant \(\mu \ge 0\), is an oscillator whose damping depends on the displacement \(x\). For \(\mu > 0\), while \(|x| < 1\) the damping coefficient \(-\mu(1 - x^2)\) is negative and pumps energy in, and while \(|x| > 1\) it is positive and drains energy out. For \(\mu = 0\) the equation is the harmonic oscillator \(x'' + x = 0\), whose solutions other than \(x = 0\) run round circles in the phase plane. For every \(\mu > 0\) there is exactly one periodic solution, a closed curve called the limit cycle, and every other solution except the equilibrium at the origin winds onto it, from outside or from inside.
For \(\mu > 0\) Mathews computes the solutions numerically. With \(y = x'\) the equation becomes the first-order system \(x' = y\), \(y' = -x + \mu(1 - x^2)\, y\), and Mathews solves that system with the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method in vector form. With the vector \(\mathbf{Z} = (x, y)\), the right-hand side \(\mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z}) = \bigl(y,\ -x + \mu(1 - x^2)\, y\bigr)\) and a fixed step \(h = (b - a)/n\), each step is
\[
\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} = \mathbf{Z}_j + \frac{1}{6}\bigl(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4\bigr),
\]
where the four vectors \(\mathbf{k}_i\) are \(h\) times \(\mathbf{F}\) evaluated at the start, twice at the middle and once at the end of the step (equation (5) below). Mathews’ module has six examples, \(\mu = 0, \tfrac{1}{16}, \tfrac14, \tfrac12, 1, 4\), and plots the solution of Example 1 as a path in the \(xy\)-plane. Example 1 (\(\mu = 0\)) survives in full: it starts at \((x, y) = (0, 3)\) and takes \(n = 400\) steps over one turn, \(0 \le t \le 6.283185\). For Examples 2 to 6 the archive keeps only the value of \(\mu\), so this page keeps Example 1’s starting point and integrates over \(0 \le t \le 60\) with \(n = 6000\) steps (\(h = 0.01\)). Every number below has been recomputed.

title: van der Pol System
text:
The van der Pol Equation






NoteDefinition — van der Pol equation



The van der Pol equation is the second-order differential equation
\[
x'' - \mu \left(1 - x^2\right) x' + x = 0,
\tag{1}
\]
where \(\mu\) is a constant. Mathews takes \(\mu > 0\) in the definition, and his first example uses \(\mu = 0\).


When \(\mu = 0\) the equation reduces to \(x'' + x = 0\), which has the familiar solution
\[
x(t) = c_1 \cos t + c_2 \sin t .
\]
For \(\mu > 0\) the middle term \(-\mu(1 - x^2)\, x'\) acts like friction or resistance where its coefficient \(-\mu(1 - x^2)\) is positive, that is where \(|x| > 1\). Where \(|x| < 1\) the coefficient is negative, the case of “negative resistance”, which feeds energy into the motion. Mathews notes that vacuum-tube circuits of early radios showed such negative resistance; the equation is named after Balthasar van der Pol (1889–1959), who studied it, and its solutions show orbital stability: nearby solutions are drawn onto the same closed path.

The equivalent first-order system
With \(y = x'\), equation (1) becomes the system
\[
x' = y, \qquad y' = -x + \mu\left(1 - x^2\right) y .
\tag{2}
\]


Energy
The energy of the harmonic oscillator, \(E = \tfrac12 (x^2 + y^2)\), is the squared distance from the origin, halved. Along a solution of (2),
\[
\frac{dE}{dt} = x x' + y y' = x y + y\bigl(-x + \mu(1 - x^2)\, y\bigr) = \mu \left(1 - x^2\right) y^2 .
\tag{3}
\]
For \(\mu = 0\) the energy is constant, so every solution runs round a circle centred at the origin. For \(\mu > 0\) the energy grows while \(|x| < 1\) and decays while \(|x| > 1\) (wherever \(y \ne 0\)), so small oscillations are pushed outwards and large ones pulled inwards.


The equilibrium at the origin
The only equilibrium of (2) is \((0, 0)\), since \(x' = 0\) forces \(y = 0\) and then \(y' = 0\) forces \(x = 0\). The Jacobian matrix of (2) at the origin and its eigenvalues are
\[
\mathbf{J}(0, 0) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & \mu \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \lambda^2 - \mu \lambda + 1 = 0, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\mu \pm \sqrt{\mu^2 - 4}}{2} .
\]
For \(\mu = 0\) the eigenvalues are \(\pm i\) and the origin is a centre, surrounded by the circles. For \(0 < \mu < 2\) they are complex with positive real part \(\mu/2\), so solutions spiral away from the origin; for \(\mu = 2\) there is the double eigenvalue \(1\), and for \(\mu > 2\) both eigenvalues are real and positive, so solutions leave the origin without spiralling. In every case with \(\mu > 0\) the origin repels.

The limit cycle






NoteDefinition — Limit cycle



A limit cycle of a system \(x' = f_1(x, y)\), \(y' = f_2(x, y)\) is a closed path traced by a periodic solution that has no other closed paths arbitrarily close to it. It is stable when the solutions that start near it approach it as \(t \to \infty\).


The circles of the case \(\mu = 0\) are closed paths, but each has others arbitrarily close to it, so none of them is a limit cycle.






TipTheorem — Liénard’s theorem, applied to the van der Pol equation (general)



Write (1) as \(x'' + f(x)\, x' + g(x) = 0\) with \(f(x) = \mu(x^2 - 1)\) and \(g(x) = x\), and let \(F(x) = \int_0^x f(s)\, ds = \mu\bigl(\tfrac13 x^3 - x\bigr)\). Liénard’s theorem gives a unique stable limit cycle when \(F\) and \(g\) have continuous derivatives, \(g\) is odd with \(x g(x) > 0\) for \(x \ne 0\), \(F\) is odd with \(F'(0) < 0\), \(F\) has a single positive zero \(x = a\), and \(F\) increases to \(\infty\) for \(x \ge a\). For \(\mu > 0\) all of these hold, with \(F'(0) = -\mu\), \(a = \sqrt3\) and \(F'(x) = \mu(x^2 - 1) > 0\) for \(x \ge \sqrt3\). So for every \(\mu > 0\) the van der Pol equation has exactly one periodic solution up to a shift in time, and every solution other than the equilibrium \(x = 0\) approaches it as \(t \to \infty\).


The theorem does not say where the cycle is. Its size for small \(\mu\) follows from the energy equation (3): when \(\mu\) is small a solution is nearly a circle \(x = A \sin t\), \(y = A \cos t\) over one turn, and the net energy gained over that turn is
\[
\int_0^{2\pi} \mu \left(1 - A^2 \sin^2 t\right) A^2 \cos^2 t \, dt = \frac{\pi \mu A^2}{4}\left(4 - A^2\right) .
\tag{4}
\]
This is positive for \(A < 2\) and negative for \(A > 2\), so for small \(\mu\) the limit cycle is close to the circle of radius \(2\). This is an approximation for small \(\mu\); the computed cycles below have their largest \(x\) between \(2.00004\) (for \(\mu = \tfrac{1}{16}\)) and \(2.02296\) (for \(\mu = 4\)), and their period grows from close to \(2\pi\) to \(10.2035\).

title: van der Pol System
section: The Runge-Kutta Method for a System
text:
The Runge-Kutta Method for a System






NoteInitial value problem in the plane



Compute approximations to the solution of
\[
x' = f_1(t, x, y), \quad x(a) = \alpha, \qquad y' = f_2(t, x, y), \quad y(a) = \beta, \qquad a \le t \le b,
\]
at a discrete set of points \(t_0 = a < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = b\). In vector form, with \(\mathbf{Z} = (x, y)\) and \(\mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z}) = \bigl(f_1(t, x, y),\ f_2(t, x, y)\bigr)\), the problem is \(\mathbf{Z}' = \mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z})\), \(\mathbf{Z}(a) = (\alpha, \beta)\).


The Runge-Kutta method in two dimensions is the “vector form” of the one-dimensional method: the function \(f\) is replaced by the vector function \(\mathbf{F}\), and every stage is computed for both components at once.






ImportantRunge-Kutta method of order 4 for a system



With \(h = (b - a)/n\), \(t_j = a + j h\) and \(\mathbf{Z}_0 = (\alpha, \beta)\), for \(j = 0, 1, \ldots, n - 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{k}_1 &= h\, \mathbf{F}(t_j, \mathbf{Z}_j), \\
\mathbf{k}_2 &= h\, \mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2},\ \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac12 \mathbf{k}_1\bigr), \\
\mathbf{k}_3 &= h\, \mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2},\ \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac12 \mathbf{k}_2\bigr), \\
\mathbf{k}_4 &= h\, \mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + h,\ \mathbf{Z}_j + \mathbf{k}_3\bigr), \\
\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} &= \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac16 \bigl(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]


Mathews’ subroutine builds the list of times \(t_j\) and the list of points \(\mathbf{Z}_j\) and returns the points, which are then joined by line segments to draw the path in the \(xy\)-plane. For a smooth \(\mathbf{F}\) the method has global error of order \(h^4\) (a general result): doubling \(n\) divides the error by about \(16\), as both sets of examples below confirm. For the van der Pol system \(\mathbf{F}\) does not depend on \(t\), so the times \(t_j\) only label the points.

title: van der Pol System
text:
Example 1 — \(\mu = 0\): the harmonic oscillator
Solve the van der Pol equation with \(\mu = 0\),
\[
x'' + x = 0, \qquad x(0) = 0, \quad x'(0) = 3,
\]
over \(0 \le t \le 6.283185\) with \(n = 400\) steps. These are the values in Mathews’ notebook.
Step 1: Write the equation as the system (2) with \(\mu = 0\):
\[
x' = y, \qquad y' = -x, \qquad \mathbf{F}(t, (x, y)) = (y, -x), \qquad \mathbf{Z}_0 = (0, 3).
\]
Step 2: The step size is
\[
h = \frac{6.283185 - 0}{400} = 0.0157079625 .
\]
Step 3: The first step, from \(t_0 = 0\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{k}_1 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(0, (0, 3)) = h\,(3, 0) = (0.0471238875,\ 0), \\
\mathbf{k}_2 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(\tfrac{h}{2}, (0.02356194375,\ 3)\bigr) = (0.0471238875,\ -0.000370110129), \\
\mathbf{k}_3 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(\tfrac{h}{2}, (0.02356194375,\ 2.999814945)\bigr) = (0.0471209807,\ -0.000370110129), \\
\mathbf{k}_4 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(h, (0.0471209807,\ 2.999629890)\bigr) = (0.0471180738,\ -0.000740174597), \\
\mathbf{Z}_1 &= \mathbf{Z}_0 + \tfrac16 (\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4) = (0.0471219496,\ 2.999629897).
\end{aligned}
\]
The exact value \(\bigl(3\sin h, 3\cos h\bigr) = (0.0471219496, 2.999629897)\) agrees to all the digits shown; the error in \(x\) is \(-2.4 \times 10^{-11}\).
Step 4: Repeating the step \(400\) times gives the end point
\[
\mathbf{Z}_{400} = \bigl(-9.311010 \times 10^{-7},\ 2.99999999987\bigr) \approx \bigl(-9.31101 \times 10^{-7},\ 3.\bigr),
\]
which is the end point Mathews prints, \(\{-9.31101 \times 10^{-7}, 3.\}\).
The exact solution is \(x(t) = 3 \sin t\), \(y(t) = 3 \cos t\), the circle of radius \(3\) traced clockwise from its top point \((0, 3)\). Mathews plots the \(400\) segments in the \(xy\)-plane with both axes marked from \(-3\) to \(3\), and they close up into that circle.

text:
Examples 2 to 6 — \(\mu = \tfrac{1}{16}, \tfrac14, \tfrac12, 1, 4\)
Mathews solves the van der Pol equation with \(\mu = \tfrac{1}{16}\) (Example 2), \(\tfrac14\) (Example 3), \(\tfrac12\) (Example 4), \(1\) (Example 5) and \(4\) (Example 6):
\[
x'' - \tfrac{1}{16}\left(1 - x^2\right) x' + x = 0, \quad \ldots, \quad x'' - 4\left(1 - x^2\right) x' + x = 0 .
\]
Each is the system (2) with \(\mathbf{F}(t, (x, y)) = \bigl(y,\ -x + \mu(1 - x^2)\, y\bigr)\), solved by (5). For these examples the archive keeps only the value of \(\mu\); the notebook cells with the interval, the number of steps and the starting point, and the plots, are lost. This page therefore keeps Example 1’s starting point \((x, y) = (0, 3)\), that is \(x(0) = 0\), \(x'(0) = 3\), and integrates over \(0 \le t \le 60\) with \(n = 6000\) steps, \(h = 0.01\).
Each solution is followed through the points where \(x\) has a local maximum, which are the points where the path crosses the positive \(x\)-axis (\(y = 0\), \(x > 0\)). Comparing those maxima with the largest \(x\) on the cycle (the table above) measures how far the solution still is from the limit cycle after each turn. The maxima below are located exactly (to the digits shown) with the order-8 reference solver; the Runge-Kutta points agree with it to within the errors listed in the verification table at the end of this section.

Example 2 — \(\mu = \tfrac{1}{16}\)
The cycle passes through the positive \(y\)-axis at \(y = 2.0007\), so \((0, 3)\) is outside it, and the solution spirals inwards. The ten maxima of \(x\) in \(0 \le t \le 60\) are
\[
2.849009,\ 2.464188,\ 2.279308,\ 2.175986,\ 2.113772,\ 2.074697,\ 2.049523,\ 2.033042,\ 2.022140,\ 2.014879,
\]
decreasing towards the cycle’s \(2.000041\). The gap shrinks by the factors \(0.547, 0.602, 0.630, \ldots, 0.671\) per turn, approaching \(\rho = 0.675\), so at the tenth maximum (\(t = 58.12\)) the solution is still \(0.0148\) outside the cycle. This is the slowest approach of the five: it takes many turns of a nearly circular path.


Example 3 — \(\mu = \tfrac14\)
The cycle crosses the positive \(y\)-axis at \(y = 2.0111\), so the solution again starts outside it. The maxima of \(x\) are
\[
2.593435,\ 2.083519,\ 2.016735,\ 2.003912,\ 2.001313,\ 2.000781,\ 2.000672,\ 2.000650,\ 2.000645,\ 2.000644,
\]
decreasing to the cycle’s \(2.000644\); from the sixth maximum on each gap is \(\rho = 0.2053\) times the one before (to four digits), down to \(2.4 \times 10^{-7}\) at the tenth maximum.


Example 4 — \(\mu = \tfrac12\)
The cycle crosses the positive \(y\)-axis at \(y = 2.0441\). The maxima of \(x\) are
\[
2.418210,\ 2.012688,\ 2.002883,\ 2.002503,\ 2.002489,\ 2.002488, \ldots
\]
and from the sixth on they equal the cycle’s \(2.002488\) to six decimals. From the fourth maximum on each gap is \(\rho = 0.0392\) times the one before, until the gap reaches rounding level (\(3.8 \times 10^{-14}\) at the tenth maximum).


Example 5 — \(\mu = 1\)
The cycle crosses the positive \(y\)-axis at \(y = 2.1727\). The maxima of \(x\) are
\[
2.240070,\ 2.008728,\ 2.008620, \ldots
\]
and from the third on (at \(t = 14.70\)) they equal the cycle’s \(2.008620\) to six decimals. The gaps are \(0.23\), \(1.1 \times 10^{-4}\), \(9.3 \times 10^{-8}\), \(8.0 \times 10^{-11}\) and \(6.8 \times 10^{-14}\), and from the third on each is about \(\rho \approx 8.6 \times 10^{-4}\) times the one before; from the sixth maximum on the solution is on the cycle to rounding level. The cycle is visibly no longer a circle: on it \(|y|\) reaches \(2.6784\) while \(|x|\) stays below \(2.0087\).


Example 6 — \(\mu = 4\)
Now the cycle crosses the positive \(y\)-axis at \(y = 3.7623\), so the starting point \((0, 3)\) is inside the cycle. The first maximum of \(x\) is \(1.956754\), below the cycle’s \(2.022963\), and the second, at \(t = 10.47\), already equals \(2.022963\) to rounding level (\(\rho = 1.3 \times 10^{-25}\)). The cycle is a relaxation oscillation, made of slow and fast parts. From its largest value \(2.023\), \(x\) takes \(3.860\) time units, \(76\%\) of the half period \(5.102\), to drift down to \(x = 1\); it then falls from \(1\) to \(-1\) in only \(0.829\) time units, and during that fall, at \(x = -0.9805\), \(|y|\) peaks at \(6.3442\). The other half of the cycle is the mirror image, since (2) is unchanged when \((x, y)\) is replaced by \((-x, -y)\). Over the whole cycle \(|y|\) exceeds \(2\) only \(10.8\%\) of the time.


Starting inside the cycle
To see the cycle attract from inside as well, the same computation was repeated from \((x, y) = (0, 0.5)\), which is inside the cycle for all five values of \(\mu\). The maxima of \(x\) now increase towards the same values until they reach them: for \(\mu = \tfrac14\) they are \(0.606543, 1.140036, 1.664822, 1.913297, 1.981599, \ldots\), reaching \(2.000637\) at the tenth maximum. For \(\mu = \tfrac{1}{16}\) the approach is again the slowest, with the tenth maximum still at \(1.692056\); for \(\mu = \tfrac12\) the tenth maximum is within \(2.0 \times 10^{-12}\) of the cycle, and for \(\mu = 1\) and \(4\) the solution reaches the cycle to rounding level within \(0 \le t \le 60\), as from outside.
