title: Projectile Motion
text:
Description
A projectile moves under gravity and, in a real medium, under air resistance that opposes its velocity. Without air resistance the equations of motion can be integrated by hand and the path is a parabola. With air resistance proportional to the velocity there is still a closed-form solution, but with resistance proportional to the square or the \(\tfrac32\) power of the speed the formulas become awkward or unavailable, and a numerical solution is the practical route. Each model is a second-order differential equation, or a pair of them, for the position.
The method is the classical fourth-order Runge–Kutta method (RK4), applied to the first-order system obtained by introducing the velocity as a second unknown. For one second-order equation \(y'' = f(t, y, y')\) with \(y(a) = \alpha\), \(y'(a) = \beta\), write \(\mathbf{Z} = (y, v)\) with \(v = y'\) and \(\mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z}) = \bigl(v,\ f(t, y, v)\bigr)\), and step with \(h = (b - a)/n\):
\[
\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} = \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac16\left(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4\right),
\qquad
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{k}_1 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j, \mathbf{Z}_j), &
\mathbf{k}_2 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + \tfrac h2, \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac12\mathbf{k}_1\bigr),\\
\mathbf{k}_3 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + \tfrac h2, \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac12\mathbf{k}_2\bigr), &
\mathbf{k}_4 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j + h, \mathbf{Z}_j + \mathbf{k}_3).
\end{aligned}
\]
Mathews’ module has two parts. In the first (Examples 1–4) an arrow is shot straight up at \(300\) ft/s and the four drag laws are compared through the ascent time, the maximum height, the descent time and the impact velocity. In the second (Examples 5–8) the same method, applied to two coupled second-order equations for \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\), traces the flight of a long-hit baseball. Throughout, \(g = 32\) ft/s² and lengths are in feet.

title: Projectile Motion
text:
Motion without air resistance
If a projectile leaves the origin with speed \(v_0\) at angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal and only gravity acts, its position is
\[
x(t) = v_0 \cos(\theta)\, t, \tag{1}
\]
\[
y(t) = v_0 \sin(\theta)\, t - \tfrac12 g t^2. \tag{2}
\]
Solving (1) for \(t = \dfrac{\sec(\theta)}{v_0}\, x\) and substituting in (2) gives the parabola
\[
y = \tan(\theta)\, x - \frac{g \sec^2(\theta)}{2 v_0^2}\, x^2 .
\]
The highest point is reached when \(y'(t) = v_0 \sin(\theta) - g t = 0\), at time \(t_1\), and the projectile is back at height \(0\) at time \(t_2\):
\[
t_1 = \frac{v_0 \sin(\theta)}{g}, \qquad
y_{\max} = y(t_1) = \frac{v_0^2 \sin^2(\theta)}{2g}, \qquad
t_2 = \frac{2 v_0 \sin(\theta)}{g} = 2 t_1 .
\]
So without air resistance the descent takes exactly as long as the ascent. The range is
\[
x_{\text{range}} = x(t_2) = \frac{v_0^2}{g}\,\sin(2\theta).
\]






TipTheorem — Angle of maximum range



For a fixed launch speed \(v_0\), no air resistance, and launch and landing at the same height, the range \(x_{\text{range}} = \frac{v_0^2}{g}\sin(2\theta)\) is largest when \(\theta = \pi/4\). The conditions matter: with drag, or with a launch point above the landing level, the best angle differs from \(45^\circ\). For a ball hit at \(127\) ft/s from \(3\) ft above the ground (Example 5 below) the longest carry comes at \(\theta = 44.83^\circ\), and at \(207\) ft/s with the linear drag of Example 6 at \(\theta = 31.8^\circ\).


For example, with \(v_0 = 300\) ft/s the range is \(2812.5\) ft at \(\theta = 45^\circ\) and \(2435.70\) ft at both \(30^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\).

title: Projectile Motion
text:
Vertical motion with air resistance
Now fire the projectile straight up, so \(x(t) = 0\), and let \(y(t)\) be its height and \(v = y'\) its velocity. The drag force \(F_R\) always opposes the motion. A very slow object in a viscous fluid feels a drag proportional to its speed; faster objects (and Millikan’s oil drops, as Mathews notes) are better described by a drag proportional to the square of the speed. The Reynolds number decides which regime applies. Mathews compares four laws.






NoteDefinition — Vertical drag models (Projectile Motion I)



With mass \(m\) and drag constant \(k > 0\):

No air resistance: \(\; m \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -mg\), \(\quad y'' = -g\).
Drag proportional to the velocity: \(\; m \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -kv - mg\), \(\quad y'' = -\dfrac{k}{m}\, y' - g\).
Drag proportional to the square of the velocity: \(\; m \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -kv^2 - mg\) on the ascent (\(v > 0\)) and \(m \dfrac{dv}{dt} = kv^2 - mg\) on the descent (\(v < 0\)); both are the single equation \(\; y'' = -\dfrac{k}{m}\, y' \lvert y' \rvert - g\).
Drag proportional to the \(\tfrac32\) power of the speed: \(\; y'' = -\dfrac{k}{m}\, y' \sqrt{\lvert y' \rvert} - g\).



The factor \(y'\lvert y'\rvert\) in (iii) is what makes the drag point the right way: it is \(+v^2\) going up and \(-v^2\) coming down. Writing \(-k v^2\) for both halves of the flight is a mistake that Example 3 examines.
When the drag grows with the speed, a falling object approaches a terminal velocity at which drag balances gravity: \(-mg/k\) for law (ii), \(-\sqrt{mg/k}\) for law (iii), and \(-(mg/k)^{2/3}\) for law (iv). (These are the limits of the descent equations as \(t \to \infty\); an arrow that hits the ground first never reaches them.)

Runge–Kutta solution
Mathews solves each case with the RK4 scheme of the Description, starting from \(y(0) = 0\), \(y'(0) = 300\). In Examples 2–4 he uses \([a, b] = [0, 20]\) with \(n = 100\) steps, so \(h = 0.2\) s, and plots the height \(y(t)\) in the window \(0 \le t \le 20\), \(0 \le y \le 1500\); the images of Example 1’s inputs and plots are lost. In Examples 1–3 he finds the top of the flight and the moment of impact by solving \(v(t) = 0\) and \(y(t) = 0\) with a root finder (FindRoot in Mathematica) applied to the closed-form solution. The values below were located in the same way: from the closed forms with a root finder, and checked against an independent high-accuracy integration (scipy’s DOP853 with relative tolerance \(10^{-13}\) and event detection) and, for Example 4, against quadrature formulas.


Example 1 — No air resistance
An arrow is shot upward from the origin at \(300\) ft/s with no air resistance: \(m\,\dfrac{dv}{dt} = -mg\), that is
\[
y'' = -32, \qquad y(0) = 0, \quad y'(0) = 300 .
\]
Find the velocity and position, the ascent time, the descent time, the maximum height and the impact velocity.
Step 1: Integrate twice:
\[
v(t) = 300 - 32t, \qquad y(t) = 300t - 16t^2 .
\]
Step 2: The top of the flight is where \(v(t) = 0\):
\[
t_{\max} = \frac{300}{32} = 9.375 \text{ s}, \qquad y_{\max} = y(9.375) = 1406.25 \text{ ft}.
\]
Step 3: Impact is where \(y(t) = 0\) with \(t > 0\):
\[
t_{\text{impact}} = \frac{300}{16} = 18.75 \text{ s}, \qquad v(18.75) = -300 \text{ ft/s}.
\]
The descent time is \(18.75 - 9.375 = 9.375\) s, equal to the ascent time, and the arrow lands at the speed it was fired, as the formulas of the previous section require. Mathews notes that the maximum comes near \(t = 9\) and the impact near \(t = 19\).
Verification: \(v' = -32\), \(y(0) = 0\), \(v(0) = 300\). The exact solution is a polynomial of degree two, and RK4 with \(h = 0.2\) (the step of Examples 2–4) reproduces it at every grid point on \([0, 20]\) to within \(1.3 \times 10^{-12}\) ft (rounding error). (The legacy pages for this example have lost their output images, so Mathews’ printed values cannot be compared.)


Example 2 — Drag proportional to the velocity
The same arrow, with drag \(F_R = 0.04\,m v\), so \(k/m = 0.04 = \tfrac1{25}\):
\[
y'' = -32 - \frac{y'}{25}, \qquad y(0) = 0, \quad y'(0) = 300 .
\]
Step 1: The velocity equation \(v' = -32 - v/25\) is linear. With \(v(0) = 300\),
\[
v(t) = -800 + 1100\, e^{-t/25}.
\]
Step 2: Integrate from \(0\) with \(y(0) = 0\):
\[
y(t) = 27500 - 27500\, e^{-t/25} - 800\, t .
\]
Step 3: Top of the flight: \(v(t) = 0\) gives \(e^{-t/25} = \tfrac{8}{11}\), so
\[
t_{\max} = 25 \ln\tfrac{11}{8} = 7.96134 \text{ s}, \qquad y_{\max} = 1130.93 \text{ ft}.
\]
Step 4: Impact: the root of \(y(t) = 0\) near \(t = 17\) is
\[
t_{\text{impact}} = 16.8675 \text{ s}, \qquad v(t_{\text{impact}}) = -239.760 \text{ ft/s}.
\]
The descent time is \(16.8675 - 7.96134 = 8.90615\) s, longer than the ascent time, and the impact speed is below the launch speed. As \(t \to \infty\), \(v(t) \to -800\) ft/s, the terminal velocity \(-mg/k\); at impact the arrow is still far from it. Mathews’ values (\(7.96134\), \(1130.93\), \(16.8675\), \(-239.76\), \(8.90615\)) agree.
Verification: \(v'(t) = -44\, e^{-t/25} = -\tfrac1{25}\bigl(v(t) + 800\bigr) = -32 - \tfrac{v(t)}{25}\) and \(v(0) = -800 + 1100 = 300\). Mathews’ RK4 solution (\(h = 0.2\)) differs from \(y(t)\) by at most \(3.4 \times 10^{-7}\) ft at the grid points of \([0, 20]\), so the two curves coincide in his comparison plot.


Example 3 — Drag proportional to the square of the velocity
The same arrow, with drag \(F_R = \tfrac{1}{2048}\, m v^2\), so \(k/m = \tfrac1{2048}\):
\[
m \frac{dv}{dt} = \mp k v^2 - mg, \qquad y'' = -\frac{y'\lvert y'\rvert}{2048} - 32, \qquad y(0) = 0,\ y'(0) = 300,
\]
with the upper sign on the ascent and the lower sign on the descent.
Step 1 (ascent): On the way up, \(v' = -32 - v^2/2048\), whose solution with \(v(0) = 300\) is
\[
V(t) = 256 \tan\!\left(\frac{t_{\max} - t}{8}\right), \qquad t_{\max} = 8 \arctan\tfrac{75}{64},
\]
and integrating with \(Y(0) = 0\),
\[
Y(t) = 2048 \ln\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{9721}}{64}\, \cos\!\left(\frac{t_{\max} - t}{8}\right)\right).
\]
Step 2 (top): \(V(t_{\max}) = 0\), with
\[
t_{\max} = 8 \arctan\tfrac{75}{64} = 6.91496 \text{ s}, \qquad y_{\max} = Y(t_{\max}) = 1024 \ln\frac{9721}{4096} = 885.020 \text{ ft}.
\]
Step 3 (the wrong continuation): Mathews first uses the ascent formula \(Y(t)\) for the whole flight, as if the drag kept pointing down. Then \(Y\) is symmetric about \(t_{\max}\): it returns to \(0\) at \(t = 2t_{\max} = 13.8299\) s with \(V = -300\) ft/s, so the ascent and descent times are both \(6.91496\) s, as with no air at all. Worse, \(V(t)\) has a vertical asymptote at \(t = t_{\max} + 4\pi = 19.4813\) s, where \(V \to -\infty\): a “drag” that pulls downward makes the fall accelerate without limit. With air resistance the descent must take longer than the ascent, and on the descent the \(v^2\) term must have a positive sign.
Step 4 (descent): On the way down, \(u' = -32 + u^2/2048\) with \(u(t_{\max}) = 0\) and \(Z(t_{\max}) = y_{\max}\). Its solution is
\[
U(t) = -256 \tanh\!\left(\frac{t - t_{\max}}{8}\right), \qquad Z(t) = y_{\max} - 2048 \ln \cosh\!\left(\frac{t - t_{\max}}{8}\right).
\]
Mathews prints these as \(U(t) = \dfrac{256\,(1 - e^{(t - t_{\max})/4})}{1 + e^{(t - t_{\max})/4}}\) and \(Z(t) = 4074.82 + 256\,t - 2048 \ln\bigl(5.63355 + e^{t/4}\bigr)\), where \(5.63355 = e^{t_{\max}/4}\) and \(4074.82\) is \(y_{\max} + 256\, t_{\max} + 2048 \ln 2 = 4074.816\) rounded.
Step 5 (impact): \(Z(t) = 0\) when \(\cosh\bigl((t - t_{\max})/8\bigr) = e^{y_{\max}/2048}\), so the descent time is
\[
t_{\text{impact}} - t_{\max} = 8\, \operatorname{arccosh}\!\left(e^{y_{\max}/2048}\right) = 7.98274 \text{ s},
\qquad t_{\text{impact}} = 14.8977 \text{ s}, \qquad U(t_{\text{impact}}) = -194.736 \text{ ft/s}.
\]
Now the descent is longer than the ascent, and as \(t \to \infty\), \(U(t) \to -256\) ft/s \(= -\sqrt{mg/k}\), a finite terminal velocity. Mathews’ values (\(6.91496\), \(885.02\), \(14.8977\), \(-194.736\), \(7.98274\)) agree. He notes the maximum near \(t = 7\) and the impact near \(t = 15\).
Step 6 (Runge–Kutta): None of this case analysis is needed numerically. The single equation \(y'' = -32 - y'\lvert y'\rvert/2048\) switches the sign of the drag by itself when \(y'\) changes sign, and Mathews’ RK4 solution with \(h = 0.2\) follows the two-piece closed form \(Y\), \(Z\) to within \(1.7 \times 10^{-4}\) ft at every grid point while the arrow is in the air (\(0 \le t \le 14.8\)). He plots the analytic curves alone in \([0, 17] \times [0, 1200]\), and the RK4 and analytic solutions together in \([0, 15] \times [0, 900]\).
Verification: \(V' = -32 \sec^2\!\bigl(\tfrac{t_{\max} - t}{8}\bigr) = -32\bigl(1 + \tfrac{V^2}{65536}\bigr) = -32 - \tfrac{V^2}{2048}\), and \(V(0) = 256 \cdot \tfrac{75}{64} = 300\). Likewise \(U' = -32\,\operatorname{sech}^2\!\bigl(\tfrac{t - t_{\max}}{8}\bigr) = -32 + \tfrac{U^2}{2048}\), with \(U(t_{\max}) = 0\).


Example 4 — Drag proportional to the 3/2 power of the velocity
The same arrow, with drag of magnitude \(0.005\, m \lvert v \rvert^{3/2}\), so \(k/m = \tfrac1{200}\):
\[
y'' = -\frac{1}{200}\, y' \sqrt{\lvert y'\rvert} - 32, \qquad y(0) = 0, \quad y'(0) = 300 .
\]
Mathews’ attempt at a closed-form solution with Mathematica’s DSolve does not produce a usable formula (dropping the initial condition gets it only a little further), so he relies on the RK4 solution (\([0, 20]\), \(n = 100\), \(h = 0.2\)), plotted in \([0, 20] \times [0, 1500]\). He asks for the velocity, the position and a plot; we also located the top and the impact.
Step 1: Top of the flight and impact (event detection on a DOP853 solution, confirmed by quadrature: \(t_{\max} = \int_0^{300} \frac{dv}{32 + 0.005\,v^{3/2}}\) and \(y_{\max} = \int_0^{300} \frac{v\,dv}{32 + 0.005\,v^{3/2}}\), then the impact speed \(U\) from \(\int_0^{U} \frac{u\,du}{32 - 0.005\,u^{3/2}} = y_{\max}\)):
\[
t_{\max} = 7.31383 \text{ s}, \quad y_{\max} = 984.199 \text{ ft}, \quad t_{\text{impact}} = 15.7413 \text{ s}, \quad v(t_{\text{impact}}) = -210.634 \text{ ft/s}.
\]
The descent time is \(8.42746\) s, longer than the ascent. The terminal speed of the descent equation is \((32 \cdot 200)^{2/3} = 344.7\) ft/s.
Step 2: Mathews expects the graph to lie between those of Examples 2 and 3, and it does; his comparison plot shows the three curves in \([0, 20] \times [0, 1500]\). On a grid of \(200\,001\) points in \(0.001 \le t \le 20\), \(y_3(t) < y_4(t) < y_2(t)\) at every point. This is not obvious from the drag laws, because the forces are not ordered at every speed: \(0.005\,v^{3/2}\) exceeds \(v^2/2048\) below \(v = 104.86\) ft/s and is less than \(0.04\,v\) below \(v = 64\) ft/s. Along these trajectories the ordering of the heights still holds throughout.
Verification: Mathews’ RK4 heights differ from the high-accuracy solution by at most \(1.3 \times 10^{-3}\) ft at the grid points while the arrow is in the air, and the two independent locations of \(t_{\max}\), \(y_{\max}\), \(t_{\text{impact}}\) and \(v(t_{\text{impact}})\) agree to the digits shown.

title: Projectile Motion
text:
The trajectory of a baseball
Now the projectile moves in the plane, with horizontal position \(x(t)\) and height \(y(t)\). Air resistance acts along the velocity \(\mathbf{v} = (x', y')\), opposite to it. If its magnitude is \(k\lvert\mathbf{v}\rvert^2\) per unit mass, its direction is \(-\mathbf{v}/\lvert\mathbf{v}\rvert\) and the force per unit mass is \(-k\lvert\mathbf{v}\rvert\,\mathbf{v}\), whose components are
\[
-k\, x' \sqrt{(x')^2 + (y')^2} \quad\text{and}\quad -k\, y' \sqrt{(x')^2 + (y')^2}.
\]






NoteDefinition — Planar drag models (Projectile Motion II)




No air resistance: \(\quad x'' = 0, \qquad y'' = -g\).


Drag proportional to the velocity: \(\quad x'' = -k x', \qquad y'' = -k y' - g\).
Drag proportional to the square of the velocity:

\[
x'' = -k\, x' \sqrt{(x')^2 + (y')^2}, \qquad y'' = -k\, y' \sqrt{(x')^2 + (y')^2} - g .
\]


Models (v) and (vi) separate into one equation for \(x\) and one for \(y\); model (vii) couples them through the speed.

Runge–Kutta method for two second-order equations
For \(x'' = f(t, x, x', y, y')\), \(y'' = f_2(t, x, x', y, y')\) with \(x(a) = \alpha\), \(x'(a) = \beta\), \(y(a) = \gamma\), \(y'(a) = \delta\), the state is \(\mathbf{Z} = (x, x', y, y')\) and \(\mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z}) = \bigl(x',\ f,\ y',\ f_2\bigr)\). The RK4 step is the same formula as in the Description, applied to these four components. Mathews launches the ball from \((0, Y_0)\) with speed \(V\) (ft/s) at angle \(\theta\) (degrees), so \(x'(0) = V\cos\theta\) and \(y'(0) = V\sin\theta\). Each case runs from \(a = 0\) to a final time \(b\) with \(n = 100\) steps and prints the final point \((x(b), y(b))\) and the launch speed in miles per hour, \(V \cdot 60/88\). His trajectory plots of \(y\) against \(x\) use Mathematica’s automatic plot ranges.
Mathews aims the cases at four long hits that he quotes: Willie Stargell’s blasts out of Dodger Stadium of \(506.5\) ft (1969) and \(470\) ft (1973), which give landing points \((506.5, 0)\) and \((470, 0)\), and two balls that struck high above the field, Mickey Mantle’s of May 22, 1963 at \(370\) ft from home plate and \(115\) ft up, and Dick Allen’s of July 6, 1974 at \(415\) ft and \(85\) ft, which give the points \((370, 115)\) and \((415, 85)\).


Example 5 — No air resistance
\[
x''(t) = 0, \qquad y''(t) = -32 .
\]

Example 8 — A model that is not quadratic drag
Mathews contrasts the quadratic drag model of Example 7 with the plausible-looking but wrong system
\[
x''(t) = -k\,\bigl(x'(t)\bigr)^2, \qquad y''(t) = -k\,\bigl(y'(t)\bigr)^2 - 32, \qquad k = 0.002,
\]
with the same initial conditions as the first case of Example 7. (Mathews’ text introduces it as “the model in Example 3”, but the comparison and his concluding sentence refer to Example 7.) As Example 7’s inputs are lost, we use our reconstructed case 1: \(Y_0 = 3\), \(V = 206.79\) ft/s, \(\theta = 42^\circ\).
Step 1: Compare the two at the time \(t = 6.3536\) s at which the quadratic drag ball lands at \((506.5, 0)\). The wrong model’s ball is then at \((541.37,\ 30.55)\), still in the air. It peaks at \((348.73,\ 199.73)\) instead of \((296.71,\ 165.96)\) and lands at \(x = 553.27\) ft at \(t = 6.5850\) s.
Step 2: Why it differs. The quadratic drag force per unit mass is \(-k\lvert\mathbf{v}\rvert\,\mathbf{v}\), whose components were derived above: the speed \(\lvert\mathbf{v}\rvert = \sqrt{(x')^2 + (y')^2}\) multiplies each velocity component. The wrong model replaces \(\lvert\mathbf{v}\rvert\, x'\) by \((x')^2\), which equals \(\lvert x'\rvert\, x'\) while \(x' > 0\), and \(\lvert\mathbf{v}\rvert\, y'\) by \((y')^2 = \lvert y'\rvert^2\), which has the wrong sign whenever \(y' < 0\). So:

Its drag is too small: \(\lvert x'\rvert\) and \(\lvert y'\rvert\) are each at most the speed, so on the way up the ball is slowed less, climbs higher and travels farther.
On the way down its vertical “drag” \(-k(y')^2\) points down instead of up. The vertical equation is then \(y'' = -g - k(y')^2\), the ascent equation of Example 3 used on the descent, whose velocity \(-\sqrt{g/k}\,\tan\bigl(\sqrt{gk}\,(t - t_{\text{top}})\bigr)\) would become infinite at \(t = 9.491\) s. The ball lands with vertical velocity \(-139.89\) ft/s, already faster than the terminal speed \(126.5\) ft/s of the correct model, at a total speed of \(148.84\) ft/s against \(95.51\) ft/s for the correct model.

Verification: The wrong model’s position at \(t = 6.3536\) s from Mathews’ RK4 with \(n = 100\) agrees with the DOP853 solution to four decimals, and the vertical velocity at landing from the closed form above, \(-139.89\) ft/s, agrees with the numerical value.

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Description
The harvesting model adds a constant removal rate \(k\) (fish caught, trees cut, animals hunted per unit time) to the logistic model of bounded population growth:
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = a x - b x^2 - k, \qquad x(0) = x_0, \qquad a, b, k > 0 .
\]
Its right-hand side is a downward parabola in \(x\), so everything depends on the stationary solutions, the constant solutions \(x(t) = r\) with \(a r - b r^2 - k = 0\). When \(a^2 > 4bk\) there are two of them, \(r_1 < r_2\): populations that start above \(r_1\) settle at \(r_2\), and populations that start below \(r_1\) die out in finite time. When \(a^2 = 4bk\) the two merge into the single value \(a/(2b)\), and when \(a^2 < 4bk\) there are none, so every population dies out. In each case the equation is separable and Mathews writes the solution as a formula: a rational function of \(t\), a quotient of exponentials, or a tangent.
Mathews then solves the same equations numerically with the modified Euler method in its midpoint form, with step \(h = (b - a)/m\) on an interval \([a, b]\):
\[
y_{k+1} = y_k + h\, f\!\left(t_k + \tfrac{h}{2},\ y_k + \tfrac{h}{2} f(t_k, y_k)\right),
\]
always with \(m = 110\) steps. He works one example for each case, \((a, b, k) = (2, 1, 1)\), \((4, 1, 3)\) and \((3, 3, 3)\), draws families of solution curves from many starting values \(x_0\), and shows that the numerical curves reproduce the formulas. Every formula below has been checked symbolically, and every number recomputed.

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Background: the Logistic Equation
The exponential model \(y' = a y\) describes unchecked growth; its solution is \(y(t) = c\, e^{a t}\). Subtracting a crowding term \(b y^2\) gives the logistic model of bounded growth.






NoteDefinition — Logistic differential equation



For constants \(a, b > 0\) the logistic differential equation is
\[
y' = a y - b y^2, \qquad y(0) = y_0 .
\tag{1}
\]


For \(y_0 > 0\) one form of its solution is
\[
y(t) = \frac{a}{b + \left(\dfrac{a}{y_0} - b\right) e^{-a t}},
\tag{2}
\]
where the constants have been arranged so that \(y(0) = y_0\). Its limit is
\[
L = \lim_{t \to \infty} y(t) = \frac{a}{b}.
\]
For \(0 < y_0 < a/(2b)\) the graph is the familiar S-shaped curve. Mathews takes \(a = 0.01\), \(b = 0.00001\) and \(y_0 = 100\), for which \(a/y_0 - b = 0.00009\) and
\[
y(t) = \frac{0.01}{0.00001 + 0.00009\, e^{-0.01 t}}, \qquad L = 1000 .
\]
He plots it for \(0 \le t \le 1000\); at the right end \(y(1000) = 999.59\). Since \(y'' = (a - 2 b y)\, y'\), the curve changes from concave up to concave down where \(y = a/(2b) = 500\), which happens at \(t = 100 \ln 9 \approx 219.72\).

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Harvesting a Logistic Population
Incorporating a constant harvesting term \(-k\) into the bounded population model gives
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = a x - b x^2 - k .
\tag{3}
\]






NoteDefinition — Stationary points



The stationary points of (3) are the constants \(r\) for which \(x(t) = r\) is a solution, that is, \(dx/dt \equiv 0\). They are the roots of the characteristic equation
\[
a r - b r^2 - k = 0, \qquad r = \frac{a \pm \sqrt{a^2 - 4 b k}}{2 b} .
\tag{4}
\]


Because \(x(t)\) is real, there are no stationary solutions when \(a^2 - 4bk < 0\). The sign of \(a^2 - 4bk\) therefore splits the problem into three cases, each with its own form of the solution. In all three the right-hand side of (3) is largest at \(x = a/(2b)\), and each formula below satisfies (3) and the initial condition \(x(0) = x_0\) identically (checked with sympy).

Case (i): \(a^2 = 4bk\), one stationary solution
When \(k = a^2/(4b)\) the right-hand side is a perfect square, \(a x - b x^2 - \tfrac{a^2}{4b} = -b\left(x - \tfrac{a}{2b}\right)^2\), and the only stationary solution is \(x_1(t) = a/(2b)\). The general solution, written as Mathews writes it with an arbitrary constant \(c\), is
\[
x(t) = \frac{a}{2b} + \frac{1}{b}\,\frac{1}{t - 4 b c},
\]
and the solution with \(x(0) = x_0\) is
\[
x(t) = \frac{a}{2b} + \frac{1}{b}\,\frac{1}{t - \dfrac{2}{a - 2 b x_0}} .
\tag{5}
\]






TipTheorem — Case (i)



Let \(a^2 = 4bk\) and \(x_0 \ge 0\).

If \(x_0 \ge a/(2b)\), then \(\displaystyle\lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) = \frac{a}{2b}\).
If \(x_0 < a/(2b)\), then \(x(t)\) has a vertical asymptote at \(t_1 = \dfrac{2}{a - 2 b x_0}\), and the population becomes extinct at the time \(t_0 = t_1 - \dfrac{2}{a} = \dfrac{4 b x_0}{a\,(a - 2 b x_0)}\), with \(0 \le t_0 < t_1\) and \(x(t_0) = 0\).



Since \(dx/dt = -b\,(x - a/(2b))^2 \le 0\), every solution decreases. One that starts above \(a/(2b)\) approaches it from above; one that starts below falls through \(0\) at \(t_0\) and on toward \(-\infty\) at \(t_1\). Mathews’ module states the extinction time only as some \(t_0\) between \(0\) and \(t_1\); the formula for \(t_0\) comes from setting (5) equal to zero.


Case (ii): \(a^2 > 4bk\), two stationary solutions
Write \(s = \sqrt{a^2 - 4bk} > 0\). The two real roots of the characteristic equation are
\[
r_1 = \frac{a - s}{2b}, \qquad r_2 = \frac{a + s}{2b},
\]
and the stationary solutions are \(x_1(t) = r_1\) and \(x_2(t) = r_2\). Mathews’ general solution is
\[
x(t) = \frac{a}{2b} + \frac{s}{2b}\left(1 - \frac{2}{1 + c\, e^{s t}}\right),
\]
and the solution with \(x(0) = x_0\) is
\[
x(t) = \frac{a}{2b} + \frac{s}{2b} - \frac{a + s - 2 b x_0}{2b}\cdot\frac{2 s}{(s + a - 2 b x_0) + (s - a + 2 b x_0)\, e^{s t}} .
\tag{6}
\]






TipTheorem — Case (ii)



Let \(a^2 > 4bk\) and \(x_0 \ge 0\).

If \(x_0 > r_1\), then \(\displaystyle\lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) = r_2 = \frac{a + \sqrt{a^2 - 4bk}}{2b}\).
If \(0 < x_0 < r_1\), then the population becomes extinct at the time \[
t_0 = \frac{1}{s}\ln\frac{r_1\,(r_2 - x_0)}{r_2\,(r_1 - x_0)} > 0, \qquad x(t_0) = 0,
\] and \(x(t)\) has a vertical asymptote later, at \(t_1 = \dfrac{1}{s}\ln\dfrac{r_2 - x_0}{r_1 - x_0}\).



Here \(dx/dt = -b\,(x - r_1)(x - r_2)\), so a solution that starts between \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) increases to \(r_2\), one that starts above \(r_2\) decreases to \(r_2\), and one that starts below \(r_1\) decreases through \(0\). Mathews’ module gives only the existence of \(t_0\); the formulas for \(t_0\) and \(t_1\) come from setting (6) and its denominator equal to zero.


Case (iii): \(a^2 < 4bk\), no stationary solutions
Write \(w = \sqrt{4bk - a^2} > 0\). Mathews’ general solution is
\[
x(t) = \frac{a}{2b} - \frac{w}{2b}\tan\!\left(\frac{w t}{2} - c\right),
\]
and the solution with \(x(0) = x_0\) has \(c = \arctan\dfrac{2 b x_0 - a}{w}\):
\[
x(t) = \frac{a}{2b} - \frac{w}{2b}\tan\!\left(\frac{w t}{2} - \arctan\frac{2 b x_0 - a}{w}\right).
\tag{7}
\]






TipTheorem — Case (iii)



Let \(a^2 < 4bk\) and \(x_0 \ge 0\). Then \(x(t)\) has a vertical asymptote at
\[
t_1 = \frac{2}{w}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + c\right), \qquad c = \arctan\frac{2 b x_0 - a}{w},
\]
and the population becomes extinct at the earlier time \(t_0 = \dfrac{2}{w}\left(\arctan\dfrac{a}{w} + c\right)\), where \(x(t_0) = 0\).


Here \(dx/dt = -b\,(x - a/(2b))^2 - w^2/(4b) < 0\) for every \(x\), so every population decreases, whatever its size. The tangent in (7) becomes infinite when its argument \(w t/2 - c\) reaches \(\pi/2\), which gives the formula for \(t_1\) above. Mathews’ module prints \(t_1 = 2(\pi/2 - c)/w\) with a minus sign, which is not where (7) is infinite; in Example 18 below (\(x_0 = 1\)) his formula gives \(0.4031\), which is the extinction time, while the asymptote is at \(0.8061\), and for \(x_0 = 6\) it gives \(0.0601\), where the population is still \(3.182\).

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Numerical Solutions
If only the graph of the solution is needed, and not the formula, an efficient way to solve (3) is a numerical method such as the modified Euler method or the Runge-Kutta method; if an accurate table of values is wanted, Mathews recommends the Runge-Kutta method. His program for the modified Euler method approximates the solution of \(y' = f(t, y)\), \(y(a) = \alpha\), on \([a, b]\) at the points \(t_k = a + k h\), \(h = (b - a)/m\), by
\[
y_{k+1} = y_k + h\, f\!\left(t_k + \frac{h}{2},\ y_k + \frac{h}{2} f(t_k, y_k)\right), \qquad k = 0, 1, \ldots, m - 1 .
\tag{8}
\]
This is the midpoint form of the method: an Euler half-step to the middle of the interval, and a full step with the slope found there. It is of second order; in Example 8 below, doubling \(m\) from \(110\) to \(220\) and then to \(440\) divides the largest error for \(x_0 = 6\) by \(4.5\) and then by \(4.3\). Mathews passes a list of starting values as \(\alpha\), so one call computes a whole family of curves.

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Example 1 — A Computer Algebra Solution
Problem. Use Mathematica to solve \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = a x - b x^2 - k\).
Solution. Mathews applies Mathematica’s DSolve to (3) with \(a\), \(b\) and \(k\) left as symbols (the output images of this example are missing from the archive). His caveat is that the general solution found by Mathematica, and by Maple too, is the one for case (iii) only; the formulas for cases (i) and (ii) are left for the reader to prove. A computer algebra system returns one formula for the “general solution”, and it may be the least significant of the three forms. When numbers are substituted for \(a\), \(b\) and \(k\), as in the examples that follow, Mathematica does find the solution of the right form.

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Example 2 — Stationary Solutions
Problem. Find the roots of \(a r - b r^2 - k = 0\) and the equilibrium solutions of (3).
Solution. Solving the quadratic gives the two roots (4),
\[
x_1(t) = \frac{a - \sqrt{a^2 - 4bk}}{2b}, \qquad x_2(t) = \frac{a + \sqrt{a^2 - 4bk}}{2b},
\]
and substituting each constant into (3) shows that \(a x_i - b x_i^2 - k = 0 = x_i'\). These are the two stationary solutions of case (ii). For case (i) the substitution \(k = a^2/(4b)\) must be made before solving, which leaves the single root \(a/(2b)\).

title: Harvesting Model

Case (i) Examples: \(x' = 2x - x^2 - 1\)

Example 3 — The general solution
Problem. Solve \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = a x - b x^2 - k\) with \(a = 2\), \(b = 1\), \(k = 1\), and explore this situation.
Step 1. Here \(a^2 = 4 = 4bk\), so this is case (i), and the equation is
\[
x' = -1 + 2x - x^2 = -(x - 1)^2 .
\]
Step 2. Mathematica’s DSolve gives the general solution
\[
x(t) = \frac{1 + t - C}{t - C} = 1 + \frac{1}{t - C},

with \(x(0) = (C - 1)/C\).
Step 3. The constant solution is the root of \(-1 + 2X - X^2 = 0\), namely \(x_1(t) = 1 = a/(2b)\).
Step 4. For every \(C\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{1 + t - C}{t - C} = 1\), the constant solution. As the next examples show, this limit is reached only by solutions with \(x_0 \ge 1\); for \(0 < x_0 < 1\) the constant is \(C = 1/(1 - x_0) > 0\) and the solution reaches \(0\), and then the pole at \(t = C\), before \(t\) can grow large.

Example 6 — Reading the graph of Example 5
Problem. In the plot of Example 5, what are the vertical lines? What are the curves below \(x = 1\), and those above \(x = 1\)? What use are they?
Solution. The vertical lines are the asymptotes \(t = C\) of the solutions. The curves below \(x = 1\) are the solutions with the initial conditions we wanted. The curves above \(x = 1\) are extraneous: they are the parts of the same formulas beyond the pole, which are not connected to \(x(0) = x_0\) and are of no use here. To get rid of them, Mathews gives each solution its own domain, from \(t = 0\) up to the asymptote, and draws all the curves on one graph (the images of this example are missing from the archive). The composite graph shows that the solutions with \(x_0 > 1\) tend to \(1\) as \(t \to \infty\) (Mathews’ text says \(x_0 > 0\) here, which contradicts his next sentence and the computation), that the solutions with \(0 < x_0 < 1\) reach \(0\) at a finite time and the population becomes extinct, and that the constant solution \(x = 1\) divides the two cases.


Example 7 — The formula for the solution with \(x(0) = x_0\)
Problem. Solve \(x' = 2x - x^2 - 1\) with \(x(0) = x_0\) using formula (5).
Solution. With \(a = 2\), \(b = 1\), (5) becomes
\[
x(t) = 1 + \frac{1}{t - \dfrac{1}{1 - x_0}},
\]
which is (9) with \(C = 1/(1 - x_0)\). Mathews checks the general formula and this one against the equation (his images for this example are missing).

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Case (ii) Examples: \(x' = 4x - x^2 - 3\)

Example 9 — The general solution
Problem. Solve \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = a x - b x^2 - k\) with \(a = 4\), \(b = 1\), \(k = 3\), and explore this situation.
Step 1. Here \(a^2 = 16 > 12 = 4bk\), so this is case (ii), and the equation is
\[
x' = -3 + 4x - x^2 = -(x - 1)(x - 3) .
\]
Step 2. DSolve gives the general solution
\[
x(t) = \frac{3 e^{2t} - e^{2C}}{e^{2t} - e^{2C}},
\tag{10}
\]
with \(x(0) = (3 - e^{2C})/(1 - e^{2C})\), so that \(e^{2C} = (x_0 - 3)/(x_0 - 1)\).
Step 3. The constant solutions are the roots of \(-3 + 4X - X^2 = 0\): \(x_1(t) = 1\) and \(x_2(t) = 3\), in agreement with \(r_{1,2} = (a \mp s)/(2b)\) for \(s = \sqrt{16 - 12} = 2\).
Step 4. For every constant \(C\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) = 3\), the second constant solution. Mathews remarks that it takes more investigation to see what is happening, and the next examples show that the limit is reached only from \(x_0 > 1\).
Verification. Substituting (10) into \(x' = -3 + 4x - x^2\) gives a zero residual for every \(C\).

Problem. Plot the solutions of \(x' = 4x - x^2 - 3\) with \(x(0) = \tfrac43, \tfrac53, 2, \tfrac73, \tfrac83\).

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
Description
This page covers the finite difference method for a hyperbolic partial differential equation, the one-dimensional wave equation, as Mathews’ module “Finite Difference Method for Hyperbolic Equations” does. The problem is to find the displacement \(u(x, t)\) of a vibrating string with fixed ends, \(u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx}\) for \(0 < x < a\) and \(0 < t < b\), given its initial position \(u(x, 0) = f(x)\) and initial velocity \(u_t(x, 0) = g(x)\).
The method covers the rectangle \(0 \le x \le a\), \(0 \le t \le b\) with a grid of spacing \(h\) in \(x\) and \(k\) in \(t\), replaces both second derivatives by central differences, and solves the resulting difference equation for the newest time level. With \(u_{i,j} \approx u(x_i, t_j)\) and the ratio \(r = ck/h\), each new row of the grid comes from the two rows before it:
\[
u_{i,j+1} = (2 - 2r^2)\,u_{i,j} + r^2\,(u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j}) - u_{i,j-1}.
\]
The first row is \(f\), and a second row is built from \(f\) and \(g\) with a Taylor expansion. This is an explicit method: the rows are computed one after another, with no system of equations to solve. As a general result, it is stable when \(r \le 1\); for \(r > 1\) the shortest wavelengths that a fine enough grid can carry grow geometrically. When \(r = 1\) and the second row is exact, every value it computes is exact. Mathews’ three examples show both sides: Examples 1 and 2 use \(r = 1\) and reproduce the exact solution to rounding error, and Example 3 takes \(r = 1.02\) and is unstable.

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
The Wave Equation






NoteDefinition — The wave equation problem



Find \(u(x, t)\) satisfying
\[
u_{tt}(x, t) = c^2\, u_{xx}(x, t) \qquad \text{for } 0 < x < a \text{ and } 0 < t < b,
\tag{1}
\]
with the boundary and initial conditions
\[
\begin{aligned}
u(0, t) &= 0 \quad \text{and} \quad u(a, t) = 0 && \text{for } 0 \le t \le b, \\
u(x, 0) &= f(x) && \text{for } 0 \le x \le a, \\
u_t(x, 0) &= g(x) && \text{for } 0 < x < a.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]


The wave equation models the displacement \(u\) of an elastic string held fixed at \(x = 0\) and \(x = a\); \(c\) is the speed at which waves travel along it. Analytic solutions can be found with Fourier series or with d’Alembert’s formula below, but the problem serves as the prototype of a hyperbolic equation, and the same difference method applies where no formula is available.

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
Derivation of the Difference Equation
Partition the rectangle \(R = \{(x, t) : 0 \le x \le a,\ 0 \le t \le b\}\) into \(n - 1\) by \(m - 1\) rectangles with sides \(h = a/(n - 1)\) and \(k = b/(m - 1)\). Following Mathews, the grid points are numbered from \(1\):
\[
x_i = (i - 1)h, \quad i = 1, \ldots, n, \qquad t_j = (j - 1)k, \quad j = 1, \ldots, m,
\]
and \(u_{i,j}\) denotes the approximation to \(u(x_i, t_j)\). The bottom row \(j = 1\) is the known initial position, \(u_{i,1} = f(x_i)\), and the end columns are the fixed ends, \(u_{1,j} = u_{n,j} = 0\).
The central-difference formulas for the two second derivatives are
\[
u_{tt}(x, t) = \frac{u(x, t + k) - 2u(x, t) + u(x, t - k)}{k^2} + O(k^2),
\tag{3}
\]
\[
u_{xx}(x, t) = \frac{u(x + h, t) - 2u(x, t) + u(x - h, t)}{h^2} + O(h^2).
\tag{4}
\]
Dropping the \(O(k^2)\) and \(O(h^2)\) terms and substituting into (1) gives the difference equation
\[
\frac{u_{i,j+1} - 2u_{i,j} + u_{i,j-1}}{k^2} = c^2\, \frac{u_{i+1,j} - 2u_{i,j} + u_{i-1,j}}{h^2}.
\tag{5}
\]
With the substitution \(r = ck/h\) it becomes \(u_{i,j+1} - 2u_{i,j} + u_{i,j-1} = r^2 (u_{i+1,j} - 2u_{i,j} + u_{i-1,j})\), which is solved for the value on the newest row:






ImportantExplicit formula for the wave equation



\[
u_{i,j+1} = (2 - 2r^2)\,u_{i,j} + r^2\,(u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j}) - u_{i,j-1}, \qquad i = 2, 3, \ldots, n - 1,
\tag{6}
\]
where \(r = ck/h\).


Formula (6) computes row \(j + 1\) from four known values: three neighbouring values \(u_{i-1,j}\), \(u_{i,j}\), \(u_{i+1,j}\) in row \(j\) and the value \(u_{i,j-1}\) directly below in row \(j - 1\). This four-point pattern is the stencil of the method. Because it reaches back two rows, two starting rows are needed.

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
Starting Values
The first row is \(u_{i,1} = f(x_i) = f_i\). The second row, at \(t = k\), is not given, so it is built from Taylor’s formula in \(t\) about \((x_i, 0)\). To first order, \(u(x_i, k) = u(x_i, 0) + u_t(x_i, 0)\,k + O(k^2)\), and with \(g_i = g(x_i)\) this gives
\[
u_{i,2} = f_i + k\,g_i, \qquad i = 2, 3, \ldots, n - 1.
\tag{7}
\]
Errors in the second row are carried through the rest of the grid by formula (6), so a better second row is worth having. When \(f\) has a second derivative, the wave equation turns the unknown \(u_{tt}\) at \(t = 0\) into a known \(x\)-derivative of \(f\):
\[
u_{tt}(x_i, 0) = c^2 u_{xx}(x_i, 0) = c^2 f''(x_i) = c^2\, \frac{f_{i+1} - 2f_i + f_{i-1}}{h^2} + O(h^2).
\]
Taylor’s formula of order 2, \(u(x, k) = u(x, 0) + u_t(x, 0)\,k + \tfrac12 u_{tt}(x, 0)\,k^2 + O(k^3)\), then gives
\[
u(x_i, k) = f_i + k g_i + \frac{c^2 k^2}{2h^2}\,(f_{i+1} - 2f_i + f_{i-1}) + O(h^2)\,O(k^2) + O(k^3),
\]
and with \(r = ck/h\) this simplifies to the second-row formula that Mathews’ program uses:






ImportantSecond row



\[
u_{i,2} = (1 - r^2) f_i + k g_i + \frac{r^2}{2}\,(f_{i+1} + f_{i-1}), \qquad i = 2, 3, \ldots, n - 1.
\tag{8}
\]

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
Stability
Mathews calls the method stable if an error made at one stage of the calculation is eventually damped out, and states that stability of formula (6) requires \(r = ck/h \le 1\). The condition is a general result, and a Fourier analysis shows where it comes from; it also shows that for \(r \le 1\) errors are not damped but stay bounded. Since the boundary values are zero, look for solutions of (6) of the form \(u_{i,j} = \lambda^{j} \sin(p\pi x_i/a)\), one for each mode \(p = 1, 2, \ldots, n - 2\) that the grid can represent. Substituting into (6) and dividing by \(\lambda^{j-1}\sin(p\pi x_i/a)\) gives
\[
\lambda^2 - (2 - 4r^2 s_p)\,\lambda + 1 = 0, \qquad s_p = \sin^2\!\left(\frac{p\pi h}{2a}\right).
\tag{9}
\]
The two roots have product \(1\). If \(|2 - 4r^2 s_p| < 2\), that is \(r^2 s_p < 1\), they are complex conjugates of modulus \(1\), and the mode neither grows nor decays. If \(r^2 s_p = 1\) they coincide at \(\lambda = -1\) and the mode can grow, but only linearly. If \(r^2 s_p > 1\), they are real and negative, and one of them has modulus greater than \(1\): the mode grows geometrically and changes sign at every step. Since \(s_p < 1\) for every mode, \(r \le 1\) gives \(r^2 s_p < 1\), and all modes stay bounded. As \(h \to 0\) the largest \(s_p\) approaches \(1\), so \(r \le 1\) is the condition that works for every grid.






TipStability condition (general result)



The explicit formula (6) for the wave equation is stable when
\[
r = \frac{ck}{h} \le 1.
\]
For \(r > 1\), on any grid fine enough that \(r^2 s_{n-2} > 1\), the highest modes the grid can carry grow without bound as the rows are computed.


The condition has a physical reading. The exact value \(u(x, t)\) depends on the initial data in \([x - ct,\ x + ct]\), while the value \(u_{i,j}\) computed by (6) can depend only on initial values in \([x_i - (j-1)h,\ x_i + (j-1)h]\), because each row reaches one grid point further to each side. The numerical interval contains the true one only when \(h/k \ge c\), which is \(r \le 1\) (the Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition). Implicit methods, which are more work to implement, have no stability restriction on \(r\).






WarningOn a coarse grid the threshold is slightly above 1



Only the modes \(p \le n - 2\) exist on a given grid, so the exact threshold there is \(r = 1/\sqrt{s_{n-2}}\), slightly above \(1\). For the grid of Examples 1 to 3 (\(n = 11\), \(h = 0.1\)) it is \(1/\sin(9\pi/20) \approx 1.0125\); only mode \(p = 9\) is unstable at \(r = 1.02\).

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
D’Alembert’s Solution and Exact Rows
The French mathematician Jean Le Rond d’Alembert (1717–1783) found that
\[
u(x, t) = F(x + ct) + G(x - ct)
\tag{10}
\]
solves the wave equation (1), as direct substitution shows: \(u_{tt} = c^2 F''(x + ct) + c^2 G''(x - ct) = c^2 u_{xx}\). The boundary conditions \(u(0, t) = u(a, t) = 0\) hold when \(F\) and \(G\) are odd and have period \(2a\): \(F(-z) = -F(z)\), \(F(z + 2a) = F(z)\), and likewise for \(G\). The solution with \(u(x, 0) = f(x)\) and \(u_t(x, 0) = 0\) is
\[
u(x, t) = \tfrac12 \bigl(\tilde f(x + ct) + \tilde f(x - ct)\bigr),
\tag{11}
\]
where \(\tilde f\) is the odd extension of \(f\) with period \(2a\). The initial shape splits into two halves that travel left and right at speed \(c\) and are reflected, upside down, at the fixed ends.
When \(r = 1\), that is \(k = h/c\), the grid lines line up with the characteristics \(x \pm ct = \text{const}\), and the method becomes exact.






TipTheorem — Two exact rows give an exact grid



Assume that the two rows \(u_{i,1} = u(x_i, 0)\) and \(u_{i,2} = u(x_i, k)\), \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, n\), are exact values of the solution of (1). If the step \(k = h/c\) is chosen, then \(r = 1\) and formula (6) becomes
\[
u_{i,j+1} = u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} - u_{i,j-1},
\tag{12}
\]
and the values it produces throughout the grid are exact values of the solution (apart from computer rounding).


Proof. With \(ck = h\), \(x_i - ct_j = (i - 1)h - (j - 1)h = (i - j)h\) and \(x_i + ct_j = (i + j - 2)h\), so by (10) every exact grid value has the form \(u_{i,j} = F((i - j)h) + G((i + j - 2)h)\). Substituting this into the right side of (12),
\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} - u_{i,j-1}
&= F((i + 1 - j)h) + F((i - 1 - j)h) - F((i - j + 1)h) \\
&\quad + G((i + j - 1)h) + G((i + j - 3)h) - G((i + j - 3)h) \\
&= F((i - (j + 1))h) + G((i + (j + 1) - 2)h) = u_{i,j+1}. \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]
The theorem needs an exact second row, and formulas (7) and (8) generally do not give one. There is one common case where they do. When \(g = 0\) and \(r = 1\), formula (8) reduces to
\[
u_{i,2} = \frac{f_{i-1} + f_{i+1}}{2}, \qquad i = 2, 3, \ldots, n - 1,
\tag{13}
\]
and by (11) the exact value is \(u(x_i, k) = \tfrac12\bigl(\tilde f(x_i + h) + \tilde f(x_i - h)\bigr)\), which is the same thing, because \(ck = h\) and the points \(x_i \pm h\) are grid points in \([0, a]\), where \(\tilde f = f\). So with \(g = 0\) and \(r = 1\) the method reproduces the exact solution at every grid point. Examples 1 and 2 are of this kind.

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
Algorithm
Mathews’ program has two parts.

Starting rows. Set \(h = a/(n - 1)\), \(k = b/(m - 1)\) and \(r = ck/h\). Fill row 1 with \(u_{i,1} = f(x_i)\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), and fill row 2 by formula (8) for \(i = 2, \ldots, n - 1\). All other entries start at \(0\), so the end columns \(u_{1,j}\) and \(u_{n,j}\) stay \(0\) for \(j \ge 2\).
Later rows. For \(j = 3, 4, \ldots, m\) and \(i = 2, \ldots, n - 1\), compute \[
u_{i,j} = (2 - 2r^2)\,u_{i,j-1} + r^2\,(u_{i+1,j-1} + u_{i-1,j-1}) - u_{i,j-2}.
\]

The result is an \(n \times m\) array whose column \(j\) is the shape of the string at time \(t_j\). Mathews plots this array as a surface over the index grid (the axes are labelled \(x(i)\) and \(t(j)\) and carry the indices \(i = 1, \ldots, 11\) and \(j = 1, \ldots, 21\), not the values of \(x\) and \(t\)), seen from the viewpoint \((4, 2, 3)\) and coloured by height.
In all three examples below \(c = 2\) (so \(c^2 = 4\)), the string has length \(a = 1\), \(g(x) = 0\), and the grid has \(n = 11\) columns and \(m = 21\) rows. The examples differ in the initial position \(f\) and the time interval \([0, b]\).

title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
text:
Description
The gradient method, also called the method of steepest descent, looks for a local minimum of a function \(f(\mathbf{X})\) of \(n\) variables, \(\mathbf{X} = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)\), whose first partial derivatives can be evaluated. At the current point \(\mathbf{P}_k\) the gradient \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) points in the direction in which \(f\) increases fastest, so the unit vector opposite to it is the direction of steepest descent. The method searches along the line through \(\mathbf{P}_k\) in that direction for the lowest value of \(f\) and moves there:
\[
\mathbf{S}_k = -\frac{\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)}{\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) \rVert}, \qquad
\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + h_k\,\mathbf{S}_k, \qquad
h_k \approx \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\gamma \ge 0}\, f(\mathbf{P}_k + \gamma\,\mathbf{S}_k).
\]
Each iteration needs only the gradient and a one-variable minimisation along a line. When that line minimisation is exact, \(f\) decreases at every step and each new search direction is perpendicular to the previous one, so the path to the minimum is a zigzag. In a long, narrow valley the zigzag steps are short and the method is slow. Mathews carries out the line search with a single quadratic interpolation per step (the quadratic interpolative search idea), and his examples work in two variables, \(\mathbf{P}_k = (x_k, y_k)\): a quadratic, Rosenbrock’s banana-shaped valley, a quartic with three local minima and a rational function. Every tabulated run below was recomputed with his line search and stopping rule in 60-digit arithmetic and agrees with a 120-digit run to within \(10^{-50}\).

title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
text:
Animations
Each animation below follows one run of the gradient method, one line search per frame, in three panels. The left panel is a fixed window over the whole run. It has cyan contours of \(f\), the dashed search line through the current point \(\mathbf{P}_k\), the level curve of \(f\) through \(\mathbf{P}_k\) in blue, the steps taken so far in magenta, the points \(\mathbf{P}_k\) in red and the minimum \(\mathbf{P}^{*}\) as a green cross. The middle panel zooms on the current line search, so that steps far too small for the left panel stay visible. Its axes are offsets from \(\mathbf{P}^{*}\), multiplied by the power of ten in the axis label. It draws what Mathews’ drawing program of Example 5 draws: cyan contours at the levels \(f^{*} + \bigl(f(\mathbf{P}_k) - f^{*}\bigr)\{0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8\}\), where \(f^{*} = f(\mathbf{P}^{*})\), the level curve through \(\mathbf{P}_k\) in blue, and the trial points \(\mathbf{P}_k\) (red), \(\mathbf{P}_k + h\mathbf{S}_k\) (blue) and \(\mathbf{P}_k + 2h\mathbf{S}_k\) (green) on a pink segment. Here the trial points are the ones after the bracketing loop, the three that the parabola (3) is fitted to; Mathews’ program draws them before the loop and draws the search segment out to \(5h\). A red dot with a black ring marks the new point \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + h_k\mathbf{S}_k\), an orange curve the level curve of \(f\) through it, and a black cross the exact minimum of \(f\) along the search line. title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
section: The Gradient and the Direction of Steepest Descent
text:
The Gradient and the Direction of Steepest Descent






NoteDefinition — Gradient



Let \(z = f(\mathbf{X})\) be a function of \(\mathbf{X} = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)\) such that \(\partial f(\mathbf{X})/\partial x_k\) exists for \(k = 1, 2, \ldots, n\). The gradient of \(f\) is the vector
\[
\nabla f(\mathbf{X}) = \left( \frac{\partial f(\mathbf{X})}{\partial x_1},\ \frac{\partial f(\mathbf{X})}{\partial x_2},\ \ldots,\ \frac{\partial f(\mathbf{X})}{\partial x_n} \right).
\tag{1}
\]








TipTheorem — Direction of steepest descent (general)



Let \(f\) be differentiable at \(\mathbf{P}\) with \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \neq \mathbf{0}\). The rate of change of \(f\) at \(\mathbf{P}\) in the direction of a unit vector \(\mathbf{u}\) is \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \cdot \mathbf{u}\). By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality it lies between \(-\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \rVert\) and \(\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \rVert\), with the largest value for \(\mathbf{u} = \nabla f(\mathbf{P}) / \lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \rVert\) and the smallest for
\[
\mathbf{u} = -\frac{\nabla f(\mathbf{P})}{\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}) \rVert}.
\]


So locally \(f\) increases fastest along \(\nabla f\) and decreases fastest along \(-\nabla f\). The decrease is local only: a long step in the direction \(-\nabla f\) can overshoot, which is why the method looks for the best step length along the line.

Illustrations — two gradients
Mathews starts by finding the gradients of two functions that reappear in the examples.
For the quartic of Example 3,
\[
f(x, y) = 5x^2 + x^4 - 9x^2 y + 3y^2 + 2y^4 + \tfrac14 x, \qquad
\nabla f(x, y) = \bigl(10x + 4x^3 - 18xy + \tfrac14,\ \ -9x^2 + 6y + 8y^3\bigr).
\]
For the rational function of Example 4, the quotient rule gives
\[
f(x, y) = \frac{x - y}{x^2 + y^2 + 2}, \qquad
\nabla f(x, y) = \left( \frac{-x^2 + 2xy + y^2 + 2}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^2},\ \ \frac{-x^2 - 2xy + y^2 - 2}{(x^2 + y^2 + 2)^2} \right),
\]
and at the point \((-3, -2)\), where \(x^2 + y^2 + 2 = 15\),
\[
\nabla f(-3, -2) = \left( \frac{9}{225},\ -\frac{19}{225} \right) = \left( \frac{1}{25},\ -\frac{19}{225} \right) \approx (0.04,\ -0.0844444).
\]
Verification: both gradients were checked symbolically against direct differentiation (the differences simplify to \(0\)), and the value at \((-3, -2)\) was computed in exact rational arithmetic.

title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
text:
The Gradient Method
Start at \(\mathbf{P}_0\) and search along the line through \(\mathbf{P}_0\) in the direction \(\mathbf{S}_0 = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0)/\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0) \rVert\). The point \(\mathbf{P}_1\) is where \(f\), restricted to the line \(\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{P}_0 + \gamma\,\mathbf{S}_0\), has a local minimum. Then compute \(\mathbf{S}_1\) from \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_1)\), search along the line through \(\mathbf{P}_1\), and so on.






ImportantOutline of the gradient method



Suppose \(\mathbf{P}_k\) has been found.

Evaluate the gradient vector \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k)\).
Compute the search direction \(\mathbf{S}_k = -\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) / \lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) \rVert\).
Minimise the function of one variable \[\varphi_k(\gamma) = f(\mathbf{P}_k + \gamma\,\mathbf{S}_k) \tag{2}\] on an interval \([0, b]\), where \(b\) is large. This gives a value \(\gamma = h_k\) at which \(\varphi_k\) has a local minimum, so \(f(\mathbf{P}_k + h_k \mathbf{S}_k)\) is a minimum of \(f\) along the search line.
Construct the next point \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + h_k\,\mathbf{S}_k\).
Termination test: are \(f(\mathbf{P}_k)\) and \(f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1})\) close enough, and is the distance \(\lVert \mathbf{P}_{k+1} - \mathbf{P}_k \rVert\) small enough? If not, repeat.









TipTheorem — Properties with an exact line search (general)



Let \(f\) be continuously differentiable and let each \(h_k > 0\) be the first local minimiser of \(\varphi_k\) in (2) on \((0, \infty)\), with \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) \neq \mathbf{0}\).

Descent. \(\varphi_k'(0) = \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) \cdot \mathbf{S}_k = -\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_k) \rVert < 0\) and \(\varphi_k\) has no local minimum in \((0, h_k)\), so \(\varphi_k(h_k) < \varphi_k(0)\) and \(f\) decreases strictly: \(f(\mathbf{P}_0) > f(\mathbf{P}_1) > \cdots > f(\mathbf{P}_k) > \cdots\).
Zigzag. \(\varphi_k'(h_k) = \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1}) \cdot \mathbf{S}_k = 0\), and \(\mathbf{S}_{k+1}\) is a negative multiple of \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1})\), so \(\mathbf{S}_{k+1} \cdot \mathbf{S}_k = 0\): consecutive search directions are perpendicular.
Limit. Every limit point \(\mathbf{P}\) of the sequence \(\{\mathbf{P}_k\}\) satisfies \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}) = \mathbf{0}\).



Mathews states that if \(\mathbf{P}_k \to \mathbf{P}\) then \(f(\mathbf{P})\) is a local minimum. That is what happens in every run on this page, but in general the theory guarantees only a stationary point. Because \(f\) decreases at every step, the limit cannot be a strict local maximum, but a saddle point can be reached from special starting points: for \(f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2\) from \((1, 0)\), the first exact line search lands on the saddle point \((0, 0)\), where the gradient is zero and the method stops. With an approximate line search such as Mathews’ single quadratic fit, properties 1 and 2 hold exactly only when \(\varphi_k\) is a quadratic, as in Example 1. In the other examples they hold approximately, and each case says how closely.






TipTheorem — Rate on a quadratic (general)



Let \(f(\mathbf{X}) = f^{*} + \tfrac12 (\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X}^{*})\,\mathbf{A}\,(\mathbf{X} - \mathbf{X}^{*})^{T}\), where \(\mathbf{A}\) is symmetric positive definite with smallest and largest eigenvalues \(\lambda_{\min}\) and \(\lambda_{\max}\), and let \(\kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}\). With exact line searches the gradient method satisfies
\[
f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1}) - f^{*} \le \left( \frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1} \right)^{2} \bigl( f(\mathbf{P}_k) - f^{*} \bigr).
\]


When \(\kappa\) is large, the level curves of \(f\) are long, thin ellipses and the factor is close to \(1\).






WarningSlow convergence



Convergence to a minimum can be slow. In Mathews’ words, the geometry of a minimum often makes \(h_k\) small, so the method returns to the line search (step 3) many times. In four of the six runs below (Examples 1, 2, 3(ii) and 3(iii)) Mathews’ program reaches its work limit before its tolerance.

title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
text:
Mathews’ Implementation
Mathews’ Mathematica program has two parts: a line search that takes one step along \(\mathbf{S}_k\), and an outer loop that repeats it.
Line search. It carries a trial step \(h\) from one iteration to the next (\(h = 1\) at the start of a run). With \(Y_0 = \varphi_k(0)\), \(Y_1 = \varphi_k(h)\) and \(Y_2 = \varphi_k(2h)\) it repeats, at most \(15\) times:

if \(Y_0 \le Y_1\), the step is too long: halve \(h\) (the old middle point becomes the new right point) and evaluate the new middle point;
otherwise, if \(Y_2 < Y_1\), \(\varphi_k\) is still falling at \(2h\): double \(h\) (the old right point becomes the middle point) and evaluate the new right point;
otherwise \(Y_1 < Y_0\) and \(Y_1 \le Y_2\), so the points \(0\), \(h\), \(2h\) bracket a minimum: stop;
after each pass, the loop also stops if \(h < \delta\), the tolerance of the stopping rule below.

In every run on this page, including those with the work counter removed, \(h\) stays above \(\delta\) in the loop, so the test \(h < \delta\) never acts and the scripts leave it out.
The step is the vertex of the parabola through \((0, Y_0)\), \((h, Y_1)\), \((2h, Y_2)\),
\[
h_k = \frac{h\,(4Y_1 - 3Y_0 - Y_2)}{2\,(2Y_1 - Y_0 - Y_2)},
\tag{3}
\]
and \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1} = \mathbf{P}_k + h_k \mathbf{S}_k\). This is one quadratic fit, not repeated: \(h_k\) is the exact minimiser of \(\varphi_k\) only when \(\varphi_k\) is itself a quadratic. The trial step for the next iteration is the smallest of \(h\), \(|h_k|\), \(|h_k - h|\) and \(|h_k - 2h|\).
Outer loop and stopping rule. The program keeps \(\mathrm{Err}\), the smallest nonzero difference \(|Y_i - f(\mathbf{P}_{k+1})|\) (\(i = 0, 1, 2\)) met so far in the run, starting from \(\mathrm{Err} = 1\). It stops as soon as both \(h \le \delta\) and \(\mathrm{Err} \le \varepsilon\), or when a work counter reaches \(60\); each iteration adds \(j + 1\) to the counter, where \(j\) is the number of passes through the bracketing loop. Mathews uses \(\delta = \varepsilon = 10^{-10}\) in Examples 1, 2, 3(i) and 4, and \(\delta = \varepsilon = 10^{-14}\) in Examples 3(ii) and 3(iii).
In the tables below \(h_k\) is the step taken from \(\mathbf{P}_k\); since \(\lVert \mathbf{S}_k \rVert = 1\) it is also the distance from \(\mathbf{P}_k\) to \(\mathbf{P}_{k+1}\). \(\mathbf{P}^{*}\) is the minimum the run approaches. Mathews’ own tables, computed in machine arithmetic, print \(12\) decimal places (in scientific notation for the smallest values). Each example says how far they agree with the recomputation. In every one of his tables the first line pairs \(\mathbf{P}_0\) with a function value left over from the previous computation (his program prints \(f(\mathbf{P}_0)\) before evaluating it), so the tables here give the correct \(f(\mathbf{P}_0)\).

Example 2 — Rosenbrock’s parabolic valley, \(f(x, y) = 100(y - x^2)^2 + (1 - x)^2\), from \((0.99, 1.01)\)
Use the gradient method to find the minimum of Rosenbrock’s function (circa 1960),
\[
f(x, y) = 100\,(y - x^2)^2 + (1 - x)^2, \qquad \mathbf{P}_0 = (0.99,\ 1.01).
\]
Step 0 (gradient and minimum):
\[
\nabla f(x, y) = \bigl(-400x\,(y - x^2) - 2(1 - x),\ \ 200\,(y - x^2)\bigr).
\]
The minimum is \(f(1, 1) = 0\), at the end of the curved valley floor \(y = x^2\). There
\[
\mathbf{H}(1, 1) = \begin{pmatrix} 802 & -400 \\ -400 & 200 \end{pmatrix}
\]
has eigenvalues \(0.3993608\) and \(1001.601\), a ratio \(\kappa \approx 2508\): the valley is very narrow.
Step 1 (first iteration): \(f(\mathbf{P}_0) = 0.089501\), \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0) = (-11.8604,\ 5.98)\) and \(\mathbf{S}_0 = (0.8929225,\ -0.4502105)\), almost straight across the valley. The trial step \(h = 1\) is far too long: \(\varphi_0(1) = 892.1648\). The line search halves \(h\) six times, to \(1/64 = 0.015625\), where \(Y_1 = \varphi_0(1/64) = 0.002469813\) lies below both \(Y_0 = 0.089501\) and \(Y_2 = \varphi_0(1/32) = 0.1619027\). Formula (3) then gives
\[
h_0 = 0.01333, \qquad \mathbf{P}_1 = (1.001903,\ 1.003999), \qquad f(\mathbf{P}_1) = 7.222046 \times 10^{-6}.
\]
\(\varphi_0\) is not a quadratic, and its exact minimum is at \(\gamma = 0.01341122\), where \(\varphi_0 = 3.907525 \times 10^{-6}\). Because the step stops short of it, \(\mathbf{S}_1 = (0.8852766,\ -0.4650649)\) points almost the same way as \(\mathbf{S}_0\) (the two differ by \(0.96^\circ\)) instead of turning a right angle.
Step 2 (the full run): the counter reaches \(61\) after \(9\) iterations.

section: Example 3 — Three local minima, \(f(x, y) = 5x^2 + x^4 - 9x^2 y + 3y^2 + 2y^4 + \tfrac14 x\)

title: Steepest Descent - Gradient Search
text:
Example 4 — \(f(x, y) = (x - y)/(x^2 + y^2 + 2)\) from \((-3, -2)\)
Use the gradient method to find the minimum of
\[
f(x, y) = \frac{x - y}{x^2 + y^2 + 2}, \qquad \mathbf{P}_0 = (-3,\ -2).
\]
Step 0 (the minimum): \(\nabla f(-1, 1) = (0, 0)\), \(f(-1, 1) = -\tfrac12\) and \(\mathbf{H}(-1, 1) = \tfrac14 \mathbf{I}\). The minimum is round: near it the level curves are almost circles. The function is also symmetric about the line \(y = -x\), since \(f(-y, -x) = f(x, y)\).
Step 1 (first iteration): from the illustration above, \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0) = (0.04,\ -0.0844444)\) and \(\lVert \nabla f(\mathbf{P}_0) \rVert = 0.09343909\), so
\[
\mathbf{S}_0 = (-0.4280863,\ 0.9037378), \qquad
\varphi_0(\gamma) = \frac{-1 - 1.331824\,\gamma}{2 + (-3 - 0.4280863\,\gamma)^2 + (-2 + 0.9037378\,\gamma)^2}.
\]
The line search starts with \(h = 1\): \(Y_0 = -0.06666667\), \(Y_1 = \varphi_0(1) = -0.1559377\) and \(Y_2 = \varphi_0(2) = -0.2166925\). It doubles \(h\) twice, to \(4\), where \(Y_1 = \varphi_0(4) = -0.2359675\) and \(Y_2 = \varphi_0(8) = -0.1650125\). Formula (3) gives
\[
h_0 = 4.818676, \qquad \mathbf{P}_1 = (-5.062809,\ 2.354820), \qquad f(\mathbf{P}_1) = -0.2235760 .
\]
The exact minimum of \(\varphi_0\) is at \(\gamma = 3.292600\), where \(\varphi_0 = -0.2404550\): the parabola through \(\gamma = 0, 4, 8\) overshoots it. Mathews’ textbook works this same iteration (its Example 8.9), and there \(4.8186760\) is called the minimum of \(\varphi_0\). It is the single quadratic-interpolation estimate, not the minimum.
Step 2 (second iteration): \(\nabla f(\mathbf{P}_1) = (-0.03809377,\ 0.001596349)\) and \(\mathbf{S}_1 = (0.9991231,\ -0.04186903)\), at \(117.75^\circ\) to \(\mathbf{S}_0\). The trial step \(0.8186760\) is doubled twice, to \(3.274704\), and
\[
h_1 = 2.770828, \qquad \mathbf{P}_2 = (-2.294411,\ 2.238808), \qquad f(\mathbf{P}_2) = -0.3692574,
\]
while the exact minimum of \(\varphi_1\) is at \(\gamma = 3.891620\). The textbook’s \(\mathbf{P}_1\), \(\mathbf{S}_1\), \(h_1\) and \(\mathbf{P}_2\) agree with these values.
Step 3 (the full run): the run ends after \(8\) iterations because the tolerances are met (the counter stands at \(47\)).

The first step lowers \(f\) but moves away from the minimum, from a distance of \(3.606\) to \(4.283\), and the first directions are far from perpendicular (\(117.75^\circ\) and \(40.86^\circ\)). From \(\mathbf{P}_2\) on, every search direction is within \(1.75^\circ\) of \((1, -1)/\sqrt2\), within \(0.18^\circ\) from \(\mathbf{P}_3\) on, and the iterates close in on the mirror line \(y = -x\) (\(x_3 + y_3 = -0.002002\), \(x_4 + y_4 = -1.117 \times 10^{-4}\)). Near the round minimum \(-\nabla f\) points almost straight at \((-1, 1)\), so there is no zigzag. Each step lands much closer than the last: the distances fall by factors \(0.31\), \(0.19\), \(0.049\), \(0.0026\), \(5.0 \times 10^{-6}\) and \(8.2 \times 10^{-10}\).

Mathews’ table agrees with rows \(1\) to \(7\) to within \(9.1 \times 10^{-13}\), but it has a ninth iteration and prints \((-0.999999998992,\ 0.999999998992)\) for both \(\mathbf{P}_8\) and \(\mathbf{P}_9\). That is rounding error: so close to the minimum, \(f\) differs from \(-\tfrac12\) by less than machine arithmetic can resolve, and the quadratic fit (3) divides one rounding error by another.

Example 5 — Drawing the iterations
Mathews’ last example returns to the quadratic of Example 1 with a version of the program that draws each step. On a contour plot of \(f\) over \([2.5, 3.05] \times [1.6, 2.15]\) it draws the level curve of \(f\) through \(\mathbf{P}_k\), the search line from \(\mathbf{P}_k\) in the direction \(\mathbf{S}_k\), and the three trial points \(\mathbf{P}_k\), \(\mathbf{P}_k + h\mathbf{S}_k\) and \(\mathbf{P}_k + 2h\mathbf{S}_k\), then marks the new point. This version also differs in detail from the program above: it starts with \(h = 0.2\), stops when the counter reaches \(20\), and takes \(h_k = h/3\) when the three trial values do not lie on an upward parabola. The starting point and the output of this example survive only in images that are missing from the archive, so the run cannot be reproduced. Its plotting window contains \((3, 2)\), the minimum of Example 1, whose run is tabulated in full above.

title: Nelder Mead Method
text:
Description
The Nelder-Mead method searches for a local minimum of a function \(f\) of \(n\) variables using only values of \(f\), never its derivatives. It keeps a simplex of \(n + 1\) points, which for two variables is a triangle. At each step the vertices are ranked by their function values as best \(\mathbf{B}\), good \(\mathbf{G}\) and worst \(\mathbf{W}\), and \(\mathbf{W}\) is replaced by a better point on the line from \(\mathbf{W}\) through the midpoint \(\mathbf{M}\) of the opposite side. If the test points on that line fail, the whole triangle is shrunk toward \(\mathbf{B}\). In the examples below the triangles change shape as they move downhill and become much smaller as they close in on a minimum: in the 50-step run of Example 1 the last triangle is more than \(100{,}000\) times smaller across than the first. Nelder and Mead introduced the method, and it is also known as the polytope method.
The candidate points are the reflection \(\mathbf{R}\) of \(\mathbf{W}\) through \(\mathbf{M}\), the expansion \(\mathbf{E}\) beyond it, and two contraction points \(\mathbf{C}_1\) and \(\mathbf{C}_2\) halfway between \(\mathbf{M}\) and \(\mathbf{W}\) or \(\mathbf{R}\):
\[
\mathbf{M} = \frac{\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{G}}{2}, \qquad
\mathbf{R} = 2\mathbf{M} - \mathbf{W}, \qquad
\mathbf{E} = 2\mathbf{R} - \mathbf{M}, \qquad
\mathbf{C}_1 = \frac{\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{M}}{2}, \qquad
\mathbf{C}_2 = \frac{\mathbf{M} + \mathbf{R}}{2}.
\]
The shrink replaces \(\mathbf{G}\) by \(\mathbf{M}\) and \(\mathbf{W}\) by \(\mathbf{S} = (\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{W})/2\). Mathews works in two variables. He gives two sets of rules for choosing among these points, the decision table of his textbook and the shorter rule of his Mathematica program, and both are set out below. Every run on this page has been computed in exact rational arithmetic.

title: Nelder Mead Method
text:
Animations
Each animation below shows the triangles of a Nelder-Mead search on a contour plot of \(f\), one step per frame. As in the pictures Mathews’ graphics program draws in Example 4, every triangle so far is outlined, the current triangle is filled cyan and the vertices are red dots; grey contours of \(f\) and a green × at each minimum are added. All three runs use Mathews’ subroutine rule (accept the first of \(\mathbf{E}\), \(\mathbf{R}\), \(\mathbf{C}_1\), \(\mathbf{C}_2\) whose value is below \(f(\mathbf{W})\), otherwise shrink), computed in exact rational arithmetic with the tie conventions given in Logical Decisions for Each Step, and their triangles are those of the tables in the worked examples. In Cases 1 and 2 the right panel shows the step just taken: the triangle before the step (dashed, with its vertices labelled \(\mathbf{B}\), \(\mathbf{G}\), \(\mathbf{W}\)), the midpoint \(\mathbf{M}\), the dotted line from \(\mathbf{W}\) through \(\mathbf{M}\), the test points in the order the subroutine evaluates them (a hollow circle for each one rejected, a star for the one accepted) and the new triangle. Its title compares each test value with \(f(\mathbf{W})\), printing as many digits as it takes to tell them apart.
Mathews’ module links one animation, “Nelder-Mead Search”, but the archived animation page shows only an “Under Construction” banner and no animation, so it is not known whether he ever made it. Case 1 turns the 16 static pictures of his Example 4 into an animation, in his window; Cases 2 and 3 are new, with no Mathews original. Not animated are the textbook rules of Table 8.5 and their run in Example 1 (Mathews’ Table 8.6), steps 16 to 50 of the 50-step run of Example 1, the run with \(\epsilon = 10^{-10}\) in Example 2, the FindMinimum comparisons of Exercise 3, and Mathews’ static surface and contour plots of \(f\) in Examples 1 and 4 and Exercise 3.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Mathews’ Example 4, \(f(x, y) = x^2 - 4x + y^2 - y - xy\), starting triangle \((0, 0)\), \((1.2, 0)\), \((0, 0.8)\), \(15\) steps
Behavior: Steps 1 and 2 expand to \(\mathbf{E} = (1.8, 1.2)\) and reflect to \(\mathbf{R} = (3, 0.4)\). At step 3 the subroutine takes \(\mathbf{E} = (4.8, 2.4)\), because \(f(\mathbf{E}) = -4.32 < f(\mathbf{W}) = -3.36\), and step 4 rejects \(\mathbf{E} = (-2.4, -2.4)\) and \(\mathbf{R} = (0, -0.8)\) and contracts to \(\mathbf{C}_1 = (3.6, 1.6)\), the reflection point that step 3 passed over. The frame of step 6 shows the tie \(f(\mathbf{R}) = f(\mathbf{W}) = -5.88\): \(\mathbf{R} = (4.2, 2.8)\) fails the strict test, and the triangle contracts to \(\mathbf{C}_1 = (2.4, 1.6)\). Mathews’ floating-point run took \(\mathbf{R}\) there, so from step 6 on each new triangle in his pictures is the mirror image through \((3, 2)\) of the triangle here one step earlier (see Example 4). The \(15\) steps are \(2\) expansions, \(3\) reflections and \(10\) contractions to \(\mathbf{C}_1\), and steps 10 to 15 are all contractions, which close in on the minimum: after step 15, \(\mathbf{B} = (2.989709, 1.979285)\) is \(0.0231\) from \((3, 2)\), with \(f(\mathbf{B}) = -6.999678\). The left panel is Mathews’ window \([0, 5] \times [0, 3]\), widened by \(0.1\) on each side so that the vertices on its edges show whole.

title: Nelder Mead Method
section: The Triangle and Its Test Points
text:
The Triangle and Its Test Points






NoteDefinition — The triangle \(\mathbf{BGW}\)



Let \(f(x, y)\) be the function to be minimised, and let \(\mathbf{V}_k = (x_k, y_k)\), \(k = 1, 2, 3\), be the vertices of a triangle. Evaluate \(z_k = f(x_k, y_k)\) and renumber the vertices so that \(z_1 \le z_2 \le z_3\). Then \[
\mathbf{B} = (x_1, y_1), \qquad \mathbf{G} = (x_2, y_2), \qquad \mathbf{W} = (x_3, y_3)
\tag{1}
\] are the best, good (next to best) and worst vertices.


Midpoint of the good side. The construction uses the midpoint of the side \(\mathbf{BG}\), the side opposite \(\mathbf{W}\): \[
\mathbf{M} = \frac{\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{G}}{2} = \left( \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2},\ \frac{y_1 + y_2}{2} \right).
\tag{2}
\]
Reflection. The values fall from \(\mathbf{W}\) to \(\mathbf{B}\) and from \(\mathbf{W}\) to \(\mathbf{G}\), so \(f\) may well take smaller values on the far side of the line \(\mathbf{BG}\), away from \(\mathbf{W}\). The test point \(\mathbf{R}\) is found by reflecting the triangle through the side \(\mathbf{BG}\): if \(d\) is the length of the segment from \(\mathbf{W}\) to \(\mathbf{M}\), extend that segment a further distance \(d\) through \(\mathbf{M}\). In vector form, \[
\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{M} + (\mathbf{M} - \mathbf{W}) = 2\mathbf{M} - \mathbf{W}.
\tag{3}
\]
Expansion. If \(f(\mathbf{R})\) is smaller than \(f(\mathbf{W})\), the move was in a good direction, and the minimum may lie a little farther on. Extend the segment through \(\mathbf{M}\) and \(\mathbf{R}\) by another distance \(d\) to the point \[
\mathbf{E} = \mathbf{R} + (\mathbf{R} - \mathbf{M}) = 2\mathbf{R} - \mathbf{M},
\tag{4}
\] which forms the expanded triangle \(\mathbf{BGE}\).
Contraction. If \(f(\mathbf{R})\) is no better than \(f(\mathbf{W})\), another point must be tested. The function may be smaller at \(\mathbf{M}\), but \(\mathbf{W}\) cannot be replaced by \(\mathbf{M}\), because \(\mathbf{B}\), \(\mathbf{G}\) and \(\mathbf{M}\) lie on one line and would not form a triangle. Instead, take the midpoints of the segments \(\mathbf{WM}\) and \(\mathbf{MR}\): \[
\mathbf{C}_1 = \frac{\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{M}}{2}, \qquad \mathbf{C}_2 = \frac{\mathbf{M} + \mathbf{R}}{2}.
\tag{5}
\] In the textbook rules, the one with the smaller function value is called \(\mathbf{C}\), and the new triangle is \(\mathbf{BGC}\). Mathews notes that the choice between \(\mathbf{C}_1\) and \(\mathbf{C}_2\) may seem unnecessary in two dimensions but matters in higher dimensions.
Shrink toward \(\mathbf{B}\). If \(f(\mathbf{C})\) is not less than \(f(\mathbf{W})\), the points \(\mathbf{G}\) and \(\mathbf{W}\) are shrunk toward \(\mathbf{B}\). \(\mathbf{G}\) is replaced by \(\mathbf{M}\), the midpoint of \(\mathbf{BG}\), and \(\mathbf{W}\) by the midpoint of \(\mathbf{BW}\), \[
\mathbf{S} = \frac{\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{W}}{2}.
\tag{6}
\]
All the test points lie on the line through \(\mathbf{W}\) and \(\mathbf{M}\), at \(\mathbf{M} + t\,(\mathbf{M} - \mathbf{W})\) with \(t = 1\) for \(\mathbf{R}\), \(t = 2\) for \(\mathbf{E}\), \(t = -\tfrac12\) for \(\mathbf{C}_1\) and \(t = \tfrac12\) for \(\mathbf{C}_2\), and the shrink halves the distances from \(\mathbf{B}\). In general terms, these are reflection, expansion, contraction and shrink coefficients of \(1\), \(2\), \(\tfrac12\) and \(\tfrac12\).
More variables. Mathews states the algorithm for a continuous function \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\) of \(n\) variables, starting from \(n + 1\) points \(\mathbf{V}_k = (v_{k,1}, \ldots, v_{k,n})\), \(k = 1, \ldots, n + 1\). In the general form of the method the vertices are ordered so that \(f(\mathbf{V}_1) \le \cdots \le f(\mathbf{V}_{n+1})\). The worst vertex \(\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{V}_{n+1}\) is then moved along the line through the centroid of the other \(n\) vertices, \[
\mathbf{M} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \mathbf{V}_k,
\] with formulas (3) to (5) unchanged, and the shrink replaces every \(\mathbf{V}_k\), \(k \ge 2\), by \((\mathbf{V}_1 + \mathbf{V}_k)/2\). For \(n = 2\) this is the triangle construction above.

title: Nelder Mead Method
text:
Logical Decisions for Each Step
An efficient implementation evaluates \(f\) only where it needs to. Each step finds one new vertex to replace \(\mathbf{W}\) (or performs the shrink), and the step ends as soon as that vertex is found. Mathews’ textbook (Mathews and Fink, Numerical Methods Using MATLAB, 4th edition, 2004, Section 8.2, Table 8.5, which the module’s proof page links) gives the decisions as two cases:






ImportantAlgorithm — Nelder-Mead step, textbook rules



Order the vertices as \(\mathbf{B}, \mathbf{G}, \mathbf{W}\), and compute \(\mathbf{M}\), \(\mathbf{R}\) and \(f(\mathbf{R})\).
Case (i), \(f(\mathbf{R}) < f(\mathbf{G})\) (reflect or expand):

if \(f(\mathbf{B}) < f(\mathbf{R})\), replace \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{R}\);
otherwise compute \(\mathbf{E}\) and \(f(\mathbf{E})\). If \(f(\mathbf{E}) < f(\mathbf{B})\), replace \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{E}\); otherwise replace \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{R}\).

Case (ii), \(f(\mathbf{R}) \ge f(\mathbf{G})\) (contract or shrink):

if \(f(\mathbf{R}) < f(\mathbf{W})\), replace \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{R}\);
compute \(\mathbf{C}_1 = (\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{M})/2\) and \(\mathbf{C}_2 = (\mathbf{M} + \mathbf{R})/2\), and let \(\mathbf{C}\) be the one with the smaller value of \(f\);
if \(f(\mathbf{C}) < f(\mathbf{W})\), replace \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{C}\); otherwise compute \(\mathbf{S} = (\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{W})/2\), replace \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{S}\) and \(\mathbf{G}\) with \(\mathbf{M}\).



Read as printed, case (ii) goes on to the contraction even after \(\mathbf{W}\) has been replaced by \(\mathbf{R}\). In that event the new \(\mathbf{W}\) is \(\mathbf{R}\), and both contraction points are the midpoint of \(\mathbf{MR}\).
The Mathematica subroutine Nelder2D in Mathews’ module, which produces the runs in every example whose output survives, uses a shorter rule. It tests the candidates in a fixed order and takes the first one that is better than \(\mathbf{W}\):






ImportantAlgorithm — Nelder-Mead step, Mathews’ subroutine



Compute \(\mathbf{M}\), \(\mathbf{R}\), \(\mathbf{E}\), and then, as needed, \(\mathbf{C}_1\) and \(\mathbf{C}_2\).

If \(f(\mathbf{E}) < f(\mathbf{W})\), replace \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{E}\).
Otherwise, if \(f(\mathbf{R}) < f(\mathbf{W})\), replace \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{R}\).
Otherwise, if \(f(\mathbf{C}_1) < f(\mathbf{W})\), replace \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{C}_1\).
Otherwise, if \(f(\mathbf{C}_2) < f(\mathbf{W})\), replace \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{C}_2\).
Otherwise shrink: replace \(\mathbf{W}\) with \((\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{W})/2\) and \(\mathbf{G}\) with \((\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{G})/2 = \mathbf{M}\).

Then reorder the three vertices as \(\mathbf{B}, \mathbf{G}, \mathbf{W}\).


The two rules use the same points but can choose differently:

The subroutine accepts \(\mathbf{E}\) whenever it is better than \(\mathbf{W}\), even when \(\mathbf{R}\) is better still. The textbook expands only when \(f(\mathbf{R}) \le f(\mathbf{B})\), and keeps \(\mathbf{E}\) only if \(f(\mathbf{E}) < f(\mathbf{B})\). Step 3 of Example 4 shows the subroutine taking a worse point this way.
The subroutine accepts \(\mathbf{R}\) whenever it is better than \(\mathbf{W}\). The textbook, when \(f(\mathbf{G}) \le f(\mathbf{R}) < f(\mathbf{W})\), replaces \(\mathbf{W}\) with \(\mathbf{R}\) and then still tries a contraction.
The subroutine tries \(\mathbf{C}_1\) before \(\mathbf{C}_2\). The textbook takes the better of the two.

Stopping. Mathews’ first subroutine runs a fixed number of steps. His “more efficient” version stores the function values instead of recomputing them and stops as soon as \[
f(\mathbf{W}) \le f(\mathbf{B}) + \epsilon .
\tag{7}
\] It always takes at least one step and never more than \(99\). This is a test on function values only: it stops when the three vertices have nearly equal values, not when the triangle is small.
What every step guarantees. These facts hold for both rules and any \(f\). A step that is not a shrink replaces \(\mathbf{W}\) by a point whose value is less than \(f(\mathbf{W})\), because each replacement above is made only after such a test. No step removes \(\mathbf{B}\) unless it finds a point with a smaller value, and a shrink keeps \(\mathbf{B}\). So \(f(\mathbf{B})\) never increases. Nothing in the rules makes the triangle converge to a minimum, though: the method is a search heuristic, and the module gives no convergence theorem.






WarningTies and round-off



All the tests are strict inequalities, so when two values are equal the result depends on how the tie is broken, and in floating-point arithmetic on how the rounding falls. In the runs below, vertices with equal values are listed with the smaller \(x\)-coordinate first, then the smaller \(y\), and \(\mathbf{C}_1\) is taken when \(f(\mathbf{C}_1) = f(\mathbf{C}_2)\). Example 1 meets exact ties within its first six steps. Its \(f\) is symmetric about the minimum, \(f(3 + u, 2 + v) = f(3 - u, 2 - v)\), and each tie is between two points that are mirror images through \((3, 2)\). Mathews’ machine-precision run takes a different path from the sixth step on (see Example 4).

title: Nelder Mead Method
text:
Example 1 — A quadratic function
Use the Nelder-Mead method to find the minimum of \[
f(x, y) = x^2 - 4x + y^2 - y - xy
