Scanning \(r\) from \(1.0001\) to \(60\) in \(200{,}000\) steps, the largest real part of the roots of (3) is negative at every sample with \(r < 470/19\) and positive at every sample with \(r > 470/19\). Near \(C_\pm\) at \(r = r_H\) a solution turns about the point with angular frequency \(\omega = \sqrt{1760/19} \approx 9.6245\), a period of \(2\pi/\omega \approx 0.6528\).

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
Runge-Kutta Method for Systems
Mathews writes the three equations as one vector equation,
\[
\mathbf{Z}' = \mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z}), \qquad \mathbf{Z}(t_0) = \mathbf{Z}_0, \qquad \mathbf{Z} = (x, y, z), \quad \mathbf{F} = (f_1, f_2, f_3),
\]
on an interval \(t_0 \le t \le t_m\) divided into \(m\) subintervals.






ImportantRunge-Kutta method in three dimensions



With \(h = (t_m - t_0)/m\) and \(t_j = t_0 + j\,h\), for \(j = 0, 1, \ldots, m - 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{k}_1 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j, \mathbf{Z}_j), \\
\mathbf{k}_2 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + \tfrac h2, \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac12\mathbf{k}_1\bigr), \\
\mathbf{k}_3 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + \tfrac h2, \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac12\mathbf{k}_2\bigr), \\
\mathbf{k}_4 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j + h, \mathbf{Z}_j + \mathbf{k}_3), \\
\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} &= \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac16\bigl(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]


This is the scalar Runge-Kutta method of order 4 with every quantity replaced by a vector; Mathews’ subroutine returns the list of points \(\mathbf{Z}_0, \mathbf{Z}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{Z}_m\). For a smooth \(\mathbf{F}\) its global error on a fixed interval is \(O(h^4)\). On the Lorenz system this holds over a short interval: for the start of Example 1, the error at \(t = 0.5\) falls by the factors \(21.0\), \(18.4\), \(17.2\), \(16.5\) and \(16.3\) as \(h\) is halved from \(0.02\) to \(0.000625\), approaching \(2^4 = 16\). Over longer intervals the chaos takes over, as Example 1 shows. Mathews remarks that the curve “twists a lot in 3D space” and uses about \(1000\) subintervals to draw it with good resolution.






WarningWhat survives in the archive



Mathews’ module states each example’s equations and initial values, but the intervals, step counts, plots and output of his solutions were images that are missing from the archive; only his remarks between them survive. Where this page needs a value his surviving text does not give (an interval, a number of steps, and the initial values in Examples 3 and 4), it says so and states the value it uses.

title: Lorenz Attractor
text:
The Rössler Attractor
In 1976 Otto Rössler, studying oscillations in chemical reactions, proposed a system with a chaotic attractor that has only one nonlinear term. Mathews notes that Rössler was looking for a minimal system that would show chaos, and that his system looks simpler than the Lorenz system but is harder to analyze.






NoteDefinition — Rössler system



The Rössler system is
\[
x' = -(y + z), \qquad y' = x + a\,y, \qquad z' = b + x\,z - c\,z,
\tag{6}
\]
with positive parameters \(a\), \(b\), \(c\). Rössler used \(a = 0.2\), \(b = 0.2\), \(c = 5.7\); Mathews gives \(a = 0.343\), \(b = 1.82\), \(c = 9.75\) as values that produce Rössler’s “screw” chaos.


While \(z\) is small, the first two equations make a solution spiral outward around the \(z\)-axis. Once \(x\) exceeds \(c\), the factor \(x - c\) in \(z' = b + (x - c)\,z\) is positive and \(z\) grows rapidly; the large \(z\) then drives \(x\) down through \(x' = -(y + z)\), \(z\) collapses, and the solution starts a new spiral closer to the \(z\)-axis. In Example 5, after each of the first six spikes with \(z > 5\), the distance from the \(z\)-axis drops from a maximum of \(10.4\) to \(12.4\) in the three time units before the spike to a minimum of \(1.8\) to \(5.0\) within four time units after it.
Equilibrium points. From \(y' = 0\), \(y = -x/a\); from \(x' = 0\), \(z = -y = x/a\); and \(z' = 0\) then gives \(x^2 - c\,x + a\,b = 0\). When \(c^2 > 4ab\) there are two equilibria,
\[
x = \frac{c \pm \sqrt{c^2 - 4ab}}{2}, \qquad y = -\frac{x}{a}, \qquad z = \frac{x}{a}.
\tag{7}
\]

title: Frobenius Series Solution
text:
Description
A second-order linear differential equation \(P(x)\,y'' + Q(x)\,y' + R(x)\,y = 0\) with polynomial or analytic coefficients has power-series solutions \(\sum c_n (x - x_0)^n\) about any point \(x_0\) where \(P(x_0) \ne 0\). At a point such as \(x = 0\) where \(P(0) = 0\), the coefficients of the normalised equation \(y'' + (Q/P)\,y' + (R/P)\,y = 0\) blow up, and a solution may behave like \(x^{1/2}\), \(x^{-1}\) or \(\ln x\) there, which no power series can reproduce. The method of Frobenius handles the mildest such point, a regular singular point, by multiplying the power series by a power of \(x\) that is not fixed in advance:
\[
y(x) = x^{r} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n x^{n} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n x^{n+r}, \qquad c_0 \ne 0.
\]
Substituting this series into the equation and setting the coefficient of the lowest power of \(x\) to zero gives the indicial equation \(r(r-1) + p_0 r + q_0 = 0\) (with \(p_0\) and \(q_0\) read off the equation, as defined below), whose roots are the admissible exponents \(r\). Setting the coefficient of every higher power to zero gives a recurrence that produces \(c_1, c_2, \ldots\) from \(c_0\). Each root of the indicial equation can give one solution; whether the second root gives a second solution depends on how the two roots differ. Examples 2 and 3 show the usual case of two Frobenius solutions, and Examples 1, 4 and 5 the special cases of roots that are equal or differ by an integer.
Mathews works five equations: three that have elementary or Bessel-function solutions, and Bessel’s equations of order \(0\) and \(1\), whose Frobenius series define \(J_0(x)\) and (up to a factor \(2\)) \(J_1(x)\). He then uses the series to prove \(J_0'(x) = -J_1(x)\) and applies \(J_0\) to the radial vibrations of a circular drum, where the zeros of \(J_0\) fix the drum’s frequencies and the circles that stay at rest. Every coefficient, closed form, zero and radius below has been recomputed: the series by solving the equations power by power in exact rational arithmetic, and the numbers in 30- or 40-digit arithmetic.

title: Frobenius Series Solution
text:
Animations
The first animation shows partial sums of a Frobenius series closing in on the solution they define, two more powers of \(x\) (one more nonzero term) per frame. Its top row plots the partial sums against the closed form, and its bottom row the error on a logarithmic scale, with green shading over \(0 < x < x^*\), the interval where the error stays below \(10^{-3}\) (the \(x^*\) of the tables below). The other two animate the vibrating drum. The second sweeps the separation constant \(\lambda\) and shows why only the zeros of \(J_0\) give a drum whose rim stays still. The third shows the first three normal modes vibrating, as surfaces over the drum and as cross-sections through its centre. As in Mathews’ graphs of the drum, pink marks displacement above the rest position and cyan below it.
Mathews’ module links no animation, and his animation archive has none for this module, so all three animations are new, with no Mathews original. (The archive’s Maclaurin- and Taylor-series animations of Bessel functions belong to his Taylor polynomial module.) Case 1 animates Example 1. The partial sums of Examples 2 to 5 are not animated: each would look like Case 1, and their tables give the same information. Example 6 is an identity with no graph. Example 7’s static plots of \(J_0\) on \([-15, 15]\) and of \(Y_0\) are not animated, but Case 2 shows \(J_0\) in Mathews’ Example 8 window. Mathews’ disk diagrams of Example 10 are replaced by the nodal circles drawn on the surfaces of Case 3. The scripts find the zeros \(\lambda_n\) as Mathews does, with a root finder started at \(n\pi\) (here Newton’s method, in 256-bit arithmetic).
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Both Frobenius solutions of Example 1, \(r = \pm\tfrac12\), partial sums through \(x^N\) for \(N = 0, 2, \ldots, 20\), on \(0 < x \le 10\)
Behavior: The factor \(x^r\) is part of every partial sum \(S_N(x) = x^r \sum_{n=0}^{N} c_n x^n\). So the partial sums of \(y_2 = \cos x/\sqrt{x}\) grow without bound like \(x^{-1/2}\) as \(x \to 0^+\), just as \(y_2\) does, and their error still tends to \(0\) there. A partial sum fails far from \(0\), not near it. The interval where the error stays below \(10^{-3}\) widens with every new partial sum, from \(x^* = 0.1292\) at \(N = 0\) to \(x^* = 7.319\) at \(N = 20\) for \(y_1\), and from \(0.01587\) to \(6.939\) for \(y_2\). From \(N = 8\) on, each further nonzero term (two more powers of \(x\)) moves \(x^*\) about \(0.76\) farther out. For every \(N\), \(x^*\) is smaller for \(y_2\) than for \(y_1\). The values for \(N = 4, 8, \ldots, 20\) are those in the table of Example 1. On \(0.1 \le x \le 10\), \(S_N\) lies above the solution for \(N = 0, 4, 8, \ldots, 20\) and below it for \(N = 2, 6, \ldots, 18\). The only error curve that falls back below \(10^{-3}\) beyond its \(x^*\) is that of \(S_0\) for \(y_2\). There \(S_0 = x^{-1/2}\) touches \(y_2\) at \(x = 2\pi\), where \(\cos x = 1\), and the error is below \(10^{-3}\) again for \(6.213 < x < 6.354\). Mathews’ graphs of this example are lost, so the window is chosen here.

Below each, the error on a log scale with the tolerance 10⁻³ dashed. The shaded interval where the error stays below 10⁻³ grows from 0 < x < 0.1292 to 0 < x < 7.319 for y1 and from 0 < x < 0.01587 to 0 < x < 6.939 for y2




Case 2 — The rim condition \(J_0(\lambda) = 0\) (Examples 8 and 9), \(\lambda\) from \(0\) to \(\lambda_5\)
Behavior: The drum’s radial profile is \(R(r) = J_0(\lambda r)\) on \(0 \le r \le 1\). This is the stretch \(0 \le x \le \lambda\) of the graph of \(J_0\) (blue, left) squeezed into the drum’s radius (right, a cross-section through the centre). The rim value is \(J_0(\lambda)\), the red dot. At \(\lambda = 0\) the profile is flat at height \(1\). As \(\lambda\) grows in steps of \(0.2\), the rim value is zero only when \(\lambda\) is one of the zeros \(\lambda_1 = 2.405\), \(\lambda_2 = 5.520\), \(\lambda_3 = 8.654\), \(\lambda_4 = 11.79\) and \(\lambda_5 = 14.93\) of Example 8, and the animation pauses at each of them. Only these values give a drum fixed at its rim, and the profile at each pause is the mode shape \(J_0(\lambda_n x)\) of Example 9. Every time \(\lambda\) passes a zero, the rim value changes sign, because the zeros are simple (\(J_0'(\lambda_n) = -J_1(\lambda_n) \ne 0\)), and a new node enters at the rim. The nodes \(r = \lambda_k/\lambda\) then move inward as \(\lambda\) grows. So mode \(n\) has \(n - 1\) nodal circles, at the radii in the table of the vibrating-drum section below, which the titles give to four figures. Between \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) the rim value has its minimum \(J_0(3.8317) = -0.40276\). The sweep comes closest at \(\lambda = 3.8\), whose frame shows \(-0.4026\). The window on the left is Mathews’ Example 8 window \([0, 5\pi] \times [-0.5, 1]\), and on the right the window \([-1, 1] \times [-0.45, 1]\) of his Example 10 cross-sections. Both tops are raised to \(1.05\) so that the value \(J_0(0) = 1\) is not drawn on the frame edge.

Right: the drum’s cross-section J0(λ|x|) on −1 ≤ x ≤ 1, pink where positive and cyan where negative, with its nodes and its rim value. Case 3 — The normal modes \(u_n(t, r) = J_0(\lambda_n r)\cos(\lambda_n t)\) for \(n = 1, 2, 3\) (Example 10), one period each
Behavior: Each mode is a standing wave. The fixed shape \(J_0(\lambda_n r)\) is scaled by \(\cos(\lambda_n t)\), so the drum head is flat at a quarter and at three quarters of a period, and upside down at half a period, when its centre is at \(-1\). The rim and the nodal circles never move. Mode 1 has no nodal circle, mode 2 has one at \(r = 0.4357\), and mode 3 has two, at \(r = 0.2779\) and \(0.6379\). Neighbouring regions between them move in opposite directions: when pink rises, cyan falls, and vice versa. The three columns share the phase \(\lambda_n t\), not the time. Each runs through its own period, \(2.613\), \(1.138\) and \(0.7261\), in 24 frames, so in real time mode 2 vibrates \(2.2954\) and mode 3 \(3.5985\) times as fast as mode 1. Unlike a string’s overtones, these are not whole-number multiples. Mathews’ box for these surfaces, \([-1, 1]^2 \times [-0.45, 1]\) with height ratio \(0.3\), holds only the initial shapes. Over a period the centre reaches \(-1\), so the box here runs from \(-1.05\) to \(1.05\) in height and is drawn with the plotting library’s default proportions. The lines for the rim and the nodal circles are drawn over the surface, so their far halves stay visible even where the surface would hide them. The surface is drawn on a \(201 \times 201\) grid with the points outside the disk left out, which makes its edge slightly ragged.

title: Frobenius Series Solution
text:
Background
Write the equation as
\[
P(x)\,y''(x) + Q(x)\,y'(x) + R(x)\,y(x) = 0,
\tag{1}
\]
divide by \(P(x)\), and set \(f_1(x) = Q(x)/P(x)\) and \(f_2(x) = R(x)/P(x)\), so that
\[
y''(x) + f_1(x)\,y'(x) + f_2(x)\,y(x) = 0.
\tag{2}
\]






NoteDefinition — Analytic function



The functions \(f_1(x)\) and \(f_2(x)\) are analytic at \(x_0\) if they have Taylor series expansions about \(x_0\) with radii of convergence \(\rho_1 > 0\) and \(\rho_2 > 0\):
\[
f_1(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n (x - x_0)^n \quad \text{for } |x - x_0| < \rho_1, \qquad
f_2(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} b_n (x - x_0)^n \quad \text{for } |x - x_0| < \rho_2.
\]








NoteDefinition — Ordinary point and singular point



If \(f_1 = Q/P\) and \(f_2 = R/P\) are both analytic at \(x_0\), then \(x_0\) is an ordinary point of (1). Otherwise \(x_0\) is a singular point of (1).








NoteDefinition — Regular singular point



Let \(x_0\) be a singular point of (1). If \((x - x_0)\,Q(x)/P(x)\) and \((x - x_0)^2\,R(x)/P(x)\) are analytic at \(x_0\), with expansions
\[
(x - x_0)\frac{Q(x)}{P(x)} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} p_n (x - x_0)^n \quad \text{for } |x - x_0| < \rho_1, \qquad
(x - x_0)^2\frac{R(x)}{P(x)} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} q_n (x - x_0)^n \quad \text{for } |x - x_0| < \rho_2,
\]
then \(x_0\) is a regular singular point of (1). In words: \(f_1\) has at worst a simple pole at \(x_0\) and \(f_2\) at worst a double pole.


All of Mathews’ examples have their singular point at \(x_0 = 0\), and from here on \(x_0 = 0\) and \(x > 0\).

title: Frobenius Series Solution
text:
The Method of Frobenius
The method is named for the German mathematician Ferdinand Georg Frobenius (1849–1917). At a regular singular point \(x_0 = 0\) of (1), look for a solution in the form of a Frobenius series
\[
y(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n x^{n+r}, \qquad c_0 \ne 0,
\tag{3}
\]
where the exponent \(r\) may be negative or fractional. When the series is substituted into the equation, \(r\) must make the coefficient of the lowest power of \(x\) vanish; the remaining coefficients then give a recurrence for \(c_n\).






NoteDefinition — Indicial equation



The exponent \(r\) in (3) is a root of the indicial equation
\[
F(r) = r(r - 1) + p_0\, r + q_0 = 0,
\qquad
p_0 = \lim_{x \to 0} x\,\frac{Q(x)}{P(x)}, \quad
q_0 = \lim_{x \to 0} x^2\,\frac{R(x)}{P(x)}.
\tag{4}
\]
Its roots \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) are the exponents of the singular point.


Derivation. Multiply (2) by \(x^2\) and write it as
\[
x^2 y'' + x\,\bigl(x f_1(x)\bigr)\, y' + \bigl(x^2 f_2(x)\bigr)\, y = 0,
\qquad
x f_1(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} p_k x^k, \quad x^2 f_2(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} q_k x^k.
\]
With \(y = \sum c_n x^{n+r}\) we have \(x^2 y'' = \sum (n+r)(n+r-1)\,c_n x^{n+r}\) and \(x y' = \sum (n+r)\,c_n x^{n+r}\). Multiplying the series together (Cauchy products) and collecting the coefficient of \(x^{n+r}\) gives, for \(n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\),
\[
(n+r)(n+r-1)\,c_n + \sum_{k=0}^{n} c_k \bigl[(r+k)\,p_{n-k} + q_{n-k}\bigr] = 0.
\]
For \(n = 0\) this is \(c_0\,[r(r-1) + p_0 r + q_0] = 0\), and since \(c_0 \ne 0\) it is the indicial equation (4). For \(n \ge 1\), splitting off the term \(k = n\) gives the general recursive formula
\[
F(r + n)\, c_n = -\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} c_k \bigl[(r+k)\,p_{n-k} + q_{n-k}\bigr], \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots
\tag{5}
\]
Formula (5) works for any equation, but in practice the series for \(x f_1\) and \(x^2 f_2\) are short (in every example below they are polynomials with one or two terms), and substituting (3) directly gives a recurrence of only two terms. That is what the examples do. Both routes were checked against each other: formula (5) and the direct recurrence give the same coefficients through \(c_8\) for the first solution of every example and for the second solutions of Examples 2 and 3. (For \(r = -\tfrac12\) in Example 1, formula (5) would divide by \(F(\tfrac12) = 0\) at \(n = 1\); that case is treated directly.)






TipTheorem — Frobenius series solutions (general statement)



Let \(x_0 = 0\) be a regular singular point of (1), let the series for \(x f_1(x)\) and \(x^2 f_2(x)\) converge for \(|x| < \rho\), and let the roots of the indicial equation be real, with \(r_1 \ge r_2\). Then:

There is a Frobenius series solution \(y_1 = x^{r_1} \sum c_n x^n\) with \(c_0 = 1\), and the series converges at least for \(0 < x < \rho\).
If \(r_1 - r_2\) is not an integer, there is a second, independent Frobenius series solution \(y_2 = x^{r_2} \sum d_n x^n\), also convergent for \(0 < x < \rho\).
If \(r_1 = r_2\), the second solution always contains a term \(y_1(x) \ln x\), so it is not a Frobenius series (Example 4).
If \(r_1 - r_2\) is a positive integer \(N\), the recurrence for \(r_2\) breaks down at \(n = N\), where \(F(r_2 + N) = F(r_1) = 0\). If the right-hand side of (5) is not zero there, the second solution contains a \(y_1(x) \ln x\) term (Example 5); if it is zero, \(c_N\) is arbitrary and \(r_2\) gives a second Frobenius solution after all (Example 1).









WarningOnly one Frobenius solution



Mathews’ module warns that “there are some instances when only one Frobenius solution can be constructed.” His linked proof page goes further and says that when the roots differ by an integer, only one Frobenius series solution can be found. The second half of that statement is too strong: in Example 1 the roots \(\pm\tfrac12\) differ by \(1\), and both give Frobenius solutions.


All five equations below have polynomial coefficients with no other singular point, so \(\rho = \infty\) and every series converges for all \(x > 0\). This can also be read off each recurrence: the ratio \(|c_n / c_{n-2}|\) (or \(|c_n / c_{n-1}|\) in Example 2) tends to \(0\) as \(n \to \infty\), so the ratio test gives convergence for every \(x\). Convergence for every \(x\) does not mean a short partial sum is accurate for every \(x\), so each example ends with a table of how far the partial sums
\[
S_N(x) = x^{r} \sum_{n=0}^{N} c_n x^n
\]
stay within \(10^{-3}\) of the exact solution: the table gives \(x^*\), the first \(x > 0\) at which \(|S_N(x) - y(x)|\) reaches \(10^{-3}\), so that the error is below \(10^{-3}\) on \(0 < x < x^*\). Each \(x^*\) was located by a scan with step \(0.001\) followed by bisection, confirmed by a second root finder, and checked by a separate double-precision scan with step \(0.0001\) that found the largest error on \((0, x^*)\) below \(10^{-3}\) in every case. Mathews plots partial sums against the exact solutions in Examples 1 to 5, but none of the images on those examples’ solution pages survives in the archive, so the number of terms and the plot windows he used are not known.

title: Frobenius Series Solution
text:
Example 1 — \(x^2 y'' + x y' + \left(x^2 - \tfrac14\right) y = 0\)
Step 1 (classify \(x = 0\)): \(P(x) = x^2\) vanishes at \(0\), so \(0\) is a singular point. Since
\[
x\,\frac{Q(x)}{P(x)} = 1, \qquad x^2\,\frac{R(x)}{P(x)} = x^2 - \tfrac14
\]
are polynomials, \(x = 0\) is a regular singular point, with \(p_0 = 1\) and \(q_0 = -\tfrac14\).
Step 2 (indicial equation): by (4),
\[
r(r - 1) + r - \tfrac14 = r^2 - \tfrac14 = 0, \qquad r_1 = \tfrac12, \quad r_2 = -\tfrac12.
\]
The roots differ by the integer \(1\).
Step 3 (recurrence): substituting \(y = \sum c_n x^{n+r}\),
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \left[(n+r)^2 - \tfrac14\right] c_n x^{n+r} + \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n x^{n+r+2} = 0,
\]
so the coefficient of \(x^{1+r}\) gives \(\left[(1+r)^2 - \tfrac14\right] c_1 = 0\), and the coefficient of \(x^{n+r}\) for \(n \ge 2\) gives
\[
\left[(n+r)^2 - \tfrac14\right] c_n = -c_{n-2}.
\tag{6}
\]
Step 4 (first solution, \(r = \tfrac12\)): (6) becomes \(n(n+1)\,c_n = -c_{n-2}\), and \(2c_1 = 0\) forces \(c_1 = 0\), so every odd coefficient is \(0\). With \(c_0 = 1\),
\[
c_2 = -\tfrac16, \quad c_4 = \tfrac{1}{120}, \quad c_6 = -\tfrac{1}{5040}, \quad c_8 = \tfrac{1}{362880}, \quad c_{10} = -\tfrac{1}{39916800}, \qquad c_{2k} = \frac{(-1)^k}{(2k+1)!},
\]
\[
y_1(x) = x^{1/2}\left(1 - \frac{x^2}{3!} + \frac{x^4}{5!} - \frac{x^6}{7!} + \cdots\right) = \frac{\sin x}{\sqrt{x}}.
\]
Step 5 (second solution, \(r = -\tfrac12\)): (6) becomes \(n(n-1)\,c_n = -c_{n-2}\). For \(n = 1\) the equation for \(c_1\) reads \(0 \cdot c_1 = 0\), so \(c_1\) is arbitrary: this is case 4 of the theorem with a zero right-hand side. The terms that \(c_1\) generates are \(c_1 x^{-1/2}\left(x - \tfrac{x^3}{6} + \tfrac{x^5}{120} - \cdots\right) = c_1\, y_1(x)\), a multiple of the first solution, so Mathews sets \(c_1 = 0\). Then
\[
c_2 = -\tfrac12, \quad c_4 = \tfrac{1}{24}, \quad c_6 = -\tfrac{1}{720}, \quad c_8 = \tfrac{1}{40320}, \quad c_{10} = -\tfrac{1}{3628800}, \qquad c_{2k} = \frac{(-1)^k}{(2k)!},
\]
\[
y_2(x) = x^{-1/2}\left(1 - \frac{x^2}{2!} + \frac{x^4}{4!} - \frac{x^6}{6!} + \cdots\right) = \frac{\cos x}{\sqrt{x}}.
\]
Result. For \(x > 0\),
\[
\boxed{\ y(x) = C_1\,\frac{\sin x}{\sqrt{x}} + C_2\,\frac{\cos x}{\sqrt{x}}\ }
\]
This is Bessel’s equation of order \(\tfrac12\), and in Bessel-function form \(y_1 = \sqrt{\pi/2}\, J_{1/2}(x)\) and \(y_2 = \sqrt{\pi/2}\, J_{-1/2}(x) = -\sqrt{\pi/2}\, Y_{1/2}(x)\). As \(x \to 0^+\), \(y_1 \to 0\) like \(\sqrt{x}\) while \(y_2\) grows without bound like \(x^{-1/2}\).
Verification: substituting \(\sin x/\sqrt{x}\) and \(\cos x/\sqrt{x}\) into the left-hand side of the equation simplifies to \(0\) for both, and their series expansions reproduce the coefficients above. The coefficients themselves were found a second way, by solving the substituted equation power by power without the recurrence.

title: Frobenius Series Solution
text:
Example 2 — \(2x\,y'' + 3y' - y = 0\)
Step 1 (classify): \(P(x) = 2x\) vanishes at \(0\), and
\[
x\,\frac{Q(x)}{P(x)} = \frac32, \qquad x^2\,\frac{R(x)}{P(x)} = -\frac{x}{2},
\]
so \(x = 0\) is a regular singular point with \(p_0 = \tfrac32\) and \(q_0 = 0\).
Step 2 (indicial equation): \(r(r-1) + \tfrac32 r = r^2 + \tfrac12 r = 0\), so \(r_1 = 0\) and \(r_2 = -\tfrac12\). The roots differ by \(\tfrac12\), which is not an integer, so the theorem promises two Frobenius solutions.
Step 3 (recurrence): here \(y''\) is multiplied by \(x\), not \(x^2\), so the powers shift by one. Substituting,
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (n+r)(2n+2r+1)\, c_n x^{n+r-1} - \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n x^{n+r} = 0,
\]
and the coefficient of \(x^{n+r-1}\) for \(n \ge 1\) gives the one-step recurrence
\[
(n+r)(2n+2r+1)\, c_n = c_{n-1}.
\tag{7}
\]
Step 4 (first solution, \(r = 0\)): \(c_n = c_{n-1}/\bigl(n(2n+1)\bigr)\), so with \(c_0 = 1\)
\[
c_1 = \tfrac13, \quad c_2 = \tfrac{1}{30}, \quad c_3 = \tfrac{1}{630}, \quad c_4 = \tfrac{1}{22680}, \quad c_5 = \tfrac{1}{1247400}, \qquad c_n = \frac{2^n}{(2n+1)!},
\]
\[
y_1(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(2x)^n}{(2n+1)!} = \frac{\sinh\sqrt{2x}}{\sqrt{2x}}.
\]
Step 5 (second solution, \(r = -\tfrac12\)): \(c_n = c_{n-1}/\bigl(n(2n-1)\bigr)\), so
\[
c_1 = 1, \quad c_2 = \tfrac16, \quad c_3 = \tfrac{1}{90}, \quad c_4 = \tfrac{1}{2520}, \quad c_5 = \tfrac{1}{113400}, \qquad c_n = \frac{2^n}{(2n)!},
\]
\[
y_2(x) = x^{-1/2} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(2x)^n}{(2n)!} = \frac{\cosh\sqrt{2x}}{\sqrt{x}}.
\]
Result. For \(x > 0\),
\[
\boxed{\ y(x) = C_1\,\frac{\sinh\sqrt{2x}}{\sqrt{2x}} + C_2\,\frac{\cosh\sqrt{2x}}{\sqrt{x}}\ }
\]
Mathews compares the series with a computer-algebra solution, which he says takes “slight fussing around with the appropriate multiple of Sinh”. Here \(y_1(0) = 1\), while \(y_2\) grows without bound like \(x^{-1/2}\) as \(x \to 0^+\).
Verification: both closed forms make the left-hand side of the equation simplify to \(0\), and their expansions reproduce \(c_0, \ldots, c_7\) of each series. Every term of both series is positive, so each error \(y - S_N\) is a sum of positive terms that grows with \(x\).

title: Frobenius Series Solution
text:
Example 3 — \(2x^2 y'' + 3x y' - (x^2 + 1)\, y = 0\)
Step 1 (classify): with \(P(x) = 2x^2\),
\[
x\,\frac{Q(x)}{P(x)} = \frac32, \qquad x^2\,\frac{R(x)}{P(x)} = -\frac12 - \frac{x^2}{2},
\]
so \(x = 0\) is a regular singular point with \(p_0 = \tfrac32\) and \(q_0 = -\tfrac12\).
Step 2 (indicial equation): \(r(r-1) + \tfrac32 r - \tfrac12 = r^2 + \tfrac12 r - \tfrac12 = \tfrac12(2r - 1)(r + 1) = 0\), so \(r_1 = \tfrac12\) and \(r_2 = -1\). They differ by \(\tfrac32\), not an integer.
Step 3 (recurrence): with \(s = n + r\), the coefficient of \(x^{s}\) is \(\bigl[2s(s-1) + 3s - 1\bigr] c_n - c_{n-2} = (2s - 1)(s + 1)\, c_n - c_{n-2}\), so
\[
(2n + 2r - 1)(n + r + 1)\, c_n = c_{n-2}, \qquad n \ge 2,
\tag{8}
\]
and \((2r + 1)(r + 2)\,c_1 = 0\). For both roots the factor is non-zero (\(2 \cdot \tfrac52 = 5\) for \(r = \tfrac12\), \((-1) \cdot 1 = -1\) for \(r = -1\)), so \(c_1 = 0\) and every odd coefficient vanishes.
Step 4 (first solution, \(r = \tfrac12\)): \(n(2n+3)\,c_n = c_{n-2}\), and with \(c_0 = 1\)
\[
c_2 = \tfrac{1}{14}, \quad c_4 = \tfrac{1}{616}, \quad c_6 = \tfrac{1}{55440}, \quad c_8 = \tfrac{1}{8426880}, \quad c_{10} = \tfrac{1}{1938182400},
\]
\[
y_1(x) = x^{1/2}\left(1 + \frac{x^2}{14} + \frac{x^4}{616} + \frac{x^6}{55440} + \cdots\right).
\]
Step 5 (second solution, \(r = -1\)): \(n(2n-3)\,c_n = c_{n-2}\), and
\[
c_2 = \tfrac12, \quad c_4 = \tfrac{1}{40}, \quad c_6 = \tfrac{1}{2160}, \quad c_8 = \tfrac{1}{224640}, \quad c_{10} = \tfrac{1}{38188800},
\]
\[
y_2(x) = x^{-1}\left(1 + \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^4}{40} + \frac{x^6}{2160} + \cdots\right).
\]
Closed forms. Mathews finds explicit formulas for these coefficients by reading the Gamma functions in a computer-algebra solution, and notes that the computer cannot sum the resulting series. His formulas are lost with the archive’s images; the ones here come from (8). For even \(n = 2k\), (8) reads \(8k\left(k + \tfrac34\right) c_{2k} = c_{2k-2}\) for \(r = \tfrac12\) and \(8k\left(k - \tfrac34\right) c_{2k} = c_{2k-2}\) for \(r = -1\), and since \(\prod_{j=1}^{k} \left(j + \tfrac34\right) = \Gamma\!\left(k + \tfrac74\right)/\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac74\right)\) and \(\prod_{j=1}^{k} \left(j - \tfrac34\right) = \Gamma\!\left(k + \tfrac14\right)/\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac14\right)\),
\[
c_{2k} = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac74\right)}{8^k\, k!\, \Gamma\!\left(k + \tfrac74\right)} \quad (r = \tfrac12), \qquad
c_{2k} = \frac{\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac14\right)}{8^k\, k!\, \Gamma\!\left(k + \tfrac14\right)} \quad (r = -1),
\]
and comparing with the series of the modified Bessel function, \(I_\nu(z) = \sum_k (z/2)^{2k+\nu} / \bigl(k!\,\Gamma(k + \nu + 1)\bigr)\), sums both series:
\[
\boxed{\ y_1(x) = 2^{9/8}\,\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac74\right) x^{-1/4}\, I_{3/4}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt2}\right), \qquad
y_2(x) = 2^{-9/8}\,\Gamma\!\left(\tfrac14\right) x^{-1/4}\, I_{-3/4}\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt2}\right)\ }
\]
As \(x \to 0^+\), \(y_1 \to 0\) like \(\sqrt{x}\) and \(y_2\) grows without bound like \(1/x\).
Verification: the Gamma formulas reproduce \(c_0, \ldots, c_{10}\) above exactly. The Bessel closed forms agree with the full series (summed to convergence in 40-digit arithmetic) to within \(4 \times 10^{-40}\) at \(x = 0.3\), \(2\) and \(7\). All terms are positive, so the errors of the partial sums grow with \(x\).

title: Frobenius Series Solution
section: Example 4 — Bessel’s equation of order 0, \(x^2 y'' + x y' + x^2 y = 0\)
text:
Example 4 — Bessel’s equation of order 0, \(x^2 y'' + x y' + x^2 y = 0\)
Step 1 (classify): \(x\,Q/P = 1\) and \(x^2 R/P = x^2\), so \(x = 0\) is a regular singular point with \(p_0 = 1\) and \(q_0 = 0\).
Step 2 (indicial equation): \(r(r-1) + r = r^2 = 0\), a double root \(r_1 = r_2 = 0\). Only one Frobenius solution exists.
Step 3 (recurrence): the coefficient of \(x^{n}\) gives \(n^2 c_n = -c_{n-2}\) for \(n \ge 2\), and \(c_1 = 0\). With \(c_0 = 1\),
\[
c_2 = -\tfrac14, \quad c_4 = \tfrac{1}{64}, \quad c_6 = -\tfrac{1}{2304}, \quad c_8 = \tfrac{1}{147456}, \quad c_{10} = -\tfrac{1}{14745600}, \quad c_{12} = \tfrac{1}{2123366400},
\]
and in closed form \(c_{2k} = (-1)^k / \bigl(4^k (k!)^2\bigr)\). The Frobenius solution is the Bessel function of the first kind of order \(0\):
\[
\boxed{\ y_1(x) = J_0(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^k}{2^{2k} (k!)^2}\, x^{2k} = 1 - \frac{x^2}{4} + \frac{x^4}{64} - \frac{x^6}{2304} + \cdots\ }
\]
It is finite at the origin, with \(J_0(0) = 1\).
The second solution. As case 3 of the theorem says, the second solution is not a Frobenius series. It is the Bessel function of the second kind \(Y_0(x)\), which contains \(\tfrac{2}{\pi} J_0(x) \ln(x/2)\); the difference \(Y_0(x) - \tfrac{2}{\pi} \ln(x/2)\, J_0(x)\) was evaluated at \(x = 10^{-2}\), \(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-8}\) and tends to the constant \(\tfrac{2}{\pi}\gamma = 0.36747\) (Euler’s constant \(\gamma\)), so \(Y_0(x) \to -\infty\) as \(x \to 0^+\). Mathews leaves \(Y_0\) to another module.
Verification: \(J_0\) satisfies the equation (the residual simplifies to \(0\)) and its Maclaurin series matches the coefficients above through \(x^{12}\).

title: Frobenius Series Solution
section: Example 5 — Bessel’s equation of order 1, \(x^2 y'' + x y' + (x^2 - 1)\, y = 0\)
text:
Example 5 — Bessel’s equation of order 1, \(x^2 y'' + x y' + (x^2 - 1)\, y = 0\)
Step 1 (classify): \(x\,Q/P = 1\) and \(x^2 R/P = x^2 - 1\), so \(x = 0\) is a regular singular point with \(p_0 = 1\) and \(q_0 = -1\).
Step 2 (indicial equation): \(r(r-1) + r - 1 = r^2 - 1 = 0\), so \(r_1 = 1\) and \(r_2 = -1\). The roots differ by the integer \(2\).
Step 3 (recurrence): the coefficient of \(x^{n+r}\) gives \(\bigl[(n+r)^2 - 1\bigr] c_n = -c_{n-2}\) for \(n \ge 2\).
Step 4 (first solution, \(r = 1\)): \(n(n+2)\,c_n = -c_{n-2}\), \(c_1 = 0\), and with \(c_0 = 1\)
\[
c_2 = -\tfrac18, \quad c_4 = \tfrac{1}{192}, \quad c_6 = -\tfrac{1}{9216}, \quad c_8 = \tfrac{1}{737280}, \quad c_{10} = -\tfrac{1}{88473600}, \qquad c_{2k} = \frac{(-1)^k}{4^k\, k!\, (k+1)!},
\]
\[
\boxed{\ y_1(x) = x - \frac{x^3}{8} + \frac{x^5}{192} - \frac{x^7}{9216} + \cdots = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^k}{2^{2k}\, k!\,(k+1)!}\, x^{2k+1} = 2 J_1(x)\ }
\]
The Frobenius series with \(c_0 = 1\) is twice the Bessel function \(J_1(x) = \tfrac{x}{2} - \tfrac{x^3}{16} + \cdots\). Both vanish at \(0\); the series has \(y_1'(0) = 1\), while \(J_1'(0) = \tfrac12\).
Step 5 (the root \(r = -1\) fails): the recurrence becomes \(n(n-2)\,c_n = -c_{n-2}\). At \(n = 2\) it reads \(0 \cdot c_2 = -c_0\), which is impossible with \(c_0 \ne 0\). This is case 4 of the theorem with a non-zero right-hand side, and there is no Frobenius solution with \(r = -1\). The second solution is the Bessel function of the second kind \(Y_1(x)\), which contains a logarithm and behaves like \(-\tfrac{2}{\pi x}\) near \(0\) (the product \(x\,Y_1(x)\) was evaluated at \(x = 10^{-2}\), \(10^{-4}\) and \(10^{-8}\) and tends to \(-2/\pi\)).
Examples 1 and 5 have the same shape, \(x^2 y'' + x y' + (x^2 - \nu^2) y = 0\) with \(\nu = \tfrac12\) and \(\nu = 1\), and both have roots \(\pm\nu\) that differ by an integer. The difference is where the recurrence for the smaller root stalls: in Example 1 at the odd index \(n = 1\), where the right-hand side is \(0\), and in Example 5 at the even index \(n = 2\), where the right-hand side is \(-c_0 \ne 0\).
Verification: \(2J_1\) satisfies the equation (residual simplifies to \(0\)), and its Maclaurin series matches the coefficients above through \(x^{13}\).

title: Frobenius Series Solution
text:
Example 6 — The identity \(J_0'(x) = -J_1(x)\)
Use the Maclaurin series from Examples 4 and 5 to verify that \(J_0'(x) = -J_1(x)\).
Step 1 (the two series):
\[
J_0(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{2^{2n} (n!)^2}\, x^{2n}, \qquad
J_1(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{2^{2n-1}\, n!\,(n-1)!}\, x^{2n-1}.
\]
(The series for \(J_1\) is Example 5’s series divided by \(2\), with the index shifted by one.)
Step 2 (differentiate term by term): the \(n = 0\) term of \(J_0\) is constant and drops out, and
\[
J_0'(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n\, 2n}{2^{2n}\, n!\, n!}\, x^{2n-1} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{2^{2n-1}\, n!\,(n-1)!}\, x^{2n-1},
\]
using \(2n/(n!\,n!) = 2/\bigl(n!\,(n-1)!\bigr)\).
Step 3 (compare): term by term, \((-1)^n = -(-1)^{n-1}\) and the rest is identical, so
\[
\boxed{\ J_0'(x) = -J_1(x)\ }
\]
Verification (the first terms, as Mathews lists them):
\[
\begin{aligned}
J_0(x) &= 1 - \frac{x^2}{4} + \frac{x^4}{64} - \frac{x^6}{2304} + \frac{x^8}{147456} - \frac{x^{10}}{14745600} + \frac{x^{12}}{2123366400} - \cdots \\
J_0'(x) &= -\frac{x}{2} + \frac{x^3}{16} - \frac{x^5}{384} + \frac{x^7}{18432} - \frac{x^9}{1474560} + \frac{x^{11}}{176947200} - \cdots \\
J_1(x) &= \frac{x}{2} - \frac{x^3}{16} + \frac{x^5}{384} - \frac{x^7}{18432} + \frac{x^9}{1474560} - \frac{x^{11}}{176947200} + \cdots
\end{aligned}
\]
These agree with independently computed Maclaurin expansions of \(J_0\), \(J_0'\) and \(J_1\), and \(J_0'(x) + J_1(x)\) simplifies symbolically to \(0\). A consequence used below: the turning points of \(J_0\) are the zeros of \(J_1\).

title: Frobenius Series Solution
text:
Application: the Vibrating Drum
The two-dimensional wave equation is \(u_{tt} = a^2 \nabla^2 u\). In rectangular coordinates it reads \(u_{tt} = a^2 (u_{xx} + u_{yy})\), and in polar coordinates
\[
u_{tt} = a^2\left(u_{rr} + \frac{1}{r}\,u_r + \frac{1}{r^2}\,u_{\theta\theta}\right).
\]
A drum head is a flexible circular membrane of radius \(c\), fixed at its rim. If it is struck in the centre so that it vibrates radially only, the displacement \(u(t, r)\) depends only on the time \(t\) and the distance \(r\) from the centre, the \(u_{\theta\theta}\) term drops out, and
\[
u_{tt} = a^2\left(u_{rr} + \frac{1}{r}\,u_r\right), \qquad u(t, c) = 0.
\tag{9}
\]

Example 7 — Separating the variables
Take \(c = 1\) and \(a = 1\), and look for standing waves \(u(t, r) = R(r) \cos(\omega t)\).
Step 1 (substitute): \(u_{tt} = -\omega^2 R(r)\cos(\omega t)\), \(u_r = R'(r)\cos(\omega t)\) and \(u_{rr} = R''(r)\cos(\omega t)\). Dividing (9) by \(\cos(\omega t)\) and multiplying by \(r^2\),
\[
r^2 R''(r) + r R'(r) + \omega^2 r^2 R(r) = 0.
\]
Step 2 (solve): with \(s = \omega r\) this is Bessel’s equation of order \(0\) from Example 4, so
\[
R(r) = C_1 J_0(\omega r) + C_2 Y_0(\omega r).
\]
Both \(J_0(\omega r)\) and \(Y_0(\omega r)\) make the separated equation’s residual simplify to \(0\).
Step 3 (choose the bounded solution): \(Y_0(\omega r) \to -\infty\) as \(r \to 0^+\) (Example 4), and the centre of the drum does not move infinitely far, so \(C_2 = 0\) and \(R(r) = J_0(\omega r)\).
Mathews plots \(J_0(r)\) (that is, \(\omega = 1\)) over \(-15 \le r \le 15\) in the window \([-15, 15] \times [-0.5, 1]\). \(J_0\) is even and equals \(1\) at \(r = 0\). On \(0 < r \le 15\) it has four turning points, at the zeros \(3.8317\), \(7.0156\), \(10.1735\) and \(13.3237\) of \(J_1\) (Example 6), where its values \(-0.40276\), \(0.30012\), \(-0.24970\) and \(0.21836\) alternate in sign and shrink in size; the next zero of \(J_1\), \(16.4706\), lies outside the window. A bounded minimiser on \([2.5, 5.5]\) finds the same lowest point, \(J_0(3.8317) = -0.40276\). He also plots \(Y_0(r)\) for \(0.01 \le r \le 15\) in the window \([0, 15] \times [-3, 1]\) to show its fall towards \(-\infty\) at the origin. At the left end of that plot \(Y_0(0.01) = -3.0055\), just below the window.


Example 8 — The zeros of \(J_0\)
The rim condition \(u(t, 1) = 0\), i.e. \(R(1) = J_0(\omega) = 0\), means \(\omega\) must be a zero of \(J_0\). The zeros have no simple formula. Mathews says they are “close to” multiples of \(\pi\), and uses \(k\pi\) as the starting value of a root finder for the \(k\)-th zero; Newton’s method started at \(k\pi\) does converge to the \(k\)-th zero for \(k = 1, \ldots, 5\). The surface of the vibrating drum
With \(\omega = \lambda_n\), the \(n\)-th zero of \(J_0\), the rim condition \(R(1) = J_0(\lambda_n) = 0\) holds, and the fundamental solutions (normal modes) of the drum are
\[
\boxed{\ u_n(t, r, \theta) = J_0(\lambda_n r)\cos(\lambda_n t), \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\ }
\]
Each mode is a standing wave: the shape \(J_0(\lambda_n r)\) is fixed and its height is scaled by \(\cos(\lambda_n t)\), with period \(2\pi/\lambda_n\). Inside the drum, \(J_0(\lambda_n r) = 0\) exactly when \(\lambda_n r\) is one of \(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_{n-1}\), so mode \(n\) has \(n - 1\) nodal circles, of radii \(r = \lambda_k/\lambda_n\) for \(k < n\), which never move, besides the fixed rim.

For \(n = 1\) the curve is positive on \(-1 < x < 1\). The archive keeps five graph slots for this example, one for each zero of Example 8, but the graphs themselves are lost.


Example 10 — The fundamental vibrations for \(n = 1, 2, 3\)
The initial displacement of the \(n\)-th fundamental solution is \(u_n(0, r, \theta) = J_0(\lambda_n r)\). Mathews draws it for \(n = 1, 2, 3\) as a surface \(z = J_0(\lambda_n r)\) over the unit disk, parametrised by \((r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)\) with \(0 \le r \le 1\) and \(0 \le \theta \le 2\pi\), in the box \([-1, 1] \times [-1, 1] \times [-0.45, 1]\) with box ratios \(1 : 1 : 0.3\). Mode 1 stays at or above \(0\), and modes 2 and 3 go down to \(-0.40276\), so the box holds all three surfaces. For \(n = 2\) and \(3\) he also draws the cross-section \(J_0(\lambda_n x)\) on \(-1 \le x \le 1\), its positive part in pink and its negative part in cyan, and a disk diagram in the window \([-1.2, 1.2]^2\) coloured the same way, with the nodal circles drawn.

\(n = 1\), \(\lambda_1 = 2.40483\): the only node is the rim \(r = 1\). \(J_0(\lambda_1 r) > 0\) for \(0 \le r < 1\), so the whole drum head moves up and down together.
\(n = 2\), \(\lambda_2 = 5.52008\): one nodal circle, of radius \(\lambda_1/\lambda_2 = 0.435651\). The disk inside it and the ring outside it move in opposite directions; the ring’s deepest point is at \(r = 0.69414\).
\(n = 3\), \(\lambda_3 = 8.65373\): two nodal circles, of radii \(\lambda_1/\lambda_3 = 0.277895\) and \(\lambda_2/\lambda_3 = 0.637884\). The inner disk and the outer ring move together, and the ring between the circles moves the opposite way.

title: Finite Difference Method for ODE’s
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Finite Difference Method for ODE’s
text:
Description
A second-order boundary value problem asks for a function \(x(t)\) on an interval \([a, b]\) that satisfies a differential equation inside the interval and prescribed values at both ends. For the linear equation
\[
x'' = p(t)\,x' + q(t)\,x + r(t), \qquad x(a) = \alpha, \quad x(b) = \beta,
\]
the finite difference method divides \([a, b]\) into \(n\) equal subintervals of width \(h = (b - a)/n\), with mesh points \(t_j = a + jh\), and looks for numbers \(x_j \approx x(t_j)\). At every interior mesh point it replaces \(x'\) and \(x''\) by central difference quotients, which turns the differential equation into one linear equation linking \(x_{j-1}\), \(x_j\) and \(x_{j+1}\):
\[
\Bigl(-\frac{h}{2}p_j - 1\Bigr)x_{j-1} + \bigl(2 + h^2 q_j\bigr)x_j + \Bigl(\frac{h}{2}p_j - 1\Bigr)x_{j+1} = -h^2 r_j, \qquad j = 1, 2, \ldots, n-1,
\]
where \(p_j = p(t_j)\), \(q_j = q(t_j)\), \(r_j = r(t_j)\), \(x_0 = \alpha\) and \(x_n = \beta\). These \(n - 1\) equations form a tridiagonal linear system, which tridiagonal elimination solves in \(O(n)\) operations, and the solution values together with the two boundary values give the approximate solution curve.
Both difference quotients are accurate to \(O(h^2)\). Under the conditions stated below, and for a smooth solution, the error of the method is then \(O(h^2)\), so halving \(h\) cuts it by about a factor of four, and two runs with \(h\) and \(h/2\) can be combined by Richardson extrapolation into a much more accurate answer. Mathews’ examples do exactly this for one equation on \([1, 6]\) with \(25\) and \(50\) subintervals; every number below has been recomputed (the example tables in 40-digit arithmetic), and the computed solutions are compared with the exact solution.

title: Finite Difference Method for ODE’s
text:
Animations
All three animations solve Mathews’ boundary value problem (7) below, \(x'' + \tfrac1t x' + \bigl(1 - \tfrac{1}{4t^2}\bigr)x = \sqrt t\,\cos t\) with \(x(1) = 1\) and \(x(6) = -0.5\), and compare the results with its exact solution (8). Case 1 refines the grid one frame at a time and draws the finite difference solution over the interval \(1 \le t \le 6\) of Mathews’ graphs, with the exact solution in magenta (in Mathews’ graphs the magenta curve is his joined finite difference points; he never plots the exact solution). Case 2 follows his Examples 4 to 6, from the solutions \(X_1\) (\(n = 25\)) and \(X_2\) (\(n = 50\)) to the extrapolated values \(X_3\), and Case 3 continues the halving of \(h\) to \(n = 400\). In every case the right panel, or both panels in Case 3, plots errors on a logarithmic scale; the log-scale panels plotted against \(t\) leave out \(t = 1\) and \(t = 6\), where every error is exactly zero because the boundary values are imposed. Each frame shows one second in Case 1 and two seconds in Cases 2 and 3, and the last frame is held for three seconds. The scripts build the tridiagonal system (6), solve it and evaluate the exact solution in 256-bit floating point, and check their results against the tables on this page.
Mathews’ module links no animation, and his animation archive has none for this topic, so all three animations are new, with no Mathews original. They animate the graphs of his Examples 1 to 4 (the solutions for \(n = 25\) and \(n = 50\), and the difference \(X_2 - X_1\), drawn in green as he draws it) and the computations of Examples 5 and 6 (the graph of Example 5 is missing from the archive, and Example 6 has none). Not animated are the setup of the tridiagonal system in Example 1 (the coefficients and the matrix) and the counterexample \(x'' = -x\) for the boundary value theorem.

title: Finite Difference Method for ODE’s
text:
Boundary Value Problems
The boundary value problem \(x'' = f(t, x, x')\), \(x(a) = \alpha\), \(x(b) = \beta\) need not have a solution, and when it has one it need not be unique. The following theorem gives a sufficient condition. In it, \(y\) stands for the third argument of \(f\), the slot where \(x'(t)\) goes, so that the partial derivatives \(f_x\) and \(f_y\) can be written down.






TipTheorem — Boundary value problem



Assume that \(f(t, x, y)\) is continuous on the region \(R = \{(t, x, y) : a \le t \le b,\ -\infty < x < \infty,\ -\infty < y < \infty\}\) and that \(f_x\) and \(f_y\) are continuous on \(R\). If there is a constant \(M > 0\) for which
\[
f_x(t, x, y) > 0 \quad\text{and}\quad |f_y(t, x, y)| \le M \qquad \text{for all } (t, x, y) \in R,
\]
then the boundary value problem
\[
x'' = f(t, x, x'), \qquad x(a) = \alpha, \quad x(b) = \beta
\]
has a unique solution \(x = x(t)\) for \(a \le t \le b\).


For a linear equation, \(f(t, x, y) = p(t)\,y + q(t)\,x + r(t)\), so \(f_x = q(t)\) and \(f_y = p(t)\), and the theorem becomes:






TipCorollary — Linear boundary value problem



Assume that \(p\), \(q\) and \(r\) are continuous on \([a, b]\) and that
\[
q(t) > 0 \qquad \text{for all } t \in [a, b].
\]
Then the linear boundary value problem
\[
x'' = p(t)\,x'(t) + q(t)\,x(t) + r(t), \qquad x(a) = \alpha, \quad x(b) = \beta
\tag{1}
\]
has a unique solution \(x = x(t)\) over \(a \le t \le b\). (A bound \(|p(t)| \le M\) is automatic here, with \(M = \max_{a \le t \le b} |p(t)|\), because \(p\) is continuous on a closed interval.)








WarningThe condition \(q(t) > 0\) is sufficient, not necessary



The equation \(x'' = -x\) has \(q(t) = -1 < 0\), and its general solution is \(x(t) = c_1 \cos t + c_2 \sin t\). With the boundary conditions \(x(0) = \alpha\) and \(x(\pi) = \beta\), the first condition gives \(c_1 = \alpha\) and the second gives \(x(\pi) = -c_1 = -\alpha\), so the problem can be solved only when \(\beta = -\alpha\), and then \(c_2\) is arbitrary and there are infinitely many solutions. (Mathews’ footnote states the condition as \(\alpha = \beta\); the general solution gives \(\beta = -\alpha\).) This counterexample is why the theory is phrased with \(q(t) > 0\). But the condition is only sufficient: many problems with \(q(t) < 0\) somewhere, including the one solved on this page, still have exactly one solution, and they can be solved by finite differences or by the shooting method with some care.

title: Finite Difference Method for ODE’s
text:
The Finite-Difference Method

Derivation
Consider the linear equation (1) over \([a, b]\) with \(x(a) = \alpha\) and \(x(b) = \beta\). Form a partition of \([a, b]\) using the points \(a = t_0 < t_1 < \cdots < t_n = b\), where
\[
h = \frac{b - a}{n} \qquad\text{and}\qquad t_j = a + jh \quad\text{for } j = 0, 1, \ldots, n.
\]
The central difference formulas approximate the derivatives at an interior point \(t_j\):
\[
x'(t_j) = \frac{x(t_{j+1}) - x(t_{j-1})}{2h} + O(h^2),
\tag{2}
\]
\[
x''(t_j) = \frac{x(t_{j+1}) - 2x(t_j) + x(t_{j-1})}{h^2} + O(h^2).
\tag{3}
\]
For a solution with continuous fourth derivative the two error terms are \(-\tfrac{h^2}{6}x'''(c_1)\) and \(-\tfrac{h^2}{12}x^{(4)}(c_2)\) for some \(c_1, c_2\) in \((t_{j-1}, t_{j+1})\); Taylor expansion of the quotients gives \(x' + \tfrac{h^2}{6}x''' + \cdots\) and \(x'' + \tfrac{h^2}{12}x^{(4)} + \cdots\).
Write \(x_j\) for the approximation to \(x(t_j)\), drop the two \(O(h^2)\) terms, and use the notation \(p_j = p(t_j)\), \(q_j = q(t_j)\) and \(r_j = r(t_j)\). Equation (1) at \(t = t_j\) becomes the difference equation
\[
\frac{x_{j+1} - 2x_j + x_{j-1}}{h^2} = p_j\,\frac{x_{j+1} - x_{j-1}}{2h} + q_j x_j + r_j.
\tag{4}
\]
Multiply each side by \(h^2\) and collect the terms involving \(x_{j-1}\), \(x_j\) and \(x_{j+1}\):






ImportantThe finite difference equations



\[
\Bigl(-\frac{h}{2}p_j - 1\Bigr)x_{j-1} + \bigl(2 + h^2 q_j\bigr)x_j + \Bigl(\frac{h}{2}p_j - 1\Bigr)x_{j+1} = -h^2 r_j
\tag{5}
\]
for \(j = 1, 2, \ldots, n - 1\), where \(x_0 = \alpha\) and \(x_n = \beta\).


(Mathews’ module prints the left boundary value as \(x_0 = \beta\); it is \(x_0 = x(a) = \alpha\).)


The tridiagonal system
Equation (5) for \(j = 1\) contains the known value \(x_0 = \alpha\), and for \(j = n - 1\) the known value \(x_n = \beta\); moving these to the right-hand side leaves \(n - 1\) equations in the \(n - 1\) unknowns \(x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}\). Write
\[
d_j = 2 + h^2 q_j, \qquad a_j = -\frac{h}{2}p_j - 1, \qquad c_j = \frac{h}{2}p_j - 1, \qquad e_j = -h^2 r_j.
\]
Then the system is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
d_1 & c_1 & & & \\
a_2 & d_2 & c_2 & & \\
& \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\
& & a_{n-2} & d_{n-2} & c_{n-2} \\
& & & a_{n-1} & d_{n-1}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_{n-2} \\ x_{n-1} \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} e_1 - a_1\alpha \\ e_2 \\ \vdots \\ e_{n-2} \\ e_{n-1} - c_{n-1}\beta \end{pmatrix},
\tag{6}
\]
which has the familiar tridiagonal form and is solved by elimination in \(O(n)\) operations.






TipWhen the system has a unique solution (general result)



Suppose \(q(t_j) > 0\) at every interior mesh point and \(h\,|p(t_j)| \le 2\) there (for instance \(h \le 2/M\) with \(M = \max_{a \le t \le b}|p(t)|\)). Then \(a_j \le 0\) and \(c_j \le 0\), so \(|a_j| + |c_j| = \bigl(1 + \tfrac{h}{2}p_j\bigr) + \bigl(1 - \tfrac{h}{2}p_j\bigr) = 2 < 2 + h^2 q_j = d_j\). Every row of (6) is strictly diagonally dominant, so the matrix is nonsingular and the tridiagonal elimination needs no pivoting.


When \(q\) is negative, as in the example below, the matrix is not diagonally dominant and nonsingularity has to be checked another way; it does not follow from this result.
The finite difference solution also converges to \(x(t)\) as \(h \to 0\): under the conditions of the corollary, with \(h \le 2/M\), and for a solution with continuous fourth derivative, the error at the mesh points is \(O(h^2)\). This is a standard general result. The example below does not satisfy these conditions, but it shows the factor of four per halving of \(h\) numerically all the same.


Algorithm
To approximate the solution of \(x'' = p(t)x'(t) + q(t)x(t) + r(t)\) with \(x(a) = \alpha\) and \(x(b) = \beta\) over \([a, b]\) by the finite difference method of order \(O(h^2)\), Mathews’ program uses the mesh \(a = t_1 < t_2 < \cdots < t_{n+1} = b\) (numbered from \(1\), so it has \(n + 1\) points for \(n\) subintervals) and returns the solution points \(\{(t_j, x_j)\}_{j=1}^{n+1}\). Its three steps are:

Construct the tridiagonal matrix and the right-hand-side vector of (6).
Solve the system in step 1 for the ordinates strictly inside the interval.
Join the mesh points and the solution vector from step 2 into points, and put the boundary points \((a, \alpha)\) and \((b, \beta)\) at the two ends.

title: Finite Difference Method for ODE’s
text:
Worked Examples
All six of Mathews’ examples use the same boundary value problem,
\[
x'' + \frac{1}{t}\,x' + \Bigl(1 - \frac{1}{4t^2}\Bigr)x = \sqrt{t}\,\cos t, \qquad x(1) = 1, \quad x(6) = -0.5,
\tag{7}
\]
over \([1, 6]\). In the form (1) it has
\[
p(t) = -\frac{1}{t}, \qquad q(t) = \frac{1}{4t^2} - 1, \qquad r(t) = \sqrt{t}\,\cos t.
\]
Here \(q(t)\) decreases from \(q(1) = -0.75\) to \(q(6) = -0.993056\), so it is negative on the whole interval and the corollary does not apply. The problem nevertheless has exactly one solution, which can be written down.

The exact solution
The homogeneous equation \(x'' + \tfrac{1}{t}x' + \bigl(1 - \tfrac{1}{4t^2}\bigr)x = 0\) is Bessel’s equation of order \(\tfrac12\). The substitution \(x = u/\sqrt{t}\) turns (7) into
\[
u'' + u = t\cos t,
\]
whose general solution is \(u = c_1\cos t + c_2\sin t + \tfrac14 t\cos t + \tfrac14 t^2\sin t\). Hence
\[
x(t) = \frac{c_1\cos t + c_2\sin t}{\sqrt{t}} + \frac14\sqrt{t}\,\cos t + \frac14\,t^{3/2}\sin t.
\tag{8}
\]
The boundary conditions give two linear equations for \(c_1\) and \(c_2\), whose determinant is \(\cos 1\,\sin 6 - \sin 1\,\cos 6 = \sin 5 = -0.958924 \neq 0\), so there is exactly one solution:
\[
c_1 = 0.0588713451552886, \qquad c_2 = 0.740071095780206,
\]
which agree with the constants Mathews uses in Example 6 to \(14\) decimal places (his \(c_1\) ends in \(\ldots 2859\), a rounding difference of \(3 \times 10^{-15}\)). The same determinant shows that the homogeneous problem with \(x(1) = x(6) = 0\) has only the zero solution. Formula (8) satisfies (7) and both boundary conditions to 40-digit precision, and an independent numerical solution of (7) with SciPy’s solve_bvp agrees with it to within \(9 \times 10^{-16}\) on \([1, 6]\). Its minimum on \([1, 6]\) is about \(-2.9057\), near \(t = 4.78\).


Example 1 — \(25\) subintervals, step by step
Solve (7) over \([1, 6]\) with the finite difference method and \(n = 25\) subintervals (\(26\) points).
Step 1: The mesh. With \(h = (6 - 1)/25 = 0.2\),
\[
t_j = 1 + 0.2j, \qquad j = 0, 1, \ldots, 25,
\]
and the unknowns are \(x_1, \ldots, x_{24}\) at \(t = 1.2, 1.4, \ldots, 5.8\).
Step 2: The coefficient functions at the mesh points. At \(t_1 = 1.2\),
\[
p_1 = -\frac{1}{1.2} = -0.833333, \qquad q_1 = \frac{1}{4(1.44)} - 1 = -0.826389, \qquad r_1 = \sqrt{1.2}\,\cos 1.2 = 0.396943.
\]
Step 3: The first row of (6). With \(h/2 = 0.1\) and \(h^2 = 0.04\),
\[
d_1 = 2 + 0.04\,q_1 = 1.966944, \qquad c_1 = 0.1\,p_1 - 1 = -1.083333,
\]
\[
e_1 - a_1\alpha = -0.04\,r_1 + (1 + 0.1\,p_1)(1) = -0.015878 + 0.916667 = 0.900789.
\]
The second row, at \(t_2 = 1.4\), is the first full one: \(a_2 = -0.928571\), \(d_2 = 1.965102\), \(c_2 = -1.071429\) and right-hand side \(e_2 = -0.04\,r_2 = -0.008044\).
Step 4: The last row, at \(t_{24} = 5.8\), where \(p_{24} = -0.172414\), \(q_{24} = -0.992568\) and \(r_{24} = 2.132613\):
\[
a_{24} = -0.1\,p_{24} - 1 = -0.982759, \qquad d_{24} = 2 + 0.04\,q_{24} = 1.960297,
\]
\[
e_{24} - c_{24}\beta = -0.04\,r_{24} + (1 - 0.1\,p_{24})(-0.5) = -0.0853045 - 0.5086207 = -0.593925.
\]
These are the first and last entries of the four vectors Mathews prints (sub-diagonal, diagonal, super-diagonal, right-hand side), and all four agree with the recomputation to the six figures he shows.
Step 5: Solve the \(24 \times 24\) tridiagonal system. Because \(q < 0\), the diagonal entries run from \(d_1 = 1.966944\) down to \(d_{24} = 1.960297\), all below \(2\), while \(|a_j| + |c_j| = 2\) in rows \(2\) to \(23\); so the matrix is not diagonally dominant and the general result above does not apply. It is nonsingular all the same: its determinant is \(-4.903642\) and its condition number (2-norm) is about \(225\).
Step 6: Put the boundary points \((1, 1)\) and \((6, -0.5)\) at the ends of the list of points \((t_j, x_j)\). The finite difference solution, compared with the exact solution (8), is:

Example 2 — the same problem with the program
Mathews repeats Example 1 with his finite difference program, which carries out the three steps of the algorithm in one call with \(a = 1\), \(b = 6\), \(\alpha = 1\), \(\beta = -0.5\) and \(25\) subintervals, skipping the details. The program returns the same \(26\) points as the table in Example 1; the list he calls points1 and prints again in Example 4 is identical to his Example 1 list. Call these values \(X_1\).


Example 3 — \(50\) subintervals
Solve (7) again with \(n = 50\) subintervals (\(51\) points), so \(h = 0.1\) and the system has \(49\) unknowns. Call the result \(X_2\). Its first and last interior values are \(x(1.1) \approx 1.03057\) and \(x(5.9) \approx -0.868321\), as in Mathews’ output; the values at the \(26\) points \(t = 1.0, 1.2, \ldots, 6.0\) that it shares with \(X_1\) are listed in the table under Example 5.


Example 4 — how much do the two solutions differ?
The two solutions cannot be subtracted directly: \(X_1\) has \(26\) points and \(X_2\) has \(51\). The mesh of \(X_1\) is every other point of the mesh of \(X_2\), so Mathews takes points \(1, 3, 5, \ldots, 51\) of \(X_2\) (numbering from \(1\)), which lie at \(t = 1.0, 1.2, \ldots, 6.0\), and forms the difference \(X_2 - X_1\) there. It appears in the table under Example 5. The difference is negative from \(t = 1.2\) to \(t = 3.4\), positive from \(t = 3.6\) to \(t = 5.8\), and largest in size at \(t = 4.8\), where \(X_2 - X_1 = 0.01100\).
Is that small or large? Since the method is of order \(O(h^2)\), the error of \(X_2\) should be about a quarter of the error of \(X_1\), so \(X_2 - X_1 \approx -\tfrac34(X_1 - x)\), and the difference itself estimates the error: \(X_1 - x \approx -\tfrac43(X_2 - X_1)\), which at \(t = 4.8\) is \(-\tfrac43(0.01100) = -0.01467\), close to the actual error \(-0.01464\). The improvement scheme of the next example removes most of it.


Example 5 — Richardson extrapolation
Use Richardson extrapolation and the results of Examples 2 and 3 to construct a more accurate solution at the \(26\) points of the \(25\)-subinterval mesh.
If the error of the method behaves like \(C h^2\) at a fixed point \(t\), then \(X_1 \approx x + Ch^2\) and \(X_2 \approx x + C h^2/4\). Eliminating \(C\) gives the extrapolated values
\[
X_3 = \frac{4X_2 - X_1}{3} = X_2 + \frac{X_2 - X_1}{3}.
\tag{9}
\]
(The output of this example is missing from Mathews’ archive; formula (9) is the one he uses in Example 6.) At \(t = 4.8\), for instance, \(X_3 = (4(-2.908846) - (-2.919846))/3 = -2.905179\), compared with the exact value \(-2.905208\).

title: Elliptic PDE’s
text:
Description
Laplace’s equation \(u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 0\) describes a steady state, such as the temperature \(u(x, y)\) in a thin plate long after the heat has stopped flowing. Here it is solved on a rectangle \(R = [0, a] \times [0, b]\) whose edges are held at known values (a Dirichlet problem), or with one edge insulated, \(\partial u / \partial N = 0\) (a Neumann condition). The rectangle is covered by a grid of \(n \times m\) points with equal spacing \(h\) in both directions, and at every interior grid point the Laplacian is replaced by the five-point difference formula. Writing \(u_{i,j}\) for the approximation to \(u(x_i, y_j)\), the equation at each interior point says that \(u_{i,j}\) is the average of its four neighbours:
\[
u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4u_{i,j} = 0 .
\]
These equations form a large, sparse linear system. Mathews solves it by iteration: starting from a guess at every interior point, he sweeps across the grid again and again, and moves each value toward the average of its neighbours by successive over-relaxation (SOR),
\[
u_{i,j} \leftarrow u_{i,j} + \omega\, r_{i,j}, \qquad r_{i,j} = \frac{u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4u_{i,j}}{4},
\]
with the relaxation parameter \(\omega\) between \(1\) and \(2\). His programs stop once the largest correction \(\lvert \omega r_{i,j} \rvert\) in a sweep is below \(0.001\). The sweeps carry the grid from the flat starting guess to the steady state, which on a \(9 \times 9\) grid takes \(20\) sweeps for the plate whose edges are held at \(180\), \(80\), \(20\) and \(0\) (Example 1).

title: Elliptic PDE’s
text:
Elliptic Equations
Recall that the Laplacian of a function \(u(x, y)\) is
\[
\nabla^2 u = u_{xx} + u_{yy}.
\tag{1}
\]






NoteDefinition — Laplace, Poisson and Helmholtz equations



With \(f\) and \(g\) given functions of \((x, y)\), the three model elliptic equations are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\nabla^2 u &= 0 &&\text{(Laplace's equation)}, \\
\nabla^2 u &= g(x, y) &&\text{(Poisson's equation)}, \\
\nabla^2 u + f(x, y)\,u &= g(x, y) &&\text{(Helmholtz's equation)}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]


It is often the case that the values of \(u(x, y)\) are known at all points on the sides of a rectangle \(R\). Each of these equations can then be solved by the finite-difference method. This page works with Laplace’s equation, which is the subject of all of Mathews’ examples; the formulas for Poisson’s and Helmholtz’s equations are given at the end of the theory.

title: Elliptic PDE’s
text:
The Laplacian Difference Equation
For a function with four continuous derivatives, the central-difference formula for the second derivative is
\[
f''(x) = \frac{f(x + h) - 2f(x) + f(x - h)}{h^2} + O(h^2).
\tag{3}
\]
Applying it to \(u_{xx}\) and \(u_{yy}\) and adding gives
\[
\nabla^2 u = \frac{u(x + h, y) + u(x - h, y) + u(x, y + h) + u(x, y - h) - 4u(x, y)}{h^2} + O(h^2).
\tag{4}
\]

The grid
The rectangle \(R = \{(x, y) : 0 \le x \le a,\ 0 \le y \le b\}\) is covered by the grid points
\[
x_i = (i - 1)h, \quad i = 1, \ldots, n, \qquad y_j = (j - 1)h, \quad j = 1, \ldots, m,
\]
so that \(a = (n - 1)h\) and \(b = (m - 1)h\), and \(R\) is divided into \((n - 1) \times (m - 1)\) squares of side \(h\). (Mathews’ text writes \(a = nh\) and \(b = mh\), but with \(n\) grid points across there are \(n - 1\) intervals, and his own program for Example 5 uses \(h = a/(n - 1)\).) The grid points with \(i = 1\) or \(n\), or \(j = 1\) or \(m\), lie on the edges of \(R\); the others are interior points.
Dropping the \(O(h^2)\) term in (4), setting the result to zero and multiplying by \(h^2\) gives one equation for each interior point.






ImportantLaplacian computational formula (five-point formula)



At each interior grid point, \(i = 2, \ldots, n - 1\) and \(j = 2, \ldots, m - 1\),
\[
u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4u_{i,j} = 0.
\tag{5}
\]
Equivalently, \(u_{i,j}\) is the average of its four neighbours. The spacing \(h\) has dropped out, so on a square the grid values depend only on the number of grid points and the boundary values, not on the side length.


The values on the edges are known:
\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{1,j} &= u(0, y_j), & u_{n,j} &= u(a, y_j), && j = 2, \ldots, m - 1 && \text{(left and right)}, \\
u_{i,1} &= u(x_i, 0), & u_{i,m} &= u(x_i, b), && i = 2, \ldots, n - 1 && \text{(bottom and top)}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
\]
The four corner values never appear in (5), because the five-point stencil never reaches diagonally. Mathews’ programs set each corner to the average of its two neighbours on the edges, which affects only the plots.


Setting up the linear system
Applying (5) at each of the \((n - 2)(m - 2)\) interior points gives a linear system with one unknown for each interior point. For a small illustration (Example 10.5 of the textbook section that the module accompanies), take the boundary values of Examples 1 to 5 below on a \(5 \times 5\) grid: \(u = 180\) on the top edge, \(80\) on the left, \(20\) on the bottom and \(0\) on the right. Number the nine interior values row by row from the bottom left:
\[
\begin{array}{ccccc}
& 180 & 180 & 180 & \\
80 & p_7 & p_8 & p_9 & 0 \\
80 & p_4 & p_5 & p_6 & 0 \\
80 & p_1 & p_2 & p_3 & 0 \\
& 20 & 20 & 20 &
\end{array}
\]
Formula (5) at \(p_1\) reads \(p_2 + p_4 + 20 + 80 - 4p_1 = 0\), and in the same way at the other eight points, so the system \(A P = B\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
-4p_1 + p_2 + p_4 &= -100 \\
p_1 - 4p_2 + p_3 + p_5 &= -20 \\
p_2 - 4p_3 + p_6 &= -20 \\
p_1 - 4p_4 + p_5 + p_7 &= -80 \\
p_2 + p_4 - 4p_5 + p_6 + p_8 &= 0 \\
p_3 + p_5 - 4p_6 + p_9 &= 0 \\
p_4 - 4p_7 + p_8 &= -260 \\
p_5 + p_7 - 4p_8 + p_9 &= -180 \\
p_6 + p_8 - 4p_9 &= -180.
\end{aligned}
\]
Gaussian elimination in exact arithmetic gives
\[
P = \Bigl(\tfrac{390}{7},\ \tfrac{605}{14},\ \tfrac{190}{7},\ \tfrac{1115}{14},\ 70,\ \tfrac{635}{14},\ \tfrac{790}{7},\ \tfrac{1565}{14},\ \tfrac{590}{7}\Bigr)
\approx (55.7143,\ 43.2143,\ 27.1429,\ 79.6429,\ 70,\ 45.3571,\ 112.8571,\ 111.7857,\ 84.2857).
\]

The centre value \(p_5 = 70\) is exactly the average of the four edge values, \((180 + 80 + 20 + 0)/4\). This holds on any square grid with an odd number of points per side: rotating the square by quarter turns permutes the four edges, and the four rotated problems add up to the problem with the same value on every edge, whose solution is constant.
On a finer grid the system grows quickly, \((n - 2)(m - 2)\) equations, while an iterative method only has to store the \(nm\) grid values. That is the reason for the iteration in the next section.


Derivative boundary conditions
A Neumann condition prescribes the derivative of \(u\) normal to an edge. The zero normal derivative
\[
\frac{\partial u}{\partial N} = 0
\tag{7}
\]
means, for heat flow, that the edge is insulated. On the right edge \(x = a\) this is \(u_x(x_n, y_j) = 0\), and the values \(u_{n,j}\) become unknowns. The five-point formula at \((x_n, y_j)\) needs the value \(u_{n+1,j}\) at a point outside \(R\); the central difference \(\bigl(u_{n+1,j} - u_{n-1,j}\bigr)/(2h) \approx u_x(x_n, y_j) = 0\), which has error \(O(h^2)\), replaces it by \(u_{n-1,j}\). The same argument on each edge gives the Neumann stencils.






ImportantNeumann computational formulas for \(\partial u / \partial N = 0\)



\[
\begin{aligned}
2u_{i,2} + u_{i-1,1} + u_{i+1,1} - 4u_{i,1} &= 0 &&\text{(bottom edge)}, \\
2u_{i,m-1} + u_{i-1,m} + u_{i+1,m} - 4u_{i,m} &= 0 &&\text{(top edge)}, \\
2u_{2,j} + u_{1,j-1} + u_{1,j+1} - 4u_{1,j} &= 0 &&\text{(left edge)}, \\
2u_{n-1,j} + u_{n,j-1} + u_{n,j+1} - 4u_{n,j} &= 0 &&\text{(right edge)}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]


When the derivative condition holds on part of the boundary and values of \(u\) are given on the rest, the problem is called mixed. The equations at the points of an insulated edge use the matching stencil in (8), and the five-point formula (5) is used at the interior points.

title: Elliptic PDE’s
text:
Iterative Solution by Successive Over-Relaxation
Write the five-point formula (5) in a form suitable for iteration:
\[
u_{i,j} \leftarrow u_{i,j} + r_{i,j}, \qquad r_{i,j} = \frac{u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4u_{i,j}}{4},
\tag{9}
\]
for \(i = 2, \ldots, n - 1\) and \(j = 2, \ldots, m - 1\). Each update replaces \(u_{i,j}\) by the average of its four neighbours, and the residual \(r_{i,j}\) is zero exactly when (5) holds at that point. Starting values must be supplied at every interior point; Mathews’ text suggests the average of the boundary values, and every one of his set-ups that survives starts each interior point at \(70\). One iteration, or sweep, applies (9) once at every interior point, using each new value as soon as it has been computed (this is the Gauss-Seidel method). Over-relaxation moves each value further in the same direction:
\[
u_{i,j} \leftarrow u_{i,j} + \omega\, r_{i,j}, \qquad 1 \le \omega < 2.
\tag{10}
\]
With \(\omega = 1\), (10) is the Gauss-Seidel sweep (9).






TipTheorem — Optimal relaxation parameter (general result)



For the five-point equations (5) of a Dirichlet problem on an \(n \times m\) grid, swept in a row-by-row or column-by-column order, the SOR iteration converges fastest for
\[
\omega = \frac{4}{2 + \sqrt{4 - \Bigl(\cos\dfrac{\pi}{n - 1} + \cos\dfrac{\pi}{m - 1}\Bigr)^2}} .
\tag{11}
\]
It follows from Young’s theory of the eigenvalues of SOR iteration matrices. For \(n = m = 9\), (11) gives \(\omega = 1.446463\), and for \(n = m = 21\) it gives \(\omega = 1.729454\). For both grids, computing the eigenvalues of the SOR iteration matrix in Mathews’ sweep order confirms that (11) minimises its spectral radius, which is then \(\omega - 1\): \(0.446463\) against \(0.853553\) for Gauss-Seidel on the \(9 \times 9\) grid, and \(0.729454\) against \(0.975528\) on the \(21 \times 21\) grid.


If the Neumann condition holds on an edge, the stencils (8) are relaxed in the same way; for example, on an insulated bottom edge,
\[
u_{i,1} \leftarrow u_{i,1} + \omega\, \frac{2u_{i,2} + u_{i-1,1} + u_{i+1,1} - 4u_{i,1}}{4},
\tag{12}
\]
and similarly with the top, left and right stencils of (8). Formula (11) is derived for the Dirichlet problem only; Example 3 shows that it is not the best \(\omega\) for a mixed problem.

Algorithm
Mathews’ two programs carry out the following steps.

Grid and starting values. Store the \(n \times m\) grid values in a table, put the boundary values (6) on the edges, set each corner to the average of its two neighbours on the edges, and set every interior value to \(70\). The Neumann program treats an insulated bottom edge, whose values are then unknowns too; in Example 3 their starting values are interpolated linearly between the two bottom corners.
Relaxation parameter. Compute \(\omega\) from (11).
Sweep. For each column of interior points in turn, and down each column, compute the correction \(\omega\, r_{i,j}\) from (10) and add it to \(u_{i,j}\) at once. In the Neumann program, then sweep the points of the bottom edge, between the corners, with formula (12).
Record the change. Let \(E\) be the largest \(\lvert \omega\, r_{i,j} \rvert\) of the sweep, each correction computed with the values current at the moment it is made, and print it as the “max grid change”.
Stop or repeat. Repeat steps 3 and 4 while \(E > 0.001\), for at most \(71\) sweeps.







WarningThe stopping rule measures the change, not the error



A small final correction does not mean the grid values are within \(0.001\) of the solution of the linear system. In Example 3 the last sweep changes no value by more than \(0.000998\), but the result still differs from the exact solution of the difference equations by up to \(0.0027\). And for a smooth solution, the solution of the difference equations differs from that of the differential equation by an amount of order \(h^2\), which no number of sweeps removes.




Poisson’s and Helmholtz’s equations
With \(g_{i,j} = g(x_i, y_j)\) and \(f_{i,j} = f(x_i, y_j)\), the same derivation turns Poisson’s equation \(\nabla^2 u = g\) into the iteration
\[
u_{i,j} \leftarrow u_{i,j} + \frac{u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4u_{i,j} - h^2 g_{i,j}}{4},
\tag{13}
\]
and Helmholtz’s equation \(\nabla^2 u + f u = g\) into
\[
u_{i,j} \leftarrow u_{i,j} + \frac{u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - (4 - h^2 f_{i,j})\, u_{i,j} - h^2 g_{i,j}}{4 - h^2 f_{i,j}} .
\tag{14}
\]
In both, the update makes the difference equation hold at \((x_i, y_j)\), and the correction can be multiplied by \(\omega\) as in (10). Unlike (5), these equations depend on \(h\).


Improvement: the nine-point formula
A more accurate approximation to the Laplacian also uses the four diagonal neighbours:
\[
\nabla^2 u_{i,j} \approx \frac{1}{6h^2}\Bigl(u_{i+1,j-1} + u_{i-1,j-1} + u_{i+1,j+1} + u_{i-1,j+1} + 4u_{i+1,j} + 4u_{i-1,j} + 4u_{i,j+1} + 4u_{i,j-1} - 20u_{i,j}\Bigr).
\tag{15}
\]
For a function that satisfies Laplace’s equation, Mathews gives the truncation errors of the nine-point and five-point formulas as \(O(h^4)\) and \(O(h^2)\). Applied to the harmonic functions \(e^x \sin y\), \(\ln\bigl((x + 2)^2 + (y + 1)^2\bigr)\) and \(\operatorname{Re}(x + iy)^8\) at the point \((0.3, 0.4)\), the five-point error falls by a factor of \(4.0\) each time \(h\) is halved, and the nine-point error by a factor of \(64.0\), that is, \(O(h^6)\), which is better still. The advantage depends on \(\nabla^2 u = 0\): for a function that is not harmonic, such as \(e^x \sin 2y\), both formulas are only \(O(h^2)\).

section: Example 4 — Example 1 on the unit square
text:
Example 4 — Example 1 on the unit square
Solve Laplace’s equation over the square \(0 \le x \le 1\), \(0 \le y \le 1\) with the boundary values of Example 1: top \(180\), left \(80\), bottom \(20\), right \(0\).
Mathews runs exactly the set-up and program of Example 1 (\(n = m = 9\)), and its first printed change, \(66.0101\), is that of Example 1, so the grid values are those of the table in Example 1, with \(x_i = (i - 1)/8\) and \(y_j = (j - 1)/8\). The only change is in the surface plot: he labels the axes \(x\) and \(y\) and replaces the row and column numbers \(1\), \(5\), \(9\) by the coordinates \(0\), \(0.5\), \(1\) (for \(y\), row \(1\) is \(y = 1\) and row \(9\) is \(y = 0\)), with vertical ticks \(0\), \(50\), \(100\), \(150\) and the viewpoint \((4, 2, 3)\) of Example 1.

title: Elliptic PDE’s
section: Example 5 — The unit square with the grid stored by coordinates
text:
Example 5 — The unit square with the grid stored by coordinates
Solve the problem of Example 4 again: Laplace’s equation on \(0 \le x \le 1\), \(0 \le y \le 1\) with \(u(x, 0) = 20\), \(u(x, 1) = 180\), \(u(0, y) = 80\) and \(u(1, y) = 0\).
This time Mathews gives the boundary as four functions and computes the grid from them, which is the form his program statement uses: \(u(x, 0) = f_1(x)\), \(u(x, b) = f_2(x)\) for \(0 \le x \le a\), and \(u(0, y) = f_3(y)\), \(u(a, y) = f_4(y)\) for \(0 \le y \le b\).
Step 1 — Set up the grid. With \(a = b = 1\) and \(n = m = 9\), the spacing is \(h = a/(n - 1) = 1/8\) in both directions. Entry \((i, j)\) of the table is now \(u(x_i, y_j)\) with \(x_i = (i - 1)h\) and \(y_j = (j - 1)h\), so the first index runs along \(x\) and the second along \(y\), as in the theory above. The edges get \(f_1(x_i) = 20\), \(f_2(x_i) = 180\), \(f_3(y_j) = 80\) and \(f_4(y_j) = 0\), the corners are the averages \(50\), \(130\), \(10\) and \(90\) as before, and the interior starts at \(70\).
Step 2 — Sweep. The program is the same, but because the table is stored the other way round, a sweep now runs along the rows of the plate from the bottom up, and from left to right along each row. With \(\omega = 1.446463\) the largest change decreases at every sweep, from \(61.8766\) in the first to \(0.000609839\) in the \(19\)th, one sweep fewer than Example 1, the difference being the order of the sweep. Our recomputation reproduces Mathews’ \(19\) printed values.
Step 3 — Result and verification. The largest difference between the final grid values and those of Example 1 at the same points is \(0.00075\), and between them and the exact solution of the difference equations \(0.00048\); the largest residual is \(0.000116\) in size.
Mathews’ plot. He plots the triples \(\bigl(x_i, y_j, u_{i,j}\bigr)\) as a surface with ListSurfacePlot3D, so the axes carry the true coordinates: axes labelled \(x\), \(y\), \(u\), viewpoint \((1, -2, 1)\) and box ratios \(1 : 1 : \tfrac12\).

title: Elliptic PDE’s
text:
Example 6 — Continuous boundary values
Solve Laplace’s equation over the square \(0 \le x \le 1\), \(0 \le y \le 1\) with
\[
u(x, 0) = \sin(\pi x), \quad u(x, 1) = 1 \quad \text{for } 0 \le x \le 1, \qquad u(0, y) = y^2, \quad u(1, y) = y^2 \quad \text{for } 0 \le y \le 1.
\]
At the corners the edge functions agree: \(u(0, 0) = u(1, 0) = 0\) and \(u(0, 1) = u(1, 1) = 1\). Unlike Examples 1 to 5, the boundary values are continuous all the way round, and Mathews notes that Mathematica then has no trouble drawing the contour lines.
The images with Mathews’ set-up (grid and starting values), printout and plots for this example are missing from the archive. This page uses his program with \(n = m = 21\), so \(h = 0.05\), and starts every interior value at \(0\), a better guess than \(70\) for boundary values between \(0\) and \(1\).
Step 1 — Set up the grid. As in Example 5, entry \((i, j)\) is \(u(x_i, y_j)\) with \(x_i = y_i = (i - 1)/20\), and the edges are \(\sin(\pi x_i)\) at the bottom, \(1\) at the top and \(y_j^2\) on both sides. The program’s corner averages (\(0.0795\) at the bottom corners, \(0.95125\) at the top corners) differ from the true corner values \(0\) and \(1\); the corners are not used by the five-point formula, so a plot can show the true values instead.
Step 2 — Sweep. Formula (11) gives \(\omega = 1.729454\). Because the boundary values are of size \(1\) instead of \(100\), the fixed tolerance \(0.001\) is relatively looser here. The largest change falls from \(1.40154\) in the first sweep to \(0.000865966\) in the \(40\)th, where the run stops; it rises once on the way, from \(0.00187047\) in sweep \(38\) to \(0.00210206\) in sweep \(39\).
Step 3 — Exact solution. The function \(H(x, y) = y^2 - x^2 + x\) is harmonic (\(H_{xx} + H_{yy} = -2 + 2 = 0\)) and equals \(y^2\) on both sides, so \(u = H + w\), where \(w\) is harmonic, zero on both sides, and equals \(\sin(\pi x) - x(1 - x)\) on the bottom and \(-x(1 - x)\) on the top. The sine series of \(x(1 - x)\) on \([0, 1]\) has coefficients \(8/(k\pi)^3\) for odd \(k\) and \(0\) for even \(k\), so
\[
u(x, y) = y^2 - x^2 + x + \sum_{k = 1}^{\infty} \sin(k\pi x)\, \frac{A_k \sinh\bigl(k\pi(1 - y)\bigr) + B_k \sinh(k\pi y)}{\sinh(k\pi)},
\]
with \(A_1 = 1 - 8/\pi^3\), \(A_k = B_k = -8/(k\pi)^3\) for the other odd \(k\), \(B_1 = -8/\pi^3\), and \(A_k = B_k = 0\) for even \(k\).

Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Earthquake Model
text:
Description
A building of \(n\) floors is modelled as a chain of \(n\) equal masses \(m\) joined by horizontal springs of stiffness \(k\): the first floor is tied to the ground, each floor to the floor above it, and the top floor only to the floor below. If \(x_i(t)\) is the sideways displacement of floor \(i\) relative to the ground, the free vibrations of the building satisfy the linear system \(\mathbf{X}'' = \mathbf{a}\mathbf{X}\), where \(\mathbf{a} = \tfrac{k}{m}\,\mathbf{T}\) and \(\mathbf{T}\) is a tridiagonal matrix. Each eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of \(\mathbf{a}\) is negative and gives a natural frequency \(\omega = \sqrt{-\lambda}\) and a natural period \(P = 2\pi/\omega\) of the building. Computing them is an eigenvalue problem.
An earthquake that shakes the ground back and forth as \(e\cos(\omega t)\) adds the same inertial force to every floor, and the system becomes \(\mathbf{X}'' = \mathbf{a}\mathbf{X} + e\,\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\,\mathbf{b}\) with \(\mathbf{b} = (1, 1, \ldots, 1)^{T}\). It has the forced solution \(\mathbf{X}(t) = \mathbf{v}\cos(\omega t)\), whose amplitude vector solves an \(n \times n\) linear system:
\[
\bigl(\omega^2\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{a}\bigr)\,\mathbf{v} = -e\,\omega^2\,\mathbf{b}.
\]
The matrix is singular exactly when \(\omega\) equals a natural frequency, so the amplitudes blow up there: resonance. Mathews’ module, which follows a six-floor building through three examples, computes the six natural frequencies and periods, solves for the floor amplitudes at one shaking frequency, and then plots the largest amplitude \(\max_i |v_i|\) against the frequency and against the period of the earthquake. Every number below has been recomputed independently.

title: Earthquake Model
text:
The Shear-Building Model

Equations of motion
Number the floors \(i = 1, \ldots, n\) from the bottom, and set \(x_0 = 0\) for the ground. The spring between floors \(i-1\) and \(i\) pulls floor \(i\) with force \(k(x_{i-1} - x_i)\), and the spring between floors \(i\) and \(i+1\) pulls it with force \(k(x_{i+1} - x_i)\), so the net force on floor \(i\) is
\[
k(x_{i-1} - x_i) + k(x_{i+1} - x_i) = k\,(x_{i+1} - 2x_i + x_{i-1}), \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n-1,
\]
while the top floor has a spring below it only, and feels \(k(x_{n-1} - x_n)\). Newton’s second law \(m\,x_i'' = \text{force}\) for each floor gives the system
\[
\mathbf{X}'' = \mathbf{a}\,\mathbf{X}
\tag{1}
\]






NoteDefinition — Matrix of the shear building



For \(n\) floors of mass \(m\) and inter-floor stiffness \(k\),
\[
\mathbf{a} = \frac{k}{m}
\begin{pmatrix}
-2 & 1 & & & \\
1 & -2 & 1 & & \\
& \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\
& & 1 & -2 & 1 \\
& & & 1 & -1
\end{pmatrix},
\tag{2}
\]
an \(n \times n\) symmetric tridiagonal matrix whose last diagonal entry is \(-1\) instead of \(-2\) because the top floor has no floor above it.




Natural frequencies and modes
A solution of (1) in which every floor moves in step, \(\mathbf{X}(t) = \mathbf{u}\cos(\omega t)\), needs \(-\omega^2\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{a}\mathbf{u}\). So \(\mathbf{u}\) is an eigenvector of \(\mathbf{a}\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda = -\omega^2\), and
\[
\omega = \sqrt{-\lambda} = \sqrt{|\lambda|}, \qquad P = \frac{2\pi}{\omega}.
\tag{3}
\]
The eigenvector \(\mathbf{u}\) is the mode shape: the pattern of floor displacements that oscillates at that frequency.






TipTheorem — The eigenvalues are real and negative



For every \(n \ge 1\) and \(k, m > 0\), the matrix \(\mathbf{a}\) in (2) is symmetric and negative definite, since for every vector \(\mathbf{x} \ne \mathbf{0}\)
\[
\mathbf{x}^{T}\mathbf{a}\,\mathbf{x} = -\frac{k}{m}\Bigl(x_1^2 + \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(x_{i+1} - x_i)^2\Bigr) < 0 .
\]
Hence its \(n\) eigenvalues are real and negative, and the building has \(n\) real natural frequencies. For this particular matrix they are known in closed form:
\[
\lambda_j = -\frac{4k}{m}\sin^2\!\frac{(2j-1)\pi}{2(2n+1)}, \qquad
\omega_j = 2\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}\,\sin\frac{(2j-1)\pi}{2(2n+1)}, \qquad j = 1, \ldots, n,
\]
with mode shapes \(u_i^{(j)} = \sin\dfrac{i(2j-1)\pi}{2n+1}\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n\). The \(\omega_j\) are distinct and increase with \(j\); \(\omega_1\) is the fundamental frequency.


The bracket in the quadratic form is zero only when \(x_1 = 0\) and every difference \(x_{i+1} - x_i\) is zero, that is, only when \(\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}\). Mathews computes the eigenvalues numerically; the closed form is a check on that computation.


Example 1 — natural frequencies and periods of a six-floor building

\]
