title: Earthquake Model
text:
Earthquake Forcing

The forced system
Suppose the ground moves sideways as \(e\cos(\omega t)\), with amplitude \(e\) and angular frequency \(\omega\). Keep \(x_i\) as the displacement of floor \(i\) relative to the ground, so floor \(i\) is at \(x_i + e\cos(\omega t)\) in fixed coordinates. The spring forces depend only on the differences \(x_{i+1} - x_i\) and on \(x_1\), the stretch of the bottom spring, so they are unchanged, but the acceleration of floor \(i\) is now \(x_i'' - e\,\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\). Newton’s law \(m\bigl(x_i'' - e\omega^2\cos\omega t\bigr) = \text{spring force}\) moves the ground acceleration to the right-hand side as a force \(f = m\,e\,\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\) on every floor, and dividing by \(m\),
\[
\mathbf{X}'' = \mathbf{a}\,\mathbf{X} + e\,\omega^2\cos(\omega t)\,\mathbf{b},
\qquad \mathbf{b} = (1, 1, \ldots, 1)^{T}.
\tag{4}
\]


The forced solution
Substituting \(\mathbf{X}(t) = \mathbf{v}\cos(\omega t)\) into (4) gives \(-\omega^2\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{a}\mathbf{v} + e\,\omega^2\mathbf{b}\), that is,






ImportantKey formula — Amplitudes of the floors



\[
\bigl(\omega^2\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{a}\bigr)\,\mathbf{v} = -e\,\omega^2\,\mathbf{b},
\qquad
\mathbf{X}(t) = \mathbf{v}\cos(\omega t).
\tag{5}
\] Floor \(i\) swings with amplitude \(\lvert v_i \rvert\) relative to the ground.








WarningSign of the matrix



Mathews’ module writes the system as \((\omega^2\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{a})\mathbf{v} = -e\omega^2\mathbf{b}\), but his Mathematica code builds the matrix \(\omega^2\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{a}\), which is what (4) gives, and all his numbers come from that matrix. With \(\omega^2\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{a}\), whose eigenvalues \(\omega^2 + \omega_j^2\) are all positive, there would be no resonance, and Example 2 would give a largest amplitude of \(0.0736\) ft instead of \(0.388\) ft.


If \(\mathbf{u}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{u}_n\) are orthonormal eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{a}\), the matrix \(\omega^2\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{a}\) has eigenvalues \(\omega^2 - \omega_j^2\) for the same eigenvectors, and the solution of (5) is
\[
\mathbf{v} = -e\,\omega^2\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\mathbf{u}_j^{T}\mathbf{b}}{\omega^2 - \omega_j^2}\,\mathbf{u}_j .
\tag{6}
\]
The system is singular exactly when \(\omega\) equals a natural frequency \(\omega_j\). As \(\omega \to \omega_j\) the \(j\)-th term grows without bound, unless \(\mathbf{u}_j^{T}\mathbf{b} = 0\); for the building of Example 1 none of the six numbers \(\mathbf{u}_j^{T}\mathbf{b}\) is zero, so every natural frequency is a resonance. Since \(\mathbf{v}\) is proportional to \(e\), doubling the amplitude of the earthquake doubles every floor amplitude.






WarningThe forced solution is not the whole motion



The model has no damping. The general solution of (4) is \(\mathbf{v}\cos(\omega t)\) plus a free vibration \(\sum_j (A_j\cos\omega_j t + B_j\sin\omega_j t)\,\mathbf{u}_j\), and the free part never dies out. \(\mathbf{X}(t) = \mathbf{v}\cos(\omega t)\) is the motion exactly when the building starts from \(\mathbf{X}(0) = \mathbf{v}\), \(\mathbf{X}'(0) = \mathbf{0}\). A building at rest when the shaking starts, \(\mathbf{X}(0) = \mathbf{X}'(0) = \mathbf{0}\), moves as \(\mathbf{X}(t) = \mathbf{v}\cos(\omega t) - \sum_j \gamma_j\cos(\omega_j t)\,\mathbf{u}_j\), where \(\gamma_j\) is the coefficient of \(\mathbf{u}_j\) in (6). Mathews, and this page, study the forced part \(\mathbf{v}\cos(\omega t)\) only.




Example 2 — the floor amplitudes for \(\omega = 2.1\) and \(e = 0.075\) ft

\[

\]

title: Crank-Nicolson Method
text:
Description
The one-dimensional heat equation \(u_t = c^2 u_{xx}\) describes the temperature \(u(x, t)\) in an insulated rod \(0 \le x \le a\) whose ends are held at fixed temperatures and whose initial temperature is \(u(x, 0) = f(x)\). A finite-difference method lays a grid over the rectangle \(0 \le x \le a\), \(0 \le t \le b\), with spacing \(h\) in \(x\) and time step \(k\), and computes the temperatures row by row, from the initial row \(t = 0\) forward in time. How the method behaves depends on the dimensionless ratio \(r = c^2 k / h^2\). The simplest method, the explicit forward-difference method, computes each new temperature directly from three old ones, but it is stable only when \(r \le \tfrac12\). For larger \(r\), rapidly oscillating error components can grow at every step until they swamp the solution, as in Example 2 below.
The Crank-Nicolson method, due to John Crank and Phyllis Nicolson, centres the difference equation halfway between two time rows. It averages the second-difference approximation of \(u_{xx}\) over the old row \(j\) and the new row \(j+1\):
\[
-r\,u_{i-1,j+1} + (2 + 2r)\,u_{i,j+1} - r\,u_{i+1,j+1} \;=\; r\,u_{i-1,j} + (2 - 2r)\,u_{i,j} + r\,u_{i+1,j}.
\]
The new temperatures are coupled, so every time step solves a tridiagonal linear system. In return, the method is second-order accurate in both \(h\) and \(k\) and stable for every \(r > 0\) (general results, stated below). Mathews’ module first runs the forward-difference method twice, with \(r = 0.5\) and with the “too large” \(r = 0.875\) (Examples 1 and 2), and then runs Crank-Nicolson with \(r = 1\) and \(r = 2\) (Examples 3 and 4). Every number below has been recomputed: Examples 1 and 2 in exact rational arithmetic, Examples 3 and 4 in double precision, and all four compared with the Fourier series solution of the heat equation.

Mathews draws all the rows at once as a three-dimensional surface over the indices \(i\) and \(j\); each frame here is one row of that surface. The second panel shows what the profile alone does not: the error at the grid points (Case 1), the sizes of the two sine modes in the data (Case 2), the largest error in each row (Case 3), or the part of the solution caused by a small perturbation (Case 4). The exact solution of Examples 1 and 2 is the Fourier series below, summed over the odd terms up to \(p = 1999\); that of Examples 3 and 4 is the closed form given there. The numbers in the titles and legends agree with the tables in the examples.
Mathews’ module links no animation, and his animation archive has none for partial differential equations, so all four animations are new, with no Mathews original. Case 4 animates the sawtooth experiment of Example 4 (“What stability buys”), which is not in the module. Not animated are Mathews’ three-dimensional surfaces themselves (including his surfaces of the exact solution in Examples 3 and 4, drawn here as the black curves), the refinement table of Example 3, and the sawtooth figures for \(r = 1\).

title: Crank-Nicolson Method
section: The Heat Equation and the Grid
text:
The Heat Equation and the Grid






NoteProblem — heat equation with fixed end temperatures



Find \(u(x, t)\) on \(R = \{(x, t) : 0 \le x \le a,\ 0 \le t \le b\}\) with
\[
u_t(x, t) = c^2\, u_{xx}(x, t) \quad \text{for } 0 < x < a,\ 0 < t < b,
\tag{1}
\]
the initial condition \(u(x, 0) = f(x)\) for \(0 \le x \le a\), and the boundary conditions \(u(0, t) = c_1\) and \(u(a, t) = c_2\) for \(0 \le t \le b\).


The heat equation can be solved analytically with Fourier series. Mathews uses it as the prototype of a parabolic equation for numerical solution, and the series solution then serves as the check on the numerical one.
Following Mathews, the grid has \(n\) columns and \(m\) rows:
\[
h = \frac{a}{n - 1}, \qquad k = \frac{b}{m - 1}, \qquad x_i = (i - 1)h,\ i = 1, \ldots, n, \qquad t_j = (j - 1)k,\ j = 1, \ldots, m,
\]
and \(u_{i,j}\) approximates \(u(x_i, t_j)\). The first row holds the initial values \(u_{i,1} = f(x_i)\), and the first and last columns hold the boundary values \(u_{1,j} = c_1\) and \(u_{n,j} = c_2\). The methods below compute the interior values \(u_{2,j}, \ldots, u_{n-1,j}\) one row at a time, and the ratio
\[
r = \frac{c^2 k}{h^2}
\tag{2}
\]
appears in all of them.
All four of Mathews’ examples use \(a = 1\), \(c = 1\) and \(c_1 = c_2 = 0\): a rod of length one whose ends are held at temperature zero.

title: Crank-Nicolson Method
text:
The Forward-Difference Method
At a grid point \((x, t)\), replace \(u_t\) by the forward difference and \(u_{xx}\) by the central second difference:
\[
u_t(x, t) = \frac{u(x, t + k) - u(x, t)}{k} + O(k), \qquad
u_{xx}(x, t) = \frac{u(x - h, t) - 2u(x, t) + u(x + h, t)}{h^2} + O(h^2).
\]
Substituting both into (1), dropping the error terms and multiplying by \(k\) gives the forward-difference (explicit) method.






ImportantForward-difference formula



\[
u_{i,j+1} = (1 - 2r)\,u_{i,j} + r\,\bigl(u_{i-1,j} + u_{i+1,j}\bigr), \qquad i = 2, \ldots, n - 1.
\tag{3}
\]


Each new value comes directly from three values in the row below, so no equations have to be solved. When \(r \le \tfrac12\), the three weights \(r\), \(1 - 2r\) and \(r\) are nonnegative and add up to \(1\), so each new value is a weighted average of old ones and can be neither larger than the largest old value nor smaller than the smallest. When \(r > \tfrac12\) the centre weight \(1 - 2r\) is negative and this argument fails.






TipTheorem — Stability of the forward-difference method (general)



For the problem (1) with fixed end temperatures, write the error at the interior grid points of a row as a combination of the discrete sine modes \(\sin(p\pi x_i/a)\), \(p = 1, \ldots, n - 2\). Formula (3) multiplies the coefficient of mode \(p\) by
\[
G_p = 1 - 4r \sin^2\!\Bigl(\frac{p\pi h}{2a}\Bigr)
\]
at each step. Every \(|G_p| \le 1\) on every grid exactly when \(r \le \tfrac12\). For \(r > \tfrac12\) the highest modes of a fine enough grid have \(G_p < -1\), so they grow and change sign at every step. The method’s local truncation error is \(O(k + h^2)\).



Example 1 — Forward differences with \(r = 0.5\)
Solve \(u_t = u_{xx}\) for \(0 \le x \le 1\), \(0 \le t \le 0.2\), with \(u(0, t) = u(1, t) = 0\) and initial temperature
\[
u(x, 0) = f(x) = 4x - 4x^2.
\]
Use the forward-difference method with \(h = 0.2\) and \(k = 0.02\), and find the temperatures for \(t = 0.02, 0.04, \ldots, 0.20\).
Mathews’ grid has \(n = 6\) columns and \(m = 11\) rows, so \(h = 1/5\), \(k = 0.2/10 = 0.02\) and
\[
r = \frac{c^2 k}{h^2} = \frac{1\,(0.02)}{(0.2)^2} = 0.5.
\]
(The module’s statement of this example says “\(r = 1\)”, but the parameters it then uses give \(r = 0.5\), which is what Mathews’ program computes. The “\(r = 1\)” is probably meant to be \(c = 1\).)
Step 1: with \(r = \tfrac12\) the centre weight \(1 - 2r\) vanishes, and (3) becomes the average of the two neighbours:
\[
u_{i,j+1} = \tfrac12\bigl(u_{i-1,j} + u_{i+1,j}\bigr).
\]
Step 2: the initial row is \(f(0), f(0.2), \ldots, f(1) = 0,\ 0.64,\ 0.96,\ 0.96,\ 0.64,\ 0\). The first time step gives
\[
u_{2,2} = \tfrac12(0 + 0.96) = 0.48, \qquad u_{3,2} = \tfrac12(0.64 + 0.96) = 0.80,
\]
and by symmetry \(u_{4,2} = 0.80\), \(u_{5,2} = 0.48\).
Step 3: the second time step gives \(u_{2,3} = \tfrac12(0 + 0.80) = 0.40\) and \(u_{3,3} = \tfrac12(0.48 + 0.80) = 0.64\), and so on.
Because \(f\) is symmetric about \(x = \tfrac12\), so is every row: the values at \(x = 0.6\) and \(0.8\) equal those at \(0.4\) and \(0.2\), and the end values are \(0\). The table lists the two independent columns. With \(r = \tfrac12\) every value is a terminating decimal, and the table gives them exactly (Mathews prints six significant digits, for example \(0.117813\) for \(0.1178125\)). Example 2 — Forward differences with \(r = 0.875\): the step is too large

\]

f(x_i) = 1.031357\,\sin(\pi x_i) + 0.035522\,\sin(3\pi x_i), \qquad i = 1, \ldots, 6.

title: Crank-Nicolson Method
text:
The Crank-Nicolson Method
The forward-difference method evaluates \(u_{xx}\) on the old row only, and that is the source of both its first-order accuracy in \(t\) and its stability limit. Crank and Nicolson instead centred the approximation at the point \((x, t + k/2)\), halfway between the rows \(t\) and \(t + k\). There the forward difference becomes a central difference, and it is second-order accurate:
\[
u_t\Bigl(x, t + \frac{k}{2}\Bigr) = \frac{u(x, t + k) - u(x, t)}{k} + O(k^2).
\tag{4}
\]
For \(u_{xx}(x, t + k/2)\) they used the average of the central second differences on the two rows. The average of the values at \(t\) and \(t + k\) also differs from the value at \(t + k/2\) by \(O(k^2)\):
\[
u_{xx}\Bigl(x, t + \frac{k}{2}\Bigr) = \frac{1}{2h^2}\Bigl[\bigl(u(x - h, t + k) - 2u(x, t + k) + u(x + h, t + k)\bigr) + \bigl(u(x - h, t) - 2u(x, t) + u(x + h, t)\bigr)\Bigr] + O(h^2 + k^2).
\tag{5}
\]
Setting (4) equal to \(c^2\) times (5), dropping the error terms and multiplying by \(2k\) gives
\[
2\bigl(u_{i,j+1} - u_{i,j}\bigr) = r\bigl(u_{i-1,j+1} - 2u_{i,j+1} + u_{i+1,j+1}\bigr) + r\bigl(u_{i-1,j} - 2u_{i,j} + u_{i+1,j}\bigr).
\]
Collecting the unknown values of row \(j + 1\) on the left:






ImportantCrank-Nicolson formula



\[
-r\,u_{i-1,j+1} + (2 + 2r)\,u_{i,j+1} - r\,u_{i+1,j+1} = r\,u_{i-1,j} + (2 - 2r)\,u_{i,j} + r\,u_{i+1,j}, \qquad i = 2, \ldots, n - 1.
\tag{6}
\]


Mathews’ program divides (6) by \(r\), so its matrix has \(2 + 2/r\) on the diagonal and \(-1\) beside it, and its right-hand side is \(u_{i-1,j} + (2/r - 2)\,u_{i,j} + u_{i+1,j}\). With \(r = 1\) the formula is especially simple:
\[
-u_{i-1,j+1} + 4u_{i,j+1} - u_{i+1,j+1} = u_{i-1,j} + u_{i+1,j}.
\]

The tridiagonal system
The values \(u_{1,j+1} = c_1\) and \(u_{n,j+1} = c_2\) are known, so their terms in (6) move to the right-hand side. That leaves a system of \(n - 2\) equations in the \(n - 2\) unknowns \(u_{2,j+1}, \ldots, u_{n-1,j+1}\):
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
2 + 2r & -r & & & \\
-r & 2 + 2r & -r & & \\
& \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\
& & -r & 2 + 2r & -r \\
& & & -r & 2 + 2r
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} u_{2,j+1} \\ u_{3,j+1} \\ \vdots \\ u_{n-2,j+1} \\ u_{n-1,j+1} \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} b_2 + r c_1 \\ b_3 \\ \vdots \\ b_{n-2} \\ b_{n-1} + r c_2 \end{pmatrix},
\tag{7}
\]
where \(b_i = r\,u_{i-1,j} + (2 - 2r)\,u_{i,j} + r\,u_{i+1,j}\) is the right side of (6). The matrix is the same at every time step. It is strictly diagonally dominant (\(2 + 2r > 2r\)) and symmetric with eigenvalues \(2 + 2r - 2r\cos\bigl(p\pi/(n - 1)\bigr) > 2\), so it is nonsingular for every \(r > 0\). A tridiagonal system is solved by Gaussian elimination without pivoting in \(O(n)\) operations: one forward sweep eliminates the subdiagonal, and back substitution finds the unknowns (see Tri-Diagonal Matrices). Mathews’ TriDiagonal routine does exactly this. His program keeps all \(n\) rows, including the two boundary rows, which become the trivial equations \(u_{1,j+1} = c_1\) and \(u_{n,j+1} = c_2\). As he remarks, \(n - 2\) rows would do.






TipTheorem — Accuracy and stability of Crank-Nicolson (general)



If the solution \(u\) is smooth, the local truncation error of (6) is \(O(h^2 + k^2)\). With fixed end temperatures, formula (6) multiplies the coefficient of the discrete sine mode \(p\) by
\[
G_p = \frac{1 - 2r\, s_p}{1 + 2r\, s_p}, \qquad s_p = \sin^2\!\Bigl(\frac{p\pi h}{2a}\Bigr),
\]
at each step. Since \(r s_p > 0\), \(-1 < G_p < 1\) for every mode and every \(r > 0\). The method is unconditionally stable: no restriction on \(r\) is needed for stability.


Stability does not mean accuracy. A larger \(k\) still gives a larger error, and when \(2r s_p > 1\) the factor \(G_p\) is negative. Such a mode is not amplified, but it changes sign at every step while it decays. For large \(r\) the factors of the highest modes approach \(-1\), so these modes die out slowly, while the true solution damps them almost at once. When the initial data are rough, for example a discontinuity or a mismatch between \(f\) and the end temperatures, Crank-Nicolson with a large \(r\) can therefore show slowly fading oscillations. This is a general property of the method; Example 4 below checks it on a computed perturbation.


Algorithm






ImportantAlgorithm — Crank-Nicolson method for the heat equation



Given \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(f\), \(c_1\), \(c_2\) and the grid sizes \(n\) and \(m\):

Set \(h = a/(n - 1)\), \(k = b/(m - 1)\) and \(r = c^2 k/h^2\).
Fill the first row with \(u_{i,1} = f(x_i)\), \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), and the end columns with \(u_{1,j} = c_1\), \(u_{n,j} = c_2\), \(j = 1, \ldots, m\).
Form the tridiagonal matrix of (7): \(2 + 2r\) on the diagonal and \(-r\) on the sub- and superdiagonals.
For \(j = 1, \ldots, m - 1\): compute the right-hand side of (7) from row \(j\), and solve the tridiagonal system for row \(j + 1\).





Example 3 — Crank-Nicolson with \(r = 1\)

\[
u(x, 0) = f(x) = \sin(\pi x) + \sin(3\pi x).
\]

The time error speeds it up: the factor \((1 - z/2)/(1 + z/2)\) is smaller than \(e^{-z}\). With the larger \(k\) the time error is larger and cancels more of the spatial error.
What stability buys. On these smooth initial data the forward-difference method would not blow up either, at least not visibly in ten steps. The data contain only the modes \(p = 1\) and \(p = 3\), whose explicit factors are \(0.902113\) and \(0.175571\) for \(r = 1\) and \(0.804226\) and \(-0.648859\) for \(r = 2\), all less than \(1\) in size. Run on the grid of this example it stays bounded but is far less accurate (largest error \(0.80\), compared with \(0.074\) for Crank-Nicolson). The difference shows as soon as the data contain high modes. Add the sawtooth perturbation \(\pm 0.001\), alternating in sign, to the interior initial values. With \(r = 2\) the forward-difference method amplifies the perturbation to about \(2.6 \times 10^{5}\) by \(t = 0.2\), because its factor for the mode \(p = 9\) is \(-6.804226\). (With \(r = 1\) on Example 3’s grid the figures are \(53\) for forward differences and \(1.2 \times 10^{-5}\) for Crank-Nicolson.)

Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Compartment Model
text:
Description
A compartment model follows a dissolved substance as it is carried by a liquid through a chain of well-mixed tanks. Tank \(i\) holds a fixed volume \(V_i\) of liquid and an amount \(x_i(t)\) of the substance; liquid flows from tank to tank at the constant rate \(r\), so the substance leaves tank \(i\) at the rate \(r\,x_i/V_i = k_i x_i\) and enters the next tank at the same rate. Writing “rate in minus rate out” for every tank gives a linear system of differential equations with constant coefficients,
\[
\mathbf{X}'(t) = \mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{X}(t), \qquad \mathbf{X}(0) = \mathbf{X}_0, \qquad k_i = \frac{r}{V_i},
\]
whose matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) records which tank drains into which. The method is the eigenvalue method for linear systems: find the eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) and eigenvectors \(\mathbf{V}_j\) of \(\mathbf{A}\), form the general solution \(\mathbf{X}(t) = \sum_j c_j e^{\lambda_j t}\mathbf{V}_j\), and choose the constants \(c_j\) to match the initial amounts. (When the eigenvalues are complex the real and imaginary parts of \(e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{V}\) are used instead; equivalently, \(\mathbf{X}(t) = e^{\mathbf{A}t}\mathbf{X}_0\) with the matrix exponential.)
Mathews works three examples, all solved in closed form with no numerical integration and all starting with \(10\) units of the substance in the first tank and none in the others: an open chain of three tanks fed by pure water, where the substance is washed out of the system; a closed loop of three tanks, where it is only redistributed; and an open chain of five tanks. Every solution below has been checked by substituting it into the differential equations and by comparing it with a high-accuracy numerical solution.

title: Compartment Model
text:
Animations
Each animation below runs one of Mathews’ three examples forward in time. The top of each frame draws the tanks with widths proportional to their volumes and a common height, so the shaded height in a tank is the concentration \(x_i/V_i\) of the substance and the shaded area is proportional to the amount \(x_i\); arrows show the flow, and the labels under each tank give its amount and concentration at the time in the title. Since every pipe carries the same rate \(r\), each tank fills exactly while its shaded height is below that of the tank feeding it (\(x_i' = r\,(x_{i-1}/V_{i-1} - x_i/V_i)\); tank 1 of an open chain is fed pure water and only drains), and a tank reaches its maximum when the two shaded heights are level. Below the tanks, the amounts \(x_i(t)\) and their sum \(S(t)\) grow in time, with a dot on the newest value of each. The curves are the exact solutions found below by the eigenvalue method: the scripts compute the eigenvectors and the constants in exact rational arithmetic and evaluate the sums of exponentials in 256-bit arithmetic.
Mathews’ module links no animation, and his animation archive has none for the compartment model, so all three animations are new, with no Mathews original. They follow his three examples, with his parameters and, where his output survives, his plot windows and colours (his green darkened for legibility). Not animated are his matrix-exponential construction in Example 2, which gives the same solution as Case 2; the plots of his Example 2, whose images are lost from the archive, including his plot of how the three curves stack up; the generalized-eigenvector case of equal volumes, which he mentions in a remark but does not work, and the equal-volume example in the callout below.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Mathews’ Example 1, open chain, \(V = (80, 100, 120)\), \(r = 20\), \(\mathbf{X}_0 = (10, 0, 0)\), \(0 \le t \le 40\)
Behavior: Tank 1 drains from the start, \(x_1 = 10e^{-t/4}\), while the substance passes down the chain. Tank 2 fills until its shaded height is level with that of tank 1, at its maximum \(x_2 = 4.096\) at \(t = 4.463\), and tank 3 until it is level with tank 2, at \(x_3 = 3.248\) at \(t = 9.866\); a diamond marks each maximum once it has passed, and afterwards both tanks drain. The total \(S(t)\) starts flat, because nothing leaves the system until tank 3 fills (\(S' = -\tfrac16 x_3\)), and then decreases in every frame. The dashed tray on the right collects the washed-out amount \(10 - S(t)\), drawn to the same area scale as the tanks; at \(t = 40\) it holds \(9.851\), and the \(S = 0.1488\) left in the system is mostly in tank 3 (\(x_3 = 0.1339\)). The bottom right panel is Mathews’ filled plot, with bands for \(x_1\), \(x_1 + x_2\) and \(S\) in his red, blue and green; the gray band above \(S\) is the washed-out amount, so the bands always add up to \(10\). Mathews plots the single curves on \([0, 20] \times [0, 10]\); both panels here use the \([0, 40] \times [0, 10]\) of his sum and filled plots.

Case 2 — Mathews’ Example 2, closed loop, \(V = (40, 20, 40)\), \(r = 20\), \(\mathbf{X}_0 = (10, 0, 0)\), \(0 \le t \le 12.5\)
Behavior: The liquid leaving tank 3 returns to tank 1, so the total stays \(S = 10\) in every frame and the substance is only redistributed: the shaded heights level out at the common equilibrium concentration \(10/100 = 0.1\) (the dashed line in each tank), so the amounts tend to \((4, 2, 4)\), in proportion to the volumes. Tank 2, the smallest, is the first to reach its equilibrium value: its shaded height passes the dashed line at \(t = 0.6435\) and overshoots it, to the concentration \(0.1294\) (\(x_2 = 2.588\)) at \(t = \pi/2\). On the linear scale of the left panel the curves look settled by \(t = 5\), the end of Mathews’ interval (dotted line), where no tank is more than \(0.035\) from its equilibrium value. The right panel plots the distance \(|x_i - \text{equilibrium}|\) on a log scale, solid while \(x_i\) is above its equilibrium value and dashed while below, and shows that the approach goes on as a damped oscillation. Each distance stays under its envelope, \(2\sqrt{10}\,e^{-t}\) for tanks 1 and 2 and \(4\sqrt5\,e^{-t}\) for tank 3, the straight lines of the log plot, and drops out of the bottom of the panel each time the tank crosses its equilibrium value: tank 2 at \(t = 0.6435\) and \(6.927\), tank 1 at \(3.785\) and \(10.07\), tank 3 at \(5.356\) and \(11.64\), consecutive crossings of a tank being \(2\pi\) apart. At \(t = 12.5\) the largest distance is \(2.21 \times 10^{-5}\). Mathews’ plots of this example are lost, so the window \([0, 12.5] \times [0, 10.5]\) and the colours, those of his Example 1, are chosen here; the clock runs past his \(t = 5\) so that every tank crosses its equilibrium value twice.

Case 3 — Mathews’ Example 3, open chain, \(V = (60, 80, 100, 120, 150)\), \(r = 24\), \(\mathbf{X}_0 = (10, 0, 0, 0, 0)\), \(0 \le t \le 50\)
Behavior: The pulse of substance travels down the chain of five tanks. Each of tanks 2 to 5 fills until its shaded height is level with that of the tank before it, and the maxima, marked by diamonds, come later and lower from tank to tank: \(4.219\) at \(t = 2.877\), \(3.383\) at \(6.527\), \(2.967\) at \(10.97\) and \(2.828\) at \(16.48\). With five tanks to pass, the total stays near \(10\) longer than in Case 1 (\(S(5) = 9.916\), against \(9.178\) for the three tanks of Case 1), since only tank 5 empties out of the system (\(S' = -\tfrac4{25}x_5\)), and then it decreases in every frame. At \(t = 50\) the tray holds \(9.878\), and of the \(S = 0.1219\) left nearly all is in tanks 4 and 5 (\(x_4 = 0.01188\), \(x_5 = 0.1093\)). title: Compartment Model
text:
Modelling the Tanks






NoteDefinition — Well-mixed tank



A tank is well mixed if the substance is spread uniformly through its liquid at every instant, so that its concentration is \(x_i(t)/V_i\) everywhere in the tank, including in the liquid that flows out.


If liquid enters and leaves tank \(i\) at the same rate \(r\), its volume \(V_i\) stays constant, and the substance leaves it at the rate (flow rate) \(\times\) (concentration) \(= r\,x_i/V_i\). The balance law for tank \(i\) is
\[
\frac{dx_i}{dt} = (\text{rate in}) - (\text{rate out}).
\tag{1}
\]
Mathews abbreviates the outflow coefficients as
\[
k_1 = \frac{r}{V_1}, \qquad k_2 = \frac{r}{V_2}, \qquad k_3 = \frac{r}{V_3}, \ \ldots
\tag{2}
\]
so that the substance leaves tank \(i\) at the rate \(k_i x_i\). A large tank (large \(V_i\)) has a small \(k_i\) and holds on to its substance longer. Mathews’ proof and program pages for this module were never written (both are empty placeholder pages in the archive), so the derivation here is the standard one.

title: Compartment Model
section: Model I — The Open Three-Stage System
text:
Model I — The Open Three-Stage System
Pure water flows at the rate \(r\) into the first tank; the mixture flows at the rate \(r\) from tank 1 into tank 2, from tank 2 into tank 3, and out of tank 3. Applying (1) to each tank,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1' &= -k_1 x_1, \\
x_2' &= \phantom{-}k_1 x_1 - k_2 x_2, \\
x_3' &= \phantom{-}k_2 x_2 - k_3 x_3,
\end{aligned}
\qquad x_1(0) = a_1,\ x_2(0) = a_2,\ x_3(0) = a_3,
\tag{3}
\]
or \(\mathbf{X}' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}\) with the lower triangular matrix
\[
\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} -k_1 & 0 & 0 \\ k_1 & -k_2 & 0 \\ 0 & k_2 & -k_3 \end{pmatrix}.
\]

Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a chain
Because \(\mathbf{A}\) is triangular, its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries, \(\lambda_j = -k_j\). All of them are negative, so every solution of (3) decays to \(\mathbf{0}\). For the eigenvalue \(-k_j\) an eigenvector \(\mathbf{V}_j\) has zeros above position \(j\), a \(1\) (or any convenient nonzero number) in position \(j\), and below it
\[
v_i = \frac{k_{i-1}}{k_i - k_j}\, v_{i-1}, \qquad i = j+1, \ldots, n,
\tag{4}
\]
which follows from row \(i\) of \((\mathbf{A} + k_j\mathbf{I})\mathbf{V}_j = \mathbf{0}\). The same recursion holds for a chain of any length \(n\); it requires \(k_i \ne k_j\) for \(i > j\).






TipTheorem — Solution of the open chain



If the tank volumes \(V_1, \ldots, V_n\) are all different, then \(k_1, \ldots, k_n\) are distinct, \(\mathbf{A}\) has \(n\) independent eigenvectors given by (4), and the solution is
\[
\mathbf{X}(t) = c_1 e^{-k_1 t}\mathbf{V}_1 + c_2 e^{-k_2 t}\mathbf{V}_2 + \cdots + c_n e^{-k_n t}\mathbf{V}_n,
\tag{5}
\]
where \(c_1, \ldots, c_n\) solve the triangular system \(c_1\mathbf{V}_1 + \cdots + c_n\mathbf{V}_n = \mathbf{X}_0\).








WarningEqual volumes need generalized eigenvectors



Mathews remarks that ordinary eigenvectors suffice “if the size of the tanks is increasing” and otherwise “the system might require generalized eigenvectors”. The condition that matters is that the volumes be different, not that they increase: with \(V = (120, 100, 80)\) or \((100, 80, 120)\) the matrix is still diagonalizable. If two volumes are equal, even in tanks that are not next to each other, the matrix is never diagonalizable. Deleting the first row and last column of \(\mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I}\) leaves a triangular matrix with \(k_1, \ldots, k_{n-1} \ne 0\) on its diagonal, so every eigenvalue has a one-dimensional eigenspace, and a repeated eigenvalue \(-k_i = -k_j\) is short of eigenvectors. For example, \(V = (80, 80, 120)\), \((80, 120, 80)\) and \((100, 100, 100)\) with \(r = 20\) all give defective matrices. The general solution then contains terms such as \(t e^{-k t}\); with \(V = (80, 80, 120)\), \(r = 20\) and Example 1’s initial amounts \((10, 0, 0)\), for instance, \(x_2(t) = \tfrac52\,t\,e^{-t/4}\).








TipTheorem — The substance is washed out



Suppose every \(k_i > 0\), \(a_1 > 0\) and \(a_2 = \cdots = a_n = 0\). Then for \(t > 0\):

every \(x_i(t) > 0\), because \(x_1 = a_1 e^{-k_1 t}\) and, by variation of parameters, \(x_i(t) = k_{i-1}\int_0^t e^{-k_i(t-s)}x_{i-1}(s)\,ds\);
the total \(S(t) = x_1 + \cdots + x_n\) satisfies \(S' = -k_n x_n < 0\) (adding the equations, the transfer terms cancel and only the outflow of the last tank remains), so \(S\) decreases strictly;
\(S(t) \to 0\) as \(t \to \infty\), because every eigenvalue \(-k_i\) is negative.



For two tanks the solution of (3) is short enough to write in general. With \(x_1(0) = a_1\), \(x_2(0) = 0\) and \(k_1 \ne k_2\),
\[
x_2(t) = \frac{a_1 k_1}{k_2 - k_1}\left(e^{-k_1 t} - e^{-k_2 t}\right),
\]
which is zero at \(t = 0\), rises, and has its maximum where \(k_1 e^{-k_1 t} = k_2 e^{-k_2 t}\), at
\[
t^* = \frac{\ln(k_1/k_2)}{k_1 - k_2}.
\tag{6}
\]
More generally, at a maximum of any \(x_i\) (\(i \ge 2\)) the derivative is zero, so by (3) the inflow equals the outflow there: \(k_{i-1}x_{i-1}(t^*) = k_i x_i(t^*)\).


Example 1 — Three tanks, \(V_1 = 80\), \(V_2 = 100\), \(V_3 = 120\), \(r = 20\)
Find the solution of (3) with \(V_1 = 80\), \(V_2 = 100\), \(V_3 = 120\), \(r = 20\) and the initial conditions \(x_1(0) = 10\), \(x_2(0) = 0\), \(x_3(0) = 0\), and plot \(x_1(t)\), \(x_2(t)\), \(x_3(t)\) for \(0 \le t \le 40\).
Step 1 (rate constants): by (2),
\[
k_1 = \frac{20}{80} = \frac14, \qquad k_2 = \frac{20}{100} = \frac15, \qquad k_3 = \frac{20}{120} = \frac16,
\qquad
\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} -\tfrac14 & 0 & 0 \\[1mm] \tfrac14 & -\tfrac15 & 0 \\[1mm] 0 & \tfrac15 & -\tfrac16 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 2 (eigenvalues and eigenvectors): the eigenvalues are \(-\tfrac14\), \(-\tfrac15\), \(-\tfrac16\). By (4), with integer scaling,
\[
\mathbf{V}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -5 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\mathbf{V}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -6 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\mathbf{V}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
For instance, for \(\mathbf{V}_1\): \(v_2 = \dfrac{1/4}{1/5 - 1/4} = -5\) and \(v_3 = \dfrac{(1/5)(-5)}{1/6 - 1/4} = 12\). Mathews’ eigenvectors are the same vectors scaled to end in \(1\): \(\bigl(\tfrac1{12}, -\tfrac5{12}, 1\bigr)\), \(\bigl(0, -\tfrac16, 1\bigr)\), \((0, 0, 1)\).
Step 3 (general solution):
\[
\mathbf{X}(t) = c_1 e^{-t/4}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -5 \\ 12 \end{pmatrix} + c_2 e^{-t/5}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ -6 \end{pmatrix} + c_3 e^{-t/6}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 4 (constants): at \(t = 0\) the system \(c_1 = 10\), \(-5c_1 + c_2 = 0\), \(12c_1 - 6c_2 + c_3 = 0\) gives \(c_1 = 10\), \(c_2 = 50\), \(c_3 = 180\).
Step 5 (solution):
\[
\boxed{\
\begin{aligned}
x_1(t) &= 10\,e^{-t/4}, \\
x_2(t) &= -50\,e^{-t/4} + 50\,e^{-t/5}, \\
x_3(t) &= 120\,e^{-t/4} - 300\,e^{-t/5} + 180\,e^{-t/6},
\end{aligned}\ }
\]
which is Mathews’ solution.
Verification: substituting into (3) leaves residuals that simplify to \(0\), the initial values are \((10, 0, 0)\), and the formula equals \(e^{\mathbf{A}t}(10, 0, 0)^T\) computed symbolically. A numerical solution (Runge–Kutta, relative tolerance \(10^{-13}\)) agrees with it to within \(4 \times 10^{-14}\) at every time in the table:

How the substance moves. The first tank empties exponentially. The second and third tanks each fill and then drain, and each has exactly one maximum (the sign of \(x_i'\) was checked on a grid of step \(0.25\) over \(0 < t \le 500\) in 60-digit arithmetic). By (6) the second tank peaks at \(t^* = 20\ln\tfrac54 \approx 4.463\), where \(e^{-t^*/20} = \tfrac45\) and \(x_2(t^*) = 50\bigl((\tfrac45)^4 - (\tfrac45)^5\bigr) = 4.096\) exactly. The third tank peaks later and lower, at \(t \approx 9.866\) with \(x_3 \approx 3.248\); this time was found as a root of \(x_3'(t) = 0\) and confirmed by locating the zero of the right-hand side \(k_2x_2 - k_3x_3\) along a numerical solution, the two agreeing to \(12\) digits.
The total amount. Adding the three solutions,
\[
S(t) = 80\,e^{-t/4} - 250\,e^{-t/5} + 180\,e^{-t/6}, \qquad S'(t) = -\tfrac16\, x_3(t),
\]
so the total decreases for all \(t > 0\) and \(\lim_{t\to\infty} S(t) = 0\), answering Mathews’ question about the limit of the sum. The substance can only leave through the third tank, so the total starts to fall only as the third tank fills: \(S'(0) = 0\). At \(t = 40\) about \(1.5\%\) of the original \(10\) units is still in the system.

Finally a filled plot stacks the curves \(x_1\), \(x_1 + x_2\) and \(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = S\) on \([0, 40] \times [0, 10]\), so that the coloured bands show how much of the substance is in each tank at each time.

title: Compartment Model
section: Model II — The Closed Three-Stage System
text:
Model II — The Closed Three-Stage System
Now no fresh water enters: the liquid that leaves tank 3 returns to tank 1. Tank 1 therefore gains \(k_3 x_3\), and (1) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1' &= -k_1 x_1 + k_3 x_3, \\
x_2' &= \phantom{-}k_1 x_1 - k_2 x_2, \\
x_3' &= \phantom{-}k_2 x_2 - k_3 x_3,
\end{aligned}
\qquad
\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} -k_1 & 0 & k_3 \\ k_1 & -k_2 & 0 \\ 0 & k_2 & -k_3 \end{pmatrix}.
\tag{7}
\]






TipTheorem — Conservation and equilibrium in the closed loop



For (7) with \(k_1, k_2, k_3 > 0\):

Each column of \(\mathbf{A}\) sums to \(0\), so \(S' = x_1' + x_2' + x_3' = 0\): the total amount \(S\) never changes.
The equilibria (\(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{0}\)) are the states with \(k_1 x_1 = k_2 x_2 = k_3 x_3\), that is, \(x_1/V_1 = x_2/V_2 = x_3/V_3\): the same concentration in every tank. With total \(S\) this is \(x_i = S\,V_i/(V_1 + V_2 + V_3)\).
The characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda\bigl(\lambda^2 + (k_1 + k_2 + k_3)\lambda + k_1k_2 + k_2k_3 + k_3k_1\bigr)\). Its quadratic factor has positive coefficients, so its two roots have negative real parts, and every solution approaches the equilibrium with the same total. The deviations from equilibrium are damped oscillations (complex roots) when \((k_1 + k_2 + k_3)^2 < 4(k_1k_2 + k_2k_3 + k_3k_1)\).




Example 2 — Closed loop, \(V_1 = 40\), \(V_2 = 20\), \(V_3 = 40\), \(r = 20\)
Find the solution of (7) with \(V_1 = 40\), \(V_2 = 20\), \(V_3 = 40\), \(r = 20\) and \(x_1(0) = 10\), \(x_2(0) = 0\), \(x_3(0) = 0\), and plot \(x_1(t)\), \(x_2(t)\), \(x_3(t)\) for \(0 \le t \le 5\).
Step 1 (rate constants):
\[
k_1 = \frac{20}{40} = \frac12, \qquad k_2 = \frac{20}{20} = 1, \qquad k_3 = \frac{20}{40} = \frac12,
\qquad
\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} -\tfrac12 & 0 & \tfrac12 \\[1mm] \tfrac12 & -1 & 0 \\[1mm] 0 & 1 & -\tfrac12 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 2 (eigenvalues): the characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda\bigl(\lambda^2 + 2\lambda + \tfrac54\bigr)\), so
\[
\lambda_1 = 0, \qquad \lambda_{2,3} = -1 \pm \tfrac12 i.
\]
Here \((k_1 + k_2 + k_3)^2 = 4 < 5 = 4(k_1k_2 + k_2k_3 + k_3k_1)\), so the approach to equilibrium oscillates.
Step 3 (eigenvectors):
\[
\lambda_1 = 0:\ \ \mathbf{V}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad
\lambda = -1 + \tfrac12 i:\ \ \mathbf{W} = \begin{pmatrix} -1 - i \\ -1 + i \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}} + i\,\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}}_{\mathbf{b}},
\]
and the conjugate \(\overline{\mathbf{W}}\) belongs to \(-1 - \tfrac12 i\). The eigenvector for \(0\) is proportional to the volumes \((40, 20, 40)\), as the theorem says.
Step 4 (real general solution): the real and imaginary parts of \(e^{(-1 + i/2)t}\mathbf{W}\) are two real solutions,
\[
\mathbf{U}(t) = e^{-t}\bigl(\mathbf{a}\cos\tfrac t2 - \mathbf{b}\sin\tfrac t2\bigr), \qquad
\mathbf{Z}(t) = e^{-t}\bigl(\mathbf{a}\sin\tfrac t2 + \mathbf{b}\cos\tfrac t2\bigr),
\]
and \(\mathbf{X}(t) = c_1\mathbf{V}_1 + c_2\mathbf{U}(t) + c_3\mathbf{Z}(t)\).
Step 5 (constants): \(c_1\mathbf{V}_1 + c_2\mathbf{a} + c_3\mathbf{b} = (10, 0, 0)^T\) gives \(c_1 = 2\), \(c_2 = -2\), \(c_3 = -4\).
Step 6 (solution):
\[
\boxed{\
\begin{aligned}
x_1(t) &= 4 + 2e^{-t}\bigl(3\cos\tfrac t2 + \sin\tfrac t2\bigr), \\
x_2(t) &= 2 + 2e^{-t}\bigl(3\sin\tfrac t2 - \cos\tfrac t2\bigr), \\
x_3(t) &= 4 - 4e^{-t}\bigl(\cos\tfrac t2 + 2\sin\tfrac t2\bigr).
\end{aligned}\ }
\]
Matrix exponential. Mathews also builds the solution as \(\mathbf{X}(t) = e^{\mathbf{A}t}\mathbf{X}_0\). Here
\[
e^{\mathbf{A}t} = \frac15\begin{pmatrix}
2 + e^{-t}(3\cos\tfrac t2 + \sin\tfrac t2) & 2 - 2e^{-t}(\cos\tfrac t2 + 2\sin\tfrac t2) & 2 - e^{-t}(2\cos\tfrac t2 - \sin\tfrac t2) \\[1mm]
1 - e^{-t}(\cos\tfrac t2 - 3\sin\tfrac t2) & 1 + e^{-t}(4\cos\tfrac t2 - 2\sin\tfrac t2) & 1 - e^{-t}(\cos\tfrac t2 + 2\sin\tfrac t2) \\[1mm]
2 - 2e^{-t}(\cos\tfrac t2 + 2\sin\tfrac t2) & 2 - 2e^{-t}(\cos\tfrac t2 - 3\sin\tfrac t2) & 2 + e^{-t}(3\cos\tfrac t2 + \sin\tfrac t2)
\end{pmatrix},
\]
and \(10\) times its first column is the solution above, the same as by eigenvectors. As \(t \to \infty\) every column tends to \(\tfrac15(2, 1, 2)^T\).
Verification: the residual of (7) simplifies to \(0\), the initial values are \((10, 0, 0)\), and a numerical solution (Runge–Kutta, relative tolerance \(10^{-13}\)) agrees to within \(2 \times 10^{-13}\) at the times in the table. The last column confirms that the total stays at \(10\).

How the substance moves. The total \(10\) ends up spread in proportion to the volumes, \(40 : 20 : 40\), so \(\mathbf{X}(t) \to (4, 2, 4)\); the deviation from this equilibrium is \(e^{-t}\) times a combination of \(\cos\tfrac t2\) and \(\sin\tfrac t2\). The derivatives are
\[
x_1' = -5e^{-t}\bigl(\sin\tfrac t2 + \cos\tfrac t2\bigr), \qquad
x_2' = 5e^{-t}\bigl(\cos\tfrac t2 - \sin\tfrac t2\bigr), \qquad
x_3' = 10\,e^{-t}\sin\tfrac t2,
\]
so the turning points are exact. On Mathews’ interval \(0 \le t \le 5\):

\(x_1\) falls from \(10\), passes the equilibrium value \(4\) at \(t = 2\pi - 2\arctan 3 \approx 3.785\), and reaches its minimum \(4 - 2\sqrt2\,e^{-3\pi/2} \approx 3.9746\) at \(t = 3\pi/2 \approx 4.712\). It then rises again, to \(3.9757\) at \(t = 5\).
\(x_2\) rises past \(2\) at \(t = 2\arctan\tfrac13 \approx 0.6435\) to its maximum \(2 + 2\sqrt2\,e^{-\pi/2} \approx 2.5880\) at \(t = \pi/2 \approx 1.571\), then falls, staying above \(2\) until \(t = 2\pi + 2\arctan\tfrac13 \approx 6.927\).
\(x_3\) increases on the whole interval, since \(x_3' > 0\) for \(0 < t < 2\pi\), and reaches \(3.9893\) at \(t = 5\). It overshoots only after the interval ends, crossing \(4\) at \(t = 2\pi - 2\arctan\tfrac12 \approx 5.356\) and peaking at \(4 + 4e^{-2\pi} \approx 4.0075\) at \(t = 2\pi\).

At \(t = 5\) no tank is more than \(0.035\) from its equilibrium value. Successive turning points of each tank are \(2\pi\) apart, and from one to the next the deviation from equilibrium changes sign and shrinks by the factor \(e^{-2\pi} \approx 0.0019\).
Mathews’ plots. The problem asks for the plot on \(0 \le t \le 5\). His notebook goes on to plot the three amounts, their sum, and a stacked plot of how “the three curves stack up”, but the output images for this example are missing from the archive, so his plot windows and colours cannot be read.

title: Compartment Model
text:
Model III — The Five-Stage System
The open chain extends to any number of tanks. For five tanks with pure water flowing in at the rate \(r\) and the mixture passing through tanks 1 to 5 in turn,
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1' &= -k_1 x_1, \\
x_2' &= \phantom{-}k_1 x_1 - k_2 x_2, \\
x_3' &= \phantom{-}k_2 x_2 - k_3 x_3, \\
x_4' &= \phantom{-}k_3 x_3 - k_4 x_4, \\
x_5' &= \phantom{-}k_4 x_4 - k_5 x_5,
\end{aligned}
\qquad x_i(0) = a_i,
\tag{8}
\]
with \(k_i = r/V_i\). The eigenvalues are \(-k_1, \ldots, -k_5\), the eigenvectors come from (4), and when the five volumes are different the solution is the sum (5) of five exponentials.

Example 3 — Five tanks, \(V = (60, 80, 100, 120, 150)\), \(r = 24\)
Find the solution of (8) with \(V_1 = 60\), \(V_2 = 80\), \(V_3 = 100\), \(V_4 = 120\), \(V_5 = 150\), \(r = 24\) and \(x_1(0) = 10\), \(x_2(0) = x_3(0) = x_4(0) = x_5(0) = 0\), and plot \(x_1(t), \ldots, x_5(t)\) for \(0 \le t \le 50\). (Mathews’ statement of the initial conditions lists \(x_5(0) = 0\) twice and omits \(x_4(0)\); it is meant to be \(0\), as his solution shows.)
Step 1 (rate constants):
\[
k_1 = \frac{24}{60} = \frac25, \quad k_2 = \frac{24}{80} = \frac3{10}, \quad k_3 = \frac{24}{100} = \frac6{25}, \quad k_4 = \frac{24}{120} = \frac15, \quad k_5 = \frac{24}{150} = \frac4{25}.
\]
Step 2 (eigenvalues and eigenvectors): the eigenvalues are \(-\tfrac25, -\tfrac3{10}, -\tfrac6{25}, -\tfrac15, -\tfrac4{25}\), and (4) with integer scaling gives
\[
\mathbf{V}_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ -8 \\ 15 \\ -18 \\ 15 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{V}_2 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ -7 \\ 35 \\ -84 \\ 120 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{V}_3 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ -6 \\ 15 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{V}_4 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}, \quad
\mathbf{V}_5 = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 3 (constants): solving \(c_1\mathbf{V}_1 + \cdots + c_5\mathbf{V}_5 = (10, 0, 0, 0, 0)^T\) from the top down gives
\[
c_1 = 5, \quad c_2 = -\tfrac{40}{7}, \quad c_3 = 125, \quad c_4 = -360, \quad c_5 = \tfrac{3750}{7}.
\]
Step 4 (solution):
\[
\boxed{\
\begin{aligned}
x_1(t) &= 10\,e^{-2t/5}, \\
x_2(t) &= -40\,e^{-2t/5} + 40\,e^{-3t/10}, \\
x_3(t) &= 75\,e^{-2t/5} - 200\,e^{-3t/10} + 125\,e^{-6t/25}, \\
x_4(t) &= -90\,e^{-2t/5} + 480\,e^{-3t/10} - 750\,e^{-6t/25} + 360\,e^{-t/5}, \\
x_5(t) &= 75\,e^{-2t/5} - \tfrac{4800}{7}\,e^{-3t/10} + 1875\,e^{-6t/25} - 1800\,e^{-t/5} + \tfrac{3750}{7}\,e^{-4t/25},
\end{aligned}\ }

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
Description
This page covers the finite difference method for a hyperbolic partial differential equation, the one-dimensional wave equation, as Mathews’ module “Finite Difference Method for Hyperbolic Equations” does. The problem is to find the displacement \(u(x, t)\) of a vibrating string with fixed ends, \(u_{tt} = c^2 u_{xx}\) for \(0 < x < a\) and \(0 < t < b\), given its initial position \(u(x, 0) = f(x)\) and initial velocity \(u_t(x, 0) = g(x)\).
The method covers the rectangle \(0 \le x \le a\), \(0 \le t \le b\) with a grid of spacing \(h\) in \(x\) and \(k\) in \(t\), replaces both second derivatives by central differences, and solves the resulting difference equation for the newest time level. With \(u_{i,j} \approx u(x_i, t_j)\) and the ratio \(r = ck/h\), each new row of the grid comes from the two rows before it:
\[
u_{i,j+1} = (2 - 2r^2)\,u_{i,j} + r^2\,(u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j}) - u_{i,j-1}.
\]
The first row is \(f\), and a second row is built from \(f\) and \(g\) with a Taylor expansion. This is an explicit method: the rows are computed one after another, with no system of equations to solve. As a general result, it is stable when \(r \le 1\); for \(r > 1\) the shortest wavelengths that a fine enough grid can carry grow geometrically. When \(r = 1\) and the second row is exact, every value it computes is exact. Mathews’ three examples show both sides: Examples 1 and 2 use \(r = 1\) and reproduce the exact solution to rounding error, and Example 3 takes \(r = 1.02\) and is unstable.

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
The Wave Equation






NoteDefinition — The wave equation problem



Find \(u(x, t)\) satisfying
\[
u_{tt}(x, t) = c^2\, u_{xx}(x, t) \qquad \text{for } 0 < x < a \text{ and } 0 < t < b,
\tag{1}
\]
with the boundary and initial conditions
\[
\begin{aligned}
u(0, t) &= 0 \quad \text{and} \quad u(a, t) = 0 && \text{for } 0 \le t \le b, \\
u(x, 0) &= f(x) && \text{for } 0 \le x \le a, \\
u_t(x, 0) &= g(x) && \text{for } 0 < x < a.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]


The wave equation models the displacement \(u\) of an elastic string held fixed at \(x = 0\) and \(x = a\); \(c\) is the speed at which waves travel along it. Analytic solutions can be found with Fourier series or with d’Alembert’s formula below, but the problem serves as the prototype of a hyperbolic equation, and the same difference method applies where no formula is available.

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
Derivation of the Difference Equation
Partition the rectangle \(R = \{(x, t) : 0 \le x \le a,\ 0 \le t \le b\}\) into \(n - 1\) by \(m - 1\) rectangles with sides \(h = a/(n - 1)\) and \(k = b/(m - 1)\). Following Mathews, the grid points are numbered from \(1\):
\[
x_i = (i - 1)h, \quad i = 1, \ldots, n, \qquad t_j = (j - 1)k, \quad j = 1, \ldots, m,
\]
and \(u_{i,j}\) denotes the approximation to \(u(x_i, t_j)\). The bottom row \(j = 1\) is the known initial position, \(u_{i,1} = f(x_i)\), and the end columns are the fixed ends, \(u_{1,j} = u_{n,j} = 0\).
The central-difference formulas for the two second derivatives are
\[
u_{tt}(x, t) = \frac{u(x, t + k) - 2u(x, t) + u(x, t - k)}{k^2} + O(k^2),
\tag{3}
\]
\[
u_{xx}(x, t) = \frac{u(x + h, t) - 2u(x, t) + u(x - h, t)}{h^2} + O(h^2).
\tag{4}
\]
Dropping the \(O(k^2)\) and \(O(h^2)\) terms and substituting into (1) gives the difference equation
\[
\frac{u_{i,j+1} - 2u_{i,j} + u_{i,j-1}}{k^2} = c^2\, \frac{u_{i+1,j} - 2u_{i,j} + u_{i-1,j}}{h^2}.
\tag{5}
\]
With the substitution \(r = ck/h\) it becomes \(u_{i,j+1} - 2u_{i,j} + u_{i,j-1} = r^2 (u_{i+1,j} - 2u_{i,j} + u_{i-1,j})\), which is solved for the value on the newest row:






ImportantExplicit formula for the wave equation



\[
u_{i,j+1} = (2 - 2r^2)\,u_{i,j} + r^2\,(u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j}) - u_{i,j-1}, \qquad i = 2, 3, \ldots, n - 1,
\tag{6}
\]
where \(r = ck/h\).


Formula (6) computes row \(j + 1\) from four known values: three neighbouring values \(u_{i-1,j}\), \(u_{i,j}\), \(u_{i+1,j}\) in row \(j\) and the value \(u_{i,j-1}\) directly below in row \(j - 1\). This four-point pattern is the stencil of the method. Because it reaches back two rows, two starting rows are needed.

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
Starting Values
The first row is \(u_{i,1} = f(x_i) = f_i\). The second row, at \(t = k\), is not given, so it is built from Taylor’s formula in \(t\) about \((x_i, 0)\). To first order, \(u(x_i, k) = u(x_i, 0) + u_t(x_i, 0)\,k + O(k^2)\), and with \(g_i = g(x_i)\) this gives
\[
u_{i,2} = f_i + k\,g_i, \qquad i = 2, 3, \ldots, n - 1.
\tag{7}
\]
Errors in the second row are carried through the rest of the grid by formula (6), so a better second row is worth having. When \(f\) has a second derivative, the wave equation turns the unknown \(u_{tt}\) at \(t = 0\) into a known \(x\)-derivative of \(f\):
\[
u_{tt}(x_i, 0) = c^2 u_{xx}(x_i, 0) = c^2 f''(x_i) = c^2\, \frac{f_{i+1} - 2f_i + f_{i-1}}{h^2} + O(h^2).
\]
Taylor’s formula of order 2, \(u(x, k) = u(x, 0) + u_t(x, 0)\,k + \tfrac12 u_{tt}(x, 0)\,k^2 + O(k^3)\), then gives
\[
u(x_i, k) = f_i + k g_i + \frac{c^2 k^2}{2h^2}\,(f_{i+1} - 2f_i + f_{i-1}) + O(h^2)\,O(k^2) + O(k^3),
\]
and with \(r = ck/h\) this simplifies to the second-row formula that Mathews’ program uses:






ImportantSecond row



\[
u_{i,2} = (1 - r^2) f_i + k g_i + \frac{r^2}{2}\,(f_{i+1} + f_{i-1}), \qquad i = 2, 3, \ldots, n - 1.
\tag{8}
\]

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
Stability
Mathews calls the method stable if an error made at one stage of the calculation is eventually damped out, and states that stability of formula (6) requires \(r = ck/h \le 1\). The condition is a general result, and a Fourier analysis shows where it comes from; it also shows that for \(r \le 1\) errors are not damped but stay bounded. Since the boundary values are zero, look for solutions of (6) of the form \(u_{i,j} = \lambda^{j} \sin(p\pi x_i/a)\), one for each mode \(p = 1, 2, \ldots, n - 2\) that the grid can represent. Substituting into (6) and dividing by \(\lambda^{j-1}\sin(p\pi x_i/a)\) gives
\[
\lambda^2 - (2 - 4r^2 s_p)\,\lambda + 1 = 0, \qquad s_p = \sin^2\!\left(\frac{p\pi h}{2a}\right).
\tag{9}
\]
The two roots have product \(1\). If \(|2 - 4r^2 s_p| < 2\), that is \(r^2 s_p < 1\), they are complex conjugates of modulus \(1\), and the mode neither grows nor decays. If \(r^2 s_p = 1\) they coincide at \(\lambda = -1\) and the mode can grow, but only linearly. If \(r^2 s_p > 1\), they are real and negative, and one of them has modulus greater than \(1\): the mode grows geometrically and changes sign at every step. Since \(s_p < 1\) for every mode, \(r \le 1\) gives \(r^2 s_p < 1\), and all modes stay bounded. As \(h \to 0\) the largest \(s_p\) approaches \(1\), so \(r \le 1\) is the condition that works for every grid.






TipStability condition (general result)



The explicit formula (6) for the wave equation is stable when
\[
r = \frac{ck}{h} \le 1.
\]
For \(r > 1\), on any grid fine enough that \(r^2 s_{n-2} > 1\), the highest modes the grid can carry grow without bound as the rows are computed.


The condition has a physical reading. The exact value \(u(x, t)\) depends on the initial data in \([x - ct,\ x + ct]\), while the value \(u_{i,j}\) computed by (6) can depend only on initial values in \([x_i - (j-1)h,\ x_i + (j-1)h]\), because each row reaches one grid point further to each side. The numerical interval contains the true one only when \(h/k \ge c\), which is \(r \le 1\) (the Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition). Suitable implicit methods, which are more work to implement, have no stability restriction on \(r\).






WarningOn a coarse grid the threshold is slightly above 1



Only the modes \(p \le n - 2\) exist on a given grid, so the exact threshold there is \(r = 1/\sqrt{s_{n-2}}\), slightly above \(1\). For the grid of Examples 1 to 3 (\(n = 11\), \(h = 0.1\)) it is \(1/\sin(9\pi/20) \approx 1.0125\); only mode \(p = 9\) is unstable at \(r = 1.02\).

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
D’Alembert’s Solution and Exact Rows
The French mathematician Jean Le Rond d’Alembert (1717–1783) found that
\[
u(x, t) = F(x + ct) + G(x - ct)
\tag{10}
\]
solves the wave equation (1), as direct substitution shows: \(u_{tt} = c^2 F''(x + ct) + c^2 G''(x - ct) = c^2 u_{xx}\). The boundary conditions \(u(0, t) = u(a, t) = 0\) hold when \(G(z) = -F(-z)\) and \(F\) has period \(2a\), since then \(u(0, t) = F(ct) - F(ct) = 0\) and \(u(a, t) = F(ct + a) - F(ct - a) = 0\); in particular they hold when \(G = F\) with \(F\) odd and of period \(2a\), as in (11) below. The solution with \(u(x, 0) = f(x)\) and \(u_t(x, 0) = 0\) is
\[
u(x, t) = \tfrac12 \bigl(\tilde f(x + ct) + \tilde f(x - ct)\bigr),
\tag{11}
\]
where \(\tilde f\) is the odd extension of \(f\) with period \(2a\). The initial shape splits into two halves that travel left and right at speed \(c\) and are reflected, upside down, at the fixed ends.
When \(r = 1\), that is \(k = h/c\), the diagonals of the grid line up with the characteristics \(x \pm ct = \text{const}\), and the method becomes exact.






TipTheorem — Two exact rows give an exact grid



Assume that the two rows \(u_{i,1} = u(x_i, 0)\) and \(u_{i,2} = u(x_i, k)\), \(i = 1, 2, \ldots, n\), are exact values of the solution of (1). If the step \(k = h/c\) is chosen, then \(r = 1\) and formula (6) becomes
\[
u_{i,j+1} = u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} - u_{i,j-1},
\tag{12}
\]
and the values it produces throughout the grid are exact values of the solution (apart from computer rounding).


Proof. With \(ck = h\), \(x_i - ct_j = (i - 1)h - (j - 1)h = (i - j)h\) and \(x_i + ct_j = (i + j - 2)h\), so by (10) every exact grid value has the form \(u_{i,j} = F((i + j - 2)h) + G((i - j)h)\). Substituting this into the right side of (12),
\[
\begin{aligned}
u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} - u_{i,j-1}
&= F((i + j - 1)h) + F((i + j - 3)h) - F((i + j - 3)h) \\
&\quad + G((i + 1 - j)h) + G((i - 1 - j)h) - G((i - j + 1)h) \\
&= F((i + (j + 1) - 2)h) + G((i - (j + 1))h) = u_{i,j+1}. \qquad \blacksquare
\end{aligned}
\]
The theorem needs an exact second row, and formulas (7) and (8) generally do not give one. There is one common case where they do. When \(g = 0\) and \(r = 1\), formula (8) reduces to
\[
u_{i,2} = \frac{f_{i-1} + f_{i+1}}{2}, \qquad i = 2, 3, \ldots, n - 1,
\tag{13}
\]
and by (11) the exact value is \(u(x_i, k) = \tfrac12\bigl(\tilde f(x_i + h) + \tilde f(x_i - h)\bigr)\), which is the same thing, because \(ck = h\) and the points \(x_i \pm h\) are grid points in \([0, a]\), where \(\tilde f = f\). So with \(g = 0\) and \(r = 1\) the method reproduces the exact solution at every grid point. Examples 1 and 2 are of this kind.

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
Algorithm
Mathews’ program has two parts.

Starting rows. Set \(h = a/(n - 1)\), \(k = b/(m - 1)\) and \(r = ck/h\). Fill row 1 with \(u_{i,1} = f(x_i)\) for \(i = 1, \ldots, n\), and fill row 2 by formula (8) for \(i = 2, \ldots, n - 1\). All other entries start at \(0\), so the end columns \(u_{1,j}\) and \(u_{n,j}\) stay \(0\) for \(j \ge 2\).
Later rows. For \(j = 3, 4, \ldots, m\) and \(i = 2, \ldots, n - 1\), compute \[
u_{i,j} = (2 - 2r^2)\,u_{i,j-1} + r^2\,(u_{i+1,j-1} + u_{i-1,j-1}) - u_{i,j-2}.
\]

The result is an \(n \times m\) array whose column \(j\) is the shape of the string at time \(t_j\). Mathews plots this array as a surface over the index grid (the axes are labelled \(x(i)\) and \(t(j)\) and carry the indices \(i = 1, \ldots, 11\) and \(j = 1, \ldots, 21\), not the values of \(x\) and \(t\)), seen from the viewpoint \((4, 2, 3)\) and coloured by height.
In all three examples below \(c = 2\) (so \(c^2 = 4\)), the string has length \(a = 1\), \(g(x) = 0\), and the grid has \(n = 11\) columns and \(m = 21\) rows (Mathews’ grid in Examples 1 and 2; the archive has lost the lines that state Example 3’s grid, and the same grid is kept there). The examples differ in the initial position \(f\) and the time interval \([0, b]\).

title: Finite Difference Method
text:
Example 1 — \(f(x) = \sin(\pi x) + \sin(2\pi x)\), \(r = 1\)
Solve
\[
u_{tt}(x, t) = 4\,u_{xx}(x, t), \qquad 0 < x < 1, \quad 0 < t < 1,
\]
with \(u(0, t) = u(1, t) = 0\), \(u(x, 0) = f(x) = \sin(\pi x) + \sin(2\pi x)\) and \(u_t(x, 0) = g(x) = 0\), over the rectangle \(R = \{(x, t) : 0 \le x \le 1,\ 0 \le t \le 1\}\), and compare with the exact solution
\[
u(x, t) = \sin(\pi x)\cos(2\pi t) + \sin(2\pi x)\cos(4\pi t).
\tag{14}
\]
Step 1 — grid. With \(n = 11\) and \(m = 21\),
\[
h = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1, \qquad k = \frac{1}{20} = 0.05, \qquad r = \frac{ck}{h} = \frac{2(0.05)}{0.1} = 1.
\]
Step 2 — first row. \(u_{i,1} = f(x_i)\); for example \(u_{2,1} = \sin(0.1\pi) + \sin(0.2\pi) = 0.309017 + 0.587785 = 0.896802\).
Step 3 — second row. Since \(g = 0\) and \(r = 1\), formula (13) applies: \(u_{i,2} = (f_{i-1} + f_{i+1})/2\). For example
\[
u_{2,2} = \frac{f(0) + f(0.2)}{2} = \frac{0 + 1.538842}{2} = 0.769421.
\]
Step 4 — later rows. With \(r = 1\), formula (12) gives each new value from three old ones. For example, at \(x_2 = 0.1\), \(t_3 = 0.1\),
\[
u_{2,3} = u_{3,2} + u_{1,2} - u_{2,1} = 1.328438 + 0 - 0.896802 = 0.431636.
\]

What the table shows. The corner of the plucked string at \(x = 0.6\) splits into two corners, one moving left and one moving right, each one grid step \(h = 0.1\) per time step \(k = 0.05\), which is the wave speed \(c = 2\). In the row \(t = 0.05\) they are at \(x = 0.5\) and \(x = 0.7\), and in the row \(t = 0.10\) at \(x = 0.4\) and \(x = 0.8\). Between them the string is a straight segment of slope \(-0.25\), the average of the two slopes \(1\) and \(-1.5\) of \(f\). Each corner is reflected at a fixed end and comes back with the displacement turned upside down. At \(t = 0.5\) the string has the shape \(u(x, 0.5) = -f(1 - x)\), the initial shape mirrored and inverted, with its lowest point \(-0.6\) at \(x = 0.4\); it then retraces its motion and returns to \(f\) at \(t = 1\).
Verification. Here \(f\) has a corner, so the solution is d’Alembert’s formula (11) with \(\tilde f\) the odd, period-2 extension of \(f\). The computed values agree with (11) at all \(11 \times 21\) grid points to within \(4.5 \times 10^{-16}\). For example, at \(x = 0.4\), \(t = 0.5\): \(\tfrac12(\tilde f(1.4) + \tilde f(-0.6)) = \tfrac12(-f(0.6) - f(0.6)) = -0.6\), the entry in the table. Mathews prints the full \(21\)-row table, and every entry agrees with the values computed here; the textbook’s Table 10.2 gives the same rows for \(0 \le t \le 0.5\).

Example 3 — the same string with \(r = 1.02\): instability
Mathews repeats Example 2 with the same \(f\), \(g = 0\) and \(c = 2\), but over the slightly longer rectangle \(R = \{(x, t) : 0 \le x \le 1,\ 0 \le t \le 1.02\}\), and asks the reader to notice the instability this produces, as predicted by the analysis above. The archive has lost the lines of the notebook that state his grid, and the plot of his result. Keeping Example 2’s grid, \(n = 11\) and \(m = 21\), the new interval gives
\[
h = 0.1, \qquad k = \frac{1.02}{20} = 0.051, \qquad r = \frac{2(0.051)}{0.1} = 1.02 > 1.
\]

title: Galerkin’s Method
text:
Description
Galerkin’s method finds an approximate solution of a linear differential equation \(L[y(x)] + f(x) = 0\) on an interval \([a, b]\), where \(L\) is a linear differential operator such as \(L[y] = y'' + y\), together with an initial condition or two boundary conditions. Instead of looking for \(y\) among all functions, it looks only among the trial functions
\[
u(x) = \phi_0(x) + \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j\,\phi_j(x),
\]
where \(\phi_0\) satisfies the initial or boundary conditions and the basis functions \(\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_n\) satisfy the homogeneous versions of them, so every trial function satisfies the conditions whatever the coefficients \(c_j\) are. A trial function cannot usually make the residual \(r(x) = L[u(x)] + f(x)\) zero everywhere, so Galerkin’s method asks for the next best thing: the residual must be orthogonal to every basis function,
\[
\int_a^b \phi_i(x)\,\bigl(L[u(x)] + f(x)\bigr)\,dx = 0, \qquad i = 1, 2, \ldots, n.
\]
Because \(L\) is linear, these are \(n\) linear equations \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{B}\) in the \(n\) unknown coefficients, with \(a_{ij} = \int_a^b \phi_i\,L[\phi_j]\,dx\) and \(b_i = -\int_a^b \phi_i\,\bigl(L[\phi_0] + f\bigr)\,dx\). Solving them gives the Galerkin solution \(u(x)\). Mathews solves one initial value problem with the polynomial basis \(x, x^2, \ldots, x^7\), and four boundary value problems, two with polynomials that vanish at both ends and two with the sine functions \(\sin kx\). In every example below the Galerkin solution is compared with the exact solution; the largest errors range from about \(5 \times 10^{-9}\) to \(1.5 \times 10^{-2}\), depending on how well the chosen basis can represent the exact solution.

title: Galerkin’s Method
text:
Animations
Each animation below shows Galerkin solutions with more and more basis functions, one value of \(n\) per frame, against the exact solution. The left panel is the graph Mathews draws for the example, over his interval and with his colours for the exact solution (magenta) and the Galerkin solution (blue); red dots mark the initial or boundary values, and in Cases 1 and 3 the earlier Galerkin solutions are gray. The middle panel is new. Where Mathews plots the signed error \(y - u\) for his one value of \(n\), it plots the error \(|y(x) - u_n(x)|\) on a logarithmic scale, and its title gives the largest error on the interval. The error is zero at the initial or boundary points and at each change of sign, where its curve dips sharply; how deep a dip is drawn depends on how close a grid point falls to the zero, and an exact zero is drawn below the bottom of the panel. The right panel is new as well and is described with each case. Each frame is shown for one second, and the last for three. The scripts check their coefficients against Mathews’ values given on this page, evaluate the errors in 256- or 512-bit arithmetic on the grids used in the examples (6001 points on \([0, 3]\) and \([0, 1]\), 20001 points on \([0, \pi]\)), and refine each largest error by a golden-section search around the largest grid value.
Mathews’ module has no animations, and his animation archive has none for Galerkin’s method, so all three animations are new, with no Mathews original. They animate his Examples 2, 3 (b) and 4 (b) with his equations, intervals and bases, and run \(n\) past the value he uses, except in Case 2, where his basis has only five functions. Not animated are Example 1, which computes inner products and solves no differential equation; Example 3 (a), where Mathews’ three polynomials already give an error of \(5.12 \times 10^{-9}\); Example 4 (a), which uses the sine basis of Case 3 with the odd sines only, because its even coefficients are zero; and the equation stated for Example 2, \(y' + 2y + 6 + 4x = 0\), which Mathews’ notebook does not solve.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Polynomial basis for an initial value problem (Example 2), \(y' + 5y - 1 - x + \sin 2x = 0\), \(y(0) = 1\), \(u_n = 1 + c_1 x + \cdots + c_n x^n\), \(n = 1\) to \(16\) on \(0 \le x \le 3\)
Behavior: The Galerkin systems are solved in 512-bit arithmetic. The largest error falls at every step, from \(0.7296\) for \(n = 1\) through \(0.01478\) for Mathews’ \(n = 7\) to \(2.374 \times 10^{-7}\) for \(n = 16\), and the point where it occurs moves toward the initial point, from \(x = 0.668\) to \(x = 0.0327\). The right panel plots these largest errors against \(n\) (left axis) and the price paid for them, the condition number \(\operatorname{cond}_\infty(\mathbf{A}_n)\) (right axis). It grows from \(179\) at \(n = 2\) to \(1.169 \times 10^{28}\) at \(n = 16\), by a factor between \(65\) and \(86\) for each added basis function, and is \(3.316 \times 10^{11}\) at \(n = 7\), as Mathews computes. The orange diamonds, and the dashed orange curve in the middle panel, come from rounding \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) to double precision and solving with Julia’s LU solver. Up to \(n = 9\) the largest error of that solution agrees with the exact Galerkin solution’s to four significant figures, although \(\operatorname{cond}_\infty(\mathbf{A}_9) = 1.478 \times 10^{15}\). From \(n = 12\) on it no longer follows the Galerkin error down: it stays between \(4.4 \times 10^{-5}\) and \(1.8 \times 10^{-3}\), rising and falling from one \(n\) to the next. These double-precision values depend on the linear-algebra library; NumPy’s solver gives different values of the same size, \(1.4 \times 10^{-4}\) to \(6.4 \times 10^{-4}\) for \(n = 12\) to \(16\).

Galerkin solutions u_n = 1 + c1 x + … + cn x^n for y′ + 5y − 1 − x + sin 2x = 0, y(0) = 1, with n = 1 to 16 basis functions, appearing one per frame against the exact solution on [0, 3], with a log-scale panel of the error |y − u_n| and a panel of the largest error and the condition number against n: the largest error falls from 0.7296 to 2.374 × 10^−7 while cond∞(A_n) grows from 1 to 1.169 × 10^28, and from n = 12 on the largest error of the double-precision solution stays between 4.4 × 10^−5 and 1.8 × 10^−3




Case 2 — Two bases for a boundary value problem (Example 3 (b)), \(y'' + y + 2x(1 - x) = 0\), \(y(0) = 0\), \(y(1) = \tfrac12\), \(n = 1\) to \(5\) on \(0 \le x \le 1\)
Behavior: Each frame solves the problem twice, exactly, with \(n\) basis functions: the first \(n\) of Mathews’ five (blue), and \(x(x - 1), x^2(x - 1), \ldots, x^n(x - 1)\) (orange, “complete basis”), which span all polynomials of degree at most \(n + 1\) that vanish at \(0\) and \(1\). For \(n = 1\) both bases are \(x(x - 1)\) and give the same largest error, \(0.005616\). After that the complete basis pulls away: at \(n = 5\) its largest error is \(2.069 \times 10^{-8}\), about \(5 \times 10^4\) times smaller than the \(0.001014\) of Mathews’ basis, whose error barely moves from \(n = 3\) to \(n = 4\) (\(0.001824\) to \(0.001823\)). The numbers in brackets in the legend show why, as explained in Example 3 (b): every trial function built from Mathews’ basis has \(u'(0) + u'(1) = 1\), while the exact solution has \(y'(0) + y'(1) = 0.9152\); with the complete basis the sum is free, and it is \(0.9146\) for \(n = 2\) and \(3\) and \(0.9152\) for \(n = 4\) and \(5\). For \(n = 5\) the error of Mathews’ basis peaks next to the ends, at \(-0.001014\) at \(x = 0.0595\) and \(+0.001014\) at \(x = 0.9405\). In the left panel the three curves lie almost on top of each other, as in Mathews’ graph.

Galerkin solutions for y″ + y + 2x(1 − x) = 0, y(0) = 0, y(1) = 1/2, with n = 1 to 5 basis functions taken from Mathews’ basis and from the complete basis x(x − 1), x²(x − 1), …, appearing one per frame against the exact solution on [0, 1], with a log-scale panel of both errors and a panel of the largest errors against n: the two bases agree at n = 1, after which the largest error of Mathews’ basis stays between 0.001014 and 0.001824 from n = 3 on, while the complete basis reaches 2.069 × 10^−8 at n = 5




Case 3 — Sine basis (Example 4 (b)), \(y'' + 2y + 2x(x - \pi) = 0\), \(y(0) = 0\), \(y(\pi) = 1\), \(u_n = x/\pi + c_1 \sin x + \cdots + c_n \sin nx\), \(n = 1\) to \(15\) on \(0 \le x \le \pi\)
Behavior: The Galerkin matrix is diagonal, so adding \(\sin nx\) to the basis adds the coefficient \(c_n\) and leaves \(c_1, \ldots, c_{n-1}\) unchanged; the right panel gains one point per frame. Each \(c_k\) (blue dot) sits inside the circle of the Fourier sine coefficient of \(y - x/\pi\), computed separately by Simpson’s rule from the exact solution; the two agree to better than one part in \(10^{12}\), as the callout above Example 4 (b) shows they must. The coefficients alternate in sign and decay like \(1/k^3\): \(|c_k|\) is within \(2\%\) of \(4/(\pi k^3)\) for \(k \ge 11\). The slow decay comes from the right end. The function \(y - x/\pi\) vanishes at both ends and its second derivative is \(0\) at \(x = 0\) but \(-2\) at \(x = \pi\), and three integrations by parts of its Fourier coefficient then give \(c_k \approx -4(-1)^k/(\pi k^3)\) for large \(k\). The error is largest near \(x = \pi\): from \(n = 2\) on, the largest error is at a point between \(x = 2.81\) and \(3.09\) that moves toward \(\pi\) as \(n\) grows. It falls at every step, but slowly, from \(0.3397\) for \(n = 1\) through \(0.008702\) for Mathews’ \(n = 7\) to \(0.002034\) for \(n = 15\), roughly like \(1/n^2\): \(n^2\) times the largest error stays between \(0.40\) and \(0.46\) for \(n = 5\) to \(15\).

title: Galerkin’s Method
text:
Inner Products






NoteDefinition — Inner product



Consider the vector space of real functions whose domain is the closed interval \([a, b]\). The inner product of two functions \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) is
\[
\langle f, g \rangle = \int_a^b f(x)\,g(x)\,dx.
\tag{1}
\]


The inner product is a continuous, infinite-dimensional analogue of the dot product of linear algebra. If \(\langle f, g \rangle = 0\), then \(f\) and \(g\) are said to be orthogonal on \([a, b]\). All the functions used here are assumed to be square-integrable, that is, \(\langle f, f \rangle = \int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx < \infty\).

Example 1 (a) — \(f(x) = x^2 - 3x + 3\) and \(g(x) = 2x^3 + x^2 + 5x - 5\) over \([0, 2]\)
Step 1 (multiply out):
\[
f(x)\,g(x) = 2x^5 - 5x^4 + 8x^3 - 17x^2 + 30x - 15.
\]
Step 2 (antiderivative):
\[
P(x) = \frac{x^6}{3} - x^5 + 2x^4 - \frac{17x^3}{3} + 15x^2 - 15x.
\]
Step 3 (evaluate):
\[
\boxed{\ \langle f, g \rangle = P(2) - P(0) = 6 - 0 = 6\ }
\]
Verification: a symbolic integration of \(f g\) over \([0, 2]\) returns \(6\), as in Mathews’ output.


Example 1 (b) — the same \(f\) and \(g\) over \([-1, 1]\)
Over a symmetric interval the odd powers in \(f g\) integrate to zero, and only the even part \(-5x^4 - 17x^2 - 15\) contributes:
\[
\boxed{\ \langle f, g \rangle = \int_{-1}^{1} \bigl(-5x^4 - 17x^2 - 15\bigr)\,dx = 2\left(-1 - \frac{17}{3} - 15\right) = -\frac{130}{3} \approx -43.3333\ }
\]
Verification: with \(P\) from Example 1 (a), \(P(1) - P(-1) = -\tfrac{13}{3} - 39 = -\tfrac{130}{3}\).






WarningMathews’ solution uses a different pair



Mathews states Example 1 (b) with the same \(f\) and \(g\) as part (a), but his solution notebook integrates a different pair over \([-1, 1]\): \(f(x) = 5x^3 - 3x^2 - 3x + 1\) and \(g(x) = 35x^4 - 30x^2 + 7x + 3\). That pair is orthogonal: the antiderivative of \(f g\) takes the value \(-\tfrac58\) at both \(x = 1\) and \(x = -1\), so \(\langle f, g \rangle = 0\), which is his printed answer and agrees with a symbolic integration. For the pair in the problem statement the inner product is \(-\tfrac{130}{3}\), as above.




Example 1 (c) — \(f(x) = \cos x + \sin 2x\) and \(g(x) = \sin 2x + \cos 3x\) over \([0, 2\pi]\)
Multiplying out gives four products. Over a full period \([0, 2\pi]\), \(\int_0^{2\pi} \cos x \sin 2x\,dx\), \(\int_0^{2\pi} \cos x \cos 3x\,dx\) and \(\int_0^{2\pi} \sin 2x \cos 3x\,dx\) are all \(0\), and only the square survives:
\[
\boxed{\ \langle f, g \rangle = \int_0^{2\pi} \sin^2 2x\,dx = \pi\ }
\]
Verification: a symbolic integration of \(f g\) over \([0, 2\pi]\) returns \(\pi\), which is Mathews’ printed answer. (The step-by-step panel that follows it in his notebook works with \(g(x) = \cos 2x + \sin x\) instead, which is orthogonal to \(f\) on \([0, 2\pi]\) and gives \(0\).)






TipLemma



If \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\) and \(\langle w, f \rangle = 0\) for every function \(w\), then \(f(x) \equiv 0\) on \([a, b]\). (Take \(w = f\): then \(\int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx = 0\).)




Basis for a vector space
A complete basis for a vector space \(V\) of functions is a set \(S = \{\phi_i(x)\}_{i=0}^{\infty}\) of linearly independent functions such that every \(f \in V\) can be written uniquely as a linear combination
\[
f(x) = \sum_{j=0}^{\infty} c_j\,\phi_j(x).
\]
For example, if \(V\) is the set of all polynomials and power series, a complete basis is \(S = \{\phi_i(x) = x^i\}_{i=0}^{\infty}\).






TipProperty (stated without proof)



If \(f \in V\) and \(\langle \phi_i, f \rangle = 0\) for all \(\phi_i \in S\), then \(f(x) \equiv 0\).


Mathews mentions the lemma and this property only as background. Together they motivate Galerkin’s method: a function orthogonal to every basis function is zero, so a residual orthogonal to the first \(n\) basis functions should be small.

title: Galerkin’s Method
text:
Weighted Residual Methods
A weighted residual method uses a finite set of functions \(\{\phi_i(x)\}_{i=0}^{n}\). Consider the differential equation
\[
L[y(x)] + f(x) = 0 \quad \text{over } a \le x \le b,
\tag{2}
\]
where \(L[y(x)]\) denotes a linear differential operator. Multiplying (2) by an arbitrary weight function \(w(x)\) and integrating over \([a, b]\) gives
\[
\int_a^b w(x)\,\bigl(L[y(x)] + f(x)\bigr)\,dx = 0 \quad \text{for every } w(x).
\tag{3}
\]
Equations (2) and (3) are equivalent when \(L[y] + f\) is continuous: (2) gives (3) at once, and (3) for every \(w\) gives (2) by the lemma above. Now introduce a trial solution of the form
\[
u(x) = \phi_0(x) + \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j\,\phi_j(x),
\tag{4}
\]
and replace \(y(x)\) with \(u(x)\) on the left side of (2). The residual is
\[
r(x) = L[u(x)] + f(x).
\tag{5}
\]
Unless \(y\) happens to be one of the trial functions, \(r(x)\) cannot be zero everywhere. The goal is to choose the coefficients so that \(u\) satisfies (3) at least for some choices of the weight function:
\[
\int_a^b w(x)\,\bigl(L[u(x)] + f(x)\bigr)\,dx = 0 \quad \text{for some choices of } w(x).
\tag{6}
\]

title: Galerkin’s Method
text:
Galerkin’s Method
One of the most important weighted residual methods is due to the Russian mathematician Boris Grigoryevich Galerkin (1871–1945). Galerkin’s method takes the weight functions from the basis functions themselves, \(w(x) \in \{\phi_i(x)\}_{i=1}^{n}\).






ImportantGalerkin’s equations



Choose the coefficients \(c_1, \ldots, c_n\) of the trial solution (4) so that
\[
\int_a^b \phi_i(x)\,\bigl(L[u(x)] + f(x)\bigr)\,dx = 0, \qquad i = 1, 2, \ldots, n.
\tag{7}
\]


Substituting (4) and using the linearity of \(L\) turns (7) into
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j \int_a^b \phi_i(x)\,L[\phi_j(x)]\,dx = -\int_a^b \phi_i(x)\,\bigl(L[\phi_0(x)] + f(x)\bigr)\,dx, \qquad i = 1, \ldots, n,
\]
which is the linear system
\[
\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{B}, \qquad a_{ij} = \langle \phi_i, L[\phi_j] \rangle, \qquad b_i = -\langle \phi_i, L[\phi_0] + f \rangle.
\tag{8}
\]
Mathews obtains the coefficients both ways: he solves the equations (7) directly, and he sets up the matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) and the vector \(\mathbf{B}\) of (8) and solves \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{B}\). Both give the same coefficients in every example.

Algorithm

Write the equation as \(L[y] + f = 0\) and choose \(\phi_0\) to satisfy the initial or boundary conditions.
Choose basis functions \(\phi_1, \ldots, \phi_n\) that satisfy the homogeneous conditions, so that every trial solution (4) satisfies the original ones.
Form the residual \(r(x) = L[u(x)] + f(x)\) of the trial solution.
Compute the integrals in (8) and solve \(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{B}\) for \(c_1, \ldots, c_n\).
The Galerkin solution is \(u(x) = \phi_0(x) + \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j\,\phi_j(x)\).







WarningConditioning of the Galerkin system



The system (8) can be ill conditioned: its solution can be very sensitive to rounding errors in \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\). Mathews computes the condition number \(\operatorname{cond}(\mathbf{A}) = \lVert \mathbf{A} \rVert\,\lVert \mathbf{A}^{-1} \rVert\) for each example and uses the estimate
\[
\lVert \mathbf{c} - \hat{\mathbf{c}} \rVert \lesssim \lVert \mathbf{c} \rVert\,\operatorname{cond}(\mathbf{A})\,\epsilon
\]
for the error of the computed solution \(\hat{\mathbf{c}}\) when the entries of \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are rounded to machine precision \(\epsilon = 2^{-52} \approx 2.22 \times 10^{-16}\). In words: the computed coefficients lose about \(\log_{10} \operatorname{cond}(\mathbf{A})\) of their sixteen or so decimal digits. This is a first-order estimate of the typical size of the error, not a guaranteed bound. Mathews’ condition numbers are in the maximum-row-sum (\(\infty\)-)norm, and the values quoted on this page are too.

title: Galerkin’s Method
section: Galerkin’s Method for an Initial Value Problem
text:
Galerkin’s Method for an Initial Value Problem
Suppose we wish to solve the initial value problem
\[
L[y(x)] + f(x) = 0, \qquad y(a) = y_0, \qquad a \le x \le b.
\tag{9}
\]
Take \(\phi_0(x) = y_0\) and the trial function
\[
u(x) = y_0 + \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j\,\phi_j(x),
\tag{10}
\]
with basis functions that vanish at the initial point, \(\phi_j(a) = 0\), so that \(u(a) = y_0\) for every choice of the coefficients. There are \(n\) equations to solve for \(\{c_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\):
\[
\int_a^b \phi_i(x)\,\Bigl(L\Bigl[\sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j\,\phi_j(x)\Bigr] + L[y_0] + f(x)\Bigr)\,dx = 0, \qquad i = 1, 2, \ldots, n.
\tag{11}
\]

Example 2 — \(y' + 5y - 1 - x + \sin 2x = 0\), \(y(0) = 1\), over \([0, 3]\)






WarningTwo versions of Example 2



Mathews’ module states Example 2 as \(y' + 2y + 6 + 4x = 0\) with \(y(0) = 1\), but his solution notebook solves a different equation, \(y' + 5y - 1 - x + \sin 2x = 0\) with \(y(0) = 1\) on \([0, 3]\). This page works the equation of the solution, which is the one his numbers belong to, and gives the result for the stated equation at the end of the example.


Step 1 (operator and data): \(L[y] = y' + 5y\), \(f(x) = -1 - x + \sin 2x\), \(a = 0\), \(b = 3\), \(y_0 = 1\).
Step 2 (basis and trial solution): Mathews takes \(n = 7\) and the powers \(\phi_i(x) = x^i\), which all vanish at \(x = 0\):
\[
u(x) = 1 + c_1 x + c_2 x^2 + c_3 x^3 + c_4 x^4 + c_5 x^5 + c_6 x^6 + c_7 x^7.
\]
Step 3 (residual):
\[
r(x) = u'(x) + 5u(x) - 1 - x + \sin 2x = 4 - x + \sin 2x + \sum_{j=1}^{7} c_j\,\bigl(j x^{j-1} + 5x^j\bigr).
\]
Step 4 (Galerkin system): since \(L[\phi_0] = L[1] = 5\), the entries of (8) are
\[
a_{ij} = \int_0^3 x^i\bigl(j x^{j-1} + 5x^j\bigr)\,dx = \frac{j\,3^{i+j}}{i+j} + \frac{5 \cdot 3^{i+j+1}}{i+j+1}, \qquad
b_i = -\int_0^3 x^i\,\bigl(4 - x + \sin 2x\bigr)\,dx.
\]
For example \(a_{11} = \tfrac92 + 45 = 49.5\), \(a_{77} = \tfrac{14348907}{2} \approx 7.17445 \times 10^6\) and \(b_1 = -9 + \tfrac32\cos 6 - \tfrac14\sin 6 \approx -7.48989\). The entries of \(\mathbf{A}\) span more than five orders of magnitude, and \(\mathbf{A}\) is not symmetric (\(a_{12} = \tfrac{477}{4}\), \(a_{21} = \tfrac{441}{4}\)).
Step 5 (solve): the solution of the \(7 \times 7\) system, computed exactly and rounded to six significant figures, is
\[
\mathbf{c} = (-3.65784,\ 6.84171,\ -7.37284,\ 4.88613,\ -1.84964,\ 0.363990,\ -0.0289550),
\]
which agrees with Mathews’ printed values. The Galerkin solution is
\[
\boxed{\ u(x) = 1 - 3.65784\,x + 6.84171\,x^2 - 7.37284\,x^3 + 4.88613\,x^4 - 1.84964\,x^5 + 0.363990\,x^6 - 0.0289550\,x^7\ }
\]
Verification: the exact solution is
\[
y(x) = \frac{1}{725}\Bigl(116 + 559\,e^{-5x} + 145x + 50\cos 2x - 125\sin 2x\Bigr),
\]
which satisfies the differential equation and \(y(0) = 1\) (checked symbolically). Substituting the exact coefficients back into (7) gives \(0\) for all seven integrals.
