title: Galerkin’s Method
section: Galerkin’s Method for a Boundary Value Problem
text:
Galerkin’s Method for a Boundary Value Problem
Suppose we wish to solve a boundary value problem over \([a, b]\):
\[
L[y(x)] + f(x) = 0, \qquad y(a) = z_a, \quad y(b) = z_b.
\tag{12}
\]
Define \(\phi_0\) as the straight line between the boundary points,
\[
\phi_0(x) = z_a + (z_b - z_a)\,\frac{x - a}{b - a},
\tag{13}
\]
and use the trial function
\[
u(x) = \phi_0(x) + \sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j\,\phi_j(x).
\tag{14}
\]
The basis functions must all vanish at both ends,
\[
\phi_i(a) = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \phi_i(b) = 0, \qquad i = 1, 2, \ldots, n,
\]
so that \(u(a) = z_a\) and \(u(b) = z_b\) for every choice of the coefficients. There are \(n\) equations to solve for \(\{c_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\):
\[
\int_a^b \phi_i(x)\,\Bigl(L\Bigl[\sum_{j=1}^{n} c_j\,\phi_j(x)\Bigr] + L[\phi_0(x)] + f(x)\Bigr)\,dx = 0, \qquad i = 1, 2, \ldots, n.
\tag{15}
\]
For an operator \(L[y] = y'' + q\,y\) with a constant \(q\), as in Examples 3 and 4, integrating by parts and using \(\phi_i(a) = \phi_i(b) = 0\) gives \(a_{ij} = \int_a^b \bigl(q\,\phi_i \phi_j - \phi_i' \phi_j'\bigr)\,dx\), so the matrix \(\mathbf{A}\) is symmetric in those examples.

Example 3 (a) — \(y'' + y + 2x(1 - x) = 0\), \(y(0) = 0\), \(y(1) = 0\)
Step 1 (operator and data): \(L[y] = y'' + y\), \(f(x) = 2x(1 - x)\), \([a, b] = [0, 1]\), \(z_a = z_b = 0\), so \(\phi_0(x) = 0\).
Step 2 (basis and trial solution): \(n = 3\), with \(\phi_1 = x(x - 1)\), \(\phi_2 = x^2(x - 1)^2\), \(\phi_3 = x^3(x - 1)^3\):
\[
u(x) = c_1\,x(x - 1) + c_2\,x^2(x - 1)^2 + c_3\,x^3(x - 1)^3.
\]
Step 3 (Galerkin system): the integrals (15) give
\[
\begin{pmatrix} -\tfrac{3}{10} & \tfrac{5}{84} & -\tfrac{4}{315} \\[1mm] \tfrac{5}{84} & -\tfrac{11}{630} & \tfrac{61}{13860} \\[1mm] -\tfrac{4}{315} & \tfrac{61}{13860} & -\tfrac{73}{60060} \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \\ c_3 \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} \tfrac{1}{15} \\[1mm] -\tfrac{1}{70} \\[1mm] \tfrac{1}{315} \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Step 4 (solve):
\[
c_1 = -\frac{1370}{7397} \approx -0.185210, \qquad c_2 = \frac{50688}{273689} \approx 0.185203, \qquad c_3 = -\frac{132}{21053} \approx -0.00626989.
\]
These are Mathews’ values. The Galerkin solution is
\[
\boxed{\ u(x) = -\frac{1370}{7397}\,x(x - 1) + \frac{50688}{273689}\,x^2(x - 1)^2 - \frac{132}{21053}\,x^3(x - 1)^3\ }
\]
Verification: the exact solution is
\[
y(x) = 2\Bigl(-2 - x + x^2 + 2\cos x + 2\sin x\,\tan\tfrac12\Bigr),
\]
which satisfies the equation and both boundary conditions (checked symbolically).

Example 4 (a) — \(y'' + 2y + 2x(x - \pi) = 0\), \(y(0) = 0\), \(y(\pi) = 0\)
Step 1 (operator and data): \(L[y] = y'' + 2y\), \(f(x) = 2x(x - \pi)\), \([a, b] = [0, \pi]\), \(\phi_0(x) = 0\).
Step 2 (basis): Mathews takes \(n = 3\) and the odd sines \(\phi_1 = \sin x\), \(\phi_2 = \sin 3x\), \(\phi_3 = \sin 5x\), which vanish at \(0\) and \(\pi\):
\[
u(x) = c_1 \sin x + c_2 \sin 3x + c_3 \sin 5x.
\]
Step 3 (Galerkin system): since \(L[\sin kx] = (2 - k^2)\sin kx\) and the functions \(\sin kx\) are orthogonal on \([0, \pi]\) with \(\int_0^\pi \sin^2 kx\,dx = \tfrac{\pi}{2}\), the matrix is diagonal, \(a_{kk} = (2 - k^2)\tfrac{\pi}{2}\). The right-hand side is \(b_k = -\int_0^\pi \sin kx \cdot 2x(x - \pi)\,dx = \tfrac{8}{k^3}\) for odd \(k\), and the equations are
\[
\frac{\pi}{2}\,c_1 = 8, \qquad -\frac{7\pi}{2}\,c_2 = \frac{8}{27}, \qquad -\frac{23\pi}{2}\,c_3 = \frac{8}{125}.
\]
Step 4 (solve):
\[
c_1 = \frac{16}{\pi} \approx 5.09296, \qquad c_2 = -\frac{16}{189\pi} \approx -0.0269469, \qquad c_3 = -\frac{16}{2875\pi} \approx -0.00177146,
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\ u(x) = \frac{16\sin x}{\pi} - \frac{16\sin 3x}{189\pi} - \frac{16\sin 5x}{2875\pi}\ }
\]
These agree with Mathews’ values. For even \(k\) the right-hand side \(b_k\) is \(0\) (the forcing \(2x(x - \pi)\) is symmetric about \(x = \tfrac{\pi}{2}\) and \(\sin kx\) is antisymmetric about it), so adding \(\sin 2x\) and \(\sin 4x\) to the basis would give them zero coefficients; that is why Mathews skips them.
Verification: the exact solution is
\[
y(x) = 1 + \pi x - x^2 - \cos\bigl(\sqrt2\,x\bigr) - \sin\bigl(\sqrt2\,x\bigr)\tan\frac{\pi}{\sqrt2},
\]
which satisfies the equation (checked symbolically) and both boundary conditions (checked to 40 digits).

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Description
The harvesting model adds a constant removal rate \(k\) (fish caught, trees cut, animals hunted per unit time) to the logistic model of bounded population growth:
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = a x - b x^2 - k, \qquad x(0) = x_0, \qquad a, b, k > 0 .
\]
Its right-hand side is a downward parabola in \(x\), so everything depends on the stationary solutions, the constant solutions \(x(t) = r\) with \(a r - b r^2 - k = 0\). When \(a^2 > 4bk\) there are two of them, \(r_1 < r_2\): populations that start above \(r_1\) settle at \(r_2\), and populations that start below \(r_1\) die out in finite time. When \(a^2 = 4bk\) the two merge into the single value \(a/(2b)\), and when \(a^2 < 4bk\) there are none, so every population dies out. In each case the equation is separable and Mathews writes the solution as a formula: a rational function of \(t\), a quotient of exponentials, or a tangent.
Mathews then solves the same equations numerically with the modified Euler method in its midpoint form, with step \(h = (b - a)/m\) on an interval \([a, b]\):
\[
y_{k+1} = y_k + h\, f\!\left(t_k + \tfrac{h}{2},\ y_k + \tfrac{h}{2} f(t_k, y_k)\right),
\]
always with \(m = 110\) steps. He works one example for each case, \((a, b, k) = (2, 1, 1)\), \((4, 1, 3)\) and \((3, 3, 3)\), draws families of solution curves from many starting values \(x_0\), and shows that the numerical curves reproduce the formulas. Every formula below has been checked symbolically, and every number recomputed.

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Background: the Logistic Equation
The exponential model \(y' = a y\) describes unchecked growth; its solution is \(y(t) = c\, e^{a t}\). Subtracting a crowding term \(b y^2\) gives the logistic model of bounded growth.






NoteDefinition — Logistic differential equation



For constants \(a, b > 0\) the logistic differential equation is
\[
y' = a y - b y^2, \qquad y(0) = y_0 .
\tag{1}
\]


For \(y_0 > 0\) one form of its solution is
\[
y(t) = \frac{a}{b + \left(\dfrac{a}{y_0} - b\right) e^{-a t}},
\tag{2}
\]
where the constants have been arranged so that \(y(0) = y_0\). Its limit is
\[
L = \lim_{t \to \infty} y(t) = \frac{a}{b}.
\]
For \(0 < y_0 < a/(2b)\) the graph is the familiar S-shaped curve. Mathews takes \(a = 0.01\), \(b = 0.00001\) and \(y_0 = 100\), for which \(a/y_0 - b = 0.00009\) and
\[
y(t) = \frac{0.01}{0.00001 + 0.00009\, e^{-0.01 t}}, \qquad L = 1000 .
\]
He plots it for \(0 \le t \le 1000\); at the right end \(y(1000) = 999.59\). Since \(y'' = (a - 2 b y)\, y'\), the curve changes from concave up to concave down where \(y = a/(2b) = 500\), which happens at \(t = 100 \ln 9 \approx 219.72\).

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Harvesting a Logistic Population
Incorporating a constant harvesting term \(-k\) into the bounded population model gives
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = a x - b x^2 - k .
\tag{3}
\]






NoteDefinition — Stationary points



The stationary points of (3) are the constants \(r\) for which \(x(t) = r\) is a solution, that is, \(dx/dt \equiv 0\). They are the roots of the characteristic equation
\[
a r - b r^2 - k = 0, \qquad r = \frac{a \pm \sqrt{a^2 - 4 b k}}{2 b} .
\tag{4}
\]


Because \(x(t)\) is real, there are no stationary solutions when \(a^2 - 4bk < 0\). The sign of \(a^2 - 4bk\) therefore splits the problem into three cases, each with its own form of the solution. In all three the right-hand side of (3) is largest at \(x = a/(2b)\), and each formula below satisfies (3) and the initial condition \(x(0) = x_0\) identically (checked with sympy).

Case (i): \(a^2 = 4bk\), one stationary solution
When \(k = a^2/(4b)\) the right-hand side is a perfect square, \(a x - b x^2 - \tfrac{a^2}{4b} = -b\left(x - \tfrac{a}{2b}\right)^2\), and the only stationary solution is \(x_1(t) = a/(2b)\). The general solution, written as Mathews writes it with an arbitrary constant \(c\), is
\[
x(t) = \frac{a}{2b} + \frac{1}{b}\,\frac{1}{t - 4 b c},
\]
and the solution with \(x(0) = x_0\) is
\[
x(t) = \frac{a}{2b} + \frac{1}{b}\,\frac{1}{t - \dfrac{2}{a - 2 b x_0}} .
\tag{5}
\]






TipTheorem — Case (i)



Let \(a^2 = 4bk\) and \(x_0 \ge 0\).

If \(x_0 \ge a/(2b)\), then \(\displaystyle\lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) = \frac{a}{2b}\).
If \(x_0 < a/(2b)\), then \(x(t)\) has a vertical asymptote at \(t_1 = \dfrac{2}{a - 2 b x_0}\), and the population becomes extinct at the time \(t_0 = t_1 - \dfrac{2}{a} = \dfrac{4 b x_0}{a\,(a - 2 b x_0)}\), with \(0 \le t_0 < t_1\) and \(x(t_0) = 0\).



Since \(dx/dt = -b\,(x - a/(2b))^2 \le 0\), every solution decreases. One that starts above \(a/(2b)\) approaches it from above; one that starts below falls through \(0\) at \(t_0\) and on toward \(-\infty\) at \(t_1\). Mathews’ module states the extinction time only as some \(t_0\) between \(0\) and \(t_1\); the formula for \(t_0\) comes from setting (5) equal to zero.


Case (ii): \(a^2 > 4bk\), two stationary solutions
Write \(s = \sqrt{a^2 - 4bk} > 0\). The two real roots of the characteristic equation are
\[
r_1 = \frac{a - s}{2b}, \qquad r_2 = \frac{a + s}{2b},
\]
and the stationary solutions are \(x_1(t) = r_1\) and \(x_2(t) = r_2\). Mathews’ general solution is
\[
x(t) = \frac{a}{2b} + \frac{s}{2b}\left(1 - \frac{2}{1 + c\, e^{s t}}\right),
\]
and the solution with \(x(0) = x_0\) is
\[
x(t) = \frac{a}{2b} + \frac{s}{2b} - \frac{a + s - 2 b x_0}{2b}\cdot\frac{2 s}{(s + a - 2 b x_0) + (s - a + 2 b x_0)\, e^{s t}} .
\tag{6}
\]






TipTheorem — Case (ii)



Let \(a^2 > 4bk\) and \(x_0 \ge 0\).

If \(x_0 > r_1\), then \(\displaystyle\lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) = r_2 = \frac{a + \sqrt{a^2 - 4bk}}{2b}\).
If \(0 < x_0 < r_1\), then the population becomes extinct at the time \[
t_0 = \frac{1}{s}\ln\frac{r_1\,(r_2 - x_0)}{r_2\,(r_1 - x_0)} > 0, \qquad x(t_0) = 0,
\] and \(x(t)\) has a vertical asymptote later, at \(t_1 = \dfrac{1}{s}\ln\dfrac{r_2 - x_0}{r_1 - x_0}\).



Here \(dx/dt = -b\,(x - r_1)(x - r_2)\), so a solution that starts between \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) increases to \(r_2\), one that starts above \(r_2\) decreases to \(r_2\), and one that starts below \(r_1\) decreases through \(0\). Mathews’ module gives only the existence of \(t_0\); the formulas for \(t_0\) and \(t_1\) come from setting (6) and its denominator equal to zero.


Case (iii): \(a^2 < 4bk\), no stationary solutions
Write \(w = \sqrt{4bk - a^2} > 0\). Mathews’ general solution is
\[
x(t) = \frac{a}{2b} - \frac{w}{2b}\tan\!\left(\frac{w t}{2} - c\right),
\]
and the solution with \(x(0) = x_0\) has \(c = \arctan\dfrac{2 b x_0 - a}{w}\):
\[
x(t) = \frac{a}{2b} - \frac{w}{2b}\tan\!\left(\frac{w t}{2} - \arctan\frac{2 b x_0 - a}{w}\right).
\tag{7}
\]






TipTheorem — Case (iii)



Let \(a^2 < 4bk\) and \(x_0 \ge 0\). Then \(x(t)\) has a vertical asymptote at
\[
t_1 = \frac{2}{w}\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + c\right), \qquad c = \arctan\frac{2 b x_0 - a}{w},
\]
and the population becomes extinct at the earlier time \(t_0 = \dfrac{2}{w}\left(\arctan\dfrac{a}{w} + c\right)\), where \(x(t_0) = 0\).


Here \(dx/dt = -b\,(x - a/(2b))^2 - w^2/(4b) < 0\) for every \(x\), so every population decreases, whatever its size. The tangent in (7) becomes infinite when its argument \(w t/2 - c\) reaches \(\pi/2\), which gives the formula for \(t_1\) above. Mathews’ module prints \(t_1 = 2(\pi/2 - c)/w\) with a minus sign, which is not where (7) is infinite; in Example 18 below (\(x_0 = 1\)) his formula gives \(0.4031\), which is the extinction time, while the asymptote is at \(0.8061\), and for \(x_0 = 6\) it gives \(0.0601\), where the population is still \(3.182\).

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Numerical Solutions
If only the graph of the solution is needed, and not the formula, an efficient way to solve (3) is a numerical method such as the modified Euler method or the Runge-Kutta method; if an accurate table of values is wanted, Mathews recommends the Runge-Kutta method. His program for the modified Euler method approximates the solution of \(y' = f(t, y)\), \(y(a) = \alpha\), on \([a, b]\) at the points \(t_k = a + k h\), \(h = (b - a)/m\), by
\[
y_{k+1} = y_k + h\, f\!\left(t_k + \frac{h}{2},\ y_k + \frac{h}{2} f(t_k, y_k)\right), \qquad k = 0, 1, \ldots, m - 1 .
\tag{8}
\]
This is the midpoint form of the method: an Euler half-step to the middle of the interval, and a full step with the slope found there. It is of second order; in Example 8 below, doubling \(m\) from \(110\) to \(220\) and then to \(440\) divides the largest error for \(x_0 = 6\) by \(4.5\) and then by \(4.3\). Mathews passes a list of starting values as \(\alpha\), so one call computes a whole family of curves.

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Example 1 — A Computer Algebra Solution
Problem. Use Mathematica to solve \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = a x - b x^2 - k\).
Solution. Mathews applies Mathematica’s DSolve to (3) with \(a\), \(b\) and \(k\) left as symbols (the output images of this example are missing from the archive). His caveat is that the general solution found by Mathematica, and by Maple too, is the one for case (iii) only; the formulas for cases (i) and (ii) are left for the reader to prove. A computer algebra system returns one formula for the “general solution”, and it may be the least significant of the three forms. When numbers are substituted for \(a\), \(b\) and \(k\), as in the examples that follow, Mathematica does find the solution of the right form.

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Example 2 — Stationary Solutions
Problem. Find the roots of \(a r - b r^2 - k = 0\) and the equilibrium solutions of (3).
Solution. Solving the quadratic gives the two roots (4),
\[
x_1(t) = \frac{a - \sqrt{a^2 - 4bk}}{2b}, \qquad x_2(t) = \frac{a + \sqrt{a^2 - 4bk}}{2b},
\]
and substituting each constant into (3) shows that \(a x_i - b x_i^2 - k = 0 = x_i'\). These are the two stationary solutions of case (ii). For case (i) the substitution \(k = a^2/(4b)\) must be made before solving, which leaves the single root \(a/(2b)\).

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Case (i) Examples: \(x' = 2x - x^2 - 1\)

Example 3 — The general solution
Problem. Solve \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = a x - b x^2 - k\) with \(a = 2\), \(b = 1\), \(k = 1\), and explore this situation.
Step 1. Here \(a^2 = 4 = 4bk\), so this is case (i), and the equation is
\[
x' = -1 + 2x - x^2 = -(x - 1)^2 .
\]
Step 2. Mathematica’s DSolve gives the general solution
\[
x(t) = \frac{1 + t - C}{t - C} = 1 + \frac{1}{t - C},
\tag{9}
\]
with \(x(0) = (C - 1)/C\).
Step 3. The constant solution is the root of \(-1 + 2X - X^2 = 0\), namely \(x_1(t) = 1 = a/(2b)\).
Step 4. For every \(C\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{1 + t - C}{t - C} = 1\), the constant solution. As the next examples show, this limit is reached only by solutions with \(x_0 \ge 1\); for \(0 < x_0 < 1\) the constant is \(C = 1/(1 - x_0) > 0\) and the solution reaches \(0\), and then the pole at \(t = C\), before \(t\) can grow large.
Verification. \(x' = -1/(t - C)^2\) and \(-(x - 1)^2 = -1/(t - C)^2\), so (9) satisfies the equation for every \(C\).

Example 6 — Reading the graph of Example 5
Problem. In the plot of Example 5, what are the vertical lines? What are the curves below \(x = 1\), and those above \(x = 1\)? What use are they?
Solution. The vertical lines are the asymptotes \(t = C\) of the solutions. The curves below \(x = 1\) are the solutions with the initial conditions we wanted. The curves above \(x = 1\) are extraneous: they are the parts of the same formulas beyond the pole, which are not connected to \(x(0) = x_0\) and are of no use here. To get rid of them, Mathews gives each solution its own domain, from \(t = 0\) up to the asymptote, and draws all the curves on one graph (the images of this example are missing from the archive). The composite graph shows that the solutions with \(x_0 > 1\) tend to \(1\) as \(t \to \infty\) (Mathews’ text says \(x_0 > 0\) here, which contradicts his next sentence and the computation), that the solutions with \(0 < x_0 < 1\) reach \(0\) at a finite time and the population becomes extinct, and that the constant solution \(x = 1\) divides the two cases.


Example 7 — The formula for the solution with \(x(0) = x_0\)
Problem. Solve \(x' = 2x - x^2 - 1\) with \(x(0) = x_0\) using formula (5).
Solution. With \(a = 2\), \(b = 1\), (5) becomes

\]
which is (9) with \(C = 1/(1 - x_0)\). Mathews checks the general formula and this one against the equation (his images for this example are missing).

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Case (ii) Examples: \(x' = 4x - x^2 - 3\)

Example 9 — The general solution
Problem. Solve \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = a x - b x^2 - k\) with \(a = 4\), \(b = 1\), \(k = 3\), and explore this situation.
Step 1. Here \(a^2 = 16 > 12 = 4bk\), so this is case (ii), and the equation is
\[
x' = -3 + 4x - x^2 = -(x - 1)(x - 3) .
\]
Step 2. DSolve gives the general solution
\[
x(t) = \frac{3 e^{2t} - e^{2C}}{e^{2t} - e^{2C}},
\tag{10}
\]
with \(x(0) = (3 - e^{2C})/(1 - e^{2C})\), so that \(e^{2C} = (x_0 - 3)/(x_0 - 1)\).
Step 3. The constant solutions are the roots of \(-3 + 4X - X^2 = 0\): \(x_1(t) = 1\) and \(x_2(t) = 3\), in agreement with \(r_{1,2} = (a \mp s)/(2b)\) for \(s = \sqrt{16 - 12} = 2\).
Step 4. For every constant \(C\), \(\displaystyle\lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) = 3\), the second constant solution. Mathews remarks that it takes more investigation to see what is happening, and the next examples show that the limit is reached only from \(x_0 > 1\).
Verification. Substituting (10) into \(x' = -3 + 4x - x^2\) gives a zero residual for every \(C\).

Example 13 — Reading the graph of Example 12
Problem. In the plot of Example 12, what are the vertical lines? What are the curves below \(x = 1\), and those above \(x = 3\)? What use are they?
Solution. As in Example 6, the vertical lines are asymptotes, and the branches beyond them are extraneous. Mathews clears things up by giving each solution of Example 12 its own domain, from \(t = 0\) to its asymptote \(t_1\) in the table above, and draws them on one graph with the constant solutions \(x_1 = 1\) and \(x_2 = 3\) and the curves of Examples 10 and 11, in the window \([0, 1] \times [0, 8]\), with ticks every \(0.2\) in \(t\). The composite graph shows three kinds of behaviour:

solutions with \(x_0 > 3\) decrease toward \(3\) as \(t \to \infty\);
solutions with \(1 < x_0 < 3\) increase toward \(3\) as \(t \to \infty\);
solutions with \(0 < x_0 < 1\) reach \(0\) at a finite time, and the population becomes extinct.

The constant functions \(x = 1\) and \(x = 3\) are the dividing lines between these three cases. A population harvested at this rate survives only if it starts above \(1\).


Example 14 — The formula for the solution with \(x(0) = x_0\)
Problem. Solve \(x' = 4x - x^2 - 3\) using the formulas, with the initial condition \(x(0) = 4\).
Solution. Mathews first checks a general formula for case (ii), here in the form \(\dfrac{a}{2b} - \dfrac{s}{2b}\cdot\dfrac{c + e^{s t}}{c - e^{s t}}\), which for \(a = 4\), \(b = 1\), \(k = 3\) becomes
\[
x(t) = 2 + \frac{c + e^{2t}}{-c + e^{2t}} = \frac{-c + 3 e^{2t}}{-c + e^{2t}},
\]
the same as DSolve’s (10) when the arbitrary constants are related by \(c = e^{2C}\). He then substitutes \(a = 4\), \(b = 1\), \(k = 3\), \(x_0 = 4\) into (6), which gives
\[
x(t) = 3 + \frac{2}{3 e^{2t} - 1} = \frac{-1 + 9 e^{2t}}{-1 + 3 e^{2t}},
\]
the same as DSolve’s solution with \(x(0) = 4\) and the first row of the table in Example 10.
Verification. Both formulas give a zero residual in \(x' = -3 + 4x - x^2\), and the second takes the value \(8/2 = 4\) at \(t = 0\).

title: Harvesting Model
text:
Case (iii) Examples: \(x' = 3x - 3x^2 - 3\)

Example 16 — The general solution
Problem. Solve \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = a x - b x^2 - k\) with \(a = 3\), \(b = 3\), \(k = 3\).
Step 1. Here \(a^2 = 9 < 36 = 4bk\), so this is case (iii), with \(w = \sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt3\), and the equation is
\[
x' = -3 + 3x - 3x^2 .
\]
Its right-hand side is at most \(-\tfrac94\) (at \(x = \tfrac12\)), so every solution decreases at a rate of at least \(\tfrac94\), and there are no stationary solutions.
Step 2. DSolve gives the general solution
\[
x(t) = \frac12\left(1 + \sqrt3\,\tan\!\left(\frac12\left(-3\sqrt3\, t + \sqrt3\, C\right)\right)\right),
\tag{11}
\]
which is the case (iii) formula with \(a/(2b) = \tfrac12\) and \(w/(2b) = \sqrt3/2\).
Verification. Substituting (11) into the equation gives a zero residual for every \(C\).


Example 17 — Solutions with \(x_0 = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\)
Problem. Plot the solutions of the equation of Example 16 with \(x(0) = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\).
Solution. Solving \(x(0) = x_0\) for \(C\) (again Mathematica warns, and again the warnings can be ignored) gives \(C = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}\arctan\dfrac{2 x_0 - 1}{\sqrt3}\), and the solutions are
\[
x(t) = \frac12\left(1 - \sqrt3\,\tan\!\left(\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}\, t - \arctan\frac{2 x_0 - 1}{\sqrt3}\right)\right),
\]
where \(\arctan(1/\sqrt3) = \pi/6\) and \(\arctan\sqrt3 = \pi/3\) give Mathews’ forms \(\tfrac12\bigl(1 + \sqrt3\tan\tfrac16(\pi - 9\sqrt3\, t)\bigr)\) and \(\tfrac12\bigl(1 + \sqrt3\tan\tfrac16(2\pi - 9\sqrt3\, t)\bigr)\) for \(x_0 = 1\) and \(2\). Example 18 — The formula for the solution with \(x(0) = x_0\)
Problem. Solve \(x' = 3x - 3x^2 - 3\) using the formulas, with the initial condition \(x(0) = 1\).
Solution. Substituting \(a = b = k = 3\) into the general case (iii) formula gives

which is DSolve’s (11) when the arbitrary constants are related by \(C = 2c/\sqrt3\). Substituting \(x_0 = 1\) into (7) gives \(c = \arctan(1/\sqrt3) = \pi/6\) and
\[

\]
the same as DSolve’s solution with \(x(0) = 1\).
Verification. The residual in the equation is zero, and \(x(0) = \tfrac12(1 + \sqrt3 \tan\tfrac{\pi}{6}) = 1\). This solution reaches \(0\) at \(t_0 = 2\pi/(9\sqrt3) = 0.4031\), and its tangent becomes infinite at \(t_1 = 4\pi/(9\sqrt3) = 0.8061\), twice as late (see the note on Mathews’ formula for \(t_1\) under case (iii) above).

title: Logistic Curve

← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Logistic Curve
text:
Description
A population that grows without limit is modelled by the exponential equation \(y' = r\,y\). When growth is held back by limited resources, the logistic differential equation \(y' = r\,y\,(1 - y/L)\) is used instead, and its solution is the S-shaped logistic curve
\[
y = \frac{L}{1 + c\,e^{a x}},
\]
which rises (when \(a < 0\) and \(c > 0\)) from near \(0\) toward the limiting value \(L\), also called the carrying capacity. The problem on this page is the one in Mathews’ module: given data points \((x_k, y_k)\), here the population of the United States from 1900 to 1990, find the logistic curve that fits them, and use it to predict the population in 2000.
The first method, data linearization, needs a guess for \(L\). It rearranges the curve to \(L/y - 1 = c\,e^{a x}\) and takes logarithms, so that the change of variables \(X = x\), \(Y = \ln(L/y - 1)\) turns the curve into the straight line
\[
Y = \ln(c) + a X .
\]
A least squares line \(Y = AX + B\) through the transformed points then gives \(a = A\) and \(c = e^{B}\). With \(L = 800\) million this predicts \(281.75\) million people for 2000, within \(0.13\%\) of the census figure. The second method, true least squares, chooses \(L\), \(c\) and \(a\) together to minimise the sum of squared errors in \(y\) itself; the equations are nonlinear, so it is solved iteratively from starting values such as those of the first method.

title: Logistic Curve
text:
Animations
Mathews’ module links no animation, and his animation archive has none for curve fitting or the logistic equation, so all three animations below are new, with no Mathews original. His plots of the least squares line in the \(XY\)-plane and of the curve \(f_1\) in Example 1 have not survived, so their windows and colours are not known. Case 1 draws both for his \(L = 800\), as one frame of a sweep over the guessed limit \(L\), together with the prediction for 2000 of Examples 2 and 4. Case 2 animates the Gauss–Newton iteration of Example 5, and Case 3 the logistic differential equation of the background section, with the growth rate and limit of \(f_1\). Not animated are Example 3, which only looks up the census figure for 2000 (it appears as the red star in Case 1), the transformation, sums and normal equations of Steps 1 to 3 of Example 1 (Case 1 shows only their result, \(A\) and \(B\)), the breakdown of the Gauss–Newton iteration from starting values with \(L \ge 1100\) in the caution after Example 5, and the symmetry of the logistic curve about its inflection point. All the scripts compute in 256-bit arithmetic.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Data linearization as the guessed limit varies, \(L = 300, 320, \ldots, 1200\) million (Mathews’ Examples 1, 2 and 4)
Each frame is Example 1 repeated with one guess for \(L\). Top left is the \(XY\)-plane, with the transformed census points \((X_k, Y_k)\), \(Y_k = \ln(L/y_k - 1)\), and their least squares line \(Y = AX + B\). Top right is the curve \(f(t) = L/(1 + c\,e^{a(t - 1900)})\), \(a = A\), \(c = e^B\), with the census points it was fitted to and, as an open red star, the July 2000 census figure, which it was not. The bottom panels trace, as \(L\) grows, the sum of squared errors in \(y\), \(E = \sum (y_k - f(t_k))^2\) (log scale), and the prediction \(f(2000)\). The animation pauses at Mathews’ \(L = 800\).
Behavior: At \(L = 300\), not far above the largest census figure \(249.46\), the transformed points bend away from the line, below it at both ends and above it in the middle, and the curve misses the data, with \(E = 665.3\) and a prediction \(f(2000) = 252.0\) that is \(10.68\,\%\) low. For larger \(L\) the points lie close to a line: the size of the correlation coefficient of the transformed points, \(|r| = 0.988\) at \(L = 300\), is at least \(0.9978\) from \(L = 500\) on (\(r\) is negative, since the line falls). \(E\) falls to its smallest value in the sweep, \(102.13\) at \(L = 660\), and then rises again, slowly, to \(129.9\) at \(L = 1200\). Every curve has \(E\) above the true least squares minimum \(102.06\) of Example 5 (dashed green), and comes closest to it, on a finer grid, at \(L \approx 655.3\) with \(E = 102.126\), near the \(L^* = 650.03\) of that example. The prediction \(f(2000)\) increases with \(L\) across the whole sweep, from \(252.0\) to \(286.7\), and crosses the census figure \(282.1246\) near \(L = 820.0\), where \(E = 108.2\). At Mathews’ \(L = 800\) the frame shows Example 1, with \(A = -0.01609871\), \(B = 2.219304\) and \(E = 107.1\), and Examples 2 and 4, with \(f(2000) = 281.8\), \(0.1325\,\%\) below the census figure. So the guess that fits 1900–1990 best, \(L \approx 655.3\), predicts 2000 with an error of \(1.36\,\%\), and the guess that predicts 2000 exactly fits the data worse.

Case 2 — True least squares by Gauss–Newton from the \(L = 800\) fit (Example 5), \(k = 0, 1, \ldots, 10\)
One frame per iterate \(\mathbf{p}_k = (L_k, c_k, a_k)\) of the undamped step (9). On the left is the curve of iterate \(k\) from 1880 to 2200, with its limit \(L_k\) (dotted), its inflection point \((t^*, L_k/2)\) (diamond), the previous iterate (gray dashed) and the census points. Top right are the residuals \(y_k - f(t_k)\) at the census years, with those of the previous iterate as open circles. Bottom right is the distance from the minimum on a log scale: \(E_k - E_{\min}\) and \(|L_k - L^*|\), where \(E_{\min} = 102.0601\) and \(L^* = 650.0271\) are the limit of the same iteration run to 80 steps.
Behavior: The first step overshoots: \(L\) drops from \(800\) to \(596.9\), well below \(L^* = 650.03\), and \(E\) nearly doubles, from \(107.06\) to \(206.85\), as the largest residual grows from \(5.041\) (1940) to \(7.637\) (1970). The second step brings \(L\) back to \(650.84\) and \(E\) to \(102.72\), and the third step brings \(E - E_{\min}\) down to \(8.6 \times 10^{-7}\). After \(k = 3\) the curve and the residuals no longer change visibly (later steps move the curve by at most \(0.003\) million), and the largest residual stays at \(5.659\), in 1940. \(L_k - L^*\) changes sign at every step, so the iterates alternate about \(L^*\). The bottom right panel shows linear, not quadratic, convergence: from \(k = 4\) to \(k = 10\), \(|L_k - L^*|\) shrinks by a factor between \(0.039\) and \(0.042\) per step, from \(3.439 \times 10^{-4}\) to \(1.550 \times 10^{-12}\), and from \(k = 5\) on, \(E_k - E_{\min}\) shrinks by about the square of that factor, \(0.0017\) per step, to \(8.300 \times 10^{-28}\) at \(k = 10\). (In general, when the residuals at the minimum are not zero, as here, Gauss–Newton converges only linearly, if it converges at all.)

The logistic equation (1) with the growth rate \(r = 0.0160987\) (the unrounded \(-A\) of Example 1) and the limit \(L = 800\) of \(f_1\), solved from \(t_0 = 1900\) for nine starting values: \(y_0 = 5\), \(20\), \(f_1(1900) = 78.4243\) (whose solution is \(f_1\) itself), \(200\), \(400 = L/2\), \(600\), \(800 = L\), \(900\) and \(1000\) million. The exact solutions (2) grow in time from 1900 to 2300, ten years per frame, and a diamond marks each inflection point (3) once the solution reaches it. On the right is the rate \(y' = r\,y\,(1 - y/L)\), drawn sideways so that \(y\) is on the same vertical axis in both panels, with the phase line \(y' = 0\) and a dot for each solution at its current \((y', y)\).
Behavior: Every solution except the stationary \(y \equiv 800\) moves toward \(L = 800\): those below rise, those above fall. The three solutions that start below \(L/2\), and \(f_1\), are concave up until they cross \(y = 400\) at \(t^* = 1968.24\) (\(y_0 = 200\)), \(2037.86\) (\(f_1\)), \(2127.57\) (\(y_0 = 20\)) and \(2214.86\) (\(y_0 = 5\)), and concave down after. At each crossing the solution’s dot passes the tip of the parabola, where the rate is largest, \(rL/4 = 3.220\) million per year. The solution from \(y_0 = 400\) has its inflection point at \(t_0\) itself, and the one from \(600\) is concave down for all \(t \ge 1900\) (its inflection point, by (3), would be at \(1831.76\)). The solutions from \(900\) and \(1000\) fall toward \(800\) and are concave up. The census points lie along \(f_1\), which was fitted to them. Growth from a small start is slow: by 2300 the solution from \(y_0 = 5\) has reached only \(638.0\) and \(f_1\) is at \(788.4\).

title: Logistic Curve
text:
The Logistic Differential Equation
Mathews’ module is about fitting the curve; the differential equation behind it is on his separate theory page, which states the solution, its initial value, its limit \(L\), its S shape and its symmetry, but whose formula images have not survived in the archive. This section therefore gives the standard background, derived and checked here.






NoteDefinition — Logistic differential equation



For constants \(r > 0\) (the growth rate) and \(L > 0\) (the carrying capacity), the logistic differential equation is
\[
\frac{dy}{dt} = r\,y\left(1 - \frac{y}{L}\right).
\tag{1}
\]


For small \(y\) the factor \(1 - y/L\) is close to \(1\) and equation (1) is close to the exponential model \(y' = r y\), whose solution is \(y = y_0 e^{r(t - t_0)}\). As \(y\) approaches \(L\) the factor approaches \(0\) and growth stops.
Solution by separation of variables. For \(y\) between \(0\) and \(L\), write (1) as \(\dfrac{dy}{y(1 - y/L)} = r\,dt\) and use the partial fractions \(\dfrac{1}{y(1 - y/L)} = \dfrac{1}{y} + \dfrac{1}{L - y}\):
\[
\ln y - \ln (L - y) = r t + C
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{y}{L - y} = K e^{r t}.
\]
Solving for \(y\) and choosing the constant so that \(y(t_0) = y_0\) gives the solution in the theorem below (the same formula holds for \(y_0 > L\), by the same steps with \(y - L\) in place of \(L - y\)).






TipTheorem — Solution of the logistic equation



If \(r > 0\), \(L > 0\) and \(y_0 > 0\), the solution of (1) with \(y(t_0) = y_0\) is, for \(t \ge t_0\),
\[
y(t) = \frac{L}{1 + c\,e^{-r(t - t_0)}}, \qquad c = \frac{L - y_0}{y_0},
\tag{2}
\]
with derivative
\[
y'(t) = \frac{L\,r\,c\,e^{-r(t - t_0)}}{\bigl(1 + c\,e^{-r(t - t_0)}\bigr)^2}.
\]

\(y(t) \to L\) as \(t \to \infty\).
If \(0 < y_0 < L\), then \(c > 0\) and \(y\) increases; if \(y_0 > L\), then \(-1 < c < 0\) and \(y\) decreases; if \(y_0 = L\), then \(y \equiv L\).
If \(0 < y_0 < L\), formula (2) holds for all \(t\), and \(y \to 0\) as \(t \to -\infty\).









TipTheorem — Inflection point and symmetry



Let \(0 < y_0 < L\) and \(r > 0\). Then
\[
y'' = \frac{r^2\, y\,(L - y)(L - 2y)}{L^2},
\]
so the solution (2) is concave up while \(y < L/2\) and concave down while \(y > L/2\). Its single inflection point is at
\[
t^* = t_0 + \frac{\ln c}{r}, \qquad y(t^*) = \frac{L}{2}, \qquad y'(t^*) = \frac{rL}{4},
\tag{3}
\]
where the growth rate \(y'\) is largest. The curve is symmetric about the point \((t^*, L/2)\):
\[
y(t^* + s) + y(t^* - s) = L \quad \text{for every } s.
\]


Connection with Mathews’ form. Mathews writes the curve as \(y = L/(1 + c\,e^{a x})\) with \(x\) the time. This is formula (2) with \(a = -r\) and \(t_0 = 0\), so \(c = (L - y_0)/y_0\) where \(y_0\) is the value of the curve at \(x = 0\). A growing population therefore has \(a < 0\), and the fitted value \(-a\) is the growth rate \(r\) of equation (1).

title: Logistic Curve
section: Fitting a Logistic Curve by Data Linearization
text:
Fitting a Logistic Curve by Data Linearization
We wish to fit the curve
\[
y = f(x) = \frac{L}{1 + c\,e^{a x}}
\tag{4}
\]
to the data points \((x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)\). Rearranging (4) and taking logarithms,
\[
\frac{L}{y} - 1 = c\,e^{a x}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\ln\!\left(\frac{L}{y} - 1\right) = \ln(c) + a x .
\]
The change of variables
\[
X = x, \qquad Y = \ln\!\left(\frac{L}{y} - 1\right)
\tag{5}
\]
turns this into \(Y = \ln(c) + a X\), which is “linearized”: a straight line in the \(XY\)-plane. Apply (5) to the data, keeping the abscissas and transforming the ordinates, to get the points \((X_1, Y_1), \ldots, (X_n, Y_n)\), and fit the least squares line \(Y = AX + B\) to them. Matching it with \(Y = \ln(c) + aX\) gives
\[
a = A, \qquad c = e^{B}.
\tag{6}
\]






ImportantLeast squares line — normal equations



The line \(Y = AX + B\) that minimises \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} (Y_k - A X_k - B)^2\) solves
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Bigl(\sum X_k^2\Bigr) A + \Bigl(\sum X_k\Bigr) B &= \sum X_k Y_k, \\
\Bigl(\sum X_k\Bigr) A + n B &= \sum Y_k .
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]








WarningCaution — \(L\) must be chosen first



Data linearization needs the limiting value \(L\) in advance (Mathews’ Remark 1), and \(L\) must be larger than every \(y_k\), or \(L/y_k - 1 \le 0\) and its logarithm is not a real number. A value suited to the problem is usually found by guessing. Different guesses give different curves (see the table after Example 4), and the line minimises the squared errors in \(Y = \ln(L/y - 1)\), not in \(y\), so it is not the least squares curve for the original data.

title: Logistic Curve
text:
True Least Squares
Mathews’ Remark 2 describes the second method: let the computer find all three parameters, \(L\) included, by true least squares, starting from good estimates. As far as their surviving text shows, the module’s worked solutions use only the data linearization model \(f_1\), so the computation below is new, on the data of Example 1.
The least squares logistic curve minimises the sum of squared errors in \(y\),
\[
E(L, c, a) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left( y_k - \frac{L}{1 + c\,e^{a X_k}} \right)^2 .
\tag{8}
\]
Setting \(\partial E/\partial L = \partial E/\partial c = \partial E/\partial a = 0\) gives three equations that are nonlinear in \(c\) and \(a\), so they are solved iteratively. A standard choice is the Gauss–Newton method. Write \(\mathbf{p} = (L, c, a)\), let \(\mathbf{r}\) be the vector of residuals \(r_k = y_k - f(X_k; \mathbf{p})\), and let \(\mathbf{J}\) be the \(n \times 3\) matrix of partial derivatives of \(f(X_k; \mathbf{p})\):
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial L} = \frac{1}{1 + c\,e^{aX_k}}, \qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial c} = -\frac{L\,e^{aX_k}}{(1 + c\,e^{aX_k})^2}, \qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial a} = -\frac{L\,c\,X_k\,e^{aX_k}}{(1 + c\,e^{aX_k})^2}.
\]
Each step replaces \(f\) by its linear approximation in \(\mathbf{p}\) and solves the resulting linear least squares problem:
\[
\mathbf{p}_{k+1} = \mathbf{p}_k + \Delta\mathbf{p}_k, \qquad
\mathbf{J}^{T}\mathbf{J}\,\Delta\mathbf{p}_k = \mathbf{J}^{T}\mathbf{r}.
\tag{9}
\]

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
Description
The Lotka-Volterra equations are two coupled nonlinear differential equations for a prey population \(x(t)\) and a predator population \(y(t)\):
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = k_1 x - k_2 x y, \qquad \frac{dy}{dt} = -k_3 y + k_4 x y, \qquad k_1, k_2, k_3, k_4 > 0 .
\]
Without predators the prey grow at the rate \(k_1\), and without prey the predators die out at the rate \(k_3\); the products \(x y\) count the encounters between the two species, which cost the prey and feed the predators. Mathews does not try to write \(x(t)\) and \(y(t)\) as formulas. He computes them with the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method in vector form: with \(\mathbf{Z} = (x, y)\), \(\mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z}) = (k_1 x - k_2 x y,\ -k_3 y + k_4 x y)\) and step \(h = (b - a)/m\),
\[
\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} = \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac16\left(\mathbf{K}_1 + 2\mathbf{K}_2 + 2\mathbf{K}_3 + \mathbf{K}_4\right),
\]
where \(\mathbf{K}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{K}_4\) are \(h\) times \(\mathbf{F}\) evaluated at the start, twice at the midpoint and at the end of the step. The computed points \(\mathbf{Z}_0, \mathbf{Z}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{Z}_m\) trace a curve in the \(xy\)-plane, the phase plane.
For positive starting values other than the equilibrium, the exact curves are closed. Dividing the two equations gives a separable equation for \(dy/dx\), whose solution says that the quantity \(V(x, y) = k_4 x - k_3 \ln x + k_2 y - k_1 \ln y\) keeps its initial value along every solution in the first quadrant. Its level curves are closed loops around the equilibrium \((k_3/k_4,\ k_1/k_2)\), so the populations rise and fall periodically, the predators peaking after the prey. After a scalar warm-up (Example 1), the examples solve the case \(k_1 = k_2 = k_3 = k_4 = 1\) from \((x_0, y_0) = (2, 1)\) numerically and analytically and compare the two, and then follow a population of \(5000\) rabbits and \(100\) foxes.

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
Animations
Each animation below traces a Runge-Kutta solution in the phase plane, one step of the method (7) per frame, beside the populations against time. In the phase plane the computed points \(\mathbf{Z}_j\) are joined by straight segments, as in Mathews’ graphs, and a large dot marks the current point; the time panels plot the same points against \(t_j\). Where an exact orbit is drawn (gray, dashed), it is the level curve of the conserved quantity (4) through the starting point, computed independently of the Runge-Kutta run, so the run’s distance from it shows the part of its error across the orbit. Periods, extreme values and the times at which they occur come from a reference solution (the Runge-Kutta method with steps of about \(10^{-4}\), crossing times refined by bisection) and agree with the values in the examples below. The last frame of each animation is held for about three seconds.
Mathews’ module links no animation, and his animation archive has none for the Lotka-Volterra model, so all three animations are new, with no Mathews original. Cases 1 and 2 animate the graphs of Example 2 and its aside, in Mathews’ window \([0, 2] \times [0, 2]\) and with his colours, step counts and zoom window; Case 3 animates Example 6, whose program, step count and graphs are lost, so its window and \(m = 100\) are chosen here. Not animated are Example 1, a single equation whose graph is lost; run (c) of Example 2 and the closing run with \(m = 200\), which trace the same loop as Case 1’s two runs together; and Examples 3 to 5, which find the orbit analytically and draw static graphs: the implicit curve (9), which is the dashed curve of Case 1, Example 4’s contour plot of \(x y e^{-x-y}\), and Example 5’s graphs of halves of the orbit.
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Example 2, runs (a) and (b): forward and backward from \((2, 1)\), \(m = 50\), \(h = \pm 0.066\)
Behavior: Run (a) (magenta) goes forward from \((2, 1)\), counterclockwise over the top of the orbit, and run (b) (blue) goes backward in time, clockwise over the bottom. Both stay on the dashed exact orbit to plotting accuracy: the largest change in \(V\) along them is \(2.3 \times 10^{-7}\). In the time panel the prey start at their largest value, \(x = 2\); run (a) passes the predators’ peak, \(y = 2\) at \(t = 1.146\), and the prey’s lowest value at \(t = 2.764\), and run (b) passes the predators’ lowest value at \(t = -1.617\). After \(50\) steps the runs end at \((0.438644, 0.731545)\) and \((0.439650, 0.728073)\), Mathews’ printed end points, inside his zoom window \([0.4, 0.5] \times [0.6, 0.8]\). A closer zoom in the last frames shows the two ends \(0.003615\) apart, on either side of the exact point at \(t = \pm T/2 = \pm 3.304\): the runs cover \(6.6\) time units in all, less than the period \(T = 6.608\), so the curve does not close.

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
The Lotka-Volterra Equations






NoteDefinition — Lotka-Volterra equations



For constants \(k_1, k_2, k_3, k_4 > 0\) the Lotka-Volterra equations are
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = k_1 x - k_2 x y, \qquad \frac{dy}{dt} = -k_3 y + k_4 x y,
\tag{1}
\]
solved with initial values \(x(0) = x_0 > 0\) and \(y(0) = y_0 > 0\).



Equilibrium points
An equilibrium (critical point) is a point where \(dx/dt = 0\) and \(dy/dt = 0\) at once. Writing (1) as \(x(k_1 - k_2 y) = 0\) and \(y(-k_3 + k_4 x) = 0\) shows there are exactly two:
\[
(0, 0) \qquad \text{and} \qquad (x_e, y_e) = \left(\frac{k_3}{k_4},\ \frac{k_1}{k_2}\right).
\tag{2}
\]
Mathews states that there is one critical point, \((k_3/k_4,\ k_1/k_2)\); that is the only one with both populations positive, but the origin is an equilibrium too.
The Jacobian matrix of the right-hand side of (1) is
\[
J(x, y) = \begin{pmatrix} k_1 - k_2 y & -k_2 x \\ k_4 y & -k_3 + k_4 x \end{pmatrix}.
\]
At the origin \(J = \operatorname{diag}(k_1, -k_3)\), with one positive and one negative eigenvalue: the origin is a saddle point, repelling along the \(x\)-axis (prey alone grow) and attracting along the \(y\)-axis (predators alone die out). At \((x_e, y_e)\)
\[
J(x_e, y_e) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -k_2 k_3/k_4 \\ k_1 k_4/k_2 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \lambda = \pm\, i\sqrt{k_1 k_3},
\tag{3}
\]
so the linearised system rotates around \((x_e, y_e)\) with angular frequency \(\sqrt{k_1 k_3}\), that is with period \(2\pi/\sqrt{k_1 k_3}\). Purely imaginary eigenvalues alone do not decide what the nonlinear system does near the equilibrium; the conserved quantity below does.


A conserved quantity and closed orbits






TipTheorem — Conserved quantity (general, for \(k_1, \ldots, k_4 > 0\) and \(x, y > 0\))



Along every solution of (1) with \(x_0, y_0 > 0\) the function
\[
V(x, y) = k_4 x - k_3 \ln x + k_2 y - k_1 \ln y
\tag{4}
\]
is constant. Equivalently, \(x^{k_3}\, y^{k_1}\, e^{-k_4 x - k_2 y}\) is constant.


Proof. The two axes are solution curves of (1) (\(x = 0\) gives \(dx/dt = 0\), \(y = 0\) gives \(dy/dt = 0\)), so a solution that starts in the open first quadrant stays in it and \(\ln x\), \(\ln y\) are defined. By the chain rule
\[
\frac{dV}{dt} = \left(k_4 - \frac{k_3}{x}\right)(k_1 x - k_2 x y) + \left(k_2 - \frac{k_1}{y}\right)(-k_3 y + k_4 x y)
= (k_4 x - k_3)(k_1 - k_2 y) + (k_2 y - k_1)(k_4 x - k_3) = 0. \qquad \blacksquare
\]






TipTheorem — Periodic orbits (general, for \(k_1, \ldots, k_4 > 0\))



Every solution of (1) that starts at a point \((x_0, y_0)\) with \(x_0, y_0 > 0\), other than the equilibrium \((x_e, y_e)\), is periodic: its orbit in the phase plane is a closed curve around \((x_e, y_e)\), traversed counterclockwise.


Why. The gradient of \(V\) is \((k_4 - k_3/x,\ k_2 - k_1/y)\), which vanishes only at \((x_e, y_e)\), and its Hessian \(\operatorname{diag}(k_3/x^2,\ k_1/y^2)\) is positive definite, so \(V\) is strictly convex on the quadrant with its only minimum at the equilibrium. Since \(V \to \infty\) as \(x\) or \(y\) tends to \(0\) or to \(\infty\), each level set \(V = V(x_0, y_0)\) above the minimum is a single closed curve around \((x_e, y_e)\). The solution stays on that curve, and the curve holds no equilibrium, so the solution keeps moving round it and returns to its starting point after a finite time \(T\). Below the equilibrium (\(y < y_e\)) the prey increase, so the motion is counterclockwise.






TipTheorem — Average populations (general)



For a periodic solution of (1) with period \(T\),
\[
\frac1T \int_0^T x(t)\,dt = \frac{k_3}{k_4} = x_e, \qquad \frac1T \int_0^T y(t)\,dt = \frac{k_1}{k_2} = y_e .
\tag{5}
\]


Proof. From (1), \(\dfrac{d}{dt}\ln y = -k_3 + k_4 x\). Integrating over one period, the left side gives \(\ln y(T) - \ln y(0) = 0\), so \(0 = -k_3 T + k_4 \int_0^T x\,dt\). The same argument with \(\dfrac{d}{dt}\ln x = k_1 - k_2 y\) gives the average of \(y\). \(\blacksquare\)
The period itself depends on the orbit. For small orbits around \((x_e, y_e)\) it approaches the linearised value \(2\pi/\sqrt{k_1 k_3}\) from (3); in Example 2 and Example 6 the computed periods of the larger orbits exceed it.

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
Predator-Prey Model
The study of interacting populations goes back to two independently published works by Alfred James Lotka (1880–1949) and Vito Volterra (1860–1940). Let \(x(t)\) be the number of prey (rabbits) and \(y(t)\) the number of predators (foxes). The prey have ample food and reproduce with birth rate \(c_1\) and death rate \(c_2\); successful hunting by the predators removes a further \(k_2\, y x\) prey per unit time, proportional to the number of encounters. Combining the three terms,
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = c_1 x - c_2 x - k_2\, y x = (c_1 - c_2)\,x - k_2\, x y,
\]
and the substitution \(k_1 = c_1 - c_2\) (the net growth rate of the prey) gives
\[
\frac{dx}{dt} = k_1 x - k_2 x y .
\]
The predators’ birth rate is proportional to their food supply, \(k_4 x\), and their death rate is \(k_3\), so
\[
\frac{dy}{dt} = -k_3 y + k_4 x y .
\]
These are the Lotka-Volterra equations (1). In this setting the equilibrium (2) is the pair of population sizes at which neither species changes, and (5) says that over each cycle the populations average exactly those sizes.

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
The Runge-Kutta Method

One equation
Mathews solves the equations with the classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method. For the initial value problem \(y' = f(t, y)\), \(y(a) = \alpha\), on \(a \le t \le b\), divide \([a, b]\) into \(m\) steps of length \(h = (b - a)/m\), set \(t_j = a + jh\) and \(y_0 = \alpha\), and compute






ImportantRunge-Kutta method of order 4



\[
\begin{aligned}
K_1 &= h\, f(t_j,\ y_j), \\
K_2 &= h\, f\!\left(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2},\ y_j + \tfrac{K_1}{2}\right), \\
K_3 &= h\, f\!\left(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2},\ y_j + \tfrac{K_2}{2}\right), \\
K_4 &= h\, f(t_j + h,\ y_j + K_3), \\
y_{j+1} &= y_j + \tfrac16\left(K_1 + 2K_2 + 2K_3 + K_4\right),
\end{aligned}
\qquad j = 0, 1, \ldots, m - 1.
\tag{6}
\]


Mathews names the four slopes \(k_1, \ldots, k_4\), the same letters as the model constants in (1); this page writes them as capitals. The result is a discrete set of points \((t_j, y_j)\) that approximate the solution, not a formula. For a smooth solution the error at a fixed \(t\) is \(O(h^4)\), so halving \(h\) divides it by about \(16\) (a general result for sufficiently smooth \(f\); Example 1 checks it). The Runge-Kutta method page treats the method in detail.


Systems of two equations
The method extends to a system
\[
x' = f_1(t, x, y),\quad x(a) = \alpha, \qquad y' = f_2(t, x, y),\quad y(a) = \beta, \qquad a \le t \le b,
\]
by applying (6) to the vector \(\mathbf{Z} = (x, y)\) and the vector function \(\mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z}) = \bigl(f_1(t, x, y),\ f_2(t, x, y)\bigr)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{K}_1 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j,\ \mathbf{Z}_j), &
\mathbf{K}_2 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\!\left(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2},\ \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac{\mathbf{K}_1}{2}\right), \\
\mathbf{K}_3 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\!\left(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2},\ \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac{\mathbf{K}_2}{2}\right), &
\mathbf{K}_4 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j + h,\ \mathbf{Z}_j + \mathbf{K}_3),
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} = \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac16\left(\mathbf{K}_1 + 2\mathbf{K}_2 + 2\mathbf{K}_3 + \mathbf{K}_4\right), \qquad \mathbf{Z}_0 = (\alpha, \beta).
\tag{7}
\]
This is the one-dimensional method in “vector form”: \(f\) is replaced by \(\mathbf{F}\), and both components of each \(\mathbf{K}_i\) are computed before the next one. A negative \(b\) (with \(a = 0\)) gives a negative \(h\) and integrates backward in time. Mathews’ subroutine returns only the points \(\mathbf{Z}_j\), which are joined by straight segments to draw the orbit.


Example 1 — A single equation, \(y' = t^2 - y\)
Problem. Solve \(y' = t^2 - y\), \(y(0) = 1\), over \([0, 10]\) with the Runge-Kutta method.
Only the text of this example’s solution page survives: the images holding Mathews’ program, output and graph are lost. Whether Mathews compared with the exact solution cannot be told from what survives; this page does. The equation is linear, and
\[
y(t) = t^2 - 2t + 2 - e^{-t}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
K_1 &= 0.2\,(0^2 - 1) = -0.2, \\
K_2 &= 0.2\,\bigl(0.1^2 - (1 - 0.1)\bigr) = -0.178, \\
K_3 &= 0.2\,\bigl(0.1^2 - (1 - 0.089)\bigr) = -0.1802, \\
K_4 &= 0.2\,\bigl(0.2^2 - (1 - 0.1802)\bigr) = -0.15596, \\
y_1 &= 1 + \tfrac16\bigl(-0.2 - 0.356 - 0.3604 - 0.15596\bigr) = 0.8212733,
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
section: Example 2 — The Lotka-Volterra system with \(k_1 = k_2 = k_3 = k_4 = 1\)
text:
Example 2 — The Lotka-Volterra system with \(k_1 = k_2 = k_3 = k_4 = 1\)
Problem. Solve
\[
x' = x - xy, \quad x(0) = 2, \qquad y' = -y + xy, \quad y(0) = 1,
\tag{8}
\]
with the Runge-Kutta method over (a) \(0 \le t \le 3.3\), (b) \(-3.3 \le t \le 0\), (c) \(0 \le t \le 6.6\). Does the solution form an orbit?
Here \(\mathbf{F}(t, x, y) = (x - xy,\ -y + xy)\), the equilibria are \((0, 0)\) and \((1, 1)\), and the conserved quantity (4) is \(V(x, y) = x - \ln x + y - \ln y\), with \(V(2, 1) = 3 - \ln 2 = 2.306853\). Mathews uses \(m = 50\) steps in (a) and (b) and \(m = 100\) in (c), so \(h = \pm 0.066\) throughout, and plots the orbits in the window \([0, 2] \times [0, 2]\).
Step 1 of (a) (\(h = 3.3/50 = 0.066\), \(\mathbf{Z}_0 = (2, 1)\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{K}_1 &= 0.066\,\mathbf{F}(2, 1) = (0,\ 0.066), \\
\mathbf{K}_2 &= 0.066\,\mathbf{F}(2,\ 1.033) = (-0.004356,\ 0.068178), \\
\mathbf{K}_3 &= 0.066\,\mathbf{F}(1.997822,\ 1.034089) = (-0.0044948,\ 0.0681012), \\
\mathbf{K}_4 &= 0.066\,\mathbf{F}(1.9955052,\ 1.0681012) = (-0.0089692,\ 0.0701778), \\
\mathbf{Z}_1 &= (2, 1) + \tfrac16\bigl(\mathbf{K}_1 + 2\mathbf{K}_2 + 2\mathbf{K}_3 + \mathbf{K}_4\bigr) = (1.9955549,\ 1.0681227).
\end{aligned}
\]
A reference solution (an adaptive eighth-order integrator with tolerance \(10^{-13}\)) gives \((1.9955549,\ 1.0681228)\) at \(t = 0.066\). The prey begin to fall and the predators to rise, since \(y_0 = 1\) sits exactly at the level where \(x' = 0\).

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
section: Example 3 — The orbit as a separable equation
text:
Example 3 — The orbit as a separable equation
Problem. For the system (8), combine the two differential equations into a separable first-order equation and solve it.
Step 1. In Leibniz notation, \(\dfrac{dx}{dt} = x - xy\) and \(\dfrac{dy}{dt} = -y + xy\). Divide the second by the first, using \(\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \dfrac{dy}{dx}\):
\[
\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-y + xy}{x - xy} = \frac{y\,(x - 1)}{x\,(1 - y)} .
\]
Step 2. Separate the variables:
\[
\frac{1 - y}{y}\,dy = \frac{x - 1}{x}\,dx .
\]
Step 3. Integrate both sides, writing the constant of integration as \(\ln c\):
\[
\ln y - y = x - \ln x + \ln c .
\]
Step 4. Collect the logarithms, \(\ln x + \ln y - x - y = \ln c\), and exponentiate:
\[
x\,y\,e^{-x-y} = c .
\]
Step 5. The curve passes through the initial point \((2, 1)\), so \(c = 2 \cdot 1 \cdot e^{-3} = 2/e^3 = 0.0995741\). The orbit is the curve
\[
x\,y\,e^{-x-y} = \frac{2}{e^3}.
\tag{9}
\]
Mathews graphs (9) with an implicit plot in the window \([0, 2] \times [0, 2]\); it is the closed loop of Example 2.
Verification. Equation (9) is (4) with every \(k_i = 1\): \(V(x, y) = x - \ln x + y - \ln y = -\ln\bigl(x y e^{-x-y}\bigr)\), so (9) says \(V(x, y) = 3 - \ln 2\). The general separation, with arbitrary \(k_i\), gives the constant \(x^{k_3} y^{k_1} e^{-k_4 x - k_2 y}\) of (4) in the same way.

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
section: Example 4 — The numerical and analytic solutions agree
text:
Example 4 — The numerical and analytic solutions agree
Problem. For the system (8), show that the numerical solution of Example 2 and the analytic solution of Example 3 agree. (Mathews’ statement says “the numerical solution in Example 3 and the analytic solution in Example 4”; the numerical solution is the one of Example 2 and the implicit curve the one of Example 3.)
Mathews places the Runge-Kutta orbit with \(m = 200\) steps over \([0,\ 6.6084827203]\) beside the implicit plot of (9), both in \([0, 2] \times [0, 2]\), and then draws one over the other, where the two curves coincide.
Verification. Substituting the \(201\) Runge-Kutta points into the left side of (9):
\[
\max_{0 \le j \le 200} \bigl|\, x_j y_j e^{-x_j - y_j} - 2/e^3 \bigr| = 1.4 \times 10^{-9},
\]
a relative deviation of \(1.4 \times 10^{-8}\). For the coarser runs of Example 2 the largest deviation is \(2.3 \times 10^{-8}\) (runs (a) and (c)) and \(8.3 \times 10^{-9}\) (run (b)). The numerical points lie on the analytic curve to far better than plotting accuracy.
Mathews also draws a contour plot of \(G(x, y) = x y e^{-x-y}\) over \([0, 2] \times [0, 2]\). Each level curve \(G = c\) with \(0 < c < e^{-2}\) is an orbit of (8); \(G\) takes its largest value \(e^{-2} = 0.135335\) at the equilibrium \((1, 1)\), and the orbit of Examples 2 and 3 is the level \(c = 2/e^3 = 0.0995741\).

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
Example 5 — Solving the orbit for \(y\)
Problem. For the system (8) the implicit solution is \(x y e^{-x-y} = 2/e^3\). Can \(y\) be solved as a function of \(x\)?
Step 1. Write (9) as \(y e^{-y} = \dfrac{2 e^{x-3}}{x}\), that is \((-y)\,e^{-y} = -\dfrac{2 e^{x-3}}{x}\). The equation \(w e^{w} = z\) is solved by the Lambert \(W\) function, \(w = W(z)\) (Mathematica’s ProductLog), so
\[
y = -W\!\left(-\frac{2e^{x-3}}{x}\right).
\tag{10}
\]
Step 2. For real \(w\), \(w e^w = z\) has real solutions only when \(z \ge -1/e\), and two of them when \(-1/e < z < 0\): the principal branch \(W_0(z) \in (-1, 0)\) and the lower branch \(W_{-1}(z) < -1\). Here \(z = -2e^{x-3}/x \ge -1/e\) exactly when \(x e^{-x} \ge 2/e^2\), that is for
\[
0.40638 \le x \le 2 .
\]
At both ends \(z = -1/e\) and \(W = -1\), so \(y = 1\): these are the leftmost and rightmost points \((0.40638, 1)\) and \((2, 1)\) of the orbit.
Step 3. Mathematica’s Solve returns the principal branch, \(y = -W_0\bigl(-2e^{x-3}/x\bigr)\), which Mathews plots for \(0.40638 \le x \le 2\). Since \(W_0 \in [-1, 0)\), this gives \(y \le 1\): the lower half of the orbit. Mathews concludes that only the lower half of the curve can be solved explicitly. In fact the upper half is the other branch, \(y = -W_{-1}\bigl(-2e^{x-3}/x\bigr) \ge 1\), which Solve does not return:

title: Lotka-Volterra Model
text:
Numerical Notes

Monitor the conserved quantity. Because \(V\) in (4) is constant along exact solutions, the change of \(V\) along the computed points detects drift off the orbit (though not timing error along it) without knowing the exact solution.
The Runge-Kutta method does not conserve \(V\). Over many periods the computed orbit slowly drifts off its level curve. For the system (8) from \((2, 1)\) with \(h = 0.066\), the change in \(V\) after \(100\), \(1001\) and \(10013\) steps (about \(1\), \(10\) and \(100\) periods) is \(-1.9 \times 10^{-8}\), \(-2.1 \times 10^{-7}\) and \(-2.1 \times 10^{-6}\), growing in proportion to the number of periods.
Stopping at a fixed time does not close the curve. A computed orbit closes only if the time interval is a whole number of periods. The gaps in Example 2 and the overlaps in its aside come from the interval length, not from the Runge-Kutta error.

title: Pendulum
text:
← Numerical Methods
Source inspiration: (Mathew 2000-2019).

title: Pendulum
text:
Description
A simple pendulum is a point mass \(m\) on a rigid rod of length \(l\) and negligible weight, swinging about a fixed pivot. If \(\theta(t)\) is the angle of the rod measured from the downward vertical, Newton’s second law for rotation gives the nonlinear pendulum equation
\[
\theta'' + \frac{g}{l}\sin\theta = 0 .
\]
For small swings \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\), and the equation becomes the linear equation of simple harmonic motion, whose solutions are sines and cosines with period \(2\pi\sqrt{l/g}\) whatever the amplitude. The nonlinear equation has no solution in elementary functions, so Mathews solves it numerically: the substitution \(y = x'\) turns the second-order equation \(x'' = f(t, x, x')\) into the first-order system \(x' = y\), \(y' = f(t, x, y)\), and the classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method is applied to that system in vector form, \(\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} = \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac16(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4)\) with \(\mathbf{Z}_j = (x_j, y_j)\). With a damping term \(\tfrac{1}{10}x'\) added, the module compares the linear and the nonlinear model in the \((t, x)\) plane (Examples 1 to 4).
The second half of the module draws phase portraits: curves \((x(t), y(t))\) in the plane of angle and angular velocity. Without damping (Examples 5 and 6) the energy \(E = \tfrac12 y^2 + \tfrac{g}{l}(1 - \cos x)\) is constant along every solution, so small swings are closed loops around the rest positions \(x = 2k\pi\), and swings with enough energy run over the top, round and round the pivot. With damping (Example 7) the energy decreases, the loops become spirals, and every curve of Example 7 tends to rest at one of the points \((2k\pi, 0)\). Every number on this page was recomputed: the Runge-Kutta runs with Mathews’ step counts (\(m = 100\); for Examples 5 and 6, whose inputs are lost, the \(m = 100\) of his Example 7), and the reference solutions with an adaptive eighth-order integrator at a tolerance of \(10^{-13}\).

title: Pendulum
text:
Animations
Each animation below draws Runge-Kutta solutions (8) of the pendulum three ways at once: as a swinging pendulum, a rod and a bob at the computed angle \(x_j\) measured from the downward vertical; as a curve in the phase plane of angle \(x\) and angular velocity \(y = x'\), with the computed points \(\mathbf{Z}_j\) joined by straight segments as in Mathews’ graphs; and against time. The gray dashed curve in the phase plane is the level \(E = 2\omega_0^2\) of the energy, the energy of the pendulum at rest at the top. Every curve is computed with \(m = 100\) steps, Mathews’ step count (for Examples 5 and 6, whose inputs are lost, the \(m = 100\) of his Example 7). In Case 1 and in the first part of Case 3 the frames advance by steps; where several curves with different step sizes move together, the frames advance by time, and each curve shows its points with \(t_j \le t\).
Mathews’ module links no animation, and his animation archive has none for the pendulum, so all three animations are new, with no Mathews original. Case 1 animates Examples 1, 3 and 4, Case 2 the phase portrait of Example 6 with the curves this page chose, and Case 3 all fourteen curves of Example 7 with Mathews’ starting points, time intervals, plot windows and colours. Not animated are the analytic solution of Example 2, which differs from the Runge-Kutta values of Case 1 by less than \(10^{-3}\) at every grid point and could not be told apart from them, together with Example 1’s first step, error table and step-halving check; Example 5, whose portrait is Example 6’s with \(y\) divided by \(\sqrt2\) and time multiplied by \(\sqrt2\) (Example 6, Step 1); and the separatrix runs of Examples 5 and 6, which are drawn only as the dashed level curve.

title: Pendulum
text:
The Pendulum Equation

The nonlinear pendulum
The torque of gravity about the pivot is
\[
\tau = -m g l \sin\theta,
\tag{1}
\]
where \(\theta\) is the angle of the rod measured downward from the vertical; the minus sign says the torque turns the mass back toward \(\theta = 0\). The moment of inertia of the point mass is \(I = m l^2\), and Newton’s second law for rotation, \(\tau = I\alpha\) with angular acceleration \(\alpha = \theta''\), gives
\[
\tau = I \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}.
\tag{2}
\]
Equating (1) and (2):






ImportantThe nonlinear pendulum equation



\[
\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{m g l}{I}\sin\theta = 0,
\qquad\text{and with } I = m l^2:\qquad
\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{g}{l}\sin\theta = 0 .
\tag{3}
\]


The mass cancels: the motion depends only on \(g/l\).


The linear pendulum
If the angle stays small, the approximation \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\) in (3) gives the familiar linear equation of simple harmonic motion,
\[
\frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} + \frac{m g l}{I}\,\theta = 0 .
\tag{4}
\]
With \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{m g l / I} = \sqrt{g/l}\) its general solution is
\[
\theta(t) = a_1 \cos(\omega_0 t) + a_2 \sin(\omega_0 t),
\tag{5}
\]
which has period \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{I/(g l m)} = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}\). Written with a phase shift, the solution is
\[
\theta(t) = A \cos(\omega_0 t + \delta).
\tag{6}
\]






WarningThe linear period does not depend on the amplitude; the nonlinear one does



In (5) the period \(2\pi/\omega_0\) is the same for every swing. For the nonlinear equation (3) with amplitude \(\theta_{\max} < \pi\) the period is (a general result, derived from the energy below)
\[
T = \frac{4}{\omega_0} K(k), \qquad k = \sin\frac{\theta_{\max}}{2}, \qquad K(k) = \int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{d\phi}{\sqrt{1 - k^2 \sin^2\phi}},
\]
and \(K(k)\) grows from \(\pi/2\) at \(k = 0\) to \(\infty\) as \(k \to 1\). A swing to \(29°\) takes \(1.6\%\) longer than the linear period, a swing to \(60°\) \(7.3\%\) longer, and a swing to \(143.6°\) \(65\%\) longer (Example 5).




Energy and the phase plane
With \(x = \theta\) and \(y = \theta'\), equation (3) is the system \(x' = y\), \(y' = -\omega_0^2 \sin x\). A solution traced in the \(xy\)-plane is a phase curve, and a set of phase curves is a phase portrait. Mathews puts the angle \(x\) on the horizontal axis and the angular velocity \(y\) on the vertical axis; since \(x\) increases where \(y > 0\), curves are traversed clockwise.






NoteDefinition — Energy of the pendulum



For \(x'' + c\,x' + \omega_0^2 \sin x = 0\) with \(c \ge 0\), the energy (per unit \(m l^2\)) of the state \((x, y) = (x, x')\) is
\[
E(x, y) = \tfrac12 y^2 + \omega_0^2 (1 - \cos x),
\]
kinetic energy plus potential energy, with \(E = 0\) at rest at the bottom and \(E = 2\omega_0^2\) at rest at the top.








TipTheorem — Energy is conserved without damping and decreases with damping



Along any solution of \(x' = y\), \(y' = -c\,y - \omega_0^2 \sin x\),
\[
\frac{d}{dt} E\bigl(x(t), y(t)\bigr) = y\,y' + \omega_0^2 \sin x \; x' = -c\, y^2 .
\]
So for \(c = 0\) every phase curve lies on a level curve \(E = E_0\), and for \(c > 0\) the energy never increases.


For \(c = 0\) the level curves give the whole picture. The equilibria are \((k\pi, 0)\). If \(E_0 < 2\omega_0^2\) and the start has \(|x_0| < \pi\), the pendulum swings back and forth, \(|x|\) never reaches \(\pi\), and the phase curve is a closed loop around \((0, 0)\) (and, since the equation is \(2\pi\)-periodic in \(x\), the same loops appear around every \((2k\pi, 0)\)). If \(E_0 > 2\omega_0^2\), \(y\) never vanishes and the pendulum runs over the top and round the pivot forever, \(y = \pm\sqrt{2E_0 - 2\omega_0^2(1-\cos x)}\). The level \(E_0 = 2\omega_0^2\) is the separatrix \(y = \pm 2\omega_0 \cos(x/2)\), which separates the two kinds of motion: a pendulum started on it at the bottom with speed exactly \(2\omega_0\) creeps toward the top \((\pi, 0)\) and never reaches it in finite time. Starting at \(x = 0\) with speed \(y_0\), the energy is \(E_0 = \tfrac12 y_0^2\), so the swing is a closed loop when \(y_0 < 2\omega_0\), a rotation when \(y_0 > 2\omega_0\), and the modulus in the period formula is \(k = y_0/(2\omega_0)\).
For \(c > 0\) the energy leaks away. The rest positions at the bottom, \((2k\pi, 0)\), attract nearby curves: there the linearised equation is \(u'' + c\,u' + \omega_0^2 u = 0\), and when \(c < 2\omega_0\) (as in Example 7, where \(c = \tfrac{1}{10}\) and \(2\omega_0 = 2.83\)) its solutions oscillate as they decay, so the curves spiral in. The tops \(((2k+1)\pi, 0)\) are saddle points. A curve with enough energy still runs over one or more tops, but each pass costs energy, and once the energy is below \(2\omega_0^2\) the curve is trapped in one well between two tops and tends to the rest position at its bottom.

title: Pendulum
text:
Runge-Kutta Method for Second-Order Equations
To approximate the solution of the initial value problem
\[
x'' = f(t, x, x'), \qquad x(a) = \alpha, \qquad x'(a) = \beta, \qquad a \le t \le b,
\]
substitute \(y = x'\). The second-order problem becomes the first-order system
\[
x' = y, \qquad y' = f(t, x, y), \qquad x(a) = \alpha, \quad y(a) = \beta .
\tag{7}
\]
More generally, the module’s two-dimensional solver handles any system \(x' = f_1(t, x, y)\), \(y' = f_2(t, x, y)\) with \(x(a) = \alpha\), \(y(a) = \beta\). It is the one-dimensional Runge-Kutta method in vector form, with the scalar \(f\) replaced by \(\mathbf{F}(t, \mathbf{Z}) = \bigl(f_1(t, x, y), f_2(t, x, y)\bigr)\), \(\mathbf{Z} = (x, y)\).






NoteAlgorithm — Runge-Kutta method in two dimensions (Mathews’ Runge2D)



Given \(a\), \(b\), \(\mathbf{Z}_0 = (\alpha, \beta)\) and a number of steps \(m\), set \(h = (b - a)/m\) and \(t_j = a + j h\). For \(j = 0, 1, \ldots, m - 1\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{k}_1 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j, \mathbf{Z}_j), &
\mathbf{k}_2 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2}, \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac12 \mathbf{k}_1\bigr), \\
\mathbf{k}_3 &= h\,\mathbf{F}\bigl(t_j + \tfrac{h}{2}, \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac12 \mathbf{k}_2\bigr), &
\mathbf{k}_4 &= h\,\mathbf{F}(t_j + h, \mathbf{Z}_j + \mathbf{k}_3),
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\mathbf{Z}_{j+1} = \mathbf{Z}_j + \tfrac16\bigl(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4\bigr).
\tag{8}
\]
The output is the list of points \(\mathbf{Z}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{Z}_m\). The first coordinates \(x_j\) approximate the solution \(x(t_j)\) of the second-order problem; plotting \((t_j, x_j)\) gives the solution curve, and plotting \((x_j, y_j)\) gives the phase curve.


The global error of the method is \(O(h^4)\) for a smooth \(\mathbf{F}\) (a general result), so halving the step should divide the error by about \(16\); Example 1 checks this.

title: Pendulum
text:
Example 1 — Runge-Kutta solution of \(x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2x = 0\)
Solve
\[
x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2x = 0, \qquad x(0) = 1, \qquad x'(0) = 2,
\]
over \([0, 20]\) with the Runge-Kutta method. This is a linear pendulum (or a mass on a spring) with \(\omega_0^2 = 2\) and a light damping term.
Step 1: Write the equation as \(x'' = f(t, x, x')\) with
\[
f(t, x, x') = -\tfrac{1}{10}x' - 2x .
\]
Step 2: With \(y = x'\) the system (7) is
\[
x' = y, \qquad y' = -\tfrac{1}{10}y - 2x, \qquad x(0) = 1, \quad y(0) = 2,
\qquad \mathbf{F}(t, (x, y)) = \bigl(y,\ -2x - \tfrac{y}{10}\bigr).
\]
Step 3: Mathews takes \(m = 100\) steps on \([0, 20]\), so \(h = 0.2\). The first step, from \(\mathbf{Z}_0 = (1, 2)\), is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{k}_1 &= 0.2\,\mathbf{F}(0, (1, 2)) = (0.4,\ -0.44), \\
\mathbf{k}_2 &= 0.2\,\mathbf{F}(0.1, (1.2, 1.78)) = (0.356,\ -0.5156), \\
\mathbf{k}_3 &= 0.2\,\mathbf{F}(0.1, (1.178, 1.7422)) = (0.34844,\ -0.506044), \\
\mathbf{k}_4 &= 0.2\,\mathbf{F}(0.2, (1.34844, 1.493956)) = (0.2987912,\ -0.56925512),
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
\mathbf{Z}_1 = (1, 2) + \tfrac16(\mathbf{k}_1 + 2\mathbf{k}_2 + 2\mathbf{k}_3 + \mathbf{k}_4) = (1.3512785,\ 1.4912428).
\]
The exact values (from Example 2) are \(x(0.2) = 1.3512965\) and \(x'(0.2) = 1.4912143\), so the first step is off by \(-1.8 \times 10^{-5}\) in \(x\).
Step 4: The remaining 99 steps are the same computation. The solution we want is the first coordinate \(x_j\); Mathews plots the points \((t_j, x_j)\) joined by line segments. The computed \(x_j\) range from \(-1.5140\) to \(1.6976\).

title: Pendulum
text:
Example 2 — The analytic solution of \(x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2x = 0\)
Find the analytic solution of the initial value problem of Example 1,
\[
x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2x = 0, \qquad x(0) = 1, \qquad x'(0) = 2,
\]
and plot it over \([0, 20]\).
Step 1: The characteristic equation \(r^2 + \tfrac{1}{10} r + 2 = 0\) has the complex roots
\[
r = -\frac{1}{20} \pm \frac{\sqrt{799}}{20}\, i .
\]
Mathematica’s DSolve returns the solution in terms of the complex exponentials \(e^{\frac{1}{20}(-1 \pm i\sqrt{799})t}\), divided by \(1598\).
Step 2: In terms of real functions, with \(\omega = \sqrt{799}/20 = 1.413329\),
\[
x(t) = e^{-t/20}\cos\!\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt{799}}{20}\,t\Bigr) + \frac{41}{\sqrt{799}}\, e^{-t/20}\sin\!\Bigl(\frac{\sqrt{799}}{20}\,t\Bigr).
\]
Step 3: In the phase-shift form (6), with a decaying amplitude,
\[
x(t) = A\, e^{-t/20} \cos(\omega t + \delta), \qquad A = \sqrt{\tfrac{2480}{799}} = 1.761783, \qquad \delta = -\arctan\frac{41}{\sqrt{799}} = -0.967200 .
\]
The solution oscillates with the constant quasi-period \(2\pi/\omega = 4.445662\) inside the envelope \(\pm A e^{-t/20}\). On \([0, 20]\) its largest value is \(1.703585\) at \(t = 0.6593\) and its smallest is \(-1.524389\) at \(t = 2.8822\).
Verification: Substituting \(x(t)\) into the equation gives \(x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2x = 0\) identically, \(x(0) = 1\), and \(x'(0) = -\tfrac{1}{20} + \tfrac{41}{\sqrt{799}}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt{799}}{20} = 2\). The phase form agrees: \(A\cos\delta = 1\) and \(-A\sin\delta = 41/\sqrt{799} = 1.450476\).

title: Pendulum
text:
Example 3 — The nonlinear pendulum \(x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2\sin x = 0\)
Solve
\[
x'' + \tfrac{1}{10}x' + 2\sin x = 0, \qquad x(0) = 1, \qquad x'(0) = 2,
\]
the damped nonlinear pendulum with \(g/l = 2\) and the same damping and starting values as Example 1.
Step 1: \(f(t, x, x') = -\tfrac{1}{10}x' - 2\sin x\), so the system is
\[
x' = y, \qquad y' = -\tfrac{1}{10}y - 2\sin x, \qquad x(0) = 1, \quad y(0) = 2 .
\]
Step 2: As in Example 1, Mathews runs the Runge-Kutta method on \([0, 20]\) with \(m = 100\) steps, \(h = 0.2\), and plots \((t_j, x_j)\). The computed \(x_j\) range from \(-1.6613\) to \(1.9766\).
Step 3: The energy at the start is \(E_0 = \tfrac12 \cdot 2^2 + 2(1 - \cos 1) = 2.919395\), less than the energy \(2\omega_0^2 = 4\) needed to reach the top, and by the theorem above the energy can only decrease. So the pendulum swings back and forth and never goes over the top: the largest angle, \(x = 1.976621\) at \(t = 0.9963\), is \(113.25°\), below \(\pi\). By \(t = 20\) the energy has fallen to \(0.448391\).

title: Pendulum
text:
Phase Portraits
The pendulum can also be explored with phase curves in the phase plane. Mathews solves the system (7) with the two-dimensional Runge-Kutta method (8) and plots the points \((x_j, y_j)\), joined by line segments, for several starting points; together the curves form a phase portrait that shows the features of the nonlinear pendulum that a graph of \(x(t)\) hides.

title: Pendulum
section: Example 5 — The undamped pendulum with \(g = 32\) and \(l = 32\)
text:
Example 5 — The undamped pendulum with \(g = 32\) and \(l = 32\)
Solve \(x'' + \dfrac{g}{l}\sin x = 0\) by the Runge-Kutta method applied to the system
\[
x' = y, \qquad y' = -\frac{g}{l}\sin x,
\]
with \(g = 32\) and \(l = 32\), so that \(g/l = 1\) and \(\omega_0 = 1\): \(x'' + \sin x = 0\). The linear period is \(2\pi\sqrt{l/g} = 2\pi = 6.283185\), the separatrix speed at the bottom is \(2\omega_0 = 2\), and the energy at the top is \(2\omega_0^2 = 2\).

Example 6 — The undamped pendulum \(x'' + 2\sin x = 0\)
Solve \(x'' + 2\sin x = 0\) by the Runge-Kutta method applied to the system
\[
x' = y, \qquad y' = -2\sin x .
\]
Here \(\omega_0 = \sqrt2 = 1.414214\), the linear period is \(2\pi/\sqrt2 = 4.442883\), the separatrix speed at the bottom is \(2\sqrt2 = 2.828427\), and the energy at the top is \(4\). Mathews’ text for this example repeats that of Example 5 (four closed loops around the origin, two rotations each way, loops around two further centres), and the archive has again lost his input and figures. For the rotations they give \(\tfrac52\sqrt2\) and \(3\sqrt2\), his speeds in Example 7.
Step 1 — scaling. If \(x(t)\) solves \(x'' + \sin x = 0\), then \(X(t) = x(\sqrt2\,t)\) solves \(X'' + 2\sin X = 0\), with \(X'(t) = \sqrt2\, x'(\sqrt2\, t)\). So every phase curve of Example 6 is a phase curve of Example 5 stretched by \(\sqrt2\) in the \(y\) direction, traversed in \(1/\sqrt2\) of the time. Mathews’ words “turn twice” and “turn three [times]” match these counts.
Step 3 — turning in the opposite direction (curves 7 and 8). With the same intervals and steps, curves 7′ and 8′ are exactly curves 5 and 6 reflected through the point \((3\pi, 0)\) (the system is unchanged by \((x, y) \to (6\pi - x, -y)\)), and the computed points agree with the reflected ones to \(2 \times 10^{-13}\).
Verification: Each Runge-Kutta curve was compared at \(t = b\) with the reference solution. For curves 1 to 4 and 9 to 12 the difference is at most \(1.6 \times 10^{-5}\); for the curves that go over the tops it is larger, \(2.2 \times 10^{-4}\) (curve 8), \(6.9 \times 10^{-4}\) (curve 7), \(2.2 \times 10^{-3}\) (curves 6 and 8′) and \(1.0 \times 10^{-2}\) (curves 5 and 7′); the end points in the table are given to three decimals for these curves. In all of them the energy at \(t = b\) is below its starting value, as the theorem requires.

title: Power method
