Case 1 rebuilds Mathews’ animation Heunaa.gif, a step-refinement sweep, drawn as on the Euler’s Method page: each frame is a complete run with \(m\) subintervals (\(h=5/m\)), for the values of \(m\) in Mathews’ animation, drawn over a gray reference solution (fixed-step RK4 with 50 000 steps) and labelled with the computed \(y(5)\), its error at \(t=5\) and the largest error at any grid point of the run. A light red band marks where \(h\,|\partial f/\partial y|\), evaluated along the reference solution rather than the plotted run, exceeds the method’s stability limit 2. Case 2 is new, with no Mathews original: it plots the errors of Euler’s method, Mathews’ modified Euler (midpoint) method and Heun’s method against \(h\) on log-log axes.
Legacy archive note: Mathews’ Heunaa.gif is in the archive (36 frames showing 21 runs), and every \(y(5)\) it prints agrees with the runs here when rounded to seven decimals; the module’s Example 11 links to it. Not animated: the module’s Examples 1–10, whose equations were images the archive lost (Examples 1–4 and 5–8 compare Heun’s errors with 25 and 50, and with 50 and 100, subintervals, and Examples 9–10 follow a solution with a vertical asymptote that Heun’s method steps past), and Examples 9.6 and 9.7 of the textbook section the module links as its proof, which solve \(y' = (t - y)/2\) on \([0, 3]\).
Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

Case 1 — Heun step-refinement sweep, \(y' = 1 - t\sqrt[3]{y}\), \(y(0)=1\), \(m = 12\) to \(150\) subintervals
Behavior: The frames use the 21 values of Mathews’ animation, \(m = 12, 14, 16, 18, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, 48, 52, 56, 60, 70, 80, 90, 100, 120, 150\) (the values of his modified Euler animation too), and the reference solution of the Euler page, which rises from \(y(0)=1\) to about \(1.4498\) near \(t=0.88\) and decays to \(y(5)=0.0081199\). No computed value \(y_n\) of any run is negative. For \(m=12\) to \(60\) the run falls to a minimum and then turns upward before \(t=5\), rising from that minimum by \(1.17\) at \(m=12\) and \(0.071\) at \(m=60\) and ending at \(y(5)\approx1.386\) and \(0.0832\); at \(m=36\), \(40\) and \(48\) to \(60\) the rise is interrupted by one or two downward steps of at most \(0.036\). At \(m=70\) the upturn is only \(0.0070\), too small to see at this scale, although \(y(5)\approx0.0171\) is about twice the reference value, and from \(m=80\) on the runs decrease steadily after their peak. For \(m=12\) to \(60\) some predictions \(p_{n+1}\) are negative (in this sweep none are from \(m=70\) on), so those frames depend on the real cube root.
The cause is stability. For \(m\le103\) (here \(m=12\) to \(100\)), \(h\,|\partial f/\partial y|\) along the reference solution exceeds \(2\) before \(t=5\) (the shaded region), from \(t\approx2.99\) at \(m=12\) to \(t\approx4.95\) at \(m=100\), and for each of these \(m\) the error at \(t=5\) is larger than just before the onset; for \(m=120\) and \(150\) it stays below \(2\) up to \(t=5\). Unlike Euler’s factor \(1+z\), which is below \(-1\) beyond the limit, Heun’s factor \(1+z+z^2/2\) is at least \(1/2\) for every real \(z\), so beyond the limit it is greater than \(1\) and positive: while the error is small compared with the solution, each step multiplies it by a factor greater than 1 without changing its sign. The coarse runs therefore turn upward and stay above the reference solution instead of swinging from one side of it to the other as Euler’s coarse runs do: for every \(m\) from \(12\) to \(100\) the error is positive at every grid point from the onset to \(t=5\). For \(m=12\) to \(20\) the turn comes at \(t=2.81\) to \(3.06\), just before the shaded region, where these runs are already \(15\%\) to \(77\%\) above the reference solution.
The error at \(t=5\) falls at every refinement in the sweep, from \(+1.4\) at \(m=12\) to \(+3.7\times10^{-6}\) at \(m=150\), where \(y(5)\approx0.0081236\), the value Mathews prints. For \(m=12\) to \(70\) the largest error of the run is at \(t=5\) or, at \(m=52\) and \(60\), one step before it. From \(m=80\) on it lies between \(t=3.08\) and \(3.12\), and the damping late in the run makes the error at \(t=5\) \(1.9\) to \(89\) times smaller than it: \(1.3\times10^{-3}\) against \(6.9\times10^{-4}\) at \(m=80\), and \(3.3\times10^{-4}\) against \(3.7\times10^{-6}\) at \(m=150\). From \(m=80\) to \(150\) that largest error falls by a factor of \(3.96\), close to the \((150/80)^2\approx3.5\) of a second-order method. At \(m=150\) it is about 69 times smaller than Euler’s \(2.2\times10^{-2}\) and about twice the modified Euler’s \(1.6\times10^{-4}\), while the error at \(t=5\) is about twice that of either.

text:

title: Big “O” Truncation Error
text:
Description
Most numerical methods have a step size \(h\) or an index \(n\), and their error vanishes as \(h \to 0\) or \(n \to \infty\). Big “O” notation says how fast, by comparing the error with a simple function such as \(h^p\) or \(1/n\).






ImportantBig “O” (Mathews’ definitions)



A function satisfies \(f(h) = O(g(h))\) if there are constants \(C > 0\) and \(\delta > 0\) such that \[
|f(h)| \le C\,|g(h)| \quad \text{whenever } 0 \le |h| \le \delta .
\] A sequence satisfies \(\{x_n\} = O(\{y_n\})\) if there are \(C > 0\) and \(N\) such that \[
|x_n| \le C\,|y_n| \quad \text{whenever } n \ge N .
\] If \(|f(h) - p(h)| \le M\,|h|^n\) for a constant \(M\) and all sufficiently small \(h\), then \(p(h)\) approximates \(f(h)\) with order of approximation \(O(h^n)\): \[
f(h) = p(h) + O(h^n).
\]


These describe the limit only: the inequality need hold only near \(h = 0\) or for \(n \ge N\), and the constants are not part of the notation. Mathews’ first two examples find them: for \(|h| \le 1\), \(|h^4 + 2h^5| \le |h|^4 + 2|h|^5 \le 3|h|^3\), so \(h^4 + 2h^5 = O(h^3)\) with \(C = 3\), \(\delta = 1\); and \((n^2-1)/n^3 \le 1/n\) for every \(n \ge 1\), so \(\{(n^2-1)/n^3\} = O(\{1/n\})\) with \(C = 1\), \(N = 1\).
As \(h \to 0\), orders combine by Mathews’ rules: \[
O(h^p) + O(h^p) = O(h^p), \qquad O(h^p) + O(h^q) = O(h^{\min\{p,q\}}), \qquad O(h^p)\,O(h^q) = O(h^{p+q}),
\] and \(c\,O(h^p) = O(h^p)\) for a constant \(c\). So if \(p\) and \(q\) are polynomials with \(f(h) = p(h) + O(h^n)\) and \(g(h) = q(h) + O(h^m)\), then \(p + q\) and \(pq\) approximate \(f + g\) and \(fg\) with order \(O(h^{\min\{m,n\}})\), and \(p/q\) approximates \(f/g\) with the same order provided \(q(0) \ne 0\). (Mathews’ condition, \(g(h) \ne 0\) and \(q(h) \ne 0\), is not enough if it is required only for \(h \ne 0\): with \(f = p = 1\), \(q = h\), \(g = h + h^2\), \(p/q - f/g \to 1\).) His Example 4 combines two Maclaurin expansions: \[
e^h = 1 + h + \tfrac{h^2}{2} + \tfrac{h^3}{6} + O(h^4), \qquad \cos h = 1 - \tfrac{h^2}{2} + \tfrac{h^4}{24} + O(h^6),
\] \[
e^h + \cos h = 2 + h + \tfrac{h^3}{6} + O(h^4), \qquad e^h \cos h = 1 + h - \tfrac{h^3}{3} + O(h^4), \qquad \frac{e^h}{\cos h} = 1 + h + h^2 + \tfrac{2h^3}{3} + O(h^4).
\]
Big “O” is only an upper bound. In general, if the error is \(E(h) = K h^p + O(h^{p+1})\) with \(K \ne 0\), then \(|E(h)|/h^p\) tends to \(|K|\) and halving \(h\) divides the error by about \(2^p\) once \(h\) is small (Case 1 shows both for the Taylor polynomials of \(e^h\)). For the sum above, \(E(h) = e^h + \cos h - (2 + h + h^3/6)\) has leading term \(h^4/12\):

Big “O” says nothing about a fixed \(h\), where the constants and the size of \(h\) decide which error is smaller. Mathews’ Example 3 takes the Taylor polynomials \(P_3(h) = h - h^3/6\) and \(P_5(h) = P_3(h) + h^5/120\) of \(\sin h\), with errors \(O(h^5)\) and \(O(h^7)\); at \(h = 7\) the higher-order \(P_5\) has error 89.2, against 50.8 for \(P_3\). Roundoff also stops the trend: the \(O(h^2)\) central difference \((e^h - e^{-h})/(2h)\) for the derivative of \(e^x\) at 0 has error \(1.7\times10^{-9}\) at \(h = 10^{-4}\) in double precision, but about \(6\times10^{-9}\) at \(h = 10^{-8}\).
By Taylor’s theorem, the degree-\(n\) Taylor polynomial \(T_n\) of Maclaurin and Taylor Series leaves a remainder \(O(h^{n+1})\) when \(f \in C^{n+1}\). Other pages state errors this way: the Trapezoidal Rule and Simpson’s Rule have errors \(O(h^2)\) and \(O(h^4)\) for smooth integrands, Euler’s Method has global error \(O(h)\), and Numerical Differentiation uses the central difference above.

P_1(h) = 1 + h, \qquad P_2(h) = 1 + h + \tfrac{h^2}{2}, \qquad P_3(h) = 1 + h + \tfrac{h^2}{2} + \tfrac{h^3}{6},

From one frame to the next \(h\) halves, from \(h = 1\) down to \(h = 2^{-10} = 1/1024\), and every curve gains a point; the newest point is the large marker, so it moves left, and the last frame is held. The labels give, for the newest \(h\), each error, the factor \(E(2h)/E(h)\) by which the last halving divided it, and the ratio. The errors are computed in 256-bit BigFloat arithmetic (about 77 significant digits): in double precision, \(e^h - P_3(h)\) loses digits to cancellation, and at \(h = 2^{-10}\) it would come out as \(3.775\times10^{-14}\) instead of \(3.790\times10^{-14}\).

title: Lin-Bairstow Method
text:

title: Lin-Bairstow Method
text:
Description
The Lin-Bairstow method finds the roots of a real polynomial \(P(x) = a_n x^n + \cdots + a_1 x + a_0\) two at a time, by finding a quadratic factor \(x^2 - rx - s\). It uses only real arithmetic, yet finds complex-conjugate pairs of roots as well as real ones.
Dividing \(P(x)\) by \(x^2 - rx - s\) leaves a quotient \(Q(x)\) and a remainder,
\[
P(x) = (x^2 - rx - s)\,Q(x) + b_1 (x - r) + b_0, \qquad Q(x) = b_n x^{n-2} + \cdots + b_3 x + b_2 ,
\]
where quadratic synthetic division computes the \(b\)’s, and the same recursion applied to the \(b\)’s gives the \(c\)’s:
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_n &= a_n, & b_{n-1} &= a_{n-1} + r\,b_n, & b_k &= a_k + r\,b_{k+1} + s\,b_{k+2} \quad (k = n-2, \ldots, 1, 0), \\
c_n &= b_n, & c_{n-1} &= b_{n-1} + r\,c_n, & c_k &= b_k + r\,c_{k+1} + s\,c_{k+2} \quad (k = n-2, \ldots, 2, 1).
\end{aligned}
\]
The quadratic is a factor exactly when \(b_0 = b_1 = 0\), and the method is Newton’s method on these two equations in \(r\) and \(s\). The \(c\)’s are the partial derivatives (\(\partial b_0/\partial r = c_1\), \(\partial b_0/\partial s = \partial b_1/\partial r = c_2\), \(\partial b_1/\partial s = c_3\)), so each step evaluates them at \((r_j, s_j)\) and solves, by Cramer’s rule in Mathews’ module,
\[
\begin{pmatrix} c_1 & c_2 \\ c_2 & c_3 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} \Delta r \\ \Delta s \end{pmatrix}
= -\begin{pmatrix} b_0 \\ b_1 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad r_{j+1} = r_j + \Delta r, \quad s_{j+1} = s_j + \Delta s .
\]
The method needs degree \(n \ge 3\), a starting guess \((r_0, s_0)\), and \(c_1 c_3 - c_2^2 \neq 0\) at every iterate. Real starts keep the iterates real, and a real polynomial always has a real quadratic factor. Mathews suggests \(r_0 = -a_1/a_2\), \(s_0 = -a_0/a_2\) (if \(a_2 \neq 0\)), from \(P(x) \approx a_2 x^2 + a_1 x + a_0\) near \(x = 0\).
In general, Newton’s method for a smooth system converges quadratically from close enough starts when its Jacobian is nonsingular at the solution. Here that holds exactly when \(x^2 - rx - s\) and \(Q(x)\) have no common root, as when every root of \(P\) is simple. When they share one, convergence can drop to linear: for \(P(x) = (x^2 + 1)^2\) from \((0.1, -1.2)\), the error ratio tends to \(1/2\).
For Mathews’ Example 4 (Case 1), \(P(x) = x^4 + x^3 + 3x^2 + 4x + 6\) from \((r_0, s_0) = (-2.1, -1.9)\), the iterates converge to \(x^2 + 2x + 2\), with roots \(-1 \pm i\), and \(Q(x) = x^2 - x + 3\) gives \(\tfrac12 \pm \tfrac{\sqrt{11}}{2} i\). Quadratic synthetic division extends the division by \(x - c\) of Horner’s Method, the iteration is two-variable Newton-Raphson as in Nonlinear Systems, Graeffe’s Method is another method made for polynomials, and Muller’s Method can also reach complex roots, using complex arithmetic.

title: Lin-Bairstow Method
text:
Animations
Mathews made no animation for the Lin-Bairstow method, so both animations below are new, with no Mathews original. Most frames show one Lin-Bairstow step; Case 2 also has a frame for each deflation. In the full-scale complex-plane panels (Case 1’s top right and Case 2), red dots are the two roots of the current trial factor \(x^2 - r_j x - s_j\) (Case 2 also leaves small faded dots at the roots from earlier steps); the method works only with the real numbers \(r_j\) and \(s_j\), and the roots are drawn (by the quadratic formula) only to show where the factor is heading. Open circles in those panels mark the roots of \(P\); in Case 1’s two zoom panels (top left and bottom left), an open circle marks the previous iterate instead. Case 1 follows a single factor closely, zooming in as the steps shrink; Case 2 repeats the method on the quotients until every root of a quintic is found. Mathews’ Examples 1–3, which divide the quintic once by \(x^2 + 2x - 3\) (by formula, by tableau and in vector form), are not animated as such, since each is one division rather than an iteration; they are step 0 of Case 2.

title: Bisection Method
text:
Description
The bisection method finds a root of a single equation \(f(x) = 0\) that has been bracketed: it starts from an interval \([a_0, b_0]\) on which \(f\) changes sign and halves that interval until the root is pinned down. Each step evaluates \(f\) at the midpoint and keeps the half on which the sign change survives:
\[
c_k = \frac{a_{k-1} + b_{k-1}}{2}, \qquad
[a_k, b_k] =
\begin{cases}
[a_{k-1},\, c_k] & \text{if } f(a_{k-1})\,f(c_k) < 0,\\
[c_k,\, b_{k-1}] & \text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\qquad k = 1, 2, \ldots
\]
The method assumes that \(f\) is continuous on \([a_0, b_0]\) and that \(f(a_0)\) and \(f(b_0)\) have opposite signs; the Intermediate Value Theorem then puts a root in every bracket. It needs no derivative and only one new value of \(f\) per step. It cannot find a root at which \(f\) does not change sign, such as the double root of \((x-1)^2\), and when the bracket holds several roots it finds only one of them.
Mathews’ bisection theorem gives the accuracy as a general result under those two hypotheses: the midpoints converge to a root \(x^*\) in \([a_0, b_0]\), with
\[
|c_k - x^*| \le \frac{b_0 - a_0}{2^k}, \qquad k = 1, 2, \ldots
\]
Mathews’ process stops if some \(f(c_k) = 0\), since \(c_k\) is then a root; the rule above has no such test, so an exact hit forces the right half twice, leaving the root (on \(x^2 - 4\), \([0, 4]\): \(c_1 = 2\), then \(c_k \to 4\)). For this rule the guarantee and the bound hold only while no \(f(c_k) = 0\). The bound halves every step whatever \(f\) is, so convergence is linear: one binary digit, about 0.3 decimal digits, per step. Guaranteeing a tolerance \(\delta\) takes \(k \ge \log_2\bigl((b_0 - a_0)/\delta\bigr)\) steps, so 22 for \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) on a bracket of width 3. Only the bound is monotone. In Case 1, \(f(x) = x^3 + 4x^2 - 10\) on \([-1, 2]\), the error at step 12 is \(2.40 \times 10^{-4}\), within the bound \(3/2^{12} \approx 7.32 \times 10^{-4}\), but it grew at steps 3, 6 and 8.
The guarantee needs both hypotheses, and Case 2, \(f(x) = \tan x\) on \([0, 2]\), breaks both. Its root lies exactly at \(a_0 = 0\), so \(f(a_0)\,f(b_0) = 0\) rather than negative, and the rule takes the right half \([1, 2]\) and leaves that root. On \([1, 2]\), \(\tan x\) changes sign across its asymptote at \(x = \pi/2\), not at a root, and the brackets close in on the asymptote: \(c_{12} \approx 1.570801\), where \(|f(c_{12})| \approx 2.2 \times 10^5\). A narrow bracket alone does not prove a root; checking that \(|f(c_k)|\) is small exposes this false one.
False Position keeps the same sign-change bracket but cuts it at the secant line’s \(x\)-intercept instead of the midpoint, Brent’s Method uses bisection as the safeguard behind faster interpolation steps, and Newton-Raphson and the Secant Method converge faster near a simple root but, without a bracket, can lose it.

title: Muller’s Method
text:
Description
Muller’s method solves a single equation \(f(x) = 0\), and it can find complex roots as well as real ones. Like the Secant Method, it uses only values of \(f\), not its derivative. Where the secant method draws a line through two points, Muller’s method draws a parabola through three, \(p_0\), \(p_1\) and \(p_2\), and takes the next iterate where the parabola crosses the x-axis.
Write the parabola as \(P(x) = f(p_2) + b\,(x - p_2) + d\,(x - p_2)^2\). Its coefficients come from divided differences of the three points,
\[
h_0 = p_1 - p_0, \quad h_1 = p_2 - p_1, \quad \delta_0 = \frac{f(p_1) - f(p_0)}{h_0}, \quad \delta_1 = \frac{f(p_2) - f(p_1)}{h_1}, \quad d = \frac{\delta_1 - \delta_0}{h_1 + h_0}, \quad b = \delta_1 + h_1 d,
\]
and the next iterate is the root of \(P\) nearest \(p_2\):
\[
p_3 = p_2 - \frac{2 f(p_2)}{b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4 f(p_2)\, d}},
\]
with the sign chosen to make the denominator larger in magnitude, which picks that nearer root and avoids subtracting nearly equal numbers. The oldest point is then dropped and the step repeats with \((p_1, p_2, p_3)\), so each step costs one new value of \(f\).
The three starting points must be distinct, and no sign change or bracket is needed. Convergence is only local: the starting points must be close enough to the root. In general, if \(f \in C^3\) near a simple root \(p\) (\(f'(p) \neq 0\)) and the iterates converge to it, the errors \(e_n = p_n - p\) satisfy
\[
e_{n+1} \approx -\frac{f'''(p)}{6 f'(p)}\, e_n\, e_{n-1}\, e_{n-2},
\]
so, when \(f'''(p) \neq 0\), the order is about 1.84, the real root of \(\alpha^3 = \alpha^2 + \alpha + 1\) (if \(f'''(p) = 0\) it is higher). That is faster than the secant method’s 1.62 and, as Mathews puts it, almost as fast as Newton’s method. All three cases on this page have double roots instead, where the order drops: in Case 2 and Case 3 the computed order settles near 1.23 as the iteration continues past the frames shown. That is still superlinear, while Newton’s method is only linear at a double root.
The parabola need not cross the x-axis. Then \(b^2 - 4 f(p_2)\, d < 0\) and the next iterate is complex, so a real-arithmetic program cannot take the step. In Case 1 this happens at every step; the animation takes the parabola’s vertex instead, and Mathews’ program drops the square root. With complex arithmetic the method itself goes on from the same start: its iterates leave the real line (the first is \(1.2873 + 0.3563i\) or its conjugate, equally near \(p_2\)) and still converge to the double root \(p = 1\).
The Newton-Raphson Method needs \(f'\) and converges quadratically at simple roots, Accelerated and Modified Newton-Raphson restore that rate at multiple roots, Brent’s Method fits a parabola in the other direction (inverse quadratic interpolation) inside a sign-change bracket, and the Lin-Bairstow Method reaches complex roots of polynomials using only real arithmetic.

title: False Position or Regula Falsi Method
text:
Description
The false position, or regula falsi, method solves a single equation \(f(x) = 0\) for a real root inside an interval \([a, b]\) on which \(f\) changes sign. Starting from \([a_1, b_1] = [a, b]\), it keeps a sign-change bracket \([a_n, b_n]\) at every step and takes as the new point the x-intercept of the secant line through \((a_n, f(a_n))\) and \((b_n, f(b_n))\):
\[
c_n = \frac{a_n f(b_n) - b_n f(a_n)}{f(b_n) - f(a_n)}.
\]
If \(f(a_n)\) and \(f(c_n)\) have opposite signs, the next bracket is \([a_n, c_n]\); otherwise it is \([c_n, b_n]\). Unlike bisection (which uses the midpoint), Regula Falsi weights the new point toward whichever endpoint has a smaller \(|f|\) value, often giving faster convergence — but one endpoint can remain fixed for many iterations.
The method needs only that \(f\) be continuous on \([a, b]\) with \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) of opposite signs. Mathews’ Regula Falsi theorem then guarantees that the points \(c_n\) converge to a zero \(x^*\) of \(f\) in \([a, b]\). If \([a, b]\) contains several zeros, the method finds one of them, and a sign change across a discontinuity need not enclose a zero at all.
The guarantee says nothing about speed. In general, if \(f''\) is positive throughout \([a, b]\) or negative throughout, so that \(f\) is convex or concave there, the same endpoint stays in the bracket at every step and the convergence is only linear. With \(b\) as that fixed endpoint and \(e_n = c_n - x^*\),
\[
e_{n+1} \approx C\, e_n, \qquad C = 1 - \frac{f'(x^*)\,(b - x^*)}{f(b)}, \qquad 0 < C < 1,
\]
for large \(n\) (with \(a\) in place of \(b\) when \(a\) is the endpoint that stays). Both animations have \(f\) convex and \(b\) fixed. In Case A, the error ratios \(e_{n+1}/e_n\) of the computed iterates settle at \(0.2513\), and in Case B at \(0.0501\), matching \(C\) and beating the factor \(1/2\) of bisection.
Two consequences can mislead. Because one endpoint never moves, the bracket width \(b_n - a_n\) does not go to zero: in Case A it stays above \(2 - x^* \approx 0.6348\), so a stopping test must use \(|c_n - c_{n-1}|\) or \(|f(c_n)|\), not the width. And when \(f\) is strongly curved, \(C\) is close to 1: for \(f(x) = x^{10} - 1\) on \([0, 1.3]\), \(C \approx 0.765\), and regula falsi needs 61 steps to bring \(|c_n - 1|\) below \(10^{-6}\), where bisection needs 20.
Bisection keeps the same kind of bracket but always halves it, the Secant Method applies the same formula to the two most recent iterates without keeping a sign change, converging faster at a simple root (order about \(1.618\)) but without the guarantee, Newton-Raphson uses the tangent line instead of a secant, and Brent’s Method combines a bracket with interpolation steps and falls back on bisection.

title: Fixed Point Iteration
text:
Description
Fixed point iteration solves an equation written in the form \(x = g(x)\). A solution \(x^*\), with \(g(x^*) = x^*\), is a fixed point of \(g\), where the curve \(y = g(x)\) meets the line \(y = x\). An equation \(f(x) = 0\) can be rewritten in this form in many ways, and the choice of \(g\) decides whether the method works. Starting from \(x_0\), apply \(g\) repeatedly:
\[
x_{n+1} = g(x_n), \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots
\]
If \(g\) is continuous and the iterates converge, their limit is a fixed point of \(g\). Mathews’ fixed point theorems give conditions that guarantee convergence: if \(g\) and \(g'\) are continuous on \([a, b]\), \(g\) maps \([a, b]\) into itself, and \(|g'(x)| \le K < 1\) for all \(x \in [a, b]\), then \(g\) has a unique fixed point \(x^*\) in \([a, b]\), the iterates converge to it from every \(x_0 \in (a, b)\), and \(|x^* - x_n| \le K^n\,|x^* - x_0|\). The theorem’s conditions are sufficient, not necessary: Case 1 starts at \(x_0 = 0.1\), where \(g'(x_0) \approx 2.24\), and still converges to \(x^* = 2\). For continuously differentiable \(g\): if \(|g'(x^*)| < 1\), the iteration converges to \(x^*\) for every starting value close enough to \(x^*\); if \(|g'(x^*)| > 1\), iterates near \(x^*\) (other than \(x^*\) itself) move away from it.
In general, write \(e_n = x_n - x^*\). If \(g\) is continuously differentiable near \(x^*\) and the iterates converge to \(x^*\) without reaching it, the mean value theorem gives \(e_{n+1} = g'(c_n)\,e_n\) for some \(c_n\) between \(x_n\) and \(x^*\), so
\[
\frac{e_{n+1}}{e_n} \to g'(x^*).
\]
Convergence is therefore linear when \(0 < |g'(x^*)| < 1\): each step multiplies the error by about \(|g'(x^*)|\), and the closer that factor is to 1, the slower the iteration. If \(g'(x^*) > 0\) the iterates eventually stay on one side of \(x^*\) (monotone); if \(g'(x^*) < 0\) they eventually alternate sides (oscillating). If \(g'(x^*) = 0\) the convergence is faster than linear. title: Secant Method
text:
Description
The secant method solves a single equation \(f(x) = 0\) without using the derivative \(f'\). From two starting approximations \(p_0\) and \(p_1\), each step draws the secant line through the two most recent points \((p_{n-1}, f(p_{n-1}))\) and \((p_n, f(p_n))\) and takes its x-intercept as the next approximation:
\[
p_{n+1} = p_n - \frac{f(p_n)\,(p_n - p_{n-1})}{f(p_n) - f(p_{n-1})}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots
\]
This is Newton’s step with \(f'(p_n)\) replaced by the slope of the secant line, so each step needs only one new value of \(f\). The formula is the one False Position uses, but the secant method always keeps the two most recent points, so its iterates need not bracket the root.
The step needs \(f(p_n) \neq f(p_{n-1})\); otherwise the secant line is horizontal and has no x-intercept. Mathews’ secant theorem gives the guarantee: if \(f \in C^2[a, b]\), \(f(p) = 0\) for some \(p \in [a, b]\), and \(f'(p) \neq 0\), then there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that the iterates converge to \(p\) for starting values \(p_0, p_1 \in [p - \delta, p + \delta]\).
In general, write \(e_n = p_n - p\). If the iterates converge to a simple root (\(f'(p) \neq 0\)) and \(f\) is in \(C^2\) near it, then
\[
e_{n+1} \approx \frac{f''(p)}{2\,f'(p)}\, e_n\, e_{n-1} \quad \text{for large } n,
\]
and when \(f''(p) \neq 0\) this makes the order of convergence \((1+\sqrt5)/2 \approx 1.618\). Two secant steps cost about as much as one Newton step when \(f'\) costs as much as \(f\), and together they have order \(1.618^2 \approx 2.618\), better than Newton’s 2. In Case 1, \(f(x) = 3e^x - 4\cos(x)\) with root \(p = 0.254850059029\), the ratio \(e_n/(e_{n-1}e_{n-2})\) settles at \(f''(p)/\bigl(2f'(p)\bigr) \approx 0.7933\) (computed in extended precision):

When \(f''(p) = 0\) the convergence is faster: for \(\arctan\) at \(p = 0\) (Case 3, Case 6), \(e_{n+1}/(e_n e_{n-1}^2) \to -1/3\) and the order is 2. At a multiple root, where \(f'(p) = 0\), the convergence is only linear. In Case 2, \(f(x) = 25(x - 0.2)^2\), the step reduces exactly to \(e_{n+1} = e_n e_{n-1}/(e_n + e_{n-1})\), and \(e_{n+1}/e_n\) settles at \((\sqrt5 - 1)/2 \approx 0.618\), slower than Newton’s \(1/2\) on the same double root.
Convergence is only local. On \(f(x) = xe^{-x}\), starting from \(p_0 = 1.5\) and \(p_1 = 2\) on the decreasing tail, the secant lines are shallow and the iterates run off to \(+\infty\) while \(f(p_n) \to 0\), so a stopping test on \(|f(p_n)|\) alone would eventually accept a point far from the root (Case 5). Even when the iterates converge, the path can be erratic: on \(f(x) = x^3 - x + 3\), starting from \(p_0 = 2\) and \(p_1 = 1\), the iterates wander as far as \(3.16\) and \(-3.03\) before they converge to the root near \(-1.672\) (Case 4).
Newton-Raphson uses the tangent line instead, False Position and Bisection keep a sign-change bracket, Muller’s Method fits a parabola through the last three iterates, Brent’s Method safeguards secant and inverse quadratic interpolation steps with bisection, and Broyden’s Method carries the secant idea to systems of equations.

title: The Tangent Parabola
text:
Description
The tangent parabola is the parabola that matches a function \(f\) and its first two derivatives at a single point \(x_0\), and this page shows where it comes from. The secant line through two points on a graph tends to the tangent line as the points merge. With three points, \(x_0 - h\), \(x_0\) and \(x_0 + h\), the same idea gives the secant parabola, the Newton interpolating polynomial of degree 2 through them:
\[
P_h(x) = f(x_0) + \frac{f(x_0+h) - f(x_0-h)}{2h}\,(x - x_0) + \frac{f(x_0+h) - 2f(x_0) + f(x_0-h)}{2h^2}\,(x - x_0)^2 .
\]
As \(h \to 0\) the two difference quotients tend to \(f'(x_0)\) and \(\tfrac12 f''(x_0)\), so the limit, the tangent parabola, is the Taylor polynomial of degree 2:
\[
T_2(x) = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x-x_0) + \tfrac{1}{2}f''(x_0)(x-x_0)^2 .
\]
The limit needs only that \(f''(x_0)\) exists. The error results below need more smoothness, as stated with each.
In general, if \(f \in C^3\) on an interval containing \(x\) and the three nodes, Mathews gives the interpolation remainder
\[
f(x) - P_h(x) = \frac{(x-x_0+h)(x-x_0)(x-x_0-h)}{3!}\,f'''(c)
\]
for some \(c\) in that interval. Letting \(h \to 0\) gives the Taylor remainder \(\tfrac{1}{3!}f'''(c)(x-x_0)^3\), so the error of \(T_2\) is \(O(|x - x_0|^3)\) near \(x_0\). If \(f \in C^4\), the two coefficients of \(P_h\) differ from their limits by \(\tfrac{1}{6}h^2 f'''(\xi)\) and \(\tfrac{1}{24}h^2 f^{(4)}(\eta)\), so they converge at rate \(O(h^2)\). Case 1, with \(f(x) = \sin(x)\) and \(x_0 = 1\), shows this: each tenfold cut in \(h\) cuts both coefficient errors about a hundredfold.

The tangent parabola is accurate near \(x_0\), not over a wide interval. In Case 1, within \(|x - 1| \le 0.3\) its error is at most 0.0027, about ten times smaller than the \(h = 1\) secant parabola’s 0.026; but over the whole window \([0, \pi]\) its error reaches 0.120 at \(x = 0\), against 0.072 for that secant parabola, as the first and last frames show. Without enough smoothness the limit may not exist: for \(f(x) = |x|\) at \(x_0 = 0\) the coefficient of \((x - x_0)^2\) is \(1/h\), which grows without bound. Computing \(P_h\) in floating point with very small \(h\) also fails, because \(f(x_0+h) - 2f(x_0) + f(x_0-h)\) cancels: for Case 1 in double precision at \(h = 10^{-8}\) that coefficient is off by about 0.13. The animation stops at \(h = 0.01\), far from this.
The secant parabola is a Newton Interpolation Polynomial (equivalently a Lagrange one), its coefficients are the central-difference approximations of \(f'(x_0)\) and \(\tfrac12 f''(x_0)\) from Numerical Differentiation, its limit is a Taylor polynomial, and Hermite Interpolation carries the idea of merged nodes further by interpolating derivative values.

title: Legendre Polynomials
text:
Description
The Legendre polynomials \(P_n(x)\) are the polynomials orthogonal on \([-1,1]\) with weight 1. Their main numerical use is continuous least squares approximation: given \(f\) on \([-1,1]\), find the polynomial \(S_N\) of degree at most \(N\) that makes \(\int_{-1}^{1}\bigl(f(x)-S_N(x)\bigr)^2\,dx\) as small as possible. Mathews builds them by Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization of \(1, x, x^2, \ldots\), normalized so that \(P_n(1)=1\); the animations compute them by the equivalent three-term recurrence
\[
P_0(x)=1, \qquad P_1(x)=x, \qquad (n+1)\,P_{n+1}(x)=(2n+1)\,x\,P_n(x)-n\,P_{n-1}(x).
\]
They are orthogonal on \([-1,1]\):
\[
\int_{-1}^{1}P_m(x)\,P_n(x)\,dx=\begin{cases}0, & m\neq n,\\[2pt] \dfrac{2}{2n+1}, & m=n.\end{cases}
\]
So the least squares problem needs no system of normal equations: each coefficient is a single integral,
\[
S_N(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{N}c_n\,P_n(x), \qquad c_n=\frac{2n+1}{2}\int_{-1}^{1}f(x)\,P_n(x)\,dx.
\]
Case 1 draws \(P_0\) to \(P_5\), and Case 2 adds the terms of this series one per frame.
The coefficients need only \(f\) square-integrable on \([-1,1]\), as Mathews assumes. On another interval \([a,b]\), Mathews uses the shifted polynomials \(P_n\bigl((2x-a-b)/(b-a)\bigr)\). The integrals are usually computed numerically; Case 2 uses 20-point Gauss-Legendre quadrature.
In general, \(S_N\) is the best polynomial of degree at most \(N\) in the integrated squared error, so adding a term never increases that error, and for every square-integrable \(f\) the error tends to zero as \(N\to\infty\). For continuous \(f\), the maximum error is bounded by the tail of the series: since \(|P_n(x)|\le 1\) on \([-1,1]\), \(|f(x)-S_N(x)|\le\sum_{n>N}|c_n|\) whenever that sum converges. If \(f\) is analytic on a region containing \([-1,1]\), the \(c_n\) shrink geometrically, and so does that bound. In Case 2 the integrated error \(\bigl(\int_{-1}^{1}(f-S_N)^2\,dx\bigr)^{1/2}\) falls at every frame, from 0.560 for \(S_0\) to \(2.33\times10^{-6}\) for \(S_8\).
Least squares is not minimax, so the maximum error need not fall at every step. In Case 2 it rises from 0.699 for \(S_0\) to 1.09 for \(S_1\), while the integrated error falls from 0.560 to 0.461. In every frame of Case 2 the largest error sits at an endpoint, \(x=-1\) or \(x=1\), where each \(|P_n|\) reaches 1. For a function with a jump, the partial sums converge in the mean but not uniformly: for \(\operatorname{sign}(x)\) they overshoot the jump by about 9 % of its height, the same at \(N=21\), 41, 81 and 161.
Gauss-Legendre Quadrature uses the zeros of \(P_n\) as its nodes, Least Squares Polynomials is the discrete counterpart that fits data points, the Chebyshev Approximation Polynomial interpolates at the zeros of the Chebyshev polynomials, which are orthogonal on \([-1,1]\) with weight \(1/\sqrt{1-x^2}\), Fourier Series is the same orthogonal expansion with sines and cosines, and Maclaurin and Taylor Series are accurate near one point rather than across the whole interval.

title: Catenary
text:
Description
A catenary is the curve of a flexible cable of uniform weight hanging from two supports. With its lowest point at the origin, Mathews writes it as
\[
y = c\cosh\!\left(\frac{x}{c}\right) - c, \qquad c > 0,
\]
where \(c\) is the ratio of the cable’s horizontal tension to its weight per unit length. The numerical questions are how well a parabola approximates this curve, how long the cable is, and which \(c\) fits a given span and sag.
The curve is even, and its Maclaurin series has only even powers:
\[
c\cosh\!\left(\frac{x}{c}\right) - c = \frac{x^2}{2c} + \frac{x^4}{24c^3} + \frac{x^6}{720c^5} + \cdots = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^{2n}}{(2n)!\,c^{2n-1}} .
\]
Its first term \(x^2/(2c)\) is the parabola in the animation. Since \(1 + \sinh^2 u = \cosh^2 u\), the arc length over \([0, a]\) has a closed form, while the \(c\) of the catenary through \((\pm a, b)\) solves a nonlinear equation:
\[
L = \int_0^a \cosh\!\left(\frac{x}{c}\right) dx = c\sinh\!\left(\frac{a}{c}\right), \qquad c\cosh\!\left(\frac{a}{c}\right) - c = b .
\]
The model assumes a perfectly flexible cable, uniform in weight per unit length, loaded only by gravity and its supports. Balancing forces on a piece of cable gives \(y'' = \sqrt{1 + (y')^2}/c\), and the catenary is its solution with \(y(0) = y'(0) = 0\).
In general, because the fourth derivative of \(\cosh\) is \(\cosh\), Taylor’s theorem bounds the gap between the curves for every \(x \neq 0\):
\[
\frac{x^4}{24c^3} \le c\cosh\!\left(\frac{x}{c}\right) - c - \frac{x^2}{2c} \le \frac{x^4}{24c^3}\cosh\!\left(\frac{x}{c}\right).
\]
So the catenary lies above the parabola, the gap is \(O(x^4)\) as \(x \to 0\), and relative to the parabola it is about \(x^2/(12c^2)\), which depends only on \(x/c\). The parabola is good where \(|x|\) is small compared with \(c\): a taut cable, or a slack one near its lowest point. In the last frame of Case 1, \(c = 4\), the gap at the window’s edge \(x = 4\) is 0.172, between the bounds 0.167 and 0.257; halving \(x\) to 2 and then 1 divides it by 16.4 and 16.1, the \(x^4\) rate.
For a slack cable the parabola misleads: in the first frame of Case 1, \(c = 0.5\), the catenary is already 38% above it at \(x = 1\) (1.381 against 1). The parabola fits a different load: a cable carrying weight uniform per horizontal distance satisfies \(y'' = 1/c\) and hangs exactly in \(y = x^2/(2c)\). Mathematica cannot solve the fit equation for \(c\) analytically, Mathews notes, so \(c\) is found numerically. In general its left side falls strictly from \(\infty\) to 0 as \(c\) grows, so it has exactly one root for every \(a, b > 0\), which a bracketing method can find.
The series is the Maclaurin and Taylor Series applied to \(\cosh\); Bisection or the Newton-Raphson Method solves the fit equation for \(c\); and Simpson’s Rule approximates the arc length integral, as in Mathews’ Example 1, with \(c\sinh(a/c)\) as a check.

title: Taylor Series Method for ODE’s
text:
Description
The Taylor series method solves an initial value problem \(y' = f(t,y)\), \(y(t_0) = y_0\) on \([t_0, b]\) at the nodes \(t_n = t_0 + nh\). The Taylor method uses the ODE to compute higher derivatives analytically, then advances via a truncated Taylor series \(y_{n+1} = y_n + hy'_n + \frac{h^2}{2}y''_n + \cdots\). The method of order \(p\) keeps the terms through \(h^p\):
\[
y_{n+1} = y_n + h\,y'_n + \frac{h^2}{2!}\,y''_n + \cdots + \frac{h^p}{p!}\,y^{(p)}_n ,
\]
where each \(y^{(k)}_n\) comes from differentiating the ODE with the chain rule and evaluating at \((t_n, y_n)\): \(y' = f\), \(y'' = f_t + f_y\,f\), and so on. For this page’s \(f(t,y) = 1 - t\sqrt[3]{y}\), \(y'' = -\sqrt[3]{y} - \tfrac{t}{3}\,y^{-2/3}\,y'\).
Mathews assumes that \(f\) is continuous and satisfies a Lipschitz condition in \(y\); the method also needs the partial derivatives of \(f\) through order \(p-1\). Here \(f\) is smooth wherever \(y > 0\), and the solution stays positive on \([0, 5]\), decreasing after its peak to \(y(5) \approx 0.00812\).
In general, if \(f\) is in \(C^p\) near the solution (so \(y \in C^{p+1}[t_0, b]\)), the local truncation error is \(O(h^{p+1})\) and the global error \(|y(t_n) - y_n|\) is \(O(h^p)\), including at \(t = b\). On the runs of Case 1 (\(p = 3\)) and Case 2 (\(p = 4\)), halving \(h\) from \(5/60\) to \(5/120\) divides the largest node error by \(8.8\) and by \(17.9\), close to \(2^3 = 8\) and \(2^4 = 16\). The error in \(y(5)\) printed in the frames falls less regularly: over the same halving, by \(4.0\) for order 3 and \(580\) for order 4, partly because at \(m = 60\) the last steps lie in the shaded region.
The method is explicit, so stability limits its step as well as accuracy. On \(y' = \lambda y\) with real \(\lambda < 0\), one step multiplies \(y_n\) by \(1 + h\lambda + \cdots + (h\lambda)^p/p!\), which exceeds 1 in size once \(h|\lambda|\) passes \(2.513\) for \(p = 3\) or \(2.785\) for \(p = 4\). On this page’s problem \(\partial f/\partial y = -t/(3y^{2/3})\) reaches \(-41.3\) at \(t = 5\), where \(y\) is small, so coarse steps pass the limit in the tail (the shaded regions), and the runs with \(m = 12\) to \(36\) for order 3 (Case 1) and \(m = 12\) to \(32\) for order 4 (Case 2) leave the reference there. A higher order is no cure: at \(m = 16\) the order-3 run ends at \(y(5) \approx 0.156\) and the order-4 run at \(y(5) \approx -7666\). The method’s other cost is the derivatives, which must be redone for every new \(f\) and grow quickly with \(p\): this page’s \(y''''\) has eight terms over \(27y^{8/3}\).
Euler’s method is the case \(p = 1\), and Heun’s method and the Runge-Kutta method reach orders 2 and 4 from values of \(f\) alone; all three animate a step-refinement sweep on the same problem. Big “O” Truncation Error explains the \(O(h^p)\) notation, and Maclaurin and Taylor Series covers the series itself.

title: Runge-Kutta Method
text:
Description
The Runge-Kutta method of order 4 (RK4) solves the initial value problem \(y' = f(t, y)\), \(y(t_0) = y_0\) over \([t_0, b]\). It computes approximations \(y_i \approx y(t_i)\) at the points \(t_i = t_0 + ih\), with \(m\) subintervals of width \(h = (b - t_0)/m\). Each step evaluates \(f\) four times, once at the start of the step, twice at its midpoint and once at its end, and advances by a weighted average of the four increments:
\[
\begin{aligned}
k_1 &= h\,f(t_i,\ y_i), &\qquad k_2 &= h\,f\!\left(t_i + \tfrac{h}{2},\ y_i + \tfrac{k_1}{2}\right),\\
k_3 &= h\,f\!\left(t_i + \tfrac{h}{2},\ y_i + \tfrac{k_2}{2}\right), &\qquad k_4 &= h\,f(t_i + h,\ y_i + k_3),
\end{aligned}
\]
\[
y_{i+1} = y_i + \frac{k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4}{6}.
\]
When \(f\) depends on \(t\) alone, \(k_2 = k_3\) and the step is Simpson’s rule on \([t_i, t_i + h]\), which explains the weights \(1, 2, 2, 1\).
Mathews’ theorem assumes that \(f\) is continuous and satisfies a Lipschitz condition in \(y\), so that the problem has a unique solution. The error result needs more: in general, if \(f\) has continuous partial derivatives through order 4 near the solution (which makes \(y \in C^5[t_0, b]\)), the local truncation error of a step is \(O(h^5)\) and the global error is \(|y(t_i) - y_i| = O(h^4)\), so for small enough \(h\) halving the step divides the final error by about 16.
Case 1 runs the sweep on \(f(t, y) = 1 - t\sqrt[3]{y}\), \(y(0) = 1\), over \([0, 5]\). The solution stays positive, down to \(y(5) = 0.0081199\), so \(f\) is smooth near it and the general rate applies, but only for steps smaller than the animation shows. The observed order, \(\log(e_{\text{prev}}/e)/\log(h_{\text{prev}}/h)\) for the error \(e\) in \(y(5)\), is still \(4.90\) between the last two frames, \(m = 120\) and \(150\), and \(4.07\) between \(m = 1200\) and \(1600\), runs far finer than any frame.
Large steps fail on this problem in two ways. Along the solution, \(\partial f/\partial y = -t/(3y^{2/3})\) reaches \(-41.3\) at \(t = 5\), so for every step longer than about \(h = 0.0675\) (\(m \le 74\)), \(h\,|\partial f/\partial y|\) exceeds RK4’s general linear stability limit of \(2.785\) before \(t = 5\). And \(f\) is not Lipschitz near \(y = 0\): in every run from \(m = 12\) to \(52\) some stage value falls below \(0\), where \(\sqrt[3]{y}\) has an infinite slope. In those same runs the computed curve visibly turns upward in the tail instead of decaying, ending at \(y(5) \approx 0.588\) for \(m = 12\); the case’s Behavior note separates the causes.
Euler’s method (order 1), Heun’s method (order 2) and the Taylor Series Method animate the same sweep on the same problem, Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg pairs embedded fourth- and fifth-order formulas to choose \(h\) adaptively, and Adams-Bashforth-Moulton takes its starting values from a one-step method such as RK4.

title: Foundations: From Equations to an Efficient Solve
Foundations: From Equations to an Efficient Solve
text:
Why storage and inverses matter
On paper, the fit is one least-squares problem,
\[
\min_z \|Az-b\|_2^2, \qquad
A=\begin{bmatrix}A_f\\ L\end{bmatrix},\qquad
b=\begin{bmatrix}y\\ 0\end{bmatrix},
\]
where \(A_f\) has one row per sample and \(L\) has one row per interior node. The normal equations \(A^TAz=A^Tb\) give the same \(z\). The inverse form \(z=(A^TA)^{-1}A^Tb\) is correct algebra. A program should still not compute it that way. Four habits follow.

Build products directly. \(A^TA\) can be accumulated row by row, so the program never needs a general matrix product.
Store only nonzeros. A fidelity row has at most two nonzeros and a smoothness row exactly three, however many nodes there are. Dense storage spends its memory on zeros.
Factor, do not invert. Factoring \(A^TAz=A^Tb\) gives the same \(z\) with less work. It also avoids the larger residuals a computed inverse can produce (Higham 2002, sec. 14.1).
Use the band. Each row of \(A^TA\) has at most two nonzeros on either side of the diagonal, so each elimination or substitution step touches a small, fixed number of values.

The sections below cover the habits in order.

title: Foundations: From Equations to an Efficient Solve
text:
Assembling the system from triplets
Each sample adds two fidelity entries, one for each node that brackets it. Each interior node adds three smoothness entries, one for each point of its three-point stencil. A sparse matrix stores these as three lists of equal length: row indices, column indices, and values. Such a list is a set of triplets. The sparse constructor drops zero values and adds together triplets that share a row and column.
The example file, fixtures/regularizeNdFoundationsFixtures.m, builds this page’s numbers from the equations and checks them. The five-sample example has \(x=[0.35,\ 1.00,\ 1.80,\ 2.70,\ 3.65]\) with \(y=[1.0,\ 1.4,\ 0.4,\ 1.2,\ 0.2]\), on six output-grid nodes \(g=[0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 2.5,\ 3,\ 4]\), with smoothness \(s=0.01\). The sample at \(x=1\) sits exactly on a node, so its second weight is zero.


Show the MATLAB code
% Fidelity: sample i in [g(j), g(j+1)] at local fraction t gives (i, j, 1-t) and (i, j+1, t).
lowerNode = @(g) discretize(x, g);
frac      = @(g) (x - g(lowerNode(g))) ./ (g(lowerNode(g)+1) - g(lowerNode(g)));
fidelityTriplets = @(g) deal(repelem((1:nF)', 2), ...
    reshape([lowerNode(g), lowerNode(g)+1]', [], 1), ...
    reshape([1-frac(g), frac(g)]', [], 1));

% Smoothness: interior row r gives three nonzeros in columns r, r+1, r+2.
hL = @(g) diff(g(1:end-1));  hR = @(g) diff(g(2:end));
smoothnessTriplets = @(g) deal(repelem((1:numel(g)-2)', 3), ...
    reshape(((1:numel(g)-2)' + (0:2))', [], 1), ...
    reshape(smooth*sqrt(nF/(numel(g)-2))*(g(end)-g(1))^2 * ...
      [2./(hL(g).*(hL(g)+hR(g))), -2./(hL(g).*hR(g)), 2./(hR(g).*(hL(g)+hR(g)))]', [], 1));

[iF, jF, vF] = fidelityTriplets(g);
[iL, jL, vL] = smoothnessTriplets(g);
Af = sparse(iF, jF, vF, nF, nNodes);
Lm = sparse(iL, jL, vL, nR, nNodes);
A  = [Af; Lm];

assert(max(abs(full(Af - fx.system.fidelity)), [], 'all') < 1e-14)
assert(max(abs(full(Lm - fx.system.regularization)), [], 'all') < 1e-14)
disp(table(iF, jF, vF, VariableNames=["row i", "column j", "value"]))
fprintf('%d fidelity triplets, %d stored nonzeros; %d smoothness triplets, %d stored nonzeros\n', ...
    numel(vF), nnz(Af), numel(vL), nnz(Lm))


    row i    column j    value

isF = ia <= nF;

title: Foundations: From Equations to an Efficient Solve
Foundations: From Equations to an Efficient Solve
text:
The band of \(A^TA\)
Each row of \(A\) has its nonzeros in a few consecutive columns: two for a fidelity row, three for a smoothness row. The normal matrix is the sum of the outer products \(a_i^Ta_i\) over the rows. The outer product of one row, whose nonzeros fall in a window of \(w\) consecutive columns, changes only entries inside that window. Two columns add to the same entry only when one row’s window contains both. A window of width three keeps every such pair within two places of the diagonal, so \(A^TA\) has bandwidth 2.
The Cholesky factor keeps the band. Factoring a banded matrix in its natural order produces no fill outside the band, so the factor has at most two nonzeros to the right of its diagonal.


Show the MATLAB code
AtA = A' * A;
R = chol(AtA);                          % R'*R = AtA, R upper triangular, natural order
[ip, jp] = find(AtA);  bandAtA = max(abs(ip - jp));
[iR, jR] = find(R);    bandR   = max(jR - iR);
assert(bandAtA == 2 && bandR == 2 && nnz(AtA) == 5*nNodes - 6)

close all
tiledlayout(1, 2, TileSpacing="compact")
k = 1:nNodes-2;
nexttile
spy(AtA, 'o', 10); hold on
plot(k+2, k, ':', k, k+2, ':', 'Color', [0.4 0.4 0.4])
title('A^TA (normal matrix)')
nexttile
spy(R, 'o', 10); hold on
plot(k+2, k, ':', 'Color', [0.4 0.4 0.4])          % R is upper triangular: only the upper edge
title('R (upper Cholesky factor)')








Figure 2: Left: the normal matrix \(A^TA\) is pentadiagonal, with every nonzero within two places of the diagonal. Right: its upper Cholesky factor \(R\) has the same bandwidth, with no fill outside the band. Dotted lines mark the band edges.

title: Foundations: From Equations to an Efficient Solve
section: Factoring and solving without an inverse
text:
Factoring and solving without an inverse
With \(A^TA=R^TR\) and \(R\) upper triangular, the solve is two triangular steps. First solve \(R^Tw=A^Tb\) from the top down. Then solve \(Rz=w\) from the bottom up. Neither step forms an inverse. Each is a run of substitutions.


Show the MATLAB code
zChol = R \ (R' \ (A' * b));           % two triangular solves, no inverse formed
fprintf('max difference from the example file solution: %.3g\n', max(abs(zChol - fx.system.solution)))
assert(max(abs(zChol - fx.system.solution)) < 1e-14)


max difference from the example file solution: 2.22e-16


MATLAB’s own AtA \ (A'*b) chooses a sparse factorization internally. This page shows the explicit two-step form so the band is visible in the loops that follow.

title: Foundations: From Equations to an Efficient Solve
text:
Forming \(A^TA\) by accumulation
The loop never multiplies matrices. It visits each row and adds its contribution. Each fidelity row contributes \(w^Tw\) to the entries of \(A^TA\) at its nonzero columns, and \(y_i w^T\) to \(A^Ty\). Each smoothness row contributes \(w^Tw\) and nothing to the right-hand side, because its entry in \(b\) is zero.


Show the MATLAB code
AtAacc = zeros(nNodes);  Atbacc = zeros(nNodes, 1);
for i = 1:nF                              % fidelity rows: two triplets each
  c = jF(2*i-1:2*i);  w = vF(2*i-1:2*i);
  AtAacc(c, c) = AtAacc(c, c) + w*w';
  Atbacc(c)    = Atbacc(c) + y(i)*w;
end
for i = 1:nR                              % smoothness rows: three triplets each
  c = jL(3*i-2:3*i);  w = vL(3*i-2:3*i);
  AtAacc(c, c) = AtAacc(c, c) + w*w';
end
assert(max(abs(AtAacc - full(AtA)), [], 'all') < 1e-14)
assert(max(abs(Atbacc - fx.projection.AfTy)) < 1e-14)
fprintf('accumulated A^TA agrees with the product A^TA to round-off\n')


accumulated A^TA agrees with the product A^TA to round-off


Sample 3 sits at \(x=1.8\) with \(y=0.4\). It lies in the interval \([1,2]\), 0.8 of the way across, so its fidelity row has weight \(0.2\) on column 2 and \(0.8\) on column 3. Its contribution to \(A^TA\) is the outer product
\[
\begin{bmatrix}0.2\\ 0.8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0.2 & 0.8\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}0.04&0.16\\0.16&0.64\end{bmatrix},
\]
and its contribution to \(A^Ty\) is \(0.4\,[0.2,\ 0.8]^T=[0.08,\ 0.32]^T\).


Show the MATLAB code
sel = iF == 3;
c3 = jF(sel);  w3 = vF(sel);
contribution3 = w3 * w3';
rhs3 = y(3) * w3;
disp(table(c3, w3, VariableNames=["column", "weight"]))
disp(contribution3)
disp(rhs3)
assert(isequal(c3', [2 3]) && max(abs(w3' - [0.2 0.8])) < 1e-12)
assert(max(abs(contribution3 - [0.04 0.16; 0.16 0.64]), [], 'all') < 1e-12)
assert(max(abs(rhs3 - [0.08; 0.32])) < 1e-12)


    column    weight
    ______    ______
      2        0.2  
      3        0.8  
    0.0400    0.1600
    0.1600    0.6400
    0.0800
    0.3200

title: Foundations: From Equations to an Efficient Solve
text:
Projecting one regularization row into \(L^TL\)
The smoothness rows follow the same rule, with scaled weights. Row 2 is centred on the node at \(x=2\) and reaches the nodes at \(x=1\) and \(x=2.5\), so its columns are 2, 3, and 4. Its unscaled weights, from the spacings \(h_1=1\) and \(h_2=0.5\), are \([\tfrac43,\ -4,\ \tfrac83]\). Multiplying by the smoothness multiplier \(0.1788854382\) gives \([0.238514,\ -0.715542,\ 0.477028]\).
Its outer product adds \(0.512\) to the \((3,3)\) entry of \(L^TL\), the entry for column 3. The total there is \(1.056\). Rows 1 and 3 supply the other \(0.544\).


Show the MATLAB code
sel = iL == 2;
cL2 = jL(sel);  wL2 = vL(sel);
contributionL2 = wL2 * wL2';
disp(table(cL2, wL2, VariableNames=["column", "scaled weight"]))
disp(contributionL2)
LTL = full(Lm' * Lm);
fprintf('(3,3) entry of L^TL: %.6g, from row 2: %.6g\n', LTL(3,3), contributionL2(2,2))
assert(max(abs(wL2' - [0.238514 -0.715542 0.477028])) < 1e-6)
assert(abs(LTL(3,3) - 1.056) < 1e-12 && abs(contributionL2(2,2) - 0.512) < 1e-9)


    column    scaled weight
    ______    _____________
      2          0.23851   
      3         -0.71554   
      4          0.47703   
    0.0569   -0.1707    0.1138
   -0.1707    0.5120   -0.3413
    0.1138   -0.3413    0.2276
(3,3) entry of L^TL: 1.056, from row 2: 0.512


Summing the fidelity and smoothness contributions gives \(A^TA=A_f^TA_f+L^TL\). Figure 3 shows the two blocks and their sum.


Show the MATLAB code
cmap = [linspace(0,1,128)', linspace(0,1,128)', ones(128,1); ...
        ones(128,1), linspace(1,0,128)', linspace(1,0,128)'];
AfAf = full(Af' * Af);
panels = {AfAf, LTL, full(AtA)};
titles = {'A_f^T A_f (fidelity)', 'L^T L (smoothness)', 'A^T A (sum)'};
close all
figure('Position', [100 100 1020 350]); tiledlayout(1, 3, TileSpacing="compact")
for p = 1:3
  M = panels{p};
  nexttile
  imagesc(M); axis image
  mx = max(abs(M(:)));  clim([-mx mx]);  colormap(cmap)
  for i = 1:nNodes
    for j = 1:nNodes
      if abs(M(i,j)) > 1e-12
        text(j, i, sprintf('%.3f', M(i,j)), HorizontalAlignment='center', FontSize=6.5)
      end
    end
  end
  title(titles{p});  xlabel('column j');  ylabel('row i')
  set(gca, 'XTick', 1:nNodes, 'YTick', 1:nNodes, 'YDir', 'reverse')
end








Figure 3: Contributions to the normal matrix for the six-node example: the fidelity block \(A_f^TA_f\) (left), the smoothness block \(L^TL\) (middle), and their sum \(A^TA\) (right). Blue is negative and red positive. Entries outside the band are zero and blank.

section: How this differs from the original
text:
How this differs from the original

Interface. The original is an Excel array function written in VBA, and its inputs and outputs live in spreadsheet ranges. This page has no spreadsheet function and no VBA. The ideas carry over.
Inversion. The original article says the spreadsheet solved the system with MINVERSE(), because that was what Excel offered. Its VBA function used Gaussian elimination and back-substitution. The companion spreadsheet used an explicit inverse. The teaching point here is “do not invert,” and this page takes no position on the spreadsheet beyond that.
Storage. The original describes a compressed layout for the pentadiagonal matrix, with the diagonal in the third of five stored columns. This page uses MATLAB sparse triplets for \(A\) and a three-diagonal array for \(R\). regularizeNd uses MATLAB sparse matrices.
Solver. The original’s solve is hand-written elimination specialized to five bands. regularizeNd passes the normal system to MATLAB’s sparse backslash. It also offers backslash on the stacked matrix and the iterative solvers covered in the deep dive.
Symmetry. The original notes that symmetry lets the second-derivative outer product be computed in six products instead of nine. The loop above computes the full outer product for clarity.
Terminology. The original calls its inputs “input points” and its outputs “output points.” Its title says “2D data” for one input variable and one output. This site uses samples, output-grid nodes, and 1D input. This page reuses none of the article’s example values. Every number here comes from the example file or from a cell on this page.

title: Foundations: Regularizing Data with One Input
section: The problem: scattered samples, one output table
text:
The problem: scattered samples, one output table
You have measurements \((x_i, y_i)\), \(i = 1,\dots,m\). The \(x_i\) fall wherever the experiment put them, and the \(y_i\) carry noise. What you want is a table \(z_j\) at the nodes \(g_j\) of an output grid that you choose. Between nodes, the table is read by interpolation. That lets you resample the data and smooth it in one step.
The unknowns are the table entries \(z = (z_1,\dots,z_N)^T\). No formula with a few coefficients is fitted. Every node value is free. The task is to choose them so the table agrees with the samples and behaves sensibly between them.
This page follows one small example throughout. It has five samples and a six-node grid:



Sample \(i\)
\(x_i\)
\(y_i\)




1
0.35
1.0


2
1.00
1.4


3
1.80
0.4


4
2.70
1.2


5
3.65
0.2



The output grid is \(g = [0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 2.5,\ 3,\ 4]\). It is nonuniform. The spacing is 1, then 0.5 between \(x=2\) and \(x=3\), then 1 again. The samples are irregular too, and sample 2 lands exactly on node 2. Figure 1 shows the layout.


Show the MATLAB code
close all
figure
hold on
for k = 1:N
  plot([g(k) g(k)], [-0.45 1.7], '--', 'Color', [0.65 0.65 0.65], 'HandleVisibility', 'off');
end
plot(x, y, 'o', 'MarkerSize', 8, 'MarkerFaceColor', [0.85 0.33 0.1], ...
  'MarkerEdgeColor', 'k', 'DisplayName', 'samples (x_i, y_i)');

  'MarkerEdgeColor', [0.4 0.4 0.4], 'DisplayName', 'output-grid nodes g_j');

xlabel('x'); ylabel('y');

title: Foundations: Regularizing Data with One Input
section: Interpolation: each sample becomes a row of weights
text:
Interpolation: each sample becomes a row of weights
Suppose sample \(i\) lies in the grid interval \([g_j, g_{j+1}]\). Its position in that interval is
\[
t_i = \frac{x_i - g_j}{g_{j+1} - g_j}, \qquad 0 \le t_i \le 1 .
\]
Linear interpolation reads the table at \(x_i\) as a weighted average of the two neighboring nodes:
\[
\hat z(x_i) = (1 - t_i)\, z_j + t_i\, z_{j+1}.
\]
The weights are nonnegative and sum to one. A constant table is therefore read as that constant everywhere. The same weights also reproduce \(x_i\) from the node coordinates, so a table whose values are linear in the node positions is read exactly.
Asking the table to agree with sample \(i\) gives one linear equation:
\[
(1 - t_i)\, z_j + t_i\, z_{j+1} \approx y_i .
\]
This is a fidelity equation. The \(\approx\) is there on purpose. The samples are noisy, so the equation is not required to hold exactly.
For sample 3, \(x_3 = 1.8\) lies in \([g_2, g_3] = [1, 2]\). Then \(t_3 = 0.8\), so the weights are \(0.2\) on node 2 and \(0.8\) on node 3:
\[
0.2\, z_2 + 0.8\, z_3 \approx 0.4 .
\]
For sample 4, \(x_4 = 2.7\) lies in \([2.5, 3]\), an interval of width \(0.5\). So \(t_4 = (2.7 - 2.5)/0.5 = 0.4\), and the weights are \(0.6\) on node 4 and \(0.4\) on node 5. The interval width is in the denominator. That is how the nonuniform spacing enters the weights.
For sample 2, \(x_2 = 1.00\) equals \(g_2\). So \(t_2 = 0\), and its row has a single weight of 1 on node 2:
\[
z_2 \approx 1.4 .
\]
The code below builds all five rows the same way. discretize finds the interval for each sample, and sparse stores only the nonzero weights, so the zero weight in the exact-node row is never stored.


Show the MATLAB code
j = discretize(x, g);                   % interval index: g(j) <= x < g(j+1)
t = (x - g(j)) ./ (g(j+1) - g(j));      % position inside that interval
Af = sparse([(1:m)'; (1:m)'], [j; j+1], [1 - t; t], m, N);

assert(max(abs(full(Af - fx.system.fidelity)), [], 'all') < 1e-14)
assert(max(abs(sum(Af, 2) - 1)) < 1e-14)            % each row sums to one
assert(abs(t(3) - 0.8) < 1e-14 && abs(t(4) - 0.4) < 1e-14 && t(2) == 0)
assert(nnz(Af(2, :)) == 1)                          % the on-node row


Each output node gets a weight from each sample. As a function of the sample’s x position, the weight from node \(j\) is a tent. It equals 1 at \(g_j\) and falls in a straight line to zero at the neighboring nodes. Figure 2 plots these tents. Each column of \(A_f\) is one tent, read at the five sample positions. Each row of \(A_f\) collects the weights that one sample gives the nodes.
Figure 2 marks the samples with dashed lines. At each dashed line, the dots are that sample’s weights, and they add up to 1.


Show the MATLAB code
close all
xq = linspace(0, 4, 801)';
H = interp1(g, eye(N), xq, 'linear');   % weight curve of each node on a fine axis
nodeColor = lines(N);
figure
hold on
for j = 1:N
  plot(xq, H(:, j), '-', 'Color', nodeColor(j, :), 'LineWidth', 1.5, 'DisplayName', sprintf('node %d', j));
end
for i = 1:m
  plot([x(i) x(i)], [-0.05 1.2], '--', 'Color', [0.35 0.35 0.35], 'HandleVisibility', 'off');
  text(x(i), 1.12, 'sum = 1', 'HorizontalAlignment', 'center', 'FontSize', 9);
end
[rr, cc, vv] = find(full(Af));
for k = 1:numel(vv)
  plot(x(rr(k)), vv(k), 'o', 'MarkerSize', 6, 'MarkerFaceColor', nodeColor(cc(k), :), ...
    'MarkerEdgeColor', 'k', 'HandleVisibility', 'off');
  text(x(rr(k)) + 0.06, vv(k), sprintf('%.2f', vv(k)), 'FontSize', 9, ...
    'BackgroundColor', 'w', 'Margin', 1);
end
xlabel('x'); ylabel('weight');
xlim([0 4]); ylim([-0.05 1.2]);
title('Weight curves of the output nodes, with each sample''s weights');
legend('Location', 'eastoutside');








Figure 2: Weight curves of the six output nodes. Each curve gives one node’s weight as a function of the sample’s x position: a tent that peaks at its node and falls to zero at the neighboring nodes. The dashed lines mark the five samples. The dots on each dashed line are that sample’s weights, labeled with their values, and they sum to 1.

title: Foundations: Regularizing Data with One Input
Foundations: Regularizing Data with One Input
text:
Second differences: the smoothness rows
The smoothness rows penalize a table whose slope changes quickly. Take three consecutive nodes. The table rises or falls across the first interval at one rate and across the second at another. The more those two rates disagree, the more the table bends and the larger the penalty. A straight line keeps one slope, so its penalty is zero. The penalty grows only when the slope jumps. For a triple of nodes \(g_a, g_b, g_c\) with values \(z_a, z_b, z_c\), the penalty is a linear combination of the three values, with weights set by the node spacing:
\[
f'' \approx \sum_{q \in \{a,b,c\}} \frac{2\, z_q}{\prod_{p \in \{a,b,c\},\, p \ne q}(g_q - g_p)} ,
\]
where the product runs over the other two nodes of the triple. The weights change wherever the spacing changes.
Three nodes give one row, so \(N = 6\) nodes give \(N - 2 = 4\) rows. The matrix \(D\) collects them:

Rows 1 and 2 are the first two triples. Row 1 covers nodes 1–3, which are evenly spaced, and has weights \([1, -2, 1]\). Row 2 covers nodes 2–4, at positions \(1\), \(2\), and \(2.5\), and has weights \([\tfrac{4}{3}, -4, \tfrac{8}{3}]\). The weights change because the spacing changes.
Row 3 covers nodes 3–5, at positions \(2\), \(2.5\), and \(3\), and has weights \([4, -8, 4]\).
Row 4 covers nodes 4–6, at positions \(2.5\), \(3\), and \(4\), and has weights \([\tfrac{8}{3}, -4, \tfrac{4}{3}]\).

A straight line has zero second derivative, so every row gives zero when applied to linear data. The example file, fixtures/regularizeNdFoundationsFixtures.m, builds this page’s numbers from the equations and checks them. The code below builds \(D\) from that formula and checks it against the example file.


Show the MATLAB code
a = g(1:N-2); b = g(2:N-1); c = g(3:N);        % left, centre, right node of each triple
w1 = 2 ./ ((a - b) .* (a - c));                % Lagrange second-derivative weights
w2 = 2 ./ ((b - a) .* (b - c));
w3 = 2 ./ ((c - a) .* (c - b));
rr = (1:N-2)';
D = sparse([rr; rr; rr], [rr; rr+1; rr+2], [w1; w2; w3], N-2, N);

assert(max(abs(full(D - fx.system.d2)), [], 'all') < 1e-14)
assert(max(abs(D * g)) < 1e-12)                % zero for a straight line
assert(max(abs(D * ones(N, 1))) < 1e-12)       % zero for a constant


Figure 4 shows \(D\) with its values. Blank cells are zeros, so the band of three weights per row is visible.


Show the MATLAB code
close all
M = full(D);
vmax = max(abs(M), [], 'all');
figure
imagesc(M); axis image; colormap(cmap); clim([-vmax vmax]);
[rr, cc, vv] = find(M);
text(cc, rr, cellstr(compose('%.3g', vv)), 'HorizontalAlignment', 'center');
xticks(1:N); xticklabels(compose('g_%d', 1:N));
yticks(1:N-2); yticklabels(compose('row %d', 1:N-2));
title('Second-difference matrix D (unscaled)');








Figure 4: The unscaled second-difference matrix \(D\). Each row has three weights on consecutive nodes. Rows 2 and 4 are the ones whose coefficients change where the spacing changes.






Scaling the smoothness rows
The smoothness rows are scaled before they are stacked:
\[
\mu = s\,\sqrt{\frac{m}{N-2}}\,(g_N - g_1)^2 .
\]
Here \(s = 0.01\) is the smoothness value, \(m\) is the number of samples, and \(N - 2\) is the number of smoothness rows. The square root of the ratio of equation counts keeps the two kinds of equation in balance as the grid is refined; Section 8 returns to this. The factor \((g_N - g_1)^2\) converts second differences, which carry units of \(z\) per \(x^2\), into the units of \(z\). The smoothness rows and the fidelity rows are then measured in the same units.
For this example,
\[
\mu = 0.01 \cdot \sqrt{5/4}\cdot 4^2 = 0.1788854382 .
\]

section: Grid resolution and the row-count factor
text:
Grid resolution and the row-count factor
The original articles make a claim about resolution. Adding output points should not change the fit, because the scale factor compensates for the extra smoothness rows. Refining the grid adds rows. Each second-difference row measures local curvature, and that curvature does not shrink as the grid is refined. Without a correction, the penalty sum for a fixed curve grows with the number of rows, so the fit is pushed toward a straight line. The factor \(\sqrt{m/(N-2)}\) divides each row’s weight by the square root of the row count, up to the fixed constant \(\sqrt{m}\). That keeps the total penalty comparable across resolutions.
The example file computes the same study with and without the factor, refining each interval by \(1, 4, 16, 64, 256\). The reference is the 5121-node fit with the factor. Figure 9 and the table below show the results.

Figure 9: Left: the fidelity SSE against the number of output nodes, with and without the row-count factor. The dotted line is the least-squares straight-line SSE. Right: the largest deviation of each fit from the 5121-node reference, on log-log axes. Values come from the example file.





The data support a narrower claim than the original article makes. With the factor, the fitted curves converge, and their deviation from the reference shrinks at each refinement. They are not identical. The fidelity SSE falls by about 11 percent between 6 and 1281 nodes, from 0.271358 to 0.242395. The discrete second differences are not exactly the continuous derivative, and that accounts for the change in SSE. The remaining differences come from discretization, and they shrink as the grid is refined.

title: Foundations: Regularizing Data with One Input
text:
Connection to regularizeNd
regularizeNd builds the same two blocks. Its fidelity block is the interpolation matrix for the chosen method. Its smoothness block is the second-difference matrix scaled by the row-count and range factors derived above. The table maps this page’s symbols to the package’s outputs and inputs.



This page
regularizeNd




\(A_f\) (fidelity rows)
first output of regularizeNdMatrices


\(\mu D\) (scaled smoothness rows)
L{1}


output grid \(g\)
{g}, one vector per input


smoothness \(s\)
smoothness (one value for 1D input)


solved table \(z\)
output of regularizeNd



The check below runs when this page renders. It calls regularizeNdMatrices and regularizeNd on this page’s samples, grid, smoothness value, and linear interpolation. It compares the fidelity block, the scaled smoothness block, and the solved table with the values in the example file, and it prints the largest difference it measures. Before the check runs, the hidden setup cell adds the regularizeNd source folder to the MATLAB path. If that folder is not present, the check is skipped with a message.


Show the MATLAB code
if ~haveRegularizeNd
  fprintf('regularizeNd is not on the MATLAB path, so the package checks were skipped.\n');
else
  [Ap, Lp] = regularizeNdMatrices(x, {g}, smoothness, 'linear');
  zp = regularizeNd(x, y, {g}, smoothness, 'linear', '\');
  dF = max(abs(full(Ap - fx.system.fidelity)), [], 'all');              % fidelity block
  dL = max(abs(full(Lp{1} - fx.system.regularization)), [], 'all');     % scaled smoothness block
  dZ = max(abs(zp - fx.system.solution));                               % solved table
  fprintf('Largest difference from the example file: fidelity %.2g, smoothness %.2g, solution %.2g.\n', dF, dL, dZ);
  assert(dF < 1e-12, 'fidelity block differs from the example file')
  assert(dL < 1e-12, 'scaled smoothness block differs from the example file')
  assert(dZ < 1e-12, 'solved table differs from the example file')
end


Largest difference from the example file: fidelity 0, smoothness 0, solution 0.


The reference in the example file solves the stacked system with \. The normal-equation solve above agrees with it at 6 nodes to within \(10^{-12}\). Forming \(A^TA\) squares the condition number. At 6 nodes, \(\kappa(A) = 3.19\) and \(\kappa(A^TA) = 10.2\). At 10,001 nodes, the condition estimate of the normal matrix (condest) is \(1.8\times10^{14}\). The normal-equation solution differs from the stacked solution by up to \(8.0\times10^{-4}\).
At 10,001 nodes, the stacked solve has the smaller residual norm. Its norm is 0.6409343, against 0.6409350 for the normal equations. For fine grids, solve the stacked least-squares system directly, or use the QR and iterative options described in the deep dive’s Solve stage and in Part 7. The deep dive covers the range factor in more depth. The smoothness-count discussion covers the row-count factor.

title: Foundations: Regularizing Data with One Input
section: How this differs from the original
text:
How this differs from the original

Terminology. The articles say “2D data” for one input and one output. regularizeNd calls this 1D input. The articles speak of an output dataset; this site calls it the output grid or table.
Smoothness scale. The articles scale the derivative rows by \(S = K\sqrt{N_f/N_d}\), with \(K\) the smoothness constant. regularizeNd also multiplies by the squared range \((g_N - g_1)^2\). The same numerical smoothness value therefore gives a different penalty weight in the two schemes.
Normalization with one axis. With one input there is one set of derivative rows, so the articles’ combined count and regularizeNd’s per-axis count coincide. The difference appears only with two inputs, which the later pages cover.
Resolution claim. The articles state that the output does not change with resolution. The calculation shows convergence with the factor. The fits are not identical: the fidelity SSE changes by about 11 percent over the study, and the deviation falls by 3.9 to 7.5 times per fourfold refinement. Without the factor, the fit drifts toward a straight line.
Solver. The articles note that the pentadiagonal normal matrix suits elimination. This page solves the normal equations once as a check. The reference in the example file solves the stacked system directly. The conditioning numbers in the regularizeNd section above show why the stacked solve is the safer choice on fine grids.
Interpolation. The articles choose linear interpolation as the simplest option among several, and use it throughout. This page does too. regularizeNd also offers other fidelity methods, covered in the deep dive’s fidelity section.
Example. This page uses its own five-sample example and six-node grid. None of the original example values appears here. Every number is computed by the example file or by the code on this page.

The next page applies this system to RegularizeData2D, the spreadsheet function that the original series built on the same equations.
